per_case.prose:
A 61-year-old man with no documented history of hypertension, diabetes, tobacco use, or known coronary disease was brought to the emergency department after roughly a day of worsening nausea, repeated vomiting, and breathlessness. He did not describe classic crushing chest pain at the outset, and his complaints were initially attributed to a gastrointestinal upset.

On arrival he was afebrile (36.4°C), with a heart rate of 92 beats/min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure recorded at 146/70 mmHg. Notably, repeat readings over the next several hours were strikingly labile, swinging between near-normal values and abrupt surges into the severely hypertensive range, accompanied by pallor, diaphoresis, and palpitations that came and went in distinct episodes.

A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated ST-segment elevation across the anterior precordial leads (V1 through V6). Cardiac biomarkers were clearly abnormal: troponin I 19.8 ng/mL (reference 0–0.05), CK-MB above the upper measurable limit, and myoglobin 312 ng/mL (reference 0–107). The B-type natriuretic peptide was markedly raised at 2,870 pg/mL (reference 0–100), the D-dimer exceeded the assay ceiling at >5,000 ng/mL, and the white-cell count was elevated at 16.4 × 10⁹/L.

The presentation was read as an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and the patient was taken urgently for coronary angiography. Imaging of the coronary tree, however, showed widely patent vessels with brisk flow and no significant stenosis or thrombus in any territory. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a depressed left ventricle (ejection fraction in the mid-40s percent) with conspicuous ballooning and akinesis of the apical segments while the basal walls contracted relatively normally; the apex appeared dilated. There was mild left atrial and left ventricular enlargement.

Given the mismatch between the infarct-pattern ECG, the elevated biomarkers, and the unobstructed coronary arteries — together with the regional apical wall-motion pattern and the episodic, paroxysmal blood-pressure surges with sweating and pallor — the team broadened the workup beyond a primary coronary event in search of an extracardiac trigger.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Pheochromocytoma-mediated (catecholamine-induced) takotsubo / stress cardiomyopathy. The patient presented as an apparent acute anterior STEMI (the initial working diagnosis), but coronary imaging showed no obstruction and the left ventricle showed apical ballooning with depressed EF — i.e., takotsubo physiology — driven by an underlying catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor.

HOW CONFIRMED (held aside, NOT in the vignette): (1) Markedly elevated plasma catecholamines — norepinephrine ~12,377 pg/mL (ref <750) and normetanephrine ~23,775 pg/mL (ref <165); (2) enhanced abdominal CT showing a retroperitoneal/adrenal space-occupying lesion; (3) HISTOPATHOLOGY of the surgically resected adrenal mass confirming pheochromocytoma. Supporting: clean coronaries on CT coronary angiography excluding atherothrombotic MI; reversibility of wall-motion abnormality.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize that "STEMI" with unobstructed coronaries + apical ballooning is not atherothrombotic infarction; pursue a secondary/non-cardiac driver. Measure plasma/urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines, image the adrenals. Treat with adequate ALPHA-blockade FIRST (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) before adding a beta-blocker (never beta-block first — unopposed alpha can precipitate crisis), then refer for surgical resection (adrenalectomy). Cardiac function normalized after tumor removal (echo normal ~1 week post-op).

Original case: 52-year-old Chinese woman, no cardiovascular risk factors; troponin I 27.3 ng/mL, CK-MB >60, BNP 3,410 pg/mL, D-dimer >5,000, WBC 19.02; ECG ST elevation V1–V6; echo EF 52% then 44% with apical ballooning; clean coronaries on CTA.

uncertainties.about: Was any chest pain actually present, or truly absent? Case states 'did not describe classic crushing' which permits non-classic discomfort
Why is wall-motion dysfunction ISOLATED to apical region (typically last to succumb to ischemia, first to recover)? Mechanism unclear without imaging of other territories or prior baseline

Is D-dimer elevation (>5000) indicating active thromboembolism elsewhere, secondary to myocardial necrosis/inflammation, or consumptive coagulopathy? No imaging specified for PE, DVT, or other sources

Paroxysmal hypertension + diaphoresis + pallor could indicate pheochromocytoma, autonomic crisis, endocrine emergency, seizure-related discharge, medication effect, or neuroendocrine tumor. No imaging or hormone levels documented

Troponin 19.8 is extremely elevated. Without serial kinetics or prior value, cannot distinguish peak from trajectory, or determine if magnitude is proportionate to observed LV dysfunction (EF mid-40s, apical only)

WBC elevation (16.4) could be sterile inflammation (secondary to myocardial necrosis), acute infection (pneumonia, endocarditis), malignancy, or systemic inflammatory condition. No differential WBC or cultures documented

Timing relationship between symptom onset (nausea/vomiting/breathlessness), BP lability episodes, and ECG changes not explicitly stated. 'Over next several hours' for BP swings is not anchored to absolute timeline
BNP markedly elevated (2870). Indicates heart failure but does not distinguish systolic dysfunction due to acute injury vs chronic decompensation vs acute decompensated failure from other cause

queries.asks: What is the underlying diagnosis explaining the constellation of: acute anterior STEMI ECG pattern + markedly elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin 19.8, CK-MB >limit, myoglobin 312) + unobstructed coronary arteries + regional apical wall-motion dysfunction (ballooning + akinesis) + depressed EF (mid-40s) + episodic paroxysmal hypertension + diaphoresis + pallor + elevated D-dimer + elevated WBC?

What extracardiac condition (i.e., non-primary-coronary-disease process) should be the focus of investigation given the clinical clues of apical-predominant wall-motion dysfunction and episodic catecholamine-like symptoms?
What is the appropriate treatment for this condition, and what is the prognosis?

ir.inferred_domain: Acute cardiology / Emergency medicine with differential spanning: endocrinology (pheochromocytoma, thyroid crisis), neurology (autonomic crisis, seizure), hematology/thrombosis (embolism, DIC), pulmonology (pulmonary embolism), oncology (neuroendocrine malignancy, paraneoplastic syndrome), toxicology (drug-induced), and stress-induced cardiomyopathy. Unifying theme: acute myocardial injury from non-atherosclerotic mechanism, with systemic or paraneoplastic trigger suspected.</inferred_domain>

rulebook.rule: Apical ballooning (wall-motion abnormality confined to apex with basal wall contraction preserved) raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy; this pattern is characteristic of the classic variant (~80% of takotsubo cases)
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Transient regional wall-motion dysfunction (ballooning extending beyond single coronary artery territory) raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Absence of significant coronary artery stenosis or thrombus on angiography raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy; this is a required diagnostic criterion
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: New ST-segment elevation (typically <2mm) or T-wave inversion on ECG raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (often exceeding acute coronary syndrome levels) raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Modest (not marked) elevation of cardiac biomarkers (troponin, CK-MB) despite severe ECG and clinical findings is characteristic of takotsubo cardiomyopathy; marked troponin elevation lowers the diagnosis
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Rapid functional recovery of left ventricular dysfunction (typically within weeks) raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy and lowers acute myocardial infarction
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Identifiable preceding emotional stress (grief, fear, anger, relationship conflict) in 33-45% of cases raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy; absence of stressor in 15% does not exclude it
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy (Broken Heart Syndrome): Background, Pathophysiology, Etiology - Medscape: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1513631-overview

rulebook.rule: Identifiable preceding physical stress (acute illness, surgery, chemotherapy) in 17-22% of cases raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Postmenopausal female sex raises takotsubo cardiomyopathy; strong female predominance reported
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Sympathetic overdrive with 2-3 fold elevation of plasma catecholamines is the leading pathophysiologic mechanism of takotsubo cardiomyopathy
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Documented pheochromocytoma lowers takotsubo cardiomyopathy as a diagnosis, since pheochromocytoma is an exclusion criterion for takotsubo
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Paroxysmal (episodic) severe hypertension with sudden surges into severely hypertensive range raises pheochromocytoma; this is the most suggestive presentation
rulebook.source: Paroxysmal hypertension - Knowledge and References: https://taylorandfrancis.com/knowledge/Medicine_and_healthcare/Cardiology/Paroxysmal_hypertension/

rulebook.rule: Classic triad of episodic headache, diaphoresis (perspiration), and palpitations in hypertensive patients raises pheochromocytoma with high diagnostic value
rulebook.source: Paroxysmal hypertension - Knowledge and References: https://taylorandfrancis.com/knowledge/Medicine_and_healthcare/Cardiology/Paroxysmal_hypertension/

rulebook.rule: Pallor (pale appearance) during hypertensive episodes raises pheochromocytoma; pallor is part of the classic 5 P's (Pressure, Pain, Perspiration, Palpitations, Pallor)
rulebook.source: Paroxysmal Hypertension - an overview: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/veterinary-science-and-veterinary-medicine/paroxysmal-hypertension

rulebook.rule: Episodic (paroxysmal) pattern of blood pressure fluctuations and symptoms coming and going in distinct episodes raises pheochromocytoma
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertensive Crises in a Previously Healthy Woman: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12867173/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated plasma free metanephrines (>4-fold upper reference limit) or elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines/normetanephrines are pathognomonic for pheochromocytoma; plasma metanephrines have highest sensitivity (96%)
rulebook.source: Biochemical Diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK543224/

rulebook.rule: Catecholamine excess causes myocardial injury through three mechanisms: (1) vasoconstriction of coronary arterioles reducing blood flow, (2) direct toxicity of catecholamine metabolites, (3) receptor-mediated direct injury
rulebook.source: Catecholamine induced cardiomyopathy in pheochromocytoma - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3743380/

rulebook.rule: Pheochromocytoma can produce elevated cardiac troponin and ECG abnormalities (T-wave inversions, ST changes) in absence of coronary occlusion through catecholamine-induced microvascular dysfunction
rulebook.source: Catecholamine induced cardiomyopathy in pheochromocytoma - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3743380/

rulebook.rule: Normal coronary angiography in patient with ACS-like presentation (chest pain, troponin elevation, ECG changes) raises pheochromocytoma rather than atherosclerotic coronary disease
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9043547/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated plasma normetanephrine (>2-3 fold normal) with normal or only mildly elevated C-reactive protein (inflammation without infection) raises pheochromocytoma
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9043547/

rulebook.rule: Reversibility of cardiovascular complications after tumor resection (vs. permanent coronary damage) distinguishes pheochromocytoma from true myocardial infarction
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9043547/

rulebook.rule: Global or predominantly basal wall-motion dysfunction (rather than apical-predominant) raises pheochromocytoma-induced cardiomyopathy; absence of regional pattern in apical territory lowers takotsubo
rulebook.source: Catecholamine induced cardiomyopathy in pheochromocytoma - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3743380/

rulebook.rule: Absence of recent significant head trauma, intracranial bleeding, or myocarditis is required to exclude these diagnoses and support takotsubo as primary diagnosis
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Acute myocarditis presents with ST elevation, elevated troponin, and patent coronaries similar to takotsubo; myocarditis is an exclusion criterion for takotsubo diagnosis
rulebook.source: Acute myocarditis mimicking ST-elevation myocardial infarction: A case report and review of the literature: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4508986/

rulebook.rule: Elevated D-dimer (>5000 ng/mL) in setting of myocardial injury indicates microvascular thrombosis, inflammatory activation, or endothelial injury associated with acute myocardial necrosis or inflammation
rulebook.source: D-Dimer Is Associated With Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction in Patients With Non-obstructive Coronary Artery Disease and Preserved Ejection Fraction: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cardiovascular-medicine/articles/10.3389/fcvm.2022.937952/full

rulebook.rule: Elevated white blood cell count (16.4 × 10^9/L) without fever suggests sterile inflammation secondary to myocardial necrosis or systemic inflammatory response rather than infection
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9043547/

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented hypertension or diabetes history in patient presenting with severe hypertensive episodes raises secondary hypertension from pheochromocytoma rather than chronic essential hypertension
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertensive Crises in a Previously Healthy Woman: A Case Report - PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12867173/

rulebook.rule: Acute presentation without prior coronary disease history in male aged 61 with no documented risk factors (HTN, DM, tobacco, CAD) raises non-atherosclerotic mechanism of myocardial injury
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness (rather than classic crushing chest pain) as initial presentation raises non-cardiac or non-typical cardiac etiology
rulebook.source: IR case presentation: initial misdiagnosis as gastrointestinal upset

rulebook.rule: Discordance between severely abnormal ECG (anterior STEMI pattern), markedly elevated biomarkers (troponin 19.8), and unobstructed coronary arteries is characteristic of non-ischemic myocardial injury syndrome and requires search for extracardiac trigger
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

rulebook.rule: Depressed left ventricular ejection fraction (mid-40s) in acute presentation with new myocardial injury raises takotsubo or myocarditis; chronic cardiomyopathy would show prior ECG/imaging abnormalities
rulebook.source: Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430798/

rulebook.rule: Mild left atrial and left ventricular enlargement (rather than severe acute dilation) in acute STEMI presentation raises non-ischemic mechanism; acute anterior MI typically causes more focal apical/anteroapical remodeling
rulebook.source: Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning) - PMC - NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2000940/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy), likely triggered by a catecholamine-secreting tumor such as pheochromocytoma.

Reasoning:
The case contains multiple overlapping diagnostic pearls:

1. **Mismatch of ECG findings with coronary anatomy**: Anterior ST elevation with patent coronaries is the classic "ECG-angio mismatch" seen in takotsubo.

2. **Characteristic apical ballooning pattern**: The echo description of apical akinesis/ballooning with relatively preserved basal contraction is the hallmark of takotsubo (not typical of LAD territory MI, which would show septal/anterior base disease).

3. **Paroxysmal hypertensive surges with diaphoresis and pallor**: These episodic catecholamine surges are not explained by takotsubo alone; they suggest an underlying catecholamine source—classic for pheochromocytoma. The labile blood pressure (swinging from near-normal to severe hypertension) is highly specific.

4. **Biomarker elevation**: Troponin, CK-MB, and myoglobin are all elevated, consistent with myocardial injury (takotsubo does cause real myocardial necrosis, not just stunning).

5. **Elevated BNP and D-dimer**: BNP elevation reflects acute cardiac dysfunction; the extremely elevated D-dimer (>5,000) is unusual and may reflect acute thromboembolism risk or catecholamine-induced endothelial injury.

6. **Absence of traditional CAD risk factors or documented hypertension history**: This argues against primary coronary atherosclerosis despite the acute presentation.

Next action:
1. **Urgent 24-hour urine metanephrines and plasma free metanephrines** to screen for pheochromocytoma
2. **CT or MRI of the abdomen/pelvis** to identify adrenal or extra-adrenal tumor
3. **MIBG or PET imaging** if biochemistry is positive
4. Meanwhile, treat symptomatically with vasodilators (nitrates, calcium channel blockers) and cautiously with beta-blockers if the pheochromocytoma workup is positive (to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation)

Confidence: 85% for takotsubo as the cardiac diagnosis; 75% for pheochromocytoma as the underlying trigger (other stressors—emotional, trauma, sepsis—can precipitate takotsubo, but the paroxysmal hypertensive episodes with diaphoresis and pallor strongly raise suspicion for catecholamine excess).
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The constellation of findings is most consistent with acute myocardial injury from a non-atherosclerotic mechanism, with pheochromocytoma as the leading extracardiac trigger.

SUPPORTING PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA:
The patient exhibits the classic triad of paroxysmal hypertension (F15: severely labile BP), diaphoresis (F17), and palpitations (F18), each documented in the acute presentation (F19: episodic pattern). Rules R13 and R14 identify this triad as highly suggestive of pheochromocytoma. Pallor (F16) is also documented (R15: part of the classic 5 P's). The episodic, paroxysmal pattern of BP surges with autonomic symptoms "coming and went in distinct episodes" (F19, F40) directly matches R16's description of pheochromocytoma presentation.

Critically, the patient had no documented hypertension or diabetes history (F2, F3), yet presented with severe episodic hypertension (F15). Rule R28 indicates this pattern—secondary hypertension without chronic disease history—raises pheochromocytoma. The absence of traditional CAD risk factors (F2–F5) combined with an acute presentation (F6) in a non-female patient (F1: male age 61) supports R29: non-atherosclerotic myocardial injury mechanism.

The coronary angiography showing patent vessels with no stenosis or thrombus (F28, F29, F30) fulfills a diagnostic requirement for excluding atherosclerotic MI. Rule R20 states that normal coronary angiography in an ACS-like presentation raises pheochromocytoma. Rule R18 explains the mechanism: catecholamine excess causes myocardial injury through vasoconstriction of coronary arterioles and direct toxicity, not atherosclerotic obstruction. Rule R19 confirms that pheochromocytoma can produce elevated troponin and ECG abnormalities (including ST changes) in the absence of coronary occlusion.

The markedly elevated troponin (F21: 19.8, >395× upper limit of normal) and CK-MB above measurable limit (F22) are explained by acute catecholamine-induced myocardial damage, not atherosclerotic necrosis over a narrow territory. Rule R18 describes the three injury mechanisms. The elevated D-dimer (F25: >5000) fits R26: endothelial injury and microvascular activation in acute myocardial injury. The elevated WBC (F26: 16.4) without fever (F11: afebrile) matches R27: sterile inflammation secondary to myocardial necrosis.

SUPPORTING TAKOTSUBO (BUT WITH IMPORTANT CAVEATS):
The apical ballooning (F32) and akinesis (F33) with preserved basal contraction (F34) fit the classic takotsubo wall-motion pattern (R1). The regional apical dysfunction exceeds single coronary territory (R2). ST elevation on ECG (F20, anterior leads) matches R4. The BNP elevation (F24: 2870, well above acute MI levels) is characteristic of takotsubo (R5).

However, Rule R6 is a significant lowering factor: takotsubo typically presents with modest, not marked, biomarker elevation. This patient's troponin of 19.8 is extremely elevated—far exceeding the "modest" range typically seen in takotsubo. This marked elevation makes takotsubo alone less probable.

Additionally, Rule R10 notes takotsubo shows strong female predominance; this patient is male, which lowers (but does not exclude) that diagnosis. No preceding emotional or physical stress is documented (R8, R9), though absence of documented stress does not exclude it.

AGAINST TAKOTSUBO ALONE:
Rule R6 explicitly states that marked troponin elevation lowers takotsubo diagnosis. The degree of troponin elevation (19.8) combined with unequivocal CK-MB overflow (F22) suggests more extensive myocyte necrosis than typical takotsubo produces. If this were purely stress-induced, one would expect more modest biomarker elevation despite the ECG and wall-motion findings.

Rule R12 states that documented pheochromocytoma is an exclusion criterion for takotsubo. While pheochromocytoma is not yet documented, the clinical presentation—paroxysmal hypertension with the classic symptomatic triad—strongly suggests it should be ruled in or out before accepting takotsubo as the diagnosis.

Rule R23 notes that global or predominantly basal dysfunction (not apical) raises pheochromocytoma-induced cardiomyopathy. This patient shows apical-predominant dysfunction, which is more consistent with takotsubo, but pheochromocytoma does not exclude some apical involvement.

INTEGRATION:
The most parsimonious explanation is that a pheochromocytoma—causing recurrent catecholamine surges (explaining the paroxysmal hypertension, diaphoresis, palpitations, and pallor documented in F15–F19, F40)—has triggered acute myocardial injury via R18's mechanisms (microvascular vasoconstriction and direct toxicity). The resulting wall-motion abnormality happens to be apical-predominant, mimicking takotsubo. The marked biomarker elevation (F21, F22) and the episodic nature of the BP and symptom episodes, rather than a single identifiable stressor, fit pheochromocytoma better than takotsubo.

Takotsubo remains in the differential and cannot be excluded without biomarker testing and exclusion of pheochromocytoma, but the paroxysmal hypertensive pattern with the autonomic triad is far more specific for pheochromocytoma (R13, R14, R15, R16) than for stress-induced cardiomyopathy.
per_case.framework_top: Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-mediated acute myocardial injury) with takotsubo cardiomyopathy as a competing but lower-probability diagnosis.
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent plasma free metanephrines and 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines to confirm or exclude pheochromocytoma. If positive, proceed to imaging (CT/MRI abdomen/pelvis) to localize tumor. Simultaneously, obtain serial troponin and echocardiography in 48–72 hours to assess trajectory of ventricular function (rapid recovery favors takotsubo; slow/persistent dysfunction favors pheochromocytoma or myocarditis).
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high (65–75%) for pheochromocytoma as primary diagnosis; lower confidence for takotsubo alone due to biomarker magnitude and male sex; myocarditis remains in differential but less supported by episodic symptom pattern.

framework_citations.claim: Patient presents with paroxysmal (episodic) severe hypertension, diaphoresis, palpitations, and pallor in distinct episodes—classic triad/5 P's of pheochromocytoma
Normal coronary angiography with patent vessels in an ACS-like presentation raises pheochromocytoma rather than atherosclerotic disease
Catecholamine excess in pheochromocytoma causes myocardial injury through microvascular dysfunction and direct toxicity, producing elevated troponin and ECG changes without coronary occlusion
Absence of documented hypertension or diabetes history with acute-onset paroxysmal hypertension raises secondary hypertension from pheochromocytoma

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: pheochromocytoma-mediated (catecholamine-induced) takotsubo/stress cardiomyopathy, confirmed by markedly elevated plasma catecholamines/normetanephrines, adrenal CT lesion, and histopathology; management = measure fractionated metanephrines/catecholamines, image adrenals, ALPHA-block first then beta-block, then adrenalectomy.

OUTPUT B is the closer match. It names "Takotsubo cardiomyopathy triggered by a catecholamine-secreting tumor such as pheochromocytoma" — essentially the exact ground-truth framing (takotsubo physiology with a pheo driver). It also provides the correct confirmation pathway (plasma free + 24h urine metanephrines, CT/MRI abdomen, MIBG/PET) and, crucially, flags the unopposed-alpha hazard ("cautiously with beta-blockers... to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation"). It is well-calibrated (explicit 85%/75% confidences with acknowledged alternatives) and contains no load-bearing hallucinations (minor: mentions myoglobin not in the case). Its one shortfall vs ground truth is not explicitly stating "alpha-blockade FIRST" as the canonical sequence, though it correctly identifies the underlying unopposed-alpha danger.

OUTPUT A correctly identifies pheochromocytoma as the leading driver and explains the catecholamine mechanism well, but has three notable problems: (1) it asserts the patient is "male age 61" and uses this fabricated sex as load-bearing reasoning (female predominance argument), when the real patient is a 52-year-old woman — a defensibility-damaging hallucination; (2) it uses altered biomarker values (troponin 19.8, BNP 2870, WBC 16.4) drawn from an abstracted rulebook rather than the true case (27.3, 3410, 19.02); (3) it provides NO disposition/management at all — omitting the workup and the safety-critical alpha-before-beta blockade. Its reasoning is also heavily tied to internal F-/R- codes that cannot be independently verified against the vignette.

B wins on correctness of both diagnosis and management, calibration, and freedom from hallucination. A captures the core mechanism but is undermined by a fabricated patient demographic used as evidence and a complete absence of disposition.

per_case.prose:
A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department after a second episode of transient loss of consciousness. For roughly the past ten months he had noticed breathlessness coming on after only light exertion, such as walking from one room to another or carrying groceries up a short flight of stairs. Over that same period he had developed repeated bouts of a dry, hacking cough; on two occasions a prolonged coughing spell had ended with him briefly blacking out, once striking his shoulder against a doorframe as he slumped. He reported that the spells had become noticeably more frequent over the last three months, to the point that he had stopped driving and had taken leave from his job as a warehouse supervisor for fear of losing consciousness without warning.

Alongside these episodes he described mounting fatigue, swelling of both ankles that had appeared over the preceding several weeks, and a sense of abdominal fullness and early satiety. He denied fever, chest pain at rest, weight loss, or recent infection. His only notable prior medical event was a clotting problem in an abdominal vein that had been identified at another facility around the time his symptoms began; he admitted he had not been taking his prescribed blood thinner reliably.

On arrival he was afebrile and his oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Heart rate and blood pressure were within normal limits. Examination of the neck showed a raised jugular venous pressure with a positive hepatojugular reflux. On auscultation the first heart sound was strikingly loud, and an additional low-pitched sound was audible in early diastole, the timing of which appeared to shift slightly with changes in his position. The lung fields were clear to auscultation bilaterally. There was mild pitting edema of both lower legs.

Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated B-type natriuretic peptide of 1280 pg/mL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 14 mm/h. Routine chemistries and a complete blood count were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large, mobile echodense structure that filled most of the left atrial cavity. The mass moved with the cardiac cycle, dropping toward the mitral orifice during diastole and producing severe obstruction to inflow across the mitral valve; the left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved at 60%. The right ventricle was moderately dilated with reduced systolic function, there was moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and the estimated pulmonary artery pressures were severely elevated. A subsequent transesophageal study confirmed that the mass was anchored to the interatrial septum and showed enlargement of both atria.

Cardiac catheterization revealed only mild, non-obstructive coronary disease. A subsequent hypercoagulability evaluation identified a deficiency in one of the body's natural anticoagulant proteins.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Giant LEFT ATRIAL MYXOMA causing intermittent mitral valve inflow obstruction (presenting as cough-induced syncope and exertional dyspnea). Confirmation: surgical resection of the intracardiac mass with HISTOPATHOLOGY confirming myxoma; preoperative transthoracic + transesophageal echocardiography showed a mobile mass occupying nearly the entire left atrium, attached to the interatrial septum, prolapsing across and severely obstructing the mitral valve in diastole. CORRECT DISPOSITION: urgent referral for cardiothoracic surgical excision of the mass (not management as benign cough-syncope syndrome and not as primary mitral stenosis). Key load-bearing clues to the true dx: an early diastolic added heart sound ("tumor plop"), positional/exertional syncope, signs of left-sided inflow obstruction with secondary severe pulmonary hypertension and right-heart failure, and a concurrent hypercoagulable/thromboembolic state (here protein C deficiency with venous thrombosis). The presentation mimicked the far more common benign cough-syncope syndrome (and superficially mitral stenosis). Original case: 46-year-old man; CT 6.1 x 4.5 cm LA mass; BNP 1411 pg/mL; ESR 12 mm/h; LVEF 60-65%; discharged POD3; protein C deficiency, portal vein thrombosis. Outcome: complete resection, good recovery.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical medicine, specifically cardiovascular pathology and thromboembolism. The case presents a patient with an intracardiac thrombus causing mitral obstruction, secondary pulmonary hypertension, and right heart dysfunction, in the setting of abdominal venous thrombosis and an underlying hypercoagulability disorder. The core diagnostic challenge is determining the mechanism of thromboembolic migration, the nature of the obstructing mass, and the appropriate intervention.

rulebook.rule: Presence of large, mobile echodense mass in left atrium anchored to interatrial septum raises the candidate that the mass is a thrombus secondary to hypercoagulability disorder rather than a primary cardiac tumor (myxoma)
rulebook.bears_on: Left atrial thrombus secondary to thrombophilia
rulebook.source: Disappearing 'Myxoma': Left Atrial Thrombus Masquerading as a Myxoma (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7352731/) and Atrial Thrombus or Atrial Myxoma? Preliminary Analysis of Echocardiographic Findings of a Case Series (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11337610/) - Myxomas typically have a stalk, are solitary, and originate from the atrial septum; thrombi are anchored directly to the septum and appear as cylinder-like mobile masses without stalk

rulebook.rule: Identification of deficiency in natural anticoagulant protein (protein C, protein S, or antithrombin) raises the candidate that the patient has inherited thrombophilia predisposing to recurrent thrombosis in multiple sites
rulebook.bears_on: Inherited thrombophilia with natural anticoagulant deficiency
rulebook.source: Hereditary thrombophilia (https://thrombosisjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1477-9560-4-15) - Familial protein S deficiency is associated with recurrent thrombosis; all three proteins (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) play a role in downregulation of coagulation

rulebook.rule: Concurrent thrombosis in abdominal vein with cardiac thrombus in setting of natural anticoagulant deficiency raises the candidate of inherited thrombophilia as the underlying etiology rather than localized cardiac pathology
rulebook.bears_on: Inherited thrombophilia with natural anticoagulant deficiency
rulebook.source: Cardiac thrombi in a patient with protein-C and S deficiencies: a case report (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC415559/) - Case showed multi-chamber cardiac thrombi without underlying cardiac pathology, indicating thrombotic tendency stemmed from coagulation protein deficiencies

rulebook.rule: Large left atrial mass producing severe obstruction to mitral inflow with diastolic motion toward mitral orifice raises the candidate of functional mitral stenosis caused by the obstructing mass
rulebook.bears_on: Mitral inflow obstruction from left atrial mass
rulebook.source: Left Atrial Thrombus in the Setting of Mitral Stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10453952/) - Left atrial thrombus formation is a well-known complication that develops secondary to significant blood stasis in the dilated left atrium and produces severe obstruction to inflow across the mitral valve

rulebook.rule: Loud first heart sound (S1) on cardiac auscultation raises the candidate of mitral stenosis or functional mitral obstruction, as the transmitral pressure gradient causes the mitral valve to remain fully open throughout diastole, closing forcefully at systole onset
rulebook.bears_on: Mitral stenosis or mitral inflow obstruction
rulebook.source: Mitral Stenosis Topic Review (https://www.healio.com/cardiology/learn-the-heart/cardiology-review/topic-reviews/mitral-stenosis/introduction-and-etiology) and Mitral Stenosis - StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430742/) - Loud S1 is present in early mitral stenosis due to forceful closure of stenotic mitral valve leaflets

rulebook.rule: Early diastolic sound with positional variation heard on auscultation raises the candidate of a mobile mass (thrombus or myxoma) obstructing the mitral valve, whose motion and position change with body position
rulebook.bears_on: Mobile left atrial mass causing mitral obstruction
rulebook.source: Left atrial giant thrombus infected by Escherichia Coli (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2373784/) and Giant Left Atrial Thrombus: A Source of Systemic Emboli (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9271426/) - Mobile masses produce variable diastolic sounds that change timing with position due to mass movement across the mitral orifice

rulebook.rule: Dyspnea with light exertion (walking between rooms, carrying groceries up stairs) raises the candidate of left-sided cardiac obstruction reducing cardiac output and increasing left atrial pressure, leading to pulmonary congestion
rulebook.bears_on: Mitral inflow obstruction with secondary pulmonary congestion
rulebook.source: Left Atrial Thrombus in the Setting of Mitral Stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10453952/) - Exertional breathing difficulty is characteristic of mitral stenosis due to obstruction to left ventricular filling

rulebook.rule: Dry, hacking cough ending with syncope during sustained coughing raises the candidate of either cardiac tamponade/pericardial effusion or severe mitral inflow obstruction that compromises cerebral perfusion when intrathoracic pressure rises acutely
rulebook.bears_on: Cough-induced syncope from mitral obstruction or pericardial constraint
rulebook.source: Cough-Induced Syncope: Mechanism and Associated Conditions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5442416/) - Cough syncope occurs when increased intrathoracic pressure decreases venous return and cardiac output; associated conditions include cardiac tamponade and pericardial effusion

rulebook.rule: Increased frequency of syncope spells over 3 months raises the candidate that the obstructing mass is enlarging or organizing further, worsening the hemodynamic obstruction
rulebook.bears_on: Progressive left atrial mass with worsening mitral obstruction
rulebook.source: Left Atrial Mass with Stalk: Thrombus or Myxoma? (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3021896/) - Growth trajectory helps distinguish between thrombi (which may stabilize or resolve with anticoagulation) and myxomas (which typically enlarge)

rulebook.rule: Mounting fatigue alongside dyspnea and edema raises the candidate of heart failure secondary to mitral obstruction, as reduced cardiac output triggers compensatory neurohumoral mechanisms causing fatigue
rulebook.source: BNP: Definition, Clinical Significance, and Overview (https://www.bestheartsurgery.com/blog/bnp-definition-clinical-significance-and-overview/) - Fatigue is a cardinal symptom of heart failure and reflects reduced cardiac output

rulebook.rule: Bilateral ankle edema with abdominal fullness and early satiety raises the candidate of right-sided heart failure or systemic venous congestion secondary to elevated right atrial pressure
rulebook.bears_on: Right heart failure with systemic venous congestion
rulebook.source: Hepatojugular Reflux - StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526097/) - Elevated right atrial pressure in right heart failure causes hepatic congestion, abdominal fullness, and peripheral edema

rulebook.rule: Elevated jugular venous pressure with positive hepatojugular reflux raises the candidate of right ventricular failure and elevated right atrial pressure
rulebook.bears_on: Right heart failure with elevated right atrial pressure
rulebook.source: Hepatojugular Reflux - StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526097/) - A sustained elevation of JVP on applying abdominal pressure is a marker of right ventricular failure; almost all patients with right heart failure have abnormal jugular venous pressure

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated BNP (1280 pg/mL) raises the candidate of acute or chronic heart failure with ventricular dysfunction or increased hemodynamic load
rulebook.bears_on: Heart failure secondary to mitral obstruction or pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.source: Natriuretic Peptides in Heart Failure (https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/761722-overview) and BNP Levels — Normal Range & Heart Failure (https://mdtools.org/bnp-levels/) - Elevated BNP indicates myocardial stress from volume or pressure overload; values above 400 pg/mL indicate heart failure

rulebook.rule: Moderate tricuspid regurgitation with moderately dilated right ventricle raises the candidate of secondary (functional) tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular dilation and tricuspid annular dilatation, rather than primary valve disease
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary tricuspid regurgitation from RV dilation
rulebook.source: Pulmonary Hypertension Related to Left-Sided Cardiac Pathology (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2011/381787) - As pulmonary arterial pressure increases, right ventricular dilation and tricuspid regurgitation may develop, leading to elevated jugular venous pressure and liver congestion

rulebook.rule: Severely elevated pulmonary artery pressures with right ventricular dilation raises the candidate of secondary (passive) pulmonary hypertension from chronic elevation of left atrial pressure due to mitral obstruction
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary pulmonary hypertension from mitral obstruction
rulebook.source: Pulmonary Hypertension Related to Left-Sided Cardiac Pathology (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2011/381787) and Pulmonary artery hypertension in mitral stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3339741/) - Pulmonary hypertension in mitral stenosis develops through retrograde transmission of elevated left atrial pressure

rulebook.rule: Reduced right ventricular systolic function with elevated pulmonary pressures raises the candidate of right ventricular failure secondary to chronic pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.bears_on: Right ventricular failure from pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.source: Pulmonary Hypertension Related to Left-Sided Cardiac Pathology (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2011/381787) - Chronic right ventricular pressure overload resulting from pulmonary hypertension ultimately leads to cavity dilation and contractile dysfunction

rulebook.rule: Preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (60%) despite mitral obstruction raises the candidate that the left ventricle is underfilled due to obstruction at the mitral valve, rather than having primary myocardial dysfunction
rulebook.bears_on: Mitral inflow obstruction with preserved LV function
rulebook.source: Left Atrial Thrombus in the Setting of Mitral Stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10453952/) - In mitral stenosis with mitral thrombus, left ventricular function is preserved as the ventricle is starved of inflow

rulebook.rule: Bilateral atrial enlargement raises the candidate of chronic elevation of atrial pressures from mitral obstruction, causing adaptive chamber dilation
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic mitral obstruction with atrial remodeling
rulebook.source: Large atrial myxoma mimicking severe mitral stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3839221/) - Left atrial enlargement occurs in response to obstruction, and bilateral atrial enlargement indicates chronicity of the obstruction

rulebook.rule: History of abdominal vein thrombosis with concurrent left atrial thrombus raises the candidate of paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale or other intracardiac defect, allowing venous thrombi to cross to the arterial circulation
rulebook.source: Fatal Mesenteric Ischemia From a Presumed Paradoxical Embolism Through a Patent Foramen Ovale (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12851606/) and Thrombus in Transit Through Patent Foramen Ovale Causing Splenic Infarction (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12441429/) - Patent foramen ovale is a pathway for venous thrombi to cross to systemic circulation; coexistence of venous and arterial thromboembolism suggests paradoxical embolism

rulebook.rule: Non-adherence to anticoagulation therapy prior to symptom onset raises the candidate that inadequate anticoagulation allowed progression of thrombosis in the setting of underlying hypercoagulability
rulebook.bears_on: Thrombosis secondary to hypercoagulability and medication non-adherence
rulebook.source: Inherited Thrombophilia in the Era of Direct Oral Anticoagulants (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8837096/) - Recurrent thrombosis in inherited thrombophilia is an indication for long-term preventive anticoagulation

rulebook.rule: Absence of fever, elevated ESR, and unremarkable CBC lowers the candidate of infectious endocarditis as the etiology of the left atrial mass
rulebook.source: Left atrial giant thrombus infected by Escherichia Coli (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2373784/) - Infected thrombi typically present with fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and positive blood cultures; their absence argues against active infection

rulebook.rule: Clear lung fields on auscultation lowers the candidate of acute decompensated pulmonary edema, though chronic elevation of left atrial pressure may not produce rales if pulmonary compensation is adequate
rulebook.source: Left Atrial Thrombus in the Setting of Mitral Stenosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10453952/) - In chronic mitral stenosis, patients may have clear lungs despite elevated left atrial pressure due to chronic adaptation and reactive pulmonary vascular changes

rulebook.rule: Mild, non-obstructive coronary artery disease on catheterization lowers the candidate of acute coronary syndrome or primary myocardial infarction as the cause of symptoms
rulebook.source: Cardiac catheterization findings showing only mild non-obstructive disease argues against significant coronary flow limitation

rulebook.rule: ESR of 14 mm/h (low-normal) lowers the candidate of acute systemic inflammatory or malignant disease affecting the heart
rulebook.source: Laboratory assessment: normal ESR argues against active systemic inflammation, infectious endocarditis, or acute neoplastic disease

rulebook.rule: Unremarkable routine chemistries and CBC lowers the candidate of acute hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, or systemic infection complicating the thrombosis
rulebook.bears_on: Acute hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, or systemic infection
rulebook.source: Laboratory findings: normal CBC argues against hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or acute hematologic crisis

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Left atrial myxoma. This is the most common primary cardiac tumor and presents classically with exertional dyspnea, syncope (especially with Valsalva/coughing), and a mobile echodense mass anchored to the interatrial septum that obstructs mitral inflow. The preserved LV function, pulmonary hypertension, and RV dysfunction are secondary to the mechanical obstruction. The hypercoagulability finding is likely coincidental.

Recommended next action: Urgent cardiac surgery consultation for mass resection; confirm with cardiac MRI if feasible, but do not delay surgery given symptomatic obstruction and syncope risk.

Confidence: 75-80%

Reasoning: The clinical triad of mechanical mitral obstruction (positional symptoms, syncope), mobile septal attachment on echocardiography, and exertional dyspnea is pathognomonic for left atrial myxoma. While the hypercoagulability and prior thrombosis raise the possibility of thrombus, the echo characteristics and clinical presentation pattern are far more consistent with a primary cardiac tumor. Myxomas can occasionally be associated with systemic features (fever, rash, constitutional symptoms) but this presentation is primarily mechanical. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathology post-resection.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
CLINICAL SYNTHESIS:

The primary diagnosis is a left atrial thrombus secondary to inherited thrombophilia, with secondary hemodynamic consequences of severe mitral inflow obstruction, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular failure.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FOR PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS:

The patient has a large, mobile echodense mass in the left atrium anchored to the interatrial septum [F16, F22], which raises the candidate of a thrombus rather than a primary cardiac tumor (R1). This is further supported by concurrent thrombosis in an abdominal vein [F7] identified around the time symptoms began, and the identification of a deficiency in a natural anticoagulant protein [F25]. The concurrent presence of thrombosis in two anatomically distant sites (abdominal vein and left atrium) in a patient with documented anticoagulant deficiency raises the candidate of inherited thrombophilia rather than localized cardiac pathology (R3). The patient's non-adherence to prescribed anticoagulation [F7] prior to symptom onset raises the candidate that inadequate anticoagulation allowed progression of thrombosis in the setting of underlying hypercoagulability (R20).

EVIDENCE FOR MITRAL INFLOW OBSTRUCTION AND HEMODYNAMIC SEQUELAE:

The large left atrial mass produces severe obstruction to mitral inflow, with diastolic motion toward the mitral orifice [F17], which raises the candidate of functional mitral stenosis caused by the obstructing mass (R4). This obstruction is supported on auscultation by a strikingly loud first heart sound [F10], which raises the candidate of mitral stenosis or functional mitral obstruction, as the transmitral pressure gradient causes forceful valve closure at systole onset (R5). An early diastolic sound with positional variation [F10] raises the candidate of a mobile mass obstructing the mitral valve, whose timing changes with body position (R6).

The exertional dyspnea—occurring after only light exertion such as walking between rooms or carrying groceries up stairs [F2]—raises the candidate of left-sided cardiac obstruction reducing cardiac output and increasing left atrial pressure, leading to pulmonary congestion (R7). The dry, hacking cough ending with syncope during sustained coughing [F3] raises the candidate of severe mitral inflow obstruction that compromises cerebral perfusion when intrathoracic pressure rises acutely during cough (R8). The increasing frequency of syncope spells over three months [F4] raises the candidate that the obstructing mass is enlarging or organizing further, worsening the hemodynamic obstruction (R9).

EVIDENCE FOR SECONDARY PULMONARY HYPERTENSION AND RIGHT HEART FAILURE:

Severely elevated pulmonary artery pressures with right ventricular dilation [F21, F19] raise the candidate of secondary (passive) pulmonary hypertension from chronic elevation of left atrial pressure due to mitral obstruction (R15). The reduced right ventricular systolic function [F19] with elevated pulmonary pressures raises the candidate of right ventricular failure secondary to chronic pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension (R16).

The elevated jugular venous pressure with positive hepatojugular reflux [F9] raises the candidate of right ventricular failure and elevated right atrial pressure (R12). The bilateral ankle edema, abdominal fullness, and early satiety [F5] raise the candidate of right-sided heart failure or systemic venous congestion secondary to elevated right atrial pressure (R11). The moderate tricuspid regurgitation with moderately dilated right ventricle [F20, F19] raise the candidate of secondary (functional) tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular dilation, rather than primary valve disease (R14).

EVIDENCE FOR HEART FAILURE AND CHRONICITY:

The markedly elevated BNP of 1280 pg/mL [F13] raises the candidate of heart failure with ventricular dysfunction or increased hemodynamic load (R13). The mounting fatigue alongside dyspnea and edema [F5] raises the candidate of heart failure secondary to mitral obstruction, as reduced cardiac output triggers compensatory mechanisms causing fatigue (R10). Bilateral atrial enlargement [F23] raises the candidate of chronic elevation of atrial pressures from mitral obstruction, causing adaptive chamber dilation (R18).

EVIDENCE AGAINST ALTERNATIVE DIAGNOSES:

The absence of fever, elevated ESR (14 mm/h [F14]), and unremarkable CBC [F15] lower the candidate of infectious endocarditis (R21) and acute systemic inflammatory disease (R24). The mild, non-obstructive coronary artery disease on cardiac catheterization [F24] lowers the candidate of acute coronary syndrome or primary myocardial infarction (R23). Clear lung fields on auscultation [F11] lower the candidate of acute decompensated pulmonary edema, though chronic elevation of left atrial pressure may not produce rales if pulmonary compensation is adequate (R22). The preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% [F18] raises the candidate that the left ventricle is underfilled due to obstruction at the mitral valve, rather than having primary myocardial dysfunction (R17).

UNRESOLVED UNCERTAINTIES AND NEXT STEPS:

The specific anticoagulant protein deficiency (protein C, protein S, or antithrombin [U1]) remains unidentified and should be determined to guide long-term management. The precise mechanism by which thromboembolism from an abdominal vein reached and lodged in the left atrium and interatrial septum [U2] is not explicitly established; paradoxical embolism via a patent foramen ovale is a candidate raised in the rulebook (R19) but would require confirmation via bubble study. The exact composition of the mass [U5]—whether true thrombus or other pathology—has not been pathologically confirmed. The identity of the specific abdominal vein involved [U3] does not alter the primary diagnosis but may inform the mechanism of embolism.

CLINICAL SUMMARY:

This is a case of inherited thrombophilia (natural anticoagulant deficiency) complicated by thrombosis in two anatomically distinct sites: an abdominal vein and the left atrium. The left atrial thrombus causes severe mitral inflow obstruction, leading to elevated left atrial pressure, secondary pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dilation and failure, systemic venous congestion, and syncope. The patient's non-adherence to anticoagulation prior to symptom onset permitted progression of the thrombotic tendency. The diagnosis is supported by the constellation of echocardiographic findings (large mobile mass anchored to septum), hemodynamic signs of mitral obstruction (loud S1, positional early diastolic sound, severe inflow obstruction on echo), and secondary signs of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (elevated PA pressures, RV dilation, elevated BNP, elevated JVP, hepatojugular reflux, peripheral edema).

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: confirmed left atrial myxoma (histopathology after resection), with the hypercoagulable state (protein C deficiency, venous thrombosis) a concurrent finding; correct disposition is urgent cardiothoracic surgical excision. The case is explicitly designed to trap responders into thrombus/mitral-stenosis/benign cough-syncope readings.

OUTPUT A names left atrial myxoma as the most likely diagnosis (correct), correctly frames pulmonary HTN and RV dysfunction as secondary to mechanical obstruction, treats the hypercoagulability as likely coincidental (consistent with GT), recommends urgent cardiac surgery consult for resection with histopathologic confirmation (correct disposition), and gives a defensible, well-calibrated 75-80% confidence. No hallucinations. Its only minor blemish is suggesting MRI confirmation, but it explicitly says not to delay surgery.

OUTPUT B is far more elaborate and traceable, and accurately maps nearly all secondary hemodynamic findings, but it commits to the WRONG primary diagnosis: left atrial thrombus secondary to inherited thrombophilia. It explicitly argues against a primary cardiac tumor, anchors on the protein C deficiency/abdominal-vein thrombosis, and reframes the early diastolic sound as functional mitral stenosis rather than the diagnostic 'tumor plop' — i.e., it falls squarely into the case's intended trap. Its disposition leans toward thrombophilia management and confirmatory bubble study rather than urgent surgical resection. Although B appropriately flags uncertainty about mass composition (good calibration hedging), the load-bearing conclusion (diagnosis + disposition) is incorrect.

Correctness on the primary diagnosis and disposition is the dominant criterion; A is right on both, B is wrong on both despite superior thoroughness. A wins decisively.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after two hours of crushing central chest pressure accompanied by breathlessness, queasiness, and profuse sweating. She reported that for roughly three days beforehand she had noticed milder, on-and-off tightness behind the breastbone that she had attributed to stress. She had no known cardiac history and took no regular medications. She had smoked about a pack a day for many years. There was no family history of premature heart disease, and she denied prior chest complaints.

On arrival she appeared anxious and diaphoretic. Blood pressure was 178/96 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 24 per minute, temperature 37.8 C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed tachycardia without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; the lungs were clear. There were no peripheral edema and no calf tenderness. On neck examination a small, firm nodule was palpable in the thyroid gland; there were no eye signs, no lid lag, and no obvious goiter. She had no resting tremor noted at the bedside.

A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia with widespread horizontal ST-segment depression across the inferior leads and the lateral precordial leads (V4 through V6), with associated T-wave inversion, together with ST-segment elevation in lead aVR and in V1.

Initial laboratory testing showed a high-sensitivity troponin T of 0.392 microgram/L (reference 0 to 0.05) and an NT-proBNP of 268 ng/L (reference 0 to 249). A complete blood count, renal panel, and electrolytes were within normal limits. The patient was treated for a presumed acute coronary syndrome with aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor, weight-based heparin, an intravenous beta-blocker, and a nitroglycerine infusion, and was taken urgently to the catheterization laboratory.

Invasive coronary angiography demonstrated severe narrowing involving the proximal right coronary artery and the ostium of the left main stem. Repeated intracoronary boluses of nitroglycerine produced prompt and near-complete resolution of these narrowings, restoring normal vessel caliber. Intravascular optical coherence tomography of the affected segments showed smooth vessel walls without atherosclerotic plaque, without intraluminal thrombus, and without evidence of dissection. Left ventriculography demonstrated preserved global systolic function with no regional wall-motion abnormality.

Given the angiographic findings, additional bloodwork was sent. This revealed a free thyroxine of 54.6 pmol/L (reference 12 to 22), a thyroid-stimulating hormone below 0.001 mE/L (reference 0.5 to 5), and a TSH-receptor antibody titre of 17.4 E/L (reference 0 to 1.8). A dedicated thyroid ultrasound was not obtained during the admission.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Acute myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) due to multivessel epicardial coronary artery vasospasm precipitated by thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease. The presentation mimicked an obstructive acute coronary syndrome.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Invasive coronary angiography demonstrated severe spasm of the right coronary artery and the left main ostium, which was RELIEVED by repeated intracoronary nitroglycerine (vasospasm proven reversible). (2) Intravascular optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed NO atherosclerotic plaque, thrombus, or dissection — excluding obstructive/plaque-rupture MI. (3) Left ventricular angiography showed no wall-motion abnormalities. (4) Biochemical thyrotoxicosis: suppressed TSH (<0.001 mE/L), markedly elevated free T4 (59.9 pmol/L), and elevated TSH-receptor antibody (20.2 E/L), establishing Graves' disease as the etiology of the autonomic/thyrotoxic vasospasm. Note: there were minimal/absent classic hyperthyroid clinical features (only a small thyroid nodule on exam, no ophthalmopathy) — the thyroid disease was occult, which is the diagnostic trap.

CORRECT DISPOSITION/MANAGEMENT: Treat the vasospasm and the underlying thyrotoxicosis, NOT obstructive ACS. Stop the dual antiplatelet/anticoagulant ACS regimen (it is inappropriate and exposes the patient to bleeding without benefit). Start a coronary vasodilator regimen (long-acting nitrate + dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker) and antithyroid therapy (thionamide, e.g. methimazole/thiamazole). Beta-blocker monotherapy without vasodilator cover should be avoided as it can worsen coronary spasm. Patient was discharged within ~2 days and was symptom-free at 1-week follow-up. Source: Klomp M, Siegelaar SE, van de Hoef TP, Beijk MAM. European Heart Journal: Case Reports, 2020 (PMC7501938).

per_case.blind_answer:
Diagnosis: Acute coronary vasospasm secondary to Graves' disease (thyrotoxicosis).

Reasoning: The angiographic hallmark—completely reversible vasospasm of proximal RCA and left main ostium with smooth vessel walls and no atherosclerotic substrate on OCT—combined with biochemical confirmation of Graves' (elevated free T4, suppressed TSH, positive TSH-receptor antibodies) and clinical thyrotoxic features (tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, diaphoresis, palpable thyroid nodule) point unambiguously to thyroid hormone-mediated coronary vasospasm. Troponin elevation reflects demand ischemia, not infarction.

Next action: Initiate definitive antithyroid therapy (propylthiouracil or methimazole) immediately; optimize beta-blocker dosing; arrange thyroid ultrasound to confirm diagnosis morphologically; consult thyroid endocrinology for long-term management.

Confidence: 92%

The diagnosis is biochemically proven and angiographically compelling. Confidence is not higher solely because thyroid ultrasound was not obtained, though lab results are diagnostic.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
DIAGNOSIS: Acute coronary vasospasm secondary to Graves' disease with thyroid storm.

ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC AND ANGIOGRAPHIC FOUNDATION:
The 12-lead ECG shows widespread ST-segment depression in inferior and lateral leads (V4–V6) with ST elevation in aVR and V1 [F037–F041], a pattern that raises high suspicion for left main coronary artery involvement (R001). The urgent coronary angiogram revealed severe narrowing of the proximal right coronary artery and the ostium of the left main stem [F054–F055]. Critically, repeated intracoronary boluses of nitroglycerine produced prompt and near-complete resolution of these narrowings, restoring normal caliber [F056–F057]—a finding that confirms a reversible vasospastic mechanism rather than fixed atherosclerotic stenosis (R002). This vasospastic pattern is further supported by intravascular optical coherence tomography showing smooth vessel walls without atherosclerotic plaque, intraluminal thrombus, or dissection [F058–F061], which excludes atherosclerotic disease and strongly supports vasospasm (R003).

THYROID PATHOLOGY:
Subsequent bloodwork revealed profound thyroid hypermetabolism: free thyroxine 54.6 pmol/L (nearly 2.5× the upper normal limit of 22) [F064], thyroid-stimulating hormone suppressed below 0.001 mE/L [F065], and TSH-receptor antibody titre 17.4 E/L (well above the normal ceiling of 1.8) [F066]. This serologic triad definitively confirms Graves' disease with thyroid storm (R005). Clinical corroboration includes sinus tachycardia at 118 bpm [F018], elevated blood pressure (178/96 mmHg) [F016–F017], tachypnea (respiratory rate 24) [F019], marked diaphoresis [F007, F023], and heightened anxiety [F022], all consistent with adrenergic hyperactivation in thyroid storm.

MECHANISTIC LINK:
The mechanism linking thyroid storm to the acute coronary vasospasm is multifold. First, thyrotoxicosis amplifies adrenergic sensitivity, leading to enhanced vasospastic response to circulating catecholamines (R006). Second, the elevated metabolic rate and increased heart rate create a severe oxygen supply-demand mismatch (R007), predisposing to myocardial ischemia in the absence of fixed coronary stenosis. Third, thyrotoxicosis induces endothelial dysfunction, causing abnormal vasospastic reactivity in angiographically normal or minimally diseased vessels (R009). This pattern—angiographically clean arteries undergoing severe vasospasm that resolves with nitrates—is characteristic of thyroid-mediated, not idiopathic, vasospasm (R010).

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FOR THYROID-MEDIATED VS. IDIOPATHIC VASOSPASM:
The patient has no conventional cardiac risk factors (no prior cardiac history [F011], no baseline medications [F012], no prior chest complaints [F013], negative family history for premature disease [F015]), which would ordinarily raise suspicion for idiopathic Prinzmetal angina. However, the concurrent confirmation of Graves' disease with suppressed TSH and elevated TSH-receptor antibodies makes thyroid-mediated vasospasm far more likely than coincidental idiopathic vasospasm (R010, R011). The presence of a palpable thyroid nodule [F031], though not further characterized by ultrasound [F067], is consistent with Graves' disease.

CARDIAC INJURY PATTERN:
The elevated high-sensitivity troponin T (0.392 µg/L) [F043] despite preserved global left ventricular systolic function [F062] and absence of regional wall-motion abnormality [F063] is entirely consistent with reversible myocardial ischemia rather than overt infarction (R004). The borderline-elevated NT-proBNP (268 ng/L, just above the normal ceiling of 249) [F044] reflects the combined cardiac stress of acute ischemia and tachycardia from thyrotoxicosis. This micro-myocardial injury pattern—elevated troponin without necrotic wall-motion changes—is characteristic of thyrotoxicosis-mediated cardiac stress (R008).

PRODROMAL COURSE:
The three-day history of milder, on-and-off central chest tightness [F008, F010] that the patient attributed to stress likely represents initial episodes of vasospasm in the setting of rising thyroid hormone levels, culminating in the acute severe vasospastic episode requiring hospitalization.

RISK STRATIFICATION:
The ECG pattern of widespread ST abnormalities with aVR/V1 elevation and lateral depression defines a high-risk acute coronary syndrome presentation (R012). Additionally, the concurrent thyroid storm significantly elevates the risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (R013), warranting intensive monitoring and rapid antithyroid therapy.

CONCLUSION:
This is a case of acute coronary vasospasm mechanistically driven by Graves' disease with thyroid storm, not atherosclerotic coronary artery disease or idiopathic Prinzmetal angina. The complete angiographic reversibility, clean vessel wall pathology, suppressed TSH, markedly elevated free T4, and elevated TSH-receptor antibodies together establish the diagnosis. Urgent management must include both coronary support (continued beta-blockade, nitrates, consideration of calcium-channel blockade) and definitive thyroid control (antithyroid drugs, beta-blockade) to prevent recurrent vasospasm and life-threatening arrhythmias.
per_case.framework_top: Acute coronary vasospasm in the setting of Graves' disease with thyroid storm, presenting as reversible left main and right coronary artery stenosis responsive to nitrates.
per_case.framework_next_step: Initiate urgent antithyroid therapy (propylthiouracil or methimazole) and beta-blockade; obtain thyroid ultrasound to characterize the palpable nodule and confirm Graves' disease morphology; admit to monitored bed with continuous cardiac telemetry; consider empiric calcium-channel blocker (e.g., diltiazem) for vasospasm prophylaxis pending cardiology input; arrange endocrinology consultation for thyroid storm management and long-term thyroid control.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85–90%). The constellation of angiographic, electrocardiographic, biochemical, and physiologic findings aligns cohesively with thyroid-mediated coronary vasospasm. The main residual uncertainty is the precise characterization and significance of the palpable thyroid nodule (U003) and whether the thyroid disease was acute presentation vs. chronic unrecognized disorder (U004), but these do not materially alter the acute management or diagnosis.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly identify the core diagnosis: reversible coronary vasospasm (RCA + left main ostium) confirmed by intracoronary nitroglycerine and clean OCT, driven by Graves' thyrotoxicosis (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4, elevated TSH-receptor antibody). Both correctly trace the angiographic and biochemical confirmation chain, which matches the ground truth's confirmation method well.

KEY DIFFERENTIATORS:

1) "Thyroid storm" overcall: Output A explicitly and repeatedly diagnoses "thyroid storm" and adds risk-stratification claims about "malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death." The ground truth and source describe occult/minimally symptomatic thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease, NOT thyroid storm — indeed the source emphasizes minimal/absent classic hyperthyroid features (only a small nodule, no ophthalmopathy) as the diagnostic trap. Thyroid storm is a specific, severe, often-fatal decompensation with altered mentation/fever; diagnosing it here is an overcall/hallucination. Output B says "thyrotoxicosis" without the storm label — more accurate.

2) Management/disposition — the decisive correctness gap. Ground truth is explicit: STOP the dual antiplatelet/anticoagulant ACS regimen, start a vasodilator regimen (long-acting nitrate + dihydropyridine CCB) plus antithyroid therapy, and AVOID beta-blocker monotherapy without vasodilator cover because beta-blockers can worsen coronary spasm. 
   - Output A recommends "continued beta-blockade, nitrates, consideration of calcium-channel blockade." It treats beta-blockade as a mainstay and only "considers" CCB — partially contradicting the guidance that vasodilators (nitrate + CCB) are primary and that beta-blocker cover without vasodilators is hazardous. It does mention nitrates/CCB so it is partially right, but it foregrounds beta-blockade.
   - Output B says "optimize beta-blocker dosing" without pairing it with mandatory vasodilator cover and omits the nitrate/CCB vasospasm regimen entirely. This is a real management miss — and arguably more dangerous given the spasm context. Neither output mentions stopping the ACS antiplatelet/anticoagulant regimen, which both miss.

   On management, A is closer (it at least names nitrates and CCB), while B's "beta-blocker dosing" with no vasodilator is weaker. This favors A.

3) Calibration/defensibility: Output A is heavily padded with finding-IDs and rule-IDs ([F0xx], R0xx), which improves traceability but also introduces specific numeric values that DIFFER from ground truth (free T4 54.6 vs 59.9; TSH-Rab 17.4 vs 20.2; troponin 0.392). These could be from a slightly different case variant, but as stated they don't match the ground-truth figures — minor numeric discrepancies that, combined with the false thyroid-storm framing, hurt A's calibration despite its show-of-work. Output B is concise, states a calibrated 92% confidence, and explicitly reasons about why it is not higher (no ultrasound), which is well-calibrated and honest. B's ultrasound recommendation is reasonable though not strictly needed for the diagnosis.

WEIGHING: A's main advantage is more complete vasospasm-directed management (naming nitrates/CCB). A's main faults are the thyroid-storm overcall (a substantive diagnostic error vs the 'occult thyrotoxicosis' ground truth), unsupported arrhythmia/SCD risk claims, and numeric mismatches. B is cleaner, avoids the storm overcall, is well-calibrated, but has a weaker management plan (beta-blocker-centric, omits the vasodilator regimen). 

Both are fundamentally correct on the central diagnosis and confirmation. The thyroid-storm overcall plus fabricated risk claims in A are clinically meaningful inaccuracies that degrade its trustworthiness more than B's management terseness, and B's calibration is superior. I give B a narrow edge. Both are "partial" overall because each has a notable management/diagnostic shortfall relative to ground truth (A: storm overcall + beta-blocker-forward plan; B: missing vasodilator regimen). Decision is close to a tie, but B's avoidance of the storm overcall and better calibration tip it.

per_case.prose:
A 71-year-old retired man was referred to a regional cardiology service for evaluation of recurrent chest discomfort. He first sought care roughly three years earlier, describing pressure-like central chest pain that came on with exertion — climbing the stairs to his apartment, carrying groceries — and eased with rest. He had no prior cardiac history of note; his only regular medications were for mild hypertension. He had never smoked.

At that first work-up, a treadmill exercise test reproduced his symptoms and showed horizontal ST-segment depression. He was taken for coronary angiography, which demonstrated smooth, widely patent epicardial coronary arteries with no significant stenosis. A provocation test to look for coronary spasm was negative. With angina, an abnormal stress test, normal-appearing coronaries, and (at that time) normal ventricular function on echocardiography, he was told his vessels were structurally fine and was managed accordingly with anti-anginal medication and reassurance.

Over the following years his exercise tolerance steadily declined. He returned this admission with worsening breathlessness on minimal exertion, ankle swelling, and a recurrence of the chest discomfort. On examination he had signs of fluid overload.

Laboratory testing showed a high-sensitivity troponin I of 0.13 ng/mL (upper reference limit 0.1 ng/mL) and a B-type natriuretic peptide of 4980 pg/mL (reference < 100 pg/mL). Renal and hepatic panels were within normal limits.

A 12-lead ECG showed strikingly small QRS complexes, with low voltages in the limb leads and poor R-wave progression across the precordial leads. Repeat echocardiography now showed a mildly increased thickness of the interventricular septum and free wall, a dilated left ventricular cavity, and severely depressed systolic function with global hypokinesis; the estimated ejection fraction was 31%. Diastolic assessment revealed a restrictive filling pattern with a transmitral E/A ratio of 2.1, and tissue-Doppler imaging showed a markedly reduced mitral annular early diastolic velocity (E') of 3 cm/s. Repeat coronary angiography again showed no obstructive epicardial disease.

He was supported with mechanical circulatory assistance while further management was arranged.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Cardiac amyloidosis (infiltrative restrictive cardiomyopathy). The patient was initially and incorrectly labeled as having cardiac syndrome X (microvascular angina) — a comparatively benign attribution — because of anginal chest pain with exertional ST-segment depression on treadmill testing, angiographically normal epicardial coronary arteries, a negative ergonovine provocation test for vasospasm, and initially preserved LV function. Over ~3 years he developed progressive congestive heart failure with a falling ejection fraction.

HOW CONFIRMED: Tissue/pathology. The patient ultimately underwent orthotopic heart transplantation, and pathologic examination of the EXPLANTED HEART was diagnostic: gross deposition of pale amorphous material in vessel walls and interstitium with degenerated myofibers; H&E showing myxoid/amorphous perivascular and interstitial deposits; and Congo-red staining demonstrating APPLE-GREEN BIREFRINGENCE under polarized light — pathognomonic for amyloid. (Original case: 77-year-old man; troponin-I 0.15 ng/mL, BNP 5643 pg/mL, EF 29%, restrictive filling E/A 2.3, mitral annular E' 2 cm/s, low-voltage limb leads with poor precordial R-wave progression, normal coronaries.)

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT benign syndrome X. The discordance between low-voltage ECG and increased/normal-to-thick LV wall thickness, restrictive diastolic physiology with a severely reduced tissue-Doppler E', markedly elevated natriuretic peptide, low-level troponin elevation, anginal chest pain with angiographically NORMAL coronaries (microvascular involvement by amyloid), and progressive refractory heart failure should prompt evaluation for an infiltrative cardiomyopathy — i.e., cardiac amyloidosis. Correct workup: serum/urine free light chains and immunofixation, bone scintigraphy (e.g., 99mTc-PYP/DPD) for ATTR, cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement, and endomyocardial (or fat-pad) biopsy with Congo-red staining and amyloid typing. Management is amyloid-type-specific (anti-plasma-cell therapy for AL, tafamidis/stabilizers for ATTR) plus heart-failure care and advanced therapies (transplant) for end-stage disease, NOT reassurance or anti-anginal-only management appropriate to syndrome X.

OUTCOME in source: Bridged with an intra-aortic balloon pump for ~3 months, then heart transplantation; NYHA class I and well at 2-year follow-up.
