per_case.prose:
A 52-year-old man was referred to a regional respiratory clinic for a second opinion regarding poorly controlled "asthma." About fourteen months earlier he had developed recurrent episodes of breathlessness together with a cough productive of a moderate amount of clear phlegm, and intermittent discomfort located in the centre of his chest. He had been started on a short-acting bronchodilator inhaler and subsequently a combination maintenance inhaler containing an inhaled corticosteroid and a long-acting bronchodilator, with the dose stepped up over the following months.

Despite frequent use of his reliever inhaler and several courses of oral corticosteroids, his symptoms never settled for long. He himself had never smoked. He reported no childhood wheezing, no eczema or hay fever, and no relatives with asthma or allergic disease. He could identify no consistent trigger for his attacks — they were not clearly provoked by exercise, cold air, pets or dust — and he denied any tendency for the breathlessness to be worse at night or in the early morning.

Roughly four months before referral, he began to notice occasional flecks of blood in his sputum. On one occasion this progressed to coughing up an estimated 20-30 mL of frank blood, which prompted escalation of his care. He remained afebrile and reported no weight loss, night sweats or foreign travel.

On examination he was comfortable at rest with normal oxygen saturations. There were no signs of clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Chest auscultation was largely unremarkable between episodes.

A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest was obtained, which demonstrated a focal soft-tissue lesion arising within the trachea. The surrounding lung parenchyma appeared normal and there was no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.

He was referred for flexible bronchoscopy. This revealed a broad-based lesion with a nodular surface arising from the lower half of the trachea, occluding more than two-thirds of the tracheal lumen.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Primary tracheal adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC), a low-grade salivary-gland-type airway malignancy, presenting as a fixed central-airway obstruction that had been mislabeled and treated as adult-onset asthma for ~1 year.

HOW CONFIRMED: New-onset hemoptysis prompted a chest CT, which showed a focal intratracheal lesion with normal lung parenchyma and no lymphadenopathy. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a broad-based, nodular-surfaced tumor in the lower half of the trachea obstructing more than two-thirds of the lumen. Endobronchial biopsies were diagnostic: histology showed uniform small cuboidal cells in tubular/cribriform and solid patterns with small basophilic nuclei and cystic spaces filled with pale-blue mucoid material — characteristic of adenoid cystic carcinoma.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT asthma. The non-resolving "asthma" with no atopic history, no triggers, no diurnal variation, poor response to escalating bronchodilators/repeated oral steroids, and especially the new hemoptysis are red flags for fixed central-airway obstruction mandating imaging of the airway and bronchoscopy rather than further asthma step-up. Definitive treatment was surgical: tracheal resection with end-to-end anastomosis via posterolateral thoracotomy, with complete symptom resolution. ACC is indolent but recurs — this patient developed bilateral lung metastases ~6 years later, treated with lobectomy and radiofrequency ablation, and remained well. Key teaching point: tracheal/central-airway tumors classically masquerade as refractory adult-onset asthma; a flow-volume loop would show fixed obstruction (plateau), and any adult with "asthma" not responding to therapy — and certainly with hemoptysis — needs airway imaging/bronchoscopy.

SOURCE: Afriyie-Mensah JS, Gbadamosi H, Darkwah Abrahams AO. "A rare mimic of adult-onset asthma: Case report and review of the literature." Respirology Case Reports, 2023. (Index case, 45-year-old male.)

rulebook.rule: Hemoptysis (frank blood in sputum) raises the candidate of primary tracheal malignancy, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, which presents with hemoptysis in early course. Hemoptysis is NOT a typical presenting feature of uncomplicated asthma.
rulebook.source: StatPearls: Tracheal Cancer (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538437/) — 'Squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with hemoptysis'

rulebook.rule: Intraluminal focal soft-tissue lesion on CT arising from the tracheal wall, particularly in the lower half with >50% luminal obstruction, raises the candidate of primary tracheal neoplasm (benign or malignant) and lowers asthma as the sole diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Merck Manual (https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/oncology/tumors-of-the-lungs/tracheal-tumors) — 'Diagnosis relies on bronchoscopic biopsy combined with imaging studies to evaluate tumor location and extent'; StatPearls — 'symptoms manifest only when the mass occupies more than 50 to 75% of the lumen diameter'

rulebook.rule: Broad-based lesion with nodular surface morphology on bronchoscopy raises the candidate of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) over other benign or low-grade tumors, which typically appear smooth, sessile, or with intact overlying mucosa.
rulebook.bears_on: Squamous cell carcinoma (over adenoid cystic carcinoma or benign tumors)
rulebook.source: Tracheobronchial Tumors radiologic-pathologic review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7115773/) — 'Squamous cell carcinoma presents as a polypoid or sessile lesion with irregular margins'; ACC 'appears as a submucosal mass with smooth contours and intact overlying mucosa'

rulebook.rule: Treatment failure despite escalating doses of inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators raises the candidate of mechanical airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal tumor or stenosis) and lowers asthma as the primary diagnosis. Mechanical obstruction does not respond to anti-inflammatory or bronchodilator therapy because the obstruction is structural, not inflammatory.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary tracheal tumor or stenosis (not asthma)
rulebook.source: StatPearls: Tracheal Cancer — 'A high index of suspicion for tracheal cancer should be raised when respiratory symptoms are not responding to initial medical therapy'; Journal of Medical Case Reports (https://jmedicalcasereports.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13256-024-04915-3) — Tracheal stenosis case demonstrates treatment failure with asthma regimens

rulebook.rule: Absence of personal history of atopy (no childhood wheezing, eczema, hay fever) lowers the likelihood of asthma but does NOT exclude it. However, combined with other atypical features (hemoptysis, structural lesion, treatment failure), it raises the suspicion for alternative diagnoses such as tracheal tumor.
rulebook.bears_on: Asthma (lowers); primary tracheal tumor (raises as alternative)
rulebook.source: Asthma Diagnosis Criteria (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK536620/) — 'A personal history of atopic disorders has sensitivity 54.2-55% and specificity 67.8-73.7% for asthma diagnosis'; medline search on atopy and asthma — indicates atopy is supportive but not required for asthma diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Absence of identifiable asthma triggers (not worse with exercise, cold air, pets, dust; no nocturnal/early morning pattern) lowers asthma as the diagnosis and raises consideration of mechanical obstruction or structural lesion causing persistent symptoms independent of external triggers.
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: asthma is typically triggered by identifiable environmental or time-based factors. Structural obstruction causes symptoms that are independent of classic asthma triggers.

rulebook.rule: Non-smoker status (negative smoking history) slightly lowers the likelihood of squamous cell carcinoma, which is strongly associated with tobacco smoking. However, adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) has no strong smoking association and affects non-smokers equally, and benign tumors are independent of smoking status.
rulebook.bears_on: Squamous cell carcinoma (lowers, relatively); adenoid cystic carcinoma (raises, equally common); benign tracheal tumor (neutral)
rulebook.source: Tracheal Cancer epidemiology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11654256/) — 'The etiology of squamous cell carcinoma is strongly associated with tobacco smoking'; StatPearls — 'Adenoid cystic carcinoma occurs equally in both sexes' with no smoking association

rulebook.rule: Age 52 years raises the candidate of adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC), which typically presents in the 4th-5th decades (40-50 years), and slightly lowers squamous cell carcinoma, which typically presents in 60-70 years in smokers.
rulebook.bears_on: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (raises); squamous cell carcinoma (lowers, relatively)
rulebook.source: Tracheal Cancer epidemiology (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12943-024-02188-4) and Frontiers (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2025.1568589/full) — 'Adenoid cystic carcinoma occurs predominantly in the fourth and fifth decades; squamous cell carcinoma exhibits male predisposition and occurs between 60 to 70 years of age'

rulebook.rule: Chronic course over 14 months (productive cough, recurrent dyspnea) raises adenoid cystic carcinoma, which grows slowly over months to years, over acute-onset asthma or rapidly progressive squamous cell carcinoma.
rulebook.bears_on: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (raises); acute asthma exacerbation (lowers)
rulebook.source: StatPearls: Tracheal Cancer — 'Adenoid cystic tumors develop slowly with symptoms progressing over a period of months to years'; PMC Carcinoid case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10129234/) — 'Progressive nonexertional shortness of breath over one year prior to diagnosis'

rulebook.rule: Absence of systemic constitutional symptoms (afebrile, no weight loss, no night sweats) lowers infectious or granulomatous causes (tuberculosis, fungal disease, sarcoidosis) but does NOT exclude malignancy. Tracheal tumors often present without systemic symptoms in early stages.
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, or granulomatous disease (lowers); primary tracheal tumor (neutral to raises, as early-stage tumors often lack systemic symptoms)
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis differential (https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0200/p144.html) — 'Fever and weight loss suggest infection or malignancy, but their absence does not exclude either'

rulebook.rule: Normal chest radiography (aside from the intratracheal lesion on CT) raises consideration of tracheal or central airway pathology, as the trachea is a 'blind spot on the chest radiograph.' This increases suspicion for tracheal tumor and explains why standard imaging missed the lesion initially.
rulebook.source: PMC Carcinoid case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10129234/) — 'Chest radiography showed no abnormalities; the trachea functions as a blind spot on the chest radiograph, enabling tumors to evade detection through standard imaging'

rulebook.rule: Pulmonary function tests showing reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and bronchospasm reversibility with bronchodilators raises the candidate of asthma but is NOT specific. The same pattern can occur in tracheal obstruction (fixed or variable obstruction). Flow-volume loops are more diagnostic: fixed obstruction pattern supports central airway obstruction (tracheal lesion); variable pattern supports asthma.
rulebook.bears_on: Asthma; primary tracheal obstruction (both can mimic, differentiated by flow-volume loop pattern)
rulebook.source: Tracheal Stenosis misdiagnosis review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11607920/) and Frontiers (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2022.898208/full) — 'Flow-volume loops remain the most effective method for detecting upper airway obstruction'; 'Resistance at 5-20 Hz and reactance can discriminate between variable and fixed central airway obstruction'

rulebook.rule: Trepopnea (breathing difficulty in specific body positions) is a rare symptom that raises suspicion for tracheal pathology. Its presence in a patient with asthma-like symptoms should prompt investigation for central airway obstruction or tracheal lesion.
rulebook.source: PMC Carcinoid case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10129234/) — 'The patient displayed trepopnea, a rare symptom' that helped distinguish tracheal carcinoid from asthma

rulebook.rule: Persisting or worsening respiratory symptoms despite one year of escalating asthma therapy raises the candidate of alternative diagnosis (mechanical obstruction, tracheal tumor) and significantly lowers the likelihood that inadequately treated asthma alone explains the clinical picture.
rulebook.bears_on: Asthma (lowers as sole diagnosis); primary tracheal tumor (raises)
rulebook.source: PMC Carcinoid case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10129234/) — 'Symptoms worsened without any significant improvement after one year of asthma therapy' was a key diagnostic clue; StatPearls — 'A high index of suspicion for tracheal cancer should be raised when respiratory symptoms are not responding to initial medical therapy'

rulebook.rule: Benign intraluminal lesions (hemangioma, fibroepithelial polyp, leiomyoma) typically present with hemoptysis and are small (<10 mm), sessile, smooth, or polypoid with intact mucosa. They may present as asthma-like symptoms (wheezing, dyspnea) with airway obstruction. Absence of constitutional symptoms and normal systemic imaging favor benign over malignant pathology.
rulebook.bears_on: Benign intraluminal tracheal lesion (hemangioma, fibroepithelial polyp, leiomyoma)
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis review (https://clinicalgate.com/hemoptysis/) — 'Tracheal lobular capillary hemangioma usually presents as a painless red-purple nodule with hemoptysis and appears as a small (<10 mm), sessile or polypoid lesion with distinctive glinting vascular appearance'; Fibroepithelial polyp case — 'presents with airway stenosis, refractory asthma, dyspnea and hemoptysis'

rulebook.rule: Bronchoscopic biopsy revealing histologic features (cell morphology, immunostains) is the definitive diagnostic test that resolves the differential between primary tracheal tumor (benign or malignant), carcinoid, and other pathologies versus asthma. Histopathology is required to confirm tissue diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Merck Manual and StatPearls — 'Diagnosis relies on bronchoscopic biopsy combined with imaging studies'; PMC Carcinoid case — 'Bronchoscopy and biopsy identified nests of uniform bland cells characteristic of carcinoid tumors, confirmed by positive immunostains'

per_case.blind_answer: Most likely diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the trachea (primary tracheal malignancy). Recommended next action: Urgent bronchoscopic biopsy for histological confirmation and staging, followed by high-resolution CT and PET-CT for treatment planning. Confidence: 85-90%. Reasoning: 52-year-old with 14 months progressive dyspnea refractory to guideline-directed asthma therapy, hemoptysis, and a focal broad-based nodular tracheal lesion occluding >2/3 of lumen. SCC is the most common primary tracheal cancer; classic presentation includes chronic cough, dyspnea from obstruction, and hemoptysis. Absence of asthma triggers, lack of atopic history, and no response to high-dose corticosteroids strongly argues against asthma. The structural lesion seen on both CT and bronchoscopy is diagnostic of a neoplastic process, not reversible airway disease.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The clinical presentation is NOT poorly controlled asthma but rather PRIMARY TRACHEAL NEOPLASM.

**Key diagnostic reasoning:**

(1) **Treatment failure refutes asthma as the primary diagnosis.** The patient failed escalating doses of inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting bronchodilators, and multiple courses of oral corticosteroids over 14 months [f4]. Per r4, mechanical airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal tumor) does not respond to anti-inflammatory or bronchodilator therapy because the obstruction is structural, not inflammatory. Combined with the 14-month duration of progressive symptoms despite escalation [f2, f3, f4], this strongly raises tracheal tumor and lowers asthma as the sole diagnosis [r14].

(2) **Hemoptysis is not a feature of uncomplicated asthma.** The patient developed frank hemoptysis (20-30 mL) four months before referral [f8]. Per r1, hemoptysis is NOT a typical presenting feature of asthma and raises squamous cell carcinoma. The combination of hemoptysis with chronic dyspnea and productive cough is characteristic of malignant tracheal lesions.

(3) **Imaging and bronchoscopy demonstrate a focal intraluminal lesion.** CT shows a focal soft-tissue lesion arising within the trachea [f11], and bronchoscopy reveals a broad-based lesion with nodular surface from the lower trachea, occluding >66% of the lumen [f12]. Per r2, intraluminal focal soft-tissue lesion on CT with >50% obstruction raises primary tracheal neoplasm and lowers asthma. Per r3, broad-based morphology with nodular surface raises squamous cell carcinoma over benign tumors (which typically appear smooth with intact mucosa).

(4) **Atypical asthma presentation lowers asthma.** The patient lacks identifiable asthma triggers [f7] and has no personal history of atopy (no childhood wheezing, eczema, hay fever, family history of asthma) [f6]. Per r5, while atopy is not required for asthma, its absence combined with other atypical features raises alternative diagnoses. Per r6, absence of trigger-sensitivity and nocturnal/early-morning pattern lowers asthma.

(5) **Differential between squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC), and benign lesion.**

- **SCC vs. ACC by age and epidemiology:** The patient is 52 years old [f1]. Per r8, age 52 raises ACC (typically 4th-5th decades) and slightly lowers SCC (typically 60-70 years). Per r7, the patient's non-smoker status [f5] slightly lowers SCC (strongly associated with tobacco) but does not exclude it; ACC has no smoking association. Thus age and smoking history favor ACC over SCC, but both remain candidates.

- **Chronic slow progression favors ACC.** Per r9, the 14-month chronic course with progressive dyspnea and productive cough raises ACC, which grows slowly over months to years. SCC can present acutely; the slow indolent course is more consistent with ACC.

- **Morphology (nodular/broad-based) raises SCC over ACC.** Per r3, nodular surface morphology raises SCC; ACC typically appears as a smooth submucosal mass. However, SCC is less likely given age and non-smoker status.

- **Benign lesion cannot be excluded.** Per r15, benign intraluminal lesions (hemangioma, fibroepithelial polyp) can present with hemoptysis and airway obstruction mimicking asthma. Absence of constitutional symptoms [f9] and normal surrounding lung parenchyma [f11] are consistent with benign pathology. However, the broad-based nodular morphology is less typical of benign lesions.

(6) **Absence of systemic constitutional symptoms does not exclude malignancy.** The patient is afebrile, without weight loss or night sweats [f9]. Per r10, absence of constitutional symptoms lowers infectious/granulomatous causes but does NOT exclude primary tracheal tumor, which often presents without systemic symptoms in early stages.

(7) **Definitive diagnosis requires histology.** Per r16, bronchoscopic biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test. Histopathology will definitively distinguish squamous cell carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, benign tumor, carcinoid, and other pathologies.

**Conclusion:** The clinical presentation—persistent dyspnea and productive cough refractory to 14 months of escalating asthma therapy, hemoptysis, focal intraluminal tracheal lesion with >66% obstruction on imaging and bronchoscopy—is diagnostic of PRIMARY TRACHEAL NEOPLASM, NOT asthma. The differential narrows to squamous cell carcinoma (morphology favors, but age and smoking history less typical), adenoid cystic carcinoma (age and chronic indolent course favor), or benign lesion (less likely given morphology, but not excluded). Urgent histopathologic diagnosis via biopsy is required.
per_case.framework_top: Primary tracheal neoplasm, most likely squamous cell carcinoma or adenoid cystic carcinoma; benign intraluminal lesion cannot be excluded without histology.
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent bronchoscopic biopsy of the tracheal lesion to obtain histopathologic diagnosis, combined with staging imaging (chest/abdomen/pelvis CT or PET-CT) to assess for metastatic disease if malignancy is confirmed.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85-90%) that the diagnosis is NOT asthma and IS a tracheal structural lesion; moderate (50-60%) confidence between squamous cell carcinoma vs. adenoid cystic carcinoma vs. benign tumor pending histology.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly reject asthma and identify a primary tracheal neoplasm as the diagnosis, citing the correct red flags (refractory "asthma," no atopy/triggers, hemoptysis, focal intraluminal lesion, >2/3 obstruction). The decisive difference is the specific tumor type. Ground truth is adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC).

OUTPUT A explicitly works the differential among SCC, ACC, and benign lesions and correctly reasons that age (52, 4th-5th decade typical), non-smoker status (no tobacco association for ACC), and the slow indolent multi-month progression favor ACC over SCC. It names ACC as a leading candidate, correctly notes ACC has no smoking association, and appropriately concludes that histology is required for definitive distinction — matching how the real case was confirmed (biopsy). Its calibration is strong: it does not overcommit to a single type, presents traceable rule-based reasoning [r-tags], and lands ACC squarely in the candidate set with supporting epidemiology. Minor imperfection: it slightly overweights "nodular/broad-based morphology favors SCC" (the real ACC was broad-based and nodular), but it correctly subordinates that to age/smoking/course favoring ACC.

OUTPUT B commits firmly (85-90% confidence) to squamous cell carcinoma, which is the WRONG specific diagnosis. While SCC is indeed the most common primary tracheal cancer (a defensible population prior), B's high confidence ignores the discriminating features that point away from SCC and toward ACC: the patient is a relatively young non-smoker with an indolent course — all of which argue against SCC. B's recommended next step (urgent bronchoscopic biopsy + imaging) is correct, and its rejection of asthma is correct, but its confident wrong commitment to SCC is poorly calibrated and less defensible.

A is correct at the level of disease category (tracheal neoplasm) and correctly surfaces ACC as a favored candidate with sound, traceable reasoning, declining to overcommit before histology — so it is essentially right where it matters. B reaches the right category but confidently names the wrong specific malignancy. A wins on correctness of the specific diagnosis and on calibration.

per_case.prose:
A 61-year-old man, a retired commercial fisherman who had never smoked, was referred to a regional respiratory service after several months of unexplained illness. His trouble had begun the previous spring with a persistent dry cough that he and his family doctor at first blamed on seasonal allergies. Over the autumn the cough failed to settle, and around the new year he noticed streaks of dark, old-looking blood in his sputum on most mornings. Shortly afterward he developed low-grade fevers and felt increasingly worn out, tiring after only modest exertion such as walking up a single flight of stairs. Two short courses of oral antibiotics prescribed in the community produced no improvement.

He had no notable prior medical history, took no regular medications, drank little alcohol, and kept no birds or other unusual pets. He had not travelled abroad recently.

On admission he was afebrile at the bedside but appeared pale and fatigued. Chest auscultation was largely unremarkable. Initial bloods showed a white-cell count of 10.4 ×10^9/L with a marked neutrophil predominance (around 85 percent), a haemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL, a C-reactive protein of 78 mg/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 74 mm/h. Rheumatoid factor was mildly raised at 29 IU/mL. A vasculitis and autoimmune panel — antinuclear antibody, both cytoplasmic and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti-endothelial-cell antibody — was sent and returned negative or within normal limits. Renal function and urinalysis were normal. Cardiac markers and an electrocardiogram showed no acute changes.

A chest radiograph taken early in the admission was reported as showing scattered bilateral opacities. A contrast CT of the thorax demonstrated multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules of varying size with well-defined borders, several surrounded by a faint rim of ground-glass change; the largest measured roughly 1.8 cm. An 18F-FDG PET/CT showed mild-to-moderate uptake in the nodules, with a maximum standardised uptake value of about 3.9, and no other dominant focus.

During the workup the patient developed a crop of palpable purpuric spots over his left shin. Sputum studies were sent; a molecular/next-generation sequencing assay flagged a non-tuberculous mycobacterial species, raising the possibility of an atypical pulmonary infection, though cultures were not confirmatory.

The combination of bilateral nodules, haemoptysis, high inflammatory markers and a purpuric rash prompted concern for a systemic small-vessel vasculitis. A punch biopsy of the skin lesion was reported as showing changes of a leukocytoclastic vasculitis. A CT-guided percutaneous core-needle biopsy of one of the larger lung nodules was reported as organising pneumonia, and a subsequent bronchoscopic transbronchial biopsy showed only chronic inflammatory change. At a multidisciplinary meeting the working impression centred on an ANCA-negative pulmonary-renal-type vasculitis, with a granulomatous vasculitis felt to be difficult to exclude, and immunosuppression was discussed.

Because none of the lung or skin samples had yielded a unifying explanation, attention turned to a small, slowly enlarging soft-tissue swelling that had appeared near the angle of the patient's left jaw. This lesion was felt to be more readily accessible, and an excisional biopsy of it was arranged.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Metastatic angiosarcoma (cutaneous/soft-tissue angiosarcoma with diffuse pulmonary metastases presenting as multiple bilateral lung nodules with hemoptysis).

HOW CONFIRMED: The diagnosis was missed on every initial sampling — CT-guided percutaneous core-needle biopsy of a lung nodule showed only "organizing pneumonia"; bronchoscopic lung biopsy showed "chronic inflammation"; skin biopsy of the lower-leg purpura showed "vasculitis"; and a multidisciplinary panel concluded granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) "could not be excluded." Definitive diagnosis came only from a surgical excisional biopsy of a soft-tissue lesion (beside the submandibular gland). Histopathology showed irregular dilated vascular lacunae lined by pleomorphic, atypical malignant endothelial cells; immunohistochemistry was positive for the endothelial/vascular markers CD31 and CD34, confirming angiosarcoma. PD-L1 expression was 70%.

KEY MISLEADING FEATURES (the trap): bilateral pulmonary nodules + hemoptysis + high inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) + anemia + a vasculitic skin rash + multiple biopsies reading as organizing pneumonia/chronic inflammation/vasculitis strongly mimic an ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA/Wegener's) or infection. The discriminating facts: ANCA, ANA and anti-endothelial-cell antibodies were all negative/unremarkable, and the lung-biopsy "organizing pneumonia" was non-specific reactive change overlying metastatic vascular tumor. Angiosarcoma metastatic to lung classically produces multiple nodules that bleed (hemoptysis) and is frequently mistaken for vasculitis.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is a malignancy, not vasculitis or infection — immunosuppression for presumed GPA would have been harmful. Correct path is excisional/surgical biopsy of an accessible lesion for definitive histology + IHC, then oncology referral for systemic therapy (the index patient received anti-angiogenic anlotinib plus pembrolizumab, with transient partial response). Prognosis is poor: the index patient died of progressive metastatic disease ~5 months after diagnosis (respiratory failure, multi-serosal effusions, hepatic and cardiac failure, DIC).

ORIGINAL CASE (held aside): 73-year-old male nonsmoker; dry cough from mid-2019, hemoptysis by Dec 2019, fever Jan 2020; WBC ~9.9-11.0×10^9/L with 82-87% neutrophils, CRP 69-92 mg/L, ESR 65-95 mm/h, Hb 86 g/L, RF 33.5 IU/mL; ANCA/ANA/anti-endothelial-cell Ab negative; bilateral pulmonary nodules (largest ~1.5×1.6 cm) with GGO halos, PET SUVmax 4.29; sputum NGS suggested Mycobacterium chelonae (red herring). Final dx metastatic angiosarcoma, CD31+/CD34+, PD-L1 70%.

uncertainties.about: Which specific non-tuberculous mycobacterial species? Species identity required to assess clinical significance.
Hemoptysis volume, duration per episode, progression pattern. 'Most mornings' specifies timing only, not severity.
Fever temperatures (exact range), daily pattern, peak, response to antipyretics. 'Low-grade' is subjective.
Community antibiotic agents, dosing, duration, coverage spectrum. 'Two short courses' is non-specific.
Vasculitis serology panel timing relative to symptom onset; assay methodologies; ANCA detection limits.
Laboratory reference range for RF; clinical threshold for 'mildly raised'; contextual significance of 29 IU/mL.
Assay platforms and upper normal limits for ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, anti-AECA. Only qualitative result stated.
Ground-glass halo distribution: what percent of nodules? Which nodules? Extent of opacity?
Specimen tracking: which specific lung nodule was core-needle biopsied if multiple were similar size?
Multidisciplinary meeting attendees, specialist opinions, competing diagnoses explicitly considered.
Why 'pulmonary-renal-type vasculitis' when renal function and urinalysis are both normal? Anatomic assumption or other rationale?
Which immunosuppressive agents considered? Induction vs maintenance regimen? Dosing? Contraindications assessed?
Jaw lesion physical examination details: size, consistency, color, fixation, overlying skin changes.
Jaw lesion chronology: when did it first appear relative to other symptoms? Growth rate quantified in what interval?
Occupational/environmental exposure history: which waters (marine vs fresh)? Chemical/organic exposures during commercial fishing?

queries.asks: What is the unifying diagnosis explaining: bilateral pulmonary nodules (FDG-avid), hemoptysis, organising pneumonia, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, chronic lung inflammation, ANCA-negative serology, elevated acute-phase reactants, and NGS-detected NTM with negative cultures?
Is the NGS-detected non-tuberculous mycobacterium clinically significant pathogen or a colonizer/contaminant? Why are cultures negative while molecular assay is positive?

How do the pathologic findings from three distinct sites (skin: leukocytoclastic vasculitis; lung core: organising pneumonia; transbronchial: chronic inflammation) relate? Single disease or multiple overlapping processes?
Why is 'pulmonary-renal-type vasculitis' invoked as working diagnosis when renal function and urinalysis are entirely normal? What diagnostic logic underpins this nosologic choice?
What is the nature and diagnostic significance of the new jaw lesion (soft-tissue swelling near mandibular angle)? Will its excisional biopsy clarify or break the systemic diagnosis?
What is the appropriate immunosuppressive regimen for ANCA-negative vasculitis? Which induction and maintenance agents are indicated given the histopathologic pattern?

ir.inferred_domain: Internal Medicine / Respiratory Medicine with differential diagnosis of systemic small-vessel vasculitis (rheumatology, pulmonology, pathology, medical microbiology)

rulebook.rule: Bilateral pulmonary nodules with well-defined borders and varying size on CT imaging raises the diagnostic probability of sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), organizing pneumonia, or lymphoma
rulebook.source: Pulmonary and extra-pulmonary manifestations of sarcoidosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26759510/) and Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: clinical characteristics and updates in diagnosis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11385631/)

rulebook.rule: Faint ground-glass rim surrounding pulmonary nodules raises likelihood of organizing pneumonia or infectious/inflammatory etiology rather than primary malignancy
rulebook.source: Bilateral pulmonary nodules in an adult patient with bronchiolitis obliterans-organising pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21691403/) and Clinical features of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33793625/)

rulebook.rule: FDG-PET SUV uptake of 3.9 in pulmonary nodules falls in the mild-to-moderate range, consistent with infection, inflammation, or low-grade malignancy; cannot reliably discriminate between these categories
rulebook.source: Maximum Standardized Uptake Value of 18F-deoxyglucose PET Imaging Increases the Effectiveness of CT Radiomics (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8718929/) and Association Between 18F-FDG PET/CT-Based SUV Index and Malignant Status of Persistent Ground-Glass Nodules (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33842310/)

rulebook.rule: Hemoptysis with dark/old-appearing blood on most mornings raises suspicion for pulmonary vasculitis, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, or pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis: evaluation and management (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25955625/) and Pulmonary hemorrhagic syndromes (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11921063/)

rulebook.rule: Hemoptysis as a rare or atypical presenting symptom of organizing pneumonia has been documented in literature, particularly when BOOP is associated with systemic disease
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis as the presenting symptom in bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9187212/)

rulebook.rule: Organising pneumonia on core-needle lung biopsy raises likelihood of idiopathic organizing pneumonia, drug-induced OP, infection-associated OP, or systemic disease (hypersensitivity pneumonitis, vasculitis, connective tissue disease)
rulebook.source: Clinical features of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33793625/) and Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis: Essential Radiologic and Pathologic Findings (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26839033/)

rulebook.rule: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis on skin biopsy (palpable purpura with neutrophilic fibrinoid necrosis and leukocytoclasia) raises suspicion for ANCA-associated vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, immune complex vasculitis, or drug reaction
rulebook.source: Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis: An Early Skin Biopsy Makes a Difference (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7263727/) and Diagnosis and management of leukocytoclastic vasculitis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8195763/)

rulebook.rule: ANCA-negative serology with leukocytoclastic vasculitis and necrotizing features lowers probability of ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and raises probability of IgA vasculitis, immune complex vasculitis, ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis, or drug-induced vasculitis
rulebook.source: ANCA-Negative Pauci-immune Necrotizing Glomerulonephritis: A Case Series and a New Clinical Classification (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34119564/)

rulebook.rule: Negative c-ANCA, p-ANCA, and anti-AECA serology lowers probability of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and ANCA-associated vasculitis, but does not exclude ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis or other small-vessel vasculitides
rulebook.source: Clinical Presentation and Outcomes of Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Autoantibody-Negative Pauci-Immune Glomerulonephritis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12142597/)

rulebook.rule: Mildly elevated rheumatoid factor (29 IU/mL) raises suspicion for connective tissue disease (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) or may be associated with immune activation in vasculitis, but is non-specific
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and differential diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/diagnosis-and-differential-diagnosis-of-rheumatoid-arthritis/print)

rulebook.rule: Negative ANA serology lowers probability of systemic lupus erythematosus and other ANA-associated autoimmune diseases but does not exclude systemic vasculitis or other systemic diseases
rulebook.source: ANCA-Negative Pauci-immune Necrotizing Glomerulonephritis: A Case Series and a New Clinical Classification (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34119564/)

rulebook.rule: Elevated CRP (78 mg/L) and ESR (74 mm/h) raise the probability of acute systemic inflammation/vasculitis and indicate increased disease activity; however, these markers are non-specific and can accompany infection, malignancy, or other inflammatory conditions
rulebook.source: Acute Phase Reactants: Relevance in Dermatology (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36776186/) and Acute Phase Reactants as Novel Predictors of Cardiovascular Disease (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3767354/)

rulebook.rule: Mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL) with elevated acute-phase reactants raises suspicion for chronic systemic disease including vasculitis, chronic infection, or malignancy; indicates disease chronicity and severity
rulebook.source: Treatment of giant cell arteritis (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/treatment-of-giant-cell-arteritis)

rulebook.rule: Normal renal function and normal urinalysis with negative c-ANCA and p-ANCA lowers probability of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis or necrotizing vasculitis with renal involvement; however, pulmonary-renal vasculitis can present with entirely normal renal indices initially
rulebook.source: ANCA-negative pulmonary-renal-type vasculitis: Pulmonary renal syndrome: A case report of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage in association with ANCA negative pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5999515/)

rulebook.rule: NGS-positive molecular detection of non-tuberculous mycobacterium with negative sputum cultures raises the possibility of atypical pulmonary infection but does not meet diagnostic criteria for NTM pulmonary disease (which require two positive cultures); molecular assays may detect organisms not recovered by culture
rulebook.source: Molecular Identification of Non-tuberculous Mycobacteria in Suspected Tuberculosis Cases in Central India (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10321564/) and Development and evaluation of a multiplex molecular point-of-care assay (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12380709/)

rulebook.rule: Single positive NGS result for NTM without culture confirmation is insufficient to diagnose NTM pulmonary disease; contamination, colonization, and clinical insignificance must be excluded; NTM pulmonary disease requires at least two positive cultures from separate occasions
rulebook.source: Development and evaluation of a molecular assay for detection of nontuberculous mycobacteria (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18945835/) and High Rates of Non-Tuberculous Mycobacteria Isolation in Mozambican Children (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5240942/)

rulebook.rule: Negative antibiotic response to two short courses of oral antibiotics raises suspicion for atypical infection (NTM, fungal), malignancy, vasculitis, or chronic inflammatory disease refractory to standard agents
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis: evaluation and management (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25955625/)

rulebook.rule: Chronic illness with persistent dry cough over several months, failed response to seasonal attribution, and progression through multiple seasons raises suspicion for systemic disease (vasculitis, sarcoidosis), malignancy, or chronic infection rather than simple allergic rhinitis
rulebook.source: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: clinical characteristics and updates in diagnosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39257888/)

rulebook.rule: Occupational history as retired commercial fisherman raises consideration for hypersensitivity pneumonitis (exposure to moldy grain, fish meal, water-associated organisms) or atypical infections endemic to marine/fishing environments
rulebook.source: Occupational hypersensitivity pneumonia (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10854060/) and Occupational causes of hypersensitivity pneumonitis: a systematic review and compendium (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8486273/)

rulebook.rule: Triad of palpable purpura (leukocytoclastic vasculitis), hemoptysis with pulmonary infiltrates (organising pneumonia), and elevated acute-phase reactants raises high suspicion for systemic small-vessel vasculitis; ANCA-negativity points to ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis or alternative etiologies
rulebook.source: Clinical Presentation and Outcomes of Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Autoantibody-Negative Pauci-Immune Glomerulonephritis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12142597/)

rulebook.rule: Chronic inflammatory changes on transbronchial biopsy without diagnostic granulomas lowers specificity for sarcoidosis or GPA and raises consideration for organizing pneumonia, drug-induced pneumonitis, or non-specific chronic infection
rulebook.source: Clinical features of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33793625/)

rulebook.rule: Two distinct pathologic findings from separate lung biopsies (organising pneumonia on core biopsy vs. chronic inflammation on transbronchial biopsy) suggest sampling variation, patchy distribution of disease, or multiple overlapping pathologic processes
rulebook.source: Clinical features of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33793625/)

rulebook.rule: Development of new palpable purpura during hospital workup for pulmonary illness strongly supports diagnosis of systemic vasculitis, suggesting progression or newly apparent manifestation of multisystem disease
rulebook.source: Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis: An Early Skin Biopsy Makes a Difference (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7263727/)

rulebook.rule: Small soft-tissue swelling near mandibular angle developing during workup for pulmonary-systemic illness may represent: metastatic lymphoma, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, vasculitis, TB, fungal), infection, or sinonasal/ENT manifestation of systemic disease
rulebook.source: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: clinical characteristics and updates in diagnosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39257888/) [includes ENT manifestations of GPA]

rulebook.rule: Standard induction immunosuppression for pauci-immune vasculitis consists of corticosteroids (methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisone) combined with intravenous cyclophosphamide; remission rates approximately 80% with this combination
rulebook.source: Management of ANCA-associated vasculitis: Current trends and future prospects (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20596502/)

rulebook.rule: Maintenance immunosuppression after induction therapy for vasculitis with methotrexate or azathioprine has comparable efficacy to cyclophosphamide maintenance; choice depends on disease severity, organ involvement, and comorbidities
rulebook.source: WEGENT - Comparison of Methotrexate or Azathioprine as Maintenance Therapy for ANCA-Associated Vasculitides (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00349674) and Methotrexate versus cyclophosphamide for remission maintenance in ANCA-associated vasculitis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5634660/)

rulebook.rule: ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis with pulmonary hemorrhage and hemoptysis has fulminant potential with mortality 25-50% if untreated; rapid immunosuppression is indicated
rulebook.source: Pulmonary Renal Syndrome in ANCA-Negative Vasculitis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10874128/)

rulebook.rule: GPA diagnosis requires 2 of 4 ACR criteria: (1) granulomatous inflammation on biopsy, (2) abnormal CXR, (3) urinary RBCs/casts, (4) oral/nasal inflammation; absence of all four criteria lowers diagnostic probability for GPA
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and classification of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24485158/)

rulebook.rule: Sarcoidosis diagnosis requires compatible clinical-radiologic findings plus non-caseating granulomas on biopsy and exclusion of alternative granulomatous diseases (TB, fungal, vasculitis); negative AFB smear and cultures support but do not exclude sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: Pulmonary and extra-pulmonary manifestations of sarcoidosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26759510/)

rulebook.rule: Elevated serum ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) found in ~60% of sarcoidosis patients and only ~1% of other conditions; high specificity when elevated but absence does not exclude sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: Predictive potential of ACE phenotyping in extrapulmonary sarcoidosis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9396819/)

rulebook.rule: Never-smoker status with occupational exposure as commercial fisherman lowers probability of primary lung malignancy but does not exclude lymphoma, carcinoid, or metastatic disease
rulebook.source: Hemoptysis: evaluation and management (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25955625/)

rulebook.rule: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis diagnosis requires occupational/environmental exposure history, compatible clinical presentation, and characteristic pathology (interstitial inflammation, bronchiolitis, organizing pneumonia, non-caseating granulomas); organizing pneumonia is frequent but not required for diagnosis
rulebook.source: Occupational hypersensitivity pneumonia (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10854060/) and Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis: Essential Radiologic and Pathologic Findings (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26839033/)

per_case.blind_answer: Most likely diagnosis: Sarcoidosis (systemic, pulmonary and cutaneous involvement). Recommended next action: Obtain non-caseating granulomas on excisional biopsy of jaw/submandibular lesion; if positive, measure serum calcium, ACE, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D to confirm diagnosis and initiate corticosteroids. Confidence: 65-70%. Reasoning: Multi-system presentation (bilateral pulmonary nodules with organizing pneumonia, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, systemic inflammation) combined with ANCA-negative serology, normal renal function, and granulomatous lung pathology is classic for sarcoidosis. The jaw lesion appearing during workup is the diagnostic keystone—tissue from this more accessible site should reveal non-caseating granulomas. The NTM finding likely reflects secondary colonization (cultures were not confirmatory). Sarcoidosis unifies the entire clinical picture better than alternatives (e.g., granulomatous vasculitis, occult mycobacterial disease), though final diagnosis depends on jaw biopsy histology.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
## Diagnostic Reasoning

The patient presents with a multisystem illness centered on three pathologic pillars:

### Pillar 1: Systemic Vasculitis (High Confidence)

The combination of **bilateral pulmonary nodules with hemoptysis** (F11, F38, F39, F42), **palpable purpuric lesions** (F47, F48), and **leukocytoclastic vasculitis on skin biopsy** (F54) constitutes a classic triad that "raises high suspicion for systemic small-vessel vasculitis" (R20). The **elevated acute-phase reactants (CRP 78, ESR 74)** further support acute systemic inflammation consistent with vasculitis (R12). The **development of new palpable purpura during hospital workup** (F46) provides temporal evidence of disease progression, "strongly supporting diagnosis of systemic vasculitis" (R23).

### Pillar 2: ANCA-Negativity Points Away from Classical ANCA-Associated Vasculitis

The **negative c-ANCA, p-ANCA, and anti-AECA serology** (F31, F32, F33) "lower[s] probability of granulomatosis with polyangiitis and ANCA-associated vasculitis" (R9). However, per R8, ANCA-negative serology with leukocytoclastic vasculitis "raise[s] probability of IgA vasculitis, immune complex vasculitis, ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis, or drug-induced vasculitis." The normal renal function (F34) and urinalysis (F35) lower—but do not exclude—pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (R14); importantly, the rulebook notes that "pulmonary-renal vasculitis can present with entirely normal renal indices initially" (R14).

### Pillar 3: Pulmonary Organising Pneumonia as a Manifestation, Not a Competing Diagnosis

The **organizing pneumonia on core-needle lung biopsy** (F56) initially appears as a competing diagnosis. However, R6 indicates that organizing pneumonia "raise[s] likelihood of...systemic disease (hypersensitivity pneumonitis, vasculitis, connective tissue disease)," explicitly positioning OP as a potential manifestation of vasculitis. The **hemoptysis preceding the nodule discovery** and the **palpable purpura appearing simultaneously** argue that OP is a secondary pathologic consequence of the vasculitic process rather than a primary independent disease. The **faint ground-glass rim surrounding nodules** (F41) raises likelihood of "organizing pneumonia or infectious/inflammatory etiology" (R2), consistent with vasculitis-driven OP.

### Addressing Confounders

**The NGS-positive non-tuberculous mycobacterium (F50):** Although F49-F52 document NGS detection of NTM, R15 and R16 establish that a single positive molecular assay without culture confirmation "is insufficient to diagnose NTM pulmonary disease; contamination, colonization, and clinical insignificance must be excluded." The negative cultures (F52) are critical: NTM disease "require[s] at least two positive cultures from separate occasions" (R16). Therefore, the NTM finding raises suspicion for atypical infection but cannot stand as a primary diagnosis given the definitive serology-negative, culture-negative status and the compelling vasculitis picture.

**The normal renal indices:** R14 explicitly addresses this conundrum: "Normal renal function and normal urinalysis...lower[s] probability of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis...however, pulmonary-renal vasculitis can present with entirely normal renal indices initially." This provides a mechanistic pathway to diagnose pulmonary-renal vasculitis despite absent renal involvement to date.

**The negative autoimmune panel:** Negative ANA (F30) "lower[s] probability of systemic lupus erythematosus and other ANA-associated autoimmune diseases but does not exclude systemic vasculitis" (R11). The mildly elevated rheumatoid factor (F29) is "non-specific" (R10) but "raises suspicion for...immune activation in vasculitis" (R10).

**The chronic inflammatory changes on transbronchial biopsy (F58):** R22 notes that "two distinct pathologic findings from separate lung biopsies...suggest sampling variation, patchy distribution of disease, or multiple overlapping pathologic processes." This is consistent with vasculitis affecting lung tissue heterogeneously.

### Ruling Out Major Differentials

**Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA):** GPA diagnosis requires 2 of 4 ACR criteria (R28). The patient has: (1) no documented granulomatous inflammation (lung biopsies show OP and chronic inflammation, not granulomas); (2) abnormal CXR (F38); (3) no renal involvement; (4) no documented oral/nasal inflammation. Additionally, the negative c-ANCA is highly atypical for GPA, which is c-ANCA-positive in ~90% of cases. The absence of granulomas on biopsy lowers GPA probability.

**Sarcoidosis:** While R1 lists sarcoidosis among diagnoses raised by bilateral nodules, R29 requires "non-caseating granulomas on biopsy." Neither lung biopsy documented granulomas. R30 notes elevated serum ACE has high specificity (~99%) when present; no ACE level is documented. Sarcoidosis is less likely than vasculitis given the cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis and absence of granulomas.

**Primary occupational hypersensitivity pneumonitis:** R19 appropriately raises HP consideration given the fisherman occupational history. However, R32 requires characteristic pathology including "non-caseating granulomas" or at minimum "bronchiolitis." The transbronchial biopsy (F57) showed "only chronic inflammatory change" (F58)—a non-specific finding. HP is possible but less parsimonious than vasculitis, which directly explains both the lung and skin pathology.

### The Jaw Lesion as a Diagnostic Wildcard

The **slowly enlarging soft-tissue swelling near the mandibular angle** (F63, F64) is clinically significant. R24 states such a lesion "may represent: metastatic lymphoma, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, vasculitis, TB, fungal), infection, or sinonasal/ENT manifestation of systemic disease." If the biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation consistent with vasculitis, it would strengthen the vasculitis diagnosis and potentially clarify the pathologic mechanism (granulomatous vs. pauci-immune). If it shows lymphoma, the diagnosis would pivot entirely. This biopsy result is pivotal.

### Conclusion on Mechanism

The most parsimonious unifying diagnosis is **ANCA-negative pauci-immune systemic small-vessel vasculitis** with:
- **Pulmonary manifestation:** leukocytoclastic vasculitis affecting pulmonary vasculature → hemoptysis (F11), nodular infiltrates (F39), organizing pneumonia (F56) as a secondary inflammatory consequence
- **Cutaneous manifestation:** small-vessel vasculitis → palpable purpuric leukocytoclastic lesions (F47, F54)
- **Possible ENT/jaw involvement:** swelling near angle of jaw (F63) pending biopsy
- **Laboratory profile:** elevated acute-phase reactants (F27, F28), mild anemia (F26), neutrophilic predominance (F25)—all consistent with active vasculitis
- **Seronegative status:** ANCA-negative pauci-immune type per R8

The organizing pneumonia represents an inflammatory response to vasculitis-induced injury, not a competing diagnosis. The NTM positivity is a molecular artifact (colonizer/contaminant) unconfirmed by culture and clinically insignificant in the context of a clear vasculitic presentation.

### Therapeutic Implications

Per R27, "ANCA-negative pauci-immune vasculitis with pulmonary hemorrhage and hemoptysis has fulminant potential with mortality 25-50% if untreated; rapid immunosuppression is indicated." The patient's hemoptysis (F11), organizing pneumonia (F56), and elevated inflammatory markers (F27, F28) indicate pulmonary involvement requiring urgent induction therapy. R25 specifies that "standard induction immunosuppression for pauci-immune vasculitis consists of corticosteroids (methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisone) combined with intravenous cyclophosphamide; remission rates approximately 80% with this combination." Maintenance therapy with methotrexate or azathioprine (R26) would follow consolidation of remission.

per_case.framework_next_step: Proceed with excisional biopsy of the jaw lesion (already arranged) to determine if it represents granulomatous vasculitis, lymphoma, or another systemic manifestation. Simultaneously initiate induction immunosuppression (corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide) pending jaw biopsy results, given the fulminant potential of untreated pauci-immune vasculitis with pulmonary hemorrhage.

The clinical triad of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, hemoptysis with pulmonary nodules/organizing pneumonia, and elevated acute-phase reactants strongly supports systemic vasculitis. However, confidence is not higher because: (1) the jaw lesion pathology is not yet known and could pivot the diagnosis (e.g., to lymphoma or sarcoidosis); (2) the NTM organism remains unidentified and unconfirmed by culture, leaving a possibility of occult infection; (3) the normal renal function and urinalysis are somewhat atypical for pulmonary-renal vasculitis, though not exclusionary per rulebook.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: the correct diagnosis is metastatic angiosarcoma (a malignancy), confirmed only by excisional biopsy of the submandibular/jaw soft-tissue lesion showing pleomorphic malignant endothelial cells, CD31+/CD34+. The clinical trap is that bilateral lung nodules + hemoptysis + purpura + organizing pneumonia/vasculitis biopsies + high inflammatory markers + negative ANCA mimic ANCA-associated/seronegative vasculitis or infection. Critically, immunosuppression for presumed vasculitis would be HARMFUL.

OUTPUT A — Diagnosis: sarcoidosis. This is incorrect; it is not the angiosarcoma malignancy, and sarcoidosis is not even a strongly supported differential here (no granulomas were found on any biopsy; the actual missed diagnosis is a vascular malignancy). However, A's recommended NEXT ACTION is partially right by luck: it correctly identifies the jaw/submandibular excisional biopsy as the diagnostic keystone and the more accessible site to sample — which is exactly how the real diagnosis was made. It also correctly flags the NTM as a likely non-confirmatory colonizer. But the unifying diagnosis is wrong, and it would proceed to corticosteroids (immunosuppression) on a positive granuloma finding — directionally harmful reasoning for the actual entity. Confidence 65-70% is overconfident for a wrong diagnosis.

OUTPUT B — Diagnosis: ANCA-negative pauci-immune systemic vasculitis. This is the central misdiagnosis the case was designed to trap — the EXACT wrong answer, and worse, B concludes with "urgent induction immunosuppression" (steroids + cyclophosphamide), the disposition that would have harmed the index patient. B never considers malignancy/angiosarcoma at all, which is a significant miss. Its reasoning is extensively traceable to the cited findings/rulebook (F/R tags), well-calibrated to its own internal evidence, and rigorously rules out competing differentials — but it is rigorously wrong about the core question, and its therapeutic recommendation is actively dangerous.

Comparison: Both miss the malignancy entirely (both incorrect on the headline diagnosis). The decisive factors are (1) defensibility/traceability and (2) the value of the recommended next step toward truth. A stumbles onto the correct next action (excisional biopsy of the jaw lesion — the actual route to diagnosis) and correctly handles the NTM red herring, despite a wrong unifying label and an unverifiable, hallucinated sarcoidosis-confirmation pathway (ACE/vitamin D framing). B is far more thoroughly reasoned and traceable, but commits fully to the textbook trap diagnosis AND recommends harmful empiric immunosuppression without securing tissue first; it treats the pivotal jaw biopsy as merely confirmatory rather than recognizing that no diagnosis should be acted on before that histology.

This is close. A is incorrect on diagnosis but its actionable recommendation (biopsy the accessible jaw lesion before treating) is the safer, diagnosis-yielding path and avoids prematurely committing to harmful immunosuppression. B's superior reasoning quality is undermined by landing squarely in the engineered trap and advocating immediate cytotoxic/steroid therapy that would harm the patient. On clinical safety and the practical next step toward the true answer, A edges ahead; on traceability and rigor, B is stronger. Weighing patient-safety disposition heavily (the ground truth explicitly notes immunosuppression would have been harmful), I lean toward A. However, A's headline diagnosis (sarcoidosis) is no closer to angiosarcoma than B's, and A's confidence is poorly calibrated.

On balance I give a narrow edge to B for defensibility and because its hedged emphasis that the jaw biopsy "would pivot the diagnosis entirely" if it shows malignancy/lymphoma at least leaves the door open to the true answer, whereas A confidently asserts a wrong unifying diagnosis with a fabricated confirmation pathway. Both are wrong; B is the better-reasoned, more verifiable response despite the dangerous treatment recommendation, which tips it from a clean win to a marginal one.

per_case.prose:
A 56-year-old woman presented to a community hospital emergency department with three days of dry cough, low-grade fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration. She had a long-standing history of asthma managed with an inhaled corticosteroid, and a remote 14-pack-year smoking history (quit several years earlier). She denied recent travel, sick contacts, occupational dust exposure, or pet ownership.

On arrival she was afebrile to mildly febrile, with oxygen saturation of 93% on room air and decreased breath sounds over the right lower zone. Initial bloodwork showed a white-cell count of 14.6 x 10^9/L, a D-dimer of 720 ng/mL, and an alkaline phosphatase of 168 IU/L. Renal function, transaminases, and a serum eosinophil count were all within normal limits. Sputum and blood cultures were sent.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a right suprahilar soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 6 cm with adjacent peripheral consolidation, together with a separate lower infrahilar mass measuring roughly 9 x 6 cm associated with peripheral atelectasis. There was bulky mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy and a moderate right pleural effusion with features concerning for a malignant process. The radiologic impression favored a primary thoracic malignancy.

Given the appearance, an extensive workup for malignancy was undertaken. CT-guided percutaneous sampling of the masses was performed on more than one occasion, and flexible bronchoscopy with endobronchial and transbronchial biopsies was carried out. Thoracentesis was done and pleural fluid was sent for cytology; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was also examined cytologically. A staging evaluation including CT of the abdomen and pelvis, MRI of the brain, and a whole-body bone scan was completed. Cytology and histology from every sampling site, as well as the pleural and lavage cytology, returned no evidence of carcinoma, lymphoma, or other neoplasm; the staging studies showed no distant disease.

Microbiologic studies, including the cultures and stains sent during the admission, were unrevealing, and there was no clinical or radiographic response to a course of empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. During one of the bronchoscopic procedures, the cell differential of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was notable for 31% eosinophils. A further dedicated parasitic serologic workup was deferred after the peripheral eosinophil count was confirmed to be normal.

Because the masses persisted and remained undiagnosed, repeat CT-guided core biopsy of the right upper-lobe lesion was obtained for definitive histopathology.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP).

HOW CONFIRMED: CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy of the lung mass showed cellular interstitial chronic inflammation with alveolar mucus extravasation, bronchiolitis with prominent eosinophils, and Charcot-Leyden crystals — histology diagnostic of chronic eosinophilic pneumonia. Supporting: bronchoalveolar lavage with markedly elevated eosinophils (28%). Critically, an EXHAUSTIVE malignancy workup was NEGATIVE — multiple CT-guided biopsies, repeat bronchoscopies with biopsies, pleural fluid cytology, BAL cytology, and full metastatic staging (CT abdomen/pelvis, MRI brain, bone scan) all showed NO malignancy — despite imaging that strongly suggested lung cancer/lymphoma (large suprahilar and infrahilar masses ~5 cm and 10x5 cm, extensive mediastinal/hilar adenopathy, malignant-appearing pleural effusion). A misleading feature: peripheral/serum eosinophil count was WITHIN NORMAL LIMITS, which argues against an eosinophilic process and is one reason CEP can be missed; the eosinophilia was compartmentalized to the lung (BAL + tissue).

KEY DISCRIMINATORS the solver should land on: (a) a malignant-looking pulmonary mass/consolidation with adenopathy and effusion that is repeatedly biopsy-negative for cancer; (b) airway/tissue eosinophilia (BAL ~28%, tissue eosinophils + Charcot-Leyden crystals) even with NORMAL blood eosinophils; (c) background of asthma; (d) dramatic response to corticosteroids. The combination of mass-like radiographic disease, negative malignancy workup, tissue eosinophilia with Charcot-Leyden crystals, and steroid responsiveness = chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, NOT lung cancer/lymphoma/infection.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Oral corticosteroids (prednisone taper) with close pulmonary follow-up. Outcome: near-complete radiographic resolution of the mass, consolidation, and pleural effusion at ~7-month follow-up. NO oncologic resection/chemotherapy and NO prolonged antibiotics were warranted. CEP characteristically relapses on steroid withdrawal, so prolonged/tapered steroids and monitoring are appropriate.

SOURCE: Amoda O, et al. "Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia Masquerading as a Lung Mass." Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports, 2022. PMC8744161.

rulebook.rule: BAL eosinophilia ≥25% (this case: 31%) raises the likelihood of eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP or AEP), as BAL eosinophil count is a hallmark diagnostic finding
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia; Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Medicine 2024 (eosinophilic pneumonia overview); AJRCCM 1990 (Diagnostic Significance of Increased Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid Eosinophils)

rulebook.rule: BAL eosinophilia ≥40% is the threshold for chronic eosinophilic pneumonia; this case has 31% eosinophils, slightly below the CEP threshold but consistent with acute forms
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Medicine 2024; PMC7121898

rulebook.rule: BAL eosinophilia >25% in the context of acute febrile illness and respiratory symptoms is diagnostic for acute eosinophilic pneumonia
rulebook.source: AJRCCM 2017 (Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia. Causes, Diagnosis, and Management)

rulebook.rule: Acute febrile illness of <1 month (this case: 3 days) with respiratory symptoms meets the temporal criterion for acute eosinophilic pneumonia
rulebook.source: AJRCCM 2017; European Respiratory Journal 2016

rulebook.rule: Normal serum eosinophil count with elevated BAL eosinophils is consistent with eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP or AEP), where tissue-specific eosinophilia occurs without peripheral blood eosinophilia
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia; Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Medicine 2024; Merck Manual

rulebook.rule: Lung masses with adjacent consolidation and atelectasis can present as CEP masquerading as lung cancer; CEP commonly causes mass-like focal infiltrates
rulebook.source: PMC8744161 (Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia Masquerading as a Lung Mass)

rulebook.rule: Bulky mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy is rare in CEP (~25% of cases) and when prominent, should raise concern for alternative diagnoses; however, CEP with atypical lymphadenopathy is documented and warrants biopsy
rulebook.source: CHEST journal (Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia With Prominent Mediastinal Lymphadenopath: Worth a Biopsy?)

rulebook.rule: Pleural effusion can occur in CEP, though it is less common than in acute forms; its presence is consistent with both CEP and AEP
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia; Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Medicine 2024; AJRCCM references

rulebook.rule: Pleural effusion occurs in 60-100% of acute eosinophilic pneumonia cases, making it a common AEP feature
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Medicine 2024

rulebook.rule: History of asthma is a major predisposing factor for ABPA (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis); patient has long-standing asthma on inhaled corticosteroid
rulebook.source: NCBI Bookshelf (Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis); PMC10130996

rulebook.rule: ABPA can present with mass-like lesions on imaging due to mucus plugging of bronchi and distal secretion accumulation; these masses can mimic lung tumors but are benign in nature
rulebook.source: PMC9208993 (Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis with an Atypical Mass-Like Presentation)

rulebook.rule: Only ~40% of ABPA patients present with eosinophilia, so normal serum eosinophil count does not exclude ABPA; elevated BAL eosinophils support ABPA diagnosis
rulebook.source: PMC10130996; NCBI Bookshelf

rulebook.rule: Negative cultures and stains do not exclude ABPA, as the chance of culturing Aspergillus from tissue is low and diagnosis relies on immunological markers (IgE), not mycological confirmation
ABPA can present with perihilar opacities that mimic hilar lymphadenopathy on imaging, though true lymphadenopathy is possible
EGPA (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) typically begins with adult-onset asthma and rhinosinusitis; this patient has long-standing asthma, consistent with prodromal phase
rulebook.source: NCBI Bookshelf (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis); Nature Reviews Rheumatology 2023

rulebook.rule: EGPA is characterized by peripheral blood eosinophilia >1×10^9 cells/L (or >10% differential); normal serum eosinophils lower the likelihood of EGPA
rulebook.source: Nature Reviews Rheumatology 2023; NCBI Bookshelf

rulebook.rule: EGPA causes eosinophilic infiltrates and masses in lungs during the eosinophilic phase; elevated BAL eosinophils would be consistent with this phase
rulebook.source: Cleveland Clinic; NCBI Bookshelf

rulebook.rule: EGPA diagnosis (ACR-EULAR 2022) gains +5 points for maximum eosinophil count ≥1×10^9 cells/L; normal serum eosinophils significantly reduce diagnostic probability unless other high-scoring criteria (airway disease, biopsy) are present
rulebook.source: Nature Reviews Rheumatology 2023

rulebook.rule: Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with parenchymal nodules or opacities is the classic presentation of pulmonary sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: UpToDate (Clinical manifestations and diagnosis of sarcoidosis); Merck Manual

rulebook.rule: Confluent nodular opacities or large masses are rare in sarcoidosis, but nodular sarcoidosis presents with multiple peripheral masses accompanied by mediastinal lymphadenopathy
rulebook.source: UpToDate

rulebook.rule: Pleural effusion is unusual in sarcoidosis (1-2% prevalence); its presence lowers the likelihood of sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: CHEST journal (Pleural Effusion: An Unusual Complication of Sarcoidosis)

rulebook.rule: Sarcoidosis diagnosis requires biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas; negative histology (as in this case) excludes sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: UpToDate; Multiple sources

rulebook.rule: Elevated alkaline phosphatase in sarcoidosis suggests hepatic granulomatous involvement; ALP elevation is consistent with systemic sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: CHEST journal; Gastroenterology Research

rulebook.rule: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is characterized by BAL lymphocytosis (mean 42.8% in chronic HP), not eosinophilia; elevated BAL eosinophils (31%) argues against HP

rulebook.rule: Mediastinal lymphadenopathy is uncommon in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, thereby distinguishing it from sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases; its presence lowers HP likelihood

rulebook.rule: Negative cytology and histology from multiple sampling sites (CT-guided biopsy, endobronchial biopsy, pleural fluid) definitively excludes malignancy

rulebook.rule: Negative sputum and blood cultures, combined with negative stains and lack of response to broad-spectrum antibiotics, excludes bacterial, fungal (culture-dependent), and mycobacterial infection

rulebook.rule: Elevated D-dimer (720 ng/mL) is nonspecific: seen in pulmonary embolism, malignancy, infection, and inflammatory states including eosinophilic pneumonia; does not discriminate between candidates

rulebook.rule: Patient is on inhaled corticosteroid for asthma; long-term inhaled corticosteroid use could mask peripheral eosinophilia (which is often suppressed by corticosteroids) while allowing tissue-specific BAL eosinophilia to persist

Drug-induced pulmonary eosinophilia with mass-like infiltrates has been documented in asthmatic patients on certain medications (NSAIDs, specific agents); patient's inhaled corticosteroid use is unlikely culprit, but other concurrent medications should be reviewed
