rulebook.rule: FINDING: Acute-onset severe abdominal pain (especially periumbilical or localized to lower quadrant) with minimal peritoneal signs (appearing comfortable at first exam) RAISES mesenteric ischemia. Early mesenteric ischemia is characterized by severe pain disproportionate to physical examination findings, with the abdomen remaining soft and non-rigid initially. As ischemia progresses to transmural necrosis, peritoneal signs develop (guarding, rebound, rigidity).
rulebook.bears_on: Acute mesenteric ischemia (arterial or venous thrombosis)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431068/ (StatPearls Acute Mesenteric Ischemia, clinical presentation)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 612 U/L, reference 120-250) RAISES mesenteric ischemia. LDH elevation is part of the 'Triple L' (Leukocytosis, Lactate, and LDH) constellation that predicts mesenteric ischemia; raised levels of at least two of the three markers are indicators of mesenteric ischemia in more than 80% of cases.
rulebook.source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12262-020-02495-2 (Triple L Predictors of Mesenteric Ischemia, Indian Journal of Surgery)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Normal abdominal ultrasound and CT on first visit, with severe evolving pain on second visit (pain migration and increased CRP), LOWERS initial exclusion of mesenteric ischemia. False-negative early CT occurs because early ischemia (superficial mucosal) produces minimal imaging findings before transmural necrosis develops. Decreased arterial enhancement may be the earliest sign, appearing within 1 hour of arterial occlusion, before traditional CT markers (bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis) become visible. Early non-contrast CT particularly lacks sensitivity for subtle ischemic changes.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute mesenteric ischemia (argues against dismissing based on initial 'normal' imaging)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3807105/ (Imaging of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia in Porcine Model, PMC); https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/370688-overview (Mesenteric Ischemia Imaging, Medscape)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: CRP markedly elevated on second visit (54 mg/L, rising from 0.08 mg/L on first visit, a 675-fold increase over 4 days) RAISES mesenteric ischemia. Inflammatory markers rise with evolution of ischemia and development of tissue necrosis. The lag between initial presentation (low CRP) and second visit (high CRP) reflects the time needed for ischemic tissue to develop transmural necrosis and evoke systemic inflammation.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute mesenteric ischemia (supports progressive ischemic process)
rulebook.source: https://turkjsurg.com/articles/diagnostic-utility-of-inflammatory-ratios-and-nutritional-scores-in-acute-mesenteric-ischemia-a-retrospective-single-center-study/doi/turkjsurg.2025.2025-4-7 (Diagnostic utility of inflammatory ratios in acute mesenteric ischemia)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Serum creatinine elevation (first visit 108, second visit 131 micromol/L, reference 49-90 for women) RAISES mesenteric ischemia with systemic complications. Renal dysfunction in mesenteric ischemia reflects reduced splanchnic perfusion, absorption of bacterial toxins from ischemic bowel, and subsequent septic shock with decreased renal perfusion. Serum creatinine >2 mg/dL is an independent predictor of mortality in acute mesenteric ischemia.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute mesenteric ischemia (with systemic complications and prognostic implications)
rulebook.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1015958414000815 (Length of necrosis and renal insufficiency predict outcome of acute mesenteric ischemia)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Mildly elevated homocysteine (17.1 micromol/L, reference ≤15) RAISES risk of mesenteric thrombosis. Homocysteine at 17.1 falls into the moderate hyperhomocysteinemia range (16-30 micromol/L) and is an independent risk factor for thrombotic disorders, particularly deep vein and arterial thrombosis. Mechanism involves endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, enhanced platelet activation, and elevated coagulation factors creating a prothrombotic state.
rulebook.bears_on: Mesenteric arterial or venous thrombosis (thrombophilia etiology)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554408/ (Hyperhomocysteinemia, StatPearls); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11585337/ (Hyperhomocysteinemia causing vascular occlusion, PMC)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Tobacco exposure (~4 cigarettes/day for 9 years) RAISES risk of mesenteric arterial thrombosis. Smoking induces prothrombotic state through multiple mechanisms: increased fibrinogen, elevated tissue factor activity, decreased tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and abnormal fibrin dynamics with resistance to fibrinolysis. Smoking is a documented risk factor for visceral arterial thrombosis in young women, particularly with concurrent other risk factors.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6053680/ (Smoking Out the Cause of Thrombosis, Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology); https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3375998/ (Intimal hyperplasia and visceral arterial thrombosis in young woman with smoking and oral contraceptives)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Pain migration from left lower quadrant to periumbilical region over 4 days IS CONSISTENT WITH mesenteric ischemia progression. In mesenteric arterial thrombosis, pain typically begins periumbilical (SMA distribution). In venous thrombosis, pain is diffuse and may localize to region of affected bowel (ileojejunal territory). Pain migration reflects progression of ischemia, involvement of additional segments, and evolution toward transmural necrosis and peritonitis.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute mesenteric ischemia (arterial or venous thrombosis)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431068/ (StatPearls Acute Mesenteric Ischemia, clinical presentation); https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459184/ (Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis, StatPearls)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Cessation of stool and flatus passage on second visit (4 days into illness) RAISES mesenteric ischemia with transmural necrosis. Complete failure of bowel transit occurs when ischemia progresses to transmural wall involvement, causing ileus through dysfunction of normal migrating motor complexes. This represents progression from mucosal/submucosal ischemia (initial loose stools) to transmural necrosis (absent bowel function).
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9534705/ (Mesenteric Ischemia and Its Need for Timely Recognition, PMC); https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/002234689390232A (Effects of ischemia and reperfusion on intestinal motility)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Low-grade fever (38.1°C) at first visit RAISES concern for evolving mesenteric ischemia with inflammatory response. Fever reflects systemic inflammatory response to mucosal injury and bacterial translocation from ischemic bowel. The combination of fever with elevated WBC and later marked CRP elevation indicates progressive tissue damage.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431068/ (StatPearls Acute Mesenteric Ischemia, clinical presentation)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Nausea and three loose stools at first visit RAISE early mesenteric ischemia (mucosal stage). GI symptoms in the setting of acute abdominal pain suggest intestinal involvement. Diarrhea reflects mucosal ischemia with impaired absorption and secretory fluid loss. Progression from loose stools to absent bowel function over 4 days marks transition from mucosal to transmural ischemia.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431068/ (StatPearls Acute Mesenteric Ischemia, clinical presentation)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Negative thrombophilia panel (antiphospholipid antibodies, ANA, rheumatoid factor, ANCA all negative) LOWERS risk of primary autoimmune or antiphospholipid-mediated thrombosis but DOES NOT EXCLUDE mesenteric venous thrombosis. Mesenteric venous thrombosis occurs in 60-75% of cases with acquired or inherited hypercoagulable states; negative standard autoimmune markers indicate inherited thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, prothrombin G20210A) or acquired prothrombotic state (smoking, homocysteine, prior VTE) rather than autoimmune etiology.
rulebook.bears_on: Mesenteric venous thrombosis (argues for inherited or acquired thrombophilia rather than autoimmune)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459184/ (Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis, StatPearls)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Normal transthoracic echocardiogram (no intracardiac thrombus, sinus rhythm), normal troponin, normal fasting lipids and glucose LOWERS cardioembolic and primary cardiac ischemic etiologies but DOES NOT EXCLUDE mesenteric arterial thrombosis from non-cardiac sources. Mesenteric ischemia is predominantly caused by thrombosis or embolism secondary to local prothrombotic state (smoking, homocysteine, thrombophilia) or arterial dissection rather than cardiac embolism.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513354/ (Mesenteric Artery Ischemia, StatPearls)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: No evidence of aortic or renal artery dissection on imaging LOWERS arterial dissection as primary etiology but DOES NOT EXCLUDE mesenteric arterial or venous thrombosis. Dissection is one mechanism of mesenteric ischemia but represents minority of cases; thrombotic/embolic occlusion is the predominant mechanism.
rulebook.bears_on: Mesenteric arterial or venous thrombosis (argues for occlusive thrombosis rather than dissection)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431068/ (StatPearls Acute Mesenteric Ischemia, etiology)

rulebook.rule: FINDING: Elevated WBC (14.2 × 10^9/L with 92% neutrophils and left shift on first visit) RAISES acute mesenteric ischemia with tissue necrosis. WBC elevation reflects acute inflammatory response to ischemic injury. Left shift indicates acute bacterial translocation from ischemic bowel mucosa. Normalization of WBC (11.3 × 10^9/L on second visit) with resolution of left shift (70% neutrophils) suggests ongoing systemic response despite worsening clinical course, consistent with progressive transmural necrosis.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Acute superior mesenteric artery (SMA) thrombosis or embolism.

Recommended next action: Urgent CT angiography (or MR angiography) of the abdomen and pelvis to visualize mesenteric vasculature and confirm diagnosis. This is time-critical and should prompt same-day imaging. If positive, immediate vascular surgery consultation.

Confidence: 75-80%. This is a high-risk diagnosis with significant morbidity/mortality if missed.

Reasoning: The clinical triad of (1) pain out of proportion to initial imaging findings, (2) progressive deterioration with rising inflammatory markers (CRP 0.08→54, LDH 612, elevated creatinine) over 4 days, and (3) evolving obstructive pattern (absent flatus/stool) strongly suggest mesenteric ischemia. Early non-contrast CT has limited sensitivity before frank bowel necrosis; pain-imaging discordance is characteristic. Smoking and mildly elevated homocysteine are minor prothrombotic factors. Negative echo and troponin lower embolic risk from cardiac source, but do not exclude thrombosis. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate vascular imaging to prevent bowel necrosis and sepsis.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient presents a classic clinical picture of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) with progressive evolution over 4 days. The diagnosis is supported by convergent evidence across multiple domains:

**Acute Presentation with Pain-Examination Disproportion:**
The patient presented with abrupt, severe left lower abdominal pain (F6) and appeared comfortable on examination (F15) with hemodynamic stability (F16). This disproportionality between severe pain and benign appearance is a cardinal feature of early mesenteric ischemia, in which severe pain reflects mucosal and early submucosal ischemia before peritoneal signs develop (R1-mesenteric-pain).

**Laboratory Trajectory Consistent with Progressive Ischemic Necrosis:**
- The markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 612 U/L, reference 120–250) on the second visit (F35) is part of the "Triple L" constellation (Leukocytosis, Lactate, and LDH) that predicts mesenteric ischemia in >80% of cases (R2-ldh-mesenteric).
- The CRP trajectory is striking: 0.08 mg/L on first visit (F19) rising to 54 mg/L on second visit (F33)—a ~675-fold increase over 4 days (R4-crp-trajectory). This lag reflects the natural history of mesenteric ischemia, in which early mucosal ischemia produces minimal systemic inflammation, but progression to transmural necrosis over 3–5 days triggers marked inflammatory response.
- Serum creatinine rose from 108 to 131 micromol/L (F20, F34), consistent with reduced splanchnic perfusion and secondary systemic complications that predict mortality in AMI (R5-creatinine-elevation).
- WBC elevated initially (14.2 × 10^9/L with 92% neutrophils, F17–F18) reflecting acute response and bacterial translocation; normalization on second visit (11.3 × 10^9/L, F31) despite clinical worsening is consistent with ongoing transmural necrosis (R15-wbc-pattern).

**Early Imaging Falsely Reassuring:**
The benign appearance of abdominal ultrasound and non-contrast CT on the first visit (F24, F25) is explained by the known insensitivity of early imaging to mucosal and early submucosal ischemia (R3-early-imaging-false-negative). Non-contrast CT particularly lacks sensitivity for early ischemic changes; decreased arterial enhancement may be the earliest sign (appearing within 1 hour of occlusion) before bowel wall thickening or pneumatosis becomes visible. The clinical team recognized this imaging-reality gap when "pain disproportionate to benign-appearing initial workup" prompted further imaging (F37).

**Pain Migration and Bowel Dysfunction Reflect Ischemic Progression:**
Pain migration from left lower quadrant (F6) to periumbilical region (F28) over 4 days is consistent with progression of mesenteric ischemia as additional bowel segments become involved (R8-pain-migration). Progression from three loose stools (F9) on first visit to complete absence of stool and flatus passage (F30) on second visit marks transition from mucosal ischemia (with impaired absorption) to transmural necrosis with ileus (R9-bowel-obstruction-ischemia, R11-nausea-diarrhea-ischemia).

**Risk Factors for Thrombotic Mesenteric Ischemia:**
The patient has identifiable prothrombotic factors:
- Cigarette smoking (~4 cigarettes/day for 9 years, F3) creates a documented prothrombotic state that is a risk factor for visceral arterial thrombosis in young women (R7-smoking-thrombosis).
- Mildly elevated homocysteine (17.1 micromol/L, reference ≤15, F36) falls into the moderate hyperhomocysteinemia range and is an independent risk factor for thrombotic disorders via endothelial dysfunction and enhanced platelet activation (R6-homocysteine-thrombotic).

**Negative Workup Does Not Exclude Mesenteric Ischemia:**
- Normal transthoracic echocardiogram, negative troponin, and normal fasting lipids/glucose (F38–F43) rule out cardioembolic and primary cardiac ischemic sources but do not exclude mesenteric arterial or venous thrombosis from non-cardiac etiologies (R13-normal-echo-rules-out-cardioembolic).
- Negative thrombophilia and autoimmune panels (antiphospholipid antibodies, ANA, rheumatoid factor, ANCA; F44–F47) lower risk of autoimmune-mediated thrombosis but redirect suspicion toward inherited thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, prothrombin G20210A) or acquired prothrombotic state (smoking, homocysteine), both of which cause mesenteric venous thrombosis in 60–75% of cases (R12-mvt-negative-autoimmune).
- Negative dissection imaging (F48–F49) argues against dissection but supports occlusive thrombosis as the predominant mechanism (R14-negative-dissection-imaging).

**Clinical Summary:**
The constellation of (1) severe pain disproportionate to initial benign imaging, (2) progressive inflammatory markers (CRP rising 675-fold, LDH markedly elevated), (3) progressive bowel dysfunction, (4) rising creatinine indicating systemic compromise, (5) identifiable prothrombotic risk factors (smoking, homocysteine), and (6) exclusion of cardiac, autoimmune, and dissection etiologies converges on acute mesenteric ischemia as the working diagnosis. The 4-day delay between presentation and clinical deterioration is consistent with the natural history of thrombotic mesenteric ischemia, in which early mucosal ischemia may be clinically and radiologically subtle, but progression to transmural necrosis is accompanied by marked systemic inflammation and organ dysfunction.
per_case.framework_top: Acute mesenteric ischemia (arterial or venous thrombosis), likely with progression from mucosal to transmural necrosis over the 4-day interval
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent CT angiography (CTA) of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to visualize mesenteric arterial and venous patency. If CTA confirms occlusion, immediate vascular surgery consultation for revascularization or resection depending on extent of necrosis. If CTA is equivocal, consider diagnostic laparoscopy or laparotomy given clinical deterioration and imaging-reality gap. Measure baseline lactate and consider repeat lactate trending as prognostic marker. Initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover gram-negative and anaerobic organisms pending culture results.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (approximately 75-80%). The constellation of findings—severe pain disproportionate to benign initial imaging, progressive inflammatory markers, evolving bowel dysfunction, and supported risk factors—is highly consistent with acute mesenteric ischemia. However, confidence is not absolute because: (1) the case lacks direct angiographic confirmation of vascular occlusion, (2) detailed abdominal exam findings at both visits are not documented, and (3) the specific imaging modality used in the follow-up is unspecified, leaving some diagnostic uncertainty.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs reach the WRONG diagnosis: each says acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA thrombosis / AMI), whereas ground truth is idiopathic acute renal infarction (partial right renal artery infarct) confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT. So neither nails the diagnosis. The tiebreaker is calibration, hallucination, and actionability. Output A is appropriately hedged (75-80% confidence), avoids fabricated statistics, and — critically — recommends the CORRECT next action: urgent CT angiography of the abdomen/pelvis. That CTA is essentially the ground-truth diagnostic action (contrast cross-sectional imaging/CTA triggered by pain out of proportion + rising LDH/creatinine) and would have revealed the renal infarct, so A's disposition is right even though its suspected target vessel is wrong. Output B reaches the same wrong diagnosis but is dangerously overconfident ('classic clinical picture', 'convergent evidence', no hedging) and is riddled with likely hallucinated/unverifiable claims ('Triple L predicts MI in >80% of cases', 'MVT in 60-75% of cases', '675-fold increase'). Its elaborate F-tag/R-tag scaffolding gives a false impression of traceability while the underlying assertions are wrong or fabricated. B also never states a concrete next action (no explicit CTA-now or anticoagulation recommendation), only declaring a 'working diagnosis', which is clinically less useful and less defensible. A is therefore the stronger response on calibration, hallucination control, and actionability despite both missing the diagnosis.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old man of mixed European descent was referred to the nephrology service of a regional teaching hospital after the abrupt development of generalized swelling. Roughly five months earlier he had been evaluated at a community cardiology clinic for several weeks of exertional chest tightness with an atypical, non-anginal quality; that workup had not yielded a clear cardiac diagnosis and he had been discharged on as-needed nitrates. He remained reasonably well until about ten days before the current admission, when he noticed puffiness around the eyes on waking and then progressive swelling of both legs. In the days before presentation he also developed nausea, two episodes of vomiting, and vague cramping abdominal pain, which prompted him to seek care.

On arrival he was afebrile and normotensive at 118/76 mmHg. Examination showed periorbital and facial edema and bilateral pitting edema to the mid-shins. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable, and there was no rash, joint swelling, or lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies on admission showed a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL with a blood urea nitrogen of 29 mg/dL and an estimated GFR of approximately 49 mL/min/1.73 m². The serum albumin was low at 1.8 g/dL. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was in the nephrotic range at roughly 10 g/g, and urinalysis showed 3+ protein with oval fat bodies on microscopy; there was no significant hematuria. A standard autoimmune and infectious serologic panel, including complement levels, antinuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and viral hepatitis screening, was unremarkable. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys without obstruction.

During the first days of hospitalization his urine output fell and the serum creatinine climbed, reaching a peak near 2.5 mg/dL before stabilizing. A percutaneous kidney biopsy was performed. On light microscopy, approximately sixteen glomeruli were available for assessment; several showed segmental areas of sclerosis, and the podocytes appeared enlarged with conspicuous cytoplasmic vacuolization and a finely foamy quality. Immunofluorescence showed no significant immune-complex deposition. Ultrastructural examination demonstrated diffuse, widespread effacement of the podocyte foot processes; in addition, the podocyte cytoplasm was packed with numerous dense, concentrically laminated osmiophilic inclusions arranged in stacked, whorled lamellae.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Late-onset Fabry disease (X-linked α-galactosidase A deficiency) presenting with FSGS-pattern nephrotic syndrome. The light-microscopy FSGS read and the rapid nephrotic syndrome were the "common disease" masquerade; the rare underlying diagnosis is Fabry disease.

HOW CONFIRMED (multi-modal, definitive):
- Electron microscopy: abundant lamellar/myelin (zebra) bodies within podocyte cytoplasm plus widespread foot-process effacement (pathognomonic for a glycosphingolipid storage disorder).
- Leukocyte α-galactosidase A enzyme activity markedly low: 1 nmol/h/mg protein (normal 20–80).
- Plasma globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) elevated: 7.4 nmol/L (normal 0.14–0.75).
- Genetic testing: GLA gene M296I missense mutation, a well-described late-onset Fabry variant.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT idiopathic primary FSGS to be managed with immunosuppression alone. Recognize the storage disease on EM, do NOT stop at the FSGS light-microscopy label. Confirm with α-Gal A enzyme assay + lyso-Gb3 + GLA sequencing. Initiate enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase-beta 1 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks). In this case concurrent immunosuppression (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day + cyclosporine 100 mg/day) was used for the superimposed nephrotic-range proteinuria; proteinuria resolved and renal function normalized (creatinine to 0.6 mg/dL, albumin to 4 g/dL, proteinuria 0.15 g/gCr) with sustained remission and no adverse events. Also screen for the cardiac involvement (the antecedent anginal/cardiac presentation) and counsel/screen family given X-linked inheritance.

ORIGINAL (pre-perturbation) FACTS, held aside: 67-year-old Japanese man; admitted Dec 2016 for atypical angina, transferred to Kurume University Hospital; rapid nephrotic syndrome April 2017, leg edema 1 week pre-admission; Cr 1.10 mg/dL rising to peak 2.7, BUN 27.4, albumin 1.63 g/dL, urine protein 11.13 g/gCr, eGFR 52.3; 15 glomeruli, segmental sclerosis + podocyte vacuolization/foamy change on LM.

rulebook.rule: Segmental areas of glomerular sclerosis on light microscopy combined with diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy and negative immunofluorescence raises the diagnosis of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

rulebook.bears_on: Lysosomal storage disease (Fabry disease, other metabolic podocytopathies); differential includes nonspecific lamellar bodies
rulebook.source: https://www.nature.com/articles/3800634; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK6177/

rulebook.rule: Non-branching randomly arranged electron-dense fibrils (8–12 nm diameter) protruding into podocyte cytoplasm and GBM on electron microscopy, combined with Congo red negativity on light microscopy in ~half of cases, raises the diagnosis of renal amyloidosis (AL or ATTR).
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic amyloidosis (AL or ATTR) with renal involvement
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10601942/; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7812497/

rulebook.rule: Prior undiagnosed exertional chest tightness with atypical, non-anginal quality combined with acute nephrotic syndrome raises the possibility of systemic disease linking cardiac and renal manifestations, such as amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, or occult malignancy.
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary multisystem disease (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, paraneoplastic syndrome)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5741539/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6119393/

rulebook.rule: Cardiac amyloidosis presents with exertional chest tightness or chest pain due to angina-like symptoms from amyloid infiltration of small arterioles, and is associated with systemic nephrotic syndrome from concurrent renal involvement.
rulebook.bears_on: Cardiac amyloidosis (AL or ATTR) as manifestation of systemic amyloidosis
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5741539/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5829326/

rulebook.rule: Nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR >3 g/g or urine protein >3.5 g/day) with normal-sized kidneys on ultrasound lowers the likelihood of chronic kidney disease and raises the likelihood of acute glomerulonephritis or podocytopathy.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute glomerulonephritis or acute podocytopathy (versus chronic CKD)
rulebook.source: https://www.ajkd.org/article/S0272-6386(15)00636-8/fulltext

rulebook.rule: Rapidly rising serum creatinine (doubling within days from 1.2 to 2.5 mg/dL) with oliguria in nephrotic syndrome raises the diagnosis of acute kidney injury superimposed on glomerulonephritis.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6681356/; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12230872/

rulebook.rule: BUN:creatinine ratio of ~24:1 (BUN 29, Cr 1.2) is compatible with but not diagnostic of prerenal azotemia; however, the BUN:Cr ratio of >20:1 alone has poor discriminatory accuracy (ROC ~0.5) and cannot reliably distinguish prerenal from intrinsic AKI.
rulebook.bears_on: Prerenal azotemia vs intrinsic acute kidney injury
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5445342/; https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/238545-overview

rulebook.rule: Severe hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin 1.8 g/dL) is associated with 7.37-fold increased risk of progression to end-stage renal disease and portends worse renal prognosis independent of biopsy histology.
rulebook.bears_on: Poor renal prognosis in kidney disease
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10018824/; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6398001/

rulebook.rule: Segmental glomerular sclerosis on biopsy combined with diffuse foot process effacement and normal immunofluorescence raises the diagnosis of primary FSGS; the negative immunofluorescence helps exclude immune-complex glomerulonephritis.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532272/; https://www.emjreviews.com/nephrology/article/focal-segmental-glomerulosclerosis-histopathology-discussion-j120121/

rulebook.rule: Normal blood pressure (118/76 mmHg) at time of AKI and nephrotic syndrome does not exclude prerenal azotemia or volume depletion, as blood pressure can be maintained through compensatory mechanisms.
rulebook.bears_on: Volume status assessment in nephrotic syndrome with AKI
rulebook.source: https://www.osmosis.org/learn/Prerenal_azotemia; https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/238545-overview

rulebook.rule: Absence of hematuria (no RBCs on microscopy) lowers the likelihood of post-infectious glomerulonephritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis, which typically present with active urinary sediment.
rulebook.source: https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneyfsgs.html; https://journals.lww.com/cjasn/fulltext/2017/03000/focal_segmental_glomerulosclerosis.18.aspx

rulebook.rule: Absence of rash, joint swelling, and lymphadenopathy lowers the likelihood of systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases, though lupus serology must still be negative to exclude lupus podocytopathy.
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic connective tissue disease (SLE, vasculitis, rheumatologic disease)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4964690/

rulebook.rule: Nephrotic syndrome with negative autoimmune serology (ANA, ANCA, complement normal) in a patient with abnormal podocytes on EM raises the diagnosis of primary podocytopathy (MCD, FSGS, collapsing GN) over secondary immune-mediated GN.
rulebook.source: https://academic.oup.com/ndt/article/38/Supplement_1/gfad063d_2907/7196121; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4964690/

rulebook.rule: Periorbital and facial edema with bilateral leg swelling onset over ~10 days, combined with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, raises the diagnosis of acute nephrotic syndrome with fluid retention.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12230872/; https://www.ajkd.org/article/S0272-6386(15)00636-8/fulltext

rulebook.rule: Podocyte foot process effacement exceeding 80% of capillary surface area on electron microscopy in primary FSGS is indistinguishable from minimal change disease and requires light microscopy findings of sclerosis to differentiate.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532272/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12683193/

rulebook.rule: Oval fat bodies on urine microscopy indicate lipiduria and support the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome with significant proteinuria and hyperlipidemia.
rulebook.source: https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneyminchange.html; https://www.ajkd.org/article/S0272-6386(15)00634-4/pdf

rulebook.rule: Paraneoplastic nephrotic syndrome can present with FSGS or minimal change disease; membranous nephropathy is more common with solid tumors, while minimal change disease associates with lymphomas.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10148753/; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1609192/full

rulebook.rule: Podocyte hypertrophy and compensatory proliferation ('podocyte proliferation') in collapsed glomeruli raises the diagnosis of collapsing glomerulopathy and suggests podocyte response to loss of neighboring cells.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3008952/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9890309/

rulebook.rule: FSGS with nephrotic proteinuria has 5-year renal survival of 76% and 10-year survival of 57%, indicating unfavorable prognosis; segmental sclerosis is associated with worse outcomes than other histologic variants.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11763650/

rulebook.rule: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (anti-CTLA-4, anti-PD-1) use can induce podocytopathy with collapsing glomerulopathy and acute kidney injury; timing varies (6–12 weeks for anti-CTLA-4, 3–12 months for anti-PD-1).
rulebook.bears_on: Drug-induced collapsing glomerulopathy (immune checkpoint inhibitor nephrotoxicity)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12523462/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10479679/

rulebook.rule: Systemic amyloidosis (AL and ATTR) presents with concurrent cardiac and renal involvement; nephrotic syndrome progresses to CKD in amyloidosis patients, with median time to dialysis 13.8 months and survival <1 year once dialysis initiated.
rulebook.source: https://journals.lww.com/kidney360/fulltext/2024/12000/kidney_disease_in_systemic_amyloidosis__a_review.21.aspx; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9124286/

rulebook.rule: GFR of ~49 mL/min/1.73m² at presentation (Stage 3a CKD) combined with rapid rise to peak creatinine 2.5 mg/dL indicates acute superimposed injury on baseline kidney function rather than chronic disease.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute kidney injury superimposed on baseline kidney function
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6681356/

rulebook.rule: Podocyte injury with foot process effacement occurs in primary podocytopathies and does not typically regenerate; podocyte depletion is irreversible and predicts progression to sclerosis and CKD.
rulebook.bears_on: Poor long-term renal prognosis in podocytopathy
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6589822/

rulebook.rule: Lupus podocytopathy (minimal change or FSGS pattern with negative immune deposits) can occur in SLE patients; it requires negative serology (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM) to differentiate from immune-complex lupus nephritis.
rulebook.bears_on: Lupus podocytopathy vs immune-complex lupus nephritis
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4964690/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), collapsing variant, likely idiopathic though secondary causes must be excluded.

Recommended next action: Obtain detailed medication history and screen for systemic etiologies (HIV, drug use, malignancy). Initiate corticosteroid therapy empirically while investigating. Monitor renal function closely; dialysis support may be needed given rapid decline (Cr 1.2→2.5 mg/dL in days).

Confidence: 85-90%

Reasoning: The pathognomonic electron microscopy finding of concentrically laminated osmiophilic inclusions (myeloid bodies) within vacuolated podocytes, combined with diffuse foot process effacement, negative immunofluorescence (ruling out immune-complex disease), and nephrotic syndrome, is diagnostic of FSGS with podocyte injury. The rapid progression and segmental glomerulosclerosis on light microscopy indicate aggressive disease. Negative serologies make idiopathic FSGS most likely, but secondary causes (medication-related, viral, malignancy-associated) must be excluded before definitive treatment.
per_case.framework_conclusion: The patient presents with acute nephrotic syndrome (UPCR ~10 g/g [F15], albumin 1.8 g/dL [F14], periorbial and facial edema [F6], bilateral leg edema [F7]) complicated by acute kidney injury (serum creatinine doubling from 1.2 to 2.5 mg/dL [F10] with oliguria [F13]). Renal biopsy shows segmental glomerular sclerosis [F21], diffuse podocyte foot process effacement [F24], and negative immunofluorescence [F23], which together satisfy the diagnostic criteria for primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) per R2 and R15. The podocyte vacuolization [F22] and foot process effacement [F24] also raise collapsing glomerulopathy (R4), a FSGS variant. Negative autoimmune serology (ANA, ANCA, complement normal [F18]), absence of hematuria [F17], and absence of rash/arthritis/lymphadenopathy [F9] lower the likelihood of immune-mediated secondary glomerulonephritis (R3, R17, R18) and support primary podocytopathy (R19). The acute presentation with rapid AKI (R12) superimposed on baseline kidney function (GFR 49 at presentation [F12]; R28) indicates acute glomerular injury. The rapid creatinine rise (R12) and the negative immunofluorescence distinguish this from post-infectious or immune-complex disease. Prognosis is poor: severe hypoalbuminemia (1.8 g/dL [F14]; R14) confers 7.37-fold higher ESRD risk; segmental sclerosis (R25) is associated with worse outcomes (5-year renal survival 76%, 10-year 57%); and podocyte foot process effacement is irreversible (R29), predicting progression to CKD. However, the case presents two unresolved features that raise concern for secondary/systemic disease. First, the patient has unidentified podocyte inclusions described as "concentrically laminated osmiophilic stacked whorled lamellae" [F25], which are compatible with myelin-like figures seen in Fabry disease and lysosomal storage disorders (R7), but may also represent amyloid or other inclusions—definitive classification requires immunoelectron microscopy or spectroscopy, not available in the case. Second, the patient's prior undiagnosed exertional chest tightness 5 months earlier [F2] combined with acute nephrotic syndrome raises the possibility of systemic disease linking cardiac and renal involvement (R9), such as amyloidosis, which can present with both cardiac symptoms (R10: angina-like chest tightness from amyloid infiltration) and renal nephrotic syndrome (R27: concurrent cardiac and renal involvement in systemic amyloidosis). Thus, while the biopsy histology unambiguously supports primary FSGS, the combination of unexplained cardiac symptoms and uncharacterized EM inclusions makes amyloidosis and other storage disorders important diagnostic considerations that must be excluded before finalizing the diagnosis and prognosis. Immediate next steps include immunoelectron microscopy/spectroscopy of the inclusions, metabolic screening (serum free light chains, protein electrophoresis, alpha-galactosidase), and cardiac imaging to evaluate for systemic disease.
per_case.framework_top: Primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with acute kidney injury, possibly with collapsing variant; unidentified podocyte inclusions requiring further characterization (amyloidosis or other storage disorder in the differential)
per_case.framework_next_step: Complete immunoelectron microscopy or spectroscopic analysis of the stored podocyte inclusions to rule out specific etiologies (Fabry disease, amyloidosis, other metabolic disorders); obtain metabolic workup including serum free light chains, serum and urine protein electrophoresis, alpha-galactosidase level, and genetic testing if indicated; perform echocardiography and cardiac imaging to characterize the prior undiagnosed exertional chest symptoms and assess for concurrent cardiac amyloidosis or infiltrative disease; initiate immunosuppressive therapy for FSGS while awaiting further diagnostic results
per_case.framework_confidence: High for primary FSGS diagnosis (histology unambiguous: segmental sclerosis + diffuse foot process effacement + negative immunofluorescence); moderate confidence overall due to unidentified inclusions and unexplained cardiac symptoms, both of which raise concern for secondary/systemic disease (amyloidosis rank highest in differential)

per_case.rationale: Ground truth: late-onset Fabry disease masquerading as FSGS-pattern nephrotic syndrome; the load-bearing clue is the EM finding (lamellar/myelin "zebra" bodies in podocytes), which is pathognomonic for a glycosphingolipid storage disorder. Correct disposition: do NOT stop at the FSGS light-microscopy label; confirm with alpha-Gal A enzyme assay + lyso-Gb3 + GLA sequencing; treat with enzyme replacement; screen cardiac and family. Output A recognizes the trap: it flags the EM inclusions as myelin-like figures "compatible with Fabry disease and lysosomal storage disorders," explicitly links the prior cardiac symptoms to systemic disease, names alpha-galactosidase testing and cardiac imaging as next steps, and refuses to finalize a primary-FSGS diagnosis. Its weakness is hedging—overweighting amyloidosis and still calling the histology "unambiguously primary FSGS"—so it does not commit to Fabry, but it surfaces the right diagnosis and the right confirmatory test, and its reasoning is traceable and well-calibrated about uncertainty. Output B commits at 85-90% confidence to "FSGS, collapsing variant, likely idiopathic" and critically misreads the same EM inclusions as "diagnostic of FSGS with podocyte injury"—explaining away the single most important clue—then recommends empiric steroids and an HIV/drug/malignancy screen, missing Fabry entirely. That is the masquerade diagnosis stated with high (mis)calibrated confidence. A is clearly closer to ground truth and better calibrated; B is confidently wrong on the pivotal finding.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old patient, raised and living as a woman, was referred to endocrinology after a CT scan — obtained during recovery from an elective appendectomy — incidentally showed enlargement of both adrenal glands. On the left the gland measured roughly 45 x 31 x 29 mm and on the right roughly 21 x 41 x 24 mm.

Her past history was notable for hypertension first identified in her late twenties, for which she had been taking an angiotensin-receptor blocker together with a calcium-channel blocker for years. At 39 she had suffered a hemorrhagic stroke affecting the right internal capsule, leaving her with a residual left-sided weakness. Outpatient records over the preceding several years repeatedly noted a serum potassium hovering around 3.0 mmol/L, variously attributed to her antihypertensives. She reported menarche around age 13 with regular menstrual periods thereafter and natural cessation of menses at about 50.

On examination she was 167 cm tall and weighed 72 kg (BMI 25.8). Breast tissue was strikingly underdeveloped, axillary and pubic hair were sparse, and her voice was somewhat deep, though she had no facial hair. External genitalia were unambiguously female. Seated blood pressure on her usual medication was 145/80 mmHg.

Initial chemistry showed Na+ 146 mmol/L (135–147), K+ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0), and Cl- 106 mmol/L (98–108). Because of the combination of treatment-resistant hypertension, persistent hypokalemia, and an aldosterone-to-renin ratio that screened positive, the referring team's working assessment was primary aldosteronism, and a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma was suspected on the bulkier adrenal.

A broader hormonal panel was then sent. Plasma renin activity was at the very bottom of the assay (0.1 ng/L/s; 0.1–0.8). The reported aldosterone concentration came back high at 0.91 nmol/L (0.01–0.67). However, several precursor steroids were grossly abnormal: deoxycorticosterone was 5,610 pmol/L (91–997) and corticosterone 296 nmol/L (0.3–24.5). Progesterone was 20.4 nmol/L (0.0–1.9) and pregnenolone 29.1 nmol/L (0.6–4.7). In contrast, 8 a.m. cortisol was low at 84 nmol/L (102–535), with a 24-hour urinary cortisol of 71 nmol/24h (160–1111). ACTH was elevated at 36.0 pmol/L (1.6–14.1).

The sex-steroid axis was also deranged. Testosterone was undetectable (<0.1 nmol/L; female ref 0.4–1.6), androstenedione 0.3 nmol/L (0.9–4.2), and DHEA-sulfate 168 nmol/L (416–4611) — all low. Estradiol was 88 pmol/L. Gonadotropins were elevated: LH 17.9 IU/L and FSH 63.0 IU/L, with a normal prolactin. Twenty-four-hour urinary potassium was 40 mmol/24h despite the low serum value, indicating ongoing renal potassium wasting.

A short ACTH-stimulation test was performed: cortisol rose only trivially (84 to 94 nmol/L) and 17-hydroxyprogesterone barely moved (4.1 to 4.9 nmol/L). Dedicated cross-sectional imaging of the pelvis, reviewed in light of the hormonal pattern, did not demonstrate a uterus or ovaries; instead it showed immature gonadal tissue positioned within the abdomen, prostate-like soft tissue, and an immature urethral structure.
per_case.ground_truth: FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency (17OHD), a form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, in a phenotypically female adult with a 46,XY karyotype (46,XY disorder of sex development). The initial working diagnosis was primary aldosteronism (based on long-standing hypertension, hypokalemia, and an apparently high aldosterone/renin ratio). HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Genetic analysis identified compound heterozygous pathogenic mutations in CYP17A1 (c.157_159delTCC, p.Phe54del; c.1118 A>T, p.His373Leu) — definitive molecular confirmation. (2) Karyotype 46,XY despite female external genitalia. (3) Biochemistry showed the classic 17OHD pattern: markedly elevated deoxycorticosterone (5858 pmol/L; ref 91–997) and corticosterone (308 nmol/L; ref 0.3–24.5), elevated progesterone and pregnenolone, LOW cortisol (80 nmol/L; ref 102–535) with low 24-h urinary cortisol, low androgens (testosterone <0.1 nmol/L, DHEA-S low, androstenedione low), high ACTH (37.1 pmol/L) and high gonadotropins (LH 18.4, FSH 65.6 IU/L). (4) Short Synacthen/ACTH-stimulation test showed blunted cortisol and 17-OHP response, confirming the 17α-hydroxylase enzymatic block. (5) The 'high aldosterone' that suggested primary aldosteronism was an immunoassay artifact — cross-reactivity with the grossly elevated upstream mineralocorticoid precursors (DOC/corticosterone); true aldosterone was normal/suppressed, and the mineralocorticoid excess driving hypertension/hypokalemia was DOC, not aldosterone. (6) Imaging showed bilateral adrenal hyperplasia/enlargement plus immature intra-abdominal testes, prostate-like structures, and absent uterus/ovaries. CORRECT DISPOSITION: Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone ~15 mg/day) to suppress ACTH-driven DOC overproduction — NOT adrenalectomy or a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist for presumed primary aldosteronism. After hydrocortisone, blood pressure and serum potassium normalized off all antihypertensives. Management should also address the 46,XY DSD (counseling, gonadal management given malignancy risk of intra-abdominal testes, sex-steroid/estrogen replacement). KEY TEACHING POINT: low-renin hypertension with hypokalemia is not always primary aldosteronism — a suppressed/normal true aldosterone with low-renin mineralocorticoid hypertension plus hypogonadism/absent secondary sexual characteristics should trigger evaluation for non-aldosterone mineralocorticoid excess (17OHD / 11β-hydroxylase deficiency).

queries.asks: What is the diagnosis? The case presents a 58-year-old with: bilateral adrenal enlargement, striking elevation of DOC, corticosterone, progesterone, and pregnenolone (5-30 fold), suppressed cortisol and ACTH elevation, primary hypokalemia with paradoxical low urinary potassium wasting, treatment-resistant hypertension, external female genitalia, internal immature gonadal tissue, Müllerian agenesis, sparse sexual hair, underdeveloped breasts, elevated gonadotropins, and suppressed sex steroids. What syndrome or diagnosis integrates all these findings?

What is the enzymatic defect in steroid biosynthesis? The combined elevation of pregnenolone, progesterone, deoxycorticosterone, and corticosterone with suppressed cortisol suggests blocked conversion in the cortisol synthesis pathway. Is the defect in 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1), 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1), 17,20-lyase, or another enzyme? What does the minimal response to ACTH stimulation (cortisol 84→94, 17-OHP 4.1→4.9) tell about adrenal reserve and enzyme function?

How do the adrenal pathology and hormonal derangement relate to the disorder of sex development (external female, internal male-associated tissue, Müllerian absence)? The patient had regular menses from age 13 to 50 but with suppressed sex steroids (testosterone undetectable, DHEA-S critically low, androstenedione low). How can adrenal steroid enzyme deficiency explain both the gonadal development anomaly (immature tissue, Müllerian agenesis) and the paradoxical menstrual history?

Why is there a paradox of low serum potassium (3.1 mmol/L) coupled with low 24-hour urinary potassium (40 mmol/24h)? Normally, hypokalemia triggers renal potassium conservation. The low urinary excretion suggests the kidneys are attempting to conserve potassium, yet serum remains depleted. Does this indicate: (a) total body potassium depletion greater than renal wasting can explain, (b) transcellular shift (e.g., from alkalosis, catecholamine effects), (c) ongoing non-renal loss (GI, skin), or (d) altered mineralocorticoid effect on potassium despite the aldosterone-to-renin ratio pattern?

What is the nature of the bilateral adrenal enlargement, and does a single adenoma or hyperplasia explain the full hormone pattern? The initial hypothesis was a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma on the larger (left) gland. However: (a) aldosterone is elevated but DOC and other precursors are disproportionately so, (b) cortisol is low (opposite of expected in aldosterone-producing adenoma), (c) both glands are enlarged (not unilateral), and (d) ACTH is elevated. Does bilateral adrenal hyperplasia from an inherited enzyme deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia or CAH) better explain the imaging and complete hormone profile than adenoma?

rulebook.rule: Grossly elevated deoxycorticosterone (DOC) with mild elevation of corticosterone, alongside suppressed cortisol and elevated ACTH, indicates enzyme defect in cortisol synthesis pathway, specifically 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) or 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1) deficiency

rulebook.rule: Five to thirty-fold elevation of pregnenolone and progesterone suggests 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1) deficiency, which blocks conversion of pregnenolone to 17-OH-pregnenolone and progesterone to 17-OH-progesterone
rulebook.source: NIH StatPearls - 17-Hydroxylase Deficiency - elevated pregnenolone and progesterone accumulate from CYP17A1 deficiency

rulebook.rule: Pattern of elevated DOC with elevated 11-deoxycortisol response to ACTH stimulation is characteristic of 11β-hydroxylase deficiency and distinguishes it from 17α-hydroxylase deficiency
rulebook.source: PMC 7396487 - Clinical and Molecular Analysis - 11-deoxycortisol described as most robust marker for biochemical diagnosis of 11β-hydroxylase CAH

rulebook.rule: Suppressed cortisol with elevated ACTH indicates primary adrenal production failure with intact pituitary feedback, characteristic of CAH enzyme deficiency rather than secondary insufficiency
rulebook.source: Merck Manual Professional Edition - diagnosis of 11β-OH CAH confirmed by marked elevation of substrates (11-deoxycortisol, DOC) and suppressed cortisol with elevated ACTH

rulebook.rule: Serum hypokalemia with paradoxically low 24-hour urinary potassium indicates kidneys are appropriately attempting to conserve potassium, suggesting ongoing mineralocorticoid-driven renal losses exceed conservation capacity
rulebook.source: American Journal of Kidney Diseases 2019 Core Curriculum - physiology of potassium conservation; low urine K+ with low serum K+ indicates appropriate renal response but overwhelmed by mineralocorticoid effect

rulebook.rule: Elevated serum sodium with borderline-high chloride in setting of DOC excess indicates mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium retention and loss of potassium via mineralocorticoid effect
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect Topics - DOC as mineralocorticoid receptor agonist with salt-retaining properties; causes hypokalemia, alkalosis, and hypertension via mineralocorticoid excess

rulebook.rule: Deoxycorticosterone excess has well-characterized mineralocorticoid agonist activity, causing hypertension and hypokalemia through mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated sodium retention and potassium wasting

rulebook.rule: Chronic hypertension onset in late twenties with resistant hypertension, combined with early hypokalemia noted over years, fits natural history of slowly progressive 11β-hydroxylase deficiency presenting in adulthood as mineralocorticoid excess syndrome

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, CAH type 2).

The pathognomonic findings are: primary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol, high ACTH, poor ACTH response), massive precursor accumulation especially deoxycorticosterone (5,610 pmol/L — 56× normal) and corticosterone (296 nmol/L — 12× normal) with low downstream sex steroids, hypokalemia-resistant hypertension from mineralocorticoid excess (deoxycorticosterone has weak MRA activity), and bilateral adrenal enlargement from compensatory ACTH stimulation. The pelvic imaging showing a 46,XY individual with female external genitalia but no uterus/ovaries, elevated gonadotropins, and virilization-resistant features (sparse hair, underdeveloped breasts) is consistent with 46,XY sex development.

Recommended next action: Initiate hydrocortisone or equivalent glucocorticoid replacement immediately to suppress ACTH and halt further adrenal hyperplasia and precursor accumulation. This will improve mineralocorticoid-induced hypokalemia and hypertension. Confirm diagnosis with CYP11B1 genetic testing and specialist endocrine/genetic counseling regarding sex development. Recheck potassium and blood pressure within days/weeks of glucocorticoid initiation. Consider whether prior hemorrhagic stroke at age 39 was precipitated by uncontrolled hypertension from decades of mineralocorticoid excess.

Confidence: 90%. The hormonal pattern is nearly specific for 11β-hydroxylase deficiency given the precursor stoichiometry and ACTH response profile. Main caveats are rare acquired enzyme defects or unusual variants, but lifelong CAH is far more likely.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 58-year-old patient presents with a steroid biosynthesis defect most consistent with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency CAH, superimposed on a complex disorder of sex development.

**Steroid Biochemistry — 11β-Hydroxylase Deficiency:**

The cardinal hormonal finding is grossly elevated deoxycorticosterone (DOC 5,610 pmol/L, 5.6-fold above upper limit [R1]) with elevated corticosterone (296 nmol/L, 12-fold elevation [R22]), combined with suppressed cortisol (84 nmol/L, below normal [F32]) and elevated ACTH (36.0 pmol/L [F34]). This pattern is pathognomonic for 11β-hydroxylase deficiency: the enzyme CYP11B1 catalyzes the final hydroxylation step converting 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. When deficient, substrates accumulate proximal to the block while products (cortisol) are depleted, triggering compensatory ACTH elevation. The markedly suppressed cortisol with elevated ACTH establishes primary adrenal insufficiency at the site of enzyme defect rather than secondary insufficiency [R4]. The minimal response to ACTH stimulation (cortisol rose only 10 nmol/L from baseline of 84 to 94 [F43]; 17-hydroxyprogesterone barely moved from 4.1 to 4.9 [F44]) indicates severely impaired adrenal steroid production capacity [R5], confirming end-organ enzyme deficiency rather than pituitary insufficiency.

Elevated pregnenolone (29.1 nmol/L, 6-fold above upper limit) and progesterone (20.4 nmol/L, 10-fold elevation [F30]) reflect accumulation of early pathway precursors upstream of the 11β-hydroxylase block [R1]. The minimal 17-hydroxyprogesterone response to ACTH (unlike the marked elevation expected in 21-hydroxylase deficiency) argues against 21-OH CAH and supports 11β-OH CAH or 17α-hydroxylase deficiency [R23].

**Mineralocorticoid Excess Syndrome:**

The DOC excess (5,610 pmol/L) has potent mineralocorticoid agonist activity at the mineralocorticoid receptor [R8], explaining the patient's clinical pentad: (1) treatment-resistant hypertension (145/80 mmHg on ARB+CCB for years [F21, F7]), (2) chronic hypokalemia (K+ 3.1 mmol/L [F23]; serum K+ documented as hovering around 3.0 for years [F9]), (3) borderline hypernatremia (Na+ 146 mmol/L [F22]), (4) suppressed plasma renin at assay floor (0.1 ng/L/s [F26]), and (5) paradoxical low 24-hour urinary potassium (40 mmol/24h [F42]) indicating intact renal potassium conservation mechanisms overwhelmed by mineralocorticoid-driven sodium repletion and potassium losses [R6, R7]. The low urinary potassium despite serum depletion indicates the kidneys are appropriately attempting to conserve potassium but cannot overcome the mineralocorticoid effect [R6].

**Natural History:**

The documented onset of hypertension in the patient's late twenties [F6] with progressive hypokalemia over years [F9] fits the natural history of slowly progressive adult-onset 11β-hydroxylase deficiency [R9]. The hemorrhagic stroke at age 39 with residual left-sided weakness [F8] is consistent with vascular complications from longstanding mineralocorticoid hypertension and chronic hypokalemia, which increase arrhythmia and stroke risk [R10].

**Imaging and Adrenal Pathology:**

Bilateral adrenal enlargement (left 45×31×29 mm [F4]; right 21×41×24 mm [F5]) indicates bilateral hyperplasia rather than unilateral adenoma [R11]. This bilateral pattern, combined with suppressed cortisol and elevated ACTH driving compensatory adrenal growth, is characteristic of CAH enzyme deficiency [R11]. The initial hypothesis of a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma on the bulkier left gland [F25] is inconsistent with the full hormone profile: typical aldosterone adenomas do not cause such severe DOC elevation, suppressed cortisol, or bilateral gland enlargement [R21].

**Gonadal and Sexual Development Anomaly:**

The patient's reproductive phenotype is complex and suggests a comorbid disorder of sex development. She was raised and living as a woman [F2] with external genitalia unambiguously female [F20], menarche at 13 [F10], regular menstrual periods thereafter [F11], and natural menopause at age 50 [F12]. However, physical exam revealed strikingly underdeveloped breast tissue [F16], sparse axillary and pubic hair [F17], no facial hair [F19], and a somewhat deep voice [F18]. Hormone levels show undetectable testosterone (<0.1 nmol/L [F35]), markedly suppressed DHEA-sulfate (168 nmol/L, critically low at 4% of lower reference limit [F37]), and low androstenedione (0.3 nmol/L [F36]). Gonadotropins are elevated (LH 17.9, FSH 63.0 IU/L [F39, F40]), indicating a hypergonadotropic hypogonadism pattern of primary gonadal insufficiency [R15, R24].

Pelvic imaging is striking: absence of uterus and ovaries [F45] with immature intra-abdominal gonadal tissue [F46], prostate-like soft tissue [F47], and an immature urethral structure [F48]. This constellation—female external genitalia with absent Müllerian structures, immature gonadal tissue, and prostate-like tissue—indicates a complex disorder of sex development inconsistent with typical 11β-hydroxylase deficiency alone [R18, R19].

The sparse secondary sexual characteristics despite elevated gonadotropins, combined with low sex steroids, suggests either intrinsic gonadal androgen production failure or androgen insensitivity [R17]. The paradoxical history of regular menses until age 50 despite profoundly suppressed sex steroids implies either residual ovarian stroma capable of menstrual cycling or adrenal androgen conversion to estrone in peripheral tissues, maintained in compensatory fashion by the chronically elevated androgen precursors (though circulating androgens are now suppressed) [R20].

**Synthesis:**

The data most strongly support **11β-hydroxylase deficiency CAH as the primary endocrine diagnosis**, explaining: (1) the pathognomonic steroid pattern (DOC and corticosterone elevation with cortisol suppression and ACTH elevation), (2) bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, (3) mineralocorticoid excess syndrome with hypertension, hypokalemia, and suppressed renin, and (4) the natural history of progressive hypertension and hypokalemia from the patient's twenties onward [R26].

However, the **gonadal dysgenesis is not explained by 11β-hydroxylase deficiency alone**. The absence of Müllerian structures (uterus, ovaries), presence of immature gonadal tissue with prostate-like differentiation, and paradoxical menstrual history despite suppressed sex steroids suggest a **comorbid or overlapping disorder of sex development**—potentially mixed gonadal dysgenesis, 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis with anomalous internal differentiation, or another genetic/developmental basis [R18].

The undetectable testosterone and critically suppressed DHEA-sulfate [F35, F37] could represent either: (a) suppression secondary to chronic adrenal enzyme deficiency with impaired C19 steroid synthesis, or (b) primary gonadal/adrenal androgen deficiency contributing to the DSD phenotype. The diagnosis cannot be completed without karyotype analysis to establish genetic sex, and imaging/histology to characterize the gonadal tissue phenotype.

**Key Citations:**
- Steroid pattern and bilateral hyperplasia diagnostic of 11β-hydroxylase CAH: R26, R4, R5, R22
- DOC mineralocorticoid excess explaining hypertension, hypokalemia, renin suppression: R8, R7, R12
- Natural history of adult-onset presentation: R9
- Vascular complications from hypertension and hypokalemia: R10
- Bilateral hyperplasia vs. adenoma: R11, R21
- Gonadal dysgenesis phenotype: R18, R19, R24
- Low androgens with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism): R15, R24

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs land on the WRONG enzyme: they diagnose 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP11B1), whereas the confirmed diagnosis is 17α-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP17A1). This is a substantive error in both — and notably, the biochemistry actually points away from 11β-OHD. In 11β-OHD, 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) accumulate, androgens are typically HIGH (causing virilization), and the 46,XY DSD with absent androgen effect, low testosterone/DHEA-S, and elevated progesterone/pregnenolone is the hallmark of 17OHD, not 11β-OHD. The classic 17OHD pattern (low androgens + hypogonadism + DOC/corticosterone-driven mineralocorticoid hypertension + cortisol block) is precisely what the case shows. So both A and B chose an enzyme deficiency inconsistent with the low-androgen, hypogonadal phenotype.

CORRECTNESS OF SHARED CORE: Both correctly identify (a) it is a CAH/steroidogenic enzyme block, (b) primary adrenal-level cortisol deficiency with high ACTH, (c) DOC-driven mineralocorticoid excess (not true aldosterone) causing the hypertension/hypokalemia, (d) bilateral adrenal hyperplasia rather than an aldosterone-producing adenoma, (e) the correct disposition: glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) replacement to suppress ACTH/DOC — NOT adrenalectomy or an MRA. These are the highest-value clinical conclusions and both got them right. Crucially, both correctly rejected the initial primary-aldosteronism working diagnosis and explained the mineralocorticoid-excess mechanism via DOC — the central teaching point of the case.

WHERE B WINS: (1) B explicitly entertains 17α-hydroxylase deficiency in its differential ("supports 11β-OH CAH or 17α-hydroxylase deficiency"), and the minimal 17-OHP response it cites is in fact more consistent with 17OHD — so B is nearer the truth and shows the correct reasoning even though it commits to the wrong primary label. (2) B repeatedly flags that the gonadal/DSD picture is NOT explained by 11β-OHD alone and that karyotype is needed — this is well-calibrated humility that correctly senses the model is incomplete. (3) B grounds nearly every claim in traceable findings/rules ([F##]/[R##]), making the reasoning auditable and far more defensible. (4) B correctly characterizes the hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, the immature intra-abdominal gonads/prostate-like tissue, absent Müllerian structures, and recommends karyotype — capturing the DSD dimension the ground truth emphasizes.

WHERE A IS WEAKER: A is confidently wrong — 90% confidence on 11β-OHD, calling the pattern "nearly specific" and "pathognomonic," and recommending CYP11B1 testing (would return negative). A does note the 46,XY DSD and gives the correct hydrocortisone disposition, which is valuable, but it shows no awareness that the androgen-low phenotype conflicts with 11β-OHD and offers no traceability. A's overconfidence on an incorrect molecular target is a calibration failure.

NET: Both are partially correct — right mechanism class, right red-herring rejection, right treatment, wrong specific enzyme. B is the better answer because it surfaces 17OHD in its reasoning, expresses appropriate uncertainty about the DSD, recommends the karyotype that would have cracked the case, and is fully traceable. A is more confidently wrong with less hedging and less defensible reasoning.

per_case.prose:
A 49-year-old woman was referred to the medical service after two emergency presentations within a fortnight. For roughly the preceding year and a half she had been vomiting two to three times most weeks, and over the last twelve months she had lost about 12 kg without trying. She was emphatic that she was not attempting to lose weight and had no concerns about her body shape; she explained that she simply could not bring herself to eat, blaming profound tiredness and a difficult stretch at home and at work. An earlier admission about ten days before, prompted by the persistent vomiting, had included upper GI endoscopy and abdominal imaging, all of which were unremarkable.

On account of the weight loss, food refusal, and psychosocial stressors, the admitting team raised the possibility of an eating disorder and arranged a psychiatric opinion, with a plan to consider transfer to a psychiatric unit once she was medically stable. The consulting psychiatrist, however, concluded that she met criteria for neither anorexia nervosa nor bulimia nervosa.

Background history was notable for autoimmune hypothyroidism on stable thyroid hormone replacement, plus a chronic seronegative inflammatory back condition followed by rheumatology and a myeloproliferative blood disorder.

On examination she appeared fatigued and thin, with a current weight of 52 kg and a body mass index of about 18.5 kg/m2. Blood pressure was 92/58 mmHg and heart rate 108 beats per minute. Mucocutaneous and skin-crease darkening was noted.

Initial bloodwork showed sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 6.1 mEq/L, magnesium 1.31 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.52 mg/dL. Targeted serological testing was sent.

She was started on parenteral corticosteroid therapy, with a striking response: the vomiting and exhaustion resolved over the following days and her biochemistry corrected, with sodium rising to 136 mEq/L, potassium falling to 4.1 mEq/L, magnesium to 1.8 mg/dL, and creatinine to 0.9 mg/dL. By later follow-up her appetite had returned, she had regained weight to roughly 64 kg (BMI about 23), and she expressed no distress about the weight gain. She was discharged from psychiatric care and is maintained on long-term replacement therapy under endocrinology.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) due to autoimmune adrenalitis. Confirmation: positive anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies (serology) establishing autoimmune adrenalitis, together with a dramatic clinical and biochemical response to glucocorticoid replacement (electrolytes normalized, vomiting/asthenia resolved, weight regained). The combination of chronic weight loss with recurrent vomiting and fatigue, hyponatremia + hyperkalemia, hypotension with relative tachycardia, skin hyperpigmentation, and coexisting autoimmune hypothyroidism (autoimmune polyglandular background) is the classic constellation. Correct disposition: this is NOT an eating disorder — it is a life-threatening (incipient adrenal crisis) endocrine emergency. Correct management is urgent stress-dose glucocorticoid (e.g., hydrocortisone), volume/electrolyte correction, and lifelong glucocorticoid (and mineralocorticoid) replacement with endocrinology follow-up; psychiatric admission/refeeding for a presumed eating disorder would be harmful and delay treatment. In the source case the patient had been initially worked up for and nearly admitted as a suspected eating disorder; psychiatry concluded she met criteria for neither anorexia nervosa nor bulimia. Original surface details (held aside, not shown to arms): 56-year-old woman; Na 127 mEq/L, K 6.3 mEq/L, Mg 1.23 mg/dL, Cr 1.65 mg/dL, BP 95/54, HR 113, weight 50 kg / BMI 18; 10 kg loss over a year, vomiting 2-3x/week for ~18 months; comorbid hypothyroidism, HLA-B27-negative sacroiliitis, JAK2-positive polycythemia; post-treatment Na 135, K 4.2, Mg 1.7, Cr 1.0, weight 65 kg / BMI 23.6.
