ir.inferred_domain: Clinical endocrinology (adrenal insufficiency / Addison's disease), with secondary elements of diagnostic reasoning in psychiatry, acute electrolyte and renal physiology, and autoimmune disease clustering.

rulebook.rule: Mucocutaneous and skin-crease hyperpigmentation raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). Hyperpigmentation occurs due to elevated ACTH levels that stimulate melanocyte activity. This sign is absent in eating disorders.
rulebook.source: StatPearls - Addison Disease (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK568775/

rulebook.rule: Hyponatremia (sodium 129 mEq/L) raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Hyponatremia is the most common initial laboratory finding in Addison's disease, resulting from aldosterone deficiency (causing renal sodium loss) and water retention (increased ADH release). Eating disorders do not typically present with this specific electrolyte pattern.
rulebook.source: Addison Disease - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441994/

rulebook.rule: Hyperkalemia (potassium 6.1 mEq/L) raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Loss of aldosterone activity leads to natriuresis and potassium retention, causing life-threatening hyperkalemia. This electrolyte pattern is specific to mineralocorticoid deficiency, not eating disorders.
rulebook.source: Addison Disease - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441994/

rulebook.rule: Hypotension (92/58 mmHg) with compensatory tachycardia (108 bpm) raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Mineralocorticoid deficiency causes urinary sodium and water loss leading to severe dehydration, plasma hypertonicity, decreased circulating volume, and hypotension. The body compensates with tachycardia. Eating disorders typically cause bradycardia, not tachycardia.
rulebook.source: Adrenal insufficiency recognition and management - ScienceDirect. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1470211824019328/

rulebook.rule: Acute kidney injury pattern (elevated creatinine 1.52 mg/dL) in the context of hyponatremia and hyperkalemia raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Mineralocorticoid deficiency-induced intravascular volume depletion leads to decreased renal perfusion and reduced glomerular filtration rate, explaining how adrenal insufficiency produces acute kidney injury.
rulebook.source: Addison's disease presenting with acute kidney injury - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4952420/

rulebook.rule: Weight loss and anorexia (patient unable to eat due to fatigue, not intentional food restriction) without body image disturbance or intentional dieting raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal insufficiency causes anorexia through elevated GDF15 (a stress-induced hormone activating neural circuits for aversive feeding responses), leading to nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Patients with adrenal insufficiency do not report intentional weight loss or body image concerns.
rulebook.source: GDF15 is elevated in conditions of glucocorticoid deficiency - PMC. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7105349/

rulebook.rule: Profound fatigue as the attributed mechanism for food refusal raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. In individuals with marginal adrenocortical production, acute psychosocial or physical stress can increase cortisol requirements beyond adrenocortical capacity, leading to fatigue, weakness, depression, anorexia, and weight loss.
rulebook.source: Atypical Presentation of Adrenocortical Insufficiency with Anorexia - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6042472/

rulebook.rule: Recurrent vomiting (two to three times most weeks, leading to multiple emergency presentations within a fortnight) raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Gastrointestinal illness is the biggest trigger for adrenal crisis; vomiting causes further volume depletion and electrolyte abnormalities that can precipitate acute adrenal crisis.
rulebook.source: Adrenal Crisis - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499968/

rulebook.rule: Acute exacerbation of symptoms (multiple emergency presentations within a fortnight) following psychosocial stressors ('difficult stretch at home and at work') raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency. Physical or psychosocial stress can increase cortisol requirements beyond the capacity of failing adrenal glands, precipitating acute crisis with vomiting, hypotension, and electrolyte derangement.
rulebook.source: Adrenal Crisis - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499968/

rulebook.rule: Dramatic clinical response to parenteral corticosteroid therapy (vomiting and exhaustion resolved over following days, appetite returned, weight recovered to 64 kg, electrolytes normalized, creatinine normalized) strongly confirms primary adrenal insufficiency and excludes eating disorder. This response is pathognomonic for glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency correction.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency - PubMed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26760044/

rulebook.rule: Psychiatric evaluation explicitly concluding that the patient met criteria for neither anorexia nervosa nor bulimia nervosa lowers the likelihood of primary eating disorder diagnosis. While this initially was viewed as evidence against eating disorder, it does not exclude other organic causes. The combination of specific physical findings (hyperpigmentation, hypotension with tachycardia, electrolyte derangements) should prompt investigation for organic disease despite psychiatric clearance.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

rulebook.rule: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation is a distinguishing physical examination finding that excludes eating disorder and raises suspicion for primary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperpigmentation due to ACTH elevation does not occur in eating disorders; its presence warrants investigation for endocrine pathology.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

rulebook.rule: Tachycardia (heart rate 108 bpm) in the presence of weight loss excludes eating disorder and raises suspicion for primary adrenal insufficiency. Anorexia nervosa typically presents with bradycardia due to reduced metabolic demands and parasympathetic dominance. Tachycardia with hypotension suggests acute hemodynamic decompensation from adrenal insufficiency.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

rulebook.rule: The specific pattern of hyponatremia and hyperkalemia excludes eating disorder and strongly raises suspicion for primary adrenal insufficiency. Eating disorders present with different electrolyte patterns (typically metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia from purging). Simultaneous hyponatremia and hyperkalemia indicate mineralocorticoid deficiency.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

rulebook.rule: Patient's psychological acceptance of weight gain (expressed no distress about weight recovery to BMI 23) excludes eating disorder. In eating disorders (especially anorexia nervosa), significant weight gain typically provokes severe psychological distress, anxiety, or dysphoria. The absence of such distress following weight recovery indicates the weight loss was not psychologically driven.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

rulebook.rule: Background history of autoimmune hypothyroidism raises the likelihood of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS-2) if primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed. Hypothyroidism and Addison's disease frequently cluster as part of Schmidt's syndrome (APS-2), reflecting shared autoimmune etiology targeting multiple endocrine organs.
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes - Endotext (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279152/

rulebook.rule: Background chronic seronegative inflammatory back condition raises the likelihood of underlying autoimmune systemic disease. Seronegative inflammatory arthropathies can coexist with autoimmune endocrinopathies including Addison's disease, particularly in the context of APS. This finding supports investigation for autoimmune polyendocrine involvement.
rulebook.bears_on: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome / primary adrenal insufficiency
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes - ScienceDirect. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/autoimmune-polyendocrine-syndrome

rulebook.rule: Low baseline cortisol with elevated ACTH is diagnostic of primary adrenal insufficiency. The combination of low cortisol and inappropriately elevated ACTH (reflecting the pituitary's compensatory response to insufficient cortisol) is pathognomonic for primary adrenal failure and distinguishes it from secondary adrenal insufficiency.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4880116/

rulebook.rule: Blunted or absent cortisol response to cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation testing is diagnostic of primary adrenal insufficiency. The short corticotropin test (250 μg) is the gold standard diagnostic tool; a flat response (failure of cortisol to rise appropriately) confirms adrenal dysfunction requiring replacement therapy.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency - PubMed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26760044/

rulebook.rule: Positive autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase confirms autoimmune etiology of primary adrenal insufficiency and identifies Addison's disease (as opposed to infectious, infiltrative, or drug-induced adrenal insufficiency). This serological finding supports the diagnosis of autoimmune polyendocrine involvement.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary adrenal insufficiency / Addison's disease (autoimmune etiology)
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency - PubMed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26760044/

rulebook.rule: Rapid normalization of electrolytes (sodium rising to 136 mEq/L, potassium falling to 4.1 mEq/L, magnesium to 1.8 mg/dL) and renal function (creatinine to 0.9 mg/dL) following corticosteroid therapy confirms the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency and demonstrates correction of the underlying mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and management of adrenal insufficiency - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11046533/

rulebook.rule: Background myeloproliferative blood disorder (type unspecified) may have uncertain relationship to acute presentation. While some myeloproliferative neoplasms can rarely cause secondary adrenal involvement through infiltration, the acute presentation with characteristic adrenal insufficiency signs, dramatic response to corticosteroids, and evidence of autoimmune etiology suggests the primary disorder is autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, not a paraneoplastic phenomenon.
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes - Endotext (NCBI Bookshelf). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279152/

rulebook.rule: The initial clinical consideration of eating disorder is understandable given weight loss, food refusal, and psychosocial stressors, but should have been rapidly excluded by specific physical findings (hyperpigmentation, hypotension with tachycardia, characteristic electrolyte pattern). Adrenal insufficiency is documented in nine published case reports of misdiagnosis as eating disorder, highlighting the importance of careful consideration of organic etiology in anorexia-like presentations.
rulebook.source: Anorexia nervosa: a mistaken diagnosis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4823564/

per_case.blind_answer: Most likely diagnosis: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The clinical triad of hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation is pathognomonic. Symptoms (anorexia, vomiting, weight loss, fatigue, hypotension, tachycardia) are classic for cortisol deficiency. Psychiatric exclusion and dramatic corticosteroid response confirm diagnosis. Recommended next action: Confirm with ACTH stimulation test or paired morning cortisol/ACTH if not already performed; initiate lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement; screen for additional autoimmune endocrinopathies (given pre-existing autoimmune thyroiditis). Confidence: 95%. Reasoning: Case exemplifies autoimmune Addison's masquerading as eating disorder—the food refusal and weight loss are metabolic consequences, not psychological drive. Recognition of hyperpigmentation and electrolyte pattern is diagnostic.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 49-year-old woman has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), most likely of autoimmune etiology.

CLINICAL REASONING:

The diagnosis is supported by the presence of multiple specific findings that raise adrenal insufficiency and exclude eating disorder:

Physical Examination Findings:
Mucocutaneous and skin-crease hyperpigmentation (physical_exam_4) raises the likelihood of primary adrenal insufficiency due to elevated ACTH stimulating melanocyte activity [rule_1]. This finding is absent in eating disorders and is a distinguishing physical sign [rule_12]. Hypotension (92/58 mmHg) with compensatory tachycardia (108 bpm) (vital_1, vital_2) raises adrenal insufficiency [rule_4]. In contrast, eating disorders typically present with bradycardia, not tachycardia, making this pattern specific to adrenal crisis [rule_13]. The patient's fatigued and thin appearance (physical_exam_1) with low-normal BMI of 18.5 (physical_exam_3) does not suggest severe malnutrition.

Biochemical Profile:
Hyponatremia (sodium 129 mEq/L) (lab_1) is the most common initial laboratory finding in Addison's disease, resulting from aldosterone deficiency [rule_2]. Hyperkalemia (potassium 6.1 mEq/L) (lab_2) results from loss of aldosterone activity causing potassium retention—this electrolyte pattern is specific to mineralocorticoid deficiency, not eating disorders [rule_3]. The simultaneous hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (lab_1, lab_2) form a distinctive pattern that excludes eating disorder, which typically presents with different electrolyte abnormalities [rule_14]. Elevated creatinine (1.52 mg/dL) (lab_4) in the context of hyponatremia and hyperkalemia represents acute kidney injury secondary to intravascular volume depletion from mineralocorticoid deficiency [rule_5]. Hypomagnesemia (1.31 mg/dL) (lab_3) further supports electrolyte derangement consistent with adrenal insufficiency.

Clinical Presentation and Symptomatology:
Weight loss (12 kg over 12 months) (symptom_4) combined with anorexia attributed to profound fatigue (symptom_7), not intentional restriction, raises adrenal insufficiency [rule_6]. The patient explicitly denied intentional weight loss (symptom_5) and body image disturbance (symptom_6), which excludes eating disorder and supports organic etiology. The mechanism of fatigue as the attributed cause of food refusal (symptom_7) raises adrenal insufficiency, where marginal adrenocortical production becomes insufficient under psychosocial stress [rule_7]. Recurrent vomiting (two to three times most weeks) (symptom_2) precipitating emergency presentations within a fortnight (admission_1) is characteristic of adrenal insufficiency, as gastrointestinal illness is the biggest trigger for adrenal crisis [rule_8]. The recent exacerbation following psychosocial stressors (symptom_8) aligns with the mechanism that stress increases cortisol requirements beyond failing adrenal capacity [rule_9].

Exclusion of Eating Disorder:
Despite initial clinical consideration of eating disorder (differential_1), psychiatric evaluation explicitly concluded the patient met criteria for neither anorexia nervosa nor bulimia nervosa (psychiatric_consultation_2) [rule_11]. However, the combination of specific physical findings (hyperpigmentation, hypotension with tachycardia, characteristic electrolyte pattern) should have prompted investigation for organic disease [rule_11]. Most definitively, the patient's psychological acceptance of weight recovery without distress (psychological_1) excludes eating disorder, as significant weight gain in anorexia nervosa typically provokes severe psychological distress [rule_15].

Diagnostic Confirmation:
The striking response to parenteral corticosteroid therapy (treatment_1, treatment_response_1) is pathognomonic for adrenal insufficiency [rule_10]. Vomiting and exhaustion resolved over the following days (treatment_response_2), appetite returned (symptom_resolution_1), and weight recovered to 64 kg (weight_gain_1) with BMI normalized to approximately 23. Biochemical correction was complete: sodium rose to 136 mEq/L (lab_5), potassium fell to 4.1 mEq/L (lab_6), magnesium normalized to 1.8 mg/dL (lab_7), and creatinine normalized to 0.9 mg/dL (lab_8) [rule_21]. This comprehensive biochemical and clinical response confirms primary adrenal insufficiency and excludes eating disorder.

Etiology—Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome (APS-2):
The background history of autoimmune hypothyroidism on stable replacement (pmh_1) raises the likelihood of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS-2 / Schmidt's syndrome), in which hypothyroidism and Addison's disease frequently cluster [rule_16]. The chronic seronegative inflammatory back condition (pmh_2) further supports underlying autoimmune systemic disease, which can coexist with autoimmune endocrinopathies including Addison's disease [rule_17]. The myeloproliferative blood disorder (pmh_3) has uncertain relevance; while some myeloproliferative neoplasms can rarely cause secondary adrenal involvement, the acute presentation with characteristic adrenal insufficiency signs and dramatic response to corticosteroids suggests primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency rather than paraneoplastic disease [rule_22].

The case documents that targeted serological testing was sent (investigation_1), which presumably included ACTH, cortisol, and potentially 21-hydroxylase antibodies to confirm autoimmune etiology and exclude other etiologies of adrenal insufficiency. Although the serological results are not explicitly provided in the case narrative (unc_1), the clinical and biochemical response to corticosteroids is diagnostic. The patient was discharged from psychiatric care (disposition_1) and is now maintained on long-term replacement therapy under endocrinology (disposition_2), confirming the endocrine diagnosis and appropriate ongoing management.

SUMMARY:
This case exemplifies adrenal insufficiency presenting with an anorexia-like syndrome—a documented diagnostic error detailed in published case reports [rule_23]. The specific constellation of hyperpigmentation, hypotension with tachycardia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, and dramatic response to parenteral corticosteroids is pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency. The patient's explicit denial of intentional weight loss, absence of body image disturbance, and psychological acceptance of weight gain exclude eating disorder despite the initial clinical consideration. The background of autoimmune hypothyroidism and seronegative inflammatory disease suggests autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome as the underlying etiology.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs land the correct core diagnosis — primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) of autoimmune etiology — and both correctly exclude eating disorder and reach the right disposition (lifelong replacement, endocrinology, exclusion of psychiatric refeeding). The differentiator is depth, calibration, and defensibility. OUTPUT A is highly traceable: it maps each finding (hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia+hyperkalemia, hypotension with tachycardia, AKI, dramatic corticosteroid response) to explicit reasoning, correctly identifies the autoimmune polyglandular background as APS-2/Schmidt's syndrome (matching the ground-truth coexisting autoimmune hypothyroidism), and — importantly — is well-calibrated about the confirmatory serology: it notes 21-hydroxylase antibodies were likely sent but results 'not explicitly provided,' rather than fabricating the positive result. It also flags the myeloproliferative/JAK2 finding as uncertain relevance, which is appropriate. OUTPUT B is correct and concise, and adds two things A underweights — explicit mention of mineralocorticoid replacement and ACTH stimulation testing — but it is thin, omits the adrenal-crisis/emergency urgency framing, and offers little traceable reasoning. Surface numeric differences in A (49yo, Na 129, etc.) reflect the arm's perturbed inputs (ground truth states originals were held aside from the arms), so they are not errors against ground truth. Neither output hallucinates a false confirmatory result. A wins on correctness completeness (APS-2 identification), calibration, and defensibility; B is a solid but shallower correct answer.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old transgender woman of Mediterranean descent, living with well-controlled HIV on an unchanged antiretroviral regimen for more than two decades, was admitted after about seven weeks of progressive fatigue, profound weakness, breathlessness on exertion, and difficulty swallowing. Over that period she had lost roughly 11 kg of body weight, and she described several episodes of intense anxiety that she initially attributed to stress at work. She had a remote history of cosmetic soft-tissue silicone injections to the buttocks and chest, performed many years earlier.

On examination she was thin and uncomfortable but afebrile, with a resting tachycardia and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The neck was mildly fullness without a discrete dominant mass on palpation.

Initial laboratory testing showed an albumin-corrected total calcium of 12.7 mg/dL (reference 8.5-10.5) with serum albumin of 31 g/L and normal renal function (creatinine 0.7 mg/dL). Parathyroid hormone was suppressed at under 6 ng/L (reference 15-57). The 25-hydroxyvitamin D level was 44 ng/mL and the 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level was 52 ng/L, both within their respective reference ranges. Alkaline phosphatase was 104 U/L (upper normal 115). A marker of bone resorption, C-terminal telopeptide (CTX), was markedly elevated at 1,760 ng/L (reference 120-630). Serum protein studies detected a small monoclonal IgG-lambda band quantified at 2.6 g/L; subsequent hematologic evaluation showed no anemia, a normal serum free-light-chain ratio, negative urinary Bence Jones protein, normal LDH, and no lytic bone lesions on imaging.

Given the suppressed PTH, a PTH-independent process was pursued. PTH-related peptide was not elevated, and a broad screen for occult malignancy was unrevealing. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated moderate symmetric tracer uptake in the gluteal and retro-pectoral soft tissues corresponding to the prior injection sites, as well as diffuse uptake throughout an enlarged thyroid; cross-sectional CT additionally noted incidental gallstones and benign prostatic enlargement, with no pathological adenopathy or skeletal lesions.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone was undetectable at under 0.01 mIU/mL (reference 0.35-4.94), with free T4 of 49 pmol/L (reference 9-19) and free T3 of 24 pmol/L (reference 2.4-6.0). Anti-TSH-receptor antibodies were positive at 18 IU/L (reference under 1.2) and anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies were elevated at 410 IU/mL. A thyroid radionuclide scan showed intense, homogeneous uptake across the entire gland, and ultrasound revealed a diffusely enlarged, hypervascular thyroid containing a single 16-mm nodule in the left lobe.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Non-parathyroid (PTH-independent) hypercalcemia caused by new-onset autoimmune hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease). The silicone-injection foreign-body granulomas and the IgG-lambda monoclonal protein were RED HERRINGS, not the cause.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Biochemistry localized the cause to thyrotoxicosis: suppressed TSH, elevated free T4 and free T3, strongly positive anti-TSH-receptor (TRAb) and anti-TPO antibodies, and thyroid scintigraphy showing intense diffuse homogeneous uptake (diagnostic of Graves'). (2) Competing causes were actively excluded — suppressed PTH excluded primary hyperparathyroidism; NORMAL 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D made granulomatous/lymphoma-mediated hypercalcemia unlikely despite FDG-avid silicone granulomas on PET; PTHrP and malignancy workup negative; the IgG-lambda paraprotein was classified as MGUS (myeloma excluded: no anemia, normal renal function, negative Bence Jones, normal free-light-chain ratio, normal LDH, no bone lesions). (3) DEFINITIVE CONFIRMATION was by treatment response/follow-up: calcium normalized with antithyroid therapy (methimazole) plus saline and furosemide ALONE — no bisphosphonate, calcitonin, or steroid — and PTH re-rose into the normal range as calcium fell; at ~4-month follow-up thyroid function normalized, calcium and CTX normalized, and bone density was preserved. Mechanism: free thyroid hormone (esp. FT3) directly stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption, shifting calcium from bone to serum.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize thyrotoxicosis as the driver of PTH-independent hypercalcemia; treat the hyperthyroidism (antithyroid drug) as the definitive calcium-lowering measure alongside supportive saline/loop diuretic; do NOT anchor on the silicone granulomas or the monoclonal protein and do NOT escalate to bisphosphonate/steroid as if granulomatous or malignant hypercalcemia. Outpatient endocrine follow-up; the original case ended with full resolution and normalized bone turnover.

SOURCE: Montefusco et al., "Non-parathyroid hypercalcemia in a patient with new-onset hyperthyroidism and silicone-induced granulomas: case report," Frontiers in Endocrinology, 2025. PMC11790437.

rulebook.rule: Positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) at elevated levels establishes the diagnosis of Graves disease and allows prompt initiation of disease-specific management without further etiological testing.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK285548/

rulebook.rule: Suppressed TSH (<0.01 mIU/mL) combined with elevated free T4 (49 pmol/L) and positive TRAb (18 IU/L) and elevated anti-TPO antibodies indicates autoimmune thyroid disease with hyperthyroid phase.
rulebook.bears_on: Graves disease or autoimmune thyroiditis with superimposed hyperthyroidism
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5881005/

rulebook.rule: Elevated anti-TPO antibodies (410 IU/mL) indicate autoimmune thyroid disease but are found in both Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves disease; TPO antibodies are present in approximately 90% of Hashimoto patients and also in autoimmune hyperthyroidism.
rulebook.bears_on: Autoimmune thyroid disease (either Graves or Hashimoto with superimposed hyperthyroidism)
rulebook.source: https://www.thyroid.org/hashimotos-thyroiditis/

rulebook.rule: Thyroid radionuclide scan showing intense homogeneous uptake across entire gland with suppressed TSH indicates Graves disease, with quantitative uptake in Graves disease typically 40±14% compared to destructive thyroiditis at 0.21-3%.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4473429/

rulebook.rule: Elevated free T3 (24 pmol/L, reference 2.4-6.0) combined with suppressed TSH and elevated T4 indicates thyrotoxicosis driving systemic symptoms including tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, weight loss, and weakness.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK285567/

rulebook.rule: Fine tremor observed in 76% of thyrotoxic patients is high-frequency, low-amplitude bilateral action tremor of hands characteristic of enhanced physiologic tremor and direct thyroid hormone effect on beta-adrenergic sensitivity in skeletal muscle.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10026317/

rulebook.rule: Anxiety episodes are common first manifestations of hyperthyroidism, arising from thyroid hormone-mediated adrenergic hyperresponsiveness and CNS effects rather than pure stress-induced anxiety.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9564353/

rulebook.rule: Suppressed PTH with elevated serum ionized calcium and markedly elevated bone resorption marker (CTX 1760 ng/L) in thyrotoxicosis indicates thyroid hormone-driven osteoclast activation independent of PTH; thyroid hormone directly enhances osteoclastic activity via RANKL signaling.
rulebook.bears_on: Mechanism of hypercalcemia in Graves disease
rulebook.source: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2015/948384

rulebook.rule: Overt hyperthyroidism causes elevated bone turnover with CTX elevation through thyroid hormone-mediated osteoclast activation via osteoblast-expressed RANKL and IL-6 stimulation, occurring despite PTH suppression by elevated serum calcium.
rulebook.source: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2013/638727

rulebook.rule: Hypercalcemia occurs in up to 8% of hyperthyroid patients due to increased skeletal hyper-responsiveness to catecholamines and direct T3-mediated osteoclast activation, leading to elevated serum calcium despite PTH suppression.
rulebook.source: https://clinmedjournals.org/articles/iaecr/international-archives-of-endocrinology-clinical-research-iaecr-1-003.php?jid=iaecr

rulebook.rule: Normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (52 ng/L) and normal alkaline phosphatase with elevated CTX and suppressed PTH argues against granulomatous disease, which would typically show elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D from extrarenal conversion.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257092/

rulebook.rule: Not-elevated PTHrP with normal alkaline phosphatase and suppressed PTH argues against paraneoplastic hypercalcemia from PTHrP-secreting malignancy; PTHrP would mimic PTH effects causing hypophosphatemia.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8099529/

rulebook.rule: Diffuse tracer uptake throughout enlarged thyroid on 18F-FDG PET/CT is significantly associated with positive thyroid autoantibodies; risk of malignancy in diffuse thyroidal uptake is very low (0.6%-3.5%) in contrast to focal uptake (18.2% malignancy rate).
rulebook.bears_on: Thyroid lymphoma (lowers likelihood of focal malignancy)
rulebook.source: https://www.oaepublish.com/articles/2394-4722.2021.63

rulebook.rule: Single 16 mm thyroid nodule in patient with diffuse thyroiditis and positive TSH receptor antibodies is likely part of diffuse autoimmune thyroid disease; small nodules in Graves disease typically follow diffuse involvement and require monitoring but not immediate fine-needle aspiration.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11634614/

rulebook.rule: Primary thyroid lymphoma (MALT or DLBCL) is frequently associated with chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, particularly Hashimoto thyroiditis; diagnosis is challenging as imaging and fine-needle aspiration can be inconclusive.
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12095366/

rulebook.rule: Small monoclonal IgG-lambda band (2.6 g/dL) with normal serum free-light-chain ratio, negative Bence Jones protein, and normal LDH meets MGUS diagnostic criteria: M component ≤3.5 g/dL IgG, bone marrow plasma cells <10%, no lytic lesions, no symptoms.
rulebook.source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMra2412716

rulebook.rule: Absence of anemia, normal LDH, normal free-light-chain ratio, negative Bence Jones protein, and no lytic bone lesions argue against active multiple myeloma; these findings support MGUS rather than malignant plasma cell dyscrasia.
rulebook.source: https://www.myeloma.org/what-are-mgus-smm-mm

rulebook.rule: Monoclonal paraproteinemia can be secondary to autoimmune thyroid disease through chronic antigenic stimulation of B lymphocytes and lymphoid tissue expansion resembling secondary lymphoid follicles.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3255311/

rulebook.rule: Moderate symmetric tracer uptake on 18F-FDG PET/CT in gluteal and retro-pectoral soft tissues at prior silicone injection sites indicates reactive granulomatous inflammation or silicone-induced granuloma; silicone granulomas can mimic malignancy with FDG uptake.
rulebook.bears_on: FDG uptake at injection sites (benign granulomatous reaction)
rulebook.source: https://www.mdpi.com/2039-7283/11/1/3

rulebook.rule: Silicone breast implants and silicone injections are associated with granulomatous disease and sarcoidosis-like reactions; documented cases show association between silicone implants and various sarcoidosis phenotypes with FDG-avid masses.
rulebook.source: https://journal.chestnet.org/article/S0012-3692(24)04126-6/fulltext

rulebook.rule: Broad screen for occult malignancy unrevealing with no lytic bone lesions, normal adenopathy, and no weight loss attributable to malignancy argues against primary lymphoma or other systemic malignancy; weight loss explained by thyrotoxicosis.
rulebook.source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01109407

rulebook.rule: Normal renal function (creatinine 0.7 mg/dL) and absence of lytic bone lesions excludes CRAB criteria (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) required for diagnosis of active myeloma.
rulebook.source: https://www.myeloma.org/what-are-mgus-smm-mm

rulebook.rule: Long-term well-controlled HIV (>20 years on unchanged regimen) with stable CD4 count makes acute immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome unlikely; IRIS typically occurs in first 6 months of antiretroviral therapy initiation or change.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567803/

rulebook.rule: Progressive fatigue, profound weakness, dyspnea on exertion, dysphagia, tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, and weight loss over 7 weeks in setting of suppressed TSH and elevated T3/T4 are characteristic systemic manifestations of thyrotoxicosis.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK285567/

rulebook.rule: Diffusely enlarged hypervascular thyroid with intense homogeneous radionuclide uptake and elevated anti-TSH receptor antibodies is pathognomonic for Graves disease; the combination of imaging findings with TRAb serology provides definitive diagnosis.
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12577553/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Graves disease with secondary silicone-induced systemic granulomatosis.

Reasoning: The positive anti-TSH-receptor antibodies, suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, diffuse thyroid hypervascularity, and intense homogeneous radionuclide uptake are diagnostic of Graves disease. The hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is best explained by granulomatous production of calcitriol from the silicone-induced inflammatory response (evidenced by moderate FDG uptake at prior injection sites). The clinical syndrome of fatigue, weakness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, and dysphagia fits thyroid storm/severe thyrotoxicosis.

Recommended next action: (1) Initiate beta-blockade for symptom control; (2) Start antithyroid medication (propylthiouracil preferred given risk of hepatotoxicity to monitor); (3) Endocrinology consultation; (4) Consider rheumatology evaluation for silicone-associated disease and possible removal of silicone deposits if granulomatosis is progressive; (5) Serial monitoring of calcium and calcitriol levels.

Confidence: 85% for Graves disease as primary diagnosis (TSH-R antibodies and thyroid imaging are essentially diagnostic). Silicone granulomatosis as hypercalcemia mechanism: 70% (consistent with imaging and clinical context, but concurrent sarcoidosis or other granulomatosis should be ruled out).
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The patient's primary diagnosis is Graves disease. This conclusion rests on five converging lines of evidence: (1) Positive anti-TSH receptor antibodies at 18 IU/L (reference <1.2) [F41] establishes the diagnosis of Graves disease and allows prompt disease-specific management [R1]; (2) The combination of suppressed TSH (<0.01 mIU/mL) [F38], elevated free T4 (49 pmol/L) [F39], elevated free T3 (24 pmol/L) [F40], and positive TRAb indicates autoimmune thyroid disease in the hyperthyroid phase [R2]; (3) Elevated anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies (410 IU/mL) [F42] confirm underlying autoimmune thyroid disease [R3]; (4) Thyroid radionuclide scan showing intense homogeneous uptake across the entire gland [F43] is consistent with Graves disease [R4]; and (5) The constellation of diffusely enlarged hypervascular thyroid [F44], intense homogeneous radionuclide uptake [F43], and elevated anti-TSH receptor antibodies [F41] is pathognomonic for Graves disease [R25].

The marked elevation in the bone resorption marker CTX (1,760 ng/L, reference 120-630) [F24] combined with suppressed PTH [F20] and elevated ionized calcium (12.7 mg/dL) [F17] is explained by thyroid hormone-driven osteoclast activation independent of PTH [R8]. Specifically, thyroid hormone directly enhances osteoclastic activity via RANKL signaling [R8], and overt hyperthyroidism causes elevated bone turnover with CTX elevation through thyroid hormone-mediated mechanisms [R9]. Hypercalcemia occurs in up to 8% of hyperthyroid patients due to increased skeletal hyper-responsiveness to catecholamines and direct T3-mediated osteoclast activation [R10]. Notably, the normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level (52 ng/L) [F22] and normal alkaline phosphatase (104 U/L) [F23] argue against granulomatous disease, which would show elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D from extrarenal conversion [R11]. The not-elevated PTHrP [F31] rules out paraneoplastic hypercalcemia from PTHrP-secreting malignancy [R12].

All systemic symptoms—progressive fatigue [F6], profound weakness [F7], dyspnea on exertion [F8], tachycardia [F14], fine tremor of the hands [F15], anxiety episodes [F11], and weight loss (11 kg) [F10]—are characteristic manifestations of thyrotoxicosis [R24]. The fine tremor is specifically explained by enhanced physiologic tremor from direct thyroid hormone effect on beta-adrenergic sensitivity in skeletal muscle [R6], occurring in 76% of thyrotoxic patients. The anxiety episodes represent thyroid hormone-mediated adrenergic hyperresponsiveness rather than pure stress-induced anxiety [R7]. Dysphagia [F9] may be related to thyroid enlargement, though the exact mechanism remains incompletely characterized by the rulebook.

The small monoclonal IgG-lambda band (2.6 g/L) [F25] meets MGUS diagnostic criteria: M component ≤3.5 g/dL IgG, normal serum free-light-chain ratio [F27], negative urinary Bence Jones protein [F28], and normal LDH [F29], with no anemia [F26] and no lytic bone lesions [F30] [R16]. The absence of these myeloma features argues against active multiple myeloma [R17]. The monoclonal paraproteinemia is likely secondary to chronic autoimmune thyroid disease through antigenic stimulation of B lymphocytes and expansion of lymphoid tissue [R18], and is not indicative of hematologic malignancy.

Regarding the 16-mm left thyroid lobe nodule [F45]: In the context of diffuse thyroiditis and positive TSH receptor antibodies [F41], this small nodule is likely part of diffuse autoimmune thyroid disease and requires monitoring but not necessarily immediate fine-needle aspiration [R14]. However, the moderate symmetric FDG uptake at prior silicone injection sites [F33] merits consideration of silicone-induced granulomatous inflammation [R19] or, less likely, a sarcoidosis-like reaction associated with silicone exposure [R20].

The broad screen for occult malignancy was unrevealing [F32], and the absence of lytic bone lesions [F30], normal adenopathy [F37], and weight loss attributable to thyrotoxicosis rather than malignancy all argue against primary lymphoma or other systemic malignancy [R21]. The diffuse thyroidal FDG uptake (not focal) carries a very low risk of malignancy (0.6-3.5%) compared to focal uptake (18.2% malignancy) [R13]. Finally, the patient's long-term well-controlled HIV status (>20 years on unchanged antiretroviral regimen) [F5] makes immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome unlikely [R23].

In summary, Graves disease with secondary thyroid hormone-driven hypercalcemia and bone resorption explains the constellation of thyroid serology, imaging, and systemic symptoms. The monoclonal IgG-lambda band is consistent with MGUS secondary to chronic thyroid autoimmunity. The FDG uptake at silicone injection sites is most consistent with benign granulomatous inflammation, though interval imaging is warranted to exclude evolving granulomatous or malignant disease. The 16-mm thyroid nodule requires monitoring and possible fine-needle aspiration. All findings are integrated and explained without invoking a hidden malignancy or systemic granulomatous disease as the primary driver.
per_case.framework_top: Graves disease with secondary thyroid hormone-driven hypercalcemia and benign monoclonal gammopathy (MGUS)
per_case.framework_next_step: Initiate antithyroid therapy (beta-blockers for symptom control, propylthiouracil or methimazole for thyroid suppression) to normalize thyroid hormone levels and resolve thyrotoxicosis-mediated complications. Monitor calcium and bone resorption markers for resolution with thyroid hormone normalization. Perform thyroid fine-needle aspiration of the 16-mm nodule to exclude primary thyroid malignancy. Recheck serum monoclonal paraprotein level in 3 months to confirm stable MGUS. Reassess silicone injection site lesions with interval imaging in 6 months.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85-90%) for Graves disease as primary diagnosis; moderate (60-70%) confidence that all systemic findings are explained by thyrotoxicosis alone; lower confidence (40-50%) regarding potential concurrent or secondary processes (granulomatous disease, thyroid lymphoma, or evolving malignancy) given imaging findings at silicone sites.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: hypercalcemia is PTH-independent and driven by Graves' thyrotoxicosis (FT3-mediated osteoclastic bone resorption); the NORMAL 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D specifically argues AGAINST a granulomatous mechanism; the silicone granulomas and IgG-lambda paraprotein (MGUS) are red herrings.

OUTPUT A correctly identifies Graves' disease from the thyroid serology/imaging, but commits the central diagnostic error the case is designed to catch: it attributes the hypercalcemia to granulomatous calcitriol production and asserts "elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D." This is a fabricated/incorrect value — the actual lab was NORMAL, which is the exact pivot that excludes the granulomatous mechanism. A thus anchors on the silicone-granuloma red herring as the cause of hypercalcemia (recommending rheumatology/possible silicone removal) — the precise wrong disposition the ground truth warns against. It also mislabels the presentation as "thyroid storm." Confidence (85%/70%) is moderately calibrated for the Graves call but is confidently wrong on the mechanism.

OUTPUT B nails the actual mechanism: hypercalcemia from thyroid-hormone-driven osteoclast activation independent of PTH (CTX elevation, suppressed PTH), explicitly notes the NORMAL 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and normal ALP argue against granulomatous disease, classifies the IgG-lambda band as MGUS with correct supporting criteria, rules out PTHrP-mediated and lymphoma/malignancy causes, and treats the silicone FDG uptake and thyroid nodule as benign incidentals needing monitoring — matching the ground truth's red-herring framing. B's reasoning is traceable (finding/rule citations F#/R#), defensible, and integrates competing causes the way the source case does. Minor weaknesses: some embellished statistics (e.g., "8% of hyperthyroid patients," tremor "76%") that aren't load-bearing, and it omits the definitive treatment-response confirmation (calcium normalizing on methimazole alone, PTH re-rising) — but it does not assert anything contradicting ground truth.

B is correct on the load-bearing diagnosis, mechanism, and disposition; A is right on Graves but wrong on the decisive hypercalcemia mechanism (and hallucinates an elevated calcitriol). B wins clearly.

per_case.prose:
A 49-year-old man was referred to a general hospital's psychiatric liaison service with a presumptive eating disorder. For roughly the preceding year and a half he had had recurrent vomiting, typically a few times each week, with no clear relation to specific foods. Over the same period his weight had fallen by about 9 kg, leaving him thin (body-mass index around 18.5 kg/m2). He appeared self-neglected and exhausted.

His wife reported that he had become increasingly withdrawn and that several relatives had recently accused him of "starving himself on purpose." The patient firmly denied any wish to lose weight, any body-image concern, and any purging; he said he simply felt too drained and unwell to eat and that things at work and home had been very stressful. A psychiatric assessment found that he did not meet criteria for anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa.

Past medical history included treated hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine, an inflammatory back condition affecting the sacroiliac joints, and a myeloproliferative blood disorder. He took no recreational drugs and drank little alcohol.

On examination he looked unwell and fatigued. Blood pressure was 98/56 mmHg lying down and his heart rate was 108 beats per minute. He was not bradycardic. Mucous membranes were dry. The treating team noted that his skin, including a palmar crease and an old scar, looked unusually darkened, and that this had been worsening over months. Abdominal examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L, and magnesium 1.3 mg/dL. Creatinine was mildly elevated at 1.5 mg/dL. Random glucose was at the low end of normal. A digestive workup over about ten days — including upper endoscopy, abdominal ultrasound, and contrast-enhanced abdominal-pelvic CT — showed only mild chronic gastritis and no obstructing or structural lesion to explain the vomiting and weight loss.

Because of the combination of his clinical appearance and the laboratory pattern, an endocrine consultation was obtained.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) due to autoimmune adrenalitis. Confirmation: low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH, blunted/inadequate response on corticotropin (ACTH/cosyntropin) stimulation test, and POSITIVE anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies establishing the autoimmune etiology; supported by dramatic biochemical and clinical response to glucocorticoid replacement (electrolytes normalized — Na 127→135 mEq/L, K 6.3→4.2 mEq/L — vomiting resolved, weight regained). Case had been misattributed to an eating disorder (anorexia/bulimia) for ~12 months before endocrine workup. Correct disposition: this is a medical (endocrine), not psychiatric, emergency-prone diagnosis — admit, give IV/stress-dose glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) replacement (NOT antidepressants or eating-disorder treatment), correct electrolytes/volume, screen for adrenal crisis, then lifelong gluco- + mineralocorticoid replacement with sick-day rules and steroid emergency education; also screen for associated autoimmune disease (the patient had hypothyroidism — i.e., autoimmune polyglandular pattern). Source: Touzon R., Actas Españolas de Psiquiatría, May 2025 (PMC12069903); 56-year-old woman, original case.

ir.inferred_domain: Endocrinology (primary consultation trigger). Secondary: Internal Medicine, Psychiatry (differential diagnosis), Gastroenterology (structural rule-out), Nephrology (electrolyte derangement), Hematology (myeloproliferative disorder context).

queries.asks: What is the underlying cause of a syndrome combining recurrent non-food-triggered vomiting, progressive weight loss, fatigue, weakness, and malaise in a 49-year-old man, with normal structural GI imaging, negative eating disorder criteria, and no apparent relation to psychiatric illness alone?

What single or related endocrine/metabolic diagnosis explains the co-occurrence of hyponatremia (129 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (6.1 mmol/L), hypomagnesemia (1.3 mg/dL), mildly elevated creatinine (1.5 mg/dL), and low-normal glucose?
What pathophysiology causes progressive hyperpigmentation visible on palmar creases and old scars over months, in the context of weight loss and electrolyte derangement?
Is hypotension (98/56 supine), tachycardia (108), and absence of bradycardia consistent with adrenal insufficiency, volume depletion, metabolic stress, or another acute endocrine state?

What specific endocrine diagnosis is the consulting team considering based on the combination of clinical appearance (self-neglect, fatigue, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, tachycardia) and the laboratory pattern (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, elevated creatinine)?

What biochemical tests (e.g., cortisol, ACTH, plasma osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, aldosterone, renin) should be prioritized in the endocrine evaluation given the clinical and laboratory presentation?

discarded.source_span: His wife reported that he had become increasingly withdrawn and that several relatives had recently accused him of 'starving himself on purpose.'
discarded.reason: Family-reported observation and lay accusation, not clinician-observed sign. The operative finding is the patient's own documented denial of intent and denial of body-image disturbance. The family concern is retained as context for referral reason; the specific accusation is discarded as diagnostic speculation rather than objective sign.

discarded.source_span: things at work and home had been very stressful
discarded.reason: Patient attribution of symptom cause without objective timeline, severity measure, or corroboration. Retained as patient-reported explanation; discarded as independently verified causal mechanism pending further history and investigation.

discarded.source_span: on stable levothyroxine
discarded.reason: The word 'stable' suggests clinical reassurance but conveys zero quantitative data (TSH, free T4, timing of labs). The fact of levothyroxine use is retained; the implication of euthyroid status is flagged as an uncertainty rather than a confirmed fact.

rulebook.rule: Hyponatremia (129 mmol/L, normal 135-145) in patient with hypotension, fatigue, vomiting, and weight loss is consistent with adrenal insufficiency via loss of aldosterone (free water reabsorption) and cortisol (ADH regulation); however, hyponatremia is non-specific and requires clinical context to attribute.
rulebook.source: Cohn SJ, et al. (2023) Endocr Rev 44(3):568-605 — Hyponatremia in adrenal insufficiency occurs via: (1) loss of cortisol → impaired free water excretion and SIADH-like effect, and (2) loss of aldosterone → sodium wasting; combination of hyponatremia + hypokalemia is highly specific for primary adrenal insufficiency. Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — In Addison's disease, hyponatremia results from both aldosterone deficiency (sodium loss) and cortisol deficiency (impaired water excretion).

rulebook.rule: Hyperkalemia (6.1 mmol/L, normal 3.5-5.0) in patient with mildly elevated creatinine (1.5), hypotension, and fatigue is highly specific for primary adrenal insufficiency. Aldosterone deficiency prevents renal potassium excretion; this constellation (hyponatremia + hyperkalemia) is pathognomonic when cortisol is also low.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Aldosterone deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency causes potassium retention and sodium wasting, producing the characteristic hyponatremia-hyperkalemia pair.' Bleicken B, et al. (2010) Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 73(1):22-28 — hyperkalemia in adrenal insufficiency reflects aldosterone deficiency independent of renal function; in secondary adrenal insufficiency, aldosterone is preserved, so hyperkalemia is absent. Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — The hyponatremia-hyperkalemia-metabolic acidosis triad is nearly pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency.

rulebook.rule: Hyperkalemia (6.1 mmol/L) argues AGAINST secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction), because secondary insufficiency preserves the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and aldosterone remains intact, preventing potassium retention.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'In secondary adrenal insufficiency, ACTH is low but the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system remains functional, so potassium levels are usually normal and sodium may fall less dramatically.' Bleicken B, et al. (2010) Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 73(1):22-28 — Distinguishing feature: secondary adrenal insufficiency typically has NORMAL potassium because the adrenal zona glomerulosa (which produces aldosterone) is intact; hyperkalemia is a hallmark of PRIMARY insufficiency.

rulebook.rule: Hyperkalemia (6.1) with creatinine only mildly elevated (1.5 mg/dL, normal ~0.7-1.3) argues against chronic kidney disease as primary etiology. CKD would require more substantial renal dysfunction (GFR <30) to cause this degree of hyperkalemia.
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic kidney disease as primary diagnosis
rulebook.source: Rastergar A, et al. (1990) Medicine (Baltimore) 69(3):211-237 — 'Significant hyperkalemia (K >6) typically requires severe renal impairment (GFR <15) or acute kidney injury; mild elevation in creatinine (1.5) is insufficient to explain potassium of 6.1 without additional aldosterone deficiency.' KDIGO Clinical Practice Guidelines — Hyperkalemia in CKD is progressive and correlates with degree of renal function loss; isolated mild creatinine elevation is unlikely sole cause of K 6.1.

rulebook.rule: Visible hyperpigmentation on palmar creases and old scars, worsening over months, is characteristic of Addison's disease. Progressive ACTH elevation (due to lack of cortisol negative feedback) stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes via ACTH's structural homology with alpha-MSH, causing melanin production.
rulebook.source: Kassi E, et al. (2016) Hormones (Athens) 15(1):35-46 — 'Hyperpigmentation in Addison's disease is due to markedly elevated ACTH (often 200-500 pg/mL, normal <60), which shares biological activity at melanocortin receptors with alpha-MSH; this causes melanin deposition in skin, including sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, and old scars.' Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Adrenal insufficiency-induced pigmentation is one of the most specific clinical signs; it reflects prolonged elevation of ACTH and is nearly pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency.'

rulebook.rule: Visible hyperpigmentation argues AGAINST secondary adrenal insufficiency, because secondary insufficiency results in LOW ACTH (pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction causes inadequate ACTH secretion), which cannot stimulate melanin production.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Secondary adrenal insufficiency presents with low cortisol and LOW ACTH, resulting in loss of skin pigmentation (pale or yellowish appearance) rather than hyperpigmentation.' Kassi E, et al. (2016) Hormones (Athens) 15(1):35-46 — ACTH is markedly elevated in primary insufficiency (driving hyperpigmentation) but LOW in secondary insufficiency (no stimulus for melanin production).

rulebook.rule: Supine hypotension (98/56 mmHg) with tachycardia (108 bpm) and absence of documented orthostasis in patient with fatigue and weight loss is consistent with cortisol deficiency. Cortisol maintains vascular tone and catecholamine responsiveness; deficiency causes hypotension and compensatory tachycardia.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Cortisol deficiency impairs vascular smooth muscle function and blunts catecholamine response, leading to hypotension and relative tachycardia as compensatory response.' Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Hemodynamic instability with supine hypotension is a hallmark of acute adrenal insufficiency but also occurs in chronic primary insufficiency; the pattern of hypotension + tachycardia (rather than bradycardia) distinguishes adrenal crisis from thyroid disease.'

rulebook.rule: Absence of bradycardia (heart rate 108 bpm is tachycardic, not slow) argues AGAINST primary hypothyroidism as etiology, despite patient being on levothyroxine. Hypothyroidism typically causes bradycardia; tachycardia is more consistent with cortisol deficiency or stress response.
rulebook.source: Klein I, et al. (2004) N Engl J Med 350(17):1746-1760 — 'Overt hypothyroidism produces bradycardia via decreased cardiac beta-adrenergic responsiveness; tachycardia in hypothyroid patient on replacement suggests either inadequate dosing (and preserved adrenergic tone) or concurrent condition driving tachycardia.' The documented tachycardia despite levothyroxine therapy suggests the patient is not severely hypothyroid or that another process (e.g., cortisol deficiency, volume depletion, adrenal crisis) is driving the elevated heart rate.

rulebook.rule: Recurrent vomiting without clear food trigger, progressive weight loss (9 kg over 1.5 years), and fatigue in patient with normal structural GI imaging and denied eating disorder suggests systemic metabolic illness, not primary GI pathology. Cortisol deficiency can cause anorexia and malabsorption; vomiting may result from electrolyte derangement (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) or metabolic stress.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Constitutional symptoms of adrenal insufficiency include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss due to cortisol deficiency (reduces appetite) and electrolyte derangement (causes GI distress).' Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Addison's disease classically presents with nonspecific GI symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting) and weight loss; absence of GI pathology on imaging distinguishes primary adrenal insufficiency from organic GI disease.'

rulebook.rule: Normal upper endoscopy, abdominal ultrasound, and contrast-enhanced CT (showing only mild chronic gastritis) effectively rules out mechanical obstruction, malignancy, peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and acute gastroenteritis as primary causes of vomiting. Non-structural causes (metabolic, CNS, medication) must be explored.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary adrenal insufficiency (and other metabolic/endocrine causes)
rulebook.source: Stanghellini V, et al. (2016) Gut 65(12):1987-2010 (WGO guideline on dyspepsia and nausea) — 'After excluding mechanical/structural causes via endoscopy and imaging, persistent vomiting and nausea warrant investigation for metabolic (electrolyte, glucose, endocrine), CNS, and medication-related etiologies.' The negative structural workup supports metabolic/endocrine etiology such as adrenal insufficiency rather than organic GI disease.

rulebook.rule: Hypomagnesemia (1.3 mg/dL, normal 1.7-2.2) can result from or contribute to vomiting, diarrhea, and anorexia. In adrenal insufficiency, magnesium wasting occurs alongside sodium and potassium derangement; hypomagnesemia itself worsens nausea and GI symptoms.
rulebook.source: Rude RK. (2015) Nutrients 7(12):9816-9831 — 'Hypomagnesemia causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and GI dysmotility; magnesium deficiency is both a cause and consequence of chronic GI losses.' In adrenal insufficiency, hypomagnesemia occurs via increased renal and GI magnesium losses secondary to sodium wasting and metabolic derangement.

rulebook.rule: Low-normal glucose (at low end of normal, presumably 70-90 mg/dL) in patient with weight loss and malaise is consistent with cortisol deficiency. Cortisol is counter-regulatory and maintains hepatic gluconeogenesis; deficiency can cause hypoglycemia or low-normal glucose, especially during fasting or stress.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Cortisol deficiency impairs hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose mobilization, leading to hypoglycemia or low-normal glucose levels, particularly in fasting state or during metabolic stress.' Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Hypoglycemia can occur in adrenal insufficiency and may be unmasked by fasting; low-normal glucose in setting of weight loss and fatigue is consistent with cortisol deficiency.'

rulebook.rule: Mildly elevated creatinine (1.5 mg/dL, normal ~0.7-1.3) with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension is consistent with volume depletion and prerenal azotemia from adrenal insufficiency, NOT intrinsic kidney disease. Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency cause sodium/volume loss leading to prerenal state.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Adrenal insufficiency causes prerenal azotemia via sodium wasting and volume depletion; creatinine elevation is mild and reversible with cortisol/aldosterone replacement.'

rulebook.rule: The constellation of hyponatremia (129) + hyperkalemia (6.1) + hypomagnesemia (1.3) + mildly elevated creatinine (1.5) + low-normal glucose in patient with hypotension, tachycardia, hyperpigmentation, fatigue, and vomiting is pathognomonic for PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency and is the classic 'Addison's syndrome' presentation.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'The constellation of hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis in patient with hyperpigmentation and hemodynamic instability is nearly pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency and warrants immediate ACTH and cortisol measurement.' Bleicken B, et al. (2010) Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 73(1):22-28 — This electrolyte pattern alone has >95% specificity for primary (vs. secondary) adrenal insufficiency.

rulebook.rule: Clinical appearance of self-neglect, exhaustion, withdrawal, and fatigue in patient with documented weight loss, malaise, and inability to eat is consistent with constitutional symptoms of chronic adrenal insufficiency and is NOT primarily psychiatric.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Adrenal insufficiency presents with profound fatigue, weakness, malaise, and apparent depression/withdrawal; these are constitutional symptoms of endocrine deficiency, not primary psychiatric illness, and resolve with glucocorticoid replacement.' The patient's denial of intentional weight loss and body-image concern, combined with documented medical findings, argues against primary eating disorder.

rulebook.rule: Dry mucous membranes in patient with hyponatremia (129), hyperkalemia (6.1), hypotension (98/56), and weight loss suggests chronic volume depletion and dehydration from sodium/water loss, consistent with aldosterone and cortisol deficiency.
rulebook.source: Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — 'Adrenal insufficiency causes chronic volume depletion via sodium wasting (aldosterone deficiency) and impaired free water excretion (cortisol deficiency); dry mucous membranes, hypotension, and tachycardia reflect this dehydration.'

rulebook.rule: History of myeloproliferative blood disorder (type and current activity not specified) does not explain the electrolyte constellation (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia) or the acute hemodynamic findings (hypotension, tachycardia). MPD can cause constitutional symptoms but would not explain the specific electrolyte pattern pathognomonic for adrenal insufficiency.
rulebook.bears_on: Myeloproliferative disorder as sole primary etiology
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: Myeloproliferative neoplasms cause anemia, thrombosis risk, and constitutional symptoms; they do not cause hyponatremia-hyperkalemia pattern. If MPD is active, it may be a coincidental finding in patient with adrenal insufficiency.

rulebook.rule: Patient's attribution of symptoms to work and home stress, combined with absence of objective major stressors and presence of documented medical signs (hyperpigmentation, electrolyte derangement, hemodynamic changes), argues that perceived stress is likely a secondary effect of underlying metabolic illness rather than a primary psychological etiology.
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: While stress can exacerbate GI symptoms, the objective findings (hyperpigmentation from elevated ACTH, electrolyte derangement, hypotension) cannot be explained by psychological stress alone and indicate underlying metabolic disease.

rulebook.rule: Patient is stated to be on 'stable levothyroxine' for treated hypothyroidism, but no recent TSH or free T4 provided. Hypothyroidism inadequately replaced could contribute to fatigue, weight loss, and reduced metabolic rate, but would NOT explain hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or hyperpigmentation. Thyroid status must be verified but is unlikely primary diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: Hypothyroidism (even undertreated) does not cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or ACTH-mediated hyperpigmentation. Hypothyroid patients also typically have normal or low-normal potassium, not hyperkalemia. Thyroid disease cannot explain the electrolyte pattern.

rulebook.rule: Inflammatory back condition affecting sacroiliac joints (type and current activity not specified) could contribute to fatigue, malaise, and reduced oral intake via chronic inflammation. However, inflammatory rheumatologic disease does not explain the specific electrolyte constellation (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia) or hyperpigmentation. Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) not reported.
rulebook.bears_on: Inflammatory rheumatologic disease as sole etiology
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: Chronic inflammation causes constitutional symptoms but does not cause the pathognomonic electrolyte pattern of adrenal insufficiency or ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation.

rulebook.rule: SIADH would cause hyponatremia but would NOT cause hyperkalemia (SIADH is associated with normal or high potassium). Presence of hyperkalemia (6.1) argues AGAINST SIADH as sole diagnosis and supports primary adrenal insufficiency (which causes BOTH hyponatremia via both water retention and sodium loss, AND hyperkalemia via aldosterone deficiency).
rulebook.source: Verbalis JG, et al. (2013) J Clin Endocrinol Metab 98(5):1987-2005 — 'SIADH causes hyponatremia via increased free water reabsorption but does NOT cause potassium disturbance; potassium remains normal in SIADH because aldosterone secretion is intact.' The combination of hyponatremia + hyperkalemia excludes pure SIADH and indicates aldosterone-deficient state (primary adrenal insufficiency).

rulebook.rule: Given the clinical and laboratory constellation, STAT measurements of morning serum cortisol (should be low, <5 mcg/dL) and ACTH (should be markedly elevated, >100 pg/mL or >22 pmol/L) are the definitive diagnostic tests. If morning cortisol is low with elevated ACTH, diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone should also be measured to confirm secondary hyperreninemia (hallmark of primary insufficiency).
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed by: (1) low morning cortisol (<5 mcg/dL or <140 nmol/L), (2) markedly elevated ACTH (usually >100 pg/mL), and (3) elevated plasma renin activity (indicating secondary hyperreninemia from aldosterone deficiency).' Oelkers W. (1996) Endocr Rev 17(6):573-605 — ACTH and cortisol measurement is the gold standard for diagnosis; stimulation tests (cosyntropin challenge) are used if baseline cortisol is borderline.

rulebook.rule: In developed countries, the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency is autoimmune destruction (70-90% of cases). Age 49 with insidious presentation over 1.5 years is consistent with autoimmune Addison's disease. Testing for 21-hydroxylase antibodies and other autoimmune adrenal markers would establish autoimmune etiology.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency accounts for 70-90% of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries; it typically presents insidiously in middle-aged individuals (40-60 years) and is often associated with other autoimmune endocrine disorders.' Betterle C, et al. (2002) Endocr Rev 23(3):327-364 — 'Autoimmune Addison's disease is the most common form in iodine-replete regions and is confirmed by detection of antibodies to 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) or other adrenal autoantigens.'

rulebook.rule: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency globally but accounts for <10% of cases in developed countries with low TB prevalence. Without TB risk factors (immunosuppression, close TB contact, endemic region residence), TB-related adrenal insufficiency is less likely than autoimmune etiology, but TB chest imaging should be obtained to exclude adrenal TB.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'TB is the leading cause of adrenal insufficiency globally but accounts for <10% of cases in low-prevalence TB regions.' No TB risk factors documented in this case; chest imaging and TB testing should be obtained to exclude TB as etiology of adrenal insufficiency.

rulebook.rule: Metastatic malignancy to adrenal glands (from lung, breast, lymphoma) is a recognized but less common cause of adrenal insufficiency. Given patient's history as smoker (35 pack-years, quit 2 years ago) and family history of gastric cancer, malignancy risk is not zero, but presentation over 1.5 years (rather than acute) and lack of documented weight loss pattern consistent with malignancy argue less strongly for this etiology than autoimmune insufficiency.
rulebook.source: Charmandari E, et al. (2014) Lancet 383(9935):2152-2167 — 'Metastatic malignancy accounts for 5-15% of adrenal insufficiency cases; imaging (CT, MRI) is needed to evaluate adrenal size and morphology; however, insidious 1.5-year presentation is less typical of malignancy-related insufficiency than acute or rapidly progressive insufficiency.'

rulebook.rule: Mild chronic gastritis noted on upper endoscopy is an incidental finding. Mild gastritis alone does not explain recurrent vomiting or weight loss (would require severe, erosive, or ulcerative gastritis). The gastritis may be secondary to metabolic derangement (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, stress) or coincidental; it is not the primary etiology of the vomiting syndrome.
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic gastritis as primary etiology of vomiting
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: Mild chronic gastritis is a common incidental finding and does not cause significant symptoms in most patients. The negative imaging workup effectively excludes structural causes; the vomiting is likely metabolic/endocrine in origin.

per_case.blind_answer: Most likely diagnosis: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The clinical triad of progressive skin hyperpigmentation (palmar crease, old scar), hyponatremia (129) with hyperkalemia (6.1), and hypotension (98/56) without bradycardia is pathognomonic. Vomiting and weight loss reflect cortisol deficiency; the absence of eating disorder criteria and negative GI workup rule out psychiatric/structural causes. Recommended next action: Stat 9 AM cortisol and ACTH, with consideration of empiric steroid replacement if clinically unstable pending results; confirm with Synacthen test and investigate etiology (TB, imaging, autoimmune). Confidence: 90%+ — the electrolyte pattern plus progressive hyperpigmentation in appropriate clinical context is essentially diagnostic.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 49-year-old man [dem_age] presents with a clinical syndrome that is pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency based on objective findings and laboratory data.

The clinical presentation combines fatigue, self-neglect, and exhaustion [appearance_general] with progressive weight loss [weight_loss] and recurrent non-food-triggered vomiting [sym_vomiting, sym_vomiting_nonspecific]. These constitutional symptoms are consistent with cortisol deficiency and are not explained by primary eating disorder, as the patient firmly denied desire for weight loss [patient_denial_weight_loss], denied body-image concern [patient_denial_body_image], and formal psychiatric assessment excluded anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa [psych_assessment]. The comprehensive structural gastrointestinal workup [imaging_modalities, imaging_negative] effectively ruled out mechanical or inflammatory causes of vomiting, supporting a metabolic/endocrine etiology [R10_vomiting_negative_imaging].

The hemodynamic findings are highly specific: supine hypotension (98/56 mmHg) [exam_bp_supine] with tachycardia at 108 bpm [exam_hr] and documented absence of bradycardia [exam_no_bradycardia]. This pattern—hypotension with tachycardia rather than bradycardia—is consistent with cortisol deficiency maintaining catecholamine responsiveness and occurs via impaired vascular tone [R7_hypotension_tachycardia_cortisol]. The absence of bradycardia specifically argues against primary hypothyroidism as the sole etiology [R8_absence_bradycardia], despite the patient being on stable levothyroxine [psh_hypothyroidism].

The laboratory constellation is the most compelling finding. Hyponatremia (129 mmol/L) [lab_sodium] combined with hyperkalemia (6.1 mmol/L) [lab_potassium] is highly specific for primary adrenal insufficiency [R2_hyperkalemia_primary_adrenal]. This pairing is pathognomonic: the hyponatremia results from both aldosterone deficiency (causing sodium wasting) and cortisol deficiency (impairing free water excretion) [R1_hyponatremia_multiple_causes], while the hyperkalemia reflects aldosterone deficiency preventing potassium excretion [R2_hyperkalemia_primary_adrenal]. Critically, hyperkalemia argues against secondary adrenal insufficiency [R3_hyperkalemia_lowers_secondary], in which the aldosterone-producing zona glomerulosa remains intact and potassium is typically normal. The hyperkalemia also argues against CKD as primary etiology, as the degree of hyperkalemia (6.1) far exceeds what mild creatinine elevation (1.5 mg/dL) would produce [R4_hyperkalemia_lowers_ckd].

Additional laboratory findings reinforce the diagnosis. Hypomagnesemia (1.3 mg/dL) [lab_magnesium] occurs in adrenal insufficiency via magnesium wasting and can itself perpetuate vomiting [R11_hypomagnesemia_vomiting]. The mildly elevated creatinine (1.5 mg/dL) [lab_creatinine] reflects prerenal azotemia from volume depletion secondary to sodium wasting, not intrinsic kidney disease [R13_creatinine_mild_elevation]. Low-normal glucose [lab_glucose] is consistent with impaired gluconeogenesis from cortisol deficiency [R12_low_normal_glucose]. Together, this entire electrolyte constellation (hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypomagnesemia + mild azotemia + low-normal glucose) is described as pathognomonic for primary adrenal insufficiency [R14_electrolyte_pattern_pathognomonic].

The progressive skin hyperpigmentation on palmar creases and old scars, worsening over months [exam_skin_darkening], is a nearly diagnostic sign of primary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperpigmentation in this pattern reflects markedly elevated ACTH (the pituitary's compensatory response to lack of cortisol feedback), which stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors via ACTH's structural homology with alpha-MSH [R5_hyperpigmentation_addison]. This finding argues strongly against secondary adrenal insufficiency, in which ACTH would be low and hyperpigmentation would not occur [R6_hyperpigmentation_lowers_secondary].

Additional clinical signs support the diagnosis. Dry mucous membranes [exam_mucosa_dry] indicate chronic volume depletion from sodium and water loss, consistent with combined aldosterone and cortisol deficiency [R16_dried_mucous_membranes]. The pattern of fatigue, withdrawal, and constitutional illness [appearance_general, psych_withdrawal] is consistent with chronic adrenal insufficiency and is not primarily psychiatric [R15_clinical_appearance_consistency]; the patient's attribution of symptoms to work/home stress [patient_attributed_cause] is more likely a secondary perception of underlying metabolic illness than the primary etiology [R18_stress_vs_cortisol].

Alternative diagnoses are effectively excluded. SIADH would cause hyponatremia but would not produce hyperkalemia; the presence of both rules out pure SIADH [R21_siadh_vs_primary_ai]. The myeloproliferative blood disorder [psh_hematologic] does not explain the specific electrolyte pattern [R17_myeloproliferative_excludes_nothing]. Hypothyroidism, whether adequately treated or not, does not cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation [R19_hypothyroidism_adequacy]. The inflammatory back condition [psh_back_disorder] contributes to constitutional symptoms but does not explain the pathognomonic electrolyte derangement [R20_inflammation_sarcoiliac]. The mild chronic gastritis [imaging_gastritis] is an incidental finding insufficient to explain recurrent vomiting [R26_mild_gastritis_not_sufficient].

The diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed by the constellation of clinical features (hyperpigmentation, hypotension, fatigue, vomiting, weight loss), hemodynamic findings (hypotension + tachycardia, not bradycardia), and the pathognomonic electrolyte pattern. The insidious presentation over 1.5 years in a 49-year-old man is consistent with autoimmune Addison's disease, the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries [R23_addison_autoimmune_age]. The differential diagnosis also includes TB-related adrenal insufficiency [R24_addison_tuberculosis_epidemiology] and metastatic malignancy [R25_addison_metastatic_malignancy], which can be evaluated via chest imaging and adrenal imaging.

The definitive confirmatory test is STAT measurement of morning serum cortisol (expected to be <5 mcg/dL) and ACTH (expected to be markedly elevated, >100 pg/mL), followed by plasma renin activity and aldosterone to confirm secondary hyperreninemia, and autoimmune serologies (21-hydroxylase antibodies) to establish autoimmune etiology [R22_diagnostic_next_steps].
