rulebook.rule: Isolated aPTT prolongation (69 seconds) with normal PT/INR and normal fibrinogen raises acquired coagulation factor inhibitor (Factor VIII or Factor IX inhibitor, or antiphospholipid antibody)
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired factor inhibitor (Factor VIII/IX inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant)
rulebook.source: Differential diagnosis and clinical management of isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Medicine journal (2021) https://journals.lww.com/md-journal/fulltext/2021/07090/differential_diagnosis_and_clinical_management_of.53.aspx; Frontiers Immunology (2026) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1735963/full

rulebook.rule: 1:1 mixing study with non-correcting aPTT (did not correct after mixing patient plasma with normal plasma) is diagnostic of an inhibitor (either specific factor inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant)
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired factor inhibitor (Factor VIII/IX inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant)
rulebook.source: Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor: A Rare Etiology for Bruisability and Anemia. PMC (2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710562/

rulebook.rule: Acute onset of extensive soft-tissue ecchymoses (bruising) and mucocutaneous bleeding in an elderly patient without prior bleeding history raises acquired hemophilia (Factor VIII inhibitor)
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired Factor VIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A)
rulebook.source: Idiopathic Acquired Hemophilia A, a Rare Cause of Bleeding: A Case Report and Literature Review. PMC (2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7899955/

rulebook.rule: Large ecchymoses (purpuric patches) without petechiae, combined with normal platelet count (162 x 10^3/uL), lowers vasculitis and thrombocytopenia; consistent with coagulation factor defect
rulebook.source: Vasculitis causes small-vessel lesions (petechiae, palpable purpura, elevated lesions); large ecchymoses without petechiae with normal platelets indicates coagulopathy. Petechiae: What Are They, Causes, Treatment & Prevention. Cleveland Clinic https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21636-petechiae

rulebook.rule: Absence of lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly lowers lymphoproliferative or systemic inflammatory disease as primary cause
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic lymphoproliferative disease or DIC from sepsis/malignancy
rulebook.source: Physical examination findings guide differential diagnosis; absence of adenopathy makes systemic disease less likely in context of isolated coagulation defect

rulebook.rule: Normal WBC (8,200/uL), normal BMP, and normal LFTs raise idiopathic cause (autoimmune) and lower infectious/hepatic/malignant etiology for acquired factor inhibitor
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary causes of acquired Factor VIII inhibitor (infection, hepatic disease, malignancy)
rulebook.source: Over 50% of acquired hemophilia cases are idiopathic; secondary causes associated with autoimmune disease, malignancy, drugs, infections

rulebook.rule: Pale appearance and mild tachycardia with hemoglobin decline (10.9 to 8.1 g/dL over 2 days) raises acute bleeding with evolving anemia and blood loss
rulebook.bears_on: Active hemorrhage with ongoing blood loss
rulebook.source: Clinical signs of blood loss: pallor, tachycardia, declining hemoglobin. Acquired Hemophilia A Presenting as a Spontaneous Soft Tissue Hematoma. PMC (2024) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12188697/

rulebook.rule: Continued oozing from tongue laceration despite sutures, pressure, and observation (failed local hemostasis over hours) raises coagulopathy, lowers platelet dysfunction or vascular defect alone
rulebook.bears_on: Platelet dysfunction or local vascular defect
rulebook.source: Failure of local measures (sutures, pressure, observation) to control bleeding over hours indicates systemic coagulation defect. Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor: A Rare Etiology for Bruisability and Anemia. PMC (2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710562/

rulebook.rule: Bruising of varying ages (some old, some new) over arms and lumbar region lowers acute trauma as sole cause; suggests ongoing spontaneous/repeated bleeding episodes
rulebook.bears_on: Single acute traumatic event as cause
rulebook.source: Varying ages of ecchymoses indicates recurrent bleeding episodes rather than single inciting event, characteristic of acquired hemophilia

rulebook.rule: Lifelong normal hemostasis (uneventful childbirth, hysterectomy, dental extractions) lowers congenital coagulation disorder or platelet dysfunction
rulebook.bears_on: Congenital coagulation deficiency or platelet dysfunction
rulebook.source: Acquired vs congenital hemophilia: acquired inhibitors present suddenly in elderly after lifelong normal bleeding. Factor VIII deficiency vs Factor VIII inhibitor acquired hemophilia. iCliniq https://www.icliniq.com/articles/blood-health/acquired-factor-viii-inhibitor

rulebook.rule: No family history of bleeding disorder lowers congenital coagulation disorder
rulebook.source: Familial clustering expected in congenital disorders; absence of family history supports acquired etiology

rulebook.rule: Not on anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin) or antiplatelets (aspirin) lowers medication-induced coagulopathy and heparin contamination
rulebook.bears_on: Medication-induced bleeding or heparin contamination artifact
rulebook.source: Heparin contamination mimics inhibitor in mixing study (non-correcting aPTT). Detecting Heparin Contamination in Prolonged APTT. PMC (2024) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12669527/

rulebook.rule: Contact factor deficiency (Factor XII/XI/prekallikrein) causes prolonged aPTT but does NOT cause clinical bleeding; absence of contact factor deficiency in presence of significant bleeding
rulebook.bears_on: Contact factor deficiency (Factor XII, Factor XI, prekallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen)
rulebook.source: Contact system activation does not contribute to in vivo hemostasis. Factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding despite prolonged aPTT. Factor XI deficiency causes only mild postoperative bleeding at high-fibrinolysis sites, not spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding. Factor XII Deficiency Mimicking Bleeding Diathesis. PMC (2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6093754/

rulebook.rule: Lupus anticoagulant (antiphospholipid antibody) causes non-correcting aPTT but is associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding unless complicated by thrombocytopenia or factor deficiency; clinical bleeding without these complications lowers lupus anticoagulant as primary cause
rulebook.source: Lupus anticoagulants typically associated with thrombosis, not bleeding. Coagulation mixing studies: Utility, algorithmic strategies and limitations for lupus anticoagulant testing. American Journal of Hematology (2020) https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ajh.25669

rulebook.rule: Time-incubation mixing study (incubating at 37 degrees C for 1-2 hours before repeating aPTT) can differentiate lupus anticoagulant from specific factor inhibitor: if time-corrected aPTT difference <3 seconds favors LA; if >3 seconds favors factor inhibitor
rulebook.bears_on: Lupus anticoagulant vs Factor VIII/IX inhibitor
rulebook.source: Differentiating Factor Inhibitors from Lupus Anticoagulant. Case report in Hashimoto thyroiditis-associated thyroid cancer. PMC (2024) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8270622/

rulebook.rule: Severe clinical bleeding (continued oral oozing, extensive ecchymoses, declining hemoglobin requiring transfusion) in setting of non-correcting aPTT and normal PT raises high-titer Factor VIII inhibitor over low-titer or lupus anticoagulant
rulebook.source: Severity of bleeding correlates with inhibitor titer. Acquired hemophilia mortality 8-22% due to severity. Incidence 1-5 per million. NORD: Acquired Hemophilia A https://rarediseases.org/rare-diseases/acquired-hemophilia/

rulebook.rule: Corticosteroid responsiveness (clinical and serological improvement with prednisone) supports diagnosis of acquired autoimmune Factor VIII inhibitor rather than congenital deficiency or heparin contamination
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired autoimmune Factor VIII inhibitor (as opposed to congenital deficiency or artifact)
rulebook.source: Corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) are first-line therapy for acquired hemophilia to eradicate autoantibodies. Influence of factor VIII level and inhibitor titer on therapeutic response to corticosteroids in acquired hemophilia. PMC (2016) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5134779/

rulebook.rule: Antifibrinolytic agent (tranexamic acid or epsilon-aminocaproic acid) as supportive therapy indicates mucocutaneous (oral) and potentially gastrointestinal bleeding sites where fibrinolysis is high
rulebook.bears_on: Mucocutaneous and gastrointestinal bleeding as predominant clinical pattern
rulebook.source: Antifibrinolytic agents adjunctive therapy for acquired hemophilia when bleeding in high-fibrinolysis tissues (oral cavity, GI tract, urogenital)

rulebook.rule: Amlodipine (calcium channel blocker) use lowers medication-induced coagulopathy as primary cause; calcium channel blockers do not typically cause coagulation factor inhibitors
rulebook.source: Acquired Factor VIII inhibitors linked to pregnancy, some drugs, malignancies, autoimmune disorders; amlodipine not classically associated

rulebook.rule: No alcohol use lowers alcohol-related coagulopathy, vitamin K deficiency, and hepatic disease as primary etiology
rulebook.source: Alcohol contributes to vitamin K deficiency and liver disease; normal LFTs and negative history lowers these causes

rulebook.rule: Age 88 years (elderly, greater than 60 years) raises acquired Factor VIII inhibitor; incidence strongly peaks in elderly population (biphasic distribution: 20-30 years postpartum and greater than 60 years)
rulebook.source: Acquired hemophilia most common in elderly (>60 years). Incidence 1-5 per million per year; majority of cases occur in elderly. Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor: A Rare Etiology for Bruisability and Anemia. PMC (2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710562/

rulebook.rule: Low Factor VIII activity (less than 1 percent in some cases) combined with detectable Factor VIII inhibitor (Bethesda units) and non-correcting mixing study confirms diagnosis of acquired Factor VIII inhibitor
rulebook.source: Diagnostic criteria: (1) prolonged aPTT, (2) normal PT/INR, (3) non-correcting mixing study, (4) low Factor VIII with detectable inhibitor measured in Bethesda units. Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor: A Rare Etiology for Bruisability and Anemia. PMC (2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710562/

rulebook.rule: Factor V inhibitor (rare acquired inhibitor) can also cause non-correcting aPTT but presents similarly to Factor VIII inhibitor with severe bleeding; distinguishable by low Factor V activity and Factor V-specific inhibitor assay
rulebook.source: Acquired Factor V inhibitors rarer (0.038-0.29 per million) than Factor VIII inhibitors. Autoimmune etiology similar to Factor VIII inhibitor. Acquired factor V inhibitor with life-threatening bleeding. Thrombosis Journal (2012) https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/1607845412Y.0000000072

rulebook.rule: No recent surgeries or invasive procedures raises idiopathic acquired inhibitor; recent surgery can precipitate acquired hemophilia
rulebook.source: Acquired Factor VIII inhibitors can be triggered by surgery, trauma, pregnancy, transfusions, infections. Absence of recent precipitant supports idiopathic etiology (>50% of cases)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Acquired Hemophilia (Factor VIII Inhibitor)

Reasoning: The acute onset of spontaneous bleeding (oral, skin) in an 88-year-old with no prior bleeding history, combined with a markedly prolonged aPTT that fails to correct on mixing study (indicating a circulating inhibitor), is classic for acquired hemophilia. The normal PT, normal fibrinogen, and normal platelet count exclude other coagulopathies. The hemorrhagic (rather than thrombotic) presentation helps distinguish this from lupus anticoagulant.

Recommended next action: 
1. Measure Factor VIII level (will be low/undetectable)
2. Quantify Factor VIII inhibitor titer via Bethesda assay
3. Continue/escalate corticosteroids and consider second-line immunosuppression (rituximab)
4. Use bypassing agents (Factor VIIa or prothrombin complex concentrate) for life-threatening bleeding
5. Screen for underlying malignancy or autoimmune conditions

Confidence: 85%

The diagnosis fits the clinical and laboratory pattern well, though lupus anticoagulant remains a consideration given the identical laboratory finding of non-correcting aPTT on mixing study.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 88-year-old woman presents with acute onset severe mucocutaneous and soft-tissue bleeding that is best explained by acquired Factor VIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A).

DIAGNOSTIC RATIONALE:

The coagulation pattern is pathognomonic for an acquired factor inhibitor:
- Isolated aPTT prolongation (69 seconds) with normal PT/INR and normal fibrinogen (F26, F25, F27) raises acquired factor inhibitor by R1
- The 1:1 mixing study failed to correct the prolonged aPTT (F29), which is diagnostic of an inhibitor rather than a simple factor deficiency, per R2
- These findings eliminate contact factor deficiency (which does not cause clinical bleeding per R13) and substantially lower lupus anticoagulant as the primary cause (R14 predicts thrombosis, not spontaneous hemorrhage)

The clinical presentation is characteristic of acquired hemophilia:
- Acute onset extensive soft-tissue ecchymoses and mucocutaneous bleeding in an elderly patient without prior bleeding history (F2, F3, F4, F6) raises acquired Factor VIII inhibitor per R3
- The bruising pattern—large ecchymoses without petechiae, with normal platelets (F6, F18, F22)—is consistent with coagulation defect rather than vasculitis or thrombocytopenia per R4
- Failure of local hemostatic measures (sutures, pressure, overnight observation) to control tongue bleeding (F4) raises systemic coagulopathy and lowers platelet dysfunction or local vascular defect alone per R8
- Bruising of varying ages (F6) lowers single acute trauma and suggests ongoing spontaneous bleeding per R9

Strong supporting epidemiologic and clinical features:
- Age 88 years strongly raises acquired Factor VIII inhibitor; incidence peaks in elderly >60 years per R21
- Lifelong normal hemostasis despite childbirth, hysterectomy, and dental extractions (F12) lowers congenital disorder per R10
- Absence of family history of bleeding (F13) lowers congenital etiology per R11
- Not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets (F11) lowers medication-induced coagulopathy and heparin contamination per R12
- Clinical deterioration with pale appearance, tachycardia, hemoglobin decline from 10.9 to 8.1 g/dL, and need for transfusion (F15, F16, F30, F32) indicates active hemorrhage consistent with significant inhibitor titer per R7 and R16
- Normal WBC, normal BMP, normal LFTs (F20, F23, F24) raise idiopathic (autoimmune) cause and lower infection, hepatic disease, and malignancy per R6
- No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly (F19) lowers systemic disease per R5
- No recent surgery or trauma raises idiopathic inhibitor per R24
- Does not use alcohol (F14), lowering alcohol-related coagulopathy per R20
- Takes amlodipine, which does not cause inhibitors per R19

NEXT STEPS REQUIRED:
The case reports initiation of corticosteroid and antifibrinolytic therapy (F33, F34), which is appropriate first-line management. Corticosteroid response would further support autoimmune Factor VIII inhibitor diagnosis per R17. However, definitive diagnosis requires Factor VIII activity assay (expected to be <1% in severe inhibitor) and Bethesda inhibitor titer per R22. A time-incubation mixing study would help exclude lupus anticoagulant, which typically shows time-dependent correction (>3 second difference favors inhibitor per R15). Factor V inhibitor should be excluded with Factor V assay per R23, though it is much rarer.

CONFIDENCE ASSESSMENT:
Confidence is high (85-90%) because the complete coagulation pattern (isolated aPTT prolongation, normal PT/INR, non-correcting mixing study), acute severe mucocutaneous and soft-tissue bleeding in an elderly patient with lifelong normal hemostasis, and epidemiologic features all converge on acquired Factor VIII inhibitor. However, confidence is not absolute (not 95%+) because definitive confirmation requires Factor VIII activity and inhibitor titer assays, which are noted as pending ("further coagulation studies were sent" per case text) but results are not yet reported (U6). Lupus anticoagulant and Factor V inhibitor remain in differential until excluded.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct final diagnosis: acquired hemophilia A / acquired factor VIII inhibitor. Both correctly anchor on the key discriminators from the ground truth: isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT/INR and normal platelets, a mixing study that fails to correct (indicating a circulating inhibitor rather than factor deficiency), spontaneous bleeding in an elderly patient with no prior or family bleeding history, and the hemorrhagic-not-thrombotic presentation that distinguishes it from lupus anticoagulant. So both are diagnostically correct.

The differentiation is in completeness, traceability, and calibration:

OUTPUT A is more thorough and far more defensible/traceable. It maps each clinical and lab feature to explicit findings (F-numbers) and rules (R-numbers), making the reasoning fully auditable. It correctly recommends the confirmatory tests the ground truth specifies (Factor VIII activity assay, expected <1%, and a Bethesda inhibitor titer), correctly notes the differential that should still be excluded (lupus anticoagulant via time-incubation mixing study; the rarer Factor V inhibitor), and notes corticosteroid/antifibrinolytic therapy is appropriate first-line management — consistent with the source case (prednisone + aminocaproic acid). Its calibration (85-90%, explicitly not 95%+ because confirmatory FVIII activity/titer are pending) is well-justified and honest. Minor nit: it does not name the bypassing-agent/factor-replacement strategy as explicitly as the ground truth describes (rFVIIa/aPCC vs high-dose FVIII concentrate based on titer), focusing more on diagnosis than acute hemostatic management.

OUTPUT B is correct but terser. It does cover management more directly than A on the hemostatic side — it correctly names bypassing agents (Factor VIIa or PCC) for life-threatening bleeding and second-line immunosuppression (rituximab), and screening for underlying malignancy/autoimmune conditions, all consistent with the ground truth's management. However, it provides much less traceable reasoning (no feature-to-rule mapping), and its calibration is a bare "85%" without justification. Its discriminators are accurate but thin.

Neither output hallucinates. A's claim that FVIII activity is "expected <1%" matches the ground-truth value of 1%. Both correctly keep lupus anticoagulant in the differential.

A wins on defensibility, traceability, completeness of the diagnostic workup, and honest calibration. B has a slight edge on naming acute bypassing-agent management, but loses overall on rigor and verifiability. Both are fundamentally correct diagnoses, so this is a close call decided on reasoning quality.

per_case.prose:
A 76-year-old man was admitted to a regional hospital after several weeks of recurrent, alarming bruising and soft-tissue bleeding. Roughly three months earlier he had slipped on an icy driveway; in the workup that followed, a pulmonary embolism had been identified, and he had been started on a therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin), with a plan to bridge to an oral agent. His other problems were longstanding: ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction, emphysema requiring home inhalers, and morbid obesity (body mass index 54 kg/m2). He took no antiplatelet agents and had no personal or family history of a bleeding tendency, and had previously tolerated surgery and dental extractions without abnormal bleeding.

Over the four months from his fall, he had multiple presentations for bleeding that was repeatedly ascribed to his anticoagulation. He developed large, spreading bruises over the abdominal wall and flank, then a tense, painful swelling of one thigh. On the index admission he was pale and tachycardic. Hemoglobin was 61 g/L, prompting transfusion. The platelet count was normal and the prothrombin time was within the reference interval. The activated partial thromboplastin time was prolonged at 38 seconds (reference 21–31), and on repeat testing over the following days it lengthened further to 46 and then 64 seconds. A 1:1 mix of the patient's plasma with normal pooled plasma, tested after incubation at 37 C, failed to correct the prolonged aPTT.

Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large rectus sheath hematoma measuring approximately 16.5 by 9.0 cm, together with an extraperitoneal collection in one side of the pelvis and a smaller hematoma within a psoas muscle. During the hospitalization he subsequently developed a large hematoma of the calf (about 12 by 5 by 5 cm) and a sizable hematoma over a buttock. He ultimately required transfusion of approximately 15 units of packed red cells over the course of admission.

Targeted coagulation studies were obtained. Factor VIII activity was markedly low at 0.05 U/mL (reference 0.50–2.00). Von Willebrand factor antigen was elevated at 3.95 IU/mL (reference 0.50–2.00). An anti-Xa level drawn to assess the contribution of the anticoagulant was less than 0.10 U/mL. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identified a small IgM-kappa monoclonal protein quantified at 3.6 g/L; a skeletal survey and other staging studies showed no end-organ involvement.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Acquired Hemophilia A (AHA) — an autoantibody (inhibitor) directed against coagulation Factor VIII — with an associated underlying IgM-kappa monoclonal gammopathy. The bleeding was NOT due to the anticoagulant the patient was receiving.

HOW CONFIRMED: Isolated prolongation of aPTT with normal PT; the prolonged aPTT did NOT correct on a mixing study (incubated mix), indicating an inhibitor rather than a factor deficiency; markedly reduced Factor VIII activity (0.04 U/mL; reference 0.50–2.00); positive FVIII-specific inhibitor by Bethesda assay (5.6 Bethesda Units; reference <0.6); anti-Xa level <0.10 U/mL confirming the bleeding was not attributable to the LMWH/DOAC. Von Willebrand antigen was normal/high (4.12 IU/mL), excluding acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation showed an IgM-kappa monoclonal protein (3.2 g/L).

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize that this is an inhibitor-mediated bleeding disorder, NOT anticoagulant toxicity. Stop attributing bleeding to the anticoagulant. Achieve hemostasis with a bypassing agent (e.g., recombinant activated FVII or aPCC) for the acute life-threatening bleeds (do NOT rely on FVIII concentrate or simple transfusion to stop bleeding), support with packed RBC transfusion (patient received ~15 units), and ERADICATE the inhibitor with immunosuppression — first-line corticosteroids (prednisone 100 mg/day) plus cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day). Investigate for and manage the underlying associated condition (the monoclonal gammopathy). FVIII normalized to 0.72 U/mL after ~4 weeks of immunosuppression; patient remained relapse-free for ~20 months. Anticoagulation was later cautiously resumed once the inhibitor was eradicated.

KEY TEACHING POINT: An acquired FVIII inhibitor in an older patient was masquerading as ordinary anticoagulant-related bleeding; the isolated non-correcting aPTT prolongation with normal PT and a low/undetectable anti-Xa is the discriminating clue.

uncertainties.about: Anticoagulation adequacy and adherence. Patient was on 'therapeutic-dose' enoxaparin but anti-Xa <0.10 U/mL (subtherapeutic). Discrepancy could reflect non-adherence, malabsorption (obesity, GI disease), renal clearance variation, timing of draw relative to dosing, or possible dosing reduction not documented.

Nature of the aPTT inhibitor. Mixing study failure suggests inhibitor (not factor deficiency), but the inhibitor could be: (a) residual unfractionated/LMWH heparin effect, (b) acquired Factor VIII inhibitor (anti-Factor VIII antibody), or (c) another inhibitor. Bethesda assay for anti-Factor VIII not reported.

Causal role of IgM monoclonal protein. When was the M-protein first detected? Is it incidental dysproteinemia or causative of acquired hemophilia (IgM-producing B-cell clone generating anti-Factor VIII antibody)? Timing and clonal analysis not provided.

Reason for Factor VIII/vWF dissociation. Patient has severely low Factor VIII (0.05 U/mL) but elevated vWF (3.95 IU/mL). This pairing is unusual; vWF is elevated (stress/reactive response) yet Factor VIII is not supported by it (suggesting consumption, inhibitor, or acquired loss). Type 2 vWD or acquired hemophilia A are in differential.

APTT progressive worsening (38 → 46 → 64 seconds) over days. Mechanism unclear: Is inhibitor accumulating? Is Factor VIII being consumed/produced at accelerating rate? Is there parallel acquisition of additional inhibitor or ongoing hemolysis/bleeding driving consumption?

Timing of Factor VIII assay relative to anticoagulant dosing and in vitro effect. No mention of when Factor VIII activity was drawn relative to enoxaparin dose. Could heparin in the sample affect Factor VIII measurement? (Unlikely to cause selective Factor VIII loss, but timing matters for interpretation.)

Relationship between anti-Xa subtherapeutic level and the hematologic crisis. Why was the patient subtherapeutically anticoagulated despite PE indication? Did this drive hypercoagulability with downstream inhibitor generation (alternative to anticoagulation excess as cause)?

queries.asks: Why did this patient, on therapeutic-dose anticoagulation for PE, develop severe, progressive spontaneous bleeding over several weeks, when the anti-Xa level is actually subtherapeutic?

What explains the severe Factor VIII deficiency (0.05 U/mL, ~10% of normal) in the presence of elevated vWF (3.95 IU/mL, ~200% of normal)? This pairing suggests inhibitor, consumption, or acquired Factor VIII loss rather than inherited deficiency.
Is the IgM-kappa monoclonal protein (3.6 g/L) causative of acquired hemophilia A (via anti-Factor VIII antibody), or is it an incidental finding? When did it first appear?
What is the mechanism driving the progressive aPTT prolongation (38 → 46 → 64 seconds) over days, given the mixing study's failure to correct (indicating an inhibitor rather than factor deficiency)?

What is the source of the aPTT inhibitor: (a) residual anticoagulant effect, (b) acquired anti-Factor VIII antibody secondary to the monoclonal protein, or (c) another inhibitor (e.g., lupus-like anticoagulant, anti-prothrombin)?

Why is the patient's anti-Xa level subtherapeutic (<0.10 U/mL) despite being on 'therapeutic-dose' enoxaparin? Does this reflect non-adherence, malabsorption, renal clearance variation, or dosing error?
Could the subtherapeutic anticoagulation have driven a hypercoagulable state with secondary inhibitor generation, rather than excess anticoagulation causing the bleeding?

rulebook.rule: Isolated prolonged aPTT (38 → 46 → 64 sec) with normal PT and normal platelets raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired hemophilia A, residual anticoagulant effect, or other inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, anti-prothrombin).
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired hemophilia A; Anticoagulation-related coagulopathy; Lupus anticoagulant
rulebook.source: International recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of acquired hemophilia A (Haematologica, PMC7327664); Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494)

rulebook.rule: Mixing study failure to correct (1:1 mix with pooled normal plasma at 37°C incubation) indicates the presence of a time- and temperature-dependent inhibitor, NOT a simple factor deficiency.
rulebook.source: Pathology Outlines (coagulation mixing studies); International recommendations (PMC7327664) — 'Most inhibitors in AHA are heat and time dependent'

rulebook.rule: Severe Factor VIII deficiency (0.05 U/mL, ~10% of normal) raises acquired hemophilia A as a mechanism via antibody-mediated consumption or inactivation of Factor VIII.
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494); Acquired Hemophilia A case series (PMC11270631)

rulebook.rule: Elevated von Willebrand factor (3.95 IU/mL, ~200% of normal) paired with severely low Factor VIII (0.05 U/mL) is unusual and suggests Factor VIII consumption or inhibition by anti-Factor VIII antibody, as vWF is reactive but unable to support Factor VIII levels in the presence of inhibitor.
rulebook.source: New Developments in Diagnosis and Management of Acquired Hemophilia and Acquired vWD (PMC8171371); Mayo Clinic Labs Factor VIII overview

rulebook.rule: Presence of IgM-kappa monoclonal protein (3.6 g/L) concurrent with Factor VIII deficiency and inhibitory aPTT raises the possibility that the monoclonal protein acts as a causative anti-Factor VIII antibody.
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia A (AHA) associated with monoclonal gammopathy case series (Blood ASH 146:3088) — 'Monoclonal proteins produced by myeloma cells can act as factor VIII inhibitors'

rulebook.rule: IgM isotype (rather than IgG, the more common isotype in acquired hemophilia) raises consideration of atypical autoimmune mechanism with potential for inhibitor activity, as IgM molecules bind with high capacity to coagulation factors and platelets.
rulebook.source: IgMk paraprotein case report (BMC Immunology, PMC5482953); International recommendations (PMC7327664) note IgG is predominant in AHA

rulebook.rule: Progressive aPTT prolongation over days (38 → 46 → 64 seconds) raises the mechanism of accumulating inhibitor or progressive Factor VIII consumption, distinct from static anticoagulant effect.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired hemophilia A (with active inhibitor generation/accumulation)
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494); International recommendations (PMC7327664) — time-dependent kinetics of inhibitors in vivo

rulebook.rule: Subtherapeutic anti-Xa level (<0.10 U/mL, vs. therapeutic target 0.5–1.0 U/mL) despite reported therapeutic-dose enoxaparin lowers the explanation of anticoagulation excess as the primary cause of bleeding, raising alternative pathophysiology (underlying hemophilia unmasked or worsened by marginal anticoagulation).
rulebook.source: Anti-Factor Xa Level Monitoring for Enoxaparin (PMC10324872)

rulebook.rule: Multiple large spontaneous hematomas at distant anatomical sites (rectus sheath 16.5×9.0 cm, pelvic, psoas, calf, buttock) with massive transfusion requirement (~15 units PRBCs) raises severe Factor VIII deficiency with inhibitor as the mechanism, more than anticoagulation excess alone (which would show more modest bleeding).
rulebook.source: Spontaneous rectus sheath hematoma literature (PMC10519645); Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494) — 'Spontaneous, extensive subcutaneous hematomas' are hallmark of AHA

rulebook.rule: Age >75 years with male sex and prior negative bleeding/surgical history raises acquired hemophilia A, which can develop de novo without prior bleeding tendency, and lowers congenital hemophilia A.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired hemophilia A; Congenital hemophilia A
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494) — 'occurs in both men and women without a previous history of bleeding'

rulebook.rule: Triggering PE event with initiation of therapeutic-dose anticoagulation, followed 3–4 months later by bleeding crisis, raises both anticoagulation-induced bleeding and acquired hemophilia A (enoxaparin may have unmasked underlying hemophilia or triggered secondary immune activation).
rulebook.source: Anticoagulation-related bleeding mechanisms (PMC5135167)

rulebook.rule: Comorbidities of morbid obesity (BMI 54), emphysema, and ischemic cardiomyopathy raise the risk of malabsorption affecting anticoagulant bioavailability, contributing to subtherapeutic anti-Xa levels, and underlying inflammatory dysregulation promoting dysproteinemia and acquired hemophilia.
rulebook.bears_on: Subtherapeutic anticoagulation; Dysproteinemia-mediated acquired hemophilia A
rulebook.source: Anti-Factor Xa Level Monitoring in High-Risk Patient Groups (PMC10324872)

rulebook.rule: Severe anemia at admission (Hemoglobin 61 g/L) with massive transfusion requirement (~15 units PRBCs) raises the severity of underlying bleeding disorder (acquired hemophilia A with inhibitor) rather than minor anticoagulation-related bleeding.
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia – StatPearls (NBK560494) — 'Life-threatening hemorrhage is a defining feature of acquired hemophilia A'

rulebook.rule: Absence of antiplatelet medications lowers the contribution of platelet dysfunction or drug-drug interactions to the coagulation disorder.
rulebook.source: Clinical context

rulebook.rule: Negative staging studies for end-organ involvement (no evidence of multiple myeloma, lymphoma, or solid malignancy) raises the dysproteinemia as MGUS or incidental finding, pointing to idiopathic acquired hemophilia A, and lowers malignancy-associated Factor VIII inhibitor.
rulebook.bears_on: Idiopathic acquired hemophilia A; Malignancy-associated AHA
rulebook.source: Acquired Hemophilia A (AHA) associated with monoclonal gammopathy (Blood ASH 146:3088)

rulebook.rule: Heparin in plasma sample can artifactually lower measured Factor VIII activity in vitro, but does NOT explain the inhibitor-mediated aPTT prolongation pattern (which reflects true inhibitor-factor VIII interaction in vivo).
rulebook.direction: lowers (true inhibitor specificity); raises (need for artifact control)
rulebook.source: Heparin neutralization is essential for accurate Factor VIII measurement (PubMed 10882230)

per_case.blind_answer:
**Diagnosis:** Acquired Factor VIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia) associated with IgM monoclonal protein.

**Recommended Next Action:** 
1. Quantify inhibitor strength via Bethesda assay
2. Discontinue enoxaparin immediately (non-contributory at subtherapeutic levels; harmful)
3. Start rFVIIa or PCC for acute hemostasis
4. Initiate immunosuppression (corticosteroids, rituximab) for long-term control
5. Further characterize paraprotein; consider bone marrow if needed

**Confidence:** 90–95%

**Reasoning:** The non-correcting aPTT with severely depressed Factor VIII (0.05 U/mL) in the setting of an IgM monoclonal protein is pathognomonic for acquired Factor VIII inhibitor. The clinical picture of progressive, severe multi-site soft-tissue and muscle bleeding, initially misattributed to anticoagulation, is classic for acquired hemophilia in an elderly patient with a paraproteinemia. Elevated vWF antigen reflects reactive upregulation due to low Factor VIII. The anti-Xa level below therapeutic range explains why anticoagulation was ineffective, supporting the diagnosis of an acquired coagulation inhibitor as the primary problem rather than over-anticoagulation.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 76-year-old man presents with a life-threatening bleeding disorder characterized by multiple large spontaneous hematomas and massive transfusion requirement over the course of hospitalization.

**Coagulation Laboratory Pattern (Rules R1, R2, R3):**
The key diagnostic constellation is isolated prolonged aPTT (38 → 46 → 64 seconds, F20, F21) with normal PT (F19) and normal platelet count (F18). A 1:1 mixing study with normal pooled plasma failed to correct the prolonged aPTT (F22), which per R2 indicates a time- and temperature-dependent inhibitor rather than simple factor deficiency. Targeted coagulation studies revealed severely low Factor VIII activity at 0.05 U/mL (F29, ~10% of normal per R3) paired with elevated von Willebrand factor at 3.95 IU/mL (F30, ~200% of normal). This dissociation (low Factor VIII with elevated vWF) per R4 is unusual and characteristic of Factor VIII consumption or inhibition by antibody, as vWF is elevated (reactive response to bleeding) but cannot support Factor VIII levels in the presence of an inhibitor.

**Severe Bleeding Phenotype (Rules R9, R13):**
The clinical severity—multiple large spontaneous hematomas at distant anatomical sites (rectus sheath 16.5×9.0 cm, F23; pelvic extraperitoneal collection, F24; psoas muscle, F25; calf 12×5×5 cm, F26; buttock, F27), severe anemia at admission (Hemoglobin 61 g/L, F16), and massive transfusion requirement (~15 units packed red cells, F28)—fits R9 and R13 for severe Factor VIII deficiency with inhibitor as the mechanism more than anticoagulation excess alone. Isolated anticoagulation excess would produce more modest bleeding.

**Role of Monoclonal Protein (Rules R5, R6, R15):**
Serum protein electrophoresis identified a small IgM-kappa monoclonal protein at 3.6 g/L (F32). Per R5, the presence of IgM-kappa concurrent with Factor VIII deficiency and inhibitory aPTT raises the possibility that this monoclonal protein acts as a causative anti-Factor VIII antibody. R6 notes that IgM isotype (rather than the more common IgG in acquired hemophilia) raises consideration of atypical autoimmune mechanism, as IgM molecules bind with high capacity to coagulation factors. Staging studies showed no end-organ involvement (F33); per R15, this lowers malignancy-associated Factor VIII inhibitor and points toward idiopathic acquired hemophilia A or dysproteinemia-mediated disease.

**Against Anticoagulation Excess (Rule R8):**
The patient's anti-Xa level was <0.10 U/mL (F31), which is subtherapeutic (normal target 0.5–1.0 U/mL). Per R8, this subtherapeutic level lowers the explanation of anticoagulation excess as the primary cause of bleeding and raises alternative pathophysiology. While anticoagulation may have unmasked or contributed to the bleeding (R11), the severe Factor VIII deficiency, inhibitory mixing study, elevated vWF/low Factor VIII dissociation, and monoclonal protein point to acquired hemophilia A as the underlying mechanism.

**Age and Bleeding History (Rule R10):**
The patient is 76 years old, male, with no prior bleeding tendency (F9) and previously uneventful surgical and dental procedures. Per R10, acquired hemophilia A can develop de novo without prior bleeding history in older adults, and this demographic pattern lowers congenital hemophilia A.

**Progressive Mechanism (Rule R7):**
The aPTT progression from 38 to 64 seconds over several days (F21) per R7 suggests accumulating inhibitor or progressive Factor VIII consumption, distinct from a static anticoagulant effect, consistent with active acquired hemophilia A.

**Synthesis:**
The clinical and laboratory evidence converges on acquired hemophilia A, likely mediated by the IgM-kappa monoclonal protein acting as an anti-Factor VIII antibody. The anti-Xa level subtherapeutic at the time of bleeding argues against anticoagulation alone driving the hemorrhage. The patient's age, absent prior bleeding history, massive spontaneous hematomas, severe Factor VIII deficiency with elevated vWF (indicating inhibitor), and concurrent monoclonal protein are hallmarks of acquired hemophilia A. Whether the IgM protein is primary causative or secondary epiphenomenon to activated B cells driven by immune dysfunction remains to be determined by Bethesda assay.
per_case.framework_top: Acquired hemophilia A (anti-Factor VIII antibody-mediated), likely monoclonal protein-associated
per_case.framework_next_step: Perform Bethesda assay (anti-Factor VIII inhibitor titer) to confirm acquired hemophilia A diagnosis; test samples for lupus anticoagulant and anti-prothrombin to exclude alternative inhibitors; proceed with immunosuppression (corticosteroids ± rituximab) and bypassing agent therapy (activated prothrombin complex concentrate or recombinant Factor VIIa) for acute hemostasis pending inhibitor confirmation.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85–90%). The constellation of isolated prolonged aPTT with failure to correct on mixing (R2), severe Factor VIII deficiency with elevated vWF (R3, R4), concurrent IgM-kappa monoclonal protein (R5, R6), progressive aPTT worsening (R7), massive spontaneous hematomas at distant sites (R9), and exclusion of malignancy (R15) fit acquired hemophilia A. Subtherapeutic anti-Xa (R8) lowers anticoagulation excess as the sole cause. Residual uncertainty remains about whether the IgM protein is causative versus incidental, timing of monoclonal protein emergence, and Bethesda assay confirmation.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct core diagnosis: Acquired Hemophilia A (an acquired Factor VIII inhibitor) associated with an IgM(-kappa) monoclonal gammopathy, with the bleeding NOT attributable to anticoagulation. Both correctly cite the discriminating evidence: isolated prolonged aPTT, normal PT, non-correcting mixing study, severely low FVIII, elevated vWF, and subtherapeutic anti-Xa (<0.10). So on diagnosis both are correct.

The deciding factor is DISPOSITION/management, which the ground truth emphasizes heavily. OUTPUT A explicitly gives the correct, complete management plan: Bethesda assay to quantify inhibitor, discontinue anticoagulant, bypassing agents (rFVIIa or PCC) for acute hemostasis, and immunosuppression for inhibitor eradication, plus paraprotein workup. This matches the ground truth's correct disposition closely. OUTPUT A is also well-calibrated (90–95%) and defensible.

OUTPUT B is a very thorough, traceable rule-by-rule derivation of the diagnosis and strongly supports the same conclusion, but it essentially STOPS at diagnosis — it never states the management/disposition (no bypassing agents, no immunosuppression, no 'stop the anticoagulant' action plan). The ground truth stresses recognizing this is inhibitor-mediated and treating with bypassing agents + immunosuppression; B omits this entirely, ending with 'remains to be determined by Bethesda assay.' B is also slightly more hedged/uncertain about whether the IgM is causative vs epiphenomenon (ground truth frames it as an associated condition, so B's caution is defensible, not wrong).

Minor factual notes: both report FVIII ~0.05 U/mL vs ground truth 0.04 (rounding, acceptable); both report vWF ~3.95/elevated vs ground truth 4.12 IU/mL (consistent); both report IgM-kappa ~3.6 g/L vs 3.2 (minor numeric drift, B's figure is closer in nature but slightly off). Neither hallucinates materially.

Both nail the diagnosis and the key teaching point (anti-Xa/non-correcting aPTT as discriminator). A wins because it additionally delivers the correct clinical disposition the ground truth requires, while B—though more rigorously traceable—leaves the actionable management unstated.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old woman was referred to the oncology clinic for evaluation of progressively worsening mid-to-lower back pain. The pain had been building over roughly three months, was centered over the lower thoracic and upper lumbar region, and was notably worse when she lay flat at night. She denied fever, drenching sweats, weight loss, or fatigue, and the remainder of her review of systems was unremarkable.

Her relevant history was a hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-positive invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, diagnosed about a year and a half earlier. At diagnosis the tumor was 1.5 cm and grade 2; the estrogen and progesterone receptors were strongly expressed, HER2 was 3+ by immunohistochemistry, and the proliferation index (Ki-67) was around 15%. One of several sampled sentinel nodes had contained tumor with extracapsular spread. She had undergone a breast-conserving lumpectomy with sentinel node sampling, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, anti-HER2 antibody therapy, locoregional radiation, and was on an aromatase inhibitor. A surveillance mammogram several months after surgery had shown no residual or recurrent disease in either breast. She presented for this new problem only a few weeks after finishing her planned year of anti-HER2 antibody treatment.

Given the history, recurrent disease was the leading clinical concern, and cross-sectional and functional imaging were obtained. MRI of the spine showed abnormal marrow signal with enhancement at several levels (notably L1, L3, and the sacrum) together with additional lesions in the iliac bones and sacrum, a pattern read as compatible with skeletal metastatic disease. Whole-body PET/CT then demonstrated multiple foci of increased metabolic activity distributed across the mediastinum, both hila, the spleen, the liver, abdominal and inguinal lymph nodes, and several bones. The intensity of uptake was modest across these sites, with maximum standardized uptake values in the range of about 2.8 to 5.6.

Because the imaging-based impression of widespread metastasis would substantially change her management, tissue confirmation was pursued. A biopsy of one of the liver lesions was performed first. It showed granulomatous inflammation of the liver with numerous well-formed, non-caseating epithelioid granulomas, and no malignant cells were identified. To resolve the discrepancy, image-guided biopsies were then taken from an iliac bone lesion and from an involved lumbar vertebral body; both likewise showed a non-necrotizing granulomatous process without any evidence of carcinoma.

An infectious evaluation was undertaken to account for the granulomas. An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative, and urine and serum antigen/antibody studies for histoplasma, blastomyces, coccidioides, and treponemal infection were all negative. Molecular testing of the liver tissue for acid-fast bacilli and for fungal organisms returned negative as well. On reviewing her older studies, imaging obtained roughly a year before her breast cancer had been diagnosed was noted to have shown findings that, in retrospect, were compatible with a chronic inflammatory process.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Systemic sarcoidosis (non-caseating/non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomatous inflammation involving liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone) presenting as a metastatic-mimic in a breast cancer survivor — NOT metastatic breast cancer recurrence.

HOW CONFIRMED: Multiple tissue biopsies were the decisive step. An initial liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis with multiple non-caseating epithelioid granulomas and no malignancy. A second set of CT-guided biopsies (iliac bone and an involved vertebral body) again showed a non-necrotizing granulomatous pattern with no evidence of malignancy. A full infectious workup was negative (QuantiFERON/TB negative; urine and serum antigen/antibody testing for histoplasma, blastomyces, coccidioides, and treponema all negative; tissue PCR negative for acid-fast bacilli and fungi), excluding the main granulomatous mimics. Supporting context: imaging roughly a year before the cancer diagnosis had already shown findings compatible with sarcoidosis; relatively low PET SUVmax (~3–5.75) and clinically indolent multi-organ pattern were atypical for aggressive widespread breast-cancer metastases. Final attribution made with rheumatology correlation.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize the lesions as benign granulomatous (sarcoid) disease rather than metastatic recurrence — biopsy before committing to palliative/systemic oncologic treatment. Do NOT escalate to metastatic-breast-cancer therapy. Manage sarcoidosis expectantly (the patient deferred corticosteroids after rheumatology review since she was largely asymptomatic and the back pain was attributed to osteoarthritis). Follow-up surveillance imaging at ~4 months showed stable lesions, supporting the benign diagnosis. Original case: 71-year-old Caucasian woman, ER 90%/PR 95%/HER2 3+, Ki67 13%, pT1N1aMx infiltrating ductal carcinoma; PET SUVmax range 3–5.75; PMC7813063.

rulebook.rule: Multiple marrow signal abnormalities on MRI (hypointense T1, hyperintense T2/STIR) with gadolinium enhancement at multiple vertebral levels and iliac bones indicates bone marrow granulomatous inflammation
rulebook.source: RadioGraphics (2006) 26(6):2025-2072 - Musculoskeletal sarcoidosis: spectrum of appearances at MR imaging; MDPI Biomedicines (2022) 11(7):1866 - Imaging plays a key role in diagnosis of bone sarcoidosis

rulebook.rule: Multifocal FDG-PET uptake with modest SUV intensity (2.8-5.6) across mediastinal, hilar, visceral, and osseous sites indicates granulomatous inflammatory process rather than high-grade malignancy
rulebook.source: Clinical Nuclear Medicine (2008) 33(10):712-716 - Bone marrow granulomatous inflammation: FDG PET findings; Annals of Nuclear Medicine (2013) 27(4):339-350 - FDG PET/CT evaluation in endemic granulomatous disease

rulebook.rule: Multivisceral distribution of granulomatous disease involving liver, spleen, mediastinal-hilar lymph nodes, abdominal nodes, iliac bones, and vertebral bodies is characteristic of systemic sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: MDPI Biomedicines (2022) 11(7):1866; European Respiratory Society (2024) - CT findings in pulmonary and abdominal sarcoidosis

rulebook.rule: MRI-detected intramedullary marrow lesions without cortical destruction or periosteal involvement can mimic metastatic disease but lack destructive features typical of true bone metastases

rulebook.rule: Liver biopsy demonstrating numerous well-formed non-caseating epithelioid granulomas without malignant cells strongly supports granulomatous disease diagnosis and excludes hepatic metastatic carcinoma

rulebook.rule: Consistent non-caseating granulomatous histology across multiple independent biopsy sites (liver, iliac bone, lumbar vertebra) without malignant cells indicates systemic granulomatous disease process
rulebook.source: UpToDate (2024) - Clinical manifestations and diagnosis of sarcoidosis; IntechOpen - Pathology of sarcoidosis and differential diagnostics

rulebook.rule: Absence of malignant cells on hepatic biopsy excludes metastatic breast cancer involvement of liver despite imaging findings suggestive of metastatic disease
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect - Bone marrow metastasis overview; Wiley Online Library (2018) - Diffuse bone marrow metastasis as initial presentation of occult breast cancer

rulebook.rule: Absence of carcinoma on iliac bone and lumbar vertebral biopsies excludes metastatic disease as explanation for osseous marrow abnormalities and imaging findings

rulebook.rule: Negative interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis substantially reduces probability of active or latent TB infection in immunocompetent patient

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: SARCOIDOSIS with multisystem involvement (osseous, hepatic, lymphatic, splenic).

Recommended next action: Check serum/urine calcium and ACE level; obtain chest radiograph; perform ophthalmologic exam for uveitis; consider bronchoscopy with mediastinal node biopsy if diagnostic confirmation is needed.

Confidence: 85%

Reasoning: The biopsies from three separate sites (liver, iliac bone, lumbar vertebra) all show non-caseating granulomas without malignant cells. Combined with negative TB (IGRA-negative, AFB-negative) and comprehensive negative fungal testing (serology and molecular), metastatic cancer and common infections are ruled out. The multisystem imaging pattern (mediastinal/hilar uptake, hepatic/splenic involvement, osseous disease) with modest FDG avidity and the documented chronic inflammatory changes on imaging from a year prior support sarcoidosis as a systemic granulomatous disease. The absence of constitutional symptoms is consistent with indolent sarcoidosis.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The clinical, radiologic, and pathologic findings are most consistent with **systemic sarcoidosis** rather than metastatic breast cancer, despite imaging mimicry.

**Evidence supporting sarcoidosis diagnosis:**

The cornerstone finding is biopsy-proven non-caseating granulomatous disease at three independent anatomic sites (liver, iliac bone, lumbar vertebra) without any malignant cells [F47, F48, F49, F51, F52, F54, F55]. This histology is reproduced consistently across multiple sites and is characteristic of systemic granulomatous disease [R6, R28]. A comprehensive infectious workup rules out the major granulomatous pathogens: tuberculosis is excluded by negative interferon-gamma release assay [F56, R9]; fungal organisms (histoplasma, blastomyces, coccidioides) are excluded by negative serology [F57, F58, F59, R12, R13, R14] and negative molecular testing [F62, R11]; syphilis is excluded by negative treponemal serology [F60, R15]; and acid-fast bacilli are ruled out by negative molecular testing [F61, R10]. This comprehensive negative infectious workup met against biopsy-proven non-caseating granulomas satisfies diagnostic criteria for sarcoidosis by exclusion [R24, R30].

Multisystem granulomatous involvement is documented across bone (L1, L3, sacrum, iliac bones) [F31, F32, F33, F34], liver [F47], spleen [F39], mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymph nodes [F37, F38], and abdominal-inguinal lymph nodes [F41]. This multivisceral distribution is characteristic of systemic sarcoidosis [R3, R25]. MRI marrow signal abnormalities with enhancement at multiple vertebral levels and iliac bones are consistent with bone marrow granulomatous inflammation [R1], and the modest FDG-PET uptake (SUV 2.8–5.6 across all sites) [F44] is characteristic of granulomatous inflammation rather than high-grade malignancy [R2]. The absence of constitutional B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue) [F6] is more consistent with early-stage granulomatous disease [R17]. The intramedullary marrow lesions without cortical destruction or periosteal involvement lack the destructive features typical of true bone metastases and can mimic metastatic disease [R4, R29].

**Evidence against metastatic breast cancer:**

Multiple independent biopsies—hepatic, iliac, and lumbar—all show granulomatous inflammation without malignant cells [F47–F49, F51–F55]. The absence of carcinoma on hepatic biopsy excludes metastatic breast cancer involvement of liver [R7], and absence of carcinoma on both osseous biopsies excludes metastatic disease [R8]. Surveillance mammography several months after surgery showed no residual or recurrent disease in either breast [F28, F29], making recurrence in the contralateral breast unlikely. The patient lacks constitutional symptoms typical of disseminated malignancy [F6, R17].

**On the temporal relationship and possible etiologic triggers:**

Prior imaging obtained approximately 1 year before breast cancer diagnosis showed findings compatible with chronic inflammatory process [F63, F64, R23], suggesting sarcoidosis predated the cancer by approximately 2.5 years. However, the presentation of symptomatic manifestations a few weeks after completion of anti-HER2 antibody therapy [F27] raises the possibility that immune checkpoint modulation or antibody-dependent cellular immunity triggered by trastuzumab may have activated or accelerated the granulomatous response [R19]. Ongoing aromatase inhibitor therapy could theoretically contribute to a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction [R20], though this is poorly documented. Chemotherapy completed ~18 months prior is within the typical 4–24 month window for chemotherapy-induced sarcoid-like reactions [R21], though the prior imaging suggests the granulomatous process was already present.

**On the concurrent diagnosis of breast cancer:**

The patient has biopsy-confirmed, stage IB hormone-receptor–positive, HER2-positive invasive ductal carcinoma that has completed primary treatment. Sarcoidosis has a documented association with increased malignancy risk; concurrent breast cancer and sarcoidosis may represent a paraneoplastic phenomenon or two independent diseases [R31]. The timing (cancer diagnosed 18 months ago, sarcoidosis visible on imaging ~1 year before that) suggests two independent processes.

**Diagnostic confidence and caveats:**

The diagnosis of sarcoidosis is highly supported by the combination of biopsy-proven non-caseating granulomas at multiple sites, comprehensive negative infectious serology and molecular testing, and multisystem clinical and radiologic distribution. However, the rulebook notes that nontuberculous mycobacteria can cause disseminated non-caseating granulomatous disease; negative AFB testing and negative fungal molecular testing argue against but do not exclude if cultures were not performed [R32]. The prior imaging history strengthens confidence that this is a chronic systemic process; if the prior imaging is indeed the same granulomatous disease, this provides strong chronologic support for sarcoidosis.

**Next steps should include formal staging of sarcoidosis**, confirmation of pulmonary involvement (chest X-ray or CT), measurement of serum/urine calcium, serum ACE, and ophthalmologic examination, while ensuring continued breast cancer surveillance remains on track.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly identify the core diagnosis: systemic sarcoidosis (non-caseating granulomatous disease) mimicking metastatic breast cancer recurrence, confirmed by multi-site biopsies plus a negative infectious workup. Both correctly cite the three-site biopsy pattern (liver, iliac, vertebra), the negative TB/fungal/treponemal/AFB testing, the modest FDG avidity, the prior imaging ~1 year before cancer diagnosis, and the indolent multisystem pattern. This matches the ground truth's "HOW CONFIRMED" precisely. Both are therefore substantively CORRECT on diagnosis and confirmation mechanism.

OUTPUT A is more complete and better traced. It explicitly addresses the central clinical decision the ground truth emphasizes — that these lesions should be recognized as benign granulomatous disease and NOT escalated to metastatic-breast-cancer therapy, with biopsy as the decisive gating step (it leads with "biopsy-proven... without any malignant cells" and frames the whole answer around the metastatic-mimic distinction). It grounds nearly every claim in specific finding/rule citations [F.., R..], which is highly defensible/traceable, and it appropriately flags caveats (NTM not fully excluded without cultures). Its weaknesses: some speculative etiologic theorizing (trastuzumab/aromatase-inhibitor triggers, paraneoplastic association) that the ground truth does not support and that risks mild hallucination, though A hedges these as "poorly documented"/"theoretical." It does not state the actual disposition taken (deferred corticosteroids, expectant management, stable 4-month follow-up), instead pivoting to sarcoidosis staging next steps.

OUTPUT B is correct and well-calibrated (85% confidence, clean reasoning) but thinner. It gives the diagnosis and a reasonable next-step workup (calcium, ACE, CXR, ophthalmology, possible mediastinal node biopsy) but does NOT explicitly make the key management point that recurrence therapy should be withheld in favor of recognizing benign disease — the crux of "CORRECT DISPOSITION." It also suggests further confirmatory bronchoscopy/node biopsy, which is reasonable but slightly redundant given three diagnostic biopsies already confirmed the pattern. It introduces no hallucinations and is tightly defensible, but covers less of the ground-truth content.

Neither output names the disposition details (deferred steroids, stable surveillance) exactly, so neither is fully complete on management. A's superior coverage of the metastatic-mimic framing and decision-not-to-escalate logic, plus its dense traceable citations, outweighs its speculative tangents. B is cleaner and better calibrated but less complete on the load-bearing disposition reasoning. On balance A is the stronger, more defensible answer.

per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old man presented to a community hospital with three weeks of low-grade fever, a productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest discomfort, and breathlessness when climbing stairs. He reported drenching night sweats for roughly the same period but denied weight loss, coughing up blood, or recent travel. He worked as an industrial floor-coating installer and described frequent use of solvent and resin sprays in poorly ventilated spaces, often without a respirator. He had never smoked and did not drink alcohol. There was no relevant family history and he took no regular medications.

This was his second presentation for the same problem. About ten weeks earlier he had been seen elsewhere with cough, fever, and exertional dyspnea, told he had pneumonia, and discharged on oral antibiotics. He improved only briefly each time. Over the intervening weeks he had received, in turn, a course of doxycycline for about three weeks, a short course of azithromycin, a two-week course of an oral respiratory fluoroquinolone, and most recently a week of an intravenous aminopenicillin/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combination, which produced a few days of defervescence before the fever returned.

On examination he was alert and in no acute distress. Temperature was 38.1 °C, heart rate 79/min, blood pressure 124/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 17/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Crackles were audible over the right base. There was no lymphadenopathy, clubbing, or peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and a normal comprehensive metabolic panel. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was markedly elevated at 82 mm/h (reference <15) and C-reactive protein was 7.2 mg/dL (reference <0.3). An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative, as were initial sputum studies.

A chest radiograph showed persistent consolidation in the right lower and middle zones that had not cleared since the earlier films, now with some new nodular opacities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated dense multifocal consolidation involving the left upper lobe and the right lower lobe, with focal low-attenuation areas suggesting small abscess-like cavitation within the consolidated right lower lobe, together with scattered bilateral pulmonary nodules and cavitating nodules. A whole-body PET study showed increased tracer uptake corresponding to the consolidated and nodular regions.

Given the lack of response to several appropriate antibiotic regimens, he underwent bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound and sampling of a subcarinal (station 7) node, which was non-diagnostic, followed by transbronchial lung biopsy; a surgical (thoracoscopic) sampling was also arranged.
per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Pneumonic-type lung adenocarcinoma — specifically invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung (a primary lung cancer that radiographically and clinically mimics infectious pneumonia). 

How confirmed: After failure of multiple sequential antibiotic courses for presumed community-acquired / "non-resolving" pneumonia, the diagnosis was established histopathologically by transbronchial lung biopsy showing adenocarcinoma with mucinous features consistent with invasive mucinous (adeno)carcinoma. (Bronchoscopy/EBUS sampling of the level-7 node was inconclusive; the transbronchial tissue was the positive sample; VATS was also performed. Infectious workup including IGRA for tuberculosis was negative.) No molecular results (EGFR/KRAS/ALK) were reported for the patient, though the discussion notes EGFR mutations in up to ~75% of pneumonic-type adenocarcinoma in some series.

Correct disposition: Recognize that an immunocompetent young non-smoker with "pneumonia" that fails to resolve across multiple appropriate antibiotic courses — with persistent/migratory multifocal consolidation plus cavitating nodules and bilateral nodularity — must be worked up for malignancy (and other non-infectious causes), NOT given yet another antibiotic. The key red flag is antibiotic-refractory consolidation. Definitive step = tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy/transbronchial, with VATS if needed). After histologic confirmation of invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, the patient was referred to oncology for staging and management. Source case: 27-year-old male, Hackensack Meridian Health Ocean Medical Center, Brick, NJ, USA.

rulebook.rule: Cavitary pulmonary consolidation with persistent fever and productive cough for >4 weeks raises suspicion for mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria)
rulebook.source: American Thoracic Society/CDC/IDSA Tuberculosis Guidelines (2016) - cavitary disease is hallmark of reactivation TB; consolidation without resolution on antibiotics is classic presentation for TB

rulebook.rule: Cavitary pulmonary consolidation with persistent fever and productive cough for >4 weeks raises suspicion for mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria)
rulebook.source: ATS/IDSA/Infectious Diseases Society of America NTM Guidelines (2007) - cavitary MAC disease occurs in immunocompetent hosts; MAC mimics TB radiographically and clinically

rulebook.rule: Negative interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) in patient with cavitary disease and positive clinical presentation lowers probability of tuberculosis but does not exclude it; false-negative IGRA occurs in 10-15% of patients with active pulmonary tuberculosis
rulebook.source: Mazurek et al. (2010) MMWR - Latent Tuberculosis Infection and Tuberculosis Disease; CDC reports sensitivity of IGRA in active TB is 85-90%, with lower sensitivity in cavitary disease populations; confirmation requires microbiologic evidence

rulebook.rule: Negative IGRA makes active tuberculosis diagnosis less likely but is concordant with nontuberculous mycobacterial diagnosis since MAC does not generate tuberculosis-specific interferon-gamma response
rulebook.source: Gopinath et al. (2006) J Clin Microbiol - MAC does not activate TB-specific T-cell response; IGRA negative is expected in MAC pulmonary disease

rulebook.rule: Negative IGRA is expected in fungal pulmonary infection (histoplasmosis, aspergillosis, coccidioidomycosis) since IGRA specifically detects TB-specific immune response
rulebook.source: Kauffman (2007) Clin Infect Dis - Fungal infections do not activate TB-specific gamma-interferon; IGRA will be negative in endemic mycoses and aspergillosis

rulebook.rule: Cavitary lung disease with focal low-attenuation areas ('abscess-like cavitation') suggests necrotic/mycobacterial process or fungal infection with tissue invasion; cavitation is not a feature of hypersensitivity pneumonitis
rulebook.source: Hansell et al. (2008) Radiology - Cavitation in TB typically shows thin-walled cavity with air-fluid level or central necrosis on CT; appearance matches 'abscess-like' descriptor

rulebook.rule: Cavitary consolidation with abscess-like appearance raises suspicion for fungal cavitary disease, particularly in occupational settings with mold exposure
rulebook.source: Groen et al. (2020) Lancet Infect Dis - Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis presents with single or multiple cavities, often with fungal ball; occupational exposure to Aspergillus spores in construction/industrial settings is risk factor

rulebook.rule: Cavitary lung disease is NOT a typical feature of hypersensitivity pneumonitis; absence of cavitation in occupational lung disease with exposure history supports HP diagnosis while presence of cavitation argues against pure HP
rulebook.source: Mohr et al. (2013) Eur Respir Rev - Hypersensitivity pneumonitis presents with centrilobular nodules, ground-glass opacities, and reticular patterns; cavitation is not a feature and should prompt search for alternative diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Cavitation is not a typical feature of organizing pneumonia (bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia, BOOP); presence of cavitating lesions argues against BOOP as sole diagnosis
rulebook.source: Epler (2001) Chest - Organizing pneumonia typically presents with bilateral patchy consolidation/nodules without cavitation; cavitation should raise suspicion for other entities

rulebook.rule: Failure to respond to sequential appropriate antibiotics (doxycycline, macrolide, fluoroquinolone, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combination) over 10 weeks with only brief symptomatic responses suggests organism intrinsically resistant to these agents

rulebook.source: Groen et al. (2020) Lancet Infect Dis - Fungal infections produce PET avidity; aspergillosis and histoplasmosis both FDG-avid

rulebook.rule: Absence of weight loss in patient with 10 weeks of fever and cough is atypical for classic tuberculosis presentation; weight loss occurs in majority of TB cases
rulebook.source: Blumberg et al. (2003) MMWR - TB classically presents with constitutional symptoms including weight loss; absence of weight loss is atypical but does not exclude TB

rulebook.rule: Absence of weight loss in patient with 10 weeks of fever and cough is less typical for disseminated fungal disease but does not exclude it; weight loss occurs in majority of chronic histoplasmosis cases
rulebook.source: Kauffman (2007) Clin Infect Dis - Histoplasmosis commonly causes weight loss; aspergillosis may not; absence of weight loss does not exclude fungal infection

rulebook.rule: Absence of hemoptysis is consistent with but does not exclude tuberculosis; hemoptysis occurs in minority of TB cases and is not required for diagnosis
rulebook.source: Blumberg et al. (2003) MMWR - Hemoptysis occurs in ~30% of cavitary TB; its absence does not exclude TB

rulebook.source: Groen et al. (2020) Lancet Infect Dis - Chronic cavitary aspergillosis may present without hemoptysis; hemoptysis typically occurs when secondary aspergilloma forms

rulebook.rule: Crackles on lung examination over right base correlate with right-sided consolidation seen on imaging; consistent with air-space disease (pneumonia, abscess, infarction)
rulebook.source: Hansell et al. (2008) Radiology - TB commonly involves right apex but can involve lower lobes; consolidation produces crackles on examination

rulebook.rule: Absence of lymphadenopathy on clinical examination does not exclude mediastinal/hilar lymph node involvement; EBUS-guided sampling indicates radiographic/imaging evidence of nodal enlargement
rulebook.source: Hansell et al. (2008) Radiology - TB commonly presents with hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; lymph nodes may not be palpable on exam but visible on imaging

rulebook.rule: Non-diagnostic EBUS-guided lymph node sampling (station 7) does not exclude tuberculosis or malignancy; sampling may have been insufficient, and disease may be peripheral rather than nodal
rulebook.source: Ash et al. (2015) - EBUS-TBNA sensitivity for TB is 70-80%; non-diagnostic result does not exclude TB; additional tissue sampling (transbronchial biopsy, surgical biopsy) recommended

rulebook.rule: Non-diagnostic EBUS-guided lymph node sampling (station 7) does not exclude fungal infection; sampling may have been insufficient, and disease may be peripheral parenchymal rather than nodal
rulebook.source: Current endoscopic ultrasound literature - EBUS best suited for nodal sampling; fungal infections may have minimal nodal involvement with primarily parenchymal disease

rulebook.rule: Non-diagnostic EBUS-guided lymph node sampling (station 7) does not exclude malignancy; additional imaging/biopsy needed for definitive diagnosis
rulebook.source: Ash et al. (2015) - Non-diagnostic EBUS-TBNA must be followed by additional diagnostic procedures; malignancy cannot be excluded on basis of non-diagnostic nodal sampling

rulebook.rule: Young age (34 years) with no smoking history lowers baseline probability of primary lung cancer but does not exclude it; cavitary lung lesions in young patients warrant consideration of infectious and inflammatory etiologies first
rulebook.source: Devesa et al. (1989) and subsequent epidemiologic data - Lung cancer incidence peaks in smokers >60 years; young non-smokers at very low baseline risk but cases do occur

rulebook.rule: Fever, productive cough, and night sweats (constitutional symptoms) for 3+ weeks are consistent with chronic infection including tuberculosis, mycobacterial infection, or invasive fungal disease
rulebook.source: Blumberg et al. (2003) MMWR - TB presents with gradual onset fever, cough, night sweats; classic constellation of symptoms

rulebook.rule: Fever, productive cough, and night sweats (constitutional symptoms) for 3+ weeks are consistent with chronic infection including tuberculosis, mycobacterial infection, or invasive fungal disease
rulebook.source: ATS/IDSA NTM Guidelines - MAC presents with chronic cough, fever, night sweats; symptoms often indistinguishable from TB

rulebook.rule: Fever, productive cough, and night sweats (constitutional symptoms) for 3+ weeks are consistent with chronic infection including tuberculosis, mycobacterial infection, or invasive fungal disease
rulebook.source: Kauffman (2007) Clin Infect Dis - Histoplasmosis and coccidioidomycosis present with fever, cough, night sweats; often misdiagnosed as TB initially

rulebook.source: Hansell et al. (2008) Radiology - TB can present with pleurisy; pleural involvement indicates active pulmonary TB with visceral pleural involvement
