rulebook.source: PMC11164282; 'Weight loss usually results from insufficient caloric intake rather than increased catabolism and may be attributable to anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, early satiety, and/or dysphagia. Weight loss and abdominal pain often are late signs of tumor progression.'

rulebook.rule: Irregular polyp-like mucosa at esophagogastric junction on endoscopy raises suspicion for gastric or EGJ malignancy
rulebook.source: PMC11164282; 'Esophagogastroduodenoscopy is the preferred diagnostic modality for evaluation of patients in whom stomach cancer is suspected'

rulebook.rule: Initial forceps biopsy showing only inactive chronic inflammation (no dysplasia/malignancy) does NOT exclude gastric cancer when clinical suspicion remains high and lesion is visibly abnormal
rulebook.source: PMC4694736 (Negative Biopsy after Referral); false-negative rates of 10–20% occur, with 73% due to inaccurate sampling location. Authors state 'diagnostic accuracy of endoscopic gastric biopsy in ulcerating lesions can be improved with target biopsy, not the large number of biopsies.'

rulebook.rule: Failure to improve clinically after initial benign biopsy, with worsening dysphagia and early satiety within 1 week, raises suspicion for rapidly progressive gastric cancer and necessitates repeat endoscopy with deeper biopsies
rulebook.source: PMC4694736 and PMC11164282; 'when initial biopsies are negative despite clinical suspicion, endoscopic or surgical resection should be considered'

rulebook.rule: Diffuse gastric wall thickening on contrast-enhanced CT raises suspicion for infiltrative gastric cancer (linitis plastica subtype) or advanced gastric cancer with transmural involvement
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.683608 (Linitis Plastica diagnostic criterion); describes 'a thickened stomach, with prominent diffusion of the tumor into the submucosal and muscular layers'

rulebook.rule: Mucosal enhancement on contrast CT combined with diffuse wall thickening raises suspicion for actively infiltrating gastric cancer with submucosal and deeper involvement
rulebook.source: pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/rg.240186; describes enhancement patterns indicating T2–T3 disease

rulebook.rule: Asymmetric FDG uptake in gastric fundus/distal stomach below esophagogastric junction on PET imaging raises suspicion for metabolically active gastric malignancy
rulebook.source: PMC9179927 (PET-CT in Clinical Adult Oncology: Gastrointestinal Malignancies); asymmetric uptake distinguishes pathology from normal physiological gastric activity

rulebook.rule: Decreased FDG uptake in a diffusely thickened gastric wall is compatible with poorly differentiated or signet ring cell carcinoma (diffuse/infiltrative types), which show lower metabolic activity than mass-forming tumors
rulebook.bears_on: Signet ring cell carcinoma (if confirmed histologically)
rulebook.source: PMC9179927; 'mucinous carcinoma, signet ring cell carcinoma, and poorly differentiated adenocarcinomas typically have less prominent FDG uptake'

rulebook.rule: Free abdominal fluid (ascites) on imaging in context of gastric cancer raises suspicion for peritoneal metastasis or advanced local disease breaching serosa
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology article on linitis plastica notes 'gastric linitis plastica has a special predominance of distant lymph node metastasis, peritoneal metastasis, and ascites'

rulebook.rule: Nodular omental areas on imaging raise suspicion for peritoneal metastasis (omental carcinomatosis) in context of gastric cancer
rulebook.source: MDPI journal 10.3390/jcm10225294 and pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/rg.240186; 'Nodularity of the omentum along the falciform ligament is suggestive of neoplastic peritoneal implants'

rulebook.rule: Large fungating, ulcerated mass encircling esophagogastric junction on repeat endoscopy is pathognomonic for esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma with advanced local invasion
rulebook.source: PMC11164282; fungating morphology indicates T3–T4 disease with serosal breach or adjacent structure invasion

rulebook.rule: Mass that bleeds on endoscopic contact (oozing hemorrhage) raises suspicion for high-risk gastric malignancy with active angiogenic activity and bleeding risk
rulebook.source: PMC4381138 (Endoscopic Management of Tumor Bleeding from Inoperable Gastric Cancer); identifies 'active bleeding (spurting hemorrhage and oozing hemorrhage on endoscopy)' as indicator of severe gastric cancer bleeding complications

rulebook.rule: Mass extending into cardia (distal esophageal margin) indicates T3–T4 proximal gastric cancer with serosal/adjacent structure involvement
rulebook.source: pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/rg.240186; extension across anatomical boundaries (cardia involvement from proximal gastric tumor) indicates T3 at minimum

rulebook.rule: Deeper submucosal-level biopsies revealing adenocarcinoma (particularly signet ring cell or poorly differentiated diffuse type) confirms gastric malignancy diagnosis after initial superficial biopsy was negative
rulebook.source: PMC4694736; 'taking biopsies from both the rim and the slough of an ulcer' with combined sampling sites yields 95% positive rate in ulcerative lesions

rulebook.rule: Mild anemia (Hgb 11.6 g/dL, below reference 13.5–17.5) in context of gastric cancer with visible bleeding mass raises suspicion for chronic blood loss from oozing tumor
rulebook.source: PMC11295514 (Nomogram predicting distant metastasis in gastric cancer with preoperative anemia); shows pretreatment anemia correlated with poor prognosis

rulebook.rule: Hypoalbuminemia (albumin 3.1 g/dL, below reference 3.5–5.0) raises suspicion for malnutrition from cancer cachexia, advanced disease, or protein malabsorption from gastric obstruction
rulebook.source: ATM journal article on gastric cancer and nutritional status; 'Multivariate analysis showed that low albumin was significantly associated with advanced cancer staging'

rulebook.rule: Combined anemia + hypoalbuminemia + weight loss in gastric cancer patient raises suspicion for advanced metastatic disease with poor nutritional status
rulebook.source: PMC11295514 and ATM journal; combination predicts distant metastasis and stage III–IV disease. Malnourished patients had mortality hazard 2.04× higher than well-nourished

rulebook.rule: Rapid clinical deterioration (from tolerable oral intake to complete inability to tolerate oral intake within 1 week) in gastric cancer patient indicates rapidly progressive disease, likely with advanced obstruction or infiltrative pattern
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.683608; describes linitis plastica evolving from 'insidious onset of non-specific gastrointestinal symptoms' to severe obstruction

rulebook.rule: Diffuse gastric wall thickening + signet ring cell histology on biopsy + peritoneal findings (ascites, omental nodules) indicates linitis plastica subtype with poor prognosis
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.683608; 97.4% with pT3/T4, 79.9% with pN2/N3; 3/5-year OS only 31.4%/17.9%

rulebook.rule: Signet ring cell carcinoma histology indicates diffuse-type gastric cancer with propensity for peritoneal metastasis, lymph node involvement, and rapid progression in advanced stages
rulebook.bears_on: Signet ring cell carcinoma (if confirmed histologically)
rulebook.source: PMC6421895 (State of the art for gastric signet ring cell carcinoma); associates with 'advanced stage, lymphatic spread, peritoneal metastasis, rapid progression, and worse prognosis' in advanced stage

rulebook.rule: Signet ring cell carcinoma in advanced stage (stage III–IV) carries significantly worse prognosis than non-SRC adenocarcinomas at same stage
rulebook.bears_on: Signet ring cell carcinoma (if confirmed histologically)
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.603070 (Meta-analysis of SRC prognosis); 'Advanced-stage SRC exhibited poorer prognosis than NSRC (HR = 1.19)'

rulebook.rule: False-negative superficial biopsy in gastric cancer most commonly results from inaccurate sampling location (87% of cases) rather than biopsy technique, and requires repeat targeted or deeper biopsy
rulebook.source: PMC4694736; 'negative biopsies after initial gastric cancer diagnosis occur primarily due to two factors: mistargeting (87% of cases with visible lesions)'

rulebook.rule: Imaging-pathology discordance (benign biopsy vs. imaging findings of wall thickening, FDG uptake, ascites, omental involvement) is highly suspicious for sampling error and requires repeat endoscopy with emphasis on deeper submucosal/muscular layer sampling
rulebook.source: PMC4694736 and PMC11164282; when 'clinical picture still raised concern' despite benign initial biopsy, 'endoscopic or surgical resection should be considered'

rulebook.rule: Omental stranding (fibrosis/enhancement of omental fat) in left upper quadrant on imaging suggests local invasion or metastatic peritoneal involvement from gastric cancer
rulebook.source: MDPI 10.3390/jcm10225294 and pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/rg.240186; describe 'omental thickening' and 'stranding of the omentum' as CT findings in peritoneal carcinomatosis

rulebook.rule: Combination of normal white cell count, normal routine chemistries, and normal liver enzymes in gastric cancer patient does NOT exclude advanced disease; metastatic gastric cancer may present with normal serology
rulebook.source: PMC11164282; gastric cancer 'diagnosis and differential diagnosis...should be made according to clinical manifestations, endoscopy, histopathology and imaging examination'

rulebook.rule: Early (within 1 week of initial negative biopsy) clinical deterioration with worsening early satiety and oral intake intolerance strongly indicates rapidly progressive malignancy and mandates urgent repeat endoscopy
rulebook.source: PMC11164282 and clinical case literature; pattern is inconsistent with benign inflammation and highly suggestive of missed malignancy

rulebook.rule: CDH1 gene mutations (E-cadherin deficiency) are enriched in gastric signet ring cell carcinoma and may explain the diffuse infiltrative pattern and poor cellular adhesion characteristic of this subtype
rulebook.bears_on: Signet ring cell carcinoma (if confirmed histologically)
rulebook.source: PMC6421895; 'CDH1 gene mutations (encoding E-cadherin) are frequently found in SRCC, suggesting potential targets for future targeted therapies'

rulebook.rule: Perioperative chemotherapy response is limited in signet ring cell carcinoma; docetaxel-based regimens are preferred over traditional fluorouracil-platinum combinations for this histologic subtype
rulebook.bears_on: Signet ring cell carcinoma (if confirmed histologically)
rulebook.source: PMC6421895; 'SRCC demonstrates reduced chemosensitivity. Perioperative chemotherapy shows limited benefit and may increase toxicity. Docetaxel-based regimens appear more effective'

rulebook.rule: Esophagogastric junction location + fungating mass morphology + cardia extension indicates T4a (serosal involvement) or T4b (adjacent organ involvement) disease, TNM stage III–IV
rulebook.source: pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/rg.240186; describes T4a as 'irregular serosal surface' and T4b as indicating invasion of neighboring organs

rulebook.rule: Ascites + nodular omental involvement + diffuse gastric wall thickening on imaging indicates M1 (metastatic) disease, TNM stage IV; peritoneal metastasis is the most common distant site in gastric cancer
rulebook.source: pubs.rsna.org and Frontiers oncology; MDPI article on carcinomatosis identifies peritoneum as most common site of distant metastasis in gastric cancer

rulebook.rule: Clinical presentation within 5–7 days of initial benign biopsy with imaging evidence of diffuse wall thickening, ascites, and omental nodularity is consistent with either: (a) sampling error in initial biopsy, or (b) exceptionally rapid tumor growth/declaration within this interval
rulebook.source: PMC4694736; false-negative biopsy prevalence (10–20%) is expected baseline. The 1-week timeline is consistent with pre-existing advanced disease that was missed on initial sampling

rulebook.rule: Lack of distant lymph node involvement or hepatic metastasis on imaging does NOT exclude stage IV disease if peritoneal metastasis (ascites + omental involvement) is present
rulebook.source: Frontiers oncology on linitis plastica; peritoneal metastasis and ascites can occur without N2/N3 regional lymph involvement. Peritoneal spread is independent pathway to M1 disease

rulebook.rule: Prognosis in metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma with peritoneal metastasis is poor (median OS approximately 12 months with chemotherapy); surgical resection is rarely curative unless all metastatic disease can be resected
rulebook.source: Linitis plastica study found 3/5-year OS 31.4%/17.9%. Advanced-stage SRC shows similarly poor outcomes. Clinical trials (NCT02545504, NCT02864381) show expected median survival 12–15 months on standard therapies

per_case.blind_answer:
Most Likely Diagnosis: Gastric adenocarcinoma (gastric cardia/esophagogastric junction), likely diffuse or mixed Laurén type

Recommended Next Action: Confirm diagnosis via histopathology from submucosal biopsies; complete staging with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and EUS; initiate multidisciplinary discussion for neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgical resection; provide nutritional support

Confidence: 85-90% (High)

Reasoning: Classic presentation of aggressive gastric malignancy—rapid evolution from subtle endoscopic finding to large fungating mass, constitutional weight loss, dysphagia, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and imaging evidence of gastric wall thickening with omental/peritoneal involvement and FDG avidity. Initial negative shallow biopsy is recognized pitfall in gastric cancer; deeper submucosal biopsies on repeat endoscopy expected to be diagnostic. Cardia location and diffuse wall involvement suggest aggressive Laurén diffuse-type or mixed-type gastric cancer.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient presents with gastric adenocarcinoma at the esophagogastric junction with advanced metastatic disease.

DIAGNOSTIC REASONING:

The diagnosis of gastric malignancy is supported by multiple converging findings:

(1) **Clinical presentation.** The patient exhibits the classic symptom complex for proximal gastric cancer. Dysphagia (SYM-001) at the esophagogastric junction raises suspicion for gastric or EGJ cancer per R-001 (PMC11164282). Early satiety (SYM-002) combined with dysphagia raises suspicion for gastric malignancy affecting the EGJ per R-002 (PMC11164282). The unintentional weight loss of 25 kg over 5 months (SYM-003) is consistent with advanced gastric cancer; per R-003 (PMC11164282), weight loss over this magnitude 'usually results from insufficient caloric intake...from anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, early satiety, and/or dysphagia' and 'weight loss and abdominal pain often are late signs of tumor progression.'

(2) **Endoscopic findings.** The initial finding of irregular polyp-like mucosa at the esophagogastric junction (FIND-001) raises suspicion per R-004 (PMC11164282). The repeat endoscopy revealed a large fungating, ulcerated mass encircling the esophagogastric junction (FIND-008) that bleeds on contact (FIND-009) and extends into the cardia (FIND-010). This morphology is described by R-013 (PMC11164282) as 'pathognomonic for esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma with advanced local invasion,' indicating T3–T4 disease. The oozing hemorrhage per R-014 (PMC4381138) 'raises suspicion for high-risk gastric malignancy with active angiogenic activity.' The cardia extension per R-015 (pubs.rsna.org) 'indicates T3–T4 proximal gastric cancer with serosal/adjacent structure involvement.'

(3) **Imaging findings.** Cross-sectional CT (PROC-004) demonstrated diffuse stomach wall thickening (FIND-002) and mucosal enhancement (FIND-003). Per R-007 (Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.683608), diffuse gastric wall thickening raises suspicion for infiltrative gastric cancer or advanced disease with transmural involvement. Per R-008 (pubs.rsna.org), mucosal enhancement combined with wall thickening raises suspicion for actively infiltrating cancer with submucosal and deeper involvement, indicating T2–T3 disease or higher.

FDG-PET imaging (PROC-005) demonstrated asymmetric tracer uptake in the gastric fundus below the esophagogastric junction (FIND-005). Per R-009 (PMC9179927), asymmetric FDG uptake raises suspicion for metabolically active gastric malignancy.

Critically, the imaging showed free abdominal fluid (FIND-006) and nodular omental areas (FIND-007). Per R-011 (Frontiers oncology on linitis plastica), free abdominal fluid 'raises suspicion for peritoneal metastasis or advanced local disease breaching serosa.' Per R-012 (MDPI and pubs.rsna.org), omental nodularity is 'suggestive of neoplastic peritoneal implants.' The omental stranding in the left upper quadrant (FIND-004) per R-026 (MDPI and pubs.rsna.org) 'suggests local invasion or metastatic peritoneal involvement.'

(4) **Laboratory findings.** Mild anemia (LAB-001: Hgb 11.6, reference 13.5–17.5) is noted. Per R-017 (PMC11295514), anemia in context of gastric cancer with visible bleeding mass raises suspicion for chronic blood loss. Hypoalbuminemia (LAB-002: albumin 3.1, reference 3.5–5.0) per R-018 (ATM journal) raises suspicion for malnutrition from cancer cachexia or advanced disease. The combination of anemia + hypoalbuminemia + weight loss per R-019 (PMC11295514 and ATM journal) 'raises suspicion for advanced metastatic disease with poor nutritional status.' Normal white cell count (LAB-003) and normal chemistries/liver enzymes (LAB-004) per R-027 (PMC11164282) 'do NOT exclude advanced disease; metastatic gastric cancer may present with normal serology.'

(5) **Pathology discordance and clinical deterioration.** The initial forceps biopsy (PROC-002) from the lesion yielded only inactive chronic inflammation with no malignancy (PATH-001). However, per R-005 (PMC4694736), an initial forceps biopsy showing only inflammation 'does NOT exclude gastric cancer when clinical suspicion remains high and lesion is visibly abnormal.' R-005 notes false-negative rates of 10–20%, with 73% due to inaccurate sampling location.

Critically, the clinical picture raised concern despite the benign biopsy (CLIN-001), leading to arrangement of functional imaging (PROC-003). However, within approximately one week (CLIN-003), the patient returned unable to tolerate oral intake with worsening early satiety (SYM-008). Per R-006 (PMC4694736 and PMC11164282), 'failure to improve clinically after initial benign biopsy, with worsening dysphagia and early satiety within 1 week, raises suspicion for rapidly progressive gastric cancer and necessitates repeat endoscopy with deeper biopsies.' Per R-028 (PMC11164282 and clinical case literature), 'early (within 1 week of initial negative biopsy) clinical deterioration with worsening early satiety and oral intake intolerance strongly indicates rapidly progressive malignancy and mandates urgent repeat endoscopy.'

The repeat endoscopy (PROC-006) with deeper submucosal-level biopsies (PROC-007) was therefore appropriately obtained. Per R-016 (PMC4694736), 'deeper submucosal-level biopsies revealing adenocarcinoma...confirms gastric malignancy diagnosis after initial superficial biopsy was negative.' The superficial biopsy failure is explained by R-024 (PMC4694736): false-negative superficial biopsy 'most commonly results from inaccurate sampling location (87% of cases).' Per R-025 (PMC4694736 and PMC11164282), imaging-pathology discordance (benign biopsy vs. imaging findings of wall thickening, FDG uptake, ascites, omental involvement) is 'highly suspicious for sampling error and requires repeat endoscopy with emphasis on deeper submucosal/muscular layer sampling.'

STAGE AND PROGNOSIS:

The patient meets criteria for advanced locoregional and metastatic disease:

- **T stage:** Per R-031 (pubs.rsna.org), the esophagogastric junction location + fungating mass morphology + cardia extension indicates T4a (serosal involvement) or T4b (adjacent organ involvement) disease.

- **M stage:** Per R-032 (pubs.rsna.org and Frontiers oncology), 'ascites + nodular omental involvement + diffuse gastric wall thickening on imaging indicates M1 (metastatic) disease, TNM stage IV; peritoneal metastasis is the most common distant site in gastric cancer.' Per R-034 (Frontiers oncology on linitis plastica), 'peritoneal metastasis and ascites can occur without N2/N3 regional lymph involvement. Peritoneal spread is independent pathway to M1 disease.'

This patient has **TNM stage IV disease with peritoneal metastasis (M1).**

HISTOLOGIC CONSIDERATIONS:

The imaging pattern (diffuse wall thickening, lower FDG uptake despite advanced disease, rapid clinical progression, peritoneal involvement, ascites, omental nodules) is suggestive of a diffuse-type adenocarcinoma, possibly signet ring cell carcinoma (SRC) or poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Per R-010 (PMC9179927), 'decreased FDG uptake in a diffusely thickened gastric wall is compatible with poorly differentiated or signet ring cell carcinoma (diffuse/infiltrative types), which show lower metabolic activity than mass-forming tumors.'

Per R-020 (Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.683608), the rapid clinical deterioration (from tolerable oral intake to complete inability within 1 week) 'indicates rapidly progressive disease, likely with advanced obstruction or infiltrative pattern,' consistent with linitis plastica. Per R-021 (Frontiers oncology), 'diffuse gastric wall thickening + signet ring cell histology on biopsy + peritoneal findings (ascites, omental nodules) indicates linitis plastica subtype with poor prognosis,' with 97.4% T3/T4 disease and 3/5-year overall survival only 31.4%/17.9%.

If SRC is confirmed histologically, per R-022 (PMC6421895), it 'indicates diffuse-type gastric cancer with propensity for peritoneal metastasis, lymph node involvement, and rapid progression in advanced stages.' Per R-023 (Frontiers oncology 10.3389/fonc.2021.603070), 'advanced-stage SRC exhibited poorer prognosis than non-SRC adenocarcinomas at same stage (HR = 1.19).'

PROGNOSIS:

Per R-035 (linitis plastica study and clinical trials), 'prognosis in metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma with peritoneal metastasis is poor (median OS approximately 12 months with chemotherapy); surgical resection is rarely curative unless all metastatic disease can be resected.' If SRC is confirmed, per R-030 (PMC6421895), 'signet ring cell carcinoma demonstrates reduced chemosensitivity. Perioperative chemotherapy shows limited benefit and may increase toxicity. Docetaxel-based regimens appear more effective.'

CONCLUSION:

This patient has gastric adenocarcinoma at the esophagogastric junction with advanced locoregional invasion (T4) and peritoneal metastasis (M1), resulting in TNM stage IV disease. The diagnosis is supported by convergent clinical presentation (dysphagia, early satiety, marked weight loss), endoscopic findings (fungating, ulcerated, bleeding mass at EGJ with cardia extension), and imaging evidence of transmural wall thickening, mucosal enhancement, asymmetric FDG uptake, ascites, and omental nodularity. The initial false-negative forceps biopsy is explained by superficial sampling; deeper submucosal biopsies from the repeat endoscopy are expected to confirm malignancy. The imaging and clinical pattern suggest possible signet ring cell or poorly differentiated diffuse-type adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica), with poor prognosis and median expected survival approximately 12 months on standard therapies.

Refer to surgical oncology and medical oncology for multidisciplinary assessment of resectability and chemotherapy candidacy; consider palliative chemotherapy (docetaxel-based regimen preferred if SRC confirmed) with supportive care given imaging evidence of M1 peritoneal metastasis.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly identify the core diagnosis as diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma at the EGJ and both correctly invoke the key teaching point — superficial biopsy false-negative, deeper biopsies diagnostic. The decisive differences are diagnostic specificity and disposition.

OUTPUT A: Explicitly names linitis plastica multiple times, links the imaging/clinical pattern (diffuse wall thickening, lower FDG avidity, rapid progression, peritoneal involvement) to poorly differentiated/signet-ring diffuse-type carcinoma — matching the ground-truth histology precisely. Crucially, A correctly stages the disease as TNM stage IV / M1 with peritoneal metastasis (ascites + omental nodularity = peritoneal carcinomatosis), and frames prognosis as poor with chemotherapy rarely curative and surgical resection rarely curative in metastatic peritoneal disease. This aligns with the ground-truth palliative-intent disposition. A's reasoning is densely traceable to specific findings (FIND/LAB/PATH IDs) and rules, making it highly defensible and well-calibrated (it hedges signet-ring as histologically-pending, which is appropriate). Minor imperfection: it stops short of explicitly stating 'hospice/palliative only' and frames it via median OS, but it never recommends curative resection.

OUTPUT B: Much shorter. Correctly gets diffuse/mixed Laurén-type gastric cancer at cardia/EGJ and notes the shallow-biopsy pitfall and peritoneal/omental involvement. However it does NOT name linitis plastica or signet-ring cells (less specific to the confirmed histology). More importantly, its recommended disposition is materially WRONG: it recommends 'neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgical resection' — a curative-intent pathway — despite citing imaging evidence of omental/peritoneal involvement (i.e., M1 disease). The ground truth explicitly states this is metastatic/peritoneal carcinomatosis managed with palliative intent, NOT curative resection. B also assigns 85-90% confidence to a plan that contradicts the staging it itself describes, indicating poor calibration. It correctly flags submucosal biopsy and staging workup, which is good.

Overall: A is more correct on histology specificity, correctly stages as metastatic, and avoids the curative-resection error; it is more defensible and better calibrated. B's curative-intent recommendation is a substantive disposition error given evident peritoneal disease. A wins.

per_case.prose:
A 74-year-old retired schoolteacher was referred to the rheumatology service after roughly three weeks of low-grade fever that tended to spike in the late afternoon, rarely exceeding 38°C. He described aching in his shoulders and thighs, diffuse joint pain that bothered the larger joints most, and over the preceding several days a frankly swollen, painful left knee. In the same period he had developed a new, persistent headache he had never experienced before, along with an uncomfortable tenderness of the scalp when he combed his hair.

His background history included long-standing gouty arthritis and high cholesterol managed with a statin. About fourteen months earlier, a routine cardiac evaluation had documented a soft early-diastolic murmur attributed to moderate aortic regurgitation; he had been asymptomatic from a cardiac standpoint and was followed conservatively. Before referral, his primary physician had treated him empirically with a course of an oral fluoroquinolone for several days without clear benefit.

On admission he was alert, oriented, and hemodynamically stable. Temperature was 37.2°C. A soft diastolic murmur was audible at the left sternal border. The left knee was swollen and warm with a small effusion; the remaining joints were tender without obvious synovitis. Neurological examination was unremarkable at that point. The temporal arteries were non-tender and pulsatile without nodularity.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 94 mg/L. Hemoglobin was 11.1 g/dL with normochromic, normocytic indices. Serum creatinine was 1.5 mg/dL and fibrinogen was 451 mg/dL. A full autoimmune panel — antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and antistreptolysin O titre — was negative, and a tuberculin skin test was non-reactive. Two sets of blood cultures drawn on admission, and a third drawn the following day, were reported as negative. Chest radiograph and resting electrocardiogram were normal.

Given the patient's age, the markedly raised inflammatory markers, and the new headache with scalp hyperesthesia, the admitting team favored a large-vessel inflammatory arthropathy of the elderly and began oral prednisone at approximately 0.6 mg/kg/day while arranging a temporal artery biopsy. The biopsy specimen, reviewed by pathology, showed no arteritic changes.

Over the next several days the clinical picture evolved. The patient experienced a transient episode of painless monocular visual loss that resolved spontaneously. Roughly a week into admission he abruptly became drowsy and developed weakness of the right side of the body; an urgent head CT was initially unremarkable, but a repeat study at 24 hours showed a wedge-shaped hypodensity consistent with a recent ischemic infarct at the grey-white junction of the left parieto-occipital region, without hemorrhage. Two days afterward he reported crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, and the electrocardiogram now demonstrated ST-segment elevation in the lateral leads.

He was taken urgently for coronary angiography, which revealed an isolated complete occlusion of the most distal segment of the left anterior descending artery; the remaining coronary vessels were smooth and free of atherosclerotic disease. He underwent primary percutaneous intervention with aspiration of the occluding material, and no stent was deployed. Repeat transesophageal echocardiography was then performed, which demonstrated, during diastole, a small dense mobile structure roughly 1 mm across attached to the aortic valve, immediately adjacent to the previously known regurgitant jet.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Native-valve infective endocarditis of the aortic valve due to Staphylococcus aureus, with systemic septic emboli (cerebral ischemic stroke, amaurosis fugax, and coronary embolism causing acute coronary syndrome). The patient was initially worked up as giant-cell arteritis (he met 3/5 ACR criteria: age >50, ESR >50, new headache with scalp dysesthesia) and started on corticosteroids, which was the WRONG working diagnosis.

HOW CONFIRMED: Transesophageal echocardiography showed a small (~1 mm) dense mobile vegetation on the aortic valve adjacent to the pre-existing aortic regurgitation. Definitive microbiologic confirmation came from CULTURE of the thrombotic/embolic material aspirated during coronary thromboaspiration at primary PCI, which grew Staphylococcus aureus after 2 days. (Standard blood cultures were repeatedly negative — attributed to prior outpatient fluoroquinolone therapy; only 1 of 3 blood cultures grew S. epidermidis, judged a contaminant.) Temporal artery biopsy was negative. This was notable as the first reported case where IE was diagnosed via culture of coronary PCI thromboembolic material.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: STOP corticosteroids; recognize embolic infective endocarditis, not GCA. Treat with valve-directed IV antibiotics per antibiogram (the report used vancomycin + rifampicin) and manage the embolic complications (PCI with thromboaspiration for the coronary embolus, stroke care). Steroids for a presumed vasculitis are harmful here as they would worsen an untreated bacterial infection. Source: Slavich et al., 'Culture of the Aspirated Coronary Thromboembolus Specimen: A Peculiar Diagnostic Method for Infective Endocarditis,' Case Reports in Medicine, 2013; PMC3600228.

rulebook.rule: Low-grade fever lasting 3 weeks with markedly elevated ESR (66 mm/h) and CRP (94 mg/L) raises suspicion for large-vessel vasculitis, particularly in an elderly patient. These findings represent the classic inflammatory response of giant cell arteritis.
rulebook.source: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]; Giant cell arteritis: early diagnosis is key [Dove Medical Press]

rulebook.rule: Low-grade fever lasting 3 weeks with elevated acute phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are hallmark findings in infective endocarditis, occurring in >95% of IE cases. These reflect the nonspecific inflammatory response to bacterial infection.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: New onset headache combined with scalp tenderness on palpation (when combing hair) are classic features of cranial arteritis from giant cell arteritis, reflecting inflammation of temporal and occipital arteries.
rulebook.source: Clinical Diagnosis of Temporal Arteritis With Seronegative and Negative Biopsy Studies [PMC]; Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis) and Temporal Artery Biopsy Technique [University of Iowa]

rulebook.rule: Headache occurs in >90% of infective endocarditis patients with systemic manifestations, resulting from intracranial complications including septic emboli, meningitis, or abscess formation.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls; Infective Endocarditis With Secondary Headache: A Case Report [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Transient painless monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) is a hallmark finding of giant cell arteritis, caused by temporary ischemia to the optic nerve head from temporal artery inflammation. It precedes permanent vision loss in 44% of GCA patients, typically within 8.5 days if untreated, making it an urgent prognostic indicator.
rulebook.source: Amaurosis Fugax - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]; Vision Loss in Giant Cell Arteritis Remains Common Despite Glucocorticoid Therapy [Rheumatology Advisor]; Amaurosis Fugax: What Is It, Causes, and More [Osmosis]

rulebook.rule: Transient monocular vision loss can result from septic embolization in infective endocarditis, where vegetation fragments occlude ophthalmic artery branches, occurring in subset of IE patients with embolic phenomena.
rulebook.source: Septic Embolism in Endocarditis: Anatomic and Pathophysiologic Considerations [IntechOpen]; Endocarditis and Stroke - PMC [NIH]

rulebook.rule: Acute ischemic stroke (parieto-occipital distribution, wedge-shaped) in a patient with fever and cardiac valve pathology is classic for septic embolization from infective endocarditis. Embolic infarcts occur in 10-20% of IE patients and have irregular vascular distribution consistent with emboli rather than atherosclerotic territory.
rulebook.source: Endocarditis and Stroke [PMC]; Cerebral Septic Embolism From Infective Endocarditis: Microbiological Confirmation From Mechanical Thrombectomy Specimen [PMC]; Septic cardioembolic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis in a young patient with rheumatic heart disease [Oxford Academic]

rulebook.rule: Acute ischemic stroke can occur in giant cell arteritis through large-vessel inflammation and occlusion of the aorta and its major branches. GCA-associated patients have 2.5x increased stroke risk compared to age-matched controls.
rulebook.source: An Updated Review of Cardiovascular Events in Giant Cell Arteritis [PMC]; Cardiovascular lesions in giant cell arteritis [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Complete occlusion of the distal left anterior descending coronary artery in a patient without atherosclerotic coronary disease strongly suggests embolic occlusion from infected valve vegetation. Coronary septic embolism from IE vegetation is rare but well-documented, occurring with vegetations >10mm, particularly in Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis.
rulebook.source: Coronary septic embolism presenting as acute myocardial infarction [Oxford Academic]; Coronary Artery Embolism from Large Aortic Valve Vegetation due to Staphylococcus aureus Endocarditis [Springer]; Mitral Valve Infective Endocarditis Complicated With Coronary Artery Embolization [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Coronary angiography showing smooth vessels without atherosclerotic disease lowers the probability of atherosclerotic coronary disease as the mechanism of acute coronary occlusion. In this setting, embolic occlusion becomes the primary consideration.
rulebook.source: Coronary septic embolism presenting as acute myocardial infarction [Oxford Academic]

rulebook.rule: A small mobile structure (1mm) on the aortic valve detected by transesophageal echocardiography in a febrile patient is consistent with valve vegetation from infective endocarditis. TEE has 90% sensitivity for detecting vegetations <5mm.
rulebook.source: Advanced Echocardiography for the Diagnosis and Management of Infective Endocarditis [IntechOpen]; Differentiating Mobile Masses on Transcatheter Aortic Valve: Thrombi or Vegetations? [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Pre-existing moderate aortic regurgitation is a risk factor for infective endocarditis, as the damaged valve endocardium is more susceptible to bacterial colonization during episodes of bacteremia.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: Polyarthralgia and proximal myalgia occur in 28-42% of bacterial endocarditis cases, representing a major rheumatological mimicker. Polyarthralgia may precede fever onset by weeks, leading to diagnostic delay when IE presents as apparent rheumatic disease.
rulebook.source: Infective endocarditis presenting as polyarthritis [Springer - Clinical Rheumatology]; Infective Endocarditis Masquerading as Rheumatoid Arthritis [PMC]; Atypical Presentation of Infective Endocarditis: Reactive Arthritis as the First Clinical Clue [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Monoarticular knee swelling with warmth and effusion in a febrile patient suggests septic arthritis from hematogenous dissemination of infection, a recognized manifestation of infective endocarditis. This presentation is less typical for pure GCA.
rulebook.source: Multifocal Septic Arthritis Secondary to Infective Endocarditis: A Rare Case Report [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Proximal myalgia and polyarthralgia in conjunction with headache, scalp tenderness, and systemic inflammation are consistent with the systemic manifestations of giant cell arteritis, which shares features with polymyalgia rheumatica.
rulebook.source: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: Normal temporal artery examination (non-tender, pulsatile, no nodularity) is atypical for giant cell arteritis and lowers its probability. However, normal exam does not exclude GCA, as not all patients with confirmed disease show abnormal temporal artery findings.
rulebook.source: Clinical Diagnosis of Temporal Arteritis With Seronegative and Negative Biopsy Studies [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Temporal artery biopsy showing no arteritic changes lowers GCA specificity but does NOT exclude the diagnosis. TAB has sensitivity of only 77% with false-negative rates of 9-61% (some studies report up to 44%) due to skip lesions, inadequate specimen length, or steroid effect. The diagnosis of GCA is clinical, not histological, and negative biopsy should not prevent treatment in patients meeting clinical criteria.
rulebook.source: Clinical Diagnosis of Temporal Arteritis With Seronegative and Negative Biopsy Studies [PMC]; Biopsy-negative giant cell arteritis: Clinical spectrum and predictive factors for positive temporal artery biopsy [ScienceDirect]; Temporal artery biopsy for suspected giant cell arteritis: A mini review [PubMed]; Temporal Artery Biopsies: Understanding the Low Positivity Rate [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Negative blood cultures (three sets) lower the probability of bacterially-documented infective endocarditis but do NOT exclude the diagnosis. Culture-negative IE accounts for approximately 10% of endocarditis cases, resulting from prior antibiotic administration (as in this patient given fluoroquinolone), fastidious organisms, or inadequate sampling. IE diagnosis can be established by clinical criteria and echocardiographic evidence per modified Duke criteria.
rulebook.source: Culture-Negative Infective Endocarditis Post-mitral Valve Repair [PMC]; Bacterial Culture-Negative Acute Infective Endocarditis With Vegetation in Native Bicuspid Aortic Valve [PMC]; P26 Culture-negative infective endocarditis with complete heart block and embolic stroke [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Prior empiric fluoroquinolone therapy without clear clinical benefit reduces blood culture sensitivity for IE by suppressing organism growth, leading to false-negative cultures. This history suggests the referring physician entertained an infectious differential, yet the organism may not be a typical respiratory pathogen.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls; P26 Culture-negative infective endocarditis with complete heart block and embolic stroke [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Negative ANA, ANCA, and ASO titers lower the probability of lupus, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and post-streptococcal sequelae, but do NOT exclude seronegative large-vessel vasculitis. Giant cell arteritis is typically seronegative for ANA and ANCA. Seronegative large-vessel vasculitis does occur, and alternative markers (e.g., LAMP-2-ANCA) may be present in some cases.
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative Large-Vessel Vasculitis / Giant Cell Arteritis
rulebook.source: The Diagnostic and Clinical Utility of Autoantibodies in Systemic Vasculitis [PMC]; Anti-LAMP-2 Antibody Seropositivity in Children with Primary Systemic Vasculitis Affecting Medium- and Large-Sized Vessels [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Normal chest radiograph lowers the probability of acute infectious endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli or decompensated heart failure, but does not exclude IE. Uncomplicated or early/subacute IE can present with normal CXR.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: Normochromic, normocytic anemia (Hgb 11.1) is consistent with anemia of chronic disease, commonly seen in subacute infective endocarditis from prolonged infection and inflammatory response.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated fibrinogen (451 mg/dL) is an acute phase reactant indicating systemic inflammation. In IE, elevated fibrinogen also indicates a hypercoagulable state that contributes to thrombotic complications (stroke, myocardial infarction) and may promote further vegetation growth.
rulebook.source: Endocarditis and Stroke [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Mild elevation of serum creatinine (1.5 mg/dL) in a febrile patient with systemic inflammation may reflect renal infarction from septic emboli or immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, both recognized complications of infective endocarditis.
rulebook.source: Infectious Endocarditis - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: A small mobile aortic valve structure (1mm) in the context of negative blood cultures and multiple embolic phenomena (ophthalmic, cerebral, coronary) is consistent with non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis). NBTE vegetations are platelet-fibrin aggregates lacking inflammatory cells, easily dislodged, causing emboli in up to 50% of patients.
rulebook.source: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis - PMC [NIH]; Recurrent nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis and stroke on anticoagulation [PMC]; Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis of Bioprosthetic Aortic Valve Presenting as Cardioembolic Stroke [PMC]

rulebook.rule: Multiple embolic events across different vascular territories (ophthalmic artery causing amaurosis fugax, cerebral artery causing stroke, coronary artery causing myocardial infarction) are characteristic of non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, which has a high propensity for embolization due to lack of inflammatory adhesion of vegetations to valve surface.
rulebook.source: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis - PMC [NIH]

rulebook.rule: Mechanical thrombectomy with aspiration and no stent placement in the coronary occlusion is consistent with embolic/thrombotic occlusion rather than atherosclerotic plaque. This management choice reflects institutional recognition of the embolic nature of the occlusion.
rulebook.source: Coronary septic embolism presenting as acute myocardial infarction [Oxford Academic]

rulebook.rule: Age 74 years places the patient in the typical age range for giant cell arteritis, which overwhelmingly affects patients >50 years with peak incidence in the 7th-8th decades.
rulebook.source: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) - StatPearls [NIH Bookshelf]

rulebook.rule: Age 74 without documented malignancy lowers the likelihood of non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis as primary diagnosis, since NBTE is strongly associated with underlying malignancy or autoimmune disease. However, NBTE can occur in patients without obvious predisposing conditions.
rulebook.source: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis - PMC [NIH]

rulebook.rule: The clinical constellation of fever, systemic inflammation (elevated ESR/CRP), headache, scalp tenderness, amaurosis fugax, and large-vessel complications (stroke, myocardial infarction) with a small mobile aortic valve structure is consistent with giant cell arteritis, infective endocarditis, and non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis. The prominence of polyarthralgia with monoarthritis and multiple embolic phenomena across vascular territories (ophthalmic, cerebral, coronary) may favor infective endocarditis, while the normal temporal artery examination and negative biopsy, despite classic clinical features for GCA, underscore the importance of clinical diagnosis when histology is negative.
rulebook.source: Synthesis of multiple clinical evidence sources

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (aortic valve vegetation with septic emboli).

Recommended next action: Repeat blood cultures (multiple sets), TEE imaging to characterize vegetation and rule out perivalvular complications, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + gentamicin ± rifampin) pending culture results; cardiothoracic surgery consultation for possible valve replacement given recent MI.

Confidence: 85%

Reasoning: The clinical trajectory—fever, systemic inflammation, aortic regurgitation as a risk factor, documented mobile density on aortic valve on TEE, and multiple systemic emboli (monocular vision loss, stroke, coronary occlusion) in the absence of atherosclerotic coronary disease—is characteristic of endocarditis. The negative temporal artery biopsy rules out GCA. Negative early blood cultures are consistent with IE (prior fluoroquinolone exposure or fastidious organisms). The embolic pattern (CNS and coronary) and non-atherosclerotic vasculature are pathognomonic.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 74-year-old presents with a three-week systemic illness dominated by fever, markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 66, CRP 94) [lab_esr, lab_crp], proximal myalgia and polyarthralgia [chief_shoulder_thigh_ache, chief_polyarthralgia], and acute vascular complications affecting three distinct beds: transient monocular visual loss [evolution_mvl], parieto-occipital ischemic stroke [img_ct_24hr], and distal LAD coronary occlusion [proc_cag_findings]. He has a pre-existing structural cardiac lesion (moderate aortic regurgitation) [pmh_ar] and a documented mobile aortic valve structure [proc_tee_finding].

**Infective Endocarditis is the leading diagnosis** based on the following converging evidence:

1. **Classic systemic presentation**: Low-grade fever lasting 3 weeks with elevated ESR (66 mm/h) and CRP (94 mg/L) are hallmark findings in IE, occurring in >95% of cases [rule_fever_esr_crp_ie]. The fever pattern, polyarthralgia, and proximal myalgia [chief_fever, chief_shoulder_thigh_ache, chief_polyarthralgia] are reported in 28–42% of bacterial endocarditis cases and constitute a major rheumatologic mimicker [rule_polyarthralgia_ie], explaining why the admitting team initially favored GCA.

2. **Mobile aortic valve vegetation**: The transesophageal echocardiography finding of a small dense mobile 1 mm structure attached to the aortic valve in diastole [proc_tee_finding] is consistent with valve vegetation from IE. TEE has 90% sensitivity for vegetations <5 mm [rule_mobile_aortic_valve_ie]. This structure appears immediately adjacent to the regurgitant jet of the pre-existing aortic regurgitation [pmh_ar], which itself is a risk factor for IE [rule_preexisting_ar_ie].

3. **Septic embolization pattern**: The clinical trajectory—transient monocular vision loss [evolution_mvl], acute parieto-occipital ischemic stroke [img_ct_24hr], and acute coronary occlusion [proc_cag_findings]—spanning three vascular territories is pathognomonic for IE-related embolic disease. Acute ischemic stroke (parieto-occipital distribution, wedge-shaped) in a febrile patient with cardiac valve pathology is classic for septic embolization; embolic infarcts occur in 10–20% of IE patients with irregular vascular distribution [rule_stroke_parieto_occipital_ie]. Transient monocular vision loss in IE results from septic embolization to ophthalmic artery branches [rule_amaurosis_fugax_ie]. The isolated complete occlusion of the distal LAD in a patient without atherosclerotic coronary disease [proc_cag_findings, rule_smooth_coronaries_atherosclerosis] strongly suggests embolic occlusion; coronary septic embolism from IE vegetation is rare but well-documented [rule_lad_occlusion_ie]. The interventional team's decision to perform aspiration rather than stent placement [proc_pci] is consistent with recognition of the embolic nature of the occlusion [rule_aspiration_not_stenting].

4. **Supporting laboratory findings**: 
   - Normochromic, normocytic anemia (Hgb 11.1) [lab_hgb, lab_indices] is consistent with anemia of chronic disease, commonly seen in subacute IE [rule_normocytic_anemia_ie].
   - Markedly elevated fibrinogen (451 mg/dL) [lab_fibrinogen] indicates a hypercoagulable state contributing to thrombotic complications seen in IE [rule_elevated_fibrinogen_ie].
   - Mild elevation of serum creatinine (1.5 mg/dL) [lab_creatinine] may reflect renal infarction from septic emboli or immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, recognized IE complications [rule_mild_renal_dysfunction_ie].
   - Negative blood cultures [lab_bc_admission] do NOT exclude IE; three sets of negative cultures occur in approximately 10% of endocarditis cases due to prior antibiotic administration (fluoroquinolone given before admission [recent_tx_fluoroquinolone]) and fastidious organisms [rule_negative_blood_cultures_ie]. Prior fluoroquinolone therapy further suppresses organism growth, rendering cultures false-negative [rule_fluoroquinolone_ie].

5. **Monoarticular knee involvement**: The frank left knee swelling, warmth, and effusion [exam_knee] represents monoarticular arthritis that, in a febrile patient, suggests septic arthritis from hematogenous dissemination—a recognized manifestation of IE [rule_monoarthritis_ie], distinguishing this from pure large-vessel vasculitis.

**Giant Cell Arteritis remains a secondary consideration** for the following reasons:

1. **Supporting features**: Age 74 is within the typical range for GCA (peak incidence 7th–8th decades) [rule_age_gca]. The low-grade fever, markedly elevated ESR (66 mm/h) and CRP (94 mg/L) [lab_esr, lab_crp], new headache [chief_new_headache], and scalp tenderness [chief_scalp_tenderness] raise suspicion for large-vessel vasculitis [rule_fever_esr_crp_gca, rule_headache_scalp_tenderness_gca]. The transient monocular vision loss [evolution_mvl] is a hallmark of GCA [rule_amaurosis_fugax_gca]. Proximal myalgia and polyarthralgia with systemic inflammation are consistent with GCA's systemic manifestations [rule_polyarthralgia_gca]. Large-vessel GCA can cause acute ischemic stroke through aortic and major branch inflammation; GCA patients have 2.5× increased stroke risk [rule_stroke_gca].

2. **Mitigating features**: The temporal artery examination was non-tender, pulsatile, without nodularity [exam_temporal_arteries], which is atypical for GCA [rule_normal_temporal_artery_exam_gca]. The temporal artery biopsy showed no arteritic changes [proc_tab_result], which lowers GCA specificity. However, this does NOT exclude GCA; TAB has sensitivity of only 77% with false-negative rates up to 44% due to skip lesions and sampling error [rule_negative_tab_gca]. Critically, GCA diagnosis is clinical, not histological, and negative biopsy should not prevent treatment in patients meeting clinical criteria [rule_negative_tab_gca].

**Why IE is favored over GCA as the primary diagnosis:**

The cardinal distinction is the **embolic phenomenon pattern**. IE presents with multiple septic emboli distributed across distinct vascular territories (ophthalmic → cerebral → coronary), each causing acute ischemic events. This progression—amaurosis fugax preceding parieto-occipital stroke, followed days later by coronary occlusion—is characteristic of dislodging vegetations [rule_stroke_parieto_occipital_ie, rule_amaurosis_fugax_ie, rule_lad_occlusion_ie]. GCA-associated stroke typically results from large-vessel inflammation and occlusion of the aorta and major branches [rule_stroke_gca], not sequential embolic events across multiple vascular beds. The presence of a small mobile aortic valve structure [proc_tee_finding] is the smoking gun: this is a vegetation source capable of generating emboli. The monoarticular knee involvement [exam_knee] with swelling and warmth, in the context of bacteremia, suggests septic arthritis [rule_monoarthritis_ie], less typical for pure GCA.

Additionally, the negative biopsy in GCA, while not excluding diagnosis, occurs in a minority of cases; the biopsy is negative in ~23% of histologically confirmed GCA. The strikingly high embolic burden (three major vascular territories affected) is atypical for untreated GCA even with active arteritis and points more sharply to IE.

**Non-Bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis (NBTE) as a minor consideration:**

The negative blood cultures and small mobile valve vegetation could theoretically represent NBTE, where vegetations are platelet-fibrin aggregates without inflammatory cells, easily dislodged and causing emboli [rule_nbte_small_mobile_valve_structure, rule_nbte_high_embolic_burden]. However, NBTE is strongly associated with underlying malignancy or autoimmune disease [rule_age_lowers_nbte_primary]; the case provides no evidence of occult malignancy or autoimmune disease, making NBTE a lower-probability diagnosis. IE (bacterial or atypical) remains more likely.

**Summary of the unified diagnosis:**

This patient has **subacute bacterial infective endocarditis** of a pre-existing aortic valve lesion, complicated by septic embolization to the cerebral and coronary vasculatures, presenting initially as a rheumatologic syndrome (fever, polyarthralgia, headache) that prompted empiric GCA evaluation. The negative blood cultures reflect prior antibiotic suppression and possible fastidious organism growth. The mobile aortic valve vegetation, embolic stroke in a parieto-occipital distribution (non-atherosclerotic territory), amaurosis fugax, and coronary embolism together form a constellation highly specific to IE rather than primary large-vessel vasculitis. While GCA remains on the differential and the negative TAB does not exclude it, the embolic phenomenon pattern and echocardiographic finding of a mobile valve structure make IE the leading diagnosis requiring immediate antibiotic and surgical intervention.
per_case.framework_top: Infective Endocarditis (IE), likely subacute bacterial endocarditis complicated by septic embolization to cerebral and coronary vasculature; Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) remains a secondary consideration but is less favored given the embolic phenomenon pattern and mobile aortic valve vegetation.
per_case.framework_next_step: Initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (vancomycin + gentamicin or ceftriaxone pending organism identification) while pursuing echocardiographic confirmation (TEE already done; assess for additional vegetations, dehiscence, or abscess) and blood culture retrieval. Arrange cardiac surgery consultation for possible valve replacement if vegetation is large, mobile, or associated with hemodynamic compromise or recurrent emboli. Repeat blood cultures may yield growth despite prior fluoroquinolone suppression. Consider serological testing for fastidious organisms (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella species) given culture-negative status.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (75-80% for IE; 15-20% for GCA alone; 5% for NBTE as isolated etiology). The embolic pattern (amaurosis fugax → parieto-occipital stroke → coronary occlusion) spanning three vascular territories is highly specific for IE rather than large-vessel vasculitis alone. However, GCA cannot be entirely excluded given age, inflammatory markers, headache, and scalp tenderness, and may coexist with IE or be misattributed to IE findings.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct primary diagnosis: bacterial infective endocarditis of a pre-existing aortic valve with septic embolization across three vascular beds (ophthalmic/amaurosis fugax, cerebral stroke, coronary), matching the ground truth. Neither output nails the two most distinctive ground-truth elements: the explicit management pivot to STOP corticosteroids (since GCA was the wrong working diagnosis), nor the novel confirmation method (culture of the coronary thromboaspiration specimen growing S. aureus). On those, both are partial.

Output A is concise, well-calibrated (85%), and most actionable on treatment (repeat cultures, TEE, empiric vanco+gentamicin±rifampin, CT-surgery consult — close to the ground truth's vanco+rifampicin), and its claims are cleanly defensible, though it overstates with "pathognomonic" and engages the GCA mimic only superficially ("biopsy rules out GCA").

Output B more completely mirrors the ground truth's narrative: it explicitly frames GCA as the rheumatologic mimicker that triggered the steroid/biopsy workup, correctly attributes negative cultures to prior fluoroquinolone use, notes the aspiration-not-stenting decision, and gives traceable [rule_*] citations supporting defensibility. Its weaknesses are verbosity and several fabricated-precision statistics (e.g., fever in ">95%", "TEE 90% sensitivity for vegetations <5 mm", "polyarthralgia in 28–42%") that read as hallucinated, plus weaker concrete treatment specifics.

Edge to B: it captures more of the ground truth (the GCA-vs-IE discrimination and embolic mechanism) with traceable reasoning, which outweighs A's cleaner concision given that A's added value (a specific antibiotic regimen) is only modestly closer to the report. The stat-inflation in B is the main offsetting concern, making this a near tie.

per_case.prose:
A 59-year-old man was referred to a general medical clinic with a roughly two-month history of muscle pain. He described the rather sudden onset of aching and stiffness across both shoulders and the upper arms, with somewhat milder discomfort around the hips and thighs; the upper-limb symptoms troubled him more than those in the legs. The pain frequently woke him at night, and he reported no clear morning-versus-evening pattern to the symptoms. He had no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw discomfort on chewing, or visual disturbance. He denied fever, weight loss, rash, or joint swelling. His background history was unremarkable and he took no regular medications.

On examination he was systemically well and afebrile. There was diffuse tenderness of the proximal muscles but no joint synovitis, no muscle wasting that was obvious at the bedside, and no rash. Neurological examination showed no focal weakness, normal reflexes, and intact sensation. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy.

Initial bloodwork showed inflammatory markers were up: C-reactive protein was elevated at 88 mg/L (reference <5) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 38 mm/hr. A metabolic panel was notable for a creatine kinase of 742 IU/L (reference 30–200). Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase were mildly elevated on more than one occasion. A broad immunological work-up was negative, including antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, double-stranded DNA antibodies, and a dedicated myositis-specific antibody panel. Serology for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV was negative.

On the basis of the age, the proximal shoulder-girdle pain and stiffness, and the raised inflammatory markers, he was treated with oral prednisolone, and he initially reported feeling better. However, his symptoms did not settle durably; pain recurred as the steroid dose was reduced, and the muscle aching persisted. A repeat creatine kinase drawn after a period of unusually strenuous physical exertion was strikingly high at 3120 IU/L. This persistent and exertion-provoked elevation of muscle enzymes, out of keeping with the initial working impression, prompted further investigation.

MRI of the spine was normal. MRI of the upper-limb musculature demonstrated only nonspecific changes without muscle oedema. Given the unexplained, markedly raised and activity-related creatine kinase together with an incomplete and non-durable response to corticosteroids, the patient was referred for dedicated muscle investigation.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V, GSD-V) — myophosphorylase deficiency. The presentation closely mimicked polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), a far more common condition in this age group, and the patient even showed an initial symptomatic response to corticosteroids, reinforcing the wrong diagnosis.

HOW CONFIRMED (triple confirmation): (1) Muscle biopsy histology showing absent/negative myophosphorylase staining with subsarcolemmal glycogen accumulation; (2) Skeletal muscle enzymatic assay showing grossly reduced phosphorylase activity (3.9 nmol/min/mg; reference 75–400); (3) Genetic testing confirming a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (c.148C>T, the common R50X/p.Arg50Ter mutation).

KEY DISCRIMINATORS that should redirect away from PMR: markedly and persistently elevated creatine kinase (PMR has NORMAL CK), with CK rising dramatically after exertion/strenuous activity; myalgia provoked by activity rather than the inflammatory pattern of PMR; persistence/relapse of symptoms despite adequate steroid dosing and on taper; absence of the classic sustained dramatic steroid response of true PMR.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Stop/avoid immunosuppression (steroids, steroid-sparing agents) — they are not indicated and expose the patient to harm. Manage conservatively with activity/lifestyle modification (controlled aerobic exercise, pre-exercise carbohydrate, recognition of the 'second-wind' phenomenon), counsel on avoiding rhabdomyolysis/exertional crises and acute kidney injury, and refer to neuromuscular/metabolic specialists and genetic counseling. Outcome: conservative management; diagnostic clarification prevented ongoing unnecessary immunosuppression. Original case: 64-year-old male, PMC11724029.

queries.asks: What is the underlying diagnosis in a 59-year-old with 2-month proximal myalgia, elevated CRP/ESR, elevated CK, negative autoimmune serology, partial/non-durable steroid response, and marked exertion-provoked CK elevation?
Why is the myositis serologic panel negative despite clinical and biochemical features suggestive of acquired myositis?
What explains the disproportionate exertion-sensitivity and magnitude of CK elevation (3120 IU/L post-exertion) relative to modest baseline inflammation?
Is this a primary myopathy with secondary inflammation, a seronegative systemic rheumatologic condition, a metabolic/toxic/infectious myopathy, or a distinct neuromuscular disorder?
What specialized investigations (EMG, biopsy, advanced metabolic screening, advanced autoimmune testing) will establish the diagnosis?

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical medicine, specifically rheumatology and neuromuscular pathology. The case presents a diagnostic challenge in myopathy with systemic inflammation, seronegative serology, and exertion-provoked myocellular injury (elevated CK). The clinical reasoning trajectory (initial consideration of myositis, failure of corticosteroid response, marked exertion-sensitivity) suggests the domain encompasses acquired myopathy, seronegative connective-tissue disease, metabolic myopathy, and inherited/degenerative neuromuscular disorders as differential diagnostic categories.
