rulebook.rule: Proximal myalgia (shoulders, hips) with acute onset in patients >50 years raises PMR; when accompanied by elevated CRP and ESR, diagnostic probability increases
rulebook.source: Polymyalgia rheumatica ( - PMR): https://pmrgca.org.uk/information-and-advice/what-is-pmr/

rulebook.rule: Nocturnal pain causing frequent awakening is nonspecific but consistent with inflammatory myalgias; less characteristic of primary metabolic myopathy
rulebook.source: Myositis Support and Understanding: https://understandingmyositis.org/myositis-antibody-testing/

rulebook.rule: Elevated CRP and ESR with myalgia indicates systemic inflammation and raises suspicion for inflammatory myositis or PMR; modest elevations alone do not exclude metabolic myopathy
rulebook.source: How age and sex affect the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein in early rheumatoid arthritis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4228188/

rulebook.rule: Negative myositis-specific antibody panel does NOT exclude myositis; approximately 20-40% of polymyositis/dermatomyositis cases are seronegative, and diagnosis requires integration with biopsy/EMG
rulebook.source: Myositis Support and Understanding: https://understandingmyositis.org/myositis-antibody-testing/

rulebook.rule: Negative ANA, ENA, and anti-dsDNA do NOT exclude inflammatory myopathy; seronegative myositis, IMNM, and IBM can occur with completely negative immunologic panels
rulebook.source: Blood Tests - The Myositis Association: https://www.myositis.org/about-myositis/diagnosis/blood-tests/

rulebook.rule: Mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase and GGT on multiple occasions lowers probability of primary skeletal muscle disease (myositis/myopathy); raises suspicion for hepatic involvement or other systemic process
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: CK elevation in baseline state (742 IU/L, normal 30–200) is consistent with myositis, IMNM, or metabolic myopathy; marked post-exertional rise (3120 IU/L) is disproportionate to baseline and suggests exercise-provoked myocellular injury (metabolic myopathy or acquired defect)
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative myositis; Metabolic myopathy; Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
rulebook.source: Metabolic Myopathies: Overview, Types of Myopathies, Classification: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1173338-overview/

rulebook.rule: Persistent and exertion-provoked CK elevation with disproportionality (baseline 742, post-exertion 3120) is a hallmark of metabolic myopathy (especially CPT II deficiency, mitochondrial myopathy) and raises this diagnosis significantly; such magnitude of exertional rise is less typical of primary inflammatory myositis
rulebook.bears_on: Metabolic myopathy; Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
rulebook.source: Recurrent myoglobinuria due to carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency: clinical, biochemical, and genetic features of adult-onset cases: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15776096/

rulebook.rule: Exercise-induced exacerbation of myalgia with marked CK elevation is cardinal for CPT II deficiency and metabolic myopathies; less characteristic of purely inflammatory myositis unless triggered by fever or infection
rulebook.bears_on: Metabolic myopathy; Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
rulebook.source: Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase II Deficiency - GeneReviews® - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1253/

rulebook.rule: Partial initial steroid response followed by relapse upon taper is seen in both PMR (>50% relapse rate on tapering) and seronegative myositis; does NOT strongly discriminate between them but raises suspicion for both over primary metabolic myopathy (which does not respond to steroids)
rulebook.source: Long-term glucocorticoid treatment and high relapse rate remain unresolved issues in the real-life management of polymyalgia rheumatica: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8724087/

rulebook.rule: Persistent myalgia despite steroid therapy and relapse on taper lowers diagnosis of typical PMR (which shows durable response to low-dose steroids); raises suspicion for seronegative myositis, IBM, or metabolic myopathy
rulebook.source: What Is the Best Treatment for Polymyalgia Rheumatica? | AAFP: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2010/0315/p788.html

rulebook.rule: Steroid resistance (non-durable remission despite adequate dosing and taper) is characteristic of inclusion body myositis (IBM); also seen in seronegative IMNM and metabolic myopathy; lowers likelihood of typical PMR
rulebook.source: Inclusion body myositis: explanation for poor response to immunosuppressive therapy: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7617187/

rulebook.rule: Absence of focal weakness on neurologic exam is inconsistent with severe myositis (which causes objective proximal weakness); more compatible with myalgia syndrome (PMR, fibromyalgia-like), early myopathy, or metabolic myopathy without acute necrosis
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: Normal reflexes and intact sensation argue against primary neuromuscular disease or neuropathy; compatible with myopathy (myositis, metabolic, or statin-induced)
rulebook.source: Electromyography and Metabolic Myopathies: https://pediatricneurologybriefs.com/articles/10.15844/pedneurbriefs-28-9-4

rulebook.rule: Absence of obvious muscle wasting at bedside does NOT exclude myopathy; true atrophy may be subtle early on and requires imaging (MRI/ultrasound) to detect; muscle biopsy is more sensitive than bedside exam
rulebook.source: Muscle Biopsy: A Requirement for Precision Medicine in Adult-Onset Myopathy: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8951002/

rulebook.rule: MRI showing nonspecific changes only (no edema) is less supportive of active inflammatory myositis; compatible with metabolic myopathy, chronic myopathy, or early myositis below imaging detection threshold
rulebook.source: Muscle biopsy features of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies and differential diagnosis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4386579/

rulebook.rule: Diffuse proximal muscle tenderness on exam is compatible with myositis, myalgia syndrome (PMR), metabolic myopathy, and statin-induced myopathy; nonspecific finding requiring additional diagnostic criteria
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative myositis; Polymyalgia Rheumatica; Metabolic myopathy; Statin-induced myopathy
rulebook.source: Myositis mimics: Clues for making the right diagnosis: https://blogs.the-hospitalist.org/content/myositis-mimics-clues-making-right-diagnosis

rulebook.rule: No joint synovitis on exam lowers diagnosis of seronegative myositis with connective tissue overlap (e.g., anti-synthetase syndrome); raises likelihood of primary myopathy (metabolic, toxic, or isolated inflammatory myositis)
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: Absence of rash, scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication argues against dermatomyositis and giant-cell arteritis; compatible with seronegative myositis subtypes (PM, IBM), PMR, or metabolic myopathy
rulebook.source: Evolution of Seronegative Inflammatory Myositis to Dermatomyositis With Characteristic Cutaneous Features: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10725130/

rulebook.rule: Absence of headache, scalp tenderness, and visual disturbance argues against giant-cell arteritis (PMR-associated); increases likelihood of uncomplicated PMR or alternative myopathy
rulebook.source: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) Treatment & Management: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/330815-treatment

rulebook.rule: Denying fever, weight loss, and constitutional symptoms lowers suspicion for systemic infection, malignancy, or severe connective tissue disease; raises likelihood of primary myopathy or PMR
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly on exam lowers suspicion for malignancy-associated myositis, lymphoproliferative disease, and hepatic dysfunction; argues against systemic infection
rulebook.source: Metastatic Prostate Cancer Mimicking Polymyalgia Rheumatica: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3542944/

rulebook.rule: CPT II deficiency is the most common metabolic cause of recurrent adult-onset exertional myoglobinuria and myalgia; when CK elevation is persistently exertion-provoked with disproportionate magnitude, CPT II deficiency becomes a leading diagnosis to exclude
rulebook.source: Recurrent rhabdomyolysis caused by carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214426918300120

rulebook.rule: Mitochondrial myopathy presents with exercise intolerance, myalgia, proximal weakness, and elevated CK; exertion-provoked symptom worsening and myalgia triggered by low-intensity activity raise this diagnosis
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathy presenting as fibromyalgia: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3293012/

rulebook.rule: Statin myopathy presents with myalgia and can cause CK elevation (though 96.5% of statin-myopathy cases have normal CK); history of statin use raises this diagnosis; absence of statin use makes it much less likely
rulebook.source: What Is Statin-Induced Myopathy or Muscle Pain?: https://www.healthline.com/health/what-is-statin-induced-myopathy-or-muscle-pain

rulebook.rule: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) can be seronegative (no anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP detected) and presents with marked CK elevation, myalgia, and steroid-resistant course; muscle biopsy shows necrosis without significant inflammatory infiltrate
rulebook.source: Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy - Myositis Support and Understanding: https://understandingmyositis.org/imnm-basics/

rulebook.rule: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is steroid-resistant, often seronegative for MSA, presents with myalgia and CK elevation (though often modest); age >50 raises likelihood; myopathic EMG and biopsy showing rimmed vacuoles are diagnostic
rulebook.source: Inclusion Body Myositis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf - NIH: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538200/

rulebook.rule: EMG showing myopathic pattern (short-duration, low-amplitude, polyphasic units) without denervation supports myopathy (myositis, metabolic, or toxic); fibrillations and positive sharp waves indicate myonecrosis (myositis, IMNM)
rulebook.source: Electrodiagnostic Evaluation of Myopathies: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4435557/

rulebook.rule: Muscle biopsy is essential for diagnosis when autoantibodies are negative; findings of fiber necrosis with inflammatory infiltrate favor myositis; minimal inflammation with necrosis suggests IMNM; lipid accumulation (type I fiber emphasis) suggests CPT II or other lipid-storage myopathy; ragged-red fibers suggest mitochondrial myopathy
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative myositis; Metabolic myopathy; Inclusion body myositis
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Value of Muscle Biopsy for the Evaluation of Adult Myopathy: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12732179/

rulebook.rule: Ischemic forearm exercise test showing absent CK rise or myoglobin rise (with absent phosphorylase activity on biopsy) confirms glycogen storage disease (McArdle disease); markedly elevated CK after exertion is less specific and occurs in CPT II, metabolic myopathies, and myositis
rulebook.source: How to do it: investigate exertional rhabdomyolysis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6580786/

rulebook.rule: Negative screening for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV argues against infection-related myositis or myopathy; mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT without other hepatic dysfunction raise lower probability of hepatitis
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: Unremarkable medical history and no regular medication use lower likelihood of drug-induced myopathy or secondary myositis from underlying malignancy or infection
rulebook.source: Drug-related Myopathies of Which the Clinician Should Be Aware: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3092639/

rulebook.rule: Afebrile, systemically well clinical presentation argues against acute infection-related myositis or severe systemic inflammation; compatible with indolent or subacute myositis, metabolic myopathy, or PMR
rulebook.source: Inflammatory Myopathy: When Electromyography and Autoantibodies Don't Help the Diagnosis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10914304/

rulebook.rule: Discordance between clinical severity (myalgia + elevated inflammatory markers) and expected tissue changes (nonspecific MRI, possible normal biopsy in early disease) suggests: (1) early myositis before infiltrate development, (2) metabolic myopathy with secondary inflammation, or (3) myalgia syndrome (PMR) without muscle inflammation
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative myositis; Metabolic myopathy; Polymyalgia Rheumatica
rulebook.source: Muscle biopsy features of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies and differential diagnosis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4386579/

rulebook.rule: Age 59 (older adult, >50 years) raises likelihood of PMR, inclusion body myositis, and age-related myopathy; CPT II deficiency typically presents earlier (median childhood-adolescence) but can present in adulthood
rulebook.source: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) Treatment & Management: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/330815-treatment

rulebook.rule: Mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT on multiple occasions may reflect age-related changes or bone turnover; does not strongly suggest myositis; warrants exclusion of hepatic, bone, or biliary disease as alternative diagnosis
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Approach to Proximal Myopathy - Skills in Rheumatology - NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK585737/

rulebook.rule: If statin use is later discovered in medical history or medications review, anti-HMGCR myopathy (statin-associated IMNM) becomes a strong candidate; this seronegative form presents with marked CK elevation, myalgia, and steroid resistance
rulebook.source: Statin-Induced Anti-3-Hydroxy-3-Methylglutaryl-Coenzyme A Reductase (Anti-HMGCR) Myopathy: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9947569/

rulebook.rule: Two-month disease duration favors acquired myopathy (myositis, toxic, metabolic acquired form) over inherited/congenital myopathy; rapid steroid-refractory course is more consistent with aggressive acquired myositis, IMNM, or progressive metabolic myopathy
rulebook.source: Clinical Usefulness of Autoantibodies in Idiopathic Inflammatory Myositis: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4479798/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Metabolic myopathy, specifically glycogen storage disease (McArdle disease/GSDV) or other muscle energy-metabolism disorder.

Recommended next action: Perform forearm ischemic exercise test (gold standard for glycogenoses; McArdle disease shows absent/blunted lactate response). Follow with muscle biopsy if ischemic test is suggestive, and consider genetic testing for PYGM mutations.

Confidence: 70-75%

Reasoning: The cardinal finding is exertional CK spike (to 3120 IU/L after strenuous activity) in a patient with proximal myalgia and stiffness—classic for glycogen storage myopathies. The poor/non-durable steroid response, normal neurological exam, negative myositis serology, and nonspecific MRI findings make idiopathic inflammatory myositis unlikely. The initial inflammatory markers (elevated CRP, ESR) likely reflect secondary muscle injury rather than true autoimmunity. While PMR initially appeared plausible (age, proximal pain), the exertional CK phenomenon and steroid resistance are incompatible with PMR (which shows CK normal and excellent steroid response). The ischemic exercise test is definitive: McArdle disease shows characteristic absent lactate rise with preserved ammonia/IMP response.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 59-year-old man presents with a diagnostic puzzle that initially suggested inflammatory myositis but now points more strongly toward a primary metabolic myopathy with secondary inflammation.

**Key clinical reasoning:**

1. **Exertion-provoked myocellular injury is the pivotal finding.** The baseline creatine kinase of 742 IU/L (F34) is already elevated, but the dramatic post-exertion rise to 3120 IU/L (F52) following "unusually strenuous physical exertion" (F51) is the critical clue. This persistent and exertion-provoked elevation pattern (F53) is a hallmark of metabolic myopathy, particularly CPT II deficiency and mitochondrial myopathy (R8, R9, R23). The magnitude of exertional rise (4.2-fold) is disproportionate to what is typical of primary inflammatory myositis (R8), which does not ordinarily show such dramatic activity-triggered enzyme elevations.

2. **Steroid resistance and relapse on taper argue against typical PMR.** Although the patient is age 59 (F1) and has proximal shoulder-girdle myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers (F4, F32, F33), which raises the diagnostic likelihood of Polymyalgia Rheumatica (R1), he experienced only partial initial improvement on prednisolone (F47) followed by relapse upon dose reduction (F49) and persistent myalgia (F50). This pattern of non-durable steroid response (F48) is notably atypical for typical PMR, which shows durable response to low-dose steroids in the majority of cases (R11). Steroid resistance is a feature of seronegative inflammatory myopathy, inclusion body myositis (R12), and metabolic myopathy—but metabolic myopathy does not respond to steroids at all, whereas myositis may show partial benefit. The paradox of initial subjective improvement followed by relapse is more consistent with myositis (R10) than with pure metabolic disease, but suggests a more refractory myositis subtype or a metabolic-inflammatory hybrid.

3. **Seronegative antibody status does not exclude myositis, but the imaging discordance is telling.** The negative myositis-specific antibody panel (F41), ANA, ENA, and anti-dsDNA (F38, F39, F40) raise suspicion for seronegative myositis (R4, R5). However, the MRI of the upper-limb musculature showed only nonspecific changes without muscle edema (F56, F57). This absence of edema on imaging is less supportive of active inflammatory myositis (R16) and more compatible with metabolic myopathy, chronic myopathy, or early myositis below detection threshold (R16). The discordance between clinical severity (myalgia + elevated markers) and nonspecific tissue changes suggests either early myositis before infiltrate formation or a metabolic myopathy with secondary inflammation (R34).

4. **Absence of focal weakness and normal neuromuscular exam findings are consistent with early or seronegative myopathy.** The patient has no focal weakness (F25), normal reflexes (F26), and intact sensation (F27), which argues against severe myositis (R13) but is compatible with early myopathy or myalgia syndrome. The absence of obvious muscle wasting at bedside (F23) does not exclude myopathy; true atrophy may be subtle and requires muscle biopsy for definitive assessment (R15).

5. **Metabolic myopathy fits the exertion-provoked pattern more parsimoniously than myositis.** CPT II deficiency (R23) is the most common metabolic cause of recurrent adult-onset exertional myoglobinuria and myalgia, and the disproportionate post-exertional CK rise fits this diagnosis strongly (R8, R9). Mitochondrial myopathy (R24) also presents with exercise intolerance, myalgia, proximal weakness, and elevated CK provoked by exertion. The two-month acquired presentation (F2, F3) is consistent with both CPT II deficiency (which can present in adulthood despite typically earlier onset) and metabolic myopathy (R38).

6. **Minor systemic findings lower but do not exclude broader diagnoses.** The mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase (F35, F36, F37) lower the probability of primary skeletal muscle disease (R6) but warrant exclusion of hepatic or other systemic involvement. The negative hepatitis serologies (F42, F43, F44) and negative HIV (F44) lower suspicion for infection-related myositis (R31). The absence of fever, weight loss, constitutional symptoms (F13, F14), lymphadenopathy (F31), headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication (F9, F10, F11) lower suspicion for systemic infection, malignancy-associated myositis, and giant-cell arteritis (R19, R20, R21, R22).

**Differential considerations:**

- **Seronegative inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis or IMNM):** Still possible. Seronegative myositis (R4, R5) and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) (R26) can present with marked CK elevation, myalgia, and steroid-resistant courses. However, the disproportionate exertion sensitivity and lack of muscle edema on MRI make this less likely as the primary diagnosis than a metabolic process.

- **Inclusion body myositis (IBM):** Age >50 raises likelihood (R27, R35). IBM is steroid-resistant, often seronegative, and presents with myalgia and CK elevation. However, IBM typically manifests with more selective distal weakness and is usually more indolent; the acute 2-month onset with exertion sensitivity is less typical.

- **Polymyalgia Rheumatica:** The age (F1), proximal myalgia (F4), and elevated inflammatory markers (F32, F33) raise likelihood (R1, R35). However, the persistent symptoms on steroids (F48, F49, F50) and the dramatic exertion-provoked CK rise are atypical for PMR, which would not ordinarily present with such marked enzymatic response to activity (R10, R11).

**Why the differential has shifted:**

The initial clinical reasoning (F45) focused on age + proximal myalgia + inflammation, which is classic for myositis or PMR. However, the observation that CK elevation is persistent and exertion-provoked (F53), with a 4.2-fold spike after activity, is out of keeping with the initial impression (F54) and has prompted the referral for dedicated muscle investigation (F59). This exertion sensitivity, combined with steroid refractoriness, nonspecific MRI changes, and seronegative serology, pivots the differential toward metabolic myopathy—specifically CPT II deficiency or mitochondrial myopathy—over classical inflammatory disease.

**Supporting facts and rules:**
- Baseline CK elevation (F34) + dramatic post-exertion rise (F52) = R8, R9, R23
- Persistent exertion-provoked pattern (F53) = R8
- Steroid resistance + relapse on taper (F48, F49, F50) = R11, R12
- Nonspecific MRI without edema (F56, F57) = R16
- Seronegative antibodies (F38, F39, F40, F41) = R4, R5
- No focal weakness on exam (F25) = R13
- Normal neuro exam (F26, F27) = R14
- No obvious wasting (F23) = R15
- Negative infections/malignancy markers (F31, F42, F43, F44) = R21, R22, R31

The next diagnostic maneuver must be muscle biopsy (R29), which will definitively show whether this is myositis (fiber necrosis + inflammation), IMNM (necrosis without significant inflammation), or metabolic myopathy (lipid accumulation, ragged-red fibers, or other storage patterns), combined with EMG (R28) and metabolic enzyme assays to pinpoint the underlying cause.
per_case.framework_top: Metabolic myopathy with secondary inflammation, most likely Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) deficiency or mitochondrial myopathy, with seronegative inflammatory myositis remaining in the differential.
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent muscle biopsy (to distinguish myonecrosis with inflammation vs. lipid accumulation vs. ragged-red fibers) combined with metabolic enzyme assays and genetic testing for CPT II mutations; baseline carnitine levels; ischemic forearm exercise test to assess phosphorylase activity; EMG to characterize myopathic vs. neurogenic pattern.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high (65-75%) for metabolic myopathy as primary diagnosis; lower confidence (40-50%) for PMR or classical seronegative myositis given the exertion-sensitivity pattern. Confidence limited by absence of EMG, biopsy, and metabolic enzyme data.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: McArdle disease (GSD-V, myophosphorylase deficiency), a glycogen storage metabolic myopathy mimicking PMR, with the key discriminators being persistently/exertionally elevated CK (PMR has normal CK) and non-durable steroid response. Confirmation was via biopsy, enzyme assay, and PYGM genetic testing; disposition is to stop immunosuppression and manage conservatively with neuromuscular referral.

OUTPUT B: Names the correct specific diagnosis — "glycogen storage disease (McArdle disease/GSDV)" — as most likely. It correctly identifies the cardinal discriminators (exertional CK spike incompatible with PMR's normal CK and excellent steroid response; inflammatory markers reflecting secondary muscle injury). It recommends forearm ischemic exercise test, muscle biopsy, and PYGM genetic testing, which align with the confirmation pathway. It correctly notes the absent/blunted lactate rise with preserved ammonia/IMP response characteristic of McArdle. Calibration is explicit and reasonable (70-75%). Minor caveat: the classic forearm ischemic test is somewhat dated and risks ischemic contracture, but it remains a recognized screening tool and is defensible. Overall correct, well-calibrated, traceable.

OUTPUT A: Reasons toward metabolic myopathy in general (good directional move away from PMR/myositis) but lands on the WRONG specific entities — CPT II deficiency and mitochondrial myopathy — as the favored diagnoses, never naming glycogen storage disease/McArdle. CPT II is a lipid/fatty-acid oxidation disorder, not glycogenosis, so the specific call is incorrect. It also fabricates a dense, unverifiable scaffold of "F#" facts and "R#" rules (e.g., F1 age 59 vs ground-truth 64) presented as if from a structured case, which inflates apparent rigor but is largely uncheckable and partly inconsistent. It correctly recommends muscle biopsy + EMG + enzyme assays as the next step, and correctly flags the exertional CK pattern and steroid refractoriness as the pivot away from PMR. So A gets the category and workup right but misses the specific diagnosis and is cluttered with unverifiable/hallucinated structured references.

B is more correct (exact diagnosis), better calibrated, and more defensible. A is partially correct (right category, wrong specific disease, fabricated reference apparatus). Winner: B.

per_case.prose:
A 64-year-old woman was referred to a community rheumatology clinic for evaluation of joint pain that had been troubling her for roughly five months. She first noticed aching and stiffness in both wrists, which over the following weeks spread to involve the small joints of both hands and, more recently, both elbows. She described difficulty closing her hands into a fist, particularly in the early part of the day, and reported that the stiffness lasted close to an hour each morning before loosening. She had no fevers, no chills, no drenching night sweats, and no unintentional weight loss, and she had not noticed any rashes or mouth ulcers. Her past medical history was unremarkable and she took no regular medications.

On examination her temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate were all within normal limits. Examination of the head and neck, eyes, mouth, heart, lungs, and abdomen was unremarkable, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy and no skin bruising. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrated soft-tissue swelling and tenderness across the second through fifth metacarpophalangeal joints and the proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, with similar boggy swelling, warmth, and tenderness at both wrists. Both elbows were held in a fixed flexion deformity of approximately 25 to 30 degrees.

Initial laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 11.4 x 10^9/L, a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL with a hematocrit of 31.6%, and a platelet count within normal limits. The C-reactive protein was elevated at 36 mg/L (reference <8) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 47 mm/hr (reference 0-15). Serum calcium and serum creatinine were both within the normal range. Rheumatoid factor was negative and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody was negative.

Plain radiographs of the hands and wrists showed only mild degenerative change without erosions. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the dominant hand demonstrated synovial thickening at the radiocarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints together with flexor tendon tenosynovitis.

A working diagnosis of seronegative inflammatory arthritis was made and the patient was started on oral prednisone 15 mg daily. Over the next several months methotrexate was introduced and titrated up to 25 mg weekly, and when joint symptoms persisted she was transitioned to a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor. Despite more than half a year of escalating therapy her synovitis, swelling, and pain did not meaningfully improve.
per_case.ground_truth: FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Multiple myeloma presenting as a seronegative-RA-like symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis (a myeloma arthropathy / paraneoplastic-type joint presentation). CONFIRMATION: (1) Serum protein electrophoresis positive for a monoclonal M-band; (2) Bone marrow biopsy showing >40% clonal plasma cells; (3) Congo red stain NEGATIVE — excludes amyloid arthropathy as the mechanism; (4) FISH showing monosomy 13 in ~88% of cells. CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize that a "seronegative RA" that is RF-negative AND anti-CCP-negative, has a normocytic anemia and high inflammatory markers, and fails to respond to an adequate trial of glucocorticoids + methotrexate + a TNF inhibitor, warrants a workup for an alternative/occult diagnosis rather than further escalation of DMARD/biologic therapy — specifically a plasma-cell-dyscrasia workup (SPEP/UPEP, serum free light chains, immunofixation) and bone marrow biopsy. Refer to hematology/oncology; treat with anti-myeloma therapy (e.g., bortezomib + dexamethasone). In this published case the patient achieved complete resolution of synovitis on bortezomib/dexamethasone. KEY TEACHING POINT (held from arms): treatment-refractory seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis + anemia is a red flag for multiple myeloma; the arthropathy resolves with treatment of the underlying clone, and amyloid was specifically excluded here (Congo red negative). SOURCE: Schoninger S et al., "A Case of Multiple Myeloma Misdiagnosed as Seronegative Rheumatoid Arthritis and Review of Relevant Literature," Case Reports in Rheumatology, 2018; PMC6201338.

queries.asks: What is the underlying diagnosis explaining this seronegative, symmetric polyarthritis affecting MCPJs, PIPJs, wrists, and elbows in a 64-year-old woman with elevated inflammatory markers, morning stiffness, and fixed elbow deformities?

What is the differential diagnosis for seronegative polyarticular arthritis in this clinical context, including but not limited to: seronegative RA, psoriatic arthritis, other connective tissue diseases, and non-rheumatologic etiologies?

What explains the failure to respond to standard escalating immunosuppressive therapy (prednisone, methotrexate, TNF inhibitor) over 6+ months, and what is the appropriate next diagnostic step or treatment modification?
Are there extra-articular manifestations (systemic, skin, pulmonary, renal, hematologic) that might narrow the differential or guide further investigation?

What is the significance of the specific laboratory abnormalities (WCC 11.4, anemia with Hgb 10.1, elevated CRP and ESR) in refining the diagnosis, and should additional autoimmune serologies be obtained?
What is the pathologic significance of synovial thickening and flexor tenosynovitis on MRI, and does this finding help differentiate among the diagnostic possibilities?

ir.inferred_domain: Rheumatology / Clinical Immunology: diagnosis and management of inflammatory arthritis, seronegative polyarticular joint disease, differential diagnosis of connective tissue disease, treatment resistance and therapeutic escalation

rulebook.rule: Symmetric polyarthritis involving MCPJs and PIPJs bilaterally raises suspicion for rheumatoid arthritis over other seronegative arthropathies
rulebook.source: Inflammatory Polyarthropathy Overview (ScienceDirect): Symmetric pattern of PIP, MCP, and MTP joints bilaterally while sparing DIP is characteristic of RA

rulebook.rule: PIP and MCP joint involvement in symmetric distribution is more suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis than psoriatic arthritis
rulebook.source: Hand and Wrist Involvement in Seropositive RA, Seronegative RA, and PsA (NCBI PMC10095289): Symmetric lesions in PIPs, wrists, juxta-articular osteoporosis more common in RA than PsA

rulebook.rule: Asymmetric joint involvement with DIP joint involvement favors psoriatic arthritis over rheumatoid arthritis
rulebook.source: Hand and Wrist Involvement in Seropositive RA, Seronegative RA, and PsA (NCBI PMC10095289): DIP joint involvement and proliferative bone changes more likely in PsA than RA

rulebook.rule: Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour implies inflammatory joint disease rather than mechanical arthropathy
rulebook.source: Polyarticular Joint Pain in Adults: Evaluation and Differential Diagnosis (AAFP 2023): Morning stiffness lasting longer than one hour implies presence of inflammatory joint disease

rulebook.rule: Morning stiffness lasting 1-3 hours that improves with movement is consistent with rheumatoid arthritis
rulebook.source: Rheumatoid Arthritis Morning Stiffness (Joint Relief Journal): RA patients commonly report morning stiffness lasting 1-3 hours that gradually improves with activity

rulebook.rule: Elevated WCC (>11 × 10⁹/L) in context of symmetric polyarthritis supports inflammatory arthritis diagnosis
rulebook.source: Prevalence of Anemia in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis (NCBI PMC11586881): Elevated white blood cell count seen in inflammatory arthropathies including RA

rulebook.rule: Anemia (Hgb <10.5 g/dL) in setting of elevated inflammatory markers and polyarthritis raises suspicion for rheumatoid arthritis
rulebook.source: Prevalence of Anemia in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis (NCBI PMC11586881): Anemia present in approximately 54.55% of RA patients; significantly associated with higher disease severity

rulebook.rule: Both elevated CRP and ESR in context of polyarthritis without systemic constitutional symptoms support RA over systemic disease
rulebook.source: P07 Rheumatoid arthritis, joint pain with raised CRP (NCBI PMC8524161): While elevated ESR and CRP consistent with inflammatory RA, disproportionately raised markers with systemic symptoms raise suspicion for alternative diagnoses

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated ferritin (>1000 ng/mL) with elevated CRP and ESR, especially with fever, suggests adult-onset Still's disease over RA
rulebook.source: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (NCBI PMC7123329): Inflammatory markers (notably CRP and ferritin) are higher in Still's disease than in rheumatoid arthritis subsets

rulebook.rule: Negative RF and anti-CCP in setting of symmetric polyarthritis does not exclude rheumatoid arthritis; seronegative RA remains on differential
rulebook.source: Seronegative Rheumatoid Arthritis (MDPI 2076-3271/14/1/14): Seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis; may be difficult to distinguish from other inflammatory arthritis; diagnosis possible after monitoring response to therapy

rulebook.rule: Negative RF and anti-CCP widen differential to include psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and other seronegative conditions
rulebook.source: Seronegative Rheumatoid Arthritis (MDPI 2076-3271/14/1/14): Multiple seronegative conditions mimic RA; careful review of alternate diagnoses prior to initiating pharmacotherapy suggested

rulebook.rule: Absence of systemic constitutional symptoms (fever, rash, weight loss) in 64-year-old with symmetric polyarthritis reduces suspicion for adult-onset Still's disease, drug-induced arthritis, and paraneoplastic syndrome
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Paraneoplastic Arthritis; ICI-induced Arthritis
rulebook.source: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (NCBI PMC7123329); Paraneoplastic arthritides (NCBI PMC9847110): AoSD characterized by spiking fever, skin rash, hyperleukocytosis; paraneoplastic primarily in men >50

rulebook.rule: Absence of pitting edema on dorsal hands significantly lowers suspicion for RS3PE
rulebook.source: Elderly Patients With Inflammatory Polyarthritis (NCBI PMC12033035): RS3PE characterized by pitting edema on dorsum of hands; absence substantially lowers this diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Absence of fever, night sweats, rash, and oral ulcers in setting of seronegative polyarthritis lowers suspicion for systemic lupus erythematosus and adult-onset Still's disease
rulebook.source: When Serology Fails: Recognising Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (NCBI PMC12236641): SLE and AoSD typically present with systemic constitutional symptoms

rulebook.rule: Fixed flexion deformity of elbows (approximately 25-30 degrees) in seronegative polyarthritis indicates chronic inflammatory arthritis with poor disease control
rulebook.source: Fixed Flexion Deformity in the Elbow (Academy Orthopedics); Rheumatoid Arthritis Clinical Presentation (Medscape): Fixed flexion deformity results from joint capsule fibrosis; elbow involved in 20-65% of RA patients

rulebook.rule: Synovial thickening at radiocarpal and MCPJs on MRI with gadolinium enhancement indicates active synovitis and supports inflammatory arthritis diagnosis
rulebook.source: Early Rheumatoid Arthritis MRI Findings (AJR 2214/AJR.07.2548); MR Imaging of Early RA (RSNA): MRI shows thickening of synovial sheath with marked gadolinium enhancement; synovitis is earliest RA finding

rulebook.rule: Flexor tendon tenosynovitis on MRI can occur in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and anti-synthetase syndrome; not specific for single diagnosis
rulebook.source: Isolated Flexor Tenosynovitis (NCBI PMC12237482); Flexor Tenosynovitis as Sole Presentation of Anti-synthetase Syndrome (NCBI PMC11867200): Flexor tenosynovitis secondary to multiple inflammatory arthropathies

rulebook.rule: Absence of erosions on plain radiographs at initial presentation does not exclude rheumatoid arthritis or indicate non-erosive disease will persist
rulebook.source: Seronegative Rheumatoid Arthritis: Erosive Potential (MDPI 2076-3271/14/1/14): Seronegative RA is distinct entity with erosive potential; erosions may develop over time

rulebook.rule: Mild degenerative changes on radiographs in 64-year-old can represent pre-existing osteoarthritis or may be superimposed on inflammatory arthritis process
rulebook.source: Case uncertainty U001: unclear if mild degenerative change represents pre-existing condition or is part of inflammatory process

rulebook.rule: Primary non-response to TNF inhibitor (no improvement after >6 months) may indicate dominant non-TNFα inflammatory pathway or incorrect diagnosis rather than treatment failure
rulebook.source: Treatment options in patients with rheumatoid arthritis failing initial TNF inhibitor therapy (Springer ar2666): 20-40% of TNFi patients fail to achieve ACR20; non-TNFα pathways (IL-12/23, IL-17) may dominate

rulebook.rule: Resistance to prednisone, methotrexate, and TNF inhibitor without improvement suggests either incorrect diagnosis or alternative inflammatory pathway not targeted by these agents
rulebook.source: RS3PE Response and Psoriatic Arthritis Management After TNFi Failure (NCBI PMC12033035; Rheumatology Advisor): Lack of response to escalating standard DMARDs suggests alternative diagnosis or different therapeutic approach needed

rulebook.rule: Steroid-responsive disease with rapid improvement on prednisone alone (within days) strongly suggests RS3PE rather than seronegative RA
rulebook.source: RS3PE Clinical Features and Response (NCBI PMC12033035): RS3PE characterized by immediate resolution of swelling and inflammatory marker normalization within 2 weeks

rulebook.rule: In 64-year-old with seronegative symmetric polyarthritis and morning stiffness >45 minutes, must distinguish seronegative RA from polymyalgia rheumatica
rulebook.source: Polymyalgia Rheumatica and Seronegative EORA (EMJ Reviews); Differentiating SEORA from PMR (NCBI PMC9914621): Erosions and symmetric MCP-PIP involvement favor RA; shoulder-girdle pain favors PMR

rulebook.rule: Acute onset with pitting edema, age >60, rapid steroid response in seronegative patient with upper extremity predominance should trigger assessment for RS3PE
rulebook.source: Elderly Patients With Inflammatory Polyarthritis (NCBI PMC12033035): RS3PE presents with acute onset, bilateral symptoms, pitting edema on dorsum, age >60, rapid corticosteroid response

rulebook.rule: Seronegative symmetric polyarthritis in patient >50 years with poor treatment response to standard immunosuppression warrants malignancy screening
rulebook.source: Paraneoplastic arthritides (NCBI PMC9847110): Paraneoplastic arthritis most frequent in middle-aged/older adults >50 with seronegative symmetric polyarthritis mimicking RA

rulebook.rule: History of recent cancer diagnosis or chemotherapy, or disproportionately elevated inflammatory markers relative to joint findings, raises suspicion for paraneoplastic or drug-induced arthritis
rulebook.source: ICI-related Arthritis Characteristics (NCBI PMC12846936): Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced seronegative arthritis occurs with anti-PD-1/anti-CTLA-4 therapies; may be refractory to TNFα inhibitors

rulebook.rule: Negative RF and anti-CCP alone are insufficient to exclude RA or seronegative autoimmune arthritis; additional serology (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-synthetase, ANCA) should be considered based on clinical presentation
rulebook.source: When Serology Fails: Recognising SLE (NCBI PMC12236641); Anti-synthetase Syndrome (Sage 2397198320902667): Seronegative SLE presents as polyarthritis with negative RF/anti-CCP but positive ANA; anti-synthetase syndrome presents with arthritis and flexor tenosynovitis

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Seronegative RA with atypical/refractory phenotype, or paraneoplastic/granulomatous arthritis mimicking RA.

Recommended next action: Obtain PET-CT or cross-sectional imaging to exclude occult malignancy; check serum ACE and chest HRCT for sarcoidosis; perform synovial biopsy if imaging negative to evaluate for granulomas or other pathology; consider switching to non-TNF biologic (JAK inhibitor or B-cell depleter) as salvage therapy.

Confidence: 65% seronegative RA (atypical/refractory); 35% alternative (paraneoplastic, granulomatous, or chronic infection).

Reasoning: Symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness, and elevated inflammatory markers fit RA, but seronegative status combined with profound resistance to conventional DMARDs and TNF inhibition is highly atypical. The absence of radiographic erosions after 6+ months of aggressive therapy further argues against classic RA. The prominent tenosynovitis and lack of systemic features suggest either a non-erosive inflammatory process or an occult systemic disease (malignancy, sarcoidosis, infection) masquerading as RA. Therapy refractoriness mandates investigation for alternative diagnoses before continuing to escalate immunosuppression.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 64-year-old woman presents with a symmetric polyarthritis affecting MCPJs, PIPJs, wrists, and elbows (F017-F019) with morning stiffness lasting ~1 hour (F005), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 36 mg/L, ESR 47 mm/hr; F024-F025), mild anemia (Hgb 10.1 g/dL; F022), and elevated WCC (11.4 × 10⁹/L; F021). These findings strongly support inflammatory arthritis rather than mechanical disease (R004).

The symmetric MCP and PIP involvement bilaterally (F017-F018) is more suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis than psoriatic arthritis (R001, R002), and the absence of documented DIP involvement or asymmetry further supports this pattern. Despite negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies (F028-F029), seronegative rheumatoid arthritis remains a valid diagnosis in this clinical context (R010); negative serology alone does not exclude RA and widens the differential to include other inflammatory arthropathies (R011).

The presence of fixed elbow flexion deformity (F020) indicates chronic inflammatory arthritis with suboptimal disease control (R015). MRI findings of synovial thickening at radiocarpal and MCPJs with flexor tendon tenosynovitis (F032) support active synovitis consistent with inflammatory arthritis (R016), although flexor tenosynovitis is not specific to RA and may occur in psoriatic arthritis or anti-synthetase syndrome (R017).

However, the critical finding is **primary non-response to escalating immunosuppressive therapy over 6+ months**, including prednisone, methotrexate, and TNF inhibitor (F037). This pattern raises concern that either (a) the diagnosis is incorrect, or (b) the underlying inflammatory pathway is independent of TNFα and may involve IL-17, IL-12/23, or IL-6 mechanisms not targeted by current therapy (R020, R021). Absence of rapid corticosteroid response argues against RS3PE (R022), and the lack of constitutional symptoms (F006-F007) reduces—but does not exclude—systemic etiologies such as SLE or adult-onset Still's disease (R012, R014).

Notably, the IR documents negative RF and anti-CCP testing but does not report results of additional serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-synthetase antibodies, ANCA). The presence of flexor tenosynovitis (F032) warrants particular consideration of anti-synthetase syndrome, which presents with polyarthritis and tenosynovitis and may be seronegative for RF/anti-CCP (R027). Similarly, given the patient's age (64 years) and refractory disease course, malignancy screening should be considered as seronegative symmetric polyarthritis in patients >50 years warrants assessment for paraneoplastic syndrome (R025).

**Conclusion:** While seronegative RA remains the most consistent with the clinical and laboratory pattern, the marked treatment resistance is atypical and mandates urgent expanded serologic evaluation (particularly anti-synthetase antibodies and ANA-related serologies per R027) and consideration of non-TNFα inflammatory pathways or alternative diagnoses before escalating further immunosuppression.
per_case.framework_top: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis (probable) with concurrent consideration of anti-synthetase syndrome or psoriatic arthritis as key differential diagnoses, given treatment resistance.
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain expanded serology panel including ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-synthetase antibodies (anti-Jo1, anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12), and ANCA. If negative, proceed with malignancy screening given age and treatment resistance. Consider reconsideration of TNF-independent pathways (IL-17, IL-6 inhibitors) or diagnostic re-evaluation if serology remains negative.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-High (70-75%) for seronegative RA as working diagnosis; lower confidence (40-50%) that this explains treatment resistance without additional diagnostic information.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: the answer is multiple myeloma masquerading as seronegative RA; the load-bearing correct disposition is to STOP escalating DMARD/biologic therapy and pursue a workup for an occult alternative diagnosis (specifically plasma-cell dyscrasia: SPEP/UPEP, free light chains, immunofixation, bone marrow biopsy), driven by the triad of treatment-refractory seronegative polyarthritis + anemia + high inflammatory markers.

Neither output names multiple myeloma, so neither reaches the confirmed diagnosis. Both are therefore at best partial. The discriminator is which output best captures (a) the red-flag reasoning and (b) the correct disposition (stop escalating, work up occult cause).

OUTPUT B is stronger. It explicitly anchors on the anemia (Hgb 10.1), high CRP/ESR, and—critically—the primary non-response to escalating immunosuppression as the pivotal finding, concluding that this "mandates urgent expanded evaluation... before escalating further immunosuppression." That is exactly the correct disposition in the ground truth (do not escalate; work up the refractory case). It also explicitly raises age 64 + refractory seronegative polyarthritis as warranting malignancy/paraneoplastic screening, which points (loosely) toward the myeloma-shaped answer. Its reasoning is traceable (cites specific findings/rules), well calibrated (hedged, identifies multiple plausible alternatives), and defensible. Its weaknesses: it never names a plasma-cell dyscrasia/myeloma specifically, foregrounds anti-synthetase syndrome (a plausible but ultimately wrong lead), and does not connect the anemia to the malignancy as a coherent paraneoplastic story.

OUTPUT A is weaker. It correctly flags refractoriness as mandating an alternative workup and lists occult malignancy/PET-CT among next steps, which is partially aligned. However it leads with sarcoidosis (ACE, HRCT) and granulomatous disease as primary alternatives—neither supported—and notably recommends "consider switching to non-TNF biologic (JAK inhibitor or B-cell depleter) as salvage therapy," which directly contradicts the ground-truth teaching point that further DMARD/biologic escalation is the wrong move. It does not mention anemia at all, missing the key red flag that links to myeloma. Confidence (65% RA) is mediocre calibration given the case is a refractory non-RA.

Both are partial (correct red-flag instinct, wrong/absent final diagnosis), but B better captures the correct disposition (no further escalation; expanded workup; explicit malignancy/paraneoplastic consideration in an older patient with anemia) and avoids A's affirmatively wrong salvage-biologic recommendation. B is more traceable and better calibrated. Winner: B.

per_case.prose:
A 47-year-old woman was referred to a rheumatology clinic for a second opinion regarding several years of worsening, generalized body pain. Her symptoms had begun insidiously and progressed: deep aching across her shoulders, upper and lower back, and arms; pronounced daytime fatigue; non-restorative sleep; and a striking inability to tolerate physical exertion, with even modest activity leaving her exhausted for the remainder of the day.

She had previously been diagnosed with fibromyalgia at another practice. Over the preceding two years she had cycled through several agents typically used for that condition — including a tricyclic at bedtime, duloxetine, and pregabalin — as well as graded physical therapy, with essentially no durable benefit. Frustrated by the lack of response, she sought further evaluation.

Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. She took no chronic medications apart from the trials above. Family history was notable for endometrial cancer and hypertension in her mother and a paternal history of leukemia; there was no known neuromuscular or metabolic disease in relatives. She did not smoke and drank alcohol only occasionally.

On examination she appeared well. There was mild tenderness to palpation over the paraspinal muscles of the upper and lower back and across both shoulder girdles. Muscle bulk and resting strength were preserved, deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric, and the joints showed no synovitis, deformity, or restricted motion. The remainder of the general and neurologic examination was normal.

Initial laboratory studies were broadly reassuring. A complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and liver function tests were all within normal limits. Serum creatine kinase was modestly elevated at 298 U/L (reference 0–150 U/L). Resting venous lactate was normal at 1.4 mmol/L (reference <2 mmol/L) and resting ammonia was normal at 19 umol/L (reference 0–40 umol/L).

Because of the prominent, disproportionate exercise intolerance, a timed walking test was performed with paired metabolic sampling. Lactate, normal at rest, rose abnormally to 4.6 mmol/L immediately after the walk, whereas the paired post-exertional ammonia remained within the normal range at 34 umol/L (reference 0–40 umol/L).

A skeletal muscle biopsy was obtained and submitted for quantitative respiratory-chain enzyme analysis. This demonstrated a generalized reduction in mitochondrial enzyme activities relative to control values: citrate synthase approximately 52% of normal, cytochrome c oxidase approximately 55%, succinate dehydrogenase approximately 70%, and NADH dehydrogenase approximately 75%. Targeted genomic sequencing was subsequently undertaken.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy (a primary mitochondrial respiratory-chain disorder), which had been misattributed to fibromyalgia.

HOW CONFIRMED:
1) Skeletal muscle biopsy with respiratory-chain enzyme (biochemical) assay showing globally reduced activities: citrate (citric acid) synthase ~49% of normal, cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) ~53%, succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) ~72%, and NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) ~73% — a pattern of multi-complex respiratory-chain deficiency.
2) Genomic sequencing identifying POLG1 polymorphisms (C->T at 2254, G->T at 3708) plus multiple mitochondrial-genome polymorphisms, consistent with a POLG-related mitochondrial disorder.
3) Supportive dynamic exercise physiology: normal resting lactate (1.6 mmol/L) with abnormal post-exertional lactate rise (5 mmol/L after a six-minute walk), normal post-exertional ammonia (~38 umol/L) arguing against a glycogenolytic/myoadenylate-deaminase defect, and only mildly elevated CK (325 U/L). Routine labs (CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid, liver) were normal, excluding common mimics.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize that "treatment-refractory fibromyalgia" with exercise intolerance and an abnormal post-exertional lactate is a red flag for a metabolic/mitochondrial myopathy; pursue exercise (aerobic/forearm) lactate testing and muscle biopsy with respiratory-chain enzymology plus mitochondrial/POLG genetic testing. Treat with a mitochondrial-support regimen (coenzyme Q10, creatine, L-carnitine, folic acid). OUTCOME: gradual and significant symptom resolution over several months on this regimen — confirming the metabolic etiology and refuting the fibromyalgia label.

SOURCE: Abdulhag et al. (case report), "Mitochondrial myopathy presenting as fibromyalgia," PMC3293012. 41-year-old Caucasian woman in the original.

queries.asks: What is the etiology of the generalized reduction in respiratory-chain enzyme activities? Is it mtDNA-based (point mutation, deletion, or depletion) or nuclear-encoded (mutation in respiratory-chain subunit genes or assembly factors)?

Why does the patient have disproportionate exercise intolerance and post-exertional exhaustion? Is this due to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and exaggerated lactate accumulation (as suggested by the post-exertional lactate rise to 4.6 mmol/L)?
What do the targeted genomic sequencing results reveal? Are there pathogenic variants in mtDNA, nuclear-encoded respiratory-chain subunit genes, or mitochondrial assembly factors?
Does the modestly elevated resting CK (298 U/L, approximately 2x upper limit of normal) correlate with muscle fiber damage on biopsy, and what is its clinical significance?

What is the diagnostic significance of the normal post-exertional ammonia level? Does it effectively exclude glycogen-storage disease, adenylate deaminase deficiency, and other disorders of anaerobic metabolism?

What is the mechanistic interpretation of the enzyme activity pattern (Complex I 75%, Complex II 70%, Complex IV 55%, citrate synthase 52%)? Does this suggest an assembly defect, subunit deficiency, or cofactor depletion?

What is the specific mitochondrial myopathy syndrome or syndrome variant? (e.g., MELAS, MERRF, CPEO, exercise-intolerance-associated mtDNA mutation, Leigh-like phenotype, or nuclear gene-based mitochondrial cytopathy?)

Why did the prior fibromyalgia-targeted therapies (tricyclic, SNRI, pregabalin, and graded physical therapy) fail? Is the diagnosis fundamentally different, implicating organic mitochondrial myopathy rather than central pain sensitization?

What treatment or management strategy is indicated? (e.g., CoQ10 supplementation, L-arginine during acute phases, exercise capacity-tailored physical therapy, genetic counseling if heritable mtDNA or nuclear gene involved?)

Is there an unrecognized family history of mitochondrial disease? Given the statement 'no known neuromuscular or metabolic disease in relatives,' were maternal or paternal relatives clinically screened, or is the inheritance pattern sporadic?

rulebook.rule: Disproportionate exercise intolerance with pronounced post-exertional exhaustion (inability to tolerate modest activity, leaving patient exhausted for remainder of day) raises suspicion for mitochondrial myopathy with impaired oxidative phosphorylation rather than fibromyalgia (primarily a central sensitization disorder).
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathies: diagnosis, exercise intolerance, and treatment options. PubMed 16331134. Exercise intolerance is a common but often overlooked hallmark of mitochondrial myopathies, reflecting lack of energy production due to mitochondrial dysfunction in skeletal muscle.

rulebook.rule: Post-exertional lactate elevation disproportionate to resting levels (resting 1.4 mmol/L normal, post-walk 4.6 mmol/L abnormally elevated) indicates impaired aerobic ATP synthesis and forced reliance on anaerobic metabolism, a hallmark metabolic derangement of mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy with oxidative phosphorylation defect
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathy presenting as fibromyalgia: a case report. PubMed 22325469 (PMC3293012). Patient demonstrated normal resting lactic acid 1.6 mmol/L but elevated post-exercise lactic acid 5 mmol/L (normal <2 mmol/L), indicating muscles cannot efficiently generate ATP aerobically.

rulebook.rule: Resting venous lactate within normal limits (1.4 mmol/L, normal <2 mmol/L) argues against severe mitochondrial myopathy at rest, but when combined with abnormal post-exertional elevation, demonstrates the functional, exercise-provoked nature of the metabolic defect.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Resting and exercise-induced increases of blood lactate are an easy screening tool for mitochondrial myopathy; elevated lactate at rest not always present.

rulebook.rule: Generalized reduction in respiratory chain enzyme activities on muscle biopsy (citrate synthase 52%, Complex IV 55%, Complex II 70%, Complex I 75% of normal) demonstrates impaired oxidative phosphorylation capacity and directly indicates primary mitochondrial dysfunction rather than neurogenic or myofascial pain mechanisms.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Muscle biopsy biochemical analysis reveals respiratory chain deficiencies, demonstrating impaired energy production at the molecular level and indicating mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction.

rulebook.rule: Citrate synthase activity reduced to 52% of normal (a mitochondrial matrix marker enzyme) suggests either generalized reduction in mitochondrial mass or mitochondrial proliferation as compensatory response; when normalized respiratory chain complex activities are all reduced, indicates true enzyme deficiency rather than mitochondrial depletion alone.
rulebook.source: Biochemical Assays of Respiratory Chain Complex Activity. ScienceDirect. Citrate synthase activity is a marker of mitochondrial mass; respiratory chain enzyme activities normalized to citrate synthase help distinguish mitochondrial proliferation from actual enzyme deficiency in disease states.

rulebook.rule: Pattern of progressive decline in enzyme activities across respiratory chain complexes (Complex I 75% > Complex II 70% > Complex IV 55%, with citrate synthase 52%) may suggest assembly defect, subunit deficiency, or global cofactor depletion affecting multiple complexes.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—mechanistic subtype (assembly vs. subunit vs. cofactor)
rulebook.source: Assessment of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzymes in cells and tissues. ScienceDirect. Measurement of activities of respiratory chain complexes (I-IV) normalized to citrate synthase helps identify specific respiratory chain defects and patterns of dysfunction.

rulebook.rule: Modestly elevated serum creatine kinase (298 U/L, approximately 2-fold upper limit of normal 150 U/L) is consistent with myopathic process but indicates limited myofiber necrosis; CK elevation in mitochondrial myopathy is typically mild unless accompanied by rhabdomyolysis.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy (mild form without acute muscle breakdown)
rulebook.source: The value of routine creatine kinase and thyroid stimulating hormone testing in patients with suspected fibromyalgia. PubMed 27032423. CK values in mitochondrial myopathy are normal or mildly elevated unless measured in rhabdomyolysis; abnormal CK in fibromyalgia is rare and suggests alternative diagnosis.

rulebook.rule: Normal post-exertional ammonia level (34 umol/L, within normal range 0-40 umol/L) effectively excludes myoadenylate deaminase deficiency and glycogen storage diseases (which would show disproportionate ammonia elevation with normal lactate rise), narrowing the differential to mitochondrial or other non-anaerobic metabolic myopathies.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—exclusion of glycogenoses and AMP deaminase deficiency
rulebook.source: Diagnostic Algorithm for Glycogenoses and Myoadenylate Deaminase Deficiency Based on Exercise Testing Parameters. PubMed 26207760 (PMC4514803). Adenylate deaminase deficiency shows negligible ammonia increase despite normal lactate rise; normal ammonia with elevated lactate distinguishes mitochondrial from anaerobic metabolic disorders.

rulebook.rule: Preserved muscle bulk, resting strength, normal deep tendon reflexes, and normal joint examination argue against primary inflammatory myositis, muscular dystrophy, or neurogenic atrophy; preserved baseline neuromuscular function with selective exercise intolerance points toward metabolic myopathy.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—specific phenotype (metabolic rather than dystrophic or inflammatory)
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Comprehensive diagnostic approach evaluates muscle strength, reflexes, and morphology to distinguish metabolic myopathies from dystrophic or inflammatory conditions.

rulebook.rule: Complete lack of durable response to standard fibromyalgia pharmacotherapy (tricyclic antidepressant, duloxetine, pregabalin) and graded physical therapy strongly indicates diagnosis is not fibromyalgia (central sensitization disorder) but rather organic mitochondrial myopathy, which requires metabolically targeted interventions.
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathy presenting as fibromyalgia: a case report. PubMed 22325469 (PMC3293012). Patient met fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria but did not respond to fibromyalgia therapy; improvement occurred only when underlying mitochondrial dysfunction was identified and treated.

rulebook.rule: Failure of graded physical therapy (a first-line, evidence-based treatment for fibromyalgia central sensitization) raises concern that progressive metabolic myopathy rather than pain modulation dysfunction is the primary pathology; graded exercise may worsen exercise intolerance in mitochondrial disease.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—indication for metabolic rather than neurophysiologic management
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathies: diagnosis, exercise intolerance, and treatment options. PubMed 16331134. Exercise intolerance is a hallmark of mitochondrial myopathy; therapeutic approach must differ fundamentally from fibromyalgia management.

rulebook.rule: Insidious progressive onset of generalized deep aching and fatigue with pronounced non-restorative sleep is consistent with both fibromyalgia and mitochondrial myopathy; these nonspecific symptoms require objective metabolic and biochemical testing to differentiate.
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathy presenting as fibromyalgia: a case report. PubMed 22325469 (PMC3293012). Both fibromyalgia and mitochondrial myopathy present with chronic pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbance; clinical presentation alone is insufficient to distinguish.

rulebook.rule: Normal comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and liver function tests argue against thyroid dysfunction, hepatic disease, or systemic metabolic derangement as causes of fatigue and pain; findings are consistent with primary muscle mitochondrial pathology.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy (primary muscle disease versus systemic metabolic disorder)
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Comprehensive diagnostic approach includes standard serum biochemistry to exclude systemic causes before focusing on primary mitochondrial dysfunction.

rulebook.rule: Respiratory chain enzyme deficiency demonstrated by muscle biopsy directly indicates either mtDNA-based pathology (point mutation, deletion, or depletion affecting mitochondrial gene expression) or nuclear-encoded defect (mutations in respiratory chain subunit genes or mitochondrial assembly factors); genetic sequencing is required to distinguish mechanism.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Biochemical enzyme deficiency must be followed by genetic analysis to identify mtDNA mutations, nuclear-encoded subunit mutations, or assembly factor defects.

rulebook.rule: POLG1 (mitochondrial DNA polymerase) variants in mitochondrial myopathy patients cause mtDNA depletion or point mutations, leading to generalized respiratory chain enzyme reduction and clinical manifestations of exercise intolerance and lactate accumulation during metabolic stress.
rulebook.source: Carriers of POLG1 variants require investigations for multisystem disease and for mtDNA variations. PMC9272553. POLG1 variants cause mtDNA depletion syndromes with autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance; serum and muscle lactate elevation occurs in POLG1 carriers.

rulebook.rule: Central sensitization, the proposed mechanism of fibromyalgia, is fundamentally distinct from muscle biopsy-proven respiratory chain enzyme deficiency; presence of objective myopathic findings on biopsy excludes fibromyalgia and indicates organic mitochondrial disease.
rulebook.source: Central Sensitization Syndrome and the Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Fibromyalgia: A Review. PMC4422459. Fibromyalgia is a centralized pain syndrome without tissue damage; in contrast, mitochondrial myopathy shows objective myopathic changes on biopsy indicating peripheral muscle pathology.

rulebook.rule: Absence of known neuromuscular or metabolic disease in family history does not exclude heritable mitochondrial myopathy; mtDNA mutations can arise de novo, and nuclear gene inheritance patterns may be recessive or show incomplete penetrance; genetic counseling and pedigree analysis are warranted.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—inheritance pattern and genetic counseling implications
rulebook.source: Genetic heterogeneity and respiratory chain enzyme analysis in pediatric Indian patients with mitochondrial disorder. ScienceDirect. Mitochondrial myopathies show heterogeneous inheritance including autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, and maternal (mtDNA) patterns; de novo mutations and reduced penetrance occur.

rulebook.rule: Targeted genomic sequencing results are essential to identify pathogenic variants in mtDNA, nuclear-encoded respiratory chain subunit genes (NDUFB8, SDHA, COX genes, etc.), or mitochondrial assembly factors (TMEM126B, TACO1, etc.); results determine prognosis, inheritance counseling, and potential targeted therapies.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—specific genetic etiology and treatment planning
rulebook.source: Diagnosis of mitochondrial myopathies. ScienceDirect. Genetic analysis is essential component of comprehensive diagnostic approach; identification of specific mutations informs prognosis and therapeutic strategy.

rulebook.rule: Generalized reduction in all respiratory chain complex activities (I, II, IV) plus citrate synthase suggests systemic effect on mitochondrial biogenesis, protein synthesis capacity, or cofactor availability rather than isolated single-complex defect; indicates severe mitochondrial dysfunction.
rulebook.source: An Evaluation of the Measurement of the Activities of Complexes I-IV in the Respiratory Chain of Human Skeletal Muscle Mitochondria. ScienceDirect. Measurement of multiple respiratory chain complexes normalized to citrate synthase reveals patterns of single-complex deficiency versus generalized dysfunction.

rulebook.rule: Skewed pattern of enzyme activities (minimal reduction in Complex I relative to greater reduction in Complex IV, Complex II, and citrate synthase) may indicate selective defects affecting assembly or cofactor incorporation of latter complexes, or may reflect muscle fiber-type-specific mitochondrial dysfunction.
rulebook.bears_on: Mitochondrial myopathy—mechanistic interpretation of enzyme gradient
rulebook.source: Optimization of respiratory chain enzymatic assays in muscle for the diagnosis of mitochondrial disorders. ScienceDirect. Different respiratory chain complexes may show selective reduction in specific mitochondrial disorders; patterns of enzyme activity aid mechanistic diagnosis.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Primary Mitochondrial Myopathy (likely mtDNA-related or nuclear gene variant affecting respiratory chain function).

Recommended next action: Continue with targeted genomic sequencing focusing on mtDNA mutations/deletions and nuclear genes encoding respiratory chain subunits (POLG, NDUFS family, COX genes). Consider whole mitochondrial genome or exome sequencing if targeted panel is negative. Assess inheritance pattern and consider genetic counseling.

Confidence: 90-95%

Reasoning: The triad of (1) disproportionate exercise intolerance with post-exertional malaise, (2) abnormal lactate accumulation during exertion (4.6 vs normal <2), and (3) documented generalized reduction in all four respiratory chain enzyme activities on muscle biopsy is pathognomonic for primary mitochondrial disease. The preserved resting strength, normal ammonia, and normal other metabolic markers exclude inflammatory and other metabolic myopathies. Fibromyalgia diagnosis was likely a misdiagnosis due to symptom overlap (pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance), but the objective finding of exercise-induced metabolic derangement with mitochondrial enzyme deficiency is diagnostic for mitochondrial myopathy.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 47-year-old woman initially diagnosed with fibromyalgia almost certainly has an underlying mitochondrial myopathy, not central sensitization.

The evidence supporting mitochondrial myopathy is strong:

(1) Disproportionate exercise intolerance and post-exertional exhaustion [fact_007]: Rule_001 establishes that the inability to tolerate modest activity with prolonged exhaustion—rather than pain amplification—is characteristic of mitochondrial myopathy with impaired oxidative phosphorylation.

(2) Exaggerated post-exertional lactate elevation [fact_037]: The resting lactate normal at 1.4 mmol/L [fact_034] but rising abnormally to 4.6 mmol/L immediately post-walk is pathognomonic. Rule_002 directly identifies this pattern—normal resting, exaggerated post-exertional lactate—as a hallmark of respiratory chain dysfunction, reflecting forced reliance on anaerobic metabolism when aerobic ATP synthesis fails. This objective metabolic derangement distinguishes mitochondrial disease from fibromyalgia.

(3) Normal post-exertional ammonia [fact_038]: The level of 34 umol/L (normal range 0–40) is crucial. Rule_008 establishes that normal ammonia effectively excludes myoadenylate deaminase deficiency and glycogen storage diseases (which would show disproportionate ammonia elevation). This narrows the differential to mitochondrial myopathy.

(4) Generalized respiratory chain enzyme deficiency on biopsy [fact_045]: The reduction pattern is striking—citrate synthase 52%, Complex IV 55%, Complex II 70%, Complex I 75% of normal. Rule_004 directly states that generalized reduction in respiratory chain enzyme activities demonstrates impaired oxidative phosphorylation capacity and indicates primary mitochondrial dysfunction rather than pain mechanisms. Rule_006 notes that this progressive decline across complexes may suggest assembly defect, subunit deficiency, or cofactor depletion.

(5) Preserved neuromuscular examination [facts_025, 026, 027, 028]: Muscle bulk, resting strength, reflexes, and joints were all normal. Rule_009 establishes that preserved baseline neuromuscular function with selective exercise intolerance points toward metabolic myopathy rather than dystrophy or inflammatory disease.

(6) Modestly elevated serum creatine kinase [fact_033]: CK at 298 U/L (approximately 2-fold normal) is consistent but not excessive. Rule_007 indicates that mild CK elevation in mitochondrial myopathy reflects limited myofiber necrosis without rhabdomyolysis, as seen here.

(7) Complete failure of fibromyalgia-directed therapies [facts_009, 010, 011, 012, 013]: The tricyclic, duloxetine, pregabalin, and graded physical therapy provided no durable benefit. Rule_010 states explicitly that complete lack of response to standard fibromyalgia pharmacotherapy and physical therapy indicates the diagnosis is not fibromyalgia but organic mitochondrial myopathy. Rule_011 adds that failure of graded exercise—a first-line treatment for fibromyalgia—raises concern that progressive metabolic myopathy rather than pain modulation is the primary pathology.

(8) Normal supporting laboratory work [facts_029, 030, 031, 032]: Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, TSH, and liver function tests exclude systemic metabolic disorder or thyroid/hepatic disease as causes of fatigue, per Rule_013.

This presentation does not fit fibromyalgia (Rule_012 acknowledges symptom overlap—fatigue, sleep disturbance, generalized pain—but Rule_016 is decisive: fibromyalgia is centralized pain without tissue damage, whereas this patient has objective myopathic findings on biopsy proving peripheral muscle pathology).

Regarding etiology, Rule_014 establishes that respiratory chain enzyme deficiency indicates either mtDNA-based pathology (point mutation, deletion, or depletion) or nuclear-encoded defect (subunit mutations or assembly factors). Rule_015 notes that POLG1 variants cause mtDNA depletion with the exact pattern seen here—generalized respiratory chain reduction and lactate elevation under metabolic stress. Rule_018 emphasizes that targeted genomic sequencing results are essential to identify pathogenic variants and determine inheritance, prognosis, and potential targeted therapy.

Rule_017 notes that absence of family history of neuromuscular disease [fact_019] does not exclude heritable mitochondrial myopathy; mtDNA mutations may be de novo, and nuclear inheritance may be recessive or show incomplete penetrance.

Uncertainties remain: the specific genomic etiology (mtDNA versus nuclear gene, and which gene) [fact_046 states sequencing was undertaken but results not yet provided]; histopathology details (ragged-red fibers, lipid, necrosis, paracrystalline inclusions) are not reported [unc_006]; and the exercise test protocol details (duration, intensity, specimen timing) lack specificity [unc_003, unc_004]. These gaps do not alter the diagnosis, which rests on biochemical and clinical grounds, but they would inform prognosis and management once clarified.
per_case.framework_top: Mitochondrial myopathy with generalized respiratory chain enzyme deficiency
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain and interpret results of targeted genomic sequencing to identify specific etiology (mtDNA mutation/depletion versus nuclear-encoded respiratory chain subunit or assembly factor defect) and establish inheritance pattern for genetic counseling and prognosis.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (75-85%). The constellation of objective findings—generalized respiratory chain enzyme deficiency on biopsy combined with disproportionate exercise intolerance and exaggerated post-exertional lactate elevation—is pathognomonic for mitochondrial myopathy. Uncertainty remains pending sequencing results and detailed histopathology interpretation.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs reach the correct core diagnosis — primary mitochondrial myopathy misattributed to fibromyalgia — and both correctly cite the multi-complex respiratory-chain enzyme deficiency, normal post-exertional ammonia (excluding myoadenylate deaminase/glycogen storage disease), the normal-resting/abnormal-post-exertional lactate pattern, mild CK elevation, and the failure of fibromyalgia therapy. Both also mention POLG among the genetic candidates, matching the ground truth's confirmed POLG1 finding. Numeric differences in A and B (CK ~298, lactate 4.6, enzyme percentages, age 47) vs the ground truth (CK 325, lactate 5, enzymes 49/53/72/73, age 41) reflect a differently-parameterized case instance rather than hallucination, since the qualitative pattern matches exactly. Output A wins on completeness, calibration, and defensibility: it maps every clinical and biochemical finding to explicit fact/rule IDs (fully traceable), explicitly anticipates POLG1 as the likely etiology with the exact mechanism the ground truth confirms, and is well-calibrated — it correctly flags that genomic sequencing results were not yet available in its inputs and that histopathology details are missing, without overclaiming. Output B is correct and appropriately confident (90-95%) but is thinner: it treats genetics only as a forward recommendation, omits the routine-lab exclusion detail's full role, and offers far less traceable reasoning. Neither materially hallucinates. A captures more of the ground-truth confirmatory mechanism and disposition.
