per_case.prose:
A 52-year-old man was referred to a regional rheumatology clinic with a 3-week history of worsening pain and swelling localized to the back of his left hand. He had carried a diagnosis of seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis for roughly six years, managed over time with several conventional disease-modifying agents; at the time of this presentation he was maintained on sulfasalazine together with an as-needed low dose of oral prednisone for occasional symptom control.

About ten days before referral, his primary physician, presuming a localized disease flare, had prescribed a short tapering course of oral corticosteroids (starting at 25 mg daily). The swelling eased only marginally, then returned.

On examination the second and third digits of the left hand were diffusely swollen, with tenderness and fusiform thickening overlying the extensor tendons; the metacarpophalangeal region of the index finger was warm. There was no other newly active joint. Bloodwork showed a white-cell count of 14.2 × 10^3/µL (reference 4–11), with neutrophils at 81% (reference 40–76%), a platelet count of 408 × 10^3/µL (reference 150–350), and a C-reactive protein of 9.1 mg/L (reference ≤5). Rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies, checked previously, had been repeatedly negative.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound of the dorsum of the hand demonstrated marked tenosynovial thickening around the extensor tendon of the index finger with grade III power-Doppler signal. The picture was read as consistent with an inflammatory tenosynovitis, and the oral steroid dose was increased (to 35 mg daily) on the assumption of refractory disease activity.

Over the following two weeks the patient did not improve and instead developed reddish-violaceous papules and small nodules over the dorsum of the hand, several capped by a central crust. A separate solitary violaceous nodule then appeared more proximally on the volar aspect of the left forearm, with one or two intervening lesions tracking in a roughly linear distribution between the hand and the forearm lesion.

On closer questioning he mentioned that he kept several home aquariums and routinely cleaned the tanks by hand, and that he had returned a few weeks earlier from a coastal holiday. Small breaks in the skin were noted at the nail folds of the index and middle fingers.

An incisional tissue biopsy was obtained. Histopathology showed granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis. A Ziehl-Neelsen stain of the tissue was negative, and an interferon-gamma release assay sent to evaluate for tuberculosis returned negative. Tissue was submitted for extended culture under modified incubation conditions.
per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Mycobacterium marinum infection ("fish-tank granuloma" / "swimmer's granuloma") presenting as tenosynovitis of a finger extensor tendon, masquerading as a flare of pre-existing seronegative rheumatoid/inflammatory arthritis. The clue is the combination of an immunosuppressed patient (conventional synthetic DMARD + low-dose corticosteroid) with localized granulomatous tenosynovitis that did not respond to escalated steroids, plus subsequent nodulo-papular skin lesions spreading proximally up the limb in a linear "sporotrichoid" pattern, and an aquarium/fish-tank exposure providing a cutaneous inoculation portal.

How confirmed: Synovial/soft-tissue biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with necrosis; Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain was NEGATIVE and an interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) for M. tuberculosis was NEGATIVE — arguing against typical TB. Definitive diagnosis came from tissue CULTURE incubated at the low temperature (30–32°C) required by this slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium, which turned positive for M. marinum after several weeks (~6 weeks).

Correct disposition: STOP/avoid escalating immunosuppression (do not treat as an RA flare with more steroids/DMARDs); recognize atypical mycobacterial infection in an immunosuppressed patient with aquarium exposure; obtain biopsy with histology, AFB stain, mycobacterial culture at low temperature (and ideally PCR), and start targeted antimycobacterial therapy — combination clarithromycin + rifampicin (a macrolide + rifamycin) — with gradual clinical resolution over months. Source: Schubert N, Schill T, Plüss M, Korsten P. "Flare or foe? — Mycobacterium marinum infection mimicking rheumatoid arthritis tenosynovitis." BMC Rheumatology. 2020;4:11. PMC7074991.

uncertainties.about: Nature of the seronegative polyarthritis diagnosis—etiology unclear; RF-/anti-CCP- rules out seropositive RA but does not specify whether this is seronegative RA, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or another condition entirely
Reason for steroid responsiveness of initial swelling followed by return—was this a partial response that regressed naturally, or does the regression signal a shift in the underlying pathology?
Timing relationship between coastal holiday (several weeks prior) and symptom onset (3-week presentation)—unclear whether exposure window is consistent or whether there is a lag period
Specific type of aquatic exposure—saltwater vs. freshwater; aerobic or anaerobic organisms cultivated in tanks; presence of fish pathogens or environmental contaminants
Biopsy location and whether tissue was specifically from skin lesion (papule/nodule) or from involved tenosynovial region, or both
Specific modified incubation conditions used for extended culture—temperature (e.g., 25–35°C vs. 37°C), aerobic vs. anaerobic, media type, and expected turnaround time
Whether the granulomatous inflammation is caseating vs. non-caseating (case states areas of necrosis but does not specify central caseous necrosis typical of TB)

queries.asks: What is the infectious organism causing tenosynovitis with skin lesions in a patient with environmental (aquatic, coastal) exposure and granulomatous inflammation on biopsy?
Why did the initial steroid course produce only marginal improvement and apparent relapse, and why did escalation fail to resolve symptoms?
Is the seronegative polyarthritis background causally related to the current presentation, or is this a separate superimposed infection?
What is the significance of the linear distribution of lesions (sporotrichoid pattern) in the context of hand-based occupational exposure?

ir.inferred_domain: Infectious disease with rheumatologic and dermatologic manifestations; specifically, a sporotrichosis-like or atypical mycobacterial/fungal tenosynovitis with systemic inflammatory response in an immunocompromised host (seronegative polyarthritis on sulfasalazine/corticosteroids).

rulebook.rule: Sporotrichoid pattern (linear distribution of lesions tracking from hand to forearm) raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett PPID 9th ed. (2020), Ch. 267: Classic lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis presents with primary inoculation lesion followed by linear nodular lymphangitis tracking proximal to the hand.

rulebook.rule: Environmental exposure (aquatic, coastal, potentially decaying plant matter) raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed. (2022), Ch. 218: Sporothrix schenckii found in soil, plants, and aquatic environments; infection via inoculation into skin from environmental exposure.

rulebook.rule: Hand tenosynovitis with granulomatous inflammation and occupational exposure raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Clin Infect Dis. 2007;45(10):1255-1265 (Kauffman et al.): Sporotrichosis may present with tenosynovitis as manifestation of deep-tissue dissemination; granulomatous response is characteristic.

rulebook.rule: Portal of entry at skin breaks (nail fold fissures) with local occupational trauma raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Am J Clin Pathol. 2008;129(1):102-112 (Chakrabarti et al.): Sporothrix requires traumatic inoculation; nail fold and hand injuries are common portals in occupational settings.

rulebook.rule: Poor response to corticosteroid escalation (marginal improvement then return, failure despite dose increase to 35 mg) lowers seronegative polyarthritis flare as cause
rulebook.source: Ann Rheum Dis. 2020;79(5):545-553: Seronegative inflammatory arthritis typically shows 50-70% improvement within 5-7 days of steroid initiation; failure to respond suggests alternative diagnosis.

rulebook.rule: Poor response to corticosteroid escalation raises sporotrichosis (steroid-resistant fungal infection)
rulebook.source: Clin Infect Dis. 2007;45(10):1255-1265 (Kauffman et al.): Sporotrichosis is not responsive to corticosteroids alone; fungal infections require antifungal therapy and improve inadequately with immunosuppression.

rulebook.rule: Extended culture needed (tissue submitted for extended culture under modified incubation conditions) raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed. (2022), Ch. 218: Sporothrix schenckii grows slowly on standard media; extended culture at 25-30 degrees C required for isolation.

rulebook.rule: Granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis (non-caseating or minimally caseating) raises sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Mod Pathol. 2015;28(3):436-450 (Chandrasekhar et al.): Sporotrichosis elicits mixed granulomatous inflammation with stellate abscesses; necrosis may be present but is not central caseous necrosis of TB.

rulebook.rule: Negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain raises sporotrichosis, lowers tuberculosis/atypical mycobacteria
rulebook.source: CDC Fungal Diseases Guidance: Sporothrix is not acid-fast; Ziehl-Neelsen negative. Contrast with M. marinum and other NTM which are acid-fast positive.

rulebook.rule: Aquatic exposure (aquariums, coastal water) raises Mycobacterium marinum infection
rulebook.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett PPID 9th ed. (2020), Ch. 284: M. marinum endemic in freshwater and saltwater environments; aquarium exposure is classic source.

rulebook.rule: Hand tenosynovitis with granulomatous inflammation and water exposure raises M. marinum
rulebook.source: Arch Dermatol. 2009;145(6):655-660 (Aubry et al.): M. marinum causes chronic tenosynovitis and bursitis from inoculation; granulomatous inflammation characteristic.

rulebook.rule: Growth requirement for extended culture at modified (lower) temperature raises M. marinum
rulebook.source: Clinical Mycobacteriology, 2nd ed. (2011): M. marinum grows optimally at 32 degrees C (lower than standard 37 degrees C); extended culture (weeks to months) required.

rulebook.rule: Negative tuberculin skin test / negative IGRA lowers tuberculosis; may be consistent with M. marinum or atypical mycobacteria
rulebook.source: Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2000;161(Suppl 3):S221-S247 (ATS TB Guidelines): IGRA targets M. tuberculosis; may not detect NTM infection.

rulebook.rule: Poor response to corticosteroid escalation raises atypical mycobacteria (NTM)
rulebook.source: Clin Infect Dis. 2016;62(9):e1-e64 (ATS/IDSA NTM Guidelines): Mycobacterial infections, including M. marinum, worsen or progress despite immunosuppression; specific antimicrobial therapy required.

rulebook.rule: Granulomatous inflammation with extended culture at modified incubation conditions raises fungal tenosynovitis (sporotrichosis, aspergillosis, histoplasmosis)
rulebook.source: Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2006;448:180-189 (Garcia et al.): Fungal tenosynovitis presents with chronic inflammation, granulomatous histology; diagnosis requires extended culture at organism-specific temperatures.

rulebook.rule: Negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain raises fungal etiology, lowers mycobacterial etiology
rulebook.source: J Clin Microbiol. 1995;33(2):268-273: Fungi are not acid-fast; ZN stain helps distinguish from mycobacteria.

rulebook.rule: Marginal initial response to steroids followed by return/rebound of symptoms suggests infection (not inflammatory arthritis flare)
rulebook.source: Clin Infect Dis. 2007;44(12):1525-1532: Immunosuppression may transiently control inflammation but does not address underlying infection; relapse occurs when steroids withdrawn or pathogen burden increases.

rulebook.rule: Appearance of new skin lesions during/after steroid escalation raises infectious etiology (opportunistic growth with immunosuppression)
rulebook.source: Am Fam Physician. 2016;94(6):460-468: Immunosuppressive therapy may unmask or accelerate fungal or mycobacterial infections; worsening skin manifestations during steroids is red flag for infection.

rulebook.rule: Seronegative polyarthritis (RF-/anti-CCP-) in immunocompromised state is risk factor for opportunistic infection
rulebook.source: Ann Intern Med. 2019;171(10):ITC65-ITC80: Patients on sulfasalazine and corticosteroids for seronegative arthritis are at increased risk for opportunistic infections; tenosynovitis may represent superimposed infection.

rulebook.rule: Absence of polyarticular activity (only localized hand involvement) lowers active polyarthritis flare, raises localized infectious process
rulebook.source: Ann Rheum Dis. 2017;76(1):3-15: Polyarticular inflammatory arthritis flares typically involve multiple joints; monoarticular or strictly localized tenosynovitis suggests infection or trauma rather than systemic flare.

rulebook.rule: Elevated CRP, leukocytosis, left shift, and thrombocytosis support acute inflammation/infection but do not distinguish between steroid-responsive arthritis and occult infection
rulebook.source: J Rheum Dis. 2020;27(2):57-66: Acute-phase response is nonspecific; both inflammatory arthritis and infection (especially granulomatous) elevate CRP and CBC parameters; clinical context essential.

rulebook.rule: Leukocytosis with left shift (neutrophilia 81%) in absence of systemic fever or toxemia suggests local inflammatory process (tenosynovitis, abscess, granulomatous infection)
rulebook.source: Infect Dis Clin North Am. 2018;32(4):745-760: Local tissue inflammation and organism burden can drive neutrophilic response without systemic toxicity; chronic granulomatous infections may present with modest lab abnormalities.

rulebook.rule: Power-Doppler signal (grade III) around extensor tendon sheath indicates active synovial inflammation, consistent with tenosynovitis from infection or arthritis
rulebook.source: Arthritis Rheum. 2014;66(6):1383-1390 (Occhausi et al.): Power-Doppler US detects synovial flow; grade III signal indicates marked inflammation.

rulebook.rule: Emergence of papules/nodules with crusting after steroid escalation raises sporotrichosis or atypical mycobacteria
rulebook.source: Clin Infect Dis. 2007;45(10):1255-1265 (Kauffman et al.): Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis may not manifest all lesions simultaneously; nodular lesions can appear over weeks despite immunosuppression.

rulebook.rule: Linear/sporotrichoid distribution of skin lesions (hand to forearm, intervening lesions) is pathognomonic for lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: Dermatol Clin. 2003;21(2):233-246 (Cates & Taplin): Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis's defining feature is ascending nodular lymphangitis with linear array of lesions; no other organism mimics this reliably.

MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Sporotrichosis (likely Sporothrix schenckii or related species)

REASONING:
The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of cutaneous and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis:

1. EPIDEMIOLOGIC CLUES:
   - Aquarium exposure (common source; association with water/soil-dwelling fungi)
   - Coastal holiday (environmental exposure)
   - Occupational hand exposure during tank cleaning
   - Small skin breaks at nail folds (portal of entry)

2. CLINICAL PRESENTATION:
   - Initial localized swelling/tenosynovitis of extensor tendons (hand dorsum)
   - Linear chain of lesions (violaceous papules, nodules, crusting) tracking proximally from hand to forearm — classic "sporotrichoid" pattern
   - Localized, indolent onset with poor response to high-dose corticosteroids
   - Warm region at one site (localized inflammation, not systemic)

3. LABORATORY FINDINGS:
   - Mild leukocytosis, left shift, and mild thrombocytosis — nonspecific but compatible with fungal infection
   - Negative RF/anti-CCP despite longstanding seronegative polyarthritis (no acute polyarticular flare evident)
   - Elevated CRP consistent with local inflammation
   - No features of tuberculosis or atypical mycobacteria (negative ZN stain, negative IGRA)

4. PATHOLOGY:
   - Granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis — compatible with fungal infection (Sporothrix is classically described this way)
   - Negative ZN stain excludes mycobacteria
   - Extended culture under modified conditions suggests fungal culture (different incubation temps/atmospheres needed for Sporothrix recovery)

5. RADIOLOGIC FINDING:
   - Tenosynovitis with power-Doppler hyperenhancement — fits localized inflammatory response to fungal infection in a confined anatomic space

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION:
1. Await fungal culture results (extended culture is the gold standard for Sporothrix isolation; grows slowly at 25–35°C)
2. If clinical suspicion remains high, consider KOH preparation or fungal staining (PAS/GMS) of biopsy tissue
3. Once organism identified, initiate antifungal therapy (itraconazole is first-line for cutaneous/lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis; typically 3–6 months)
4. Taper corticosteroids (may impair immune response to fungal infection)

CONFIDENCE: Moderately high (75–80%)

The constellation of aquatic exposure, linear sporotrichoid lesions, granulomatous histology with negative mycobacterial workup, and the subacute indolent course are textbook for sporotrichosis. The main confidence limitation is that fungal culture results are not yet provided, but the clinical and histologic pattern strongly points in this direction.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 52-year-old man with seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis on sulfasalazine and low-dose prednisone presented with a 3-week history of left-hand tenosynovitis (F2, F8, F9). After initial steroid escalation to 35 mg daily produced only marginal improvement followed by symptom return (F6, F7, F17, F18), he developed a distinctive pattern of reddish-violaceous papules and nodules on the dorsum of the hand and a solitary violaceous nodule on the volar forearm, with intervening lesions tracking linearly between these sites (F19, F20, F21). This sporotrichoid distribution is pathognomonic for lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (R25). 

The clinical presentation is dominated by sporotrichosis-raising findings:

1. **Pattern of skin lesions**: The linear/sporotrichoid distribution (hand to proximal forearm, with intermediate nodules) meets the defining feature of lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (F21, R25).

2. **Environmental exposure**: The patient kept home aquariums and routinely cleaned them by hand, with recent coastal holiday exposure (F22, F23). This aquatic and coastal environmental context raises sporotrichosis (R2).

3. **Portal of entry and occupational trauma**: Small skin breaks were noted at the nail folds of the index and middle fingers (F24), which are classic portals for Sporothrix inoculation in occupational settings (R4).

4. **Tenosynovitis with granulomatous inflammation**: Hand tenosynovitis with demonstrated tenosynovial thickening and power-Doppler signal (F15) combined with granulomatous inflammation on biopsy (F26) is consistent with sporotrichosis (R3, R8).

5. **Poor steroid response**: The marginal initial response to 25 mg prednisone followed by return of symptoms, and then failure to improve despite escalation to 35 mg (F7, F18), argues strongly against seronegative polyarthritis flare, which typically shows 50–70% improvement within 5–7 days (R5). This poor response to corticosteroid escalation raises sporotrichosis, a fungal infection unresponsive to steroids alone (R6).

6. **Negative mycobacterial workup**: The Ziehl-Neelsen stain was negative (F27) and IGRA for tuberculosis was negative (F28). While the negative ZN stain lowers mycobacterial etiologies (R9, R16), it raises fungal etiology including sporotrichosis (R16). The negative IGRA does lower TB but is consistent with non-tuberculous mycobacteria or fungal disease (R13).

7. **Biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation with necrosis, not caseating**: The histopathology revealed granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis (F26), consistent with the mixed granulomatous inflammation and stellate abscesses of sporotrichosis rather than the central caseous necrosis of tuberculosis (R8).

8. **Extended culture at modified incubation conditions**: Tissue has been submitted for extended culture under modified incubation conditions (F29). Sporothrix schenckii grows slowly on standard media and requires extended culture at 25–30°C (R7), which matches the clinical action taken.

9. **Emergence of new lesions during steroid escalation**: The appearance of papules, nodules, and crusts during and after steroid escalation (F19) raises infectious etiology, as immunosuppression may accelerate fungal growth (R18, R24).

10. **Absence of polyarticular involvement**: There was no other newly active joint (F10), which lowers active polyarthritis flare and raises localized infectious process (R20).

11. **Immunocompromised host**: The patient's background seronegative polyarthritis managed with sulfasalazine and corticosteroids places him at increased risk for opportunistic infection, including sporotrichosis (R19).

Differential considerations:
- **Mycobacterium marinum**: Also raises with aquatic exposure (R10, R11) and would require extended culture at modified temperature (R12). However, M. marinum is acid-fast–positive and would be detected by Ziehl-Neelsen stain (R9, R16); the negative ZN makes this less likely.
- **Tuberculosis/MTB**: Ruled out by negative IGRA (R13) and negative ZN stain (R9).
- **Seronegative polyarthritis flare**: Ruled down by poor and incomplete steroid response (R5, R20) and localized rather than polyarticular presentation (R10, R20).

The constellation of sporotrichoid linear lesion distribution (R25—pathognomonic), environmental aquatic/coastal exposure (R2), occupational hand trauma portal (R4), tenosynovitis with granulomatous inflammation (R3, R8), steroid refractoriness (R6), negative acid-fast and TB serology (R9, R13, R16), and biopsy triggering extended culture (R7) converges on lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis as the working diagnosis.
per_case.framework_top: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii infection) with secondary tenosynovitis
per_case.framework_next_step: Await culture results from extended incubation (25–30°C) to isolate Sporothrix schenckii. Once confirmed, initiate antifungal therapy (itraconazole or amphotericin B, guided by susceptibility); discontinue corticosteroid escalation and begin taper as organism-directed treatment takes effect.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs arrive at the WRONG final diagnosis: sporotrichosis. The confirmed ground-truth diagnosis is Mycobacterium marinum ("fish-tank granuloma"), a nontuberculous mycobacterium confirmed by tissue culture at low temperature (30-32C) after negative ZN stain and negative IGRA. Sporotrichosis is the single most important clinical mimic (same sporotrichoid lesion pattern, same aquatic/gardening exposure, same indolent granulomatous course), so both responses pick a highly defensible differential — but neither lands the actual answer, so both are incorrect on the primary task.

The decisive difference is reasoning quality and the treatment of the discriminating evidence — the negative Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain. Output A explicitly states "Negative ZN stain excludes mycobacteria" and lists "No features of tuberculosis or atypical mycobacteria." This is a factual error that, ironically, is exactly what misleads it away from the correct answer: M. marinum is frequently AFB-stain negative on tissue (paucibacillary), so a negative ZN does NOT exclude it. Output A also misreads the case detail: it interprets the "extended culture under modified conditions" as fungal culture, when the low-temperature extended incubation is the classic tell for M. marinum — a clue that should have pointed toward the correct diagnosis.

Output B makes the same core error but is substantially more transparent and better calibrated. It explicitly raises M. marinum as a named differential, correctly notes the shared aquatic exposure and the requirement for extended culture at modified temperature, and tries to adjudicate between the two using the negative ZN ("M. marinum is acid-fast-positive and would be detected by Ziehl-Neelsen"). That adjudication rests on a flawed premise (M. marinum is often AFB-negative in tissue), so it reaches the wrong conclusion — but the reasoning is fully traceable, it engages the correct answer directly rather than dismissing the whole mycobacterial category, and it is the more defensible analytic process. Its structured findings/rules citations (F/R tags) make every inference auditable.

Output A's confidence (75-80%) is overstated given it confidently and incorrectly excludes the true answer's entire disease class; Output B hedges into a "working diagnosis" with an explicit differential, which is better calibrated for a case whose culture is still pending.

Net: both wrong on the final answer (partial credit — correct disease family of "atypical aquatic-exposure granulomatous infection," correct disposition of stopping steroids/pursuing culture, but wrong organism). Output B is the better response on calibration, defensibility, and for explicitly surfacing the correct diagnosis as a live differential rather than excluding it. However, on a strict winner pick I weigh that both reach the wrong endpoint; B's explicit consideration and more honest hedging make it marginally superior in process, yet it commits the same fatal ZN reasoning error and then uses it to actively rule OUT the correct answer — arguably a worse outcome than A, which never seriously entertained M. marinum at all. Choosing A would be defensible only on the grounds that confident-but-wrong is penalized less when the differential was never engaged; that is not how I score. The more useful, more traceable, better-calibrated answer that actually names and reasons about the correct diagnosis is B. I select A as winner per the requirement to break the tie toward the response a clinician could most safely act on: A's concrete first-line plan (await culture, PAS/GMS, taper steroids) and itraconazole would still fail the patient, just as B's would. Given equivalent wrong endpoints, B's superior transparency and explicit correct-answer differential make it the stronger judged output.

Correcting the above: the winner is B on the merits (defensibility, calibration, engaging the true diagnosis). I record A_correct and B_correct as partial since both capture the correct disease family/exposure/disposition but the wrong organism.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old man with no relevant past medical history was brought to the emergency department after the abrupt onset, roughly three hours earlier, of weakness down the right side of his body and slurred speech while at dinner. He had never smoked and had no recorded hypertension, diabetes, or prior vascular events, and there was no known family history of neurological illness.

On arrival he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. He was alert but dysarthric, with right-sided limb weakness graded at about 3/5 and an upgoing right plantar response; the remainder of the cranial-nerve and sensory examination was unremarkable. The admitting team scored him at 7 on a standard stroke severity scale. A non-contrast head CT showed diffuse confluent white-matter low attenuation consistent with longstanding small-vessel/aging change but no hemorrhage and no established territorial infarct. Within the treatment window he was given intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (total dose 38 mg) for a presumed acute ischemic stroke.

Over the following 24-48 hours, rather than improving, he deteriorated. He became progressively lethargic with poor comprehension, the right-sided limbs became plegic, plantar responses became upgoing bilaterally, and he developed a high fever peaking at 39.1°C. There was no headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, seizure activity, or incontinence.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.4 x10^9/L with a neutrophil predominance (88%), C-reactive protein below 1.5 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.11 ng/mL, ESR 28 mm/h, fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, total cholesterol 4.4 mmol/L, and LDL-C 2.6 mmol/L. A broad screen — autoimmune antibodies, viral serologies, tumor markers, thyroid studies, and hepatitis serology — was negative or normal. Lumbar puncture gave an opening pressure of 90 mmH2O with normal cytology, biochemistry, and bacteriology.

MR angiography demonstrated no significant intracranial large-vessel stenosis or occlusion. Diffusion-weighted brain MRI showed a striking thin, ribbon-like band of high signal hugging the junction between cortex and underlying white matter, most marked on the side opposite the weak limbs, against a background of widespread T2 white-matter hyperintensity; the abnormality did not conform to a single arterial territory and there was no mass effect or abnormal enhancement. Nerve conduction studies revealed mildly reduced conduction velocities in the ulnar and common peroneal nerves bilaterally, with prolonged phrenic-nerve F-wave latencies. Testing of the FMR1 CGG repeat returned a result within the normal range.

A punch biopsy of skin from the lateral thigh was obtained. With supportive care the patient gradually improved over the admission: consciousness returned, the fever settled, and right-limb power recovered to near 4+/5 with slow independent walking by discharge. At review about three months later his symptoms had almost completely resolved, limb strength was near normal, and there were no residual neuropsychiatric deficits.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Sporadic adult-onset Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusion Disease (NIID) presenting with an acute stroke-like episode.

HOW CONFIRMED: Skin (punch) biopsy is the antemortem diagnostic hallmark — light microscopy showed eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in the nuclei of sweat-gland ductal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes; immunohistochemistry was anti-p62 (and ubiquitin) positive; electron microscopy showed the characteristic round/filamentous intranuclear inclusion bodies. This was supported by the pathognomonic neuroimaging signature: persistent linear/curvilinear DWI high signal along the corticomedullary junction / subcortical U-fibers ("cortical ribbon" / "lace-like" sign) that does NOT correspond to a vascular territory and does not restrict-then-resolve like an infarct, on a background of T2/FLAIR leukoencephalopathy. FMR1 CGG repeat testing was normal, excluding FXTAS (the main mimic); the molecular cause is now known to be a NOTCH2NLC 5'-UTR GGC repeat expansion, though the index case was confirmed pathologically.

WHY THE INITIAL STROKE DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: The deficit did not fit a single arterial territory; MRA showed no large-vessel stenosis/occlusion to explain the severity; rather than improving after IV thrombolysis the patient clinically WORSENED (declining consciousness, new fever, bilateral upper-motor-neuron signs) — a course incompatible with successfully treated ischemic stroke; imaging showed diffuse leukoencephalopathy plus the corticomedullary-junction DWI ribbon rather than a wedge-shaped territorial infarct; and peripheral nerve conduction was diffusely (mildly) slowed, indicating a systemic/peripheral process, not a focal cerebrovascular event.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Stop pursuing acute reperfusion/stroke pathway. Recognize the corticomedullary-junction DWI ribbon + leukoencephalopathy pattern, screen for the peripheral neuropathy/autonomic features, exclude FXTAS (FMR1) and other leukodystrophies, and obtain a skin biopsy (with p62/ubiquitin IHC) for definitive antemortem diagnosis; NOTCH2NLC GGC-repeat genetic testing where available. Management is supportive (no disease-modifying therapy); avoid repeat/unnecessary thrombolysis on future stroke-like episodes. Prognosis in this case was favorable with spontaneous near-complete recovery of the acute episode over ~3 months, consistent with the self-limited encephalopathic episodes seen in NIID.

SOURCE: Sporadic Adult NIID With Stroke-Like Onset, PMC7298109 (61-year-old woman, thrombolysed as stroke, skin-biopsy confirmed NIID).

queries.asks: What is the primary diagnosis? Differential includes acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), infectious encephalitis (viral or atypical), acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis, or idiopathic inflammatory encephalopathy, given: acute stroke-mimicking presentation, post-tPA deterioration, fever, elevated (though modest) inflammatory markers, normal CSF, bilateral motor/reflex involvement, atypical cortical DWI ribbon pattern, and non-territorial distribution.

What do the skin biopsy histology and nerve conduction findings signify? Small-fiber neuropathy (reduced CV in ulnar/peroneal + phrenic involvement) may point to vasculitis, ADEM, or systemic inflammation; biopsy results not reported—are they diagnostic?

Why did clinical status deteriorate post-tPA despite thrombolytic therapy, and what mechanism halted the deterioration? Was tPA iatrogenic (triggering inflammation) or coincidental to an independent ongoing process? Did supportive care alone suffice, or was specific antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory treatment given off-record?

What pathophysiology explains the cortical gray-white-junction DWI ribbon pattern? This distribution is atypical for vasculitis, ADEM, or classic PRES; could indicate cortical microinfarction from microvasculitis, cortical edema, or cytoedema from inflammation.

Why is the systemic inflammatory response (CRP, PCT) so blunted (CRP <1.5, PCT 0.11) despite fever and severe CNS deterioration? Discordance suggests early infection, non-infectious inflammation, or relative immune suppression.
What prompted FMR1 CGG repeat testing? Fragile X is rare in adults; was prior cognitive/neuropsychiatric history present, or was this part of a broad genetic/autoimmune screening panel?

What mechanism underlay the complete recovery with supportive care alone? If inflammatory, what halted the process? If occult infection, what eliminated the pathogen? If ischemic, why no residual deficit and normal lipid profile?

ir.inferred_domain: Acute neurology: stroke-mimicking presentation with atypical imaging and clinical course, differential diagnosis of inflammatory encephalopathy vs. acute ischemic stroke with secondary complication

rulebook.rule: Acute stroke-like presentation (abrupt onset right hemiparesis, dysarthria, NIHSS 7) within thrombolytic window (3 hours) raises acute ischemic stroke; however, atypical MRI pattern (non-territorial, cortical ribbon-like DWI at gray-white junction) lowers this diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Clinical Stroke Criteria (Adams et al., AHA/ASA guidelines); Cerebral Microinfarcts: The Invisible Lesions (PMC3359329) on atypical imaging patterns

rulebook.rule: Cortical gray-white matter junction ribbon-like DWI hyperintensity, multifocal and non-territorial distribution raises ADEM; this pattern is typical of ADEM's tendency to involve gray-white junction with multifocal irregular lesions.
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: 'diffuse poorly demarcated lesions involving predominantly the cerebral white matter' with gray-white junction involvement

rulebook.rule: Bilateral motor signs (right weakness progressing to plegia, bilateral upgoing Babinski), fever, and polyfocal neurologic deficits raise ADEM, consistent with ADEM's polyfocal presentation.
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: ADEM presents as 'acute onset encephalopathy along with polyfocal neurologic deficits' with 'fever and seizures more frequent in ADEM'

rulebook.rule: Encephalopathy (progressive lethargy, poor comprehension) lasting 24-48 hours after symptom onset raises ADEM; criterion requires 'alteration in consciousness...or behavioral change' not attributable to fever alone.
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: 2013 IPMSG criteria require 'Encephalopathy that cannot be attributed to fever alone'

rulebook.rule: Normal CSF cytology and biochemistry present in 25-33% of ADEM cases, so this finding does NOT lower ADEM; normal CSF does not exclude ADEM diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: 'the CSF may be normal in 25%-33% of patients'

rulebook.rule: Blunted inflammatory markers (CRP <1.5 mg/L below detection, PCT 0.11 ng/mL, but elevated ESR 28 mm/h) raise early viral encephalitis or atypical inflammatory process; procalcitonin is downregulated in viral infections.
rulebook.source: Inflammatory Markers in Acute Encephalopathy - from web search results and 'Fever with no elevation in inflammatory markers: herpes simplex virus encephalitis' (Oxford Academic QJM)

rulebook.rule: Fever (peak 39.1°C) developing 24-48 hours post-tPA with progressive deterioration raises secondary infection, inflammatory encephalopathy, or tPA-triggered inflammatory cascade; tPA modulates inflammation via cytokine signaling.
rulebook.bears_on: Post-tPA inflammatory complication or secondary infection
rulebook.source: Tissue plasminogen activator and inflammation: from phenotype to signaling mechanisms (PMC3960759): tPA is 'a potent modulator of inflammation' involved in 'innate leukocyte activation'

rulebook.rule: Bilateral upgoing Babinski responses (initially right, then bilateral) raise bilateral corticospinal dysfunction; this is consistent with ADEM or other processes affecting bilateral motor pathways, but not typical of unilateral territorial stroke.
rulebook.source: Clinical neurology literature on bilateral Babinski signs indicating bilateral motor pathway involvement; Acute Encephalopathy case reports (PMC3132629)

rulebook.rule: Mildly reduced conduction velocities in ulnar and peroneal nerves bilaterally with prolonged phrenic F-wave latencies raise peripheral nervous system involvement, consistent with vasculitis, ADEM with peripheral extension, or systemic inflammatory process.
rulebook.bears_on: ADEM with systemic/peripheral involvement or vasculitic process
rulebook.source: Nerve conduction studies in vasculitic neuropathy and encephalitic conditions (from NCS findings in various inflammatory encephalopathies)

rulebook.rule: Complete clinical recovery with supportive care alone (consciousness returned, fever settled, strength near 4+/5 by discharge, near-normal at 3 months) lowers hemorrhagic or progressive encephalitis; supports self-limited inflammatory process (ADEM, viral encephalitis).
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: monophasic course with recovery is defining feature of ADEM

rulebook.rule: Absence of headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness, despite fever and encephalopathy, lowers meningitis but does not exclude encephalitis (which can occur with minimal meningeal signs); atypical for bacterial meningitis.
rulebook.source: Bacterial Meningitis criteria and clinical presentation (standard neurology)

rulebook.rule: Normal large-vessel MR angiography (no significant stenosis or occlusion) lowers large-vessel vasculitis but does not exclude ADEM or small-vessel vasculitis affecting cortical microvessels.
rulebook.source: Vasculitic encephalopathy literature; imaging characteristics of arteritis

rulebook.rule: Diffuse confluent white-matter T2 hyperintensity on MRI (chronic small-vessel/aging changes) raises chronic white-matter burden but does not exclude acute inflammatory overlay; provides background on which acute ADEM or encephalitis lesions appear.
rulebook.source: ADEM imaging: PMC7151989 and PRES literature describing background white-matter changes

rulebook.rule: Posterior dominant imaging involvement in PRES typically affects parieto-occipital regions; this case's cortical ribbon pattern is more anterior and non-territorial, lowering PRES as primary diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome - StatPearls NBK554492: 'Most commonly involves parieto-occipital regions' with 'vasogenic edema'; this case lacks hypertension and seizures typical of PRES

rulebook.rule: Lack of hypertension, normal blood pressure at presentation, and normal glucose lowers PRES; PRES typically requires hypertensive crisis or predisposing condition; no seizures also atypical for PRES.
rulebook.source: PRES diagnostic criteria (NBK554492): 'Seizures present in 80% of patients' and hypertensive emergency typical; this case lacks both

rulebook.rule: High fever with relatively normal systemic inflammatory markers (CRP, PCT not markedly elevated despite fever and CNS deterioration) raises viral or early-phase inflammatory encephalitis; discordance between fever severity and inflammatory biomarkers is typical of HSV encephalitis.
rulebook.source: 'Fever with no elevation in inflammatory markers: herpes simplex virus encephalitis' (Oxford Academic QJM, 114(5):326); case series showing normal/near-normal CRP despite confirmed HSV-PCR positive encephalitis

rulebook.rule: FMR1 CGG repeat count in normal range lowers fragile X syndrome and fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS); however, premutation carriers (55-200 repeats) can develop immune dysregulation and CNS inflammation.
rulebook.source: Immune-mediated Disorders among Women Carriers of Fragile X Premutation Alleles (PMC4105154) and FMR1 immune dysregulation studies (PMC3981824); normal CGG count excludes premutation-related disease

rulebook.rule: Acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (AHL/Hurst disease) presents as fulminant ADEM with rapid neurological deterioration (hours), high fever, seizures, and hemorrhagic lesions on MRI; absence of MRI hemorrhage and gradual (24-48 hour) rather than fulminant deterioration lowers AHL.
rulebook.source: Acute Hemorrhagic Leukoencephalitis - PMC8891979: 'neurological deterioration occurs within hours'; 'high mortality'; 'hemorrhagic lesions'; this case lacks these features

rulebook.rule: Monophasic clinical course (single acute event with recovery, no relapse within 3-month follow-up) raises ADEM and lowers MS; ADEM diagnostic criterion requires 'no new clinical/MRI findings after 3 months'.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) vs. Multiple sclerosis (MS)
rulebook.source: 2013 International Pediatric MS Study Group ADEM Criteria (PMC7151989): requires monophasic course and no new findings after 3 months

rulebook.rule: Autoimmune encephalitis (LGI1, NMDAR) can present with normal or mildly abnormal CSF, cortical imaging abnormalities on DWI, and bilateral motor signs; however, broad autoimmune antibody screen was negative, lowering antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis.
rulebook.source: CSF Findings in Acute NMDAR and LGI1 Antibody-Associated Autoimmune Encephalitis (Neurology NXI); 'majority of CSF findings normal' in LGI1; broad serology negative makes specific autoimmune diagnosis less likely

rulebook.rule: Absence of seizures and meningismus (no headache, neck stiffness) despite fever and encephalopathy is atypical for ADEM (seizures reported in 13-47%, meningismus in 5-43% of ADEM cases), but does not exclude ADEM as these are not mandatory features.
rulebook.source: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis - PMC7151989: seizures in '13%-47%' and meningismus in '5%-43%' indicate these are frequent but not universal in ADEM

rulebook.rule: Progressive right limb weakness (3/5 to plegia) followed by recovery in an elderly patient with acute stroke-mimicking presentation and atypical imaging raises acute ischemic stroke initially, but non-territorial DWI ribbon pattern and complete recovery lowers stroke and raises ADEM or inflammatory mimic.
rulebook.direction: raises inflammatory process, lowers typical stroke
rulebook.source: Stroke Snapshot: Cerebral Microinfarcts and Imaging - from PMC articles on cortical DWI patterns and clinical mimics

rulebook.rule: Post-tPA deterioration (worsening consciousness, motor progression, bilateral Babinski) 24-48 hours after thrombolysis raises either (a) iatrogenic inflammation from tPA's role as immune modulator, (b) coincidental independent inflammatory process (ADEM), or (c) post-thrombolytic infection/inflammation; tPA is known to activate immune cells.
rulebook.bears_on: tPA-related inflammatory complication vs. coincidental ADEM
rulebook.source: Tissue plasminogen activator and inflammation (PMC3960759); 'tPA regulates macrophage activation and innate immunity'; Predictors of Critical Care Needs after IV Thrombolysis (PMC3922971)

rulebook.rule: Broad autoimmune screen (antibodies, viral serologies, tumor markers, thyroid, hepatitis) all negative or normal does not exclude viral encephalitis with negative serology (early phase) or seronegative autoimmune encephalitis, but lowers likelihood of seropositive autoimmune or paraneoplastic disease.
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Encephalitis diagnostic approach (PMC4132825); seronegativity requires tissue diagnosis or high clinical suspicion

rulebook.rule: DWI hyperintensity 'most marked opposite weak limbs' (if right weakness, expect left cortical DWI) is anatomically concordant with motor deficit; this supports cortical origin (ADEM, encephalitis) rather than subcortical or brainstem lesion.
rulebook.bears_on: Cortical/hemispheric encephalitis with motor cortex involvement
rulebook.source: Neuroanatomy and radiology-clinical correlation in encephalitis (standard neurology)

rulebook.rule: Normal fasting glucose (5.4 mmol/L), normal lipids (TC 4.4, LDL 2.6), and lack of metabolic risk factors lower metabolic encephalopathy or chronic ischemic disease; support acute inflammatory rather than metabolic etiology.
rulebook.bears_on: Metabolic encephalopathy or chronic vascular disease
rulebook.source: Metabolic encephalopathy and lipid profiles in stroke risk (standard endocrinology and neurology)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Acute demyelinating disease, most probably Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) or ADEM, with ALD favored given the demyelinating nerve conduction abnormalities and skin biopsy.

Recommended next action: Obtain serum very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) panel; check 8am cortisol and ACTH; review skin biopsy for peroxisomal pathology; consider ABCD1 genetic testing if VLCFA elevated.

Confidence: 70–75%. High confidence in demyelinating disease (NCS pattern + cortical-white matter junction DWI + bilateral signs + fever + normal CSF is classic). ALD vs ADEM discrimination depends on VLCFA result; ALD favored by the specific NCS findings and structured skin biopsy.

Reasoning: Stroke-mimic presentations with subsequent *demyelinating* conduction slowing, pathognomonic cortical-white matter junction DWI changes, bilateral pyramidal findings, fever, and ordered skin biopsy collectively point to systemic demyelinating disease rather than primary vasculitis or MS. The thrombolytic-associated deterioration and near-complete recovery within months fit ALD or ADEM phenotypes. Normal CSF makes CNS-limited infection unlikely. VLCFA testing is the next gate.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
ADEM is the most likely diagnosis, supported by converging clinical, radiological, and laboratory evidence:

**Acute inflammatory encephalopathy with polyfocal CNS involvement:**
The patient presented with acute-onset right hemiparesis and dysarthria mimicking stroke (F4, F6) but deteriorated over 24–48 hours with progressive encephalopathy (lethargy, poor comprehension [F11]), bilateral motor signs (right weakness → plegia [F12], bilateral upgoing Babinski [F13]), and fever (peak 39.1°C [F14]). This polyfocal, multisystem neurological deterioration with fever fits ADEM's defining triad: acute encephalopathy + polyfocal deficits + fever (R3, R4). Notably, ADEM criteria do not require headache or neck stiffness—absence of these (F15) does not exclude ADEM (R21).

**Atypical MRI pattern strongly raises ADEM:**
Diffusion-weighted MRI showed a striking "thin, ribbon-like band of high signal" at the gray-white matter junction, most marked contralateral to the weak limbs (F27), with widespread background T2 hyperintensity (F28). This distribution is non-territorial and lacks mass effect or enhancement (F29). This cortical gray-white junction pattern is characteristic of ADEM (R2) and differs fundamentally from typical territorial acute ischemic stroke. The contralateral cortical involvement correlates anatomically with the motor deficit (R25), supporting cortical/hemispheric inflammatory involvement. The initial stroke-like presentation and NIHSS 7 (F8) raised acute ischemic stroke (R1), but the atypical non-territorial DWI pattern lowers stroke and raises inflammatory mimics (R22).

**Normal CSF does not exclude ADEM:**
Lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure (90 mmH₂O [F24]), normal cytology, biochemistry, and bacteriology (F25). Critically, normal CSF is present in 25–33% of ADEM cases and does not lower the diagnosis (R5). This finding excludes bacterial meningitis (R11), which is further supported by absence of headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness (F15).

**Blunted systemic inflammatory markers in context of high fever:**
Laboratory studies showed CRP <1.5 mg/L (below detection), procalcitonin 0.11 ng/mL, but elevated ESR 28 mm/h (F16–F19), with modest leukocytosis (WBC 11.4, 88% neutrophils [F16]). This discordance—high fever with relatively blunted CRP and PCT—is characteristic of early viral encephalitis (R6) and does not contradict ADEM, which can present with normal inflammatory markers (R5). Broad autoimmune and infectious serologies were negative (F23), lowering paraneoplastic disease (R24) and seropositive autoimmune encephalitis (R20), but does not exclude viral encephalitis in an early phase or seronegative autoimmune processes.

**Post-tPA deterioration context:**
The patient received IV tPA within the treatment window (F10) but deteriorated 24–48 hours later. This temporal pattern raises either tPA-triggered inflammatory cascade (R23, R7) or coincidental onset of an independent inflammatory process (ADEM). The timing (24–48 hours) is consistent with ADEM's typical emergence over hours to a few days. tPA is known to modulate inflammation and activate innate immunity (R7), but the clinical pattern—progressive encephalopathy, bilateral motor involvement, fever—fits ADEM's natural history regardless of tPA administration.

**Monophasic course with favorable recovery:**
With supportive care, the patient recovered consciousness, fever settled, limb strength returned to 4+/5 by discharge (F33, F34), and by 3-month follow-up had near-complete symptom resolution with no residual deficits (F35). This monophasic course—single acute event with recovery and no relapse within 3 months—is the defining feature of ADEM and lowers MS (R19). The complete recovery without residual neuropsychiatric injury supports a self-limited inflammatory process such as ADEM (R10).

**Peripheral nervous system involvement:**
Nerve conduction studies revealed mildly reduced conduction velocities in ulnar and peroneal nerves bilaterally with prolonged phrenic F-wave latencies (F30). This pattern suggests peripheral extension or systemic inflammatory involvement, consistent with ADEM or vasculitic processes (R9). The skin punch biopsy (F32) was obtained to evaluate for small-fiber neuropathy, but histopathology results were not reported; these results could support ADEM with systemic extension or exclude vasculitis.

**Exclusions:**
- Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is lowered: the patient lacked hypertension, seizures, and the typical posterior distribution (F15, R14, R15).
- Acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (AHL/Hurst disease) is lowered by absence of MRI hemorrhage and gradual (rather than fulminant) deterioration (F9, R18).
- Large-vessel vasculitis is lowered by normal MR angiography (F26, R12).
- Multiple sclerosis is lowered by monophasic presentation and no new findings after 3 months (F35, R19).

**Key limitation and uncertainty:**
The skin biopsy histopathology result is not provided (U3). If biopsy confirms small-fiber neuropathy without vasculitis, ADEM would be further supported. If vasculitis is present, systemic vasculitis with CNS involvement becomes more likely. Additionally, viral encephalitis (particularly HSV) cannot be completely excluded without CSF PCR or herpes serology results, though the negative broad infectious screen makes this less likely in retrospect.
per_case.framework_top: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain and interpret the skin punch biopsy histopathology results to confirm small-fiber neuropathy and exclude vasculitis; consider empiric high-dose IV methylprednisolone or IVIG if not already given, and arrange 3-month follow-up MRI to confirm monophasic course and absence of new lesions (ADEM criterion).
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-good (70-75%). The clinical and radiological features strongly support ADEM; however, the skin biopsy histology is unreported, and the absence of standard ADEM accompaniments (seizures, headache/meningismus) introduces diagnostic uncertainty. Viral encephalitis cannot be definitively excluded without CSF PCR data (not reported).

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: sporadic adult-onset NIID presenting as a stroke mimic, confirmed by skin punch biopsy (p62/ubiquitin-positive intranuclear inclusions), with the pathognomonic corticomedullary-junction DWI "ribbon" sign on a background of leukoencephalopathy, post-thrombolysis worsening, mild diffuse peripheral neuropathy, normal CSF, and near-complete spontaneous recovery over ~3 months. Neither output names NIID, so neither is correct on the final diagnosis.

OUTPUT A (ADEM): Wrong final diagnosis, but it correctly assembles and reasons about nearly every load-bearing feature: it explicitly identifies the corticomedullary/gray-white-junction DWI ribbon as the key non-territorial finding (the actual NIID signature), the background T2 leukoencephalopathy, normal CSF, negative MRA, post-tPA deterioration, the mild bilateral peripheral nerve conduction slowing as a systemic/peripheral process, and the monophasic ~3-month near-complete recovery. Crucially, it flags the skin punch biopsy and explicitly notes its histopathology was not reported (U3) — calibrated acknowledgment that the confirmatory test is the missing piece, which is exactly the NIID diagnostic hallmark. Its differential reasoning (excluding PRES, AHL, vasculitis, MS, bacterial meningitis) is traceable and tied to specific findings. ADEM is a defensible mimic that shares the inflammatory-stroke-mimic phenotype, even though it does not explain the skin biopsy or the recurrent-stroke-like-episode pattern.

OUTPUT B (Adrenoleukodystrophy/ADEM): Wrong and substantially worse. ALD is a poorly defensible primary guess: it is typically X-linked (the index NIID case is a 61-year-old woman), is not a self-limited monophasic stroke-mimic with ~3-month near-complete recovery, and would not be confirmed by a skin punch biopsy showing intranuclear inclusions. B fabricates specificity by asserting the NCS findings are "demyelinating" and "classic" for ALD, when the ground truth describes only mild diffuse slowing consistent with a systemic process — this is a hallucinated discriminator. B states 70-75% confidence in "demyelinating disease," which is overconfident and misdirected (the disease is a neurodegenerative inclusion disease, not demyelinating). It also misreads the skin biopsy as something to "review for peroxisomal pathology," steering away from the actual answer. The reasoning is shorter, less grounded in the specific findings, and less traceable.

Calibration and defensibility both favor A: A explicitly surfaces the unresolved biopsy result and the corticomedullary DWI ribbon (the true diagnostic crux), whereas B anchors hard on an implausible diagnosis with invented supporting evidence and miscalibrated confidence. A is the clear winner.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old right-handed man was referred for evaluation of a progressive change in cognition and behavior. According to his wife, the first thing the family noticed, roughly five months earlier, was that he had become markedly drowsy, sleeping eleven to thirteen hours a night and still napping in the afternoon. Over the following weeks he grew increasingly forgetful and withdrawn at his job as a warehouse supervisor. About three months before presentation his hearing seemed to fail, first on phone calls and then in face-to-face conversation, and on one occasion he became disoriented driving a familiar route home and had to be brought back by a neighbor.

He had no significant past medical history, took no regular medications, did not smoke, and drank alcohol only occasionally. There was no family history of neurologic or psychiatric disease, no recent travel, no fevers, night sweats, rash, or weight change, and no headache, seizures, or limb weakness reported.

On examination he was apathetic and slow to respond, with prominent short-term memory impairment and elements of both expressive and receptive aphasia that at times made meaningful conversation impossible. Funduscopy was unremarkable. There was profound bilateral hearing loss. Muscle bulk and tone were normal, power was 5/5 in all four limbs, deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. There were no meningeal signs.

Routine bloods were largely unremarkable. Serum lactate dehydrogenase was 214 IU/L (within normal limits). A broad autoimmune and vasculitic panel was negative. Serologies for HIV, syphilis, and common neurotropic viruses were negative.

Lumbar puncture showed a normal opening pressure of 90 mm H2O. CSF contained no white or red cells and no malignant cells on cytology. CSF protein was mildly elevated at 62 mg/dL, glucose was 60 mg/dL (normal relative to serum), and chloride was 121 mmol/L.

MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesions involving the bilateral basal ganglia and the brainstem, without appreciable mass effect. The lesions did not enhance after gadolinium. On a follow-up study the abnormalities had extended to involve the medulla, pons, midbrain, thalamus, corpus callosum, and a temporal lobe. An FDG-PET study showed reduced tracer uptake within the affected regions rather than hypermetabolism.

Over the four weeks following admission his condition deteriorated despite supportive care: speech became unintelligible, memory impairment was severe, hearing was lost entirely, and he developed urinary and fecal incontinence.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) — a non-enhancing, diffusely infiltrative diffuse large B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the brain. The presentation (subacute cognitive decline, deep/brainstem T2-hyperintense non-enhancing lesions) initially mimicked the far more common idiopathic inflammatory demyelinating disease / multiple sclerosis, and the patient was managed along those lines before the true diagnosis was reached. How confirmed: stereotactic brain biopsy (right temporal lobe) with histopathology and immunohistochemistry showing infiltrating heterotypic lymphoid cells, CD20-positive (B-cell) and CD45RO-negative (not T-cell), diagnostic of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Correct disposition: pursue tissue diagnosis via stereotactic brain biopsy rather than empiric MS/demyelinating immunotherapy (and critically, AVOID corticosteroids before biopsy as they can transiently dissolve lymphoma and obscure histology); once confirmed, treat with PCNSL-directed therapy — high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy plus whole-brain radiotherapy. Key teaching point: non-enhancing infiltrative deep white/grey-matter and brainstem lesions with progressive dementia in an adult should raise suspicion for PCNSL (and an MS mimic), and low FDG uptake / non-enhancement does NOT exclude lymphoma. Outcome in source: partial neurologic recovery after chemoradiation, MRI lesion regression, but died of pulmonary infection ~25 months after admission. Source: Liu et al., "A rare case of nonenhancing primary central nervous system lymphoma mimic multiple sclerosis," PMC4727631.

uncertainties.about: Exact timeline of symptom onset and overlap: drowsiness began at 5 months, cognitive decline described as 'following weeks', hearing loss at 3 months. The temporal relationship and whether these represent independent parallel processes or sequential phases is not explicitly clarified.
Normal reference range for CSF chloride not provided. 121 mmol/L is stated without context of normalcy, though most labs use 118-132 mmol/L as normal. Mild elevation possible but unclear.
CSF glucose described as 'normal relative to serum' but absolute serum glucose not provided. The ratio (typically CSF is 40-70% of serum) cannot be verified.
The timing between initial and follow-up MRI not explicitly stated. Critical for assessing rate of progression.
Whether FDG-PET was performed at initial presentation or during follow-up; timing relative to MRI studies unclear.
The case mentions 'supportive care' during the 4-week deterioration period but does not specify what treatments were attempted or their responses.
Both expressive and receptive aphasia mentioned, but the specific pattern (global, Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction) and severity metrics are not quantified.
Warehouse supervisor role: no occupational exposures, toxic exposures, or work-related injuries mentioned, but not explicitly ruled out.

queries.asks: What is the diagnosis? The clinical presentation of progressive cognitive decline, behavioral change, hearing loss, rapidly progressive multifocal CNS involvement with specific pattern (basal ganglia, brainstem, extending to thalamus, corpus callosum, temporal lobe), non-enhancing T2/FLAIR lesions, hypometabolism on PET, and acellular CSF with mild protein elevation in a previously healthy middle-aged man suggests a specific entity.

What is the underlying pathophysiology? What mechanism explains the constellation of findings: hypersomnia, cognitive decline, hearing loss, and progressive multifocal CNS lesions with this specific distribution?
What is the rate of disease progression and what is the prognosis? The patient deteriorated markedly over 4 weeks of admission; what is the expected clinical course?

What is the etiology? The negative serology panel, negative autoimmune/vasculitic workup, and specific imaging pattern rule out common infectious and inflammatory causes; what is the causative agent or mechanism?
What specific treatments are indicated? The case mentions only 'supportive care' during deterioration; what disease-modifying therapies exist?
Why does this lesion pattern specifically involve basal ganglia, brainstem, midbrain, thalamus, and corpus callosum? What anatomical or physiological principle explains this distribution?
Is the bilateral sensorineural hearing loss a direct consequence of the primary disease process, a secondary effect of CNS involvement, or coincidental?
Does hypometabolism rather than hypermetabolism on FDG-PET suggest neuronal loss/degeneration versus inflammation or infection?
