ir.inferred_domain: Clinical Neurology / Neuropsychiatry — specifically rapid-progressive multifocal CNS disease with characteristic imaging pattern (non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in deep gray matter and brainstem), hypometabolic on PET, presenting with cognitive/behavioral decline, sensorineural hearing loss, and acellular CSF with mild protein elevation. The constellation suggests a neurodegenerative, infectious, or metabolic/toxic encephalopathy rather than primary inflammatory/demyelinating or neoplastic disease.</inferred_domain>

rulebook.rule: Subacute cognitive decline developing over months (not years) raises suspicion for rapidly progressive dementia including prion disease, infections, and metabolic encephalopathy rather than typical slow-progressing neurodegenerative disease
rulebook.source: The Evaluation of Rapidly Progressive Dementia. PMC3356774. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356774/

rulebook.rule: Marked hypersomnia at symptom onset (sleeping 11-13 hours nightly plus daytime naps) is atypical for progressive supranuclear palsy; more characteristic of encephalitis, prion disease, or metabolic encephalopathy
rulebook.source: Dementia in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy: A Narrative Review. PMC12965954. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12965954/

rulebook.rule: Multiple T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem without enhancement are characteristic of sporadic CJD, matching the cortical ribboning and deep gray matter involvement pattern (92% sensitivity, 97% specificity)
rulebook.source: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Brain MRI lesion features from 2 cases reports. PMC10767313. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10767313/

rulebook.rule: Progressive multifocal extension of lesions to medulla, pons, midbrain, thalamus, corpus callosum, and temporal lobe reflects disease propagation pattern consistent with prion pathology or some infectious encephalitides (Whipple's, CNS syphilis)
rulebook.bears_on: Sporadic CJD; CNS Whipple's Disease; Neurosyphilis
rulebook.source: Brainstem and cerebellar radiological findings in progressive supranuclear palsy. Brain Communications. https://academic.oup.com/braincomms/article/7/1/fcaf051/8002813

rulebook.rule: FDG-PET hypometabolism (reduced tracer uptake) is the predominant finding in both neurodegenerative disease and some infectious/inflammatory conditions; does not reliably distinguish between prion disease, infection, and inflammation
rulebook.source: Abnormal brain metabolism on FDG-PET/CT is a common early finding in autoimmune encephalitis. PMC5442608. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5442608/

rulebook.rule: Acellular CSF (no white cells, red cells, or malignant cells) argues against bacterial/fungal meningitis and typical viral meningitis but is compatible with prion disease, acellular infection (neurosyphilis, Whipple's disease), and neurodegenerative disease
rulebook.source: Cerebrospinal Fluid - Clinical Methods. NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK398/

rulebook.rule: Mild CSF protein elevation (62 mg/dL) without pleocytosis is consistent with neurosyphilis (70% of general paresis cases have 46-100 mg/dL protein), prion disease, Whipple's disease, and neurodegenerative disease
rulebook.source: Neurosyphilis - StatPearls. NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK540979/

rulebook.rule: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss beginning 3 months into illness and progressing to complete bilateral deafness raises suspicion for syphilitic otosyphilis (eighth cranial nerve involvement by Treponema pallidum), Whipple's disease with basilar involvement, or mitochondrial disease (MELAS, MNGIE)
rulebook.source: Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, & Otosyphilis. CDC. https://www.cdc.gov/syphilis/hcp/neurosyphilis-ocular-syphilis-otosyphilis/index.html

rulebook.rule: Negative serology for syphilis lowers probability of neurosyphilis; however, serology may be negative in early or late CNS syphilis (false-negative rate up to 25% in general paresis) and must be interpreted with CSF findings and clinical presentation
rulebook.source: Neurosyphilis - StatPearls. NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK540979/

rulebook.rule: Negative broad autoimmune and vasculitic serologies lowers probability of primary autoimmune encephalitis, vasculitis, and SLE with CNS involvement; maintains differential toward infectious, prion, and primary neurodegenerative causes
rulebook.source: Abnormal brain metabolism on FDG-PET/CT is a common early finding in autoimmune encephalitis. PMC5442608. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5442608/

rulebook.rule: Negative serology for HIV, syphilis, and common neurotropic viruses lowers suspicion for these infections but does not exclude CNS syphilis (false-negative serology possible), other rare infections, or non-infectious causes
rulebook.source: Neurosyphilis - StatPearls. NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK540979/

rulebook.rule: Apathy, bradyphrenia, and prominent short-term memory impairment are consistent with sCJD (akinetic mutism in advanced cases), neurosyphilis (general paresis with dementia), and Whipple's disease (medial temporal lobe pathology); nonspecific but fits multiple diagnoses
rulebook.source: Neuropsychological Features in Patients with General Paresis of the Insane at an Early Stage. PMC9749326. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749326/

rulebook.rule: Global aphasia (both expressive and receptive components impaired) suggests dominant hemisphere temporal-perisylvian involvement; seen in temporal lobe pathology (Whipple's predilection for medial temporal lobes), cortical ribboning (sCJD), and herpes encephalitis
rulebook.source: Central nervous system involvement in Whipple's disease: Clinical Study of 18 Patients. PMC4553994. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553994/

rulebook.rule: Absence of meningeal signs (neck stiffness, Kernig's, Brudzinski's) lowers probability of acute bacterial meningitis and some viral meningitides; compatible with acellular CNS pathology including prion disease and neurodegenerative disease
rulebook.source: The Evaluation of Rapidly Progressive Dementia. PMC3356774. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356774/

rulebook.rule: Absence of headache lowers suspicion for meningitis and inflammatory encephalitis (though absence does not exclude them); more typical of pure neurodegenerative disease progression
rulebook.source: The Evaluation of Rapidly Progressive Dementia. PMC3356774. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356774/

rulebook.rule: Preserved motor strength (5/5 throughout) and normal reflexes argue against motor neuron disease (ALS), advanced progressive supranuclear palsy (which causes postural instability and motor decline), and some polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias
rulebook.bears_on: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy; Polyglutamine Diseases; ALS
rulebook.source: Progressive supranuclear palsy: cognitive and behavioral changes. MedLink Neurology. https://www.medlink.com/articles/progressive-supranuclear-palsy-cognitive-and-behavioral-changes

rulebook.rule: Normal bilateral flexor plantar responses (normal finding) argue against significant pyramidal tract disease; compatible with non-motor-system primary pathology
rulebook.bears_on: Pyramidal Syndrome; Upper Motor Neuron Disease
rulebook.source: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creutzfeldt%E2%80%93Jakob_disease

rulebook.rule: Marked clinical deterioration within 4 weeks of admission (unintelligible speech, severe memory loss, complete hearing loss, incontinence) is consistent with rapidly progressive dementia timeline (sCJD median survival 12-14 months from symptom onset) and argues against slower-progressing neurodegenerative diseases
rulebook.source: Rapidly Progressive Dementia. Continuum. https://continuum.aan.com/doi/10.1212/CON.0000000000001089

rulebook.rule: Progression of bilateral sensorineural hearing loss to complete deafness over 5 months of illness suggests active infection/inflammation of auditory pathways (otosyphilis, Whipple's with basilar meningitis, mitochondrial disease); acute-to-complete trajectory within months favors infection over slow neurodegenerative disease
rulebook.source: Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, & Otosyphilis. CDC. https://www.cdc.gov/syphilis/hcp/neurosyphilis-ocular-syphilis-otosyphilis/index.html

rulebook.rule: Absence of reported seizures somewhat lowers probability of cortical pathology and inflammatory encephalitis (where seizures are common); compatible with subcortical/brainstem-predominant disease
rulebook.source: The Evaluation of Rapidly Progressive Dementia. PMC3356774. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356774/

rulebook.rule: Normal CSF opening pressure (90 mm H2O) excludes elevated intracranial pressure from mass lesion, obstructive hydrocephalus, or acute meningitis; compatible with acellular degenerative and infectious CNS disease
rulebook.source: Cerebrospinal Fluid - Clinical Methods. NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK398/

rulebook.rule: Gadolinium-non-enhancing lesions on MRI argue against active inflammation, brain abscess, tumor, and granulomatous disease (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, fungal infection); compatible with neurodegenerative disease, prion disease, and ischemic lesions
rulebook.source: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Brain MRI lesion features from 2 cases reports. PMC10767313. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10767313/

rulebook.rule: Temporal lobe involvement (medial temporal lobes, uncus region) on extended MRI is a known predilection site for CNS Whipple's disease and also occurs in sCJD cortical ribboning and herpes simplex encephalitis; localizing sign for differential diagnosis
rulebook.source: Central nervous system involvement in Whipple's disease: Clinical Study of 18 Patients. PMC4553994. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553994/

rulebook.rule: Absence of fever, night sweats, weight loss, and systemic inflammatory symptoms argues against tuberculosis, lymphoma, and active bacterial/fungal infections; less suggestive of systemic infection, though neurosyphilis and some CNS infections can be minimally systemic
rulebook.source: The Evaluation of Rapidly Progressive Dementia. PMC3356774. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356774/

rulebook.rule: Acute episode of disorientation while driving a familiar route suggests acute encephalopathy; consistent with prion disease, active infection (Whipple's, neurosyphilis), metabolic derangement, and severe depression
rulebook.source: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creutzfeldt%E2%80%93Jakob_disease

rulebook.rule: Cognitive impairment with memory and language dysfunction is compatible with amnestic phenotype seen in Wernicke-area pathology, temporal lobe disease, and diffuse cortical pathology in sCJD, general paresis, and Whipple's disease; nonspecific but narrows pathoanatomical distribution
rulebook.source: Neuropsychological Features in Patients with General Paresis of the Insane at an Early Stage. PMC9749326. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749326/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Mitochondrial cytopathy/mitochondrial leukoencephalopathy (possibly atypical MELAS variant).

Recommended next action: Order serum/urine organic acids, amino acids, carnitine panel, and lactate/pyruvate levels. Pursue mitochondrial genetic testing (mtDNA sequencing and nuclear mitochondrial gene panel). Consider muscle or skin biopsy for mitochondrial histochemistry if serologic workup is inconclusive.

Confidence: Moderate (60-70%). The symmetric bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with hypometabolism, combined with sensorineural hearing loss (a recognized mitochondrial disease feature), subacute cognitive decline, and apathy in a previously healthy adult, point toward mitochondrial dysfunction. The acellular CSF with normal glucose excludes active infection/inflammation. However, the absence of markedly elevated serum lactate and the atypical distribution slightly reduce confidence; metabolic/toxic leukoencephalopathy remains in differential.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 54-year-old man presents with a rapidly progressive multifocal CNS syndrome most consistent with sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD). 

The diagnosis is supported by several key findings. The MRI pattern—multiple T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem without gadolinium enhancement [fact: mri_initial], extending progressively to medulla, pons, midbrain, thalamus, corpus callosum, and temporal lobe [fact: mri_followup]—has 92% sensitivity and 97% specificity for sCJD (R3). The subacute cognitive decline developing over five months [fact: onset_drowsiness, chief_complaint] raises suspicion for rapidly progressive dementia including prion disease rather than slower-progressing neurodegenerative disease (R1). The marked hypersomnia at symptom onset [fact: onset_drowsiness] is consistent with encephalitis and prion disease (R2). 

Cognitive and behavioral features align: apathy, bradyphrenia, and prominent short-term memory impairment [fact: mental_status_exam] are characteristic of sCJD in its akinetic mutism phase (R12). Global aphasia with expressive and receptive components [fact: mental_status_exam] combined with temporal lobe involvement [fact: mri_followup] fits the cortical ribboning pattern of sCJD (R13, R26). The acute episode of disorientation while driving [fact: disorientation_event] is consistent with acute encephalopathy episodes in prion disease (R25).

CSF findings support this diagnosis. The acellular CSF [fact: csf_cell_count] is compatible with prion disease (R6). Mild CSF protein elevation at 62 mg/dL [fact: csf_protein] without pleocytosis is characteristic of prion disease (R7). Normal CSF opening pressure [fact: csf_opening_pressure] excludes mass lesion and obstructive hydrocephalus (R21).

Negative findings further support this diagnosis. The absence of meningeal signs [fact: meningeal_signs] and absence of headache [fact: systemic_symptoms_negative] lower the probability of bacterial meningitis and inflammatory encephalitis (R14, R15). Preserved motor strength (5/5 throughout) and normal reflexes [fact: motor_exam] argue against motor neuron disease and advanced progressive supranuclear palsy (R16). The absence of seizures [fact: systemic_symptoms_negative] is more consistent with subcortical/brainstem-predominant disease than cortical encephalitis (R20). Gadolinium non-enhancement [fact: mri_initial] argues against active inflammation, brain abscess, and tumor (R22). The absence of fever, night sweats, and weight loss [fact: recent_exposures_negative] lowers suspicion for systemic infection (R24). Normal LDH [fact: ldh_level], negative autoimmune and vasculitic panel [fact: autoimmune_vasculitis_panel], and negative serology for HIV, syphilis, and common neurotropic viruses [fact: serologies_negative] lower probability of autoimmune encephalitis, vasculitis, and common infections (R10, R11). FDG-PET hypometabolism [fact: pet_findings] is consistent with neurodegenerative disease including prion disease, though not pathognomonic (R5).

Rapid clinical deterioration—within four weeks of admission, speech became unintelligible, memory impairment severe, hearing completely lost, and urinary/fecal incontinence developed [fact: clinical_course_deterioration]—is consistent with the sCJD progression timeline of median 12-14 months from symptom onset (R18).

The principal diagnostic uncertainty stems from bilateral sensorineural hearing loss [fact: hearing_loss_onset], which progressed to complete bilateral deafness [fact: clinical_course_deterioration]. This raises differential suspicion for neurosyphilis with otosyphilis (eighth nerve involvement) (R8), Whipple's disease with basilar meningitis (R8, R23), or mitochondrial disease (R8, R19). While hearing loss can occur in advanced sCJD, the prominent early progression and dominance in the clinical picture is atypical. However, negative serology for syphilis [fact: serologies_negative] lowers but does not exclude neurosyphilis, as false-negative rates reach 25% in general paresis (R9, R11). The broad negative autoimmune and vasculitic panel and lack of systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, diarrhea) argue against active Whipple's disease.

The constellation of findings—especially the highly specific MRI pattern (R3), subacute multifocal CNS involvement with characteristic distribution (R1, R4), cognitive/behavioral decline with apathy and bradyphrenia (R12), acellular CSF with mild protein elevation (R6, R7), rapid progression (R18), and exclusion of inflammation/abscess/tumor (R22)—most strongly supports sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease as the primary diagnosis. Neurosyphilis (general paresis of the insane) and CNS Whipple's disease remain differential considerations given the hearing loss, but are less likely given the specific imaging pattern and negative serology.
per_case.framework_top: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (sCJD)
per_case.framework_next_step: Test for 14-3-3 protein and phosphorylated tau in cerebrospinal fluid; obtain EEG to evaluate for characteristic periodic sharp wave complexes; if serology remains equivocal, repeat CSF VDRL and consider empirical penicillin therapy to exclude neurosyphilis given the atypical hearing loss component
per_case.framework_confidence: High (approximately 75-80%). The MRI pattern is highly specific for sCJD (R3: 97% specificity), the clinical progression is consistent with rapidly progressive dementia timeline (R1, R18), and the CSF profile fits (R6, R7). However, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with progression to complete deafness (R8, R19) is atypical for sCJD and raises differential concern for neurosyphilis or Whipple's disease, reducing absolute diagnostic certainty despite strong imaging specificity.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: Primary CNS lymphoma (B-cell NHL), a non-enhancing infiltrative MS-mimic, confirmed by stereotactic brain biopsy (CD20+/CD45RO-), treated with high-dose methotrexate + whole-brain RT, with the critical caveat to avoid pre-biopsy steroids. Neither output names PCNSL/lymphoma, so both miss the final diagnosis. Critically, neither recommends the correct disposition (tissue diagnosis via stereotactic brain biopsy), which is the load-bearing clinical action.

OUTPUT A diagnoses mitochondrial cytopathy (atypical MELAS). This is wrong, but it is appropriately hedged at moderate confidence (60-70%), keeps metabolic/toxic leukoencephalopathy in the differential, and recommends a coherent, low-harm workup (lactate/pyruvate, organic acids, genetic testing, muscle/skin biopsy). It does not name lymphoma and does not recommend brain biopsy, so it misses both the diagnosis and the correct disposition. Calibration is reasonable for its degree of wrongness, and the reasoning is concise and traceable. One factual overreach: claiming acellular normal-glucose CSF "excludes active infection/inflammation" is too strong, but it's not central.

OUTPUT B diagnoses sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) with high confidence and an extensive fact-tagged chain. This is also wrong. It is far more poorly calibrated: it commits strongly to sCJD and invents a fabricated, highly specific quantitative claim ("92% sensitivity and 97% specificity for sCJD" for that MRI pattern, tagged R3), which is a hallucination presented as established evidence — basal ganglia/brainstem T2 lesions are NOT specific for CJD (cortical ribboning/DWI is the hallmark, and CJD typically does not gadolinium-enhance, which B misuses). The fact-citation scaffolding gives a veneer of defensibility but several inferences are spurious (e.g., treating brainstem T2 hyperintensity as confirming CJD). B does usefully retain neurosyphilis, Whipple, and mitochondrial disease as differentials and engages more thoroughly with the case facts, but its dominant claim is a confidently-asserted wrong diagnosis backed by a fabricated statistic — a worse failure mode for a clinical judge.

Both miss the diagnosis and both miss the correct disposition (biopsy, avoid steroids). Neither raised lymphoma despite the classic non-enhancing infiltrative MS-mimic picture in the stem. A is better calibrated and free of fabricated evidence; B is more thorough but over-confident and contains a hallucinated specificity statistic that undermines its defensibility. These roughly offset: A's safer calibration vs. B's greater (if partly spurious) differential breadth. On balance neither is clearly superior — both are incorrect on diagnosis and disposition, so this is a tie.

per_case.prose:
A 57-year-old woman with a long history of well-controlled hypertension was referred to a regional neurology service for evaluation of progressive sensory and gait disturbance. She reported that roughly six weeks earlier she had begun noticing a vague numbness affecting both hands and feet, which she initially attributed to her blood-pressure medication. Over the following weeks the numbness became more constant and crept proximally. About ten days before admission she developed a sharp, stabbing, pins-and-needles pain at the back of her neck and upper shoulders, and her family noticed she had started walking with a wide, unsteady gait and occasionally reached for furniture to steady herself.

She denied recent infection, vaccination, fever, weight loss, or night sweats at presentation. There was no preceding optic symptom and no visual loss. Past history was otherwise notable only for hypertension; she took an ACE inhibitor and a thiazide. She did not smoke and drank alcohol rarely.

On examination she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Cranial nerves, including fundoscopy and visual fields, were normal. There was mild symmetric weakness in the lower limbs with preserved bulk. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk throughout, ankle clonus was absent, and the plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Pinprick and vibration sense were diminished in a length-dependent pattern in all four limbs, and joint-position sense was reduced at the toes. Romberg testing was positive. Bladder and bowel function were intact at this stage.

MRI of the neuraxis demonstrated an abnormal intramedullary signal with patchy contrast enhancement extending from the cervicomedullary junction down through the lower cervical cord (approximately C2 to C7). The thoracic cord and conus appeared normal, and the optic nerves were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed only nonspecific scattered white-matter changes consistent with her vascular risk factors.

Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed a clear, colourless sample. Total CSF protein was elevated at 712 mg/L (reference 150–450), CSF albumin 421 mg/L (reference 100–300), CSF lactate dehydrogenase 22 U/L (reference <40), CSF IgG 67.5 mg/L (reference ≤58.6), and CSF IgA 9.0 mg/L (reference ≤7.0). Cell count was not markedly raised. A serum and CSF autoimmune panel — including aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies and a paraneoplastic screen — returned negative. A serum epithelial tumour-marker fragment was reported as marginally above the upper limit.

A working diagnosis of antibody-negative longitudinally extensive inflammatory myelopathy was made, and the patient was started on high-dose intravenous corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 1 g daily, subsequently tapered to an oral equivalent of about 100 mg). Her sensory symptoms and gait improved noticeably over the first week, and she was discharged for outpatient follow-up.

Roughly four to five weeks later she returned acutely. She now had marked weakness of both legs to the point that she could no longer stand or walk, severe boring pain across the occiput, mid-back, and lumbar region, and new urinary and faecal incontinence. She had become intermittently febrile. Repeat MRI showed that the enhancing intramedullary lesion had not regressed; instead it had become more extensive, with a new abnormal segment now visible in the thoracic cord. A second course of high-dose corticosteroid produced no meaningful benefit.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Primary intramedullary spinal cord lymphoma (PISCL) — diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), non-germinal-center subtype, an aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient was initially misdiagnosed as antibody-negative longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) and treated with steroid pulse therapy.

HOW CONFIRMED: Tissue diagnosis. After neurological deterioration ~3 months in, a vertebral/cord microscopic resection biopsy was performed. Histopathology showed aggressive lymphoma; immunohistochemistry positive for leukocyte common antigen (LCA/CD45) and CD20 (B-cell marker), consistent with DLBCL. PET/CT excluded systemic lymphoma, establishing the lesion as PRIMARY to the CNS/spinal cord.

KEY DISCRIMINATORS (load-bearing): (1) transient/partial response to high-dose steroids followed by rapid relapse and progression within ~1 month — steroid-responsive-then-resistant course is characteristic of CNS lymphoma masquerading as inflammatory myelitis; (2) serial MRI showing an ENLARGING, longitudinally extensive enhancing intramedullary lesion that extended (medulla → cervical → new thoracic level) despite immunotherapy; (3) aquaporin-4 / MOG / autoimmune antibody panel NEGATIVE; (4) nonspecific CSF (elevated protein, mildly elevated IgG) without a clear demyelinating profile; (5) clinical-radiologic mismatch — severe progressive deficits out of proportion to an 'inflammatory' label.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Do NOT settle on antibody-negative transverse myelitis when a longitudinally extensive cord lesion enhances, enlarges, and progresses despite adequate steroids — pursue tissue biopsy. Confirmed PISCL/DLBCL is treated with high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy plus rituximab, with radiotherapy and salvage targeted therapy (e.g., a BTK inhibitor) as needed. Prognosis guarded; this patient later developed systemic metastases.

ORIGINAL (un-perturbed) FACTS for reference: 49-year-old male with type 2 diabetes; ~1 month limb numbness, 7 days of pinprick posterior-neck pain, unsteady gait, brisk reflexes + Babinski; MRI abnormal enhancing signal at medulla oblongata and C1–C7; CSF protein 664 mg/L (nl 150–450), albumin 394 mg/L (nl 100–300), CSF LDH 25 U/L, IgG 64.2 mg/L (nl ≤58.6), IgA 8.2 mg/L (nl ≤7.0), autoantibodies negative, CYFRA21-1 slightly elevated; methylprednisolone 1 g pulse tapered to 120 mg with temporary improvement, then month-1 relapse with paraparesis, bowel/bladder incontinence, fever, new thoracic lesion; biopsy at month 3; treated with 8 cycles HD-MTX + rituximab, radiotherapy, later zanubrutinib; metastases by year 3.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical neurology — diagnostic reasoning in acute myelopathy with atypical presentation, steroid responsiveness followed by treatment resistance, and progressive lesion expansion. Differential diagnosis generation task for antibody-negative longitudinally extensive inflammatory myelopathy.

rulebook.rule: Longitudinally extensive cord lesion (≥3 vertebral segments) with patchy contrast enhancement on MRI
rulebook.source: Kitley et al., Neurology 2012. The differential diagnosis of longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. Defines LETM diagnostic criteria: T2 hyperintensity extending ≥3 vertebral segments with cord expansion and enhancement as hallmark inflammatory signature.

rulebook.rule: Both AQP4 and MOG antibodies negative on sensitive cell-based assays
rulebook.source: Castillo-Trivino et al., Journal of Neuroinflammation 2016. 53-patient multicenter cohort confirmed double-seronegative LETM as distinct entity; 24.5% eventually seroconvert at relapse.

rulebook.rule: Initial marked clinical response to high-dose IV methylprednisolone (sensory/gait improvement within first week)
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative LETM vs. paraneoplastic or infectious myelopathy
rulebook.source: Castillo-Trivino et al., 2016. All double-seronegative LETM patients in multicenter series received IV methylprednisolone as standard therapy; initial steroid responsiveness is typical of autoimmune-mediated LETM.

rulebook.rule: Clinical relapse within 18 months of initial presentation with new or worsening myelopathic symptoms
rulebook.source: Castillo-Trivino et al., 2016. First relapse at median 5.7 months in 24.5% of seronegative patients; relapsing course is recognized natural history of untreated seronegative LETM.

rulebook.rule: Absence of early immunosuppressive therapy (only steroids used in inter-relapse period, no azathioprine/mycophenolate/rituximab)
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative LETM with increased recurrence risk and steroid dependency
rulebook.source: Castillo-Trivino et al., 2016. Early immunosuppressive treatment (within 6 months) reduced recurrence to 9% vs. 32% untreated; absence of maintenance immunosuppression is strongest predictor of relapse.

rulebook.rule: Loss of clinical response to second course of high-dose IV methylprednisolone despite initial efficacy in first course
rulebook.bears_on: Steroid-resistant transverse myelitis; transition from responder to non-responder phenotype
rulebook.source: Mayo Clinic & Transverse Myelitis Association guidelines. Documented that some patients lose responsiveness to repeat steroid pulses, requiring escalation to plasma exchange or cyclophosphamide.

rulebook.rule: Interval neurological deterioration concurrent with inadequate maintenance immunosuppression between relapse episodes
rulebook.bears_on: Steroid-resistant recurrent disease with insufficient disease control
rulebook.source: Castillo-Trivino et al., 2016. Patients discharged on oral steroid taper without azathioprine/mycophenolate/rituximab showed 32% relapse rate vs. 9% with early immunosuppressives.

rulebook.rule: Progressive lesion expansion on repeat MRI despite steroid therapy (cephalocaudal spread, cervical to thoracic extension)
rulebook.bears_on: Steroid-resistant disease with ongoing inflammatory activity requiring alternative immunosuppression
rulebook.source: Kitley et al., 2012. Imaging progression beyond initial segment boundaries despite anti-inflammatory therapy indicates inadequate disease control.

rulebook.rule: New constitutional symptoms (fever, multisegmental boring pain) and acute autonomic dysfunction (incontinence) emerging at relapse
rulebook.bears_on: Active inflammatory flare with expanded cord involvement; not specific to steroid resistance alone
rulebook.source: Transverse Myelitis StatPearls consensus. Constitutional symptoms and autonomic involvement reflect acute spinal cord inflammation; emergence after initial steroid responsiveness suggests breakthrough inflammation.

rulebook.rule: Marginally elevated single epithelial tumor marker (non-specific serum fragment)
rulebook.bears_on: Paraneoplastic myelopathy (raises suspicion weakly, but insufficient alone)
rulebook.source: Frontiers in Neurology systematic review, 2020. Classical tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA125) are NOT recommended for screening/diagnosis in paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes; borderline elevation has high false-positive rate.

rulebook.rule: Biphasic treatment response: initial steroid responsiveness followed by steroid resistance (loss of benefit on second course)
rulebook.bears_on: Paraneoplastic myelopathy with T-cell-mediated intracellular-antigen pathophysiology
rulebook.source: Paraneoplastic Myelopathy, Neurology 2013 & Imaging review AJNR 2020. Paraneoplastic myelitis caused by intracellular-antigen antibodies (anti-Hu, etc.) is T-cell mediated and often steroid-resistant; some stabilize if underlying cancer controlled, explaining biphasic course.

rulebook.rule: Progressive myelopathic course with imaging evidence of cord expansion, longitudinally extensive involvement, and gadolinium enhancement
rulebook.source: Imaging review of paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes, AJNR 2020. Paraneoplastic myelopathies characteristically show longitudinally extensive, symmetric, tract-specific T2-hyperintensity with cord expansion/edema.

rulebook.rule: Age >50 years (patient is 57) with otherwise limited medical history and no prior malignancy diagnosis
rulebook.bears_on: Paraneoplastic myelopathy (risk factor for occult malignancy)
rulebook.source: Paraneoplastic Myelopathy review, Neurology 2013. Paraneoplastic myelopathy occurs predominantly in older adults (>50 years); age alone is non-specific but shifts baseline probability.

rulebook.rule: Negative standard paraneoplastic antibody panel (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-CRMP5, anti-CV2 absent) and no significant tumor marker elevation beyond single borderline marker
rulebook.bears_on: Paraneoplastic myelopathy (lowers confidence, does NOT exclude)
rulebook.source: Paraneoplastic Myelopathy, Neurology 2013. Antibody-seronegative paraneoplastic myelopathy exists but is rare; absence of detected antibodies makes diagnosis less likely but remains in differential if imaging/clinical course matches.

rulebook.rule: Female gender, age 57 (demographic fit); no documented ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, or complement levels in clinical record
rulebook.bears_on: SLE-related LETM (demographic consistency, but requires serologic confirmation)
rulebook.source: SLE-LETM literature, PMC 2024. SLE-LETM occurs in 1-2% of SLE patients, predominantly female; can be presenting sign (22% of cases).

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented SLE serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, C3/C4 complement) in clinical record
rulebook.source: SLE-LETM diagnostic criteria, PMC 2024. Diagnosis of SLE-LETM requires positive ANA and typically anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith; lack of serologic testing or positive results makes SLE unlikely.

rulebook.rule: Medical history notable only for well-controlled hypertension; no documented arthritis, rashes, serositis, cytopenia, or other systemic features
rulebook.source: SLE-LETM presentation patterns, PMC 2024. While LETM can be first manifestation of SLE, other systemic features (cutaneous, articular, constitutional, hematologic) frequently present; isolated neurologic presentation without systemic features makes SLE unlikely.

rulebook.rule: Afebrile at first presentation; denied recent infection; CSF lactate dehydrogenase normal (22 U/L, reference <40)
rulebook.source: Kitley et al., 2012 & Transverse Myelitis StatPearls. Normal CSF LDH argues against necrotic/infectious processes; afebrile status and absent infection history reduce likelihood of bacterial/viral etiologies.

rulebook.rule: CSF shows only mild immunoglobulin elevation (IgG 67.5, IgA 9.0) without marked pleocytosis; paraneoplastic antibody screen negative
rulebook.source: Transverse Myelitis StatPearls. Marked CSF pleocytosis (lymphocytic or mixed) is typical of infectious myelitis; absence of pleocytosis with only mild immunoglobulin elevation is atypical for infection.

rulebook.rule: Initial cervical cord lesion (C2-C7, ~5-6 segments) progresses to include new thoracic cord involvement on repeat MRI at relapse
rulebook.bears_on: Progressive inflammatory myelopathy; inadequately treated seronegative LETM or paraneoplastic disease with ongoing inflammation
rulebook.source: LETM neuroradiologic patterns, Kitley et al., 2012. Cephalocaudal progression or rostral/caudal extension beyond initial lesion boundaries indicates ongoing inflammatory activity and inadequate response to current immunosuppression.

rulebook.rule: Lesion does not regress and becomes more extensive on repeat imaging despite high-dose corticosteroid therapy
rulebook.bears_on: Steroid-resistant inflammatory process requiring escalation of immunosuppression or investigation for underlying systemic/paraneoplastic etiology
rulebook.source: Transverse Myelitis treatment response guidelines, Mayo Clinic & SRNA. Regression of lesion is expected marker of treatment response; persistent/progressive lesions despite steroids warrant alternative immunosuppression or investigation for refractory mechanisms.

rulebook.rule: Bladder and bowel function remain intact at initial evaluation despite extensive cervical cord lesion (C2-C7)
rulebook.bears_on: Atypical inflammatory pattern; suggests spared sacral-innervated autonomic pathways or preferential tract involvement (not complete transection)
rulebook.source: Cervical myelopathy clinical consensus, StatPearls & Cleveland Clinic. Bladder/bowel dysfunction typically occurs in severe cervical myelopathy; preservation despite extensive cervical involvement suggests peripheral rather than central cord involvement.

rulebook.rule: New urinary and fecal incontinence acute at relapse, concurrent with marked bilateral leg weakness and severe multisegmental pain
rulebook.bears_on: Acute severe exacerbation with now-complete cord involvement affecting previously spared sacral autonomic tracts
rulebook.source: Transverse Myelitis clinical summary, SRNA. Acute onset of bowel/bladder incontinence concurrent with paraplegia indicates acute expansive myelitis affecting sacral autonomic pathways; switch from initial preservation to acute loss suggests extension to previously spared regions.

per_case.blind_answer:
**Most Likely Diagnosis:** Paraneoplastic myelopathy associated with occult malignancy (antibody-negative)

**Recommended Next Action:** Urgent whole-body malignancy screening (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, age-appropriate breast imaging), expanded paraneoplastic serology including patient-serum CSF testing for rare antibodies, and infectious workup if imaging is negative.

**Confidence:** 65–70%

**Reasoning:** The cardinal red flag is steroid-refractory disease with radiologic progression (extension into thoracic cord despite high-dose methylprednisolone). Classic demyelinating myelitis (even seronegative) typically stabilizes or improves with corticosteroids. The constellation of progressive intramedullary myelopathy, high CSF protein with low cellularity, negative standard autoimmune serology, marginal tumor marker elevation, and clinical worsening on immune therapy points toward an underlying malignancy driving the myelopathy rather than primary demyelinating disease. While the negative AQP4/MOG serology and initial steroid response created diagnostic ambiguity, the subsequent relapse and extension are more consistent with paraneoplastic pathophysiology than antibody-negative demyelination.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 57-year-old woman presents with a clinical and radiological picture diagnostic of seronegative longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM). The cervical cord lesion extending C2–C7 with patchy contrast enhancement (F33) meets R1.1 criteria for LETM. Both aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies are negative (F44), consistent with R1.2 defining seronegative LETM as a recognized distinct entity. Her initial dramatic response to high-dose IV methylprednisolone—sensory and gait improvement within one week (F49)—aligns with R1.3, which notes that initial steroid responsiveness is typical of autoimmune-mediated LETM. She subsequently relapsed 4–5 weeks after hospital discharge (F51), conforming to R1.4's reported natural history (median first relapse at 5.7 months in untreated seronegative cohorts).

The critical pathogenic factor appears to be inadequate maintenance immunosuppression. The discharge summary (F48) documents only tapered oral corticosteroid (~100 mg), with no mention of azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, or other disease-modifying agents. R1.5 directly addresses this scenario: in a multicenter series, patients receiving early immunosuppressive therapy (within 6 months) had a 9% relapse rate, whereas untreated patients had 32% relapse—a 23 percentage-point difference. This patient's rapid relapse strongly suggests she fell into the untreated cohort.

At re-presentation, she now manifests steroid-resistant disease: a second course of high-dose corticosteroid produced no meaningful benefit (F58), in contrast to the substantial improvement from the first course. R2.1 establishes that loss of clinical response to repeat steroid pulses defines steroid-resistant transverse myelitis. Concurrent with treatment failure, repeat imaging shows the lesion has not regressed but has become more extensive, with new thoracic cord involvement (F57). R2.3 characterizes such imaging progression—expansion beyond initial segment boundaries—as evidence of inadequately controlled inflammation requiring alternative immunosuppression. R2.2 explicitly links interval neurological deterioration concurrent with inadequate maintenance immunosuppression to steroid-resistant recurrent disease.

New constitutional and neurological features emerging at relapse—fever (F55), severe boring multisegmental pain (F53), and acute bilateral sphincter dysfunction (F54)—are consistent with R2.4, which notes that constitutional symptoms and autonomic involvement reflect acute spinal cord inflammation; their emergence after initial steroid responsiveness suggests breakthrough inflammation. Notably, the patient had preserved bladder and bowel function initially (F31) despite the extensive cervical lesion, which R7.1 suggests reflects spared sacral autonomic tracts or preferential peripheral tract involvement. The acute loss of continence now (F54), concurrent with marked paraplegia (F52), indicates per R7.2 that acute expansion now involves previously spared sacral autonomic pathways.

Paraneoplastic myelopathy cannot be fully excluded and remains in the differential, though at lower confidence. The patient's age (57 years) is consistent with R3.4's observation that paraneoplastic myelopathy occurs predominantly in older adults. More importantly, R3.2 notes that biphasic treatment response—initial steroid responsiveness followed by steroid resistance—is characteristic of T-cell–mediated paraneoplastic myelopathy caused by intracellular-antigen antibodies (e.g., anti-Hu). The progressive myelopathic course with imaging evidence of cord expansion and longitudinally extensive gadolinium enhancement (F33, F57) matches R3.3's description of typical paraneoplastic myelopathy imaging. However, R3.5 explicitly lowers confidence: antibody-seronegative paraneoplastic disease is rare. The patient's standard paraneoplastic antibody screen returned negative (F45), and her serum tumor marker elevation is described as "marginal" (F46). R3.1 emphasizes that borderline elevation of non-specific epithelial tumor markers has high false-positive rates and is not recommended for screening. Thus, while the biphasic response pattern raises paraneoplastic concern, the absence of seropositive antibodies and the presence of only a marginally elevated single nonspecific marker lower confidence in this diagnosis. Further targeted paraneoplastic serologies and imaging screening for occult malignancy (chest, abdomen, pelvis) are warranted before classifying this as paraneoplastic disease.

SLE-related LETM and infectious myelitis are effectively ruled out. No ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, or complement testing is documented in the record, and R4.2 establishes that ANA positivity and typically anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith are required for diagnosis; R4.3 notes that isolated neurologic presentation without systemic features (rashes, arthritis, serositis, cytopenia) makes SLE unlikely. For infection, the patient was afebrile at initial presentation (F21), denied recent infection (F11), and had normal CSF lactate dehydrogenase (F40), all supporting R5.1. Her CSF showed only mild immunoglobulin elevation (F41, F42) without marked pleocytosis (F43), as per R5.2, atypical for infection. Infectious etiologies are therefore low in the differential.

The recommended diagnostic and therapeutic path is: (1) Immediately escalate immunosuppression to plasma exchange, IVIG, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab (R2.1 documents these as standard escalations for steroid-resistant disease); (2) Initiate maintenance disease-modifying therapy (azathioprine, mycophenolate, or rituximab) to prevent further relapses (R1.5); (3) Complete paraneoplastic workup—expanded antibody panels, clarification of the tumor marker identity and degree of elevation (U4), and imaging for occult malignancy; (4) Check ANA and complement levels if not already done; (5) Repeat MRI to assess lesion response to escalated therapy. If the patient stabilizes or improves with escalated immunosuppression, the diagnosis of seronegative LETM with relapsing-remitting course will be confirmed. If she fails escalated immunosuppression, or if advanced paraneoplastic serologies or imaging reveal evidence of malignancy, diagnosis revision toward paraneoplastic myelopathy will be warranted.
per_case.framework_top: Seronegative longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) with relapsing-remitting course and steroid dependence, worsened by inadequate maintenance immunosuppression between initial treatment and relapse.
per_case.framework_next_step: Escalate immunosuppression immediately (plasma exchange, IVIG, or cyclophosphamide/rituximab for steroid-resistant disease) and initiate long-term disease-modifying therapy (azathioprine, mycophenolate, or rituximab) to prevent further relapses. In parallel, complete paraneoplastic workup (expand antibody panel, clarify tumor marker identity and degree of elevation, consider imaging for occult malignancy) and check ANA/complement levels. Repeat MRI to assess lesion response to escalated therapy.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-High (70–75%). Seronegative LETM diagnosis is well supported by imaging morphology (R1.1), seronegative status (R1.2), initial steroid responsiveness (R1.3), and relapse timing consistent with published natural history of untreated disease (R1.4). Lack of maintenance immunosuppression directly explains the observed relapse (R1.5 establishes 32% vs. 9% relapse rates untreated vs. treated). However, confidence is not higher due to: (a) incomplete paraneoplastic workup details (U3, U4 note tumor marker identity unspecified), which prevents full exclusion of rare seronegative paraneoplastic disease (R3.2, R3.5); (b) uncertainty about exact maintenance steroid regimen between discharge and relapse (U6).

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: the answer is primary intramedullary spinal cord lymphoma (DLBCL) masquerading as antibody-negative LETM, with the load-bearing discriminators being (a) transient steroid response then rapid steroid-resistant relapse, (b) an enlarging longitudinally extensive enhancing intramedullary lesion progressing despite immunotherapy, (c) negative AQP4/MOG/autoimmune antibodies, (d) nonspecific CSF, and (e) clinical-radiologic mismatch. The correct disposition is to reject the inflammatory label and pursue tissue biopsy.

OUTPUT A is largely incorrect and poorly calibrated. It commits to seronegative LETM as the primary diagnosis and frames the entire course as 'inadequate maintenance immunosuppression,' recommending escalation to plasma exchange/IVIG/cyclophosphamide/rituximab and maintenance DMTs. This is precisely the misdiagnosis the case is built to expose — A treats the steroid-resistant, progressively enlarging lesion as breakthrough inflammation rather than a red flag for neoplasm. It does carry a secondary paraneoplastic differential and notes the biphasic response and need for malignancy imaging, which is partially in the right direction, but it explicitly relegates this to lower confidence and never reaches lymphoma or recommends biopsy. Critically, A never names neoplasm/lymphoma as the leading concern and never recommends tissue biopsy, which is the load-bearing correct disposition. It also leans heavily on fabricated-sounding rule citations (R1.x, etc.) and invented statistics, which hurts defensibility/calibration. (Note: both outputs use perturbed demographics — 57F vs the true 49M — but that is an artifact of the perturbed input, not scored against ground truth.)

OUTPUT B is substantially more correct on the key reasoning even though it lands on the wrong specific label. It correctly identifies the cardinal red flag — steroid-refractory disease with radiologic progression (thoracic extension despite methylprednisolone) — and reasons that demyelinating/seronegative myelitis should stabilize with steroids, so an underlying malignancy is driving the myelopathy. This captures the central insight: reject the inflammatory diagnosis, suspect neoplasm. Its top diagnosis (paraneoplastic myelopathy from occult malignancy) is wrong — the true answer is a PRIMARY CNS lymphoma intrinsic to the cord, and B's recommended whole-body/breast screening points away from a primary cord tumor — so it does not nail the diagnosis or the biopsy disposition. But it gets the discriminating logic right (steroid resistance, progression, high CSF protein with low cellularity, negative serology, marginal tumor marker), is honestly calibrated (65-70%), and is concise and traceable without fabricated citations.

Verdict: B wins. Both miss the exact diagnosis (lymphoma) and neither recommends biopsy, but B correctly rejects the inflammatory-LETM trap and pivots to neoplasm — the core of the case — whereas A actively endorses the misdiagnosis and prescribes more immunosuppression, the dangerous wrong move. B's brevity, honest confidence, and lack of invented evidence also make it more defensible.

per_case.prose:
A 44-year-old man was referred to a tertiary neurology service for evaluation of headaches and intermittent visual disturbance that had been recurring for roughly four years.

He first noticed episodes around age 40. Each attack began with visual symptoms: shimmering and a sense that objects to either side of his gaze were missing or smeared, sometimes a distortion of the central field on the right so that straight lines looked bent. These visual phenomena typically came a few minutes before, or occasionally an hour or two after, the onset of a one-sided throbbing head pain. The pain was usually over the left forehead and temple, sharp and pulsating, and he rated it 6 out of 10 at first; over the following years the worst attacks reached the top of his pain scale. Bright light and bouts of coughing reliably brought on an episode, and he became markedly light-sensitive during attacks. The episodes recurred over months to years without a clear progression in frequency.

At a regional hospital the picture had been read as a small-vessel inflammatory process. He was started on an antiplatelet agent together with a course of oral corticosteroids, but the attacks continued unabated on this regimen.

On examination at referral he was alert and fully oriented. Cognitive screening was near-ceiling (a Mini-Mental State Examination of 30 and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 27). Cranial nerves, motor and sensory testing, coordination, and gait were unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination was normal.

Laboratory evaluation was broadly unrevealing. Complete blood count, electrolytes, hepatic and renal panels, and a coagulation profile were all within normal limits. A serologic autoimmune panel — antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and a vasculitis-associated antibody screen — returned negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no abnormality, with normal cell count, protein, and glucose. Carotid duplex ultrasonography, transcranial Doppler, and MR angiography of the intracranial vessels were each normal.

Brain MRI was the most striking study. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed bands of high signal running along the junction between cortex and underlying white matter, and a separate focus of high signal in the splenium of the corpus callosum. Notably, these diffusion changes were still present on a repeat study about a year later rather than resolving. In addition there was atrophy of both temporal poles and of the cortex generally that the reporting radiologist judged to be greater than expected for a man of his age.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Adult-onset Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusion Disease (NIID), presenting with recurrent headache + transient visual/aura-like episodes (a "migraine-mimic"/episodic encephalopathy phenotype). 

HOW CONFIRMED (dual, definitive): (1) Genetic testing showed a pathological GGC trinucleotide repeat expansion in the NOTCH2NLC gene (~101 repeats; normal is well under ~40). (2) Skin biopsy demonstrated p62/ubiquitin-positive eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in sweat-gland epithelial cells and fibroblasts — the histologic hallmark of NIID. Supporting radiologic hallmark: persistent DWI high-signal along the corticomedullary junction ("subcortical lace/ribbon" sign) plus splenium of corpus callosum, with disproportionate bilateral temporal-pole/cortical atrophy for age; full inflammatory/vasculitic/autoimmune/CSF/vascular workup negative.

KEY DISCRIMINATOR the arms must catch: the combination of (a) DWI corticomedullary-junction ribboning that PERSISTS over a year, (b) temporal-pole atrophy out of proportion to age, and (c) negative vasculitis/inflammatory workup despite a "vasculitis/migraine" working diagnosis — should redirect toward NIID and prompt skin biopsy + NOTCH2NLC repeat analysis rather than continued anti-inflammatory/anti-platelet/migraine-prophylaxis treatment.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize the DWI corticomedullary-junction sign, stop the vasculitis/migraine framing, obtain skin biopsy and NOTCH2NLC GGC-repeat genetic testing to confirm NIID; manage symptomatically (the index patient's attacks were controlled on flunarizine/calcium-channel blocker prophylaxis after diagnosis) and counsel as a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. The original misattribution to vasculitis (steroids + antiplatelets) was ineffective and incorrect.

Source: Recurrent headache and visual symptoms in a young man: a rare neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease case report, PMC9628060.

queries.asks: What is the underlying diagnosis integrating the clinical phenotype (migrainous aura, left-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, light/Valsalva triggers, age 44, 4-year course) with the striking structural findings (persistent cortical-junction DWI bands, splenial lesion, progressive atrophy)?

Why do DWI hyperintensities persist at 1-year imaging instead of resolving as expected for acute cytotoxic edema, and what does this tell us about the underlying pathophysiology (chronic demyelination vs. recurrent lesioning vs. gliotic change)?

Does the negative serological workup (ANA, APLA, vasculitis screen), normal CSF, and normal vascular imaging definitively exclude CNS vasculitis, or are there seronegative small-vessel vasculitic syndromes that present this way?
Are the cognitive scores (MMSE 30, MoCA 27) indicating normal cognition, or could they represent cognitive decline relative to an unknown higher premorbid baseline given the structural atrophy?

What explains the bilateral temporal pole predominance in the atrophy pattern, and does it suggest a specific etiology (e.g., specific neurodegeneration, post-ictal changes from recurrent seizures, or secondary to the primary process)?

What is the anatomical relationship between the visual aura symptoms (suggesting occipital/visual cortex involvement) and the DWI lesion distribution (cortical junction bands + corpus callosum splenium)?

Why did the empirical trial of antiplatelet therapy and oral corticosteroids fail to control attacks, and does the failure refute the small-vessel inflammatory hypothesis or indicate inadequate dosing/duration?

uncertainties.about: Laterality of the lateral field-deficit visual aura
uncertainties.detail: F7 states 'objects to either side of his gaze were missing or smeared'—this phrasing could mean bilateral lateral field loss, monocular field loss in one eye, or homonymous field loss (both eyes, one side). F8 specifies 'right' field distortion, but the relationship between the bilateral phrasing in F7 and the right-sided specification in F8 is unclear; are these two subtypes of aura or the same phenomenon described twice?

uncertainties.about: Temporal relationship variability between visual aura and headache onset
uncertainties.domain: Temporal sequencing of migraine attack phases
uncertainties.detail: F9 states the typical pattern is aura 'a few minutes before' pain onset, but F10 introduces an exceptional subtype where aura occurs 'occasionally an hour or two after' pain onset. Is this a true bimodal distribution in the same patient, or are these rare outliers? Does 'occasionally' quantify frequency?

uncertainties.about: Headache laterality and its relationship to visual aura laterality
uncertainties.detail: F11 clearly specifies headache pain is 'left forehead and temple,' but F8 describes visual distortion of the 'right' field. Whether the pain ever involves the right side, or whether visual and pain laterality are consistently contralateral, is unspecified.

uncertainties.about: Temporal onset of photophobia relative to headache phases
uncertainties.detail: F17 states photophobia develops 'during attacks,' but does not specify whether it precedes, accompanies, or follows the headache onset. Preictal, ictal, and postdromal photophobia have different mechanistic implications.

uncertainties.about: Quantification of 'atrophy greater than expected for age'
uncertainties.detail: F51 employs qualitative language ('greater than expected for a man of his age'). No volumetric measurements, normative data, or comparison imaging from prior years is provided; this is radiologist's gestalt assessment.

uncertainties.about: Adequacy and duration of prior corticosteroid course
uncertainties.detail: F21–F22 report corticosteroid therapy was initiated and attacks persisted. No specification of dose regimen, duration of course, or whether the dose/duration met standard protocols for the suspected inflammatory condition. 'Unabated' could indicate true refractoriness or inadequate trial.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical Neurology with Neuroradiology — specifically, chronic headache syndrome with visual aura and imaging-detected structural brain pathology (diffusion abnormalities and atrophy). The case presents a diagnostic puzzle: reconciling a migrainous clinical phenotype with unexplained persistent DWI lesions and progressive brain atrophy despite benign vascular and serological workup.

rulebook.rule: Migraine with visual aura (scintillation, field defects, metamorphopsia) occurring in 75-90% of CADASIL cases, often with onset age 40-50 and prolonged/complex aura patterns.
rulebook.bears_on: CADASIL (Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy)
rulebook.source: Markus H et al., PMC4911105: CADASIL represents 75% migraine prevalence, 90% with aura phenotype; age of onset typically later than general population.

rulebook.rule: Anterior temporal lobe white matter involvement with high signal on T2/FLAIR has 100% specificity and ~90% sensitivity for CADASIL diagnosis.
rulebook.source: PMC4692034: 'Anterior temporal lobe involvement has nearly 100% specificity' with sensitivity ~90% in CADASIL imaging.

rulebook.rule: Bilateral temporal pole atrophy greater than expected for age is consistent with progressive CADASIL-related subcortical lacunar disease and cognitive decline.
rulebook.source: Markus H et al., PMC4911105: 'Cerebral atrophy ensues' in CADASIL and 'correlates well with the degree of cognitive decline.'

rulebook.rule: Cortical junction bands and splenial corpus callosum lesions on DWI can persist beyond acute phase in demyelinating or microvasculopathic processes, representing chronic tissue injury with gliosis rather than reversible cytotoxic edema.
rulebook.source: PMC4757308: DWI-restricted lesions can show persistent gliosis on T2 follow-up despite ADC normalization, with 'residual focal area of gliosis' persisting chronically.

rulebook.rule: Negative ANA, APLA, vasculitis serologies, normal CSF, and normal angiography do not exclude primary CNS vasculitis; seronegative small-vessel PCNSV can present with headache and DWI lesions without inflammatory CSF.
rulebook.bears_on: Seronegative CNS vasculitis (small-vessel primary CNS vasculitis)
rulebook.source: PMC12063240: 'Definitive diagnosis requires brain biopsy'; serological workup limited utility with '17.4% [of PCNSV] had completely normal CSF profiles.'

rulebook.rule: Persistent DWI lesions at 1-year follow-up in seronegative PCNSV reflect ongoing small-vessel inflammation with areas of DWI-enhancement correlation in 77% of cases, consistent with microembolization or chronic hypoperfusion.
rulebook.source: PMC12063240: 'DWI changes corresponded with areas of vessel wall enhancement in 77% of patients' and 'persistent areas of enhancement (including vessel-wall enhancement) for months or years.'

rulebook.rule: Headache and visual disturbance are cardinal presenting features of MELAS syndrome, with stroke-like lesions distributed to cortex and white matter junction (occipito-temporal predilection due to high energy demand of visual cortex).
rulebook.bears_on: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes)
rulebook.source: PMC4302172 & Cureus 2025: 'Most frequent onset symptoms of stroke-like episode are migraine or migraine-like headache...visual field defects.' 'Occipital lobe prone to stroke-like lesions due to high energy requirements of visual cortex.'

rulebook.rule: Stroke-like lesions in MELAS do not conform to known vascular territories and may be mistaken for migraine with prolonged aura; they appear as multifocal cortical edema in different stages of evolution.
rulebook.source: MELAS search results: 'Multifocal infarct-like areas of cortical edema in different stages of ischemic evolution, yet do not commonly conform to any known vascular territory.'

rulebook.rule: Photophobia is more prevalent in migraine with aura than without aura, reflecting shared underlying mechanism involving cortical spreading depression affecting retino-thalamo-cortical photic pathways.
rulebook.source: Frontiers 2019 & PMC4502959: 'Photophobia...is more prevalent in migraine with aura than in migraine without aura' with mechanistic link through 'retino-thalamo-cortical pathway.'

rulebook.rule: Visual aura of gradual onset progressing across visual field with evolution from positive (scintillation) to negative (scotoma) symptoms is consistent with cortical spreading depression of migraine, not ischemic stroke.
rulebook.source: PMC9531679: 'Gradual-onset disturbance with progression across the visual field and evolution of symptoms from positive to negative is more compatible with migraine pathology.'

rulebook.rule: Reversible splenial corpus callosum lesions with restricted diffusion (DWI hyperintensity) are a well-documented migraine aura variant, with resolution on follow-up MRI in 5 reported cases (age 10-51).
rulebook.bears_on: Migraine with visual aura (reversible corpus callosum variant)
rulebook.source: Neurology 2018 abstract & PMC11963349: 'Few case reports to date of reversible lesions of the splenium...associated with migraine with aura (n=5, age range 10–51 years)' with 'resolution of the areas of restricted diffusion' on follow-up.

rulebook.rule: Migraine with aura is associated with increased risk of subclinical posterior (occipital) infarction; ischemic strokes attributable to migraine occur within PCA territory.
rulebook.bears_on: Migrainous infarction (ischemic stroke secondary to migraine)
rulebook.source: Stroke journal & PMC9531679: 'Migraine with aura may increase risk of subclinical posterior infarct...strokes attributable to migraine commonly occur within territory of posterior cerebral arteries.'

rulebook.rule: Treatment failure with oral corticosteroids in presumed inflammatory CNS disease may indicate inadequate dosing/duration OR that the underlying diagnosis is non-inflammatory (e.g., CADASIL, MELAS), requiring reevaluation.
rulebook.source: ANCA trial protocols & Rare Disease Advisor: Corticosteroid therapy >20 mg/day prednisone equivalent required for adequacy; lower doses may represent therapeutic failure, prompting diagnosis reconsideration.

rulebook.rule: Normal cognitive testing (MMSE 30, MoCA 27) does not exclude structural brain pathology or early cognitive decline; these scores may reflect preserved function relative to unknown baseline or may be falsely reassuring if atrophy progresses.
rulebook.source: CADASIL literature: Cognitive decline in CADASIL correlates with atrophy; normal cross-sectional scores do not preclude subclinical decline relative to premorbid baseline.

rulebook.rule: Normal vascular imaging (carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler, MR angiography) excludes large-vessel occlusion and macroscopic vasculitis but does NOT exclude primary CNS microvasculitis or microembolization.
rulebook.source: PMC12063240: 'Microembolization or hypoperfusion' in PCNSV produces DWI lesions despite normal angiography; small-vessel disease is angiographically silent.

rulebook.rule: Photic trigger (bright light) reliably precipitating migraine attacks is consistent with photosensitive migraine; however, cumulative photic stress in CNS small-vessel disease (CADASIL, PCNSV) may exacerbate symptoms through different mechanism.
rulebook.bears_on: Migraine with visual aura; CNS vasculitis (differential)
rulebook.source: Migraine literature: Photic sensitivity is core migraine feature, though underlying structural disease may amplify response.

rulebook.rule: Valsalva-triggered attacks (coughing) in migraine with aura are well-recognized; however, Valsalva-induced pressure spikes may unmask hemodynamic insufficiency in microvasculopathic disease (e.g., CADASIL with lacunar ischemia).
rulebook.bears_on: Migraine with visual aura; CADASIL (differential consideration)
rulebook.source: Migraine and Valsalva literature: Both conditions can present with Valsalva-triggered symptoms; CADASIL presents added mechanism of microvasculopathic hemodynamic vulnerability.

rulebook.rule: Left forehead/temple headache pain with right field visual distortion represents contralateral pain-vision relationship, suggesting occipital/visual cortex involvement in right hemisphere with pain referral to ipsilateral temporal region.
rulebook.source: Visual aura literature: Migraine aura begins occipitally; pain localization is ipsilateral to pain-generating structures (meninges/vessels) which may be contralateral to visual disturbance site.

rulebook.rule: CADASIL predominantly affects anterior temporal lobe and external capsule white matter; cortical junction band distribution is less typical of CADASIL, which shows subcortical (U-fiber sparing) pattern.
rulebook.source: PMC4365670 & PMC4692034: CADASIL shows 'relative sparing of...U-fibers and cortex' with predilection for subcortical structures; cortical-junction bands less characteristic.

rulebook.rule: Migraine with aura can occur secondary to structural brain lesions; imaging-confirmed lesions should prompt search for underlying etiology (vascular, demyelinating, metabolic) rather than attributing symptoms to primary migraine alone.
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect 2010: 'Migraine-like visual aura due to focal cerebral lesions' can mimic primary migraine; structural lesions require etiology identification.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: CADASIL (Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy) or other inherited small-vessel disease presenting with migraine with aura as sentinel symptom.

Reasoning: While the clinical episodes (visual aura followed by unilateral throbbing pain, light/cough triggers) resemble migraine, the MRI findings are atypical for primary migraine. Persistent diffusion-weighted abnormalities at the gray-white junction and corpus callosum splenium—rather than resolving acutely—suggest recurrent ischemic events or chronic microvascular disease. Early cortical atrophy in a 44-year-old, combined with failure of standard migraine prophylaxis, argues against primary migraine. Negative autoimmune/inflammatory workup excludes vasculitis. Normal vascular imaging excludes large-vessel disease. The constellation of progressive small-vessel white matter changes, generalized atrophy, and migraine with aura strongly suggests CADASIL, which classically presents with migraine with aura in the fourth decade before progressing to recurrent strokes.

Recommended next action: (1) NOTCH3 gene sequencing for CADASIL; (2) skin biopsy with electron microscopy to look for granular osmiophilic material in arteriolar walls (pathognomonic for CADASIL); (3) mitochondrial genetic panel if CADASIL testing is negative (to rule out MELAS).

Confidence: 65–70%. The clinical presentation of migraine with aura could stand alone, but persistent imaging changes and progressive atrophy demand investigation for an inherited vasculopathy. CADASIL is the most likely inherited small-vessel disease at this age with this phenotype.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 44-year-old man presents with a 4-year history of migraine with visual aura (F4–F5, F6–F10): scintillation and field defects (F6–F7), metamorphopsia (F8), aura preceding headache (F9), left unilateral throbbing pain (F11–F12), photophobia (F17), and photic/Valsalva triggers (F15–F16). This clinical constellation alone is consistent with uncomplicated migraine with visual aura, supported by R10 (gradual-onset aura with positive-to-negative evolution fits cortical spreading depression) and R9 (photophobia prevalent in aura-migraine).

However, neuroimaging reveals persistent and progressive structural abnormalities that cannot be reconciled with primary migraine: (1) DWI hyperintensities at cortex-white matter junctions and splenium (F46–F47), which are **still present at 1-year follow-up** (F48) rather than resolving as expected for acute cytotoxic edema; (2) bilateral temporal pole atrophy (F49) and generalized cortical atrophy greater than expected for age (F50–F51). Per R20, imaging-confirmed lesions warrant search for underlying etiology, not attribution to primary migraine alone.

Differential diagnosis:

**Seronegative primary CNS vasculitis (small-vessel)** is the leading diagnosis. R5 establishes that negative ANA, APLA, vasculitis serology, normal CSF, and normal angiography do NOT exclude seronegative PCNSV; R15 confirms normal vascular imaging excludes macroscopic vasculitis but not microvasculitis or microembolization. R6 explains persistent DWI lesions at 1-year as reflecting ongoing small-vessel inflammation with DWI-enhancement correspondence in 77% of PCNSV cases. The cortical-junction band distribution (F46) aligns with R7's description of MELAS-pattern cortex-white-matter junction involvement, which also applies to microvasculopathic lesioning.

**CADASIL (Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy)** is a strong secondary consideration. R1 reports migraine with aura in 75–90% of CADASIL with typical onset age 40–50, matching this patient's age and phenotype (F1, F5). R3 links bilateral temporal pole atrophy to CADASIL-related decline. R4 explains persistent DWI changes as chronic gliosis rather than acute edema. However, R19 significantly undermines CADASIL: the expected imaging pattern in CADASIL shows anterior temporal white-matter involvement with U-fiber sparing and subcortical predilection; cortical-junction bands are **less typical of CADASIL**. This patient's DWI pattern therefore does not fit CADASIL's expected neuroradiological signature.

**MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes)** must be considered. R7 notes headache and visual disturbance are cardinal MELAS presenting features, and R8 describes multifocal cortical edema at stroke-like lesions distributed to cortex-white matter junction—precisely matching this patient's imaging (F46–F47). However, MELAS typically manifests with acute stroke-like episodes and rapid progression; this patient's 4-year indolent episodic course is atypical. MELAS onset is usually pediatric or young adult; age 44 is less common.

**Uncomplicated migraine with aura** remains a consideration for the clinical phenotype but is insufficient to explain the imaging. R11 documents rare reversible corpus callosum lesions in migraine aura (n=5 cases, age 10–51 years), which matches the splenial finding (F47); however, R11 emphasizes **resolution on follow-up**, whereas this patient's lesions persist at 1 year (F48). R12 acknowledges migraine-with-aura carries increased risk of subclinical posterior infarction, but this applies to acute ischemic events, not progressive atrophy over years.

**Integration:** The clinical phenotype satisfies criteria for migraine with visual aura (R9, R10), but the persistent cortical-junction DWI lesions and progressive atrophy indicate an **underlying small-vessel pathology**. The cortical-junction band pattern is less consistent with CADASIL's typical subcortical distribution (R19) and more consistent with either seronegative PCNSV microvasculitis (R5–R6, R15) or MELAS (R7–R8). The normal CSF (F40–F42), while uncommon in PCNSV, does not exclude it (R5: 17.4% of PCNSV have normal CSF). The failure of antiplatelet therapy and corticosteroids (F22) may indicate inadequate dosing/duration or non-inflammatory etiology (R13), but does not exclude vasculitis if the corticosteroid course was subtherapeutic.

**Top diagnosis: Seronegative primary CNS vasculitis (small-vessel),** with secondary migraine-with-aura phenotype and progressive cortical lesioning. This diagnosis best integrates: (1) cortical-junction DWI distribution; (2) persistent lesions despite normal angiography (R15); (3) normal serologies, CSF, and angiography that are compatible with seronegative disease (R5–R6); (4) progressive atrophy consistent with recurrent microinfarction.

**Differential: MELAS and CADASIL.** MELAS anatomically fits the cortex-white matter junction pattern (R7–R8) but is atypical for age and disease timeline. CADASIL fits migraine phenotype and temporal atrophy (R1, R3) but is argued against by the cortical-junction predominance (R19).

**Confidence: Moderate (50–60%),** because none of the three leading diagnoses is definitively ruled in or out by the IR alone. Seronegative PCNSV is favored on anatomical grounds (cortical bands) and because normal serology/angiography are compatible with its diagnosis (R5, R15), but the completely normal CSF and indolent 4-year episodic course are atypical. Definitive diagnosis requires brain biopsy (per R5).
per_case.framework_top: Seronegative primary CNS vasculitis (small-vessel), with secondary migraine-with-aura phenotype, causing progressive cortical lesioning and atrophy. Differential includes MELAS and CADASIL.
per_case.framework_next_step: Brain biopsy for definitive diagnosis (per R5, 'definitive diagnosis requires brain biopsy'). Concurrently, obtain serum and CSF lactate levels to evaluate for MELAS; order mitochondrial genetic testing (m.3243A>G) if metabolic workup is pending. Referral to neuro-ophthalmology to characterize aura semiology and confirm cortical spreading depression vs. ischemic mechanism. Brain MRI with contrast to assess vessel-wall enhancement pattern (R6 notes 77% DWI-correspondence with vessel wall enhancement in PCNSV).
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate (50–60%). The clinical phenotype is classic for migraine with visual aura, but persistent imaging abnormalities with progressive atrophy indicate an underlying structural etiology. The cortical-junction DWI pattern and normal serology/CSF narrow the field to seronegative PCNSV, MELAS, or CADASIL, but no single diagnosis is definitively supported by the IR alone. Seronegative PCNSV is favored because: (a) cortical-junction bands fit R7–R8 (MELAS cortex-WM junction) and (b) persistent DWI + normal vascular imaging fit R6 + R15; however, (c) the indolent 4-year episodic course is atypical for vasculitis, and (d) completely normal CSF is uncommon in PCNSV. CADASIL is undermined by cortical-junction predominance (R19 notes U-fiber sparing typical, not cortical bands). MELAS is possible but unusual age/timeline. Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: NIID, confirmed by NOTCH2NLC GGC-repeat expansion and SKIN BIOPSY (p62/ubiquitin intranuclear inclusions); key discriminator is that the persistent DWI corticomedullary-junction ribbon + temporal-pole atrophy + NEGATIVE vasculitis workup should redirect AWAY from the vasculitis/migraine framing toward skin biopsy + NOTCH2NLC testing.

Neither output names NIID/NOTCH2NLC, so both are incorrect on the specific diagnosis. The decisive difference is disposition and whether each respects the case's central lesson.

OUTPUT A (CADASIL): wrong specific diagnosis and wrong gene (NOTCH3), but correctly abandons the vasculitis/migraine framing, recognizes an inherited disorder, and — critically — recommends SKIN BIOPSY plus genetic testing. Skin biopsy is the actual confirmatory modality; A's workup pathway would plausibly surface the inclusions and lead to the real answer. Confidence 65-70% is reasonable though slightly overconfident.

OUTPUT B (seronegative primary CNS vasculitis): far more rigorous in form, with feature/rule traceability and excellent differential breadth (it even argues against CADASIL on imaging grounds and discusses MELAS), and it is best-calibrated (50-60%). But it lands on and reinforces PRIMARY CNS VASCULITIS as the top diagnosis — the exact framing the ground truth explicitly says was the wrong original misattribution and should be dropped. It explains away every negative serology/CSF/angiogram to preserve vasculitis, and recommends BRAIN biopsy rather than skin biopsy. This both perpetuates the documented error and points to the wrong confirmatory test.

So although B is more defensible/traceable as a piece of reasoning and better calibrated, A reaches the materially closer clinical disposition (skin biopsy + genetic testing; explicitly excludes vasculitis), which is what the case rewards. Closeness-to-correct-disposition and avoidance of the explicitly-rejected vasculitis path outweigh B's superior form. Winner: A. Both partial.
