per_case.prose:
A 63-year-old man was referred to a gastroenterology service for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension. About fourteen months earlier he had begun to notice generalized fatigue and bilateral ankle swelling. Over the subsequent year his abdomen became increasingly distended, and in the last several months he had developed numbness and a persistent cold sensation in both hands and feet. He also reported dryness of the mouth and eyes and an unintentional weight loss of roughly 4 kg over the year. There was no fever and no drenching night sweats.

Six to seven months before the current referral, an abdominal ultrasound at another hospital had shown moderate ascites. He underwent therapeutic paracentesis and was started on spironolactone and furosemide, but the fluid reaccumulated quickly. A contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis described multiple enlarged lymph nodes, several containing dense calcified foci. An excisional lymph-node biopsy was reported as lymphoid tissue with granuloma formation. On the basis of these findings he was presumptively treated for tuberculosis with a four-drug regimen (isoniazid 300 mg daily, ethambutol 750 mg daily, rifampicin, and after one month pyrazinamide 1 g daily) together with a low dose of oral prednisolone. After roughly a month of therapy the ascites had not improved.

On examination at referral, vital signs were normal. The skin showed several small red papulonodular lesions, each about 2–4 mm, scattered over the forehead, anterior chest and abdominal wall, with darkening of the skin around the mouth. Small firm lymph nodes were palpable in both axillae. The abdomen was distended with shifting dullness, mild epigastric tenderness, and no rebound; bowel sounds were sluggish. Both lower legs showed pitting edema. Neurological examination revealed symmetric mild distal weakness (power 4/5 in all limbs) with reduced sensation in a stocking-glove distribution.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 109 g/l, white cell count 5.9 × 10⁹/l, platelets 208 × 10⁹/l, CRP 11.8 mg/l, serum albumin 29 g/l. Thyroid testing showed TSH 7.1 µIU/ml (ref 0.4–5.0) with low-normal free T4. Morning serum cortisol was 17.9 µg/dl (ref 2.9–17.3). CA-125 was modestly elevated at 41 IU/ml. ANA and ANCA were negative. An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded clear yellow fluid with a serum-ascites albumin gradient greater than 11 g/l and no acid-fast bacilli on staining. Serum protein immunofixation demonstrated an IgG lambda monoclonal band. Bone marrow examination was hypercellular with plasma cells comprising under 1% of the marrow. Review of the prior lymph-node specimen and a repeat node sampling showed clustered plasma cells. Serum vascular endothelial growth factor was markedly elevated at 1710 pg/ml (ref 0–142).

Nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrated slowed conduction consistent with a peripheral neuropathy. Doppler ultrasound of the legs found a thrombus in a right deep leg vein. CT review additionally noted several sclerotic bony lesions of increased density involving the sternum, sacrum and iliac bones. A small forehead nodule that was excised showed a vascular (haemangiomatous) lesion; a sampled thyroid nodule was benign.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: POEMS syndrome (Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, Skin changes) — a paraneoplastic syndrome of an underlying clonal plasma-cell disorder. Presented predominantly as a gastroenterology problem: refractory ascites and distended abdomen.

HOW CONFIRMED: Diagnostic criteria fully met. BOTH mandatory criteria present — (1) peripheral neuropathy (clinical sensorimotor + EMG showing axonal/demyelinating slowing) and (2) monoclonal plasma-cell proliferative disorder (serum immunofixation/immunoelectrophoresis = IgG lambda M-protein; clonal/clustered plasma cells on lymph-node biopsy). THREE major criteria — osteosclerotic (sclerotic) bone lesions on CT (sternum, sacrum, ilium); markedly elevated serum VEGF (1595 pg/ml vs ref 0–142); and lymph-node features (Castleman-type/angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia). Multiple minor criteria — endocrinopathy (subclinical hypothyroidism TSH 6.6, mildly elevated cortisol), skin changes (perioral hyperpigmentation; multiple small red cutaneous nodules consistent with glomeruloid hemangiomas — one excised forehead nodule read as haemangioma), extravascular volume overload (ascites with SAAG >11 g/l + bilateral pitting leg edema), and a venous thrombosis (right leg DVT). KEY MISLEADING STEP: an early lymph-node biopsy showed granuloma formation and CT showed calcified/enlarged nodes, so she was misdiagnosed as tuberculosis and given full anti-TB therapy (4 drugs) + low-dose steroid for ~1 month with POOR response (ascites persisted); T-spot negative, ascitic fluid AFB-negative — i.e., anti-TB failure was the clue that reframed the workup.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize this is NOT tuberculosis and NOT primary IBD/ovarian/serositis; the refractory transudative ascites + peripheral neuropathy + monoclonal gammopathy + osteosclerotic lesions + sky-high VEGF + skin/endocrine findings define POEMS. Stop ineffective anti-TB therapy; treat the underlying plasma-cell clone. The patient received lenalidomide + dexamethasone (plasma-cell-directed therapy), plus supportive diuretics and levothyroxine, with gradual resolution of ascites and improved weakness over two cycles / 3 months; condition stable at last follow-up. (Autologous stem-cell transplant or radiotherapy to a solitary plasmacytoma are the other standard definitive options.)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: POEMS Syndrome. 

Reasoning: Classic pentad of polyneuropathy (distal, stocking-glove), organomegaly (lymphadenopathy + ascites), endocrinopathy (thyroid dysfunction, elevated cortisol), monoclonal protein (IgG lambda), and skin changes (papules + hyperpigmentation). Markedly elevated VEGF (1710) is nearly pathognomonic. Sclerotic bone lesions and thrombophilia fit. TB testing was negative and therapy failed, ruling out TB despite granulomas.

Recommended next action: Confirm POEMS diagnosis, discontinue anti-TB therapy, and initiate immunosuppression (corticosteroids, IVIG, or plasma exchange).

Confidence: 85%

The elevated VEGF in the setting of this clinical constellation is highly specific for POEMS. Ascites and granulomas can occur in POEMS, though not universally reported.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 63-year-old man with 14-month progressive multi-system disease presents with clinical and laboratory findings diagnostic of POEMS syndrome.

**POEMS Diagnostic Criteria Met (Mandatory + Major):**

*Polyneuropathy (Mandatory):* Patient demonstrates symmetric distal sensorimotor neuropathy with length-dependent stocking-glove sensory loss and symmetric mild distal weakness (4/5 all limbs, F27-F28). Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction consistent with demyelinating pattern (F46), fulfilling the mandatory neurologic criterion for POEMS (R1).

*Monoclonal protein:* Serum immunofixation demonstrates IgG lambda monoclonal band (F42), with lambda-chain restriction present in >95% of POEMS cases (R2). Bone marrow is hypercellular with plasma cells <1% (F43), and repeat lymph node sampling shows clustered plasma cells (F44)—consistent with monoclonal dyscrasia rather than classical myeloma (R16). This plasma cell clonal expansion combined with monoclonal protein on immunofixation represents the required monoclonal component.

*Endocrinopathy (Minor criterion):* Elevated TSH 7.1 µIU/ml with low-normal free T4 (F34-F35) indicates primary hypothyroidism present in 54-67% of POEMS patients (R7). Perioral hyperpigmentation (F21) with borderline elevated morning cortisol 17.9 µg/dl (F36, at upper limit 17.3) raises consideration of adrenal involvement (R19-R21), though adrenal insufficiency is not fully excluded without dynamic testing (R20).

*Organomegaly (Minor criterion):* Marked VEGF elevation at 1710 pg/ml (F45)—far exceeding the 200 pg/ml threshold—is a major diagnostic criterion for POEMS and correlates with disease activity (R3). Lymphadenopathy is documented clinically (bilateral axillary nodes, F22) and radiographically (multiple enlarged lymph nodes on CT, F13).

*Skin changes (Minor criterion):* Multiple small erythematous papulonodular lesions, 2-4 mm, distributed over forehead, anterior chest, and abdominal wall (F19-F20) with perioral hyperpigmentation (F21). Vascular manifestations occur in 68-100% of POEMS patients (R8). The excised forehead nodule showing benign hemangioma (F49) does not exclude distributed papulonodules as POEMS manifestations (R26).

**Additional Major Criterion—Bone Lesions:**
CT imaging reveals sclerotic (osteosclerotic) bone lesions in sternum, sacrum, and iliac bones (F48), a major diagnostic criterion for POEMS (R4). Osteosclerotic lesions are atypical for classical myeloma, which presents with lytic lesions (R15), and this pattern with IgG-lambda monoclonal protein and low bone marrow plasma cells further supports POEMS over myeloma.

**Minor Criteria Also Present:**
- Ascites with SAAG >11 g/l (F41), indicating high protein gradient consistent with peritoneal infiltration (R17) and listed as minor criterion for POEMS (R6). Ascites is a manifestation of POEMS-related vascular permeability or peritoneal involvement (R32).
- Peripheral edema (bilateral lower legs, F26), another minor criterion (R6).
- DVT in right deep vein (F47), an underappreciated vascular complication in ~20-30% of POEMS due to VEGF-driven coagulation activation (R9).
- Anemia (Hb 109 g/l, F29) with normal WBC and platelets and low bone marrow plasma cells, consistent with chronic disease anemia of POEMS (R18).
- Elevated CRP (11.8 mg/l, F32) with preserved WBC reflects chronic inflammatory/vascular disease rather than acute infection (R24).
- Progressive 14-month indolent course (F2-F6) characteristic of POEMS rather than acute infection (R28).

**Why Tuberculosis is Excluded:**
Initial misdiagnosis was based on granulomas reported on lymph node biopsy (F14) and lymphadenopathy on imaging (F13). However, decisive evidence against TB includes:
- Negative interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), which has high diagnostic utility for TB (F40, R10).
- Negative acid-fast bacilli in ascitic fluid on staining (F41, R10).
- Rapid failure of ascites to improve after one month of anti-TB therapy (F17, R11).
- Repeat lymph node sampling showing clustered plasma cells rather than caseating granulomas (F44, R12), indicating plasma cell dyscrasia not granulomatous inflammation.
- Absence of fever and night sweats (F7-F8), lowering inflammatory/infectious diagnoses (R22).
- Markedly elevated VEGF (1710 pg/ml) distinguishes POEMS from TB (R13).

**Why Not Classical Multiple Myeloma:**
Osteosclerotic (not lytic) bone lesions argue against classical MM (R15). Bone marrow plasma cells <1% are far below the >10% threshold for MM diagnosis (R16). Absence of hypercalcemia, lytic lesions, and high plasma cell burden makes classical myeloma unlikely.

**Why Not Waldenström Macroglobulinemia:**
Monoclonal protein is IgG, not IgM; WM typically produces IgM (R14), making WM diagnosis unlikely.

**Pathophysiology of Key Features:**
- *Ascites mechanism:* SAAG >11 g/l with no cirrhosis or hepatic synthetic failure (preserved albumin synthesis evident) suggests peritoneal infiltration by plasma cells or lymphoid tissue (R17) or VEGF-driven vascular permeability (R32) rather than portal hypertension.
- *DVT mechanism:* VEGF-induced endothelial activation and hypercoagulability (R9) in absence of immobility or documented thrombophilia.
- *Neuropathy mechanism:* Symmetric demyelinating pattern (R1, R27) consistent with POEMS pathophysiology, though distinction between primary demyelination and secondary axonal injury cannot be made without detailed NCS pattern analysis.

**Remaining Uncertainties Requiring Confirmation:**
Definitive confirmation requires: (1) detailed neurophysiology distinguishing demyelinating vs axonal predominance; (2) IL-6 and cytokine profiling to assess for Castleman disease variant (R31); (3) histopathologic verification that plasma cell lesions represent monoclonal dyscrasia; (4) exclusion of mechanical ascites mechanisms (portal vein imaging); (5) cosyntropin testing to clarify adrenal reserve. However, these refinements do not change the fundamental diagnosis, which meets POEMS criteria with high specificity.

per_case.framework_next_step: Confirmatory testing: (1) High-resolution neurophysiology to characterize demyelinating vs axonal pattern and correlate with POEMS phenotype; (2) Serum IL-6 and cytokine profiling to assess for Castleman disease variant; (3) Repeat/new lymph node imaging (PET-CT) and biopsy to define histopathology definitively (plasma cell vs Castleman); (4) Cosyntropin stimulation test to clarify adrenal reserve given borderline cortisol; (5) Thrombophilia workup and imaging of mesenteric/portal vasculature to exclude mechanical obstruction as ascites mechanism. Once POEMS confirmed, initiate immunosuppression (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis, or rituximab) per POEMS protocol.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct final diagnosis (POEMS syndrome) and both correctly identify the misleading TB step and that anti-TB therapy failure was the reframing clue. The decisive differences are in treatment recommendation, calibration, and defensibility.

CORRECTNESS — Treatment/disposition: This is where A goes materially wrong. Ground truth specifies plasma-cell-directed therapy (lenalidomide + dexamethasone, ASCT, or radiotherapy to plasmacytoma) because POEMS is driven by an underlying clonal plasma-cell disorder. Output A recommends "immunosuppression (corticosteroids, IVIG, or plasma exchange)" — this is essentially CIDP-style neuropathy management and is NOT correct POEMS disposition; it treats POEMS as if it were an immune-mediated neuropathy and misses the need to treat the clone. Output B does not name a specific drug regimen but correctly frames the disposition as confirming/treating the monoclonal plasma-cell dyscrasia and excludes the relevant differentials; it does not assert a wrong treatment. B's omission of the specific regimen is a lesser fault than A's affirmatively incorrect treatment recommendation.

DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FIDELITY: B correctly maps the mandatory (neuropathy + monoclonal protein) and major criteria (osteosclerotic lesions, VEGF, lymph node/Castleman) and minor criteria (endocrinopathy, skin, volume overload/ascites+edema, DVT) closely matching the ground-truth structure. A gives the older "pentad" framing (the P-O-E-M-S mnemonic) which is reasonable but conflates organomegaly with ascites/lymphadenopathy loosely and is less precise about mandatory-vs-major structure. B's mechanistic framing of ascites (VEGF-driven permeability / extravascular volume overload) matches ground truth better than A.

HALLUCINATION/MINOR ERRORS: Both cite VEGF as 1710 pg/ml whereas ground truth says 1595 pg/ml — both share this discrepancy equally (likely a different reported value in their input), so it does not differentiate. Both invoke specific percentages and reference tags; B's are presented as cited (R-tags, F-tags) giving traceability, though these are internal citations not independently verifiable here. A's claim that VEGF threshold context is "nearly pathognomonic" is acceptable; B's quantitative claims (e.g., lambda restriction >95%, hypothyroidism 54-67%) are plausible and standard. Neither shows egregious fabrication, but B's claims are more carefully hedged and tied to evidence items.

CALIBRATION: B explicitly enumerates remaining uncertainties (demyelinating vs axonal, IL-6/Castleman confirmation, adrenal dynamic testing, mechanical ascites exclusion) without letting them undermine the firm diagnosis — well calibrated. A gives a flat 85% confidence and a couple of caveats; adequate but shallower.

DEFENSIBILITY: B's reasoning is far more traceable — each assertion is tied to a finding/rule, differentials (classical MM, Waldenström) are explicitly excluded with correct reasoning (osteosclerotic vs lytic, plasma cells <1%, IgG not IgM), and the TB exclusion is itemized. A's reasoning is correct in gist but terse and includes the flawed treatment line.

OVERALL: Both are correct on diagnosis. B is more complete, better structured to the actual POEMS criteria, better calibrated, more defensible, and avoids A's incorrect treatment recommendation. A is partially correct: right diagnosis and right TB exclusion, but materially wrong on disposition (immunosuppression/IVIG/plasma exchange instead of plasma-cell-directed therapy). Winner: B.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old man was referred to a regional gastroenterology service after roughly two and a half years of bowel trouble that had never been pinned down. His complaints were remarkably consistent over that span: loose, watery stools several times a day, a persistent sense of upper-abdominal fullness after meals that he described as "indigestion that never quits," and diffuse, crampy abdominal discomfort that waxed and waned without clear triggers. A retired long-haul truck driver, he initially blamed years of irregular meals and roadside food, and so did his first two physicians.

Over the preceding two years he had been worked up repeatedly. He underwent three separate upper endoscopies and two colonoscopies at different facilities; the gross endoscopic appearance was each time read as essentially normal or non-specific. Random mucosal sampling on those earlier procedures had been obtained specifically to exclude inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and microscopic colitis — and on review none of those conditions were supported. Serologic celiac testing was negative, and a trial of dietary modification produced no durable benefit. With structural and inflammatory causes felt to be excluded, he carried a working label of diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and had cycled through antispasmodics, loperamide, a low-FODMAP diet, and a bile-acid sequestrant, none of which controlled his symptoms.

On admission to the tertiary center his examination was largely unremarkable apart from mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or organomegaly that was clearly appreciable. Routine bloods, including hemoglobin and white-cell differential, were within normal limits. Repeat colonoscopy was again macroscopically bland, but multiple targeted mucosal biopsies were taken from the right colon and rectosigmoid. Histology showed a dense, diffuse infiltrate of round-to-spindled cells expanding the lamina propria; on immunohistochemistry these cells stained strongly for tryptase and for CD117, and aberrant co-expression of CD25 was demonstrated. A serum tryptase drawn during the admission returned markedly elevated, well above 180 ng/mL. Given those findings a bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy were performed, which revealed multifocal compact aggregates of the same cells, again co-expressing tryptase together with the aberrant markers CD2 and CD25. Targeted molecular testing of marrow was sent and returned positive for an activating KIT codon-816 point mutation.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Systemic mastocytosis presenting as (and long misattributed to) diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D). Confirmation was multi-modal and unambiguous: (1) GI mucosal biopsies showed diffuse lamina propria infiltration by mast cells positive for tryptase and CD117 (CD25-aberrant); (2) bone marrow aspirate/biopsy demonstrated multifocal dense mast cell infiltrates co-expressing the aberrant markers CD2 and CD25 along with tryptase (meeting WHO criteria); (3) serum tryptase markedly elevated (>200 ng/mL, far above the ~11.4 ng/mL upper limit and above the 20 ng/mL minor criterion); (4) activating KIT D816V mutation positive. Correct disposition: this is NOT a functional bowel disorder — recognize the multi-system clonal mast cell disease, refer to hematology, stage with bone marrow biopsy + KIT mutation testing + serum tryptase, and treat the underlying clonal disorder rather than symptomatic IBS management. In this report the patient received midostaurin (KIT inhibitor) 100 mg PO BID with marked symptomatic improvement at 3 months (diarrhea/abdominal discomfort resolved), though clonal mast cells persisted on repeat GI biopsy. Source: Archives of Medical Science, April 2024 (PMC11493042). The key reasoning lesson: refractory IBS-D with negative IBD/celiac/microscopic-colitis workup should prompt a serum tryptase and consideration of mast cell disease before settling on a functional label.

rulebook.rule: Multifocal dense bone marrow aggregates with ≥15 mast cells in aggregate, confirmed by immunohistochemistry (tryptase and/or CD117 staining), RAISES diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis. This is the major WHO diagnostic criterion.
rulebook.source: WHO 2022 Classification; Systemic mastocytosis in adults: 2023 update on diagnosis, risk stratification and management. Am J Hematol. 2023. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ajh.26962

rulebook.rule: Aberrant co-expression of CD25 and/or CD2 on mast cells in bone marrow or extracutaneous tissues RAISES diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis as a minor WHO diagnostic criterion (one of four minor criteria).
rulebook.source: Immunophenotyping in systemic mastocytosis diagnosis: 'CD25 positive' alone is more informative than the 'CD25 and/or CD2' WHO criterion. Modern Pathology. 2012. https://www.nature.com/articles/modpathol2011192

rulebook.rule: Detection of activating KIT codon-816 (D816V) point mutation in bone marrow, peripheral blood, or extracutaneous tissue RAISES diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis as a minor WHO diagnostic criterion. >90% of adult SM patients carry somatic KIT mutations, most commonly D816V.
rulebook.source: Detection of KIT Mutations in Systemic Mastocytosis: How, When, and Why. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11507058/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated baseline serum tryptase (≥180 ng/mL or substantially above the 20 ng/mL minor criterion threshold) RAISES diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis. Baseline tryptase >20 ng/mL is a minor WHO criterion; levels >200 ng/mL correlate with elevated grades of mast cell infiltration.
rulebook.source: Systemic Mastocytosis Workup: Approach Considerations, Laboratory Studies. Medscape. https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/203948-workup

rulebook.rule: Diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis is established when patient meets 1 major criterion + 1 minor criterion, OR 3 minor criteria. Major criterion = multifocal dense BM aggregates (≥15 cells); Minor criteria = (1) ≥25% atypical mast cells, (2) KIT codon-816 mutation, (3) CD25/CD2/CD30 aberrant expression, (4) serum tryptase >20 ng/mL.
rulebook.source: WHO 2022 Classification; Detection of KIT Mutations in Systemic Mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11507058/

rulebook.rule: Chronic diarrhea (loose, watery stools multiple times daily) RAISES suspicion for systemic mastocytosis when present in context of normal or non-specific endoscopic appearance. GI symptoms occur in 14–85% of SM patients; diarrhea reported in up to 80% of patients with SM.
rulebook.source: Systemic Mastocytosis: A Rare Cause of Diarrhea. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7358960/

rulebook.rule: Chronic abdominal pain and postprandial upper abdominal discomfort RAISES suspicion for systemic mastocytosis, especially when unresponsive to antispasmodics, loperamide, and dietary modification (low-FODMAP, bile-acid sequestrants). Abdominal pain reported in ~51% of SM patients; cramping results from mast cell mediator release.
rulebook.source: Gastrointestinal manifestations of systemic mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2773867/

rulebook.rule: Chronic GI symptoms (diarrhea, cramping, indigestion) persisting for >2 years with multiple negative prior biopsies (normal or non-specific endoscopic appearance, biopsies negative for inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and microscopic colitis) RAISES concern for systemic mastocytosis and warrants immunohistochemical screening (tryptase, CD117, CD25) on repeat biopsies.
rulebook.source: Delayed Diagnosis of Adult Indolent Systemic Mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4224005/

rulebook.rule: Failure of multiple therapeutic trials (antispasmodics, loperamide, low-FODMAP diet, bile-acid sequestrants) to control chronic diarrhea and abdominal symptoms LOWERS confidence in IBS-predominant diagnosis and RAISES suspicion for systemic mastocytosis or other organic pathology.
rulebook.source: Systemic Mastocytosis: variable manifestations can lead to a challenging diagnostic process. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6721155/

rulebook.rule: Dense diffuse infiltrate of round-to-spindled mast cells expanding the lamina propria (rather than normal scattered mast cell distribution) on mucosal biopsy RAISES diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis, especially when confirmed by tryptase and CD117 immunohistochemistry.
rulebook.source: Gastrointestinal manifestations of systemic mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2773867/

rulebook.rule: Absence of morphologic atypia or spindle-cell predominance (<25% atypical/spindle mast cells) does NOT lower diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis if other major and minor criteria are met. Cell morphology is only one minor criterion; diagnosis does not require morphologic atypia.
rulebook.source: WHO 2022 Classification; Detection of KIT Mutations in Systemic Mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11507058/

rulebook.rule: Normal or non-specific gross endoscopic appearance with negative routine H&E histology does NOT exclude systemic mastocytosis. Approximately 40% of involved colonic biopsies show no corresponding endoscopic abnormalities. Immunohistochemistry (tryptase, CD117) is essential to detect microscopic mast cell infiltration.
rulebook.source: A Clinicopathologic Study of 24 Cases of Systemic Mastocytosis Involving the Gastrointestinal Tract. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4086834/

rulebook.rule: Random or limited biopsy sampling (single sites or small number of biopsies) LOWERS sensitivity for detecting systemic mastocytosis because GI involvement is often focal and multifocal rather than diffuse. Multiple systematic biopsies from different anatomic sites (right colon, rectosigmoid, etc.) with explicit instructions for immunohistochemical staining are recommended.
rulebook.source: A Clinicopathologic Study of 24 Cases of Systemic Mastocytosis Involving the Gastrointestinal Tract. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4086834/

rulebook.rule: Omission of immunohistochemical staining (tryptase, CD117) in favor of routine H&E histology alone SIGNIFICANTLY LOWERS detection sensitivity for systemic mastocytosis. Immunohistochemical stains are superior to H&E and histochemical stains (toluidine blue, chloroacetate esterase) for enumeration and confirmation of mast cells.
rulebook.source: CD117 or Mast Cell Tryptase Immunohistochemical (IHC) Stains. LabCE. https://www.labce.com/spg9857325_cd117_or_mast_cell_tryptase_immunohistochemical_ih.aspx

rulebook.rule: KIT D816V mutation causes ligand-independent constitutive activation of KIT tyrosine kinase, resulting in uncontrolled mast cell proliferation, survival, and mediator release (histamine, tryptase, PGD2). This activation loop is the pathophysiologic basis for mast cell accumulation and systemic symptoms in SM.
rulebook.source: Systemic Mastocytosis Pathophysiology. Rare Disease Advisor. https://www.rarediseaseadvisor.com/hcp-resource/systemic-mastocytosis-pathophysiology/

rulebook.rule: Diarrhea in systemic mastocytosis results from mast cell mediator release: histamine and prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) increase water and chloride secretion into the intestinal lumen and augment bowel motility. Tryptase itself contributes to protease-mediated mucosal injury and acid hypersecretion.
rulebook.source: Mast cells in digestive diseases: New insights to keep them under control. ScienceDirect. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1043661825004943

rulebook.rule: Negative celiac serology (tissue transglutaminase antibody, endomysial antibody) LOWERS likelihood of celiac disease-mediated diarrhea but does NOT exclude systemic mastocytosis as an alternative diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Systemic Mastocytosis: variable manifestations can lead to a challenging diagnostic process. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6721155/

rulebook.rule: Elevated serum tryptase levels must be interpreted cautiously: normal baseline tryptase does NOT exclude systemic mastocytosis (5–7% of indolent SM patients have tryptase <11.4 ng/mL). Conversely, mild elevations (20–50 ng/mL) can occur in non-SM conditions (myeloid neoplasms, renal disease, hereditary alpha-tryptasemia). Therefore, elevated tryptase ALONE is insufficient for SM diagnosis; bone marrow biopsy and KIT mutation analysis are required for confirmation.
rulebook.source: Defining 'Normal' basal serum tryptase levels: a context-dependent approach to improve diagnostics in systemic mastocytosis. Frontiers in Allergy. 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/allergy/articles/10.3389/falgy.2025.1592001/full

rulebook.rule: Bone marrow involvement (multifocal compact aggregates of mast cells) with KIT D816V mutation and aberrant CD2/CD25 co-expression confirms systemic mastocytosis and RAISES prognostic concern for more aggressive disease and multilineage hematopoietic involvement compared to cutaneous-only disease.
rulebook.source: Unraveling the Rare Entity of KIT D816V-Negative Systemic Mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11236357/

rulebook.rule: Bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM) is a subvariant of indolent SM characterized by bone marrow involvement WITHOUT skin lesions, often with normal or near-normal baseline tryptase levels. This phenotype is frequently underdiagnosed due to lack of typical cutaneous involvement and reliance on serum tryptase as sole screening tool.
rulebook.source: Bone Marrow Mastocytosis: A Diagnostic Challenge. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8037514/

rulebook.rule: Diagnostic delay in systemic mastocytosis is common and may persist 6–15 years because: (a) rarity of disease leads to low clinical suspicion, (b) symptoms mimic common GI disorders (IBS, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease), (c) prior biopsies lack immunohistochemical staining for mast cell markers, (d) endoscopic appearance may be normal despite microscopic infiltration, and (e) absence of skin manifestations in some patients (BMM subtype).
rulebook.source: Delayed Diagnosis of Adult Indolent Systemic Mastocytosis. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4224005/

rulebook.rule: CD25 expression alone (without CD2) is more specific for systemic mastocytosis than the WHO 'CD25 and/or CD2' criterion. Recent expert consensus recommends prioritizing CD25 positivity as the aberrant antigen marker, with CD30 increasingly recognized as significant in advanced disease. The presence of CD2 in non-SM settings limits its diagnostic specificity.
rulebook.source: Prognostic impact of expression of CD2, CD25, and/or CD30 in/on mast cells in systemic mastocytosis: a registry study of the European Competence Network on Mastocytosis. PubMed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39815050/

rulebook.rule: Highly sensitive KIT mutation detection (VAF threshold <0.01%) using allele-specific qPCR (ASO-PCR) or digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) is required because standard next-generation sequencing lacks adequate sensitivity for detecting KIT mutations in most SM patients. Standard assays may miss low-burden or subclonal mutations.
rulebook.source: Detection of KIT Mutations in Systemic Mastocytosis: How, When, and Why. PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11507058/

rulebook.rule: In patients with unexplained chronic diarrhea, normal endoscopies, unremarkable H&E histology on prior biopsies, and failure of standard IBS and functional GI therapies, systemic mastocytosis should be actively considered. This clinical picture is characteristic of missed SM diagnosis and warrants dedicated evaluation with tryptase/CD117 immunohistochemistry on repeat mucosal biopsies.
rulebook.source: Mast cells in digestive diseases: New insights to keep them under control. ScienceDirect. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1043661825004943

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Systemic Mastocytosis (Indolent type) with gastrointestinal involvement. The KIT D816V mutation is pathognomonic. The constellation of dense mast cell infiltrates (tryptase+, CD117+ with aberrant CD2/CD25) in both GI mucosa and bone marrow, markedly elevated serum tryptase (>180 ng/mL), and classic GI symptoms (chronic diarrhea, postprandial distress, cramping) in a patient with excluded IBD/celiac/microscopic colitis makes this diagnosis certain.

Recommended next action: (1) Confirm diagnosis with additional serum tryptase, 24-hour urinary histamine metabolites, and chromogranin A; (2) Risk-stratify with complete marrow morphology, flow cytometry quantitation of aberrant mast cells, and cytogenetic assessment; (3) Initiate symptomatic management with H1/H2 blockers and consider mast cell stabilizers or tyrosine kinase inhibitors depending on disease burden; (4) Establish monitoring protocol (serial tryptase, periodic marrow re-evaluation, organ involvement screening).

Confidence: 95%

Reasoning: The KIT D816V mutation is diagnostic for SM. The clinical picture—obscure GI symptoms unresponsive to standard IBS therapy, negative IBD/celiac workup, distinctive histology showing CD117+/tryptase+ cells with aberrant CD25+ in both GI and marrow, and markedly elevated serum tryptase—is highly specific for SM. The indolent presentation and absence of cytopenias or constitutional symptoms favor indolent SM over aggressive variants. GI mast cell infiltration explains the entire 2.5-year symptom complex.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 58-year-old man has systemic mastocytosis (SM) with bone marrow and gastrointestinal involvement.

The diagnosis is established by WHO 2022 criteria. The patient meets one major criterion and multiple minor criteria:

MAJOR CRITERION: The bone marrow biopsy (F25, F26) revealed multifocal compact aggregates of mast cells confirmed by immunohistochemistry co-expressing tryptase, CD2, and CD25 (F27). This multifocal dense bone marrow aggregation is the hallmark major WHO diagnostic criterion for SM (R1).

MINOR CRITERIA MET:
1. Aberrant antigen co-expression: CD25 and CD2 aberrant co-expression detected on bone marrow mast cells (F27) satisfies the minor criterion for abnormal immunophenotype (R2). CD25 expression alone is particularly specific for SM (R22).

2. KIT mutation: Activating KIT codon-816 point mutation identified in bone marrow (F28) represents a somatic mutation present in >90% of adult SM patients (R3). This fulfills the KIT D816V minor criterion (R5).

3. Elevated baseline serum tryptase: Serum tryptase markedly elevated at >180 ng/mL (F24), well above the 20 ng/mL minor criterion threshold (R4) and correlating with substantial mast cell burden (R4).

The diagnosis meets the WHO rule: 1 major criterion (bone marrow aggregates) + ≥1 minor criterion (actually 3 minor criteria present: KIT mutation, aberrant CD25/CD2, elevated tryptase) = systemic mastocytosis established (R5).

GASTROINTESTINAL INVOLVEMENT explains the 2.5-year history of chronic diarrhea (F2, F3), postprandial upper abdominal fullness (F4), and crampy abdominal discomfort (F5). Diarrhea occurs in up to 80% of SM patients (R6) and results from mast cell mediator release (histamine and PGD2) causing increased water/chloride secretion and augmented bowel motility (R16). The colonic biopsy (F19, F20) showed a dense diffuse infiltrate of round-to-spindled cells expanding the lamina propria (F20), characteristic of SM GI involvement (R10).

WHY DIAGNOSIS WAS DELAYED: The prior 5 endoscopic procedures (F7, F8) showed macroscopically normal or non-specific findings (F9), and earlier biopsies were negative for inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and microscopic colitis (F10, F11). This diagnostic odyssey illustrates three critical gaps: (a) absence of immunohistochemical staining (tryptase/CD117) on prior biopsies, per R14; (b) limited biopsy sampling strategy that may have missed focal SM infiltration (R13); and (c) low clinical suspicion due to SM rarity. Crucially, per R12, ~40% of involved colonic biopsies show no endoscopic abnormalities, yet immunohistochemistry reveals infiltration. The patient was falsely anchored to a diarrhea-predominant IBS diagnosis (F14) despite failure of multiple IBS-directed therapies (antispasmodics, loperamide, low-FODMAP, bile-acid sequestrants; F15). Per R9, therapeutic failure of these agents should have raised suspicion for organic pathology including SM. The case exemplifies R21: diagnostic delay is characteristic of SM due to rarity, symptom mimicry of common GI disorders, absence of immunohistochemical staining on prior biopsies, and normal endoscopic appearance masking microscopic disease.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: The KIT D816V mutation causes constitutive ligand-independent activation of KIT tyrosine kinase (R15), driving uncontrolled mast cell proliferation, survival, and mediator release, producing both the bone marrow aggregates and the chronic GI symptoms. Mast cell infiltration in the lamina propria releases histamine, tryptase, and prostaglandins, accounting for the patient's diarrhea, cramping, and postprandial discomfort (R16).

PROGNOSTIC CONSIDERATION: Bone marrow involvement with KIT D816V and aberrant CD2/CD25 co-expression (F27, F28) raises concern for more aggressive disease compared to cutaneous-only or indolent presentations (R19). However, the absence of documented systemic symptoms (anaphylaxis, flushing, pruritus are not mentioned) and the 2.5-year indolent course suggest this may be bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM), a subvariant of indolent SM with bone marrow involvement but often without skin lesions (R20). Further stratification (quantification of bone marrow involvement, expanded molecular profiling for TET2/ASXL1 mutations, risk scoring) is needed to confirm indolent vs. aggressive subtype.

UNCERTAINTY FLAGGED: Rule R18 notes that elevated baseline tryptase must be interpreted cautiously and is insufficient alone for diagnosis. However, in this case the markedly elevated tryptase (F24, >180 ng/mL) is corroborated by the major criterion (bone marrow aggregates) and two additional minor criteria (KIT mutation, aberrant antigen expression), rendering the tryptase result interpretable within the diagnostic constellation rather than a standalone finding.
per_case.framework_top: Systemic Mastocytosis (SM) with bone marrow and gastrointestinal involvement, meeting WHO diagnostic criteria
per_case.framework_next_step: Complete diagnostic subtyping and risk stratification: (1) confirm absence of skin lesions (rule out urticaria pigmentosa); (2) quantify bone marrow involvement (percentage of marrow cellularity replaced by aggregates); (3) expand molecular profiling to detect other SM-associated mutations (PDGFRA, TET2, ASXL1) and assess allele burden of KIT D816V; (4) perform flow cytometry on bone marrow to confirm aberrant mast cell immunophenotype; (5) establish baseline serum tryptase and determine prognosis category (indolent vs. aggressive SM); (6) initiate targeted management (imatinib or midostaurin) after risk assessment and discuss monitoring protocol.

Postprandial upper abdominal fullness and crampy discomfort are consistent with systemic mastocytosis GI involvement
Colonic biopsy shows dense diffuse infiltrate of round-to-spindled cells expanding lamina propria, characteristic of SM GI involvement

Prior diagnostic delay (2.5 years) was due to: (a) absence of immunohistochemical staining on prior biopsies, (b) focal SM infiltration missed by limited sampling, (c) normal endoscopic appearance despite microscopic disease, and (d) false anchoring to IBS diagnosis
Failure of multiple IBS-directed therapies (antispasmodics, loperamide, low-FODMAP, bile-acid sequestrants) should have raised suspicion for organic pathology including systemic mastocytosis
KIT D816V mutation causes constitutive activation of KIT tyrosine kinase, driving uncontrolled mast cell proliferation and mediator release
Bone marrow involvement with KIT D816V and aberrant CD2/CD25 expression raises concern for more aggressive disease phenotype, though indolent bone marrow mastocytosis subtype remains possible
Negative celiac serology does not exclude systemic mastocytosis; serology is relevant only to celiac disease, not to ruling in/out SM

per_case.rationale: Both outputs reach the correct final diagnosis (systemic mastocytosis with bone marrow + GI involvement, long misattributed to IBS-D) and correctly cite the confirming evidence: dense mast cell infiltrates positive for tryptase/CD117 with aberrant CD2/CD25 in both GI mucosa and marrow, markedly elevated serum tryptase, and KIT D816V. Both also capture the central reasoning lesson—refractory IBS-D with negative IBD/celiac/microscopic-colitis workup should not be left as a functional label. A is more rigorous and defensible: it maps findings to WHO major/minor criteria with explicit finding/rule references (traceable), correctly frames the diagnostic-delay mechanism (missing IHC, sampling, normal endoscopy), and—importantly for calibration—flags subtype (BMM/indolent) as needing further stratification rather than asserting it, and explicitly notes the 'tryptase alone is insufficient' caveat. B is more actionable: it gives a clean disposition (confirm, risk-stratify, treat, monitor) and mentions tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which aligns with the actual midostaurin treatment better than A (A gives no disposition/treatment). However, B over-commits by labeling KIT D816V 'pathognomonic' (it is the major molecular criterion / >90% prevalence, not strictly pathognomonic) and by asserting a definitive 'indolent type' classification that the ground truth does not establish, while stating 95% confidence—weaker calibration than A. Neither names midostaurin or notes persistent clonal cells post-treatment. Net: both are substantively correct with no significant hallucination; A wins on traceability and calibration, B wins on disposition. A's edge in rigor and calibrated uncertainty outweighs B's actionability advantage in a judging context that prizes defensible, verifiable reasoning.

per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old man was referred to a regional surgical service after roughly ten weeks of worsening right-sided lower abdominal pain. He worked outdoors as an irrigation-canal laborer and had previously been healthy, on no regular medications. Over the preceding months he had lost approximately 13 kg, with reduced appetite, intermittent low-grade fevers, and persistent constipation. On examination he was thin and febrile, with a tender, firm, ill-defined mass palpable in the right iliac fossa. There was no lymphadenopathy and no skin lesions.

Initial bloodwork showed a hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL and a total white cell count of 16,400 cells/uL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was markedly elevated at 138 mm/h. Routine liver and renal chemistry, electrolytes, and amylase were within normal limits. Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen demonstrated a bulky, partly obstructing soft-tissue mass in the right iliac fossa measuring about 9 x 7 x 6 cm, encasing adjacent small-bowel loops and appearing distinct from the ascending colon. The radiological appearance was reported as concerning for an obstructing colonic neoplasm.

Because of the obstructing mass and suspicion of malignancy, the patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy. At operation a hard, ulcerated inflammatory mass involving the cecum and terminal ileum was found. A limited right-sided resection with appendicectomy and primary anastomosis was performed. His pain and obstructive symptoms resolved quickly after surgery and he was discharged. Histological examination of the resected specimen was initially interpreted as showing chronic mucosal and transmural inflammation favoring inflammatory bowel disease, with a possibility of an eosinophil-rich colitis, and explicitly no evidence of carcinoma.

About six weeks later he returned with recurrence of the right lower quadrant mass, now accompanied by watery diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Repeat laboratory studies were notable for a strikingly high absolute eosinophil count of approximately 29,000 cells/uL, with the total white cell count again elevated and a persistently high sedimentation rate. Upper endoscopy showed several small superficial duodenal ulcers, and examination of the anastomotic region revealed multiple shallow ulcerations. Stool studies for ova and parasites were unrevealing. He had not received corticosteroids or immunosuppressive agents. Given the recurrence and the prominent eosinophilia, the surgical and pathology teams undertook a careful re-examination of the original resection material.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis (invasive subcutaneous-zygomycosis-class fungal infection caused by the environmental fungus Basidiobolus ranarum / Entomophthorales), presenting as an inflammatory abdominal mass mimicking colonic malignancy and then inflammatory bowel disease / eosinophilic colitis.

HOW CONFIRMED: Histopathology. The resected bowel mass showed mixed suppurative and granulomatous inflammation with a dense eosinophilic infiltrate and characteristic broad, thin-walled fungal hyphae surrounded by eosinophilic amorphous material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) on re-review of the original tissue blocks at the referral center. (Tissue culture, the formal gold standard, was not obtained.) The marked peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophils ~32,000/uL) and very high ESR (129 mm/h) supported the fungal-eosinophilic diagnosis after initial slides were misread as IBD/eosinophilic colitis and the CT mass was initially called malignant.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT a malignancy and NOT inflammatory bowel disease — do not treat with surgery-alone or with immunosuppression/steroids (which would worsen a fungal infection). Correct management is prolonged systemic azole antifungal therapy. In the source case: surgical resection of the obstructing mass plus ~10 months of oral azole antifungals (itraconazole ~400 mg/day, later switched to voriconazole for tolerability). Outcome: symptom-free with no recurrence at 3-year follow-up. Key teaching point: an immunocompetent agricultural/outdoor worker from an arid or tropical region with an RLQ inflammatory mass, striking peripheral eosinophilia, and tissue eosinophilic granulomas should prompt consideration of GI basidiobolomycosis, with antifungals rather than immunosuppression.

ORIGINAL CASE (held aside): 29 y/o Omani male road-construction truck driver, Sultan Qaboos University Hospital, Oman. RLQ painful mass, fever, anorexia, constipation, 10 kg weight loss x2 months; CT 8 x 8.4 x 6.3 cm mass involving ileal loops looked malignant; cecectomy + appendectomy done; slides read as IBD/eosinophilic colitis; recurred at 5 weeks with diarrhea/nausea/vomiting; Hb 10.3 g/dL, WBC 18,000/uL, eos 32,000/uL, ESR 129 mm/h; duodenal + anastomotic ulcers on endoscopy; re-review of blocks revealed Basidiobolus hyphae with Splendore-Hoeppli; treated with voriconazole then itraconazole 400 mg/day then voriconazole, ~10 months total, plus small-bowel resection; well at 3 years.

rulebook.rule: Occupational exposure to irrigation water (as canal laborer) raises risk of parasitic infection (Strongyloides, Ascaris, Ancylostoma) in differential diagnosis of eosinophilic GI disease.
rulebook.source: CDC Wastewater Irrigation & Helminth Infection (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5140065/) — farmers exposed to irrigation water 3x more likely infected with Ascaris and hookworm

rulebook.rule: Absolute eosinophil count ≥29,000 cells/µL (severe hypereosinophilia, >5,000/µL threshold) raises differential of parasitic infection, particularly nematodes in endemic-exposure patient.
rulebook.source: CDC Yellow Book Post-Travel Parasitic Disease (https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-parasitic-disease.html) & PubMed case series: eosinophilia ≥5,000/µL classified as severe; Strongyloides case with 11,466/µL reported (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3932278/)

rulebook.rule: Transmural inflammation (muscularis mucosa and deeper layers) with mucosal preservation and eosinophil-predominant infiltrate raises eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease (EGID).
rulebook.source: PMC3152953 Eosinophilic Colitis review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3152953/) — transmural disease associated with bowel-wall thickening, obstruction; diagnostic threshold ≥20 eosinophils/HPF in colonic biopsies

rulebook.rule: Isolated cecal and terminal ileal involvement with transmural inflammation and ulceration raises Crohn disease or infectious ileocolitis in differential; eosinophilic colitis involvement less common than mucosal/proximal.
rulebook.bears_on: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn) vs parasitic infection
rulebook.source: PMC3152953 Eosinophilic Colitis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3152953/) — cecal wall thickening in 71% of EC cases; terminal ileal thickening in 29%. Also standard IBD literature: Crohn commonly affects ileum and cecum with transmural disease

rulebook.rule: Multiple shallow ulcerations at anastomotic site PLUS duodenal ulcers (multifocal) raises parasitic infection (Strongyloides with mature and larval migration) over primary EGID or IBD.
rulebook.source: PMC3932278 Strongyloidiasis case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3932278/) & CDC Strongyloides Overview (https://www.cdc.gov/strongyloides/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html) — transmural eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation affecting colonic wall; extensive duodenojejunal ulceration noted in severe cases

rulebook.rule: Visualization of parasitic larvae, ova, or adult forms in duodenal/colonic tissue biopsies is pathognomonic and definitively distinguishes parasitic infection from primary EGID or IBD.
rulebook.source: PMC5775510 EGID Pathology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775510/) — 'the only etiology that can be identified histologically is parasitic infestation, if a portion of an invasive parasite is found in mucosal biopsies'; PMC3932278 strongyloides case: duodenal biopsy revealed 'parasitic ova and adult worms suggestive of S. stercoralis'

rulebook.rule: Negative stool ova and parasite test does NOT exclude parasitic infection; eosinophilia may precede adult worm maturation; low sensitivity (52.4%) of Kato-Katz technique; Strongyloides stool tests commonly negative, requiring serology or tissue diagnosis.
rulebook.source: CDC Yellow Book (https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-parasitic-disease.html) — 'stool ova and parasite tests are commonly negative, and serology is needed for diagnosis'; CDC guidelines note Kato-Katz sensitivity only 52.4%; also CDC Intestinal Parasite Guidelines (https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/26248/cdc_26248_DS1.pdf) state minimum two specimens needed

rulebook.rule: Duodenal aspiration and biopsy are more sensitive than stool examination for Strongyloides diagnosis and may reveal larvae, adult worms, or ova in mucosal crypts when stool tests negative.
rulebook.source: CDC Strongyloides Clinical Overview (https://www.cdc.gov/strongyloides/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html) — duodenal aspirate and biopsy listed as diagnostic methods more sensitive than stool; histopathology papers (PubMed 16622487, 17149952) describe larvae and worms in Lieberkuhn crypts and duodenal mucosa

rulebook.rule: Dense eosinophil sheets and eosinophil-predominant inflammation (vs. mixed acute/chronic inflammatory infiltrate) raises primary EGID; acute inflammatory cells with lymphocytes/neutrophils favors IBD.
rulebook.source: PMC5775510 EGID Pathology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775510/) — distinguishes IBD (acute inflammatory cells with chronic changes; lacks dense eosinophil sheets) from allergic/eosinophilic colitis (greater IgE/tryptase co-localization)

rulebook.rule: Recurrence 6 weeks post-resection raises incomplete parasitic treatment (residual infection not recognized/treated) or inadequately resected parasitic involvement; infectious etiologies recur if source not addressed.
rulebook.source: PMC7734700 Strongyloides case 'Rare Cause of Acute Abdomen' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7734700/) discusses recurrent symptoms when parasitic infection not diagnosed; standard treatment is ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily × 2 days with repeat stool exam in 2–4 weeks for parasite clearance verification

rulebook.rule: Serologic testing (antibody detection) is indicated when clinical suspicion for Strongyloides remains high despite negative stool examination; serologies detect active and past infection but cannot distinguish acute from chronic.
rulebook.source: CDC Yellow Book (https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-parasitic-disease.html) — recommends serology for diagnosis when stool tests inconclusive; CDC Strongyloides Overview notes cross-reactivity with other parasites and inability to distinguish active vs. past

rulebook.rule: Colonic biopsies with ≥20 eosinophils per high-power field meet diagnostic threshold for eosinophilic colitis; diagnosis of exclusion requiring exclusion of parasitic infection, drug reaction, and systemic disease.
rulebook.source: PMC3152953 Eosinophilic Colitis Review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3152953/) — diagnostic threshold ≥20 eosinophils/HPF in colonic biopsies; emphasis that EC is 'diagnosis of exclusion' with multiple mimics

rulebook.rule: Transmural eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation with granulomas and giant cells (vs. simple eosinophilic infiltration) raises Strongyloides hyperinfection or severe parasitic burden.
rulebook.source: CDC Strongyloides Overview (https://www.cdc.gov/strongyloides/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html) — severe cases show 'characteristic transmural eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation affecting mostly the colonic wall...eosinophilic granulomatous enterocolitis with formation of granulomas'

rulebook.rule: Villous atrophy (Grade 4 in most cases) and severe duodenitis (57% of cases) on duodenal histology raises Strongyloides infection; degree of villous destruction correlates with endoscopic findings.
rulebook.source: PubMed 16622487 & 17149952 Strongyloides histopathology — villous atrophy found in all cases (most Grade 4), severe duodenitis in 57%; eosinophil infiltration intensity correlates with infection intensity

rulebook.rule: Initial pathology reporting dual differential (IBD vs. eosinophil-rich colitis) without parasitic assessment raises risk of missed parasitic diagnosis; re-examination with parasitic stains essential if clinical picture evolves.
rulebook.source: Case presentation IR uncertainty unc-initial-histology-divergence and pinworm misdiagnosis literature (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11530421/) — 'parasitic infections are frequently responsible for intestinal wall eosinophilia, hampering establishment of diagnosis of primary EGID; pinworm infection often ignored'

rulebook.rule: Significant weight loss (13 kg), anemia (Hgb 9.6), and constitutional symptoms (low-grade fever) support chronic inflammation; parasitic burden (particularly hookworm causing blood loss) contributes to anemia.
rulebook.bears_on: Parasitic infection (particularly blood-loss parasites) and eosinophilic/inflammatory disease
rulebook.source: CDC Immigrant Refugee Health — Intestinal Parasites (https://www.cdc.gov/immigrant-refugee-health/hcp/domestic-guidance/intestinal-parasites.html) — hookworm causes anemia particularly in young/pregnant; CDC Yellow Book notes parasites cause malabsorption and weight loss

rulebook.rule: Palpable firm mass with partial obstruction and ileal/cecal location raises transmural inflammation (EGID, Crohn, parasitic) with wall thickening; eosinophilic colitis causes 71% cecal thickening in imaging studies.
rulebook.bears_on: Eosinophilic colitis or parasitic transmural disease
rulebook.source: PMC3152953 Eosinophilic Colitis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3152953/) — cross-sectional imaging findings: colonic wall thickening, predominantly cecal (71%), terminal ileal (29%); strictures and mucosal fold thickening noted

rulebook.rule: Quick symptom resolution post-resection without identification of underlying etiology (no cancer, negative stool parasite studies) raises concern for unrecognized parasitic infection incompletely resected or residual systemic parasitic burden.
rulebook.source: Surgical management of strictures and infectious disease literature; case reports of strongyloides presenting with recurrence post-surgical resection when parasitic diagnosis missed

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated ESR (138 mm/h) and leukocytosis (16,400 cells/µL) support active inflammation; present in both infectious and primary inflammatory conditions; not specific for parasitic vs. EGID vs. IBD.
rulebook.source: Standard pathophysiology: both parasitic infection and EGID/IBD cause systemic inflammatory response; ESR and WBC elevation nonspecific

rulebook.rule: Parasites missed on initial histology due to: (1) inadequate parasitic staining, (2) low parasite density at initial biopsy, (3) guideline emphasis on other conditions, (4) stool tests falsely reassuring but insensitive, (5) histologic similarity of parasitic and IBD inflammation.
rulebook.source: PMC11530421 Pinworm misdiagnosis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11530421/) — scotch-tape test only 50% sensitive single-day (90% with multiple days); stool tests unreliable for pinworm; CDC Yellow Book notes ova not shed early in Strongyloides infection

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Parasitic infection causing eosinophilic transmural inflammation—most consistent with Echinococcosis or Amebiasis given the recurrent mass, marked eosinophilia (~29,000 cells/uL), transmural involvement, and failure of surgical resection alone. Outdoor laborer with likely freshwater/environmental exposure, plus the clinical team's decision to re-examine histology (implying parasitic organisms were identified), supports a helminthic etiology.

Recommended next action: (1) Careful re-review of original resection material using special histologic stains (PAS, Gram, Giemsa, polarized light microscopy) to identify parasitic organisms; (2) Serologic testing for common parasites (Echinococcus, Entamoeba, Schistosoma, Ascaris, Toxoplasma); (3) Repeat stool studies with concentration methods; (4) Imaging to assess current mass; (5) Initiate antihelmintic therapy based on serology and re-histology findings.

Confidence: 65-70%. The recurrent mass + marked eosinophilia + transmural eosinophilic inflammation + failure of surgery alone strongly points to parasitic disease, but without seeing the revised histology, the exact organism cannot be definitively determined. The case structure (team re-examining original material) suggests the diagnosis hinges on parasitic identification in the specimen.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The patient presents with a clinical picture highly suggestive of parasitic infection (specifically Strongyloides stercoralis) rather than primary inflammatory bowel disease or primary eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease. 

The key evidence supporting parasitic infection:

1. **Occupational and epidemiologic risk**: The patient is an irrigation-canal laborer (occupation-fact-id: occupation), which raises risk of parasitic infection including nematodes (rule-01-occupational-water-exposure). This occupational exposure in a likely endemic setting is a critical epidemiologic marker.

2. **Severe eosinophilia is a major diagnostic clue**: The absolute eosinophil count of approximately 29,000 cells/µL (eosinophil-count) is classified as severe hypereosinophilia, well above the 5,000/µL threshold (rule-02-severe-eosinophilia-threshold). This degree of eosinophilia in a patient with occupational water exposure is a strong signal for parasitic nematode infection, particularly Strongyloides.

3. **Multifocal ulceration pattern suggests Strongyloides migration**: The patient has ulcerations at two distinct sites: duodenal ulcers (upper-endo-finding) AND multiple shallow ulcerations at the anastomotic region in the terminal ileum/cecum (anastomotic-ulcers). This multifocal pattern is characteristic of Strongyloides infection, where larvae migrate through the submucosa and mature worms migrate between anatomic sites (rule-05-multifocal-ulceration). In contrast, primary EGID typically presents with more focal or segmental involvement.

4. **Transmural inflammation with eosinophilia is compatible with parasitic disease**: The initial histology showed chronic mucosal and transmural inflammation (initial-histology) and mention of eosinophil-rich colitis as a differential. Transmural inflammation with eosinophil infiltration is described in rule-03-transmural-inflammation-mucosal as raising eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease, but crucially, rule-13-transmural-strongyloides indicates that transmural eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation with granulomas raises the likelihood of Strongyloides hyperinfection or severe parasitic burden.

5. **Negative stool studies do NOT exclude parasitic infection**: Although stool studies for ova and parasites were unrevealing (stool-studies), rule-07-negative-stool-ova-parasite explicitly states that negative stool tests do NOT exclude parasitic infection. Strongyloides in particular shows low sensitivity on stool examination (Kato-Katz sensitivity only 52.4%), and eosinophilia may precede adult worm maturation. The rule emphasizes that tissue diagnosis or serology is required.

6. **Rapid recurrence post-resection indicates incomplete eradication of the underlying etiology**: The patient experienced symptom resolution immediately after surgery (postop-immediate), but recurrence occurred at approximately 6 weeks (recurrence-timing) with return of the mass and GI symptoms (recurrence-gi-symptoms). Rule-10-rapid-recurrence-6weeks indicates that recurrence 6 weeks post-resection raises the likelihood of incomplete parasitic treatment or recognition—that is, residual parasitic infection was not identified at the time of initial resection and therefore not treated. If the diagnosis had been cancer or primary IBD, surgical resection would have aimed for curative intent; recurrence this rapid suggests a systemic parasitic burden that was not addressed.

7. **Persistent laboratory evidence of systemic inflammation**: At recurrence, the patient again showed elevated WBC (recurrence-wbc), elevated ESR (recurrence-esr), and the striking eosinophilia (eosinophil-count), all compatible with active parasitic infection.

8. **Initial diagnostic miss is explained by rule-15 and rule-20**: The initial pathology report contained a dual differential (rule-15-initial-histology-divergent-differential) favoring IBD with eosinophil-rich colitis as a possibility, but did not assess for parasitic infection. Rule-20-misdiagnosis-mechanism-parasites-ignored outlines how parasites are missed: inadequate parasitic staining, low parasite density at initial biopsy (parasites may not be uniformly distributed), guideline emphasis on other conditions, and the histologic similarity between parasitic and IBD inflammation. The stool tests, though negative, were falsely reassuring because of their low sensitivity (rule-07-negative-stool-ova-parasite).

**Why the diagnosis was initially missed:**

The pathology team did not use targeted parasitic stains on the resection material. The dual differential (IBD vs. eosinophil-rich colitis) anchored interpretation toward primary inflammatory or allergic disease rather than parasitic mimics. The negative stool ova and parasite study (stool-studies), while insensitive for Strongyloides, may have created false reassurance. The cecal and terminal ileal location, while compatible with both Crohn disease and parasitic disease (rule-04-cecal-terminal-ileal-location), was interpreted in the context of IBD differential rather than parasitic infection.

**Recommended diagnostic confirmation:**

Rule-06-parasite-identification-tissue states that visualization of parasitic larvae, ova, or adult forms in tissue biopsies is pathognomonic and definitively distinguishes parasitic infection. This is the gold standard. The re-examination of the original resection material using parasitic-specific stains is essential (rule-15-initial-histology-divergent-differential). Additionally, rule-08-duodenal-aspiration-biopsy-parasites indicates that duodenal aspiration and biopsy are more sensitive than stool examination for Strongyloides and may reveal larvae or worms in mucosal crypts when stool tests are negative. Rule-11-serology-strongyloides recommends serologic testing when stool tests are inconclusive.

**Conclusion:**

The patient almost certainly has parasitic infection (Strongyloides stercoralis), not primary inflammatory bowel disease or primary eosinophilic colitis. The occupational exposure, severe eosinophilia, multifocal ulceration pattern, transmural inflammation, negative but insensitive stool studies, rapid recurrence after surgical resection (indicating residual parasitic burden), and the initial pathology team's lack of parasitic assessment all converge on a parasitic diagnosis that was missed at the time of initial evaluation. Careful re-examination of the resection material with parasitic stains, duodenal aspiration and biopsy, and serologic testing are essential next steps to confirm the diagnosis and guide definitive treatment with antiparasitic therapy.
per_case.framework_top: Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection or severe parasitic infection (nematode) of the small and large bowel with incomplete initial recognition.
per_case.framework_next_step: Perform duodenal aspiration and biopsy with histopathologic examination for parasitic larvae, ova, and adult forms; obtain serologic testing (ELISA or immunofluorescence) for Strongyloides-specific antibodies; carefully re-examine original resection material using parasitic stains (PAS, trichrome) for larvae or ova in crypts and transmural locations; if parasites identified, initiate ivermectin treatment (200 µg/kg daily × 2 days) with repeat parasitologic assessment in 2–4 weeks.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (80–85%). The constellation of occupational water exposure, striking eosinophilia at a severe threshold, multifocal ulceration pattern (duodenal + anastomotic), rapid recurrence despite surgical resection, and negative stool studies that do not exclude parasitic infection all align with parasitic etiology. However, confidence is not absolute because (1) the original pathology re-examination findings have not been disclosed in the case, and (2) duodenal aspiration and tissue parasitic stains have not yet been performed—both would be gold-standard confirmatory tests.

per_case.rationale: Ground truth is GI basidiobolomycosis (a FUNGAL infection, Basidiobolus/Entomophthorales), confirmed by histopathology re-review showing broad fungal hyphae with Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, treated with prolonged azole antifungals — explicitly NOT immunosuppression and not surgery alone. Both outputs MISS the fungal diagnosis and instead diagnose PARASITIC infection (A: Echinococcosis/Amebiasis; B: Strongyloides), so both are wrong on the organism class and on definitive treatment (antiparasitics vs. antifungals). Both correctly reject malignancy and IBD/eosinophilic colitis, correctly frame it as an infectious mimic, and correctly identify histologic re-review of the original blocks (with special stains) plus serology as the confirmation route. The deciding factor is calibration and defensibility. Output A hedges at 65-70% confidence, offers a differential, and explicitly states the exact organism cannot be determined without revised histology — appropriately uncertain given it landed in the wrong organism class. Output B asserts the patient 'almost certainly' has Strongyloides with near-certainty, which is badly miscalibrated for a wrong answer, and it pushes a specific (incorrect) antiparasitic/hyperinfection treatment path. B also fabricates an elaborate scaffold of ~20 numbered 'rules' and invented specifics (e.g., Kato-Katz 52.4% sensitivity, 'irrigation-canal laborer') that create a false veneer of rigor and add hallucination risk without improving correctness. Both are incorrect on the core diagnosis; A's lower, hedged confidence and cleaner reasoning make it the more defensible response.

per_case.prose:
A 71-year-old retired schoolteacher was referred to the dermatology clinic with a roughly five-month history of a red, warm, swollen left lower leg. She felt systemically well throughout — no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss — and her routine bloods, including inflammatory markers, had remained unremarkable on repeated checks.

The problem had first been treated by her primary physician as an infection. Over the preceding months she had been given several separate courses of antibiotics, both oral and intravenous, on the assumption of recurrent cellulitis. None produced lasting improvement. Because she had longstanding signs of chronic venous insufficiency — including brownish hemosiderin staining over both shins — attention then shifted to a venous cause, and she was started on emollients and compression for presumed venous eczema/stasis dermatitis.

On examination there was erythema and edema over the medial and anterior aspect of the left lower leg. The affected skin had an unusually firm, almost woody texture on palpation rather than the soft pitting edema expected from simple stasis change. Hemosiderin discoloration was present over both lower limbs. Pulses were intact and there was no ulceration.

She returned earlier than her scheduled follow-up because, over the course of about a week, several lumps in the left calf had enlarged noticeably, distributed in a band running around the circumference of the limb. Cross-sectional imaging of the leg was arranged, which showed multiple soft-tissue nodules within the subcutaneous fat and the underlying muscle, the largest measuring approximately 8 cm. A tissue sample was taken from one of the masses.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type (PCDLBCL-LT), with secondary nodal involvement (Ann Arbor stage IV). HOW CONFIRMED: Core needle biopsy of the leg mass showed partly necrotic high-grade B-cell lymphoma; immunohistochemistry was CD20+, PAX5+, BCL6+, MUM1+, BCL2+ and c-Myc+, with a high MIB-1/Ki-67 proliferation index of 60-80%. MRI demonstrated multiple soft-tissue nodules in subcutaneous tissue and muscle (largest ~9 cm). CORRECT DISPOSITION: Refer urgently for tissue biopsy + staging rather than continuing antibiotics/venous-eczema care; oncology/haematology referral; treat with R-CHOP-type immunochemotherapy (6 cycles; gemcitabine substituted for doxorubicin in final cycle due to anthracycline cap) plus radiotherapy to the leg — achieved complete metabolic response. KEY TEACHING POINT: A chronic, antibiotic-refractory 'cellulitis' / 'venous eczema' with woody induration and rapidly enlarging nodules in an elderly patient must prompt biopsy to exclude cutaneous lymphoma. Source: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma-leg type masquerading as venous eczema, PMC11763905.
