rulebook.rule: Unilateral lower-limb edema (vs. bilateral) raises likelihood of local structural/neoplastic cause rather than systemic venous insufficiency
rulebook.source: Unilateral Leg Swelling: A Clinician's Differential Diagnosis (Heartcare Sydney) — notes unilateral swelling suggests local factors; Cellulitis: StatPearls notes cellulitis 'often noted in one leg'; Hemosiderin Staining (United Vein Centers) notes 'presence of hemosiderin staining in bilateral lower limbs suggests venous insufficiency is affecting both legs'

rulebook.rule: Five-month chronic course before rapid 1-week acceleration of nodule growth raises suspicion for malignancy (sarcoma or lymphoma) rather than acute infection
rulebook.source: Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Medscape/StatPearls) — 'After an interval of 1-30 years, a purplish patch appears...developing into a plaque or nodule'; Soft Tissue Sarcoma (AAFP) — 'rapidly growing nodule...should prompt further workup'; Stewart-Treves Syndrome (JAAD) — 'small satellite areas can develop and become confluent, forming an enlarging lesion'

rulebook.rule: Failure of multiple antibiotic courses (oral and IV) to produce lasting improvement lowers likelihood of bacterial infection (cellulitis)
rulebook.source: Recurrent Cellulitis: Who is at Risk (PMC 9379124) — '18% failure rate with initial antibiotic treatment; reported rates vary 6-37%, due in part to wrongful inclusion of cellulitis mimickers'; Cellulitis: Practice Essentials (StatPearls) — 'when antibiotic treatment fails or recurrence occurs, underlying risk factors should be reassessed...non-infectious causes should be considered'

rulebook.rule: Antibiotic failure despite multiple courses (cephalexin, IV agents) strongly raises likelihood of non-infectious mimicker (malignancy, rheumatologic condition)
rulebook.source: Primary Cutaneous DLBCL Leg Type (PMC 8177962) — 'lesions suspected as cellulitis that receive multiple courses of different antibiotics (such as cephalexin, Augmentin, and levofloxacin) without improvement, but rather progression'; Angiosarcoma Clinical Presentation (Medscape) — 'low grade infection was suspected and antibiotics were started, but there was no clinical response to the antibiotics'

rulebook.rule: Firm, woody texture of skin (vs. soft pitting edema) raises likelihood of fibrosis from chronic lymphedema, liposarcoma, or malignancy
rulebook.source: Stasis Dermatitis (PMC 9968263) — 'Thick, woody texture (called lipodermatosclerosis) develops in severe chronic venous insufficiency'; Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa (DermNet) — clinical features include 'Woody or mossy textured skin'; Liposarcoma StatPearls — dedifferentiated liposarcomas show 'complex and inhomogeneous' appearance with 'small fatty components'

rulebook.rule: Unremarkable inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) despite 5-month course and significant tissue pathology lowers likelihood of acute bacterial infection (cellulitis)
rulebook.source: Cellulitis & Inflammatory Markers (Annals of Dermatology 2016) — 'Procalcitonin, WBC, and CRP showed positive correlation with body temperature in cellulitis patients'; ESR/CRP in Acute Inflammation (Taming the SRU) — acute inflammatory markers CRP and ESR are 'elevated in cellulitis'; in contrast, NXP-2 Dermatomyositis (PMC 12769389) — case with unilateral leg edema showed 'CRP, ESR, C3, C4 all within normal ranges' despite severe disease

rulebook.rule: Absence of systemic constitutional symptoms (no fevers, night sweats, weight loss) and unremarkable labs lowers likelihood of lymphoma or systemic inflammatory disease
rulebook.source: Primary Cutaneous DLBCL Leg Type (PMC 7301429) — PCDLBCL-LT is 'very aggressive' but case reports document those presenting without systemic symptoms; Lymphangiosarcoma (Without a Ribbon) — rapid progression occurs; however, absence of constitutional symptoms does not exclude malignancy in cutaneous-only disease

rulebook.rule: Circum­ferential distribution of nodules around limb (band-like pattern) raises likelihood of lymphedema-related pathology (ENV, lymphangiosarcoma) or sarcoma
rulebook.source: Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa (PMC 3470531 and DermNet) — ENV presents with 'cobblestone-like nodules...on body parts with gravity-dependent blood flow'; gravity and circumferential pattern suggest dependent lymphatic obstruction

rulebook.rule: Multiple large soft-tissue nodules (up to 8 cm) within subcutaneous fat and muscle raises likelihood of liposarcoma, sarcoma, or lymphoma
rulebook.source: Soft Tissue Sarcoma (AAFP) — 'Masses that are...5 cm in diameter or larger, grow rapidly...should prompt further workup'; Liposarcoma of Lower Extremity (Applied Radiology) — well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas present as multiple nodular masses; Stewart-Treves Syndrome (StatPearls) — lesions described as 'multiple reddish blue macules or nodules that may become polypoid'

rulebook.rule: Presence of imaging-documented nodules within muscle (not just subcutaneous fat) raises concern for higher-grade malignancy (dedifferentiated liposarcoma, angiosarcoma, myogenic sarcoma)
rulebook.source: MRI Liposarcoma Characteristics (PMC 11107907) — dedifferentiated liposarcomas 'show clear boundary between fat and non-fat solid tissue'; solid muscle involvement suggests higher-grade tumor

rulebook.rule: Bilateral hemosiderin staining (over both shins) with unilateral acute edema/nodules suggests underlying bilateral venous insufficiency but localized acute pathology (not purely venous in origin)
rulebook.source: Hemosiderin Staining & Venous Insufficiency (United Vein Centers) — 'presence of hemosiderin staining in bilateral lower limbs suggests venous insufficiency is affecting both legs'; Distinguishing Cellulitis from Mimics (MDedge) — 'You can differentiate venous stasis dermatitis from cellulitis by its chronic, usually bilateral presence. Cellulitis is often noted in one leg'

rulebook.rule: Longstanding chronic venous insufficiency (hemosiderin, skin changes) raises baseline risk for ENV and secondary lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves-like syndrome)
rulebook.source: Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa (DermNet/PMC) — ENV 'results from conditions that impair lymphatic drainage, including...deep vein thrombosis, prior surgery, radiation therapy'; Stewart-Treves Syndrome (StatPearls) — 'Although it most commonly refers to malignancies associated with chronic lymphedema resulting from mastectomy and/or radiotherapy for breast cancer, it may also describe lymphangiosarcomas that result from congenital and other causes of chronic secondary lymphedema'

rulebook.rule: Intact pulses and absence of significant clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis lowers likelihood of acute venous obstruction as primary cause
rulebook.source: Unilateral Leg Swelling Differential (Heartcare Sydney) — 'Most unilateral edema is usually caused by local factors such as deep vein thrombosis, venous insufficiency, or lymphedema'; intact pulses exclude vascular emergency

rulebook.rule: Dermatology referral for nodular erythema + edema that failed antibiotics raises index of suspicion for cutaneous malignancy (PCBCL-LT, angiosarcoma) over simple infection
rulebook.source: Primary Cutaneous DLBCL Leg Type (Multiple PMC sources) — PCDLBCL-LT 'typically manifests as rapidly enlarging nodules...most commonly affecting elderly women in the seventh decade of life'; 'Lesions suspected as cellulitis that receive multiple courses of different antibiotics...without improvement, but rather progression'

rulebook.rule: Rapid growth of lesions over ~1 week (vs. slow 5-month course prior) raises likelihood of acute decompensation of chronic process (transition to malignancy) or acute phase of inflammatory/neoplastic disease
rulebook.source: Stewart-Treves Syndrome (StatPearls) — 'After an interval of 1-30 years, a purplish patch appears...The lesions of Stewart-Treves syndrome typically appear as multiple reddish blue macules or nodules that may become polypoid...around these nodules, small satellite areas can develop and become confluent, forming an enlarging lesion'

rulebook.rule: Absence of ulceration in early/nodular phase (no breaks in skin) lowers suspicion for secondary infection or necrotizing process
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma Clinical Presentation (Medscape) — 'The classical manifestation is characterized by an erythematous plaque which expands rapidly...forming blue-black nodules that often ulcerate' (ulceration is late sign); ENV typically develops ulcerations as disease progresses (DermNet)

rulebook.rule: Age 71 (elderly) with no history of mastectomy or radiation but longstanding venous disease raises risk for non-Stewart-Treves-related causes of subcutaneous sarcoma (primary soft-tissue sarcoma, liposarcoma)
rulebook.source: Liposarcoma of Lower Extremity (Applied Radiology) — liposarcoma 'most common in adults between the ages of 20 and 60' and in elderly; well-differentiated and dedifferentiated subtypes present at different ages; Soft Tissue Sarcoma (AAFP) — 'rapidly growing or presenting suddenly without explanation should prompt further workup'

rulebook.rule: Very firm (woody) palpable texture distinguishes fibrotic/sarcomatous process from soft pitting edema of simple venous stasis
rulebook.source: Stasis Dermatitis vs. Fibrosis (PMC 9968263) — 'thick, woody texture (called lipodermatosclerosis) develops in severe chronic venous insufficiency. Lipodermatosclerosis presents as a well-demarcated, woody, erythematous induration'; Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa features include 'woody or mossy textured skin' from pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and extensive fibrous tissue hyperplasia

rulebook.rule: MRI/imaging with fat-suppression showing enhancement of nodular/septal components raises likelihood of high-grade sarcoma (dedifferentiated liposarcoma) vs. well-differentiated or benign lipoma
rulebook.source: MRI Liposarcoma (PMC 11107907) — 'Dedifferentiated liposarcomas show small fatty components with a clear boundary between fat and non-fat solid tissue...DD has greater proportion of non-fatty components, with more complex and inhomogeneous MRI signals, and typically shows significant enhancement'

rulebook.rule: Histology showing pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia + dilated lymphatic channels + fibrous tissue hyperplasia supports diagnosis of ENV (vs. malignancy)
rulebook.source: Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa (Search results across multiple sources: DermNet, PMC articles) — 'Characteristic histological findings include pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, dilated lymphatic channels, widened tissue spaces, and extensive fibrous tissue hyperplasia within the dermis, subcutaneous tissue, and lymphatic vessel walls'

rulebook.rule: Histology showing atypical spindle-shaped endothelial cells forming vascular clefts supports diagnosis of lymphangiosarcoma (vs. benign lymphedema)
rulebook.source: Lymphangiosarcoma Histology (ScienceDirect) — 'Histologically, the tumor consists of vascular cavities lined with spindle-shaped endothelial cells with large nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Lymphangiosarcomas are characterized by a poorly defined proliferation of spindle-shaped endothelial cells forming vascular clefts or cavernous spaces. A key diagnostic feature distinguishing lymphangiosarcoma from hemangiosarcoma is the relative absence of erythrocytes within the abnormal vascular channels'

rulebook.rule: Histology showing atypical plump endothelial cells with CD31/CD34 positivity supports diagnosis of angiosarcoma
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma Clinical Presentation & Pathology (Medscape/PMC 5705372) — 'Histopathologic examination shows vascular proliferation lined by atypical and plump endothelial cells in the dermis; immunohistochemistry shows positivity of neoplastic endothelial cells for CD31 and CD34'

rulebook.rule: Histology showing diffuse monomorphous atypical lymphoid cells (CD20+, CD79a+, CD5–, CD3–) supports diagnosis of primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma leg type (PCBCL-LT)
rulebook.source: Primary Cutaneous DLBCL Leg Type (PMC 7301429 and 8177962) — 'Diagnosis is mainly determined by skin biopsy that shows diffuse distribution of atypical lymphoid cells showing positivity for markers of CD20+, CD79a+ and negative for CD5 and CD3'

rulebook.rule: Histology showing lipomatous tissue with thick septa, nodularity, and non-lipomatous solid components raises likelihood of well-differentiated or dedifferentiated liposarcoma
rulebook.source: Liposarcoma MRI Features (Applied Radiology & PMC 11107907) — 'well-differentiated liposarcomas typically demonstrated a very specific diagnostic appearance as a predominantly adipose mass containing nonlipomatous components seen as thick septa that may show nodularity'

rulebook.rule: Bilateral hemosiderin staining with unilateral acute erythema-edema suggests local acute process superimposed on chronic bilateral venous disease
rulebook.source: Stasis Dermatitis (PMC 9968263) — 'Stasis dermatitis is generally bilateral, has been ongoing for years...Cellulitis is often noted in one leg...It is not uncommon for patients with chronic stasis dermatitis to also develop cellulitis'

rulebook.rule: Erythema and edema localized to medial/anterior leg (not diffuse) lowers suspicion for purely systemic disease (e.g., simple congestive heart failure-related edema)
rulebook.source: Soft Tissue Sarcoma (AAFP) — 'Masses that are deep to the fascia, are 5 cm in diameter or larger, grow rapidly...localization affects differential; localized presentation suggests local pathology rather than systemic edema'

rulebook.rule: No documented fever or systemic signs during antibiotic courses lowers likelihood of acute bacterial cellulitis (which typically presents with systemic toxicity)
rulebook.source: Cellulitis StatPearls & Medscape — cellulitis is 'accompanied by other signs of infection, including fever, chills, and bright red skin with increased warmth'; absence of fever and systemic signs makes cellulitis unlikely as primary diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Normal CRP/ESR with markedly elevated muscle enzymes (CK 9x ULN, aldolase 3x ULN) raises suspicion for myositis/dermatomyositis (vs. infection or simple lymphedema)
rulebook.source: NXP-2 Dermatomyositis Unilateral Leg Edema (PMC 12769389) — case of unilateral leg edema showed 'CRP, ESR, C3, C4, and CA125 all fell within normal ranges. However, muscle enzymes were elevated—serum creatine kinase and aldolase were 9x and 3x the upper limits of normal, respectively'

rulebook.rule: Unilateral subcutaneous edema (without typical dermatomyositis rash features documented) lowers likelihood of classic dermatomyositis
rulebook.source: NXP-2 Dermatomyositis (PMC 12769389) — 'Unilateral extremity swelling is notably rare, with the article noting only 6 previously reported cases...This atypical presentation initially caused diagnostic confusion, leading to misdiagnoses of cellulitis and erythema multiforme'

rulebook.rule: Circumferential distribution pattern of nodules (band around limb) + fibrosis + chronic course suggests lymphedema-related progressive fibrosis (ENV) rather than acute localized cellulitis
rulebook.source: Elephantiasis Nostras Verrucosa (PMC 3479949, DermNet) — ENV develops in 'gravity-dependent' areas with circumferential presentation; 'Nonpitting edema and superimposed verrucose, cobblestone-like nodules on body parts with gravity-dependent blood flow are characteristic of ENV'

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Soft-tissue sarcoma (liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, or leiomyosarcoma) with secondary consideration for primary cutaneous lymphoma or sarcoidosis.

Recommended next action: Review pathology from the tissue biopsy; if malignancy confirmed, obtain MRI of the entire leg for margin assessment and staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis. If non-malignant, pursue sarcoid/lymphoproliferative workup based on histology.

Confidence: 70-75% for malignancy (based on clinical presentation); final diagnosis pending histology.

Brief reasoning: The presentation initially mimics infection/venous disease but the key red flags are the firm "woody" texture (not soft pitting edema), multiple deep subcutaneous and muscular nodules arranged in a band pattern, largest 8 cm, and indolent progression over months in a systemically well patient with normal inflammatory markers. This constellation is far more consistent with indolent soft-tissue malignancy than with infection or simple venous insufficiency.
per_case.framework_conclusion: This patient presents with a unilateral lower-limb edema and subcutaneous nodules that initially mimicked cellulitis but failed multiple antibiotic courses (F7, R3, R4), strongly lowering the likelihood of bacterial infection. Unremarkable inflammatory markers on repeated checks despite a 5-month clinical course (F5, R6) further reduce suspicion for acute infection (R27). The clinical presentation is dominated by a striking pattern: a five-month indolent course followed by rapid acceleration of nodule growth over one week (F2, F16, R2, R15), with imaging showing multiple large soft-tissue nodules (up to 8 cm) infiltrating both subcutaneous fat and underlying muscle (F18, F19, R9, R10). The woody, firm texture of the affected skin (F12, R5, R18) distinguishes this from soft pitting edema of simple venous stasis. The patient's age (71 years, F1) without a history of mastectomy or radiation (R17) supports a primary soft-tissue sarcoma rather than Stewart-Treves syndrome. The circumferential distribution of masses around the limb (F17, R8, R30) and the presence of longstanding bilateral hemosiderin staining (F8, F13, R11, R12) indicate chronic venous insufficiency as a predisposing background, raising risk for lymphedema-related malignancy including lymphangiosarcoma; however, the documented muscle involvement (F18, R10) suggests higher-grade malignancy, favoring dedifferentiated liposarcoma or lymphangiosarcoma over benign elephantiasis nostras verrucosa (which would show characteristic histology of pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and dilated lymphatics—R20). The dermatology referral for antibiotic-refractory nodular erythema also raises suspicion for cutaneous malignancy (R14). The absence of systemic constitutional symptoms (F4, R7) does not exclude cutaneous malignancy, as primary cutaneous sarcomas can present with localized disease. The definitive diagnosis requires histopathological analysis of the biopsy specimen (F20, U9, Q1), which will determine whether the lesion shows features of dedifferentiated liposarcoma (R24: lipomatous tissue with thick septa and non-lipomatous solid components), lymphangiosarcoma (R21: atypical spindle-shaped endothelial cells forming vascular clefts), or angiosarcoma (R22: atypical plump endothelial cells with CD31/CD34 positivity). Once histology is obtained, staging imaging and oncologic consultation are essential to establish grade, margins, and appropriateness for surgical resection versus neoadjuvant therapy.
per_case.framework_top: Soft-tissue sarcoma of the left lower leg, most likely dedifferentiated liposarcoma or lymphangiosarcoma, with secondary fibrotic changes superimposed on chronic bilateral venous insufficiency.
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent histopathological examination of the tissue biopsy (F20) including H&E, immunohistochemistry (CD31/CD34, CD20/CD79a, lipid markers), mitotic index, and necrosis assessment to determine exact tumor type and grade. Simultaneously arrange staging imaging (chest/abdomen CT) and oncology consultation for surgical planning and adjuvant therapy discussion.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high (70-75%). The clinical pattern (five-month slow course with abrupt 1-week acceleration, antibiotic failure despite multiple courses, large muscle-infiltrating nodules in an elderly patient, unremarkable inflammatory markers, circumferential distribution) strongly supports malignancy. However, definitive diagnosis hinges on the histology results (F20, U9), which are not provided. The muscle involvement (F18) and age (F1) favor sarcoma over ENV or PCBCL-LT, but without histology, some uncertainty remains.

per_case.rationale: Ground truth is primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type, with the correct disposition being urgent biopsy + staging (stop antibiotics) and the teaching point that antibiotic-refractory woody "cellulitis"/"venous eczema" with enlarging nodules in an elderly patient must prompt biopsy to exclude cutaneous lymphoma. Both outputs correctly converge on the disposition (biopsy + staging imaging + oncology referral) and correctly reframe the case away from infection/venous disease using the right red flags (woody induration, deep subcutaneous/muscle nodules, normal inflammatory markers, indolent course). Neither names PCDLBCL-LT exactly. The decisive difference is the differential and calibration. Output A commits hard to soft-tissue sarcoma (dedifferentiated liposarcoma, lymphangiosarcoma, angiosarcoma), explicitly favoring sarcoma and building detailed sarcoma-specific histology (CD31/CD34, spindle cells, lipomatous septa) that points away from the correct answer; lymphoma appears only obliquely as "cutaneous malignancy." It is long, overconfident, and anchored on the wrong entity. Output B also leads with sarcoma (incorrect) but explicitly names "primary cutaneous lymphoma" as a secondary consideration and calls for a lymphoproliferative workup, partially matching ground truth, while staying well-calibrated (70-75% malignancy, final dx pending histology). B captures the actual answer within its named differential and is more defensible and better calibrated; A's confident traceable reasoning leads to the wrong place and omits lymphoma as a real contender.

per_case.prose:
A 31-year-old woman was referred to a hospital dermatology clinic in a temperate-climate city for evaluation of a long-standing skin lesion on her left posterior thigh. She had emigrated several years earlier from a region where tuberculosis is endemic and recalled receiving a BCG vaccination in childhood. As a teenager she had had a small comparable nodule near her left ear that was excised at a local clinic in her country of origin; she could not recall the pathology result.

She reported that the thigh lesion had first appeared as a small reddish papule roughly five years ago, around the time of an illness, and had slowly but relentlessly enlarged ever since. Over that period she had been seen by two prior clinicians, each of whom diagnosed psoriasis. She had been treated for a prolonged period with high-potency topical corticosteroids and a keratolytic (salicylic-acid) preparation, without meaningful improvement; if anything the plaque continued to spread outward.

On examination she was well-appearing and afebrile, with normal vital signs. She denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, cough, and fatigue. The lesion was a single large, well-demarcated, reddish-brown scaly plaque with raised firm borders and central atrophy and scarring occupying much of the left posterior thigh. The plaque was warm and tender, and gentle pressure expressed a small amount of purulent material through several fissures and sinus-like openings on its surface. There was no regional or generalized lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. The remainder of the skin examination, including nails and scalp, was unremarkable.

Routine laboratory studies were largely unremarkable: white-cell count 7.4 x10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelets 268 x10^9/L. HIV serology was negative. An interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) was positive. A chest radiograph showed no active or prior parenchymal disease, and three induced-sputum specimens were negative on smear and subsequent mycobacterial workup.

A punch biopsy of the plaque margin was performed. Histopathology demonstrated pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the epidermis with intraepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses, overlying a dermal infiltrate that was mixed neutrophilic and granulomatous in character. Special staining of the tissue for acid-fast organisms revealed rare elongated acid-fast bacilli within the infiltrate. Tissue was submitted for further microbiological characterization.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Cutaneous tuberculosis (a paucibacillary chronic form, consistent with lupus vulgaris / tuberculosis verrucosa cutis), i.e. cutaneous infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis — NOT psoriasis, for which the patient had been treated unsuccessfully for years.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Skin biopsy histopathology showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with intraepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses plus a mixed neutrophilic and granulomatous dermal infiltrate; (2) acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining of tissue revealed rare/sparse acid-fast bacilli; (3) DEFINITIVE: mycobacterial CULTURE of the biopsy grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis (gold-standard organism isolation); (4) supportive: positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold (IGRA), consistent with TB infection. Systemic workup (sputum cultures negative, chest X-ray with no active pulmonary disease) showed disease was limited to the skin.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Stop ineffective topical steroid/keratolytic 'psoriasis' therapy. Start standard multidrug antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol — RIPE regimen). Outcome: lesion cleared by ~3 months on anti-TB therapy and the patient remained disease-free, confirming the diagnosis ex juvantibus as well. Key teaching point: a steroid-refractory chronic plaque with central atrophy, sinus/fissure discharge, granulomatous histology, and prior TB exposure/endemic origin should prompt AFB stain + mycobacterial culture rather than continued treatment for psoriasis.

rulebook.rule: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) detected on special staining of skin tissue raises suspicion for Mycobacterium tuberculosis cutaneous disease (including TB verrucosa, primary inoculation TB, scrofuloderma, or disseminated TB with cutaneous manifestation)
rulebook.bears_on: Mycobacterium tuberculosis cutaneous TB (vs. nontuberculous mycobacterium infection)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NIH/NCBI: AFB staining (Ziehl-Neelsen, Auramine-rhodamine) is foundational for detecting mycobacterial infection; sensitivity and specificity vary by TB form and bacillary load

rulebook.rule: Rare elongated acid-fast bacilli (as opposed to numerous bacilli) lowers likelihood of nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) multibacillary infection; NTM cutaneous infections often show variable or absent AFB on histology despite positive culture
rulebook.source: Epidemiology and clinical outcomes in skin and soft tissue nontuberculous mycobacteria infections: A retrospective study, ScienceDirect: Histopathology in NTM cutaneous infections showed variable or absent AFB despite confirmed culture

rulebook.rule: Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of epidermis with intraepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses raises suspicion for Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (TVC) or primary inoculation tuberculosis
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: A Practical Case Report and Review, PMC (JCAD): TVC characteristically shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis and microabscesses of neutrophils in papillary dermis

rulebook.rule: Mixed neutrophilic and granulomatous dermal infiltrate raises suspicion for cutaneous tuberculosis (across multiple forms including TVC, primary inoculation TB, or lupus vulgaris)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NIH/NCBI: Characteristic histology shows granulomas (caseating or non-caseating epithelioid granulomas) with surrounding mixed inflammation

rulebook.rule: Central atrophy and scarring within a chronic expanding plaque raises suspicion for tuberculosis verrucosa cutis or lupus vulgaris (chronic endogenous forms with reactivation immunity)
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis or Lupus vulgaris (cutaneous TB)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: A Practical Case Report and Review for the Dermatologist, PMC: TVC presents as 'painless, solitary, purplish or brownish-red warty plaque' with 'central atrophy or fissures'; lupus vulgaris shows 'apple-jelly nodules' with 'spontaneous healing with scarring and atrophy at the center'

rulebook.rule: Slow but relentless enlargement of skin lesion over years (5+ years) raises suspicion for cutaneous tuberculosis (particularly TB verrucosa or lupus vulgaris), which progress insidiously unlike acute bacterial or fungal infections
rulebook.bears_on: Mycobacterium tuberculosis cutaneous TB (verrucosa or lupus vulgaris)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: epidemiological, clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic update, PMC: TB verrucosa 'represents 3-19% of CTB cases, presenting as a verrucous plaque...diagnosis often occurs years after injury due to slow, asymptomatic growth'

rulebook.rule: Warm, tender plaque with purulent drainage through fissures and sinus-like openings raises suspicion for active cutaneous tuberculosis (consistent with TB verrucosa, scrofuloderma, or primary inoculation TB)
rulebook.source: Surgeon's Dilemma in Skin Manifestations of Tuberculosis, European Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine: Cutaneous TB manifests as warm, tender lesions with expression of purulent material through fissures and potential sinus tract formation

rulebook.rule: History of similar nodule/lesion in same person (years prior, in endemic region) raises suspicion that current lesion represents reactivation, relapse, or reinfection with TB rather than a new primary infection
rulebook.bears_on: Cutaneous TB (reactivation vs. relapse vs. reinfection rather than primary inoculation)
rulebook.source: Insights into Recurrent Tuberculosis: Relapse Versus Reinfection and Related Risk Factors, IntechOpen: 'TB recurrence can be due to either reactivation of the same strain...or reinfection with a new strain...recurrence due to reinfection has become an area of intense study in TB endemic settings'

rulebook.rule: Emigration from TB-endemic region raises pre-test probability for tuberculosis disease (active or latent), increasing likelihood of TB reactivation or new cutaneous manifestation
rulebook.source: Reinfection as a central constraint on tuberculosis vaccine development, Frontiers: In high endemic areas, approximately 10% of TB patients undergo recurrence, either due to reinfection or relapse

rulebook.rule: BCG vaccination in childhood combined with TB disease in adulthood raises suspicion for vaccine failure (primary or waning immunity) or reinfection exposure in endemic region
rulebook.bears_on: Mycobacterium tuberculosis TB (but suggests vaccine-escape or reinfection mechanism)
rulebook.source: The BCG vaccine, advantages, and disadvantages of introducing new generation vaccines, PMC: 'BCG is not protective against adult TB in endemic areas, and a major drawback of BCG is its variable efficacy (ranging from nil to 80%) against adult TB. Additionally, BCG-induced protection is short-lived'

rulebook.rule: Positive interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) raises suspicion for M. tuberculosis infection (either active TB or latent TB infection); particularly diagnostic utility in paucibacillary cutaneous TB where AFB staining and culture may be negative
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis Presenting as a Chronic Dermatologic Disorder, PMC: 'IGRA diagnostic utility in paucibacillary forms of cutaneous TB; strongly positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold test (>5 IU/mL) guided appropriate clinical suspicion despite negative culture and PCR'

rulebook.rule: Positive IGRA alone cannot distinguish between active TB disease and latent TB infection (LTBI); integration with clinical presentation, tissue findings, and systemic symptoms is required for diagnosis of active cutaneous TB
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis Presenting as a Chronic Dermatologic Disorder, PMC: 'IGRAs cannot accurately distinguish between latent and active TB infections' and WHO does not recommend IGRAs alone for diagnosis of active TB in low/middle-income countries

rulebook.rule: Negative sputum smear and culture from induced specimens, combined with normal chest radiograph, lowers likelihood of active pulmonary TB; consistent with cutaneous TB limited to skin or disseminated TB in early stage without pulmonary shedding
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: epidemiological, clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic update, PMC: Cutaneous TB can present as sputum-negative disease; paucibacillary forms often show negative culture and PCR results due to sparse mycobacteria

rulebook.rule: Sputum-negative status combined with AFB-positive tissue biopsy and positive IGRA is consistent with cutaneous TB (primary inoculation type or verrucosa) without active pulmonary involvement
rulebook.source: Understanding cutaneous tuberculosis: two clinical cases, PMC: Cutaneous TB is 'an unusual manifestation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, accounting for only 1.0-1.5% of cases' but sputum-negative cutaneous disease is well-documented

rulebook.rule: Absence of regional lymphadenopathy and negative systemic symptoms (no fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough) lowers likelihood of disseminated/miliary TB or active scrofuloderma with lymph node involvement; more consistent with cutaneous TB limited to skin
rulebook.bears_on: Disseminated tuberculosis or miliary TB (hematogenous form)
rulebook.source: Disseminated miliary tuberculosis with cutaneous involvement, PMC: Miliary TB 'commonly presents with nonspecific symptoms of weight loss, headache, easy fatigability, cough, hepatosplenomegaly, and fever' and 'cutaneous involvement in miliary TB presents as crops of minute papules...in a patient who is obviously ill'

rulebook.rule: Patient well-appearing and afebrile with normal vital signs lowers likelihood of acute miliary TB or severe disseminated disease; more consistent with indolent cutaneous TB (primary inoculation or verrucosa) or sputum-negative latent/paucibacillary disease
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis | Microbiology Spectrum: Cutaneous miliary TB 'is usually reported in children, HIV and immunocompromised patients' and presents in 'obviously ill' patients with systemic symptoms, contrasting with localized cutaneous TB

rulebook.rule: Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with mixed granulomatous/neutrophilic infiltrate but rare AFB and absence of extensive caseous necrosis raises suspicion specifically for TB verrucosa cutis (paucibacillary form) rather than primary inoculation TB or lupus vulgaris
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (vs. other cutaneous TB forms)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: A Practical Case Report and Review, PMC: TVC shows 'pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with noncaseating tuberculous granulomata, characteristically without visible mycobacteria' whereas primary inoculation TB shows 'suppurative infiltrate of neutrophils' with possible 'dermal necrosis' and AFB typically positive

rulebook.rule: Reddish-brown scaly plaque with firm raised borders, slowly enlarging over years, raises suspicion for TB verrucosa or lupus vulgaris (endogenous cutaneous TB forms in persons with prior TB exposure and immunity)
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis or Lupus vulgaris
rulebook.source: Cutaneous tuberculosis: epidemiological, clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic update, PMC: TVC presents as 'reddish or brownish-red warty plaque' with 'slow, asymptomatic growth' occurring over years; lupus vulgaris shows 'small reddish-brown nodules with gelatinous consistency'

rulebook.rule: History of water exposure (freshwater or saltwater, occupational as fisher or aquarium worker) raises suspicion for Mycobacterium marinum cutaneous infection; absence of reported water exposure history lowers this suspicion
rulebook.source: Mycobacterium marinum Cutaneous Infection: A Series of Three Cases and Literature Review, PMC: M. marinum 'resides in fresh or salt water (in tropical or temperate areas); it is a fish and human pathogen' transmitted through water exposure

rulebook.rule: No documented water exposure history lowers likelihood of Mycobacterium marinum as causative organism, though does not exclude other nontuberculous mycobacteria
rulebook.source: Slow-growing and Linearly Spreading Cutaneous Lesion: Often Misdiagnosed Mycobacterium Marinum Infection, PMC: M. marinum infection typically follows water exposure; epidemiological context is diagnostic clue

rulebook.rule: Single large well-demarcated plaque lowers likelihood of cutaneous miliary TB; miliary cutaneous TB typically presents as crops of multiple small papules, pustules, or vesicles distributed across body
rulebook.source: Disseminated miliary tuberculosis with cutaneous involvement in a patient with HIV, PMC: Cutaneous miliary TB 'presents as crops of minute bluish papules, vesicles, pustules, or hemorrhagic lesions' affecting substantial body areas, not solitary large lesions

rulebook.rule: Verrucous (warty) surface with scale and fissures containing purulent material is consistent with TB verrucosa cutis (TVC), which characteristically has warty appearance and may drain seropurulent material
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: A Practical Case Report and Review, PMC: TVC presents as 'warty plaque' with 'fissures exuding purulent material'; the 'verrucosa' designation refers to the warty morphology

rulebook.rule: Prior misdiagnosis as psoriasis (by two independent clinicians) and treatment with topical corticosteroids without improvement raises suspicion that diagnosis is incorrect and cutaneous TB should be reconsidered (TB can mimic inflammatory dermatoses)
rulebook.bears_on: Mycobacterium tuberculosis cutaneous TB (diagnostic bias alert)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis Presenting as a Chronic Dermatologic Disorder, PMC: 'Cutaneous TB is often misdiagnosed, particularly when it mimics other dermatological conditions' including eczematous dermatitis and psoriasis

rulebook.rule: Lack of improvement or worsening with high-potency topical corticosteroid therapy lowers likelihood of inflammatory dermatoses (psoriasis, eczema) and raises suspicion for infectious etiology (TB, fungal, mycobacterial)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis Presenting as a Chronic Dermatologic Disorder, PMC: Corticosteroid resistance is a red flag for infectious etiologies including TB

rulebook.rule: Pending culture results and molecular identification (species of AFB detected, drug susceptibility testing) means the differential between M. tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterium remains open; final diagnosis requires species-level identification
rulebook.bears_on: M. tuberculosis vs. nontuberculous mycobacterium (species identification)
rulebook.source: Detection and Differentiation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Isolates by Real-Time PCR, PMC: Molecular and culture-based methods (16S rRNA PCR, NAAT, Xpert MTB/RIF, PNA-FISH) are required for species-level differentiation

rulebook.rule: Positive culture or molecular identification (PCR, Xpert MTB/RIF) of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in tissue specimen confirms diagnosis of tuberculosis (cutaneous or disseminated); rules out nontuberculous mycobacterium
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NIH/NCBI: Culture and nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) confirm diagnosis of TB; Xpert MTB/RIF is WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic test

rulebook.rule: Identification of nontuberculous mycobacterium species (M. marinum, M. avium, M. fortuitum, etc.) on culture or molecular testing rules out M. tuberculosis and requires NTM-specific treatment regimen
rulebook.source: Epidemiology and clinical outcomes in skin and soft tissue nontuberculous mycobacteria infections: A retrospective study, ScienceDirect: NTM species identification via culture and PCR is essential for guiding appropriate NTM-specific therapy

rulebook.rule: Drug susceptibility testing showing resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin (or broader resistance) in M. tuberculosis isolate indicates multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) requiring alternative second-line regimen (fluoroquinolone, bedaquiline, linezolid, etc.)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous tuberculosis: epidemiological, clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic update, PMC: Treatment is 'WHO-recommended regimen: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for two months (intensive phase) followed by four months maintenance therapy' but requires adaptation for MDR-TB

rulebook.rule: In cases of diagnostic uncertainty (IGRA+ but sputum-, cutaneous lesion, no systemic symptoms), dramatic clinical response to anti-TB therapy within 4 weeks can be considered valuable diagnostic criterion for active TB, supporting diagnosis over latent TB infection
rulebook.bears_on: Active tuberculosis vs. latent TB infection
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis Presenting as a Chronic Dermatologic Disorder, PMC: 'In cases of strong clinical suspicion but doubtful laboratory tests, dramatic response to antituberculosis therapy after 4 weeks can be considered a valuable diagnostic criteria'

rulebook.rule: Absence of extensive caseous necrosis and predominance of microabscesses with mixed inflammation lowers likelihood of primary inoculation TB (which typically shows suppurative infiltrate with possible dermal necrosis); more consistent with TB verrucosa or lupus vulgaris
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis - StatPearls, NIH/NCBI: Primary inoculation TB shows 'suppurative infiltrate of neutrophils with possible dermal necrosis; granulomas may develop later' whereas TVC shows 'noncaseating tuberculous granulomata' with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia

rulebook.rule: Painless or low-pain lesion is consistent with most forms of cutaneous TB (TB verrucosa, lupus vulgaris, primary inoculation TB), which tend to be indolent; does not narrow differential between cutaneous TB forms
rulebook.source: Cutaneous Tuberculosis: A Practical Case Report and Review, PMC: TB verrucosa described as 'painless, solitary' and primary inoculation TB 'remaining painless' whereas scrofuloderma and lupus vulgaris also painless or minimally painful

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Tuberculosis Verrucosa Cutis (cutaneous tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis)

Reasoning: Acid-fast bacilli on histology + positive IGRA + chronic progressive verrucous plaque with drainage/sinuses + pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia + history from TB-endemic region = classic TVC. The rarity of organisms and prior similar excised lesion support this diagnosis. Prior misdiagnosis as psoriasis is typical for this entity.

Recommended next action: (1) Confirm species on culture/molecular testing of tissue; (2) obtain drug-susceptibility testing; (3) initiate standard 4-drug anti-TB therapy (RIPE) once TB confirmed; (4) assess close contacts for latent TB.

Confidence: 85-90% (histologic acid-fast bacilli + IGRA + clinical morphology are highly specific; awaiting culture confirmation).
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient most likely has active cutaneous tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, specifically TB verrucosa cutis (TVC).

EVIDENCE FOR MYCOBACTERIAL DISEASE:
Acid-fast bacilli (rare elongated organisms) were detected on special staining of skin tissue, which raises suspicion for M. tuberculosis cutaneous disease (fact: stain_afb; rule: r_afb_positive_raises_mtb). The interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) was positive, raising suspicion for M. tuberculosis infection (fact: lab_igra; rule: r_igra_positive_raises_tb). The dermal infiltrate was mixed neutrophilic and granulomatous in character, consistent with cutaneous tuberculosis (fact: histo_dermal; rule: r_mixed_granulomatous_dermal_raises_ctb).

EVIDENCE FAVORING M. TUBERCULOSIS OVER NONTUBERCULOUS MYCOBACTERIUM:
The AFB present were rare (not numerous), which lowers likelihood of nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) multibacillary infection, as NTM cutaneous infections typically show variable or absent AFB despite positive culture (fact: stain_afb; rule: r_rare_afb_lowers_ntm). There is no documented water exposure history in this case, which lowers likelihood of Mycobacterium marinum specifically (fact: lesion_site; rule: r_negative_marinum_lowers_ntm_marinum). The patient emigrated from a TB-endemic region, which raises the pre-test probability for TB disease (fact: dem_emigration; rule: r_emigration_endemic_region_raises_tb). Overall, the pattern favors M. tuberculosis, though species identification remains pending.

EVIDENCE FOR CUTANEOUS TB (SPECIFICALLY TB VERRUCOSA CUTIS) RATHER THAN OTHER FORMS:
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the epidermis with intraepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses raises suspicion for TB verrucosa cutis or primary inoculation TB (fact: histo_epidermis, histo_microabscesses; rule: r_pseudoepitheliomatous_hyperplasia_raises_tbv). The plaque has central atrophy and scarring within a chronic expanding lesion, which raises suspicion for TB verrucosa or lupus vulgaris (fact: lesion_morphology; rule: r_central_atrophy_scarring_raises_tbv_lupus). The lesion is a reddish-brown scaly plaque with firm raised borders, slowly enlarging over 5 years, consistent with TB verrucosa or lupus vulgaris (facts: lesion_morphology, lesion_course; rule: r_reddish_brown_plaque_slowly_enlarging_raises_tbv_lupus). The plaque is warm and tender with purulent drainage through fissures and sinus-like openings, consistent with active cutaneous TB (fact: lesion_warmth_tenderness, lesion_drainage; rule: r_warm_tender_drainage_raises_ctb). The verrucous surface with fissures containing purulent material is specifically consistent with TB verrucosa cutis morphology (fact: lesion_morphology; rule: r_verrucous_surface_scaly_tbv_probable). Critically, the rare AFB combined with absence of extensive caseous necrosis and presence only of microabscesses raises suspicion for TB verrucosa (the paucibacillary form) rather than primary inoculation TB, which typically shows suppurative infiltrate with possible dermal necrosis and AFB-positive findings (fact: histo_epidermis, histo_microabscesses, stain_afb; rule: r_pseudoepitheliomatous_no_caseous_necrosis_tbv). The single large well-demarcated plaque lowers likelihood of cutaneous miliary TB, which presents as crops of multiple small papules (fact: lesion_morphology; rule: r_single_large_plaque_lowers_miliary).

EVIDENCE AGAINST DISSEMINATED/MILIARY TB:
There is no regional or generalized lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly (fact: exam_lymph, exam_hsp; rule: r_no_lymphadenopathy_systemic_symptoms_lowers_disseminated). The patient is well-appearing and afebrile with normal vital signs, and denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, cough, and fatigue (facts: exam_general, exam_systemic_denials; rule: r_well_appearing_afebrile_lowers_miliary_disseminated). Three induced-sputum specimens were negative on both smear and mycobacterial culture, and the chest radiograph showed no active or prior parenchymal disease (facts: micro_sputum_specimens, micro_sputum_smear, micro_sputum_culture, img_cxr). Sputum negativity combined with AFB-positive tissue biopsy and positive IGRA is consistent with cutaneous TB limited to skin without active pulmonary involvement (fact: lab_igra, stain_afb, micro_sputum_smear, micro_sputum_culture; rule: r_sputum_negative_afb_positive_tissue_cutaneous_tb). The sputum-negative and normal CXR pattern lowers likelihood of active pulmonary TB (fact: micro_sputum_smear, micro_sputum_culture, img_cxr; rule: r_sputum_negative_cxr_clear_lowers_pulmonary_tb). Therefore, this appears to be cutaneous TB localized to skin, not disseminated disease.

EVIDENCE FOR ACTIVE DISEASE RATHER THAN LATENT TB INFECTION:
While a positive IGRA alone cannot distinguish between active TB disease and latent TB infection (rule: r_igra_positive_cannot_distinguish_active_latent), the clinical presentation strongly suggests active cutaneous TB. The tissue shows AFB-positive findings, the lesion exhibits active inflammatory signs (warmth, tenderness, purulent drainage), and the lesion has been continuously growing over 5 years (facts: stain_afb, lesion_warmth_tenderness, lesion_drainage, lesion_course). This pattern indicates active TB disease rather than merely latent infection.

CLINICAL CONTEXT AND DISEASE MECHANISM:
The patient has a prior history of a comparable nodule near her left ear, excised in her country of origin as a teenager, though the pathology result was not recalled (facts: hx_prior_lesion, hx_prior_lesion_pathology_unknown). The presence of this prior similar lesion raises suspicion that the current thigh lesion represents reactivation, relapse, or reinfection with TB rather than a new primary infection (fact: hx_prior_lesion; rule: r_prior_lesion_same_site_raises_recurrence). The patient received BCG vaccination in childhood, yet now presents with TB disease in adulthood, raising suspicion for vaccine failure (primary or waning immunity) or reinfection exposure in the endemic region (fact: hx_bcg; rule: r_bcg_vaccination_raises_tb_vaccine_failure). The lesion began approximately 5 years ago around the time of an illness episode (facts: lesion_onset_time, lesion_onset_association), though the nature of this illness is not documented. The prior treatment with high-potency topical corticosteroids and keratolytic agents was unsuccessful, which lowers likelihood of inflammatory dermatoses such as psoriasis and raises suspicion for infectious etiology (facts: prior_tx_corticosteroid, prior_tx_keratolytic, prior_tx_response; rule: r_no_response_corticosteroid_lowers_inflammatory_raises_infectious).

LIMITATIONS AND PENDING WORKUP:
Species identification of the acid-fast bacilli is pending; the differential between M. tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterium technically remains open until culture and molecular results are available (rule: r_species_identification_pending_differential_remains_open). However, the preponderance of clinical and epidemiologic evidence strongly favors M. tuberculosis. Once species is confirmed as M. tuberculosis, drug susceptibility testing must be obtained to guide appropriate therapy. If nontuberculous mycobacterium is identified instead, treatment will differ substantially. Clinical response to empiric anti-TB therapy within 4 weeks can serve as a valuable diagnostic criterion supporting active TB diagnosis in cases of strong clinical suspicion (rule: r_suspected_latent_active_clinical_response_differentiates).
per_case.framework_top: Active cutaneous tuberculosis, most likely TB verrucosa cutis (TVC), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The disease appears localized to skin without disseminated involvement and represents likely reactivation/relapse rather than primary inoculation.
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain pending culture and molecular identification (species-level PCR, Xpert MTB/RIF, or 16S rRNA) of the tissue-cultured organism to confirm M. tuberculosis vs. nontuberculous mycobacterium. Once species confirmed, obtain drug susceptibility testing. Initiate empiric anti-TB therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) while awaiting results; clinical response within 4 weeks will further support active TB diagnosis. Consider repeat chest imaging to rule out occult pulmonary TB if clinically indicated.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high (75-80%). The diagnosis is supported by strong clinical and histopathologic evidence (AFB-positive tissue, IGRA positivity, distinctive morphology, endemic exposure, and prior similar lesion history), but confidence is limited by pending species identification and the inability of IGRA alone to definitively distinguish active TB from latent TB infection.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: confirmed diagnosis is cutaneous tuberculosis (paucibacillary form, lupus vulgaris / TB verrucosa cutis) from M. tuberculosis, NOT psoriasis. Confirmation hinges on biopsy histology (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia + intraepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses + mixed neutrophilic/granulomatous dermal infiltrate), sparse AFB on Ziehl-Neelsen, definitive mycobacterial CULTURE growing M. tuberculosis, supportive positive IGRA, negative sputum/CXR (disease limited to skin), and disposition is to stop psoriasis therapy and start RIPE anti-TB therapy.

Both outputs reach the correct top-line diagnosis: cutaneous TB / TB verrucosa cutis from M. tuberculosis. Both correctly recommend culture/species confirmation, drug-susceptibility testing, and RIPE therapy — matching ground-truth disposition. Neither could state the culture result as confirmed (the case as presented leaves culture pending), so both appropriately flag culture as the pending gold-standard step, which is well-calibrated.

OUTPUT A is concise, accurate, well-calibrated (85-90%, awaiting culture), and hits every load-bearing point: AFB, IGRA, morphology, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, endemic origin, prior misdiagnosis as psoriasis, RIPE, contact tracing. No hallucinations. It is correct but minimal.

OUTPUT B reaches the same correct conclusion with far more granular, traceable reasoning: it explicitly maps each finding to the histology (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, intraepidermal microabscesses, mixed neutrophilic/granulomatous infiltrate), distinguishes paucibacillary TVC vs other forms, correctly reasons that sputum-negative + CXR-clear + AFB-positive tissue = skin-limited disease (matching ground truth's systemic workup), correctly infers psoriasis treatment failure points away from inflammatory dermatosis toward infection, and properly keeps NTM/species open pending culture. Its calibration is sound (favors M. tuberculosis but flags species pending). The rule-tag annotations are internal-system references, not external claims, and every clinical assertion is defensible and grounded in the case facts. I did not find hallucinated facts; the BCG vaccine-failure and recurrence reasoning are reasonable inferences, appropriately hedged.

Both are correct. B is the stronger answer on defensibility and traceability — it reconstructs the full diagnostic chain (including the skin-limited determination and the steroid-refractory-points-to-infection logic that is the ground truth's key teaching point) without overclaiming. A is correct but does not surface the systemic-workup reasoning or the explicit pivot away from psoriasis as a diagnostic clue. B wins on completeness and verifiable reasoning while matching A on correctness and calibration.

per_case.prose:
A 71-year-old retired man living in a rural farming district was referred to dermatology for a slowly enlarging, painful sore on his right forearm that he had first noticed about two months earlier. He recalled scratching the area on a thorny branch while pruning shrubs in his garden shortly before the lesion appeared. His only chronic medical problem was well-controlled high blood pressure, and he took no immunosuppressive medications. He felt generally well, with no fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or muscle aches.

On referral, the lesion was an indurated, erythematous plaque several centimeters across, studded with shallow ulcers that intermittently oozed serous fluid. His primary care physician had diagnosed bacterial cellulitis and had prescribed a course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate followed by a switch to intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam over roughly three weeks. Rather than improving, the plaque had continued to spread outward and the ulceration deepened.

On examination he was afebrile with normal vital signs. There was no regional lymphadenopathy and no other skin lesions. Examination of the chest, abdomen, and nervous system was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and unremarkable serum chemistries. C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 4.6 mg/dL. An HIV antibody test was negative. Serum beta-D-glucan was negative, and a serum assay for a circulating polysaccharide capsular antigen was also negative. A chest radiograph and CT of the thorax were normal, as were CT of the brain and examination of the cerebrospinal fluid.

Bacterial and fungal cultures were obtained from tissue, and an incisional skin biopsy was performed with routine histology plus special stains. Histopathology of the dermis demonstrated granulomatous inflammation composed of aggregated histiocytes and scattered multinucleated giant cells, within which numerous round, encapsulated intracytoplasmic yeast-like organisms were identified; these organisms stained strongly with Gomori methenamine silver and periodic acid–Schiff and were negative on acid-fast staining. Tissue culture subsequently grew an organism that was characterized further by sequencing of a ribosomal internal transcribed spacer region.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Primary cutaneous cryptococcosis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans (var. grubii) in an immunocompetent host, arising at a site of traumatic inoculation with plant/soil material. Key teaching point: cryptococcal skin infection occurring as a localized primary process WITHOUT immunosuppression and WITHOUT dissemination — initially mistaken for bacterial cellulitis.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Incisional skin biopsy showing granulomatous dermal inflammation (aggregated histiocytes + multinucleated giant cells) with multiple intracytoplasmic/encapsulated yeast forms highlighted on GMS and PAS special stains (acid-fast negative); (2) tissue fungal culture growing Cryptococcus, with species/variety confirmed by ITS (internal transcribed spacer) gene sequencing as C. neoformans var. grubii. Dissemination excluded: serum cryptococcal antigen negative, beta-D-glucan negative, HIV negative, CBC/serum chemistry unremarkable, chest radiograph + thoracic CT + brain CT + CSF examination all normal → confirming PRIMARY CUTANEOUS (localized) disease rather than secondary cutaneous spread of systemic cryptococcosis.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Stop antibiotics; treat as localized primary cutaneous cryptococcosis with systemic azole antifungal therapy (fluconazole), since even 'primary cutaneous' cryptococcosis is treated systemically and worked up to rule out occult dissemination. In original case: fluconazole 400 mg IV daily x4 days, then 200 mg daily x10 days, then oral 200 mg daily, later escalated to 400 mg daily x3 months; lesions resolved with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, no recurrence. Outpatient management after dissemination ruled out.

Original patient: 78-year-old woman, rural South Korea, hypertension only, sickle injury cutting grass, left forearm, 7-week course, failed cefoperazone/sulbactam x3 weeks, CRP 3.95 mg/dL.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical mycology / infectious diseases, with sub-domains: dermatology (lesion morphology, biopsy interpretation), epidemiology (geographic & environmental risk), and immunology (serology, response to antimicrobials)

rulebook.rule: Rural farming district in arid region (Southwest endemic) raises suspicion for soil-dwelling fungal pathogen with occupational exposure risk
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6787932/ — Coccidioidomycosis endemic to Southwest US (AZ, CA, NV, UT, NM, TX); farmers and soil-disturbing activities at high occupational risk

rulebook.rule: Traumatic inoculation via thorny branch scratch during gardening is classic transmission mechanism
rulebook.source: https://dermnetnz.org/topics/sporotrichosis — Sporothrix schenckii transmitted classically via rose thorns, plant material; primary infection route is cutaneous inoculation via thorns/barbs/scratches (rose gardener's disease)

rulebook.rule: Indurated erythematous plaque with shallow ulcers and serous exudate, progressive over 2 months, matches cutaneous dermatophytic and yeast infection presentation
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Cutaneous coccidioidomycosis presents with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and ulceration; https://dermnetnz.org/topics/blastomycosis — Blastomycosis cutaneous lesions present as ulcerative plaques or verrucous lesions

rulebook.rule: Failure of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and IV piperacillin-tazobactam (broad-spectrum bactericidal agents) with continued lesion progression and deepening argues against bacterial infection and for fungal etiology
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5324810/ — Antibiotic treatment is completely ineffective against fungal pathogens; delayed fungal diagnosis results from inappropriate antibiotic use in misidentified mycotic infections

rulebook.rule: Refractory course despite adequate broad-spectrum bactericidal coverage strongly indicates fungal (not bacterial) pathogen
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657236/ — Blastomycosis initially misdiagnosed as bacterial pneumonia; patients fail multiple antibiotic courses before correct fungal diagnosis established; characteristic presentation of systemic mycosis

rulebook.rule: Histopathology showing granulomatous inflammation with aggregated histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells containing round intracytoplasmic yeast-like organisms is hallmark of systemic mycosis
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122495/ — All three dimorphic fungi present with granulomatous dermal inflammation containing intracellular yeasts; characteristic histologic pattern distinguishing from bacterial or acid-fast infections

rulebook.rule: Strong Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining of organisms highlights fungal cell wall and confirms fungal etiology
rulebook.source: https://dermnetnz.org/topics/coccidioidomycosis-pathology — GMS stains fungal cell walls black; effectively highlights spherule walls and endospores; primary special stain for fungal identification in histologic tissue

rulebook.rule: Positive periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining of organisms confirms fungal cell wall polysaccharides
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122495/ — PAS stains fungal cell wall polysaccharides bright magenta; positive in all dimorphic mycoses; complements GMS for fungal diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Negative acid-fast staining excludes mycobacterial etiology (tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria) and supports fungal diagnosis
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122495/ — Fungi do not stain with acid-fast methods; acid-fast staining targets mycobacterial cell wall lipids; negative acid-fast rules out TB and MAC as causes of granulomatous dermatitis

rulebook.rule: Tissue culture growth followed by molecular ribosomal ITS sequencing provides species-level identification and definitive diagnosis
rulebook.bears_on: [Coccidioidomycosis, Blastomycosis, Paracoccidioidomycosis, or Sporotrichosis—whichever ITS identifies]
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Ribosomal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequencing is gold-standard for fungal species identification; PCR-based fungal-universal primers reliably differentiate Coccidioides, Blastomyces, Paracoccidioides, Sporothrix

rulebook.rule: Afebrile presentation with normal vital signs and absence of fever/chills despite 2-month progressive illness is consistent with chronic indolent fungal infection rather than acute bacterial sepsis
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Dimorphic fungi produce chronic indolent infections; fever is absent in many cutaneous and early-stage infections; constitutional symptoms (fever, chills) indicate systemic dissemination

rulebook.rule: Absence of regional lymphadenopathy argues against sporotrichosis, which characteristically causes lymphocutaneous spread with nodular chain
rulebook.source: https://dermnetnz.org/topics/sporotrichosis — Sporotrichosis lymphocutaneous form (most common) produces string of nodules ascending along proximal lymphatics from inoculation site; absence of regional lymphadenopathy makes sporotrichosis less likely

rulebook.rule: No systemic skin lesions, normal internal organ examination, and unremarkable imaging (CXR, CT thorax, CT brain) with normal CSF indicate absence of disseminated disease
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8883362/ — Disseminated coccidioidomycosis commonly involves skin (nodules, abscesses), bone, joints, meninges; early-stage or primary cutaneous disease may be limited to dermis without visceral involvement

rulebook.rule: Normal complete blood count (no leukocytosis, anemia, or thrombocytopenia) supports localized cutaneous infection without systemic hematologic involvement
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Systemic mycosis typically causes elevated WBC, anemia, and metabolic abnormalities; normal CBC consistent with localized cutaneous mycosis

rulebook.rule: Mild C-reactive protein elevation (4.6 mg/dL) without fever or systemic signs indicates chronic low-grade inflammation consistent with indolent mycotic infection
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657236/ — Dimorphic fungi trigger chronic low-grade inflammatory response; mild CRP elevation is consistent with chronic mycosis rather than acute bacterial sepsis

rulebook.rule: Negative serum beta-D-glucan and negative circulating polysaccharide antigen may indicate early-stage infection, localized disease, or false-negative serology
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3421794/ — Coccidioidomycosis serology negative in very early infection (first 1-3 weeks); 20-50% of immunosuppressed patients test false-negative despite active infection; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8619313/ — Blastomyces immunodiffusion 40% sensitivity within first 4 weeks post-symptom onset; beta-D-glucan more sensitive in disseminated/meningeal disease; isolated cutaneous mycosis can have negative serology despite positive culture

rulebook.rule: Negative HIV serology indicates immunocompetent host, consistent with cutaneous mycosis in setting of high inoculum or traumatic exposure
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657236/ — HIV+ patients at substantially higher risk for disseminated coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis; negative HIV serology does not exclude cutaneous mycosis in immunocompetent individual, especially with traumatic inoculation

rulebook.rule: Two-month progressive course unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics is consistent with chronic dimorphic fungal mycosis requiring antifungal therapy
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Coccidioidomycosis incubation typically 7-21 days; cutaneous disease may progress over weeks to months without antifungal treatment; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657236/ — Blastomycosis presents as chronic progressive disease unresponsive to antibiotics

rulebook.rule: ITS sequencing identifying Coccidioides species: initiate fluconazole 400-1200 mg daily or itraconazole 200 mg 2-3 times daily; treat for 3+ months
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448161/ — Fluconazole preferred first-line 400-1200 mg daily for coccidioidomycosis; itraconazole alternative with potentially superior bone/soft tissue penetration; treatment duration often 3-12+ months depending on disease extent

rulebook.rule: ITS sequencing identifying Blastomyces dermatitidis (mild-to-moderate cutaneous): initiate itraconazole 200 mg three times daily for 3 days, then twice daily for 6 months total
rulebook.source: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/296870-treatment — Itraconazole is standard therapy for mild-to-moderate blastomycosis; loading dose 200 mg 3x daily for 3 days, then maintenance 2x daily; 6-month course typical for localized disease

rulebook.rule: ITS sequencing identifying Paracoccidioides brasiliensis: initiate itraconazole 100 mg twice daily for 9-18 months
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532700/ — Azoles (itraconazole preferred) are first-line for paracoccidioidomycosis; itraconazole 100 mg 2x daily for 9-18 months more effective than ketoconazole; lower toxicity and relapse rates than sulfonamides

rulebook.rule: ITS sequencing identifying Sporothrix schenckii: initiate itraconazole as treatment of choice for cutaneous and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis
rulebook.source: https://dermnetnz.org/topics/sporotrichosis — Itraconazole is standard oral antifungal and treatment of choice for sporotrichosis; effective for cutaneous, lymphocutaneous, and fixed cutaneous forms

rulebook.rule: Organism culture growth from tissue biopsy confirms active viable fungal infection (not colonization or seropositivity alone)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122495/ — Culture growth confirms active infection vs. colonization or prior exposure; necessary for species identification and assessment of treatment response

rulebook.rule: Broad-spectrum antibiotics futile in fungal infection; diagnostic delay from antibiotic misuse increases morbidity. Early tissue biopsy with special stains and culture essential when antibiotic failure encountered
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5324810/ — Better fungal diagnosis key to reducing antibiotic resistance; invasive fungal diseases misdiagnosed as bacterial, treated inappropriately with broad-spectrum antibiotics, resulting in delayed diagnosis and escalating resistance

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Blastomycosis (cutaneous/sporotrichoid form caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis).

Recommended next action: Initiate systemic antifungal therapy with itraconazole 200 mg BID for cutaneous disease (or amphotericin B if dissemination suspected); obtain fungal culture confirmation; monitor clinical response.

Confidence: 92%

Reasoning: The histopathology is pathognomonic — granulomatous inflammation with intracellular encapsulated yeast-like organisms that are GMS/PAS-positive and acid-fast negative, housed within histiocytes and giant cells. This pattern combined with negative serum fungal markers (beta-glucan, cryptococcal antigen), sporotrichoid presentation after traumatic inoculation, normal systemic workup (chest, CSF, neuroimaging), and rural agricultural exposure makes blastomycosis the only diagnosis that fits. Failure to respond to antibiotics and the granulomatous response rule out bacterial cellulitis. The 28S rRNA sequencing would confirm Blastomyces dermatitidis identification.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
**Diagnostic Reasoning:**

This 71-year-old immunocompetent farmer from a rural district (F001, F002, F007) presented with a two-month progressive, painful dermal lesion (F003, F004) following traumatic inoculation via thorny branch scratch (F005). The lesion is a slowly enlarging, indurated erythematous plaque with shallow ulceration and serous drainage (F010).

**Exclusion of Bacterial Etiology:**
The initial clinical presumption of bacterial cellulitis (F011) was disproven by treatment failure. Despite adequate broad-spectrum bactericidal therapy—oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (F012) followed by intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam (F013)—the lesion continued to spread and deepened over three weeks (F014). Per R004 and R005, antibiotic failure with continued progression strongly argues against bacterial pathogenesis and implicates fungal etiology. Additionally, acid-fast staining was negative (F035), ruling out mycobacterial infection per R009.

**Fungal Etiology Established by Histopathology and Microbiology:**
Tissue biopsy (F030) revealed hallmark findings of systemic mycosis: granulomatous dermal inflammation with aggregated histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells (F031) containing round, encapsulated, intracytoplasmic yeast-like organisms (F032). Per R006, this granulomatous pattern with intracellular yeasts is characteristic of Coccidioidomycosis, Blastomycosis, and Paracoccidioidomycosis. The organisms stained strongly with Gomori methenamine silver (F033) and periodic acid–Schiff (F034), confirming fungal cell wall structure per R007 and R008. Tissue culture subsequently grew an organism (F036), confirming active viable infection per R023. Molecular characterization via ribosomal ITS sequencing (F037) will provide definitive species-level identification per R010.

**Geographic and Epidemiologic Context:**
The patient's residence in a rural farming district (F002) combined with traumatic inoculation during gardening (F005) raises suspicion for soil-dwelling fungal pathogens. The rural farming environment is consistent with endemic exposures to Coccidioides (R001, per Southwest endemic zones) and Blastomyces/Paracoccidioides (occupational soil exposure). The classic transmission mechanism of traumatic inoculation via thorny plant material particularly raises suspicion for Sporotrichosis (R002, rose gardener's disease presentation).

**Systemic Dissemination Status:**
The patient remains afebrile with normal vital signs (F015), no constitutional symptoms (F008), no regional lymphadenopathy (F016), no systemic skin involvement (F017), and unremarkable chest/abdominal/neurologic examination (F018). Imaging (chest radiograph F025, CT thorax F026, CT brain F027) and cerebrospinal fluid examination (F028) are all normal. Laboratory assessment shows normal complete blood count (F019), unremarkable serum chemistries (F020), and mildly elevated C-reactive protein at 4.6 mg/dL (F021). Per R011, afebrile presentation with an indolent 2-month course is consistent with chronic fungal infection. Per R013 and R014, the absence of disseminated features and normal CBC support localized cutaneous mycosis rather than systemic dissemination. Notably, serum beta-D-glucan (F023) and circulating polysaccharide antigen (F024) are both negative, but per R016, these findings do not exclude early-stage or localized infection—particularly in an immunocompetent host—and negative serology can coexist with positive tissue culture.

**Differential Diagnosis Refinement:**
Four organisms remain in the differential pending ITS sequencing:
1. **Coccidioidomycosis**: Raised by R001 (endemic/occupational risk in farming district), R003 (ulcerative plaque morphology), R005 (antibiotic failure), R006 (granulomatous histology), R011 (indolent course), R015 (mild CRP elevation), R018 (2-month progressive course). Supported by F001–F010, F014, F021, F025–F028.
2. **Blastomycosis**: Raised by R003 (ulcerative plaque), R005, R006, R011, R015, R018. Similar epidemiologic and clinical overlap with coccidioidomycosis.
3. **Paracoccidioidomycosis**: Raised by R006 (granulomatous histology with intracellular yeasts). More common in Central/South America; less likely in rural North American farming district, but cannot be excluded without geographic clarification.
4. **Sporotrichosis**: Raised by R002 (traumatic inoculation via thorny branch is classic). However, per R012, the absence of regional lymphadenopathy argues against the characteristic lymphocutaneous form, making sporotrichosis less likely (though fixed cutaneous form remains possible).

The histologic pattern and clinical course are most consistent with a dimorphic mycosis (Coccidioides, Blastomyces, or Paracoccidioides), with geographic and epidemiologic context favoring Coccidioidomycosis or Blastomycosis.

**Treatment Approach Upon Organism Identification:**
Once ribosomal ITS sequencing identifies the organism (F037), organism-specific antifungal therapy should commence:
- If **Coccidioides** (R019): Fluconazole 400–1200 mg daily or itraconazole 200 mg 2–3 times daily for ≥3 months.
- If **Blastomyces dermatitidis** (R020): Itraconazole 200 mg three times daily for 3 days, then twice daily for 6 months total.
- If **Paracoccidioides brasiliensis** (R021): Itraconazole 100 mg twice daily for 9–18 months.
- If **Sporothrix schenckii** (R022): Itraconazole as first-line oral antifungal.

Per R024, early tissue biopsy with special stains and culture—as performed here—is the correct diagnostic approach to avoid prolonged antibiotic delays.

**Conclusion:**
The patient has a cutaneous mycotic infection confirmed by histopathology (granulomatous inflammation, yeast-like organisms; F031–F035) and tissue culture growth (F036). Bacterial and mycobacterial etiologies are excluded (F014 antibiotic failure, F035 acid-fast negative). The specific organism awaits ribosomal ITS sequencing (F037); pending this result, the clinical presentation is most consistent with Coccidioidomycosis or Blastomycosis given geographic and epidemiologic context. Organism-specific azole antifungal therapy tailored by ITS identification (R019–R022) is the appropriate next step, with anticipated favorable response given the localized cutaneous disease and immunocompetent host status.

The clinical, histologic, and microbiologic findings form a coherent pattern strongly consistent with fungal etiology; however, confidence is not absolute pending molecular identification, as the differential remains broad and clinical features overlap across the four suspected organisms.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: primary cutaneous cryptococcosis (C. neoformans var. grubii), confirmed by ITS sequencing, treated with systemic fluconazole; dissemination excluded; immunocompetent host with traumatic plant/soil inoculation.

Neither output names cryptococcosis, and both omit Cryptococcus from their differential despite the described "round, encapsulated" yeast (encapsulation is the cardinal cryptococcal clue) and negative serum cryptococcal antigen — a notable shared miss, since negative crypto antigen does not exclude LOCALIZED primary cutaneous disease.

Output A: Does not commit to a wrong organism. It correctly establishes the entire framework matching ground truth — immunocompetent host, traumatic inoculation, fungal etiology confirmed by histopath + tissue culture, bacterial excluded by antibiotic failure, mycobacterial excluded by negative acid-fast, and localized/non-disseminated disease per normal CBC, imaging, CSF, beta-D-glucan and antigen. It explicitly defers species ID to pending ITS sequencing — which is exactly the actual confirmation method in ground truth — and lists systemic azole (including fluconazole) as treatment. Well-calibrated and fully traceable. Weaknesses: misplaces geography to North America; offers a 4-organism dimorphic-fungus differential (Coccidioides/Blastomyces/Paracoccidioides/Sporothrix) that misses the actual organism.

Output B: Commits at 92% confidence to Blastomycosis — the wrong organism — and recommends itraconazole as if established. It cites "28S rRNA sequencing" as the confirmatory test, but ground truth used ITS sequencing (a factual error). It correctly excludes bacterial cellulitis and gets the broad direction (systemic antifungal for localized fungal cutaneous disease) right, but the confident wrong diagnosis plus wrong confirmatory test is poorly calibrated and the most clinically harmful failure mode.

Decision: A wins on calibration, defensibility, and fidelity to the actual workup/confirmation/management pathway, despite not naming the organism. B's overconfident incorrect commitment and incorrect confirmatory-test claim are worse.
