per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old man was referred to a tertiary dermatology service for multiple chronic, painful skin ulcers that had been present for roughly 30 months and had failed to heal despite several courses of treatment.

His relevant background was ulcerative-type inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease) diagnosed about five years earlier, for which he had been on long-term immunosuppression: a thiopurine (azathioprine 75 mg daily) together with an intravenous anti-TNF biologic (infliximab 350 mg every 8 weeks). His bowel disease had been quiescent on this regimen. The skin lesions had first appeared while he was on this immunosuppressive therapy. He lived in a rural area of a Mediterranean-basin country and had not traveled abroad recently.

The lesions had originally been attributed to a neutrophilic skin condition thought to be linked to his bowel disease, and two skin biopsies taken early in the course had been interpreted as compatible with that working diagnosis. On that basis he had received, over an 18-month period, repeated tapering courses of systemic corticosteroids, weekly intralesional corticosteroid injections for about two months, and — when these failed — a switch of his biologic to adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly plus addition of cyclosporine 200 mg daily. None of these measures produced any improvement, and new lesions continued to appear.

On examination there were several well-demarcated ulcers with raised, firm, erythematous rolled edges and a base covered by necrotic, purulent slough. Lesions were distributed across the forearms, the neck, the chest, the right ear, and the lower legs. There was no regional lymphadenopathy and the patient was systemically well, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable.

Laboratory evaluation was largely unremarkable: complete blood count, coagulation studies, serum proteins, liver and renal function, and inflammatory markers were all within or near normal limits. HIV serology was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging showed no abnormality and no organomegaly.

A repeat biopsy of an active lesion was taken for histopathology and additional studies. Histology showed ulceration of the epidermis with dermal edema, dilated vessels, and a dense, nodular, multicellular granulomatous infiltrate within the dermis.
per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Disseminated/diffuse CUTANEOUS LEISHMANIASIS caused by Leishmania infantum, occurring in an immunosuppressed patient (Crohn's disease on anti-TNF + thiopurine). The chronic ulcers had been misattributed to PYODERMA GANGRENOSUM (a non-infectious neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD) — two prior biopsies were read as "suggestive of PG," and the patient failed repeated systemic/intralesional corticosteroids, a switch of biologic, and a calcineurin inhibitor before the true diagnosis was made.

How confirmed: (1) Lesional skin biopsy histopathology showed a dense nodular granulomatous dermal infiltrate (NOT the neutrophilic pattern expected in PG); (2) Leishmania serology positive; (3) PCR for Leishmania DNA on lesional tissue confirmed the organism and SPECIATED it as Leishmania infantum; (4) PCR on peripheral blood was NEGATIVE, excluding visceral/systemic dissemination. Full systemic workup (CBC, coagulation, proteins, liver/renal function, inflammatory markers, abdominal ultrasound, chest imaging) was unremarkable.

Correct disposition: Antiparasitic therapy, NOT escalation of immunosuppression. Treated with IV liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day on days 1–5, 14, and 21, followed by three monthly intralesional pentavalent antimonial injections. Complete resolution with only residual scarring; no recurrence at 12-month follow-up and IBD remained stable. KEY TEACHING POINT: a "PG" diagnosis in an immunosuppressed IBD patient that fails to respond to immunosuppression — especially with granulomatous (not neutrophilic) histology and residence in a Leishmania-endemic area — must trigger a search for an infectious mimic; intensifying immunosuppression for misread PG worsens an underlying infection.

The contrast between early biopsy interpretation (neutrophilic) and repeat biopsy findings (granulomatous) suggests either sampling error, evolution of disease, misinterpretation, or changed tissue characteristics. Not specified which.
Lesion count: 'Several' ulcers is stated, but exact number unclear. Relevant for disease burden assessment.
Lesion size: Dimensions or surface area of individual or total ulceration not specified. Relevant for severity staging.
Pain characteristics: Type (burning, sharp, throbbing), severity scale, or relationship to lesion activity not described.

Whether abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging were performed specifically to rule out systemic infection/disseminated disease, versus routine baseline. Context matters for differential diagnosis breadth.
Timing of repeat biopsy relative to referral: Was biopsy done at tertiary service or before? Affects interpretation of accumulated treatment history.

Granuloma composition: Were granulomas caseating or non-caseating? Presence/absence of epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells (type), acid-fast bacilli staining not mentioned. Critical for tuberculosis and fungal differential.

Special stains or culture performed on repeat biopsy: Acid-fast stain (TB), PAS (fungal), cultures (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal), immunohistochemistry not mentioned. Standard workup for granulomatous lesions unclear.
Skin test or IGRA for tuberculosis: Not mentioned. Critical in rural Mediterranean setting with immunosuppression.
Fungal serology or antigen panels: Not mentioned. Mediterranean basin context raises question of endemic fungi (Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces presence variable by region).
Lesion chronology: Are lesions appearing simultaneously or sequentially over the 30 months? Pattern of new appearance may indicate acute recurrence vs chronic reactivation.

Relationship between bowel disease flares and skin lesions: Case states bowel was quiescent, but does not state whether skin lesions temporally correlated with any past bowel exacerbations or are independent.

rulebook.rule: Dense nodular granulomatous infiltrate in dermis RAISES cutaneous tuberculosis (TB verrucosa cutis, scrofuloderma, or TB chancre) as a candidate diagnosis.
rulebook.source: StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf: Cutaneous Tuberculosis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/) — granulomas with caseating necrosis and acid-fast bacilli are characteristic; DermNet (https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cutaneous-tuberculosis) describes multiple clinical forms presenting as chronic ulcers with granulomatous histology

rulebook.rule: Residence in rural Mediterranean-basin country and potential exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis RAISES cutaneous tuberculosis, especially given prior TB exposure in endemic setting.
rulebook.source: StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf: Cutaneous Tuberculosis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/) — lists endemic areas including Mediterranean regions as risk factor; TB endemic in Mediterranean-basin countries

rulebook.rule: Long-term immunosuppression with TNF inhibitors (infliximab/adalimumab) and azathioprine significantly RAISES risk of TB reactivation or new TB infection, with skin ulceration as possible manifestation.
rulebook.source: Nature Reviews Rheumatology (https://www.nature.com/articles/ncprheum0336): TNF-α essential for granuloma formation; inhibition leads to increased TB risk. NCBI/PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5237312/): documented case of disseminated TB after TNF inhibitor initiation

rulebook.rule: TNF inhibitor use (infliximab/adalimumab) combined with long-term systemic corticosteroids RAISES risk of opportunistic fungal infections (histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis) with chronic granulomatous skin ulcers as manifestation.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5548176/): fungal infection rate in TNF inhibitor users includes 60% histoplasmosis, 10% coccidioidomycosis, 4% blastomycosis; prednisone use doubled infection risk. FDA warning documented in Nature Reviews Rheumatology

rulebook.rule: Combination therapy with TNF inhibitor (adalimumab) plus azathioprine plus cyclosporine RAISES risk of serious opportunistic infections more than monotherapy alone.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8788654/): significant risk for infections with combination immunosuppressive therapy in IBD; elevated risk of opportunistic infection with concomitant TNFi and immunomodulator use

rulebook.rule: Residence in Mediterranean-basin rural area with cutaneous chronic granulomatous ulcers affecting exposed skin (forearms, neck, chest, ear, lower legs) RAISES cutaneous leishmaniasis (L. infantum) as candidate diagnosis.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9867513/): Leishmania infantum endemic in Mediterranean basin; transmitted by sandfly bites; lesions on exposed skin (face, neck, arms, legs); chronic non-necrotizing granulomatous infiltrate on histology

rulebook.rule: Immunosuppression (TNF inhibitors, systemic corticosteroids) in patient with chronic leishmaniasis RAISES likelihood of ulcerative rather than nodular presentation; more chronic and intractable course.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9867513/): ulcerative lesions more common in immunosuppressed patients (13/14) than immunocompetent (20/28)

rulebook.rule: History of Crohn's disease (IBD) RAISES pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) as candidate extraintestinal manifestation, especially if bowel disease quiescent (PG can follow independent course).
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4225318/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5089702/): PG occurs in 1-2% of IBD patients; can present independent of bowel disease activity. Wiley Online Library (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/crgm/2028354): erythema nodosum and PG are first and second most common cutaneous EIMs of IBD

rulebook.rule: Well-demarcated ulcers with raised, firm, erythematous rolled edges and base with necrotic purulent slough are classic morphology of pyoderma gangrenosum, raising this diagnosis.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4225318/): PG lesions start as tender papulopustules with erythematous-violaceous rim, undergo necrosis, leading to ulceration with characteristic rolled edges

rulebook.rule: Failure of repeated systemic corticosteroid courses and intralesional corticosteroid injections to heal lesions LOWERS pyoderma gangrenosum likelihood; typical PG responds to TNF inhibitors.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4225318/): infliximab and TNF inhibitors are effective treatments for PG associated with IBD; if corticosteroids failed but TNF inhibitors (infliximab then adalimumab) also failed, suggests alternative diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Dense nodular multicellular granulomatous infiltrate on repeat biopsy RAISES granulomatous infection (TB, fungal, parasitic) or non-infectious granulomatosis (GPA, granuloma annulare) and LOWERS simple neutrophilic dermatosis.
rulebook.source: StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf: Cutaneous Tuberculosis and Chronic Granulomatous Disease differential diagnoses (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK99496/): granulomatous histology distinguishes TB, fungal, and CGD from pyogenic or purely neutrophilic processes

rulebook.rule: Discordance between early biopsies (interpreted as neutrophilic) and repeat biopsy (showing granulomatous infiltrate) RAISES possibility of: (i) sampling error in initial biopsy, (ii) evolution of histology over disease course, (iii) misinterpretation of initial specimen, or (iv) concurrent process.
rulebook.bears_on: Diagnostic interpretation; TB/fungal infection (if granulomas represent evolved/unrecognized infection)
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5594233/): palisaded neutrophilic granulomatous dermatitis shows spectrum of histologic findings; given disease may progress through stages, individual biopsy may not capture full picture. NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5746633/): repeat biopsy often necessary to establish diagnosis of granulomatous disease

rulebook.rule: Complete failure of multiple immunosuppressive agents (systemic corticosteroids ×18 months, intralesional steroids, TNF inhibitors infliximab→adalimumab, cyclosporine, azathioprine) RAISES infectious etiology (TB, fungal infection, leishmaniasis) rather than purely inflammatory/autoimmune condition.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5548176/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8788654/): immunosuppression paradoxically worsens or fails to control infections because it impairs immune containment of pathogens. TB and fungal infections reactivate or progress on TNF inhibitors

rulebook.rule: Absence of regional lymphadenopathy LOWERS cutaneous leishmaniasis and tuberculosis chancre (which typically present with draining lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy) but does NOT exclude other forms of TB (lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma, TB verrucosa cutis).
rulebook.source: DermNet (https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cutaneous-tuberculosis): leishmaniasis presents with early localized adenopathy; TB chancre followed by lymphangitis; StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/): scrofuloderma involves draining lymph node abscess; lupus vulgaris and TB verrucosa cutis less likely to have prominent adenopathy

rulebook.rule: Normal inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), normal CBC, normal coagulation, normal liver/renal function LOWERS acute inflammatory/infectious exacerbation but DOES NOT exclude chronic TB, fungal infection, or leishmaniasis (which often have minimal systemic inflammation).
rulebook.source: Multiple sources: chronic granulomatous infections localized to skin often produce minimal systemic inflammatory response. PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5548176/): TB and fungal infections in immunosuppressed patients may present without fever or leukocytosis

rulebook.rule: Normal abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging LOWERS disseminated/systemic TB or histoplasmosis but does NOT exclude localized cutaneous disease or early/limited pulmonary involvement.
rulebook.source: StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/): cutaneous TB often occurs without pulmonary involvement. CDC (https://www.cdc.gov/histoplasmosis/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html): primary cutaneous histoplasmosis rare but can occur without dissemination

rulebook.rule: Residence in Mediterranean-basin rural area; however, histoplasmosis endemic to tropical/subtropical Americas and Africa, less established in Mediterranean proper—LOWERS histoplasmosis relative to TB or leishmaniasis as first differential.
rulebook.source: CDC (https://www.cdc.gov/histoplasmosis/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html) and NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5237312/): histoplasmosis endemic to river valleys of Americas, Africa, east/south Europe, tropical Asia; specific Mediterranean prevalence not highlighted as high-risk region

rulebook.rule: Chronic granulomatous mycotic skin ulcers with lymphocutaneous or fixed cutaneous form RAISES sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) as candidate, though endemic mainly to tropical/subtropical regions with soil/plant exposure.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4295339/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5729013/): sporotrichosis presents as chronic granulomatous infection with ulceration; can mimic pyoderma gangrenosum; histology shows epithelioid granuloma with Langhans giant cells

rulebook.rule: Initial biopsy interpretation as neutrophilic skin condition combined with IBD background RAISES Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), though repeat biopsy showing pure granulomas (not neutrophilic infiltrate) LOWERS this diagnosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD)
rulebook.source: PMC (https://academic.oup.com/ibdjournal/article/31/Supplement_1/S19/7978499 and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8905119/): Sweet syndrome is rare EIM of IBD; histology shows diffuse dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis; some cases can show granulomatous component

rulebook.rule: Cutaneous blastomycosis with chronic granulomatous ulceration RAISES this fungal diagnosis in patients on TNF inhibitors; however, endemic to Ohio/Mississippi valleys and Great Lakes—LOWERS likelihood in Mediterranean setting.
rulebook.source: PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5657236/) and NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441987/): blastomycosis endemic to Ohio/Mississippi river valleys, Great Lakes, southeastern USA; cutaneous form presents as papules evolving to crusted plaques with ulceration; granulomatous histology with pyogranulomatous response

rulebook.rule: Coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever) endemic to Southwest USA/Mexico, NOT Mediterranean region—LOWERS likelihood as differential in Mediterranean-basin patient despite granulomatous skin ulcer presentation.
rulebook.source: Britannica and DermNet (https://www.britannica.com/science/disseminated-coccidioidomycosis and https://dermnetnz.org/topics/coccidioidomycosis): endemic to arid Southwest USA and Northern Mexico; search results do not support Mediterranean endemicity

rulebook.rule: Dense granulomatous infiltrate WITHOUT documented special stains (acid-fast bacilli for TB, PAS for fungal, cultures) RAISES need for additional diagnostic workup and LOWERS diagnostic certainty pending those results.
rulebook.bears_on: Diagnostic specificity; TB, fungal, and bacterial infections
rulebook.source: StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/): acid-fast staining and cultures essential for TB diagnosis; granulomatous histology alone insufficient. MDPI (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/12/7/920): PAS staining and fungal cultures needed to differentiate fungal from other granulomatous causes

rulebook.rule: No documented tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) mentioned—RAISES critical need for TB screening given immunosuppression, endemic region, and granulomatous histology.
rulebook.source: Nature Reviews Rheumatology (https://www.nature.com/articles/ncprheum0336): tuberculosis screening (TST/IGRA) recommended before TNF inhibitor initiation; essential in endemic areas

rulebook.rule: No documented fungal serology or antigen testing (histoplasma antigen, coccidioides antibody, blastomyces antigen) mentioned—RAISES need for these tests given TNF inhibitor use and granulomatous histology.
rulebook.source: CDC and NCBI: fungal serologies and antigen detection are standard workup for granulomatous skin disease in immunosuppressed TNF inhibitor users

rulebook.rule: Dense granulomatous infiltrate without documented bacterial, mycobacterial (TB), or fungal cultures—RAISES critical need for tissue culture to identify organism and guide targeted antimicrobial therapy.
rulebook.source: StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/): culture is gold standard for TB and fungal diagnosis; granulomatous histology alone cannot specify organism

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Cutaneous mycobacterial infection, specifically M. ulcerans (or disseminated cutaneous tuberculosis if pulmonary involvement is present). Key reasoning: granulomatous histology, characteristic rolled ulcer edges with necrotic slough, chronic non-healing course despite escalated immunosuppression, rural Mediterranean epidemiology, and complete resistance to anti-inflammatory therapy all point to missed mycobacterial disease.

Recommended next action: (1) Obtain tissue for mycobacterial culture (TB culture, atypical mycobacterial culture, AFB staining, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, M. ulcerans PCR); (2) Consider chest imaging to exclude pulmonary TB given profound immunosuppression.

Confidence: 75-80%. The clinical and histologic picture is highly suggestive of mycobacterial infection, though the initial misdiagnosis and lack of lymphadenopathy introduce some diagnostic uncertainty. Culture confirmation is essential before initiating antimicrobial therapy.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient presents with chronic, recurrent, painful granulomatous skin ulcers refractory to prolonged anti-inflammatory therapy (systemic and intralesional corticosteroids, two sequential TNF inhibitors, and cyclosporine) [F4, F19, F15–F18]. The repeat skin biopsy shows a dense nodular multicellular granulomatous infiltrate [F40], which is the key diagnostic finding.

The initial biopsy interpretation as "neutrophilic" [F14] contrasts sharply with the repeat finding of granulomatous infiltrate [F37–F40]. Per R12, this discordance raises the possibility of sampling error, disease evolution, misinterpretation, or concurrent pathology—particularly suggestive of an evolving infectious process not recognized on early biopsy.

The clinical context strongly implicates an infectious etiology: The patient has been on long-term immunosuppression with TNF inhibitors (infliximab 350 mg every 8 weeks, then switched to adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly) [F8, F17], azathioprine 75 mg daily [F7], and cyclosporine 200 mg daily [F18]. Per R3, TNF inhibitor use significantly raises the risk of tuberculosis reactivation or new infection, with skin ulceration as a possible manifestation. Per R13, complete failure of multiple immunosuppressive agents raises infectious etiology (TB, fungal, parasitic) rather than primary inflammatory disease—immunosuppression paradoxically worsens infections by impairing immune containment.

Three infectious candidates emerge:

**1. Cutaneous Tuberculosis (Highest Suspicion)**
- Dense nodular granulomatous infiltrate raises cutaneous TB (TB verrucosa cutis, scrofuloderma, lupus vulgaris) [F40 per R1]
- Rural Mediterranean-basin residence raises TB, especially given endemic prevalence [F11 per R2]
- Long-term TNF inhibitor therapy significantly raises TB reactivation/infection risk [F8, F17 per R3]
- Complete treatment resistance across two TNF inhibitors raises infectious etiology [F19 per R13]
- Absence of regional lymphadenopathy [F27] lowers the TB chancre form (which presents with lymphangitis) [F27 per R14], but does not exclude lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma, or TB verrucosa cutis
- Normal chest imaging [F36] lowers disseminated TB but does not exclude localized cutaneous disease [F36 per R16]
- Critically, no TB screening (TST/IGRA) and no acid-fast bacilli staining/culture have been documented, which are essential for diagnosis [per R22, R23, R25]

**2. Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (Strong Candidate)**
- Rural Mediterranean-basin residence with endemic L. infantum raises this diagnosis [F11 per R6]
- Lesion distribution across exposed skin (forearms, neck, chest, ear, lower legs) [F22–F26] is consistent with sandfly-transmitted disease [F22–F26 per R6]
- Granulomatous infiltrate on histology matches non-necrotizing granulomatous response of leishmaniasis [F40 per R6]
- Immunosuppression with TNF inhibitors and systemic corticosteroids [F7, F15, F17, F18] favors ulcerative (rather than nodular) presentation in immunosuppressed hosts and a more chronic, intractable course [per R7]
- Absence of regional lymphadenopathy [F27] lowers early localized adenopathy typical of leishmaniasis chancre [F27 per R14]
- Fungal serology/antigen testing has not been documented [per R24]

**3. Fungal Infection (Lower Likelihood but Possible)**
- Combination of TNF inhibitor (adalimumab) plus long-term systemic corticosteroids [F15, F17, F18] raises opportunistic fungal infection risk (60% histoplasmosis rate in TNF inhibitor users; prednisone use doubled risk) [per R4]
- Combination therapy with TNF inhibitor + azathioprine + cyclosporine [F7, F17, F18] raises serious opportunistic infection risk above monotherapy [per R5]
- Granulomatous histology is consistent with fungal infection [F40 per R4]
- Complete treatment resistance to immunosuppressive agents raises infectious etiology [F19 per R13]
- However, histoplasmosis is endemic to tropical/subtropical Americas and Africa, less established in Mediterranean proper [per R17]—this lowers histoplasmosis as a leading differential
- Blastomycosis endemic to Ohio/Mississippi valleys and Great Lakes [per R20]—lowers likelihood in Mediterranean setting
- Coccidioidomycosis endemic to Southwest USA and Northern Mexico [per R21]—lowers likelihood in Mediterranean setting

**Against Pyoderma Gangrenosum:**
Although PG is a recognized extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease (IBD) [F5 per R8] and the ulcer morphology (well-demarcated, raised firm erythematous rolled edges, necrotic purulent slough) [F20, F21] is classically consistent with PG [per R9], the complete failure of two sequential TNF inhibitors (infliximab then adalimumab) strongly lowers the PG diagnosis [per R10]. TNF inhibitors are standard effective treatments for PG in IBD; their failure—combined with failure of corticosteroids—is atypical for PG and redirects focus toward an alternative diagnosis.

**Why Early Treatments Failed:**
The patient received systemic corticosteroids, intralesional steroids, TNF inhibitors (infliximab, then adalimumab), and cyclosporine—all of which would be expected to control inflammatory skin disease or improve PG [F15–F18]. Their complete failure [F19], in the context of quiescent bowel disease [F9], strongly suggests that the skin condition is not a simple inflammatory manifestation of IBD but rather an infectious process that is actively worsened or sustained by immunosuppression.

**Laboratory and Imaging Context:**
Normal inflammatory markers, CBC, coagulation, liver/renal function [F29–F33] lower acute inflammatory exacerbation [per R15], but do NOT exclude chronic TB, fungal, or parasitic infection, which often produce minimal systemic inflammation [per R15]. Normal abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging [F35, F36] lower disseminated disease [per R16] but do not exclude localized cutaneous infection [per R16]. The patient is systemically well, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable [F28], consistent with a chronic localized process.

**Critical Diagnostic Gaps:**
The granulomatous histology [F40] alone cannot specify the pathogen. Per R22, R23, R24, R25, the following are essential and are not documented: (1) acid-fast bacilli staining and mycobacterial culture (for TB diagnosis) [R22, R25]; (2) TB screening via TST or IGRA [R23]; (3) fungal serology/antigen panels [R24]; (4) bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal tissue cultures [R25]. Without these results, the diagnosis remains presumptive on histology and clinical context but cannot be finalized.

**Conclusion:**
The constellation of granulomatous histology, endemic geography, long-term TNF inhibitor-mediated immunosuppression, and universal resistance to anti-inflammatory agents strongly points toward an infectious etiology, most likely **cutaneous tuberculosis** or **cutaneous leishmaniasis**. Pyoderma gangrenosum is substantially lowered by TNF inhibitor failure. Fungal infections are raised by immunosuppression risk but lowered by geographic endemicity patterns. The diagnosis cannot be confirmed without urgent special stains, cultures, and serologies to identify the causative organism.
per_case.framework_top: Granulomatous skin ulcers of infectious etiology, most likely cutaneous tuberculosis or cutaneous leishmaniasis, rather than primary inflammatory/autoimmune dermatosis.
per_case.framework_next_step: Immediate additional diagnostic workup: (1) tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for TB screening [per R23]; (2) acid-fast bacilli staining and mycobacterial culture on biopsy tissue [per R22, R25]; (3) fungal serology (histoplasma antigen, if regional endemic exposure confirmed) and fungal culture [per R24, R25]; (4) tissue bacterial culture; (5) if leishmaniasis suspected, Leishmania serology and culture. Once organism identified, initiate pathogen-specific therapy (e.g., anti-tuberculosis regimen for TB, amphotericin B or azoles for fungal, pentavalent antimony or miltefosine for leishmaniasis) and consider temporary reduction of immunosuppression (with IBD specialist coordination) if appropriate.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate (60–70%). Infectious etiology is well-supported by the constellation of granulomatous histology, immunosuppression with TNF inhibitors, endemic geography, and complete treatment resistance. However, the specific pathogen cannot be identified from histology and clinical data alone; special stains, cultures, and serologies are essential. Diagnosis cannot be finalized without these results.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: the diagnosis is disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (Leishmania infantum) in an immunosuppressed IBD patient, misattributed to pyoderma gangrenosum. Key features the correct answer must capture: (1) infectious mimic of PG, (2) leishmaniasis specifically, (3) endemic geography + immunosuppression as drivers, (4) granulomatous (not neutrophilic) histology as the pivot, (5) the danger of escalating immunosuppression, (6) need for organism confirmation (PCR/serology) rather than empiric immunosuppression.

OUTPUT A commits to a single most-likely diagnosis — mycobacterial infection (M. ulcerans / cutaneous TB) — at 75-80% confidence. This is incorrect: it never mentions leishmaniasis at all, despite the lesions being in a Leishmania-endemic Mediterranean setting. It correctly identifies the broad theme (granulomatous infectious mimic missed under immunosuppression, needs culture before treating) and correctly recommends tissue diagnostics, but its confident headline diagnosis misses the actual answer entirely and even invents M. ulcerans (which is not endemic to the rural Mediterranean — a geographic hallucination). High confidence on a wrong specific answer hurts calibration.

OUTPUT B reasons as a structured differential, explicitly listing cutaneous leishmaniasis as a "strong candidate" with the correct supporting logic (endemic L. infantum, sandfly-exposed lesion distribution, granulomatous histology, immunosuppression favoring chronic ulcerative course). It correctly argues strongly against PG (TNF-inhibitor failure), correctly frames the granulomatous-vs-neutrophilic histology discordance as the pivotal clue, correctly identifies immunosuppression worsening an infection, and correctly insists on organism-level confirmation. Its main weakness is ranking cutaneous TB as the single highest suspicion above leishmaniasis, so it does not cleanly land the exact answer as #1 — but it explicitly names and well-supports the correct diagnosis and the correct disposition (antimicrobial, not more immunosuppression; confirm organism first). Its calibration is appropriate (refuses to finalize without stains/cultures/serologies), and its reasoning is fully traceable via cited findings/rules.

Comparison: B captures the true diagnosis within a well-calibrated differential and gets the management principle right; A confidently picks a wrong specific diagnosis (and hallucinates M. ulcerans endemicity) while omitting leishmaniasis. B is clearly stronger on correctness, calibration, and defensibility.

per_case.prose:
An 81-year-old man was referred to a dermatology clinic for evaluation of facial skin changes that had persisted for roughly five months. He first noticed a small, flesh-colored bump on the left side of his forehead that had slowly grown larger over that period. Around the same time, he developed mildly itchy, red, flaky areas of skin on the opposite side of his face.

He had previously been seen by another physician, who diagnosed eczema and prescribed a topical hydrocortisone cream together with regular emollients. He reported using these faithfully for several months but said neither the bump nor the red patches improved.

On examination, there was a flesh-colored nodule beneath the skin of the left forehead, measuring approximately 1.7 by 1.0 cm, that was firm and non-tender. On the right cheek there were poorly demarcated, erythematous, scaly patches; these were most prominent over the right cheek and did not have a sharp border. There was no regional lymph node enlargement on palpation of the head and neck.

His medical history was otherwise unremarkable for the presenting problem, and routine examination was non-contributory.

The forehead nodule was removed by excisional biopsy, and separate "scouting" biopsies were taken from several points within the scaly patches on the cheek. Cross-sectional imaging of the head and neck and of the chest was obtained as part of the workup; these studies showed no enlarged lymph nodes and no evidence of spread to distant sites.

Microscopic examination of the excised tissue showed a population of atypical, markedly pleomorphic spindle-shaped cells with numerous mitotic figures. In places the cells formed irregular, interconnecting channels lined by enlarged, dark-staining cells that bulged into the lumina. Special immunohistochemical staining was performed: the tumor cells stained positively for CD31 and CD34, and were negative for S100, leukocyte common antigen, CK7, and CK20. The biopsies taken from the scaly cheek patches showed the same process as the forehead nodule, and the excision margins were involved at both the lateral and deep edges.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Cutaneous angiosarcoma of the face/scalp region. CONFIRMATION: Excisional biopsy of the nodule plus scouting biopsies of the adjacent scaly patches showed atypical, pleomorphic spindle cells with numerous mitotic figures, irregular anastomosing vascular channels, and hyperchromatic "hob-nailing" of the neoplastic endothelium; immunohistochemistry was POSITIVE for the endothelial markers CD31 and CD34 and NEGATIVE for S100, LCA (leukocyte common antigen), CK7, and CK20 — confirming a vascular endothelial malignancy and excluding melanoma, lymphoma, and carcinoma. Staging head/neck and chest CT showed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis (localized disease). CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is a malignancy, NOT eczema; topical steroids are inappropriate and dangerous as they delay diagnosis. Any persistent/enlarging facial nodule with adjacent non-resolving "eczematous" patches in an elderly patient that fails topical therapy requires biopsy. The patient was treated with definitive radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions of 2 Gy); post-treatment in-field biopsies confirmed complete pathologic response and there was no recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Cutaneous angiosarcoma of the head/scalp is a rare, aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma of the elderly that classically masquerades as a benign bruise, rosacea, or eczema, leading to diagnostic delay. Source: Cutaneous Angiosarcoma Masquerading as Eczema, PMC3814070 (original patient: 98-year-old Caucasian man).

rulebook.rule: Tumor cells positive for CD31 (pan-endothelial marker with >90% sensitivity) raises likelihood of endothelial malignancy
rulebook.source: CD31 immunoreactivity in mesenchymal neoplasms of skin and subcutis (PubMed 7593814); Pathology Outlines - Angiosarcoma

rulebook.rule: Tumor cells positive for CD34 (less specific than CD31 but useful adjunctive endothelial marker) combined with CD31 positivity strongly supports endothelial origin
rulebook.bears_on: Angiosarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma, Spindle cell hemangioma
rulebook.source: Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine - Best Practices in Diagnostic Immunohistochemistry (131/10/1517); Kaposi Sarcoma CD31 Staining (136/11/1329)

rulebook.rule: CD31+/CD34+ membranous staining pattern (strong dense linear, not granular cytoplasmic) indicates true endothelial cells rather than background histiocytes
rulebook.source: Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine - Best Practices in Diagnostic Immunohistochemistry

rulebook.rule: Negative S100 lowers likelihood of melanoma, nerve sheath tumors, and certain spindle cell tumors of neural origin
rulebook.source: Soft Tissue Special Issue: Cutaneous Pleomorphic Spindle Cell Tumors (PMC7021907)

rulebook.rule: Negative leukocyte common antigen (LCA) lowers likelihood of lymphoproliferative disorder or lymphoid malignancy
rulebook.source: Best Practices in Diagnostic Immunohistochemistry - Pleomorphic Cutaneous Spindle Cell Tumors

rulebook.rule: Negative CK7 and CK20 lowers likelihood of epithelial primary malignancy or metastatic carcinoma
rulebook.source: Soft Tissue Special Issue: Cutaneous Pleomorphic Spindle Cell Tumors (PMC7021907)

rulebook.rule: Population of atypical, markedly pleomorphic spindle-shaped cells raises concern for malignancy; marked pleomorphism and high mitotic rate are consistent with high-grade sarcoma
rulebook.source: Histopathologic Grading Significance in Angiosarcoma (PMC9974594); Angiosarcoma: clinical and imaging features from head to toe (PMC5594986)

rulebook.rule: Spindle cell morphology with vascular differentiation (irregular interconnecting channels) combined with CD31/CD34 positivity is characteristic of angiosarcoma
rulebook.source: Pathology Outlines - Angiosarcoma; Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine

rulebook.rule: Irregular, interconnecting channels lined by enlarged dark-staining cells that bulge into lumina (hobnailing) is characteristic of angiosarcoma histology
rulebook.source: Unusual Clinical Presentation of Cutaneous Angiosarcoma Masquerading as Eczema (PMC3814070)

rulebook.rule: High mitotic rate with numerous mitotic figures in vascular channels indicates aggressive biological behavior and high-grade disease
rulebook.source: Histopathologic Grading Significance in Angiosarcoma (PMC9974594)

rulebook.rule: Flesh-colored subcutaneous nodule (firm, non-tender) on facial location in elderly patient raises angiosarcoma; angiosarcoma typically presents as asymptomatic nodules on face/scalp/neck
rulebook.source: Cutaneous angiosarcoma of head, neck, and face of the elderly (PubMed 23723607); Angiosarcoma of the face and scalp in older patients

rulebook.rule: Elderly age (81 years) is strong risk factor; angiosarcoma predominantly affects older patients, with worse prognosis
rulebook.source: Review of cutaneous angiosarcoma: epidemiology, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment (Oxford Academic JJCO 55/7)

rulebook.rule: Facial/scalp location (high sun exposure site) raises angiosarcoma and lowers prognosis; angiosarcomas of scalp/face have worse prognosis than other sites
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma of the Scalp and Face: A Hard to Treat Tumor; Angiosarcoma: clinical and imaging features (PMC5594986)

rulebook.rule: Failure to respond to topical hydrocortisone and emollients over months despite faithful adherence lowers eczema diagnosis and raises suspicion for neoplastic process (angiosarcoma may mimic dermatitis)
rulebook.source: Unusual Clinical Presentation of Cutaneous Angiosarcoma Masquerading as Eczema (PMC3814070)

rulebook.rule: Flesh-colored nodule distinct from pruritic red/scaly patches raises concern for separate neoplastic process in context of treatment failure
rulebook.source: Unusual Clinical Presentation of Cutaneous Angiosarcoma Masquerading as Eczema (PMC3814070)

rulebook.rule: Identical pathological process in biopsies from separate anatomic sites (forehead + cheek) indicates multifocal disease; raises concern for systemic vascular involvement
rulebook.source: Kaposi Sarcoma - ScienceDirect Topics; Multifocal cutaneous angiosarcoma of the scalp (Wiley 10.1002/cnr2.1659)

rulebook.rule: Multifocal cutaneous lesions with same pathology lowers likelihood of isolated primary tumor and raises need for whole-body staging
rulebook.source: Multifocal cutaneous angiosarcoma of the scalp; Angiosarcoma: a review of diagnosis and current treatment

rulebook.rule: Positive excision margins at lateral and deep edges raises risk of local recurrence and overall mortality; positive margins are independent adverse prognostic factor (HR 4.73 for overall survival)
rulebook.source: Prognostic significance of positive surgical margins for scalp angiosarcoma (PubMed 32446755)

rulebook.rule: Even with negative margins, multifocal disease results in discontinuous foci throughout specimen, leading to high recurrence risk (up to 60% local recurrence)
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: a review of diagnosis and current treatment (PMC6895451)

rulebook.rule: High-grade angiosarcoma (marked pleomorphism, high mitotic rate, necrosis) exhibits disease-free survival of 20% at 5 years (vs 95% grade 1, 62% grade 2)
rulebook.source: Histopathologic Grading Significance in Primary Angiosarcoma (PMC9974594)

rulebook.rule: Facial/scalp angiosarcoma has particularly poor prognosis compared to other sites with median survival 15-24 months and 5-year survival 10-15% (improved to 38-54% with multimodality treatment)
rulebook.source: Cutaneous angiosarcoma of the head, neck, and face of the elderly (PubMed 23723607); Review of cutaneous angiosarcoma (Oxford Academic JJCO 55/7)

rulebook.rule: Positive margins, multifocal disease, and high mitotic rate are independent adverse prognostic factors; combination carries highest mortality risk
rulebook.source: Prognostic significance of positive surgical margins (PubMed 32446755); Angiosarcoma: clinical and imaging features (PMC5594986)

rulebook.rule: Positive margins with multifocal disease necessitate multimodality treatment (surgery + radiotherapy ± chemotherapy); radiation reduces postoperative recurrence risk
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: a review of diagnosis and current treatment (PMC6895451)

rulebook.rule: Multifocal unresectable lesions and metastatic disease require systemic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, ifosfamide, taxanes) with or without propranolol
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: a review of diagnosis and current treatment (PMC6895451)

rulebook.rule: TNM staging not typically applied to cutaneous angiosarcoma due to multifocal nature; traditional staging systems have limited utility
rulebook.source: Review of cutaneous angiosarcoma: epidemiology, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment (Oxford Academic JJCO 55/7)

rulebook.rule: Kaposi sarcoma presents as multifocal lesions with spindle cells and CD31+/CD34+ endothelial marker expression, mimicking angiosarcoma; distinguishing feature is HHV-8 positivity
rulebook.source: Kaposi Sarcoma - ScienceDirect Topics; Pathology Outlines - Kaposi sarcoma

rulebook.rule: Kaposi sarcoma spindle cells may also express lymphatic endothelial marker D2-40/podoplanin; lack of HHV-8 staining and KSHV negativity lowers Kaposi sarcoma diagnosis
rulebook.source: Kaposi Sarcoma - ScienceDirect Topics; Pathology Outlines - Kaposi sarcoma

rulebook.rule: Absence of risk factors for Kaposi sarcoma (HIV negativity implied, no immunosuppression mentioned) and non-endemic presentation lowers Kaposi sarcoma diagnosis
rulebook.source: Pathology Outlines - Kaposi sarcoma

rulebook.rule: Absence of regional lymph node enlargement on imaging and palpation lowers N1/N2 stage but does not exclude metastatic disease risk
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: clinical and imaging features (PMC5594986)

rulebook.rule: Absence of evidence of spread to distant sites on CT chest and head/neck imaging at time of diagnosis is favorable, but high-grade multifocal angiosarcoma carries significant risk of subsequent distant metastasis
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: clinical and imaging features (PMC5594986)

rulebook.rule: Identical histopathology in contralateral cheek patches to forehead nodule indicates either: (a) metastatic spread from primary forehead lesion, (b) multifocal primary disease (separate angiosarcomas), or (c) systemic vascular involvement
rulebook.bears_on: Paraneoplastic vs metastatic vs multifocal primary diagnosis
rulebook.source: Multifocal cutaneous angiosarcoma of the scalp (Wiley 10.1002/cnr2.1659)

rulebook.rule: Angiosarcoma characteristically presents as multifocal disease; multifocal presentation does NOT necessarily indicate paraneoplastic phenomenon but rather reflects biological nature of the tumor
rulebook.source: Angiosarcoma: a review of diagnosis and current treatment (PMC6895451)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Cutaneous angiosarcoma (vascular malignancy). The hobnail histology with CD31+/CD34+ endothelial differentiation, atypical spindle cells with mitoses, and negative carcinoma/melanoma markers are diagnostic. The multifocal facial involvement and positive excision margins indicate aggressive disease.

Recommended next action: Urgent wide re-excision (Mohs or staged excision) for margin clearance; oncology referral for chemotherapy consideration (doxorubicin-based); possible radiation therapy; close surveillance.

Confidence: 90%

Reasoning: The histopathologic findings are essentially diagnostic for angiosarcoma. The characteristic hobnail endothelial cells bulging into channels, combined with CD31/CD34 positivity and exclusion of other diagnoses via immunostains, make this the only reasonable differential. Positive margins and multifocal disease are poor prognostic features requiring urgent intervention.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 81-year-old man presents with high-grade cutaneous angiosarcoma, a vascular endothelial malignancy affecting the face with multifocal disease presentation.

DIAGNOSIS: The immunohistochemical profile strongly supports endothelial origin. CD31+ and CD34+ staining (f25, f26, R1.1, R1.2) indicates endothelial markers with >90% sensitivity for angiosarcoma, while negative staining for S100 (f27, R2.1), leukocyte common antigen (f28, R2.2), CK7, and CK20 (f29, f30, R2.3) effectively excludes melanoma, nerve sheath tumors, lymphoproliferative disorders, and epithelial malignancies. The histomorphologic findings are pathognomonic for angiosarcoma: markedly pleomorphic spindle cells (f22) with numerous mitotic figures (f23, R3.1, R4.2) and the characteristic hobnail architecture with irregular interconnecting channels and dark-staining cells bulging into luminal spaces (f24, R4.1, R3.2). The clinical presentation — an asymptomatic firm nodule (f12) on the forehead (f9, R5.1) of an 81-year-old patient (f1, R5.2) at a high-exposure site (R5.3) — is classic for angiosarcoma in the elderly. Critically, the initial misdiagnosis as eczema and subsequent treatment failure with topical hydrocortisone and emollients despite faithful adherence (f6, f7, f8, R6.1) actually raise suspicion for angiosarcoma, which can masquerade as dermatitis (R6.2).

MULTIFOCAL DISEASE: Identical pathological findings in biopsies from contralateral cheek patches (f31) indicate multifocal disease. The cheek lesions developed concurrently with the forehead nodule (f4) and show identical histopathology on separate scouting biopsies (f19, f31). This confirms multifocal angiosarcoma rather than isolated primary disease (R7.1, R7.2, R13.1, R13.2). Multifocal presentation is characteristic of angiosarcoma's biological nature rather than a paraneoplastic phenomenon (R13.2).

STAGING AND PROGNOSIS: At the time of workup, no regional lymph node enlargement was detected on palpation (f15) or imaging (f20), and chest imaging showed no evidence of distant spread (f21, R12.1, R12.2). However, the absence of nodal involvement at diagnosis does not exclude subsequent metastatic risk in this aggressive tumor type (R12.2). The patient carries multiple adverse prognostic factors: (1) high-grade histology with marked pleomorphism and high mitotic rate (f22, f23, R9.1) yields only 20% disease-free survival at 5 years; (2) facial location (f9, R9.2) confers particularly poor prognosis with median survival of 15-24 months and 5-year survival of 10-15% without multimodality treatment (improving to 38-54% with combined modality); (3) positive excision margins at lateral and deep edges (f32, R8.1) create a hazard ratio of 4.73 for overall survival; (4) multifocal disease carries up to 60% local recurrence risk even with negative margins (R8.2, R9.3). The combination of positive margins, multifocal disease, and high mitotic rate represents the highest-risk subset (R9.3).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Kaposi sarcoma enters the differential given the multifocal presentation and spindle cell morphology with CD31+/CD34+ positivity (R11.1). However, Kaposi sarcoma is distinguished by HHV-8 positivity (R11.2) and requires specific risk factors (HIV infection, immunosuppression, endemic exposure) that are not documented in this case (R11.3). In the absence of immunocompromise history and endemic risk factors, angiosarcoma remains the leading diagnosis.

TREATMENT IMPLICATIONS: Excision alone is inadequate given positive margins. Per R10.1 and R10.2, multimodality treatment is essential: surgery (already performed) combined with adjuvant radiation to reduce postoperative recurrence risk, and systemic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, ifosfamide, taxanes) with or without propranolol for multifocal disease. Standard TNM staging does not apply to cutaneous angiosarcoma (R10.3), making histologic grade and margin status the primary prognostic guides.
per_case.framework_top: High-grade cutaneous angiosarcoma with multifocal disease (forehead nodule and contralateral cheek involvement); positive margins at excision; no current evidence of regional lymph node involvement or distant metastasis.
per_case.framework_next_step: Multimodality treatment consisting of: (1) adjuvant radiation therapy to primary forehead site and surrounding tissue given positive lateral and deep margins; (2) evaluation for systemic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, ifosfamide, or taxanes) given multifocal disease, high-grade histology, and facial location; (3) close surveillance imaging and clinical follow-up for early detection of local recurrence and distant metastasis; (4) genetic testing and immunohistochemical confirmation with HHV-8 staining if not already performed to exclude Kaposi sarcoma.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85-90%). The immunohistochemical profile (CD31+, CD34+; S100-, LCA-, CK7-, CK20-), histomorphologic features (pleomorphic spindle cells, high mitotic rate, characteristic hobnailing), clinical presentation (elderly patient, facial location, asymptomatic nodule), and treatment failure of presumed eczema create a tightly concordant case for angiosarcoma. Multifocal disease is confirmed by identical pathology in separate sites. The main residual uncertainty is whether HHV-8 staining was performed to definitively exclude Kaposi sarcoma in the differential.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs correctly identify the core diagnosis — cutaneous angiosarcoma — and both correctly cite the diagnostic IHC profile (CD31+/CD34+, negative S100/LCA/CK7/CK20) and the hobnail/pleomorphic-spindle-cell histology, matching the ground truth confirmation and exclusions. Neither output gets the actual definitive disposition fully right: the ground truth treatment was definitive radiotherapy alone (60 Gy/30 fx) with complete pathologic response and no recurrence at 6 months, whereas both outputs lead with surgical re-excision and chemotherapy (B lists radiation only as "possible"; A frames surgery as already done plus adjuvant RT + chemo). The deciding factor is hallucination and calibration. Output A, despite an impressive citation scaffold (f-/R-tags), asserts numerous specifics as established fact that are NOT in the ground truth: positive excision margins (f32), confirmed multifocal/contralateral disease, and precise survival/recurrence statistics and a hazard ratio of 4.73. The ground truth describes adjacent scaly patches that were scouting-biopsied — not a confirmed multifocal malignancy — and says nothing about positive margins. A presents these inferences with high confidence, weakening defensibility. Output B stays appropriately scoped, is correct on diagnosis and IHC reasoning, is well-calibrated (states 90% confidence), and avoids unsupported claims, making it more defensible. Both miss explicitly flagging that topical steroids were dangerous/delaying, but both implicitly reject eczema by diagnosing malignancy.

per_case.prose:
A 44-year-old man with no significant past medical history other than known homozygous factor V Leiden — for which he had taken a direct oral anticoagulant uneventfully for roughly seven years — presented to a regional hospital with several weeks of vague upper-abdominal fullness for which he had been "detoxing" with an extensive program of supplements and intravenous infusions arranged through an alternative-medicine clinic.

His self-directed regimen, taken over the preceding three to four months, was elaborate. It included a daily oral copper preparation (taken for about a month), a high-dose ascorbic acid infusion, intravenous L-carnitine, N-acetylcysteine, a B-complex preparation, intravenous magnesium and bicarbonate, a daily selenium supplement, oral alpha-lipoic acid, ashwagandha capsules, a proprietary herbal weight-management product line, and assorted probiotics. He had escalated the doses shortly before becoming acutely unwell. One day after the dose increase he developed sudden right-upper-quadrant pain and noticed his urine had turned dark; he was admitted elsewhere and told he had "acute hepatitis."

He was referred to the hepatology service about two months later, now jaundiced, itchy, and profoundly fatigued. On admission, transaminases were markedly elevated in a hepatocellular pattern — AST around 880 U/L (ref 5–45) and ALT around 540 U/L (ref 0–44) — with alkaline phosphatase 296 U/L (ref 38–150), GGT 165 U/L (ref 0–49), albumin 27 g/L (ref 35–50), INR 1.5 (ref 0.8–1.2), and a rising total bilirubin of 248 µmol/L (ref 0–20.4) that was predominantly conjugated (direct 172 µmol/L). Ceruloplasmin was 305 mg/L (ref 200–600).

A broad work-up was unrevealing. Viral hepatitis A, B, C, and E serologies were all negative, as were EBV, CMV, HIV, Bartonella, syphilis, and malaria studies. An autoimmune panel — ANA, anti-LKM, anti-smooth-muscle, and anti-mitochondrial M2 antibodies — was negative. Screening for hereditary hemochromatosis and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency was negative. Alcohol was undetectable and acetaminophen levels were non-detectable. Early abdominal ultrasound showed normal hepatic architecture without cirrhosis; subsequent cross-sectional imaging during the admission demonstrated a lobulated, nodular liver contour with lobar redistribution, splenomegaly, and features of portal hypertension, and a hepatic venous pressure gradient was measured at roughly 13 mmHg (normal <5).

A liver biopsy obtained at the first hospital had shown subacute severe hepatitis with confluent panacinar hepatocyte dropout involving about half the specimen, without features of venous outflow obstruction and without established fibrosis or cirrhosis. A second biopsy on the hepatology service showed only minimal necrosis with prominent hepatocyte regeneration — and, on special staining, an abnormally high deposition of copper within the liver. The long-standing anticoagulant was considered an unlikely culprit given years of prior tolerance. Targeted testing was undertaken to pursue the copper finding: a 24-hour urinary copper collection, quantitative copper measurement on the second biopsy specimen, and a slit-lamp examination of the corneas were obtained.

He was managed supportively with oral N-acetylcysteine, a short course of vitamin K, and ursodeoxycholic acid, and all of his supplements and infusions were discontinued on admission.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) caused by a complex regimen of naturopathic/natural health products — critically including an oral COPPER supplement (plus other hepatotoxic supplements such as a proprietary herbal weight-management product, ashwagandha, selenium). The case is notable because the markedly elevated copper on liver biopsy special staining created a strong initial working impression of WILSON DISEASE, which was WRONG.

HOW THE WRONG INITIAL DIAGNOSIS AROSE: Biopsy showed "abnormally high" hepatic copper deposition on rhodanine/rhodamine staining in a young previously-healthy adult with acute hepatitis and evolving portal hypertension — a picture that classically triggers a Wilson disease work-up.

HOW WILSON DISEASE WAS REFUTED: (1) serum ceruloplasmin NORMAL (318 mg/L; ref 200–600); (2) 24-hour urinary copper NOT in the Wilson range; (3) quantitative hepatic copper on the second biopsy NOT diagnostic of Wilson disease; (4) slit-lamp exam NEGATIVE for Kayser-Fleischer rings. (Genetic ATP7B testing was deemed unnecessary given the negative functional tests.) The elevated stainable copper was instead attributed to exogenous copper ingestion from the supplement, not endogenous copper-handling failure.

HOW DILI WAS CONFIRMED: Exclusion of all competing causes — viral hepatitis A/B/C/E negative; EBV/CMV/HIV/Bartonella/syphilis/malaria negative; autoimmune panel (ANA, anti-LKM, anti-SMA, anti-M2) negative; hereditary hemochromatosis and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency negative; toxicology negative (alcohol negative, acetaminophen non-detectable). Histology showed acute/subacute hepatitis with confluent panacinar hepatocyte dropout. Temporal relationship: injury onset coincided with escalation of the supplement regimen, and liver enzymes plus synthetic function progressively normalized after all products were stopped (positive dechallenge). Long-standing rivaroxaban for homozygous Factor V Leiden was a red herring — tolerated for years, excluded as the cause.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize supplement/naturopathic-product hepatotoxicity (including iatrogenic copper) as the etiology; STOP all offending products (the key therapeutic act); supportive care (N-acetylcysteine, vitamin K, ursodeoxycholic acid); hepatology follow-up. DO NOT initiate copper-chelation/Wilson therapy. Outcome: progressive recovery of liver function over ~2 months with residual coarsened echotexture/early fibrosis but no cirrhosis.

SOURCE: Drug-induced hepatitis mimicking Wilson's disease secondary to the use of complex naturopathic regimens: a case report. PMC6882359.

queries.asks: What is the diagnosis? (i.e., is this confirmed copper-induced hepatotoxicity, and if so, are there other concurrent contributors?)
What were the final results of the targeted copper testing (24-hour urinary copper, quantitative biopsy copper, Kayser-Fleischer ring examination)?
How did liver biochemistry and synthetic function evolve during the hepatology admission and with treatment (discontinuation of supplements + supportive care)?

What explains the normal serum ceruloplasmin (305 mg/L) in a patient with clinical and histologic evidence of hepatic copper overload? (Expected pattern in inherited Wilson disease is low ceruloplasmin; normal ceruloplasmin is atypical for primary copper overload.)
Why does imaging (lobulated contour, splenomegaly, elevated HVPG ~13 mmHg) suggest portal hypertension with apparent cirrhosis when biopsies explicitly deny fibrosis and cirrhosis?
What was the clinical outcome? (recovery vs. progression to decompensated liver disease; need for transplant consideration?)
Was copper exposure the sole cause, or did ascorbic acid (high-dose IV), N-acetylcysteine, or other components of the supplement regimen contribute synergistically to hepatotoxicity?
Did the homozygous Factor V Leiden or the long-term DOAC (likely dabigatran or apixaban) influence susceptibility to supplement-induced toxicity?

rulebook.rule: Daily oral copper supplementation (reported in case as ~1 month duration) in setting of acute presentation with right-upper-quadrant pain, dark urine, and dose escalation raises the candidate diagnosis of acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity (iatrogenic from supplement overload)
rulebook.source: LiverTox® (NCBI Bookshelf): Copper toxicology overview; "Acute copper toxicity presents with characteristic gastrointestinal symptoms followed by systemic effects... Liver injury tends to arise after 24 to 72 hours following ingestion of toxic amounts (1–10 grams)." https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548090/

rulebook.rule: High-dose intravenous ascorbic acid infusion combined with oral copper supplementation raises the risk of synergistic hepatotoxicity via ascorbate-mediated mobilization and enhanced hepatic copper uptake.
rulebook.source: Published research on ascorbic acid and copper metabolism: "Ascorbate increases the efficiency of hepatic uptake of Cu, and ascorbate intravenously administered together with copper caused an increase in copper in the liver... In human studies, serum ceruloplasmin activity was significantly reduced at every data point throughout the ascorbic acid supplementation period." https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1493135/ and https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/influence-of-ascorbic-acid-supplementation-on-copper-metabolism-in-rats/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated serum aminotransferases (AST 880 U/L, ALT 540 U/L) with AST > ALT and elevated bilirubin (predominantly conjugated) in acute onset raises acute hepatocellular necrosis from a hepatotoxic agent, consistent with acute copper toxicity pattern.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute hepatocellular necrosis from hepatotoxic exposure
rulebook.source: LiverTox® copper entry: "The injury pattern reflects acute hepatic necrosis with distinctive laboratory features: marked serum aminotransferase elevations, minimal alkaline phosphatase increases, early hepatic failure signs, elevated prothrombin time." https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548090/

rulebook.rule: Histologic findings of subacute severe hepatitis with confluent panacinar hepatocyte necrosis (first biopsy: ~50% specimen involvement) progressing to minimal necrosis with prominent hepatocyte regeneration (second biopsy) raises acute toxic hepatitis with recovery phase, consistent with supplement-induced injury pattern.
rulebook.source: Clinical case of supplement-induced hepatotoxicity (PMC2931391): "Liver histopathology revealed zone 3 (centrilobular) confluent necrosis and stromal collapse with patchy portal inflammation and considerable bile stasis... After discontinuing all supplements, the patient showed dramatic improvement. Within six weeks, liver enzymes nearly normalized." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2931391/

rulebook.rule: Abnormally high copper deposition on special staining of the second liver biopsy specimen raises acute-phase copper accumulation in hepatocytes, supporting copper-induced liver injury diagnosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Confirmed hepatic copper overload from exogenous copper exposure
rulebook.source: Wilson disease and copper toxicity pathophysiology (NCBI): "In Wilson disease, impaired copper transport decreases copper secretion into the bile, causing copper overload and accumulation in the liver... The hepatic copper value in untreated Wilson disease is above 200 µg/g dry weight of tissue with the normal being 50 or less." https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1368/ and Kayser-Fleischer ring overview: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459187/

rulebook.rule: Normal serum ceruloplasmin (305 mg/L, within normal range 200–600) in a patient with clinical and histologic evidence of hepatic copper overload lowers the likelihood of primary inherited Wilson disease but does NOT exclude acquired copper-induced hepatotoxicity, as normal ceruloplasmin can occur in symptomatic copper toxicity.
rulebook.source: Wilson disease ceruloplasmin patterns (NCBI/AASLD): "In Wilson disease, serum ceruloplasmin (normally 20 to 35 mg/dL) is usually low but can be normal... Interestingly, 5–15% of symptomatic Wilson's patients may have normal or only slightly decreased ceruloplasmin." https://www.aasld.org/liver-fellow-network/core-series/clinical-pearls/metallic-liver-c-u-later and PMC12237300: "A rare presentation of Wilson disease with normal levels of serum ceruloplasmin and copper." https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12237300/

rulebook.rule: Negative serologies for viral hepatitis A, B, C, E; negative EBV, CMV, HIV, Bartonella, syphilis, malaria; and negative autoimmune panel (ANA, anti-LKM, anti-smooth-muscle, anti-mitochondrial M2) lowers the probability of infectious hepatitis or autoimmune hepatitis, directing diagnostic focus toward toxicological or metabolic etiologies.
rulebook.bears_on: Viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and other infectious etiologies
rulebook.source: Standard hepatology diagnostic workup (NCBI/Merck): Comprehensive exclusion of major infectious and autoimmune causes is fundamental to identifying drug/supplement-induced injury and metabolic liver disease. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548090/

rulebook.rule: Negative hereditary hemochromatosis and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency screening lowers the probability of genetic iron-overload or protease-deficiency liver disease, though does not exclude secondary iron accumulation from acute necroinflammatory injury.
rulebook.source: Hereditary hemochromatosis screening guidelines (NCBI/AAFP): "A normal serum ferritin level with transferrin saturation less than 45 percent has a negative predictive value of 97 percent for excluding iron overload." https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2013/0201/p183.html/ and "HFE testing should be considered in patients with unexplained chronic liver disease... Ferritin is also an acute phase reactant and thus has a significant false positive rate, particularly in patients with necroinflammatory liver disease." https://www.nature.com/articles/gim200942

rulebook.rule: Undetectable alcohol and non-detectable acetaminophen levels at presentation lowers the probability of alcohol-induced liver disease or acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity as primary etiologies.
rulebook.source: Hepatotoxicology and differential diagnosis (LiverTox® and NCBI): Standard exclusion of common hepatotoxins (alcohol, acetaminophen) is essential when evaluating drug/supplement-induced injury. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548090/

rulebook.rule: Imaging findings of lobulated nodular liver contour with splenomegaly and elevated hepatic venous pressure gradient (~13 mmHg, normal <5) in setting of biopsies denying fibrosis or cirrhosis raises the possibility of acute sinusoidal injury, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, or post-necrotic portal hypertension from severe acute hepatitis rather than established cirrhosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (non-cirrhotic portal hypertension) vs. cirrhosis from copper toxicity
rulebook.source: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia and portal hypertension pathophysiology (NCBI): "Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) is a rare liver condition characterized by a widespread benign transformation of the hepatic parenchyma into small regenerative nodules that may lead to the development of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension... NRH is complicated by clinically overt portal hypertension in at least 50% of cases." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3070012/ and "Copper sulfate is noted as a usual exposure to assess in cases of non-cirrhotic intrahepatic portal hypertension." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11730389/

rulebook.rule: Multi-ingredient proprietary supplement regimen with undisclosed composition raises uncertainty regarding causative agent(s) and synergistic toxicity, but collective discontinuation with clinical improvement supports supplement-induced hepatotoxicity as the unifying diagnosis.
rulebook.source: Clinical case (PMC2931391): A 45-year-old presented with severe hepatotoxicity after taking nine dietary supplements containing over 30 individual ingredients. "After discontinuing all supplements, the patient showed dramatic improvement. Within six weeks, liver enzymes nearly normalized... at one year, his liver enzymes were completely normal." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2931391/

rulebook.rule: N-acetylcysteine (initiated as supportive care during admission) can mitigate pro-oxidant effects of copper-ascorbate combinations; its use as treatment lowers the severity trajectory but does not address the underlying copper burden and requires supplement discontinuation for resolution.
rulebook.bears_on: Therapeutic mitigation of copper-ascorbate pro-oxidant injury
rulebook.source: NAC and copper-ascorbate toxicity (NCBI): "Systemic protein oxidation in serum, intestine, bladder, and kidney [from copper-ascorbate combination] was entirely preventable with thiol antioxidants like N-acetylcysteine, confirming the free radical mechanism." https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9181168/

rulebook.rule: Homozygous Factor V Leiden (thrombophilia) in setting of 7-year DOAC exposure lowers the likelihood that the DOAC itself caused acute hepatotoxicity (long-standing tolerance) and raises consideration of acquired susceptibility to supplement-induced injury through vascular/microcirculatory mechanisms, though direct causality is not established.
rulebook.bears_on: DOAC-induced hepatotoxicity vs. acquired susceptibility to supplement injury
rulebook.source: Factor V Leiden thrombophilia overview (GeneReviews/NCBI): Factor V Leiden is the most common hereditary blood coagulation disorder; patients on DOACs for thrombophilia are at baseline increased thrombotic risk. Hepatotoxicity from DOACs after 7 years is unlikely. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1368/ and https://www.webmd.com/dvt/factor-v-leiden

rulebook.rule: Prodromal symptoms of vague upper-abdominal fullness over several weeks preceding acute presentation raises consideration of a building toxicological burden or metabolic derangement rather than acute infectious onset, consistent with supplement-induced toxic accumulation.
rulebook.bears_on: Insidious toxic accumulation vs. acute viral or autoimmune hepatitis
rulebook.source: Hepatotoxin accumulation patterns (LiverTox): "Liver injury tends to arise after 24 to 72 hours following ingestion of toxic amounts," but chronic lower-level exposure produces gradual symptomatology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548090/

rulebook.rule: Early abdominal ultrasound showing normal hepatic architecture without cirrhosis, contrasted with later cross-sectional imaging demonstrating nodular contour and portal hypertension findings, raises the likelihood of acute/subacute parenchymal injury (hepatitis) with secondary portal hypertension developing during the clinical course, rather than pre-existing cirrhosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute hepatitis with reactive portal hypertension vs. pre-existing cirrhosis
rulebook.source: Acute hepatitis and portal hypertension development (NCBI): Acute severe hepatocellular necrosis with regeneration can cause functional portal hypertension and architectural remodeling without fibrosis. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3070012/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Acute copper hepatotoxicity from oral copper supplementation.

Recommended next action: Confirm with 24-hour urinary copper excretion (expect elevated), quantitative copper content on liver biopsy (expect >250 mcg/g dry weight; normal <50), and slit-lamp examination to rule out Descemet's membrane rings of Wilson disease. Continue supportive care (NAC, ursodeoxycholic acid) with copper-free diet and monitoring for recovery as copper is eliminated.

Confidence: 95% — The abnormal copper deposition on liver biopsy combined with documented oral copper supplementation, temporal relationship (dose escalation → acute hepatitis within 1 day), hepatocellular pattern of injury with cholestasis, negative infectious/autoimmune/genetic workup, normal ceruloplasmin (ruling out Wilson disease), and imaging evidence of severe hepatitis make this diagnosis nearly certain.

Reasoning: Copper is a known hepatotoxin. Acute high-dose exposure causes direct hepatocyte injury explaining the panacinar necrosis seen on biopsy 1. The special stain demonstrating abnormal liver copper is pathognomonic. The constellation of negative testing for common hepatitis etiologies combined with a clear source of exposure makes this straightforward toxicology rather than a systemic disease.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 44-year-old man with no prior liver disease presented with acute severe hepatotoxicity following a self-directed supplement regimen lasting 3-4 months (F5), with a marked dose escalation immediately preceding illness onset (F17). The diagnosis is acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity, with the following supporting evidence:

EXPOSURE AND CLINICAL PRESENTATION:
The patient took daily oral copper (F6) for approximately one month, escalated doses of this and other supplements, and developed acute RUQ pain with dark urine one day later (F17). This acute symptom onset following dose escalation is characteristic of acute copper toxicity (R1). He then developed jaundice, pruritus, and severe fatigue (F20), consistent with acute hepatocellular necrosis.

BIOCHEMICAL PATTERN:
Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated AST (880 U/L) and ALT (540 U/L) (F21, F22) with predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (direct 172 µmol/L of total 248 µmol/L) (F27, F28), coagulopathy (INR 1.5) (F26), and hypoalbuminemia (27 g/L) (F25) — a pattern consistent with acute hepatocellular necrosis from a hepatotoxic agent (R3).

HISTOPATHOLOGY:
The first biopsy showed subacute severe hepatitis with confluent panacinar hepatocyte necrosis involving ~50% of the specimen, without fibrosis or cirrhosis (F53, F54, F56). By the second biopsy, there was minimal necrosis with prominent hepatocyte regeneration (F57, F58) — a progression consistent with acute supplement-induced hepatotoxicity in its recovery phase (R4). Critically, special staining revealed abnormally high hepatic copper deposition (F59), directly confirming copper-induced liver injury (R5).

SYNERGISTIC MECHANISM:
The concurrent use of high-dose intravenous ascorbic acid (F7) alongside oral copper supplementation raises the likelihood of synergistic hepatotoxicity (R2), as ascorbate enhances hepatic copper uptake and mobilization, potentiating oxidative injury.

EXCLUSION OF ALTERNATIVE ETIOLOGIES:
A comprehensive diagnostic workup ruled out major infectious (negative viral serology for HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, EBV, CMV, HIV, Bartonella, syphilis, malaria [F30–F39]), autoimmune (negative ANA, anti-LKM, anti-smooth-muscle, anti-mitochondrial M2 [F40–F43]), and genetic metabolic etiologies (negative hemochromatosis and alpha-1-antitrypsin screening [F44, F45]). Alcohol and acetaminophen were undetectable (F46, F47), excluding common toxins (R7, R8, R9). The long-standing DOAC tolerance over 7 years (F3) and homozygous Factor V Leiden indication (F2) make the anticoagulant an unlikely culprit (R13). These exclusions direct the diagnosis toward supplement-induced toxicity.

PORTAL HYPERTENSION AND IMAGING:
Early abdominal ultrasound showed normal hepatic architecture without cirrhosis (F48). However, subsequent imaging demonstrated a lobulated nodular liver contour with lobar redistribution, splenomegaly, and features of portal hypertension (F49–F51), with an elevated hepatic venous pressure gradient of ~13 mmHg (normal <5) (F52). This imaging progression despite the absence of established fibrosis or cirrhosis on biopsy (F56) suggests acute sinusoidal injury, functional obstruction from severe hepatitis, or nodular regenerative hyperplasia causing secondary portal hypertension, rather than pre-existing or cirrhotic disease (R10, R15).

CERULOPLASMIN AND WILSON DISEASE:
Serum ceruloplasmin was 305 mg/L, within the normal range (200–600) (F29). While inherited Wilson disease classically presents with low ceruloplasmin, normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude acquired copper-induced hepatotoxicity, as this clinical syndrome arises from exogenous copper exposure and acute sinusoidal injury rather than defective copper transport (R6).

TREATMENT RESPONSE:
All supplements and infusions were discontinued upon admission (F62), and the patient received supportive care with N-acetylcysteine (F63), vitamin K (F64), and ursodeoxycholic acid (F65). The histological improvement between biopsies (from severe panacinar necrosis to minimal necrosis with regeneration) aligns with the expected trajectory of supplement-induced hepatotoxicity following exposure withdrawal, consistent with clinical reports of rapid recovery after discontinuation (R11).

CONCLUSION:
The diagnosis is acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity, likely potentiated by synergistic ascorbate-copper interaction, manifesting as acute hepatocellular necrosis with secondary non-cirrhotic portal hypertension. Inherited Wilson disease is excluded by the absence of classic genetic/enzymatic features and the acute, dose-dependent onset after exogenous copper exposure. The normal ceruloplasmin and regenerative histology support acquired rather than inherited disease. The marked improvement in histology post-discontinuation and the absence of cirrhosis on biopsy are consistent with acute toxic injury amenable to recovery rather than progressive liver disease.

Key uncertainties remain regarding the final results of the targeted copper testing (24-hour urinary copper, quantitative biopsy copper concentration, and Kayser-Fleischer ring examination [U4, U5, U6]) and the patient's clinical outcome trajectory (biochemical recovery, organ function recovery, need for transplantation [Q3, Q6]), which would further confirm and stage the severity of copper overload and prognosis.
per_case.framework_top: Acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity with secondary non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, potentiated by synergistic ascorbate-copper interaction
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain and report results of the three targeted copper tests (24-hour urinary copper collection, quantitative hepatic copper from biopsy specimen, slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings) to confirm and stage the degree of copper overload; assess liver biochemistry and INR trajectory during admission to document recovery vs. progression; consider long-term follow-up imaging to exclude development of true cirrhosis or persistent nodular regenerative hyperplasia
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high (70-80%) for acute copper-induced hepatotoxicity as the primary diagnosis; lower confidence (60-70%) for portal hypertension mechanism and long-term prognosis pending unreported test results and clinical course data
