per_case.rationale: Both outputs land on "copper hepatotoxicity" rather than the ground truth's broader framing of drug-induced liver injury from a complex naturopathic regimen (copper plus herbal weight product, ashwagandha, selenium), so neither nails the full final diagnosis. However, B is meaningfully closer and more defensible. B frames the etiology as supplement/DILI-induced toxicity, lists the multi-supplement regimen, correctly handles the central teaching nuance — that elevated stainable copper reflects EXOGENOUS ingestion and that normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude acquired copper toxicity — and is well-calibrated, explicitly flagging that urinary copper, quantitative biopsy copper, and Kayser-Fleischer exam are still pending (matching ground truth where those refuted Wilson). Its reasoning is fully traceable via finding/rule citations. B's weakness is a speculative, unsupported "synergistic ascorbate-copper" mechanism, but it is hedged as a likelihood. A makes two errors that the case specifically warns against: it predicts quantitative hepatic copper will be ">250 mcg/g (Wilson range)" — yet ground truth says quantitative copper was NOT diagnostic of Wilson — and it calls the copper stain "pathognomonic," which is precisely the trap that drove the wrong initial Wilson impression. A's 95% confidence is therefore overstated and its key confirmatory recommendation is backwards. Both correctly note normal ceruloplasmin excludes Wilson and both recommend stopping exposure with NAC/UDCA supportive care, but A's reasoning is less defensible.

per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old man, a former agricultural laborer who had relocated to a large coastal city about a decade earlier, was admitted for evaluation of recurrent jaundice. His scleral and skin yellowing had come and gone over roughly six years. He neither drank alcohol nor used tobacco, took no regular medications, and his family history was noncontributory. He had not traveled abroad or to any rural province since moving to the city.

The first episode, about six years before this admission, consisted of unintentional weight loss, poor sleep, and a dry cough without fever. Sputum examination for acid-fast bacilli was negative at that time, but a chest radiograph together with abdominal ultrasound and abdominal CT were interpreted as showing combined hepatic and pulmonary infection of granulomatous type. He was treated with a standard four-drug regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for six months, along with ursodeoxycholic acid, and improved: he regained the lost weight and his jaundice faded.

He remained reasonably well until about eighteen months before the current admission, when jaundice returned, now accompanied by severe, symmetric joint pain involving the shoulders, hips, and all four limbs. There was no fever, cough, or weight loss. Repeat ultrasound and CT showed the same hepatic lesions as before, plus an incidentally noted collapsed lumbar vertebra; this was attributed to skeletal extension of the prior infection and he completed a further year-long antimicrobial course with full compliance and symptom resolution.

A few months after finishing that course, his jaundice worsened again, now with vague upper-abdominal pain, vomiting, and intermittent fevers, prompting the current admission.

On arrival he appeared thin and deeply jaundiced. Temperature peaked at 38.5 C, heart rate 104/min, and the remaining vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and mildly distended with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and no rebound; an ill-defined right-upper-quadrant mass was palpable. Breath sounds were clear throughout. There was no lymphadenopathy. The working impression on admission was acute cholangitis.

Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. HIV testing was negative. A nucleic-acid amplification assay (GeneXpert) for M. tuberculosis on admission was negative.

Laboratory results:
- Alkaline phosphatase 208 U/L (ref 30-120)
- AST 71 U/L (ref <35)
- ALT 49 U/L (ref <35)
- Total bilirubin 284 micromol/L (ref 5-21)
- Direct bilirubin 139 micromol/L (ref <3.4)
- Indirect bilirubin 145 micromol/L (ref 3.4-11.9)
- Albumin 30 g/L (ref 35-52)
- Creatinine 61 micromol/L (ref 39-91)
- C-reactive protein 12.6 mg/dL (ref <1.0)
- Sodium 137 mmol/L (ref 136-146)
- Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (ref 3.5-5.1)
- Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL (ref 12.1-15.1, sex-appropriate range applied)
- Hematocrit 37% (ref 36-45)
- Leukocytes 19.4 x10^3/microL (ref 4.0-11.0)
- Neutrophils 90%
- Lymphocytes 6%
- Platelets 88 x10^3/microL (ref 140-400)
- Prothrombin time 22.6 s (ref 11.5-14.3)
- Partial thromboplastin time 31.8 s (ref 27.7-32.9)
- INR 1.74

A contrast-enhanced CT showed an enlarged liver with otherwise normal parenchymal density apart from coarse irregular calcifications in segments V and VII; comparison with the studies from several years earlier showed the same calcifications but with clear interval enlargement, especially in segment VII. No discrete enhancing mass was seen. There was no concentric periportal layered enhancement, no broad septal enhancement, and no septal calcification. Intrahepatic bile ducts were dilated. The gallbladder was distended, about 8 x 5 cm, with minimal pericholecystic fluid, in keeping with hydrops and cholecystitis. The common bile duct was widened (about 9 mm) from extrinsic compression by enlarged calcified perihilar nodes. The spleen was enlarged. The portal vein was not dilated and no collateral vessels were identified. The chest radiograph showed regressing hazy upper-zone opacities and a small stable ovoid right-upper-zone density.

No preoperative liver biopsy was obtained owing to local disease prevalence, cost, and patient preference. He was kept nil by mouth and given a proton-pump inhibitor, an antispasmodic, intravenous analgesia, and fluids; potassium was repleted. Abdominal pain resolved within hours. He was placed on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Because of the gallbladder hydrops he consented to surgery and underwent open cholecystectomy with intraoperative ultrasound. At operation the liver had a diffusely nodular surface with a firm yellow-white calcified nodule on segment VII; biopsies were taken of the hepatic nodule, the peritoneal wall, and omentum. Intraoperative ultrasound demonstrated prominently thickened portal tracts with surrounding hyperechoic change.

The postoperative course was uneventful and he was discharged after about a week, with steadily falling bilirubin.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Chronic hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (advanced, with Symmers "pipestem" periportal fibrosis), almost certainly Schistosoma japonicum given the endemic Philippine origin. The years-long course was misdiagnosed and treated as hepatic + pulmonary tuberculosis (then "bone TB").

HOW CONFIRMED: Tissue diagnosis. Liver/hepatic-nodule biopsy taken at open cholecystectomy showed multiple Schistosoma eggs on histology, establishing the diagnosis. Intraoperative findings corroborated it: grossly diffusely nodular liver, a yellow-white calcified nodule (segment VII), and intraoperative ultrasound showing thickened portal tracts characteristic of Symmers pipestem fibrosis. Supportive negatives that argue against the mimic (TB): sputum smear negative, GeneXpert/CB-NAAT negative for M. tuberculosis, and hepatic lesions that progressed despite full multi-course anti-TB therapy (with apparent clinical improvement attributable to concurrent ursodeoxycholic acid, not anti-TB drugs). CT lacked the classic schistosomiasis signs (no periportal "turtle-shell" concentric/septal enhancement or septal calcification), which is why imaging alone misled clinicians toward calcified-granuloma TB.

KEY DISCRIMINATOR: Patient originated from a rural region endemic for BOTH schistosomiasis and TB; calcified hepatic lesions are nonspecific. The lesson is that calcified hepatic granulomatous disease in such a patient is not pathognomonic for TB, and biopsy is required when lesions progress on anti-TB therapy.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize schistosomal etiology and treat with praziquantel (antihelminthic to reduce worm burden); at advanced fibrotic stage cure of fibrosis is not expected, so management also targets portal-hypertension sequelae / variceal-bleeding surveillance (UGI endoscopy) and supportive hepatic care. Avoid committing to indefinite empiric anti-TB therapy without tissue confirmation. In the actual case: open cholecystectomy for gallbladder hydrops/cholecystitis, broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole) for the cholangitis episode, then outpatient praziquantel (annual dosing), with incidental later findings of a duodenal ulcer with melena (Forrest III) and a newly detected hepatitis B infection (started tenofovir). Patient recovered with declining bilirubin and no further complaints at follow-up.

SOURCE: Albano JE, Ma-alat RBB. "Misdiagnosis of Hepatosplenic Schistosomiasis as Hepatic Tuberculosis: A Case Report." Cureus 15(2): e35169, 2023. DOI 10.7759/cureus.35169. Open access (CC-BY). Original patient: 38F housewife, Davao de Oro, Philippines.

uncertainties.about: Etiology of granulomatous infection
uncertainties.domain: Infectious disease pathology. Initial diagnosis based on imaging alone (granulomatous type); AFB negative on sputum (F12), GeneXpert negative on admission (F34). Differential remains open: tuberculosis (despite negative tests, immunocompromised TB possible), endemic fungi (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis), non-tuberculous mycobacteria (MAC), atypical infections, or sarcoidosis. Occupational history (agriculture, coastal city) and travel restrictions noted but incomplete for excluding all endemic infections.

uncertainties.about: Mechanism of relapse after first completed treatment
uncertainties.domain: Clinical microbiology and pharmacology. Patient completed full 6-month regimen (F14) with clinical improvement (F15), yet jaundice recurred (F17). Unknown whether this represents: relapse (organism persistence due to seeded foci, sanctuary sites, or inadequate penetration), reinfection (new exposure), or slow progression of underlying disease despite treatment. No repeat mycobacterial cultures or genotyping provided to discriminate these.

uncertainties.about: Pathogenesis and significance of lumbar vertebral collapse
uncertainties.domain: Spine pathology and osteomyelitis. Collapse attributed to 'skeletal extension of prior infection' (F20), but mechanism unspecified: Could represent Pott's disease (tuberculous spondylodiscitis), direct granulomatous infiltration of vertebral body, compression fracture from metabolic bone disease, or neoplastic involvement. No imaging follow-up of vertebra documented in current presentation (F19 notes collapse but no current biopsy mentioned); relationship to systemic recurrence unclear.

uncertainties.about: Etiology of second-episode polyarthralgia
uncertainties.domain: Rheumatology and immunology. Second episode featured severe symmetric polyarthralgia (shoulders, hips, all four limbs, F17) WITHOUT fever, cough, or weight loss (F18) — atypical for acute infectious exacerbation. Differential includes: immune complex arthritis, reactivity to granulomatous disease, medication side effect (rifampicin, isoniazid), paraneoplastic syndrome, or unrelated rheumatologic condition.

uncertainties.about: Identity and pathology of enlarged calcified perihilar nodes
uncertainties.domain: Diagnostic pathology and lymph node etiology. CT shows 'enlarged calcified perihilar nodes' causing CBD compression (F62), presumed granulomatous but unbiopsied. Differential diagnosis: granulomatous TB/MAC/fungal, malignancy (lymphoma, metastases), old TB with benign calcification, fungal infection, sarcoidosis. No nodal core needle biopsy or FNA documented.

uncertainties.about: Definitive histopathologic diagnosis of liver lesions
uncertainties.domain: Hepatic pathology and diagnostic confirmation. Initial imaging (F13) interpreted as 'granulomatous' but not histologically confirmed. Intraoperative biopsies obtained (F71) from hepatic nodule, peritoneal wall, and omentum, but final pathology report with organism identification, stains, and culture results not provided in case summary.

uncertainties.about: Causative relationship between biliary obstruction and gallbladder hydrops
uncertainties.domain: Hepatobiliary pathophysiology. Gallbladder hydrops in setting of 'acute cholangitis' (F29) attributed to extrinsic CBD compression by nodes (F62), but hydrops is non-specific and can arise from other causes: prolonged fasting/NPO status (patient was nil by mouth, F67), underlying hepatic disease, lymphatic obstruction, sepsis, or even unrelated gallbladder pathology. Direct causality not histologically proven.

uncertainties.about: Relationship between elevated indirect bilirubin and hepatic/obstructive etiology
uncertainties.domain: Biochemistry and liver physiology. Total bilirubin 284 (F38), direct 139 (F39), indirect 145 (F40) — indirect bilirubin exceeds reference range (3.4–11.9). Typically obstructive/hepatic jaundice is predominantly direct; elevated indirect suggests concomitant hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, or advanced cirrhosis with shunting. No hemolytic screen documented; mechanism of indirect hyperbilirubinemia unclear.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Recurrent Echinococcus (hydatid) disease, Echinococcus granulosus, with hepatic cyst calcification and secondary biliary obstruction/cholangitis. The coarse parenchymal calcifications, calcified perihilar nodes, relapsing pattern of jaundice over years despite TB treatment, agricultural background, and intraoperative findings (firm calcified nodule, portal tract thickening) are pathognomonic.

Recommended next action: (1) Review intraoperative biopsies with pathology for echinococcal cyst architecture and parasitic organisms; (2) order echinococcal-specific serology (ELISA or IHA); (3) initiate albendazole as adjunctive therapy; (4) screen for extrahepatic echinococcosis given collapsed vertebra.

Confidence: 85%. The imaging pattern and clinical recurrence are highly characteristic of echinococcosis. Remaining uncertainty reflects possible rare mimics and the need for histopathologic and serologic confirmation.

Reasoning: The prior "TB treatment" likely provided transient anti-inflammatory benefit rather than curative therapy for parasitic disease. The relapsing jaundice reflects intermittent biliary compression from progressively enlarging and calcifying cysts. Negative GeneXpert, lack of response to TB monotherapy alone, and the specific calcification pattern all point away from tuberculosis and toward helminthic infection.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
## Clinical Synthesis

**Chief Finding:** A 34-year-old former agricultural laborer with occupational and environmental exposure presents with a relapsing granulomatous hepatobiliary disease characterized by three episodes of jaundice, granulomatous imaging findings, polyarthralgia, skeletal involvement, and calcified perihilar lymphadenitis causing mechanical cholangitis over a 6-year period.

**Supporting Radiographic Evidence:**
The CT imaging reveals coarse irregular hepatic calcifications in segments V and VII with interval enlargement [F56, F57], intrahepatic bile duct dilation [F60], extrinsic CBD compression by enlarged calcified perihilar nodes [F62], and absence of periportal or septal enhancement [F59]. Intraoperatively, a firm yellow-white calcified nodule was noted on segment VII [F70] with prominently thickened portal tracts [F72]. These findings are consistent with granulomatous cholangitis with mechanical obstruction [BIL-1].

**Differential Diagnosis Evaluation:**

**Tuberculosis (TB):** Against this diagnosis:
- AFB sputum examination was negative initially [F12], lowering likelihood of cavitary TB [TB-4].
- GeneXpert MTB was negative on admission [F34], which despite >99% sensitivity for cavitary disease, does not exclude disseminated TB [TB-5].
- **Most critically**, the patient has had three episodes (initial at 6 years before admission [F10, F15], second relapse ~18 months before [F17, F21], third relapse "a few months after" completing the year-long course [F22]) within 6–7 years. Standard TB relapse rate is 4–5%, making three relapses highly unusual [TB-3, EPI-1]. 
- The imaging pattern shows calcifications consistent with hepatic TB [TB-1], and the collapsed lumbar vertebra is consistent with Pott's disease [TB-6]. However, the absence of periportal/septal enhancement [F59] lowers likelihood of the classic TB caseating pattern [HIS-2].

**Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis:** Supporting this diagnosis:
- **Occupational exposure**: Former agricultural laborer [F2] with occupational history conferring +84% increased odds for chronic fungal disease [HIS-1]. 
- **Endemic geography**: Relocated to large coastal city ~10 years ago [F3], placing him in endemic zone for *Coccidioides immitis* [COCC-1]. Notably, absence of recent rural travel [F9] does NOT exclude coccidioidomycosis, as decade-long residence is sufficient for ongoing environmental exposure [EPI-2].
- **Polyarthralgia pattern**: Second episode featured severe symmetric polyarthralgia of shoulders, hips, and all four limbs WITHOUT fever, cough, or weight loss [F17, F18]. This pattern—immune complex-mediated arthritis without constitutional symptoms—is characteristic of disseminated coccidioidomycosis [COCC-2].
- **Relapsing course**: Three relapses over 6–7 years is consistent with chronic coccidioidomycosis from ongoing or recurrent environmental exposure [HIS-3, EPI-1]. Unlike TB, endemic fungal disease commonly presents with cycling remission and relapse [EPI-1].
- **Skeletal involvement**: Vertebral collapse [F19] and calcified lymph nodes [F62] are consistent with disseminated coccidioidomycosis involving osseous and nodal systems [COCC-4].
- **Hepatic granulomas**: Granulomatous hepatitis with hepatomegaly and elevated alkaline phosphatase (208 U/L [F35]) in an endemic region is consistent with disseminated coccidioidomycosis, though symptomatic hepatitis is rare [COCC-3].
- **Calcification pattern**: Coarse hepatic calcifications [F56, F57] fit both TB and coccidioidomycosis, but the relapsing pattern and polyarthralgia favor coccidioidomycosis.

**Chronic Histoplasmosis:** Supporting:
- Occupational agricultural history raises likelihood [HIS-1].
- Relapsing course over years is consistent with chronic histoplasmosis from occupational re-exposure [HIS-3].
- Against: Absence of periportal enhancement [F59] somewhat lowers TB-like pattern [HIS-2], but this is not TB-specific. Histoplasmosis typically does not produce the degree of lymphadenitis and CBD compression seen here.

**Sarcoidosis or Non-Infectious Granulomatous Disease (SARC-1):** Supporting:
- Granulomatous lesions presumed on imaging but not confirmed by organism identification on AFB, culture, or molecular testing [F12, F34, SARC-1].
- Symmetric polyarthralgia is consistent with sarcoidosis [SARC-2].
- Against: Three episodes with recurrence after completed antimicrobial therapy argue against non-infectious etiologies, which typically present as single chronic presentations. The negative serology for HIV [F33], the elevated inflammatory markers [F43], and the response to antimicrobial therapy in episodes 1 and 2 [F15, F21] favor infection over sarcoidosis.

**Non-Tuberculous Mycobacteria (NTM):** Supporting:
- Negative AFB sputum [F12] and negative GeneXpert MTB [F34] with disseminated granulomatous disease raise likelihood of MAC, *M. kansasii*, or other NTM [NTM-1].
- Against: Patient was treated with four-drug TB regimen including rifampicin and ethambutol, both active against many NTM, yet still relapsed—less consistent with NTM than with a pathogen for which the standard regimen is ineffective.

**Blastomycosis:** Disfavored:
- Coarse hepatic calcifications are NOT commonly seen in blastomycosis [BLAST-1], lowering this diagnosis.

## Laboratory and Pathophysiologic Integration

**Obstructive Cholestasis with Indirect Hyperbilirubinemia:**
Total bilirubin is markedly elevated at 284 micromol/L [F38], with direct 139 and indirect 145 [F39, F40]. In typical obstructive jaundice, bilirubin is predominantly direct. Elevated indirect bilirubin (145 exceeds reference 3.4–11.9) raises concern for concurrent hemolysis or advanced cirrhosis with portosystemic shunting [HEM-1]. No hemolytic screen is documented, leaving this partially unexplained. The elevated indirect fraction may reflect advanced hepatic synthetic dysfunction (see below) rather than primary hemolysis.

**Hepatic Synthetic Dysfunction:**
Albumin is low at 30 g/L [F41], PT prolonged at 22.6 s [F52], INR elevated at 1.74 [F54], and platelets reduced at 88 [F51]—findings indicating advanced hepatic synthetic dysfunction consistent with cirrhosis from chronic granulomatous disease [HEM-2]. This constellation suggests not acute cholangitis alone, but rather chronic parenchymal disease with superimposed obstruction.

**Acute Inflammatory Response:**
Leukocytosis of 19.4 (ref 4.0–11.0) [F48] with left shift (neutrophils 90% [F49]) and elevated CRP of 12.6 [F43] indicate acute bacterial superinfection. The clinical presentation on admission was acute cholangitis [F29]—defined by fever [F24], biliary obstruction [F62], and signs of infection—overlaying the chronic granulomatous substrate [HEM-3]. Empiric ceftriaxone and metronidazole [F68] were appropriately initiated and the abdominal pain resolved within hours [F67], supporting bacterial superinfection on chronic disease.

## Why Standard TB Therapy Failed

The patient received a full, compliant 6-month four-drug regimen for episode 1 [F14] and a year-long course for episode 2 [F21], yet presented with a third relapse within months [F22]. Standard TB relapse rate is ~4–5% [TB-3]. Three relapses in 6–7 years is statistically inconsistent with TB and instead suggests either:
1. **Misdiagnosis**: The underlying pathogen is not *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* but rather an organism either resistant to the regimen (unlikely given the clinical improvement after each course) or for which the regimen is suboptimal—such as endemic fungi.
2. **Sanctuary sites or inadequate penetration**: Less likely if compliant, but possible in TB with poor CNS or bone penetration.
3. **Reinfection vs. relapse**: If coccidioidomycosis, recurrent exposure from environmental reservoir would explain the cycling pattern.

The data are more consistent with **relapsing disseminated coccidioidomycosis** than with TB.

## Critical Missing Diagnostic Elements

The case summary does not provide:
- **Final histopathology from intraoperative biopsies [F71]**: Organism identification (stains: GMS, PAS for fungi; Ziehl-Neelsen for AFB; culture), cell types, and extent of granulomatous inflammation would definitively resolve the differential.
- **Coccidioidal serology**: No mention of complement fixation, immunodiffusion, or antigen/antibody assays for *Coccidioides*.
- **Fungal culture results**: From sputum, tissue, or body fluids.
- **Hemolytic panel**: To exclude hemolysis as contributor to elevated indirect bilirubin.
- **Gallbladder/bile duct histology** from cholecystectomy specimen: Could show coccidioidal granulomas or organisms.

## Integration and Conclusion

The **most parsimonious diagnosis**, given available evidence, is **disseminated coccidioidomycosis** with:
- Chronic hepatic granulomas and calcifications [COCC-3]
- Perihilar lymphadenitis with mechanical CBD compression and tuberculous-cholangitis-like pattern [COCC-4, BIL-1]
- Polyarthralgia from immune complex disease [COCC-2]
- Osseous involvement (Pott's-disease-like vertebral collapse) [COCC-4]
- Relapsing course from ongoing environmental exposure [HIS-3, EPI-1, EPI-2]

**Alternative diagnoses in order of likelihood:**
1. Tuberculosis (especially if intraoperative biopsy shows caseating granulomas with AFB or TB PCR)
2. Chronic histoplasmosis
3. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria
4. Sarcoidosis (unlikely given response to antimicrobials and relapsing pattern)

The negative AFB [F12], negative GeneXpert [F34], extraordinarily high relapse rate, severe polyarthralgia without fever, occupational and endemic exposure, and decade of residence in coastal endemic zone all **support coccidioidomycosis over TB**. However, **TB cannot be excluded without histopathology**, and the calcification pattern and Pott's-like vertebral disease are classic for TB.

**The definitive diagnosis hinges on pathology [F71] and serologic/fungal culture results, which have not been reported in this summary.**
per_case.framework_top: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis with hepatic granulomas, calcified perihilar lymphadenitis, tuberculous cholangitis-like pattern, and osseous involvement, causing relapsing obstructive jaundice and polyarthralgia.
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain final histopathology and special stains from intraoperative biopsies (hepatic nodule, peritoneal, omentum) with fungal culture and PCR for Coccidioides immitis; if organism identified, initiate long-term antifungal therapy (fluconazole or itraconazole). If biopsies show granulomas without organism, perform coccidioidal serology (complement fixation, immunodiffusion, ELISA) and consider empiric antifungal trial given occupational/endemic epidemiology and relapsing pattern. Assess for immune compromise (repeat HIV, lymphocyte count trend).

Histoplasmosis and sarcoidosis are also plausible but less likely given severity and pattern.

per_case.rationale: Ground truth is chronic hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. japonicum), confirmed by liver biopsy showing Schistosoma eggs, in a Philippine patient misdiagnosed/treated as hepatic+pulmonary TB; correct management is praziquantel plus portal-hypertension surveillance, with the lesson being that biopsy is required when calcified hepatic lesions progress on anti-TB therapy. Neither output names schistosomiasis. Output B concludes recurrent Echinococcus (hydatid) disease — wrong organism, but it lands in the correct disease CLASS (a chronic parasitic helminthic liver infection misdiagnosed as TB) and its recommended workup is directionally correct: review biopsy for parasitic organisms, parasitic serology, and an antiparasitic drug (albendazole vs. the correct praziquantel). This captures the case's central, load-bearing insight ("parasite, not TB"). Output A concludes disseminated coccidioidomycosis with TB/histoplasmosis/NTM/sarcoidosis as alternatives, and never considers parasitic/helminthic disease at all — a fungal answer that is conceptually further from the egg/worm-mediated fibrotic truth. A's strengths are calibration and thoroughness: it correctly weights the negative AFB/GeneXpert, the failure of anti-TB therapy, and explicitly states the diagnosis hinges on unreported histopathology, appropriately hedging that TB cannot be excluded. A's weaknesses are anchoring on the wrong organism class and using heavy false-precision citation tags (e.g., "+84% odds [HIS-1]", "[COCC-2]") that are not traceable/defensible. B's weakness is overconfidence (85%, calls non-specific findings "pathognomonic") on a wrong specific organism. On balance, correctness toward the actual etiology and the correct management direction (the point of the case) favors B; A is better calibrated but commits to a more distant wrong answer. Both are partially correct.

per_case.prose:
A 59-year-old woman with no notable past medical history presented to the emergency department after about one month of progressive yellowing of the eyes and skin, dull right-upper-quadrant and epigastric discomfort, intermittent nausea, and two episodes of vomiting. She had been taking an over-the-counter proton-pump inhibitor for presumed dyspepsia without relief, and over the preceding week had developed generalized itching. She did not smoke, drank no alcohol, used no recreational drugs, and reported no family history of cancer. She had not traveled recently and was on no other medications.

On examination she was febrile at 38.4°C, deeply icteric, with scleral icterus and excoriations from scratching. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant; there was no palpable mass and no peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 16.8 mg/dL with direct (conjugated) bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 612 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 41 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 44 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase 588 U/L; amylase 62 U/L. The white-cell count was 12,800/µL, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, and platelets 244,000/µL. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. Alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and CA 19-9 were all within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated dilatation of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, a normal-caliber gallbladder wall initially, a small (about 14 mm) calculus impacted at the gallbladder neck, and an ill-defined hypoechoic oval area roughly 13 × 21 mm near the hepatic hilum. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a large infiltrative lesion with poorly defined margins occupying the central liver and extending into both the right and left lobes, showing only mild enhancement after contrast. The mass encased the right and left hepatic ducts and the proximal common hepatic duct, producing upstream intrahepatic biliary dilatation, while the common bile duct remained normal in caliber. The gallbladder wall appeared thickened and edematous with surrounding fluid and small calculi. No enlarged abdominal lymph nodes were identified.

The patient underwent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with placement of a biliary stent to relieve the obstruction; brush cytology specimens were obtained from the strictured ducts. She subsequently underwent cholecystectomy and a tissue sampling of the hilar lesion, and a bone-marrow sampling was also performed.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Primary hepatic lymphoma — diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) — presenting as an infiltrative perihilar liver mass causing obstructive jaundice and clinically mimicking a Klatskin-type hilar cholangiocarcinoma. CONFIRMATION: CT-/surgically obtained core biopsy of the liver hilar mass showed sheets of large lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm; immunohistochemistry was positive for CD20 with a high Ki-67 proliferation index, establishing large B-cell lymphoma. Biliary brush cytology was negative for carcinoma, and bone-marrow biopsy was normal (supporting PRIMARY hepatic, rather than secondary/disseminated, lymphoma). Disproportionate cholestatic LFT pattern (very high alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin with only mildly elevated transaminases), elevated LDH, negative viral hepatitis serologies, and normal AFP/CEA/CA19-9 were the discriminating clues. CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT a surgical/resection or palliative-stent-only biliary-cancer case — recognizing it as lymphoma changes management entirely to hematology referral, staging, and systemic chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP: rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone), which the patient responded well to. Biliary decompression (stent) is supportive only. Key teaching point: a normal-tumor-marker, markedly cholestatic, infiltrative perihilar mass with raised LDH and negative brush cytology should prompt biopsy for lymphoma before committing to a cholangiocarcinoma pathway. Source: Primary Hepatic Lymphoma Mimicking Cholangiocarcinoma, PMC5534224.

rulebook.rule: Large infiltrative hilar mass with poorly defined margins (13×21 mm hypoechoic lesion near hepatic hilum progressing to large infiltrative central lesion on CT) raises suspicion for cholangiocarcinoma versus benign stricture; poorly demarcated mass is characteristic of malignancy.
rulebook.source: Radiological diagnosis and staging of hilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3731524): hilar cholangiocarcinomas manifest as 'ill-defined hypoechoic oval areas near the hepatic hilum' with 'intrahepatic segmental biliary dilatation'

rulebook.rule: Lesion encasing both right and left hepatic ducts at their confluence (proximal common hepatic duct) is pathognomonic for hilar (Klatskin) location and raises cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis; this anatomy defines the Klatskin tumor.
rulebook.source: Hilar cholangiocarcinoma – Augusta Health and Klatskin Tumor overview (ScienceDirect Topics): Klatskin tumors arise 'at the bifurcation of the common hepatic duct' with 60-70% of cholangiocarcinomas in the perihilar region

rulebook.rule: Upstream intrahepatic biliary dilatation with normal-caliber common bile duct distal to obstruction is consistent with obstruction at or proximal to the hepatic duct confluence; this pattern preserves the distal duct because the obstruction occurs upstream of it.
rulebook.source: Biliary Obstruction – StatPearls (NBK539698): obstruction location determines which segments dilate proximally; hilar obstruction spares the common bile duct distal to the confluencce

rulebook.rule: Mild enhancement on contrast CT with only faint arterial and portal venous phase enhancement in hilar mass is consistent with cholangiocarcinoma's characteristic desmoplastic (fibrotic) nature; malignant strictures show delayed, marked enhancement patterns.
rulebook.source: Radiological diagnosis and staging of hilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3731524): periductal thickening shows 'iso-hypo enhancement in arterial/portal phases with marked delayed enhancement,' and 'some tumors may show arterial hyperenhancement' but desmoplasia limits enhancement

rulebook.rule: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia (10.2 mg/dL of 16.8 total) with elevated alkaline phosphatase (612 U/L) and normal transaminases (AST 41, ALT 44) indicates cholestasis from biliary obstruction rather than hepatocellular injury.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): perihilar cholangiocarcinoma presents with 'painless jaundice' from biliary obstruction; laboratory pattern reflects cholestasis (elevated ALP) not hepatitis (normal transaminases)

rulebook.rule: Progressive jaundice (icterus) over one month with pruritus onset over preceding week is classic for obstructive jaundice; intrahepatic cholestasis causes pruritus and incremental bilirubin rise.
rulebook.source: Acute cholangitis – Knowledge @ AMBOSS: obstructive jaundice from biliary obstruction presents with progressive jaundice, pruritus, and RUQ pain; bile duct strictures are a known cause

rulebook.rule: Fever (38.4°C) with elevated WBC (12,800/µL) and elevated inflammatory markers (LDH 588 U/L) in context of biliary obstruction and stricture raises concern for cholangitis or secondary infection; fever indicates systemic inflammatory response.
rulebook.bears_on: Cholangitis from biliary obstruction and infection
rulebook.source: Acute cholangitis – Knowledge @ AMBOSS and Biliary Obstruction (StatPearls NBK539698): fever >38°C, elevated WBC, and elevated CRP are diagnostic criteria for acute cholangitis; bile duct obstruction predisposes to ascending infection

rulebook.rule: Patient presents with Charcot's triad component (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) consistent with ascending cholangitis; full triad present only in ~70% of cholangitis cases but presence raises infection risk.
rulebook.bears_on: Cholangitis from biliary obstruction and infection
rulebook.source: Charcot's Triad – AMBOSS and Charcot's cholangitis triad (Wikipedia): classic triad of RUQ pain, jaundice, and fever occurs in ~70% of patients with ascending cholangitis, though not universally required for diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Normal serology (negative hepatitis A, B, C) lowers probability of viral hepatitis as cause of jaundice; does not exclude obstruction or malignancy.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): serological testing for viral hepatitis is part of risk-factor assessment for cholangiocarcinoma; negative results rule out viral etiology

rulebook.rule: Normal tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) do not exclude cholangiocarcinoma; CA 19-9 has 76% sensitivity at >100 U/mL but low sensitivity at lower levels, and 23% of CCA cases are CA 19-9 negative.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): CA 19-9 has sensitivity 76% and specificity 92% at >100 U/mL, but normal levels do not exclude diagnosis; combined markers (AFP, CEA) are less specific for CCA

rulebook.rule: Brush cytology from strictured ducts has low sensitivity (~20-42%) due to cholangiocarcinoma's desmoplastic nature; negative cytology does not exclude malignancy. FISH analysis increases sensitivity to 40-90%.
rulebook.source: Triple modality testing by ERCP for diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma (PMC4314305) and Clinical diagnosis (PMC6448701): brush cytology alone has sensitivity ~20-42% and 100% specificity; triple modality (cytology + biopsy + FISH) achieves 82% sensitivity and 100% specificity

rulebook.rule: Mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL) can reflect anemia of chronic disease from malignancy or may indicate bone-marrow involvement; in malignancy without marrow infiltration, hemoglobin typically >8 g/dL.
rulebook.source: Anemia of Chronic Disease – Merck Manual Professional Edition: anemia of chronic disease occurs in malignancies not causing marrow infiltration; hemoglobin typically >8 g/dL unless additional mechanism present

rulebook.rule: Elevated LDH (588 U/L) with normal transaminases can reflect systemic inflammation or tissue turnover from malignancy; LDH is nonspecific marker for cellular damage.
rulebook.source: Radiological diagnosis and staging of hilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3731524): systemic inflammatory response from malignancy can elevate LDH; nonspecific finding

rulebook.rule: No enlarged abdominal lymph nodes on CT lowers probability of extensive nodal metastases; however, ~33% of hilar cholangiocarcinomas have lymph node involvement, and absent node enlargement does not exclude N1 disease.
rulebook.source: Hilar cholangiocarcinoma: diagnosis and staging (PMC2043098): nodal metastases occur in up to one-third of hilar cholangiocarcinoma cases; imaging may underdetect microscopic nodal disease

rulebook.rule: Hilar mass encase right and left hepatic ducts but no explicit vascular involvement mentioned (hepatic artery, portal vein encasement not mentioned in imaging); vascular invasion is a major factor for prognosis and resectability.
rulebook.source: Prognostic Impact of Preoperative Imaging Parameters on Resectability of Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3687508): hepatic artery and portal vein involvement are independent predictors of unresectability; resectability ranges from 32-80%

rulebook.rule: Bone-marrow biopsy is indicated in suspected malignancy to assess for metastatic infiltration or hematologic abnormality; bone marrow involvement in cholangiocarcinoma is rare (disseminated carcinomatosis in <1% of cases) but affects prognosis.
rulebook.source: Disseminated Carcinomatosis of Bone Marrow as Initial Presentation of Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma (PMC8943367): DCBM occurs in small fraction of CCA cases but when present is associated with poor prognosis; bone metastases found in 8.3% of cases with extrahepatic disease

rulebook.rule: Impacted gallstone at gallbladder neck (14 mm calculus) with edematous thickened gallbladder wall and surrounding fluid raises secondary cholecystitis from biliary obstruction; does not explain hilar mass or cholestasis.
rulebook.source: Biliary Obstruction – StatPearls (NBK539698): gallbladder changes reflect downstream obstruction effect; gallstones alone do not explain hilar stricture at duct confluence

rulebook.rule: Absence of family history of cancer and absence of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) or liver flukes reduces risk factors typically associated with cholangiocarcinoma; however, most hilar CCA cases arise de novo without identified risk factors.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): PSC and liver flukes are key risk factors; absence of these reduces pre-test probability but does not exclude CCA

rulebook.rule: Presence of hilar mass with imaging characteristics (ill-defined margin, mild enhancement, periductal involvement) combined with normal CA 19-9 does not exclude cholangiocarcinoma; perihilar mass on MRI is diagnostic criterion for CCA even with normal markers.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): diagnosis criteria include 'perihilar mass on MRI with CA 19-9 >100' or 'positive cytology with FISH confirmation'; imaging mass alone is highly suggestive

rulebook.rule: MRI/MRCP with 90% sensitivity and 76% specificity for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is gold-standard imaging modality; CT has high sensitivity but MRI superior for detection of tumor extent and vascular/ductal involvement.
rulebook.source: Clinical diagnosis and management of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC6448701): 'MRI with MRCP is imaging technique of choice with 90% sensitivity and 76% specificity; superior for bile duct extent and vascular involvement'

rulebook.rule: Tissue diagnosis via biopsy from hilar lesion is critical for definitive diagnosis; brush cytology alone insufficient. Tissue sampling should be accompanied by FISH analysis for chromosomal aberrations to maximize sensitivity.
rulebook.source: Triple modality testing by ERCP for diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma (PMC4314305): triple modality (brush cytology + biopsy + FISH) achieves 82% sensitivity and 100% specificity vs brush cytology alone (42% sensitivity)

rulebook.rule: Wall thickening >1.5 mm at strictured ducts on imaging suggests malignancy; benign strictures typically <1.5 mm wall thickness. This patient's imaging shows periductal involvement consistent with infiltration.
rulebook.source: Radiological diagnosis and staging of hilar cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3731524): 'bile duct wall thickness greater than 1.5 mm' and 'irregular outer margins' and 'asymmetric narrowing' suggest malignancy vs benign stricture

rulebook.rule: Prognosis for hilar cholangiocarcinoma depends on resectability, TNM stage, lymph node involvement, and vascular invasion. Recent surgical series report 5-year survival >40% in resected patients vs 9% historical rates, indicating improved surgical outcomes.
rulebook.source: Prognostic Impact of Preoperative Imaging Parameters on Resectability of Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma (PMC3687508): survival of T3 tumors significantly lower than earlier stages; hepatic artery and lymph node involvement major prognostic factors; modern series show >40% 5-year survival after resection

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor) — a malignant tumor at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts.

Recommended next action: Await tissue biopsy and brush cytology results; complete staging with chest imaging and advanced liver imaging (MRCP); assess resectability and vascular involvement; consider neoadjuvant chemotherapy depending on stage.

Confidence: 90%

Reasoning: The clinical triad of progressive obstructive jaundice, a hilar mass encasing the hepatic duct confluence with upstream intrahepatic biliary dilatation, and a normal-caliber distal common bile duct is pathognomonic for Klatskin tumor. Negative hepatitis serologies and normal tumor markers don't exclude it. The interventions already performed (ERCP with stent, biopsy, cholecystectomy) are consistent with this diagnosis. Poor prognosis without resection, but the modest mass size may allow surgical consideration if no vascular invasion or metastatic disease.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 59-year-old woman presents with a clinical and radiologic picture highly consistent with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor).

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE:

The radiologic findings are strongly suggestive of malignancy at the hepatic duct confluence. The large infiltrative hilar mass (13×21 mm hypoechoic lesion progressing to large central infiltrative lesion on CT) with poorly defined margins raises suspicion for cholangiocarcinoma [R1]. The mass encases both the right and left hepatic ducts at their confluence (proximal common hepatic duct) [F45, F46, F47], which is pathognomonic for hilar (Klatskin) location and raises the cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis [R2]. The upstream intrahepatic biliary dilatation with normal-caliber common bile duct distal to the obstruction [F38, F48, F49] is consistent with obstruction at the hepatic duct confluence and reflects the anatomic location [R3]. The mild enhancement on contrast CT with only faint arterial and portal venous phase enhancement [F44] is consistent with cholangiocarcinoma's characteristic desmoplastic (fibrotic) nature [R4].

The laboratory pattern indicates obstructive rather than hepatocellular pathology. Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia (10.2 mg/dL of 16.8 total) [F23] with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (612 U/L) [F24] and normal transaminases (AST 41 U/L, ALT 44 U/L) [F25, F26] indicates cholestasis from biliary obstruction rather than hepatocellular injury [R5].

The clinical presentation is consistent with progressive obstructive jaundice. Progressive jaundice (yellowing of eyes and skin over one month) [F10, F11] with pruritus onset over the preceding week [F14] is classic for obstructive jaundice [R6]. The patient presented with fever (38.4°C) [F15], elevated white-cell count (12,800/µL) [F29], and elevated LDH (588 U/L) [F27], raising concern for cholangitis or secondary infection [R7]. The patient exhibits components of Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) [F12, F15, F16] consistent with ascending cholangitis [R8].

FACTORS LOWERING PROBABILITY (but not excluding diagnosis):

Normal tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) [F35, F36, F37] do not exclude cholangiocarcinoma, as CA 19-9 has only 76% sensitivity at >100 U/mL and 23% of CCA cases are CA 19-9 negative [R10]. The absence of identified risk factors (no family history of cancer [F6], no noted primary sclerosing cholangitis or liver flukes) [R18] reduces typical pre-test probability, though most hilar CCA cases arise de novo. No enlarged abdominal lymph nodes were identified on CT [F53], which lowers probability of extensive nodal metastases but does not exclude N1 disease, as approximately 33% of hilar cholangiocarcinomas have lymph node involvement [R14]. Negative hepatitis serology (hepatitis A, B, C) [F32, F33, F34] rules out viral hepatitis as the cause of obstruction [R9] but is irrelevant to excluding malignancy.

CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS:

The definitive diagnosis of malignancy is pending tissue diagnosis. Brush cytology obtained during ERCP [F55] has low sensitivity (20-42%) due to cholangiocarcinoma's desmoplastic nature; negative cytology alone does not exclude malignancy [R11]. Tissue sampling of the hilar lesion [F57] is critical, and FISH analysis should accompany the tissue biopsy, as triple-modality testing (brush cytology + tissue biopsy + FISH) achieves 82% sensitivity and 100% specificity versus brush cytology alone [R21].

The bone-marrow biopsy [F58] is indicated to assess for metastatic bone-marrow infiltration or hematologic abnormality [R16]. Mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL) [F30] may reflect anemia of chronic disease from malignancy or, if bone-marrow involvement is present, indicates disseminated disease with poor prognosis [R12]. Bone-marrow involvement in cholangiocarcinoma is rare (disseminated carcinomatosis in <1% of cases) but affects prognosis when present [R16].

STAGING AND PROGNOSIS:

Once malignancy is confirmed, TNM staging and assessment of resectability are essential. No vascular invasion was mentioned in the imaging report (hepatic artery and portal vein involvement not documented), which is a favorable prognostic sign [R15], though vascular involvement is a major factor for prognosis and unresectability. Hilar cholangiocarcinoma resectability ranges from 32% to 80% [R15]. Prognosis depends on TNM stage, lymph node involvement, and vascular invasion [R23]; modern surgical series report >40% five-year survival in resected patients, compared to 9% historical rates, indicating improved outcomes with modern surgical techniques [R23].

IN SUMMARY: The imaging characteristics (ill-defined hilar mass, duct encasement at the confluence, upstream biliary dilatation with spared distal CBD), laboratory pattern (cholestasis without hepatocellular injury), and clinical presentation (progressive jaundice with pruritus and fever) are highly consistent with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Definitive diagnosis awaits histopathology, brush cytology with FISH, and bone-marrow interpretation. If malignancy is confirmed, the patient requires TNM staging and resectability assessment to guide surgical versus palliative management.
per_case.framework_top: Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor) — highly likely based on imaging and clinical presentation; tissue diagnosis pending.

Confidence is limited pending tissue diagnosis, as brush cytology alone has only 20-42% sensitivity (R11). Normal tumor markers (R10) and lack of identified risk factors (R18) slightly reduce pre-test probability but do not exclude malignancy.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs arrive at the WRONG final diagnosis: cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor), which is precisely the condition the ground-truth case is mimicking. The confirmed answer is primary hepatic lymphoma (DLBCL), establishing management is hematology/R-CHOP rather than the surgical-resection/staging pathway both outputs recommend. Neither output names lymphoma at all, so neither reaches the correct diagnosis or correct disposition.

However, the two outputs differ sharply in calibration and defensibility, which is decisive for the winner.

OUTPUT A: States cholangiocarcinoma at 90% confidence and calls the imaging triad "pathognomonic for Klatskin tumor." It explicitly dismisses the two most important discriminating clues — "Negative hepatitis serologies and normal tumor markers don't exclude it" — treating them as noise rather than as the signal pointing to an alternative. It is confidently and overconfidently wrong, with no consideration of lymphoma or any differential. The high confidence on the wrong answer is poorly calibrated and would lead directly to the wrong (resection/palliative-stent) pathway the ground truth warns against.

OUTPUT B: Also concludes cholangiocarcinoma, so it is equally incorrect on the headline diagnosis. But it is substantially better calibrated and more defensible: it repeatedly hedges ("highly consistent," "pending tissue diagnosis," "definitive diagnosis awaits histopathology"), foregrounds that tissue biopsy is the critical next step, and notably flags the LDH elevation (588), the mild anemia, the indication for bone-marrow biopsy, and even raises the possibility of disseminated/hematologic disease ("hematologic abnormality," "bone-marrow involvement"). It cites the negative brush cytology's limitations and pushes for biopsy before committing — which is exactly the ground-truth teaching point's procedural recommendation, even though B fails to name lymphoma as the hypothesis driving it. Its claims are traceable (finding/rule references), specific, and quantitatively grounded, and it does not foreclose the alternative the way A does.

Neither is correct, so both are scored incorrect on the diagnosis. But on the dimensions that distinguish a defensible miss from a reckless one — calibration, acknowledgment of uncertainty, insistence on tissue diagnosis before treatment, and noticing the LDH/anemia/bone-marrow signals that point toward lymphoma — B is clearly superior. A's 90% confidence with explicit dismissal of the discriminating clues is the more dangerous and less defensible answer. B wins.

per_case.prose:
A 46-year-old man was brought to a community hospital's emergency department by his family because of two days of progressive lethargy and overwhelming tiredness; he had become difficult to rouse on the morning of presentation. He had no reported abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, or change in stool or urine colour. On arrival he was afebrile and his blood pressure was 128/84 mmHg; the remainder of his vital signs were unremarkable and he was somnolent but arousable.

Initial bloodwork was striking for a hepatocellular pattern of injury together with a coagulation defect. Alanine aminotransferase was 2710 IU/L (reference 7–41) and aspartate aminotransferase was 1830 IU/L (reference 12–38). Lactate dehydrogenase was disproportionately elevated at 3460 U/L (reference 115–221). Alkaline phosphatase was near-normal at 84 IU/L, and total bilirubin was only 1.1 mg/dL (reference 0.3–1.3). The prothrombin time was prolonged at 23 seconds (reference 12.7–15.4) with an INR of 2.8. Serum sodium was 140 mmol/L and potassium was 4.2 mmol/L. He was admitted to the intensive care unit with a working diagnosis of acute liver failure with coagulopathy.

A broad workup for the usual causes of fulminant hepatocellular injury was undertaken. A viral hepatitis panel was unrevealing: hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, and hepatitis C antibody were all negative. Autoimmune markers showed only trivial positivity, with an antinuclear antibody titre of 1/50 and an anti–smooth muscle antibody titre of 1/50, neither considered clinically significant. Abdominal ultrasonography of the liver was normal, with no biliary dilatation, mass, or vascular abnormality.

On more detailed questioning of the patient and his relatives, it emerged that he had been taking a corticosteroid (dexamethasone) regularly for a prolonged period and had stopped the medication on his own roughly three days before this admission. Endocrine testing was then obtained, which showed a serum cortisol of 2.4 µg/dL and a plasma ACTH of 13 pg/dL (reference 9–52).

He was started on glucocorticoid replacement therapy. His liver enzymes and coagulation parameters improved steadily over the subsequent days, normalising by roughly the twelfth hospital day, and he was discharged in good general condition.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Secondary (tertiary) adrenal insufficiency precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of chronic exogenous glucocorticoid (dexamethasone), presenting as a hepatocellular "acute liver failure" picture. The transaminitis/coagulopathy was a manifestation of acute adrenal/cortisol deficiency, NOT primary liver disease.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Biochemical — low serum cortisol (2.5 µg/dL) with an inappropriately non-elevated/low-normal ACTH (11 pg/dL, ref 9–52), consistent with central/secondary adrenal insufficiency from HPA-axis suppression by chronic steroid use. (2) History — chronic dexamethasone use discontinued 3 days before presentation. (3) Exclusion — negative viral hepatitis serologies (HAV IgM, HBsAg, HBcAb, HCV Ab all negative), only trivial autoimmune titres (ANA 1/50, ASMA 1/50), normal liver ultrasound, no biliary obstruction. (4) Therapeutic confirmation — rapid, complete normalization of liver enzymes and coagulopathy after glucocorticoid replacement (prednisolone), with discharge in good condition by ~day 12.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Do NOT manage as fulminant hepatic failure / transplant workup. Recognize glucocorticoid-withdrawal adrenal insufficiency; give stress-dose then maintenance glucocorticoid replacement (the case used prednisolone), supportive care, and taper/education to avoid abrupt steroid cessation. Liver recovers fully without hepatology-specific intervention. Source: Anvari E, et al. "Adrenal Insufficiency as a Cause of Acute Liver Failure: A Case Report," Case Reports in Endocrinology, 2013 (PMC3596948).

rulebook.rule: Finding: Markedly elevated aminotransferases (ALT 2710 U/L, AST 1830 U/L, both >50× reference) with ALT > AST ratio raises hepatocellular acute hepatocellular injury as primary candidate diagnosis.
rulebook.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries (acgcdn.gi.org); Liver Function Tests - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482489/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Disproportionately elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 3460 U/L, ~1.9× AST) in the context of acute hepatocellular necrosis raises hypoxic/ischemic hepatitis or severe acute hepatocellular injury.
rulebook.source: Lactate dehydrogenase production in hepatocytes is increased at an early stage of acute liver failure - PMC (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3440653/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Preserved total bilirubin (1.1 mg/dL, normal range) despite extreme aminotransferase elevations lowers cholestatic or obstructive liver disease and favors hepatocellular necrosis as primary mechanism.
rulebook.bears_on: Cholestatic or obstructive disease (e.g., biliary obstruction, primary biliary/primary sclerosing cholangitis)
rulebook.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries; Liver Test Interpretation - Cleveland Clinic (my.clevelandclinic.org)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Near-normal alkaline phosphatase (84 U/L) despite hepatic injury lowers cholestasis, obstruction, and infiltrative disease; is consistent with hepatocellular necrosis pattern.
rulebook.bears_on: Cholestatic disease; biliary obstruction; infiltrative malignancy
rulebook.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries; Merck Manual Laboratory Tests of the Liver and Gallbladder (merckmanuals.com)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Prolonged PT (23 sec) and elevated INR (2.8) in setting of acute hepatocellular injury raises severe impairment of hepatic synthetic function, a hallmark of acute liver failure.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute liver failure; severe hepatocellular dysfunction
rulebook.source: Guidance for Coagulation Management in Patients With Acute or Chronic Liver Failure - Gastroenterology & Hepatology (gastroenterologyandhepatology.net); How to assess hemostasis in patients with severe liver disease - American Society of Hematology (ashpublications.org)

rulebook.rule: Finding: PT/INR abnormality reflects impaired hepatic synthesis of Factors II, V, VII, and X (all produced by hepatocytes), confirming acute reduction in hepatocyte functional mass.
rulebook.source: Liver Function Tests - StatPearls (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482489/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Negative hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, HBcAb, HCV antibody lowers viral hepatitis (A, B, C) as primary etiology.
rulebook.source: Case presentation (negative serologies exclude acute and chronic viral hepatitis)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Trivial autoimmune markers (ANA 1/50, ASMA 1/50, both non-significant) lowers autoimmune hepatitis as primary etiology.
rulebook.source: Case presentation (autoimmune markers explicitly described as not clinically significant)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Normal abdominal ultrasound with no mass, biliary dilatation, or vascular abnormality lowers primary biliary/sclerosing cholangitis, hepatic masses, and acute vascular thrombosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Obstructive biliary disease; hepatocellular carcinoma; hepatic vascular thrombosis; cirrhosis
rulebook.source: Case presentation (imaging findings negative)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Recent chronic dexamethasone use (prolonged period) followed by abrupt self-discontinuation 3 days before symptom onset raises iatrogenic corticosteroid withdrawal as precipitant of acute hepatocellular injury.
rulebook.source: Corticosteroids - LiverTox - NCBI Bookshelf (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548400/); A case of drug-induced acute liver failure caused by corticosteroids - Springer (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12328-022-01661-1)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal causes immune reconstitution flare if underlying viral or autoimmune hepatitis present; raises severe hepatocellular injury even in seronegative cases through direct hepatotoxicity or undefined immune-mediated mechanism.
rulebook.source: Corticosteroids - LiverTox: withdrawal or pulse therapy can cause severe flares and fulminant hepatic failure; high doses of IV corticosteroids cause acute liver injury with ALF and death (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548400/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Low serum cortisol (2.4 µg/dL, below 8 AM normal ~5-25) in context of recent glucocorticoid withdrawal raises secondary adrenal insufficiency due to HPA axis suppression.
rulebook.source: Glucocorticoid-Induced Adrenal Insufficiency - Endocrine Society (endocrine.org); Adrenal Suppression - Endotext (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279047/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: ACTH at lower end of normal range (13 pg/dL, reference 9-52) paired with low cortisol (2.4 µg/dL) raises secondary adrenal insufficiency; ACTH should be elevated if adrenal glands were primary failure source.
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) adrenal insufficiency rather than primary adrenal failure
rulebook.source: Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency - Merck Manual Professional (merckmanuals.com); Physiology, ACTH - StatPearls (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500031/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Preserved serum sodium (140 mmol/L) and potassium (4.2 mmol/L, both normal) lowers primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), where hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are characteristic; consistent with secondary insufficiency where mineralocorticoid axis remains intact.
rulebook.source: Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency - Merck Manual: aldosterone secretion remains normal in secondary insufficiency, so hyponatremia and hyperkalemia do not occur (merckmanuals.com)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure >3-4 weeks causes inevitable HPA axis suppression; abrupt cessation precipitates acute secondary adrenal insufficiency with loss of endogenous cortisol production.
rulebook.source: Adrenal Suppression - Endotext: Prolonged administration of supraphysiological corticosteroid doses exceeding 3-4 weeks may result in HPA axis suppression (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279047/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Acute hepatocellular injury with coagulopathy normalizing within ~12 days of initiating glucocorticoid replacement therapy raises mechanistic link between adrenal insufficiency and transient hepatocellular dysfunction; recovery of cortisol production restores hepatic synthetic function.
rulebook.bears_on: Corticosteroid withdrawal-induced acute hepatocellular injury mediated through secondary adrenal insufficiency
rulebook.source: Case presentation (clinical response to glucocorticoid replacement); inferred from LiverTox mechanism of corticosteroid withdrawal flares (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548400/)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Lethargy, somnolence, and difficulty rousing on morning of presentation in context of acute hepatocellular injury with coagulopathy raise hepatic encephalopathy and/or acute adrenal insufficiency with CNS depression.
rulebook.bears_on: Hepatic encephalopathy; acute adrenal insufficiency with altered mental status
rulebook.source: Acute Liver Failure - Hepatology - Merck Manual (merckmanuals.com): hepatic encephalopathy is defining feature of ALF

rulebook.rule: Finding: Absence of jaundice (bilirubin 1.1, normal) despite extreme transaminase elevation consistent with rapidly evolving acute hepatocellular necrosis before bilirubin accumulation; raises fulminant course.
rulebook.bears_on: Fulminant acute liver failure; rapidly progressive hepatocellular necrosis
rulebook.source: Acute Liver Failure - Merck Manual: fulminant hepatic failure develops within days; bilirubin may not be markedly elevated in earliest phase (merckmanuals.com)

rulebook.rule: Finding: Normalization of PT, INR, and transaminases by hospital day 12 following glucocorticoid replacement, without specific antiviral or immunosuppressive therapy, lowers viral hepatitis reactivation as sole mechanism; supports metabolic/endocrine dysfunction reversible by steroid replacement.
rulebook.bears_on: Viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV reactivation) as primary mechanism
rulebook.source: LiverTox (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548400/): viral reactivation requires specific antiviral therapy; rapid recovery with glucocorticoid monotherapy suggests alternative mechanism

rulebook.rule: Finding: Afebrile status and absence of fever throughout presentation lowers fulminant infectious hepatitis or septic hepatitis as primary etiology; consistent with metabolic or immune-mediated hepatocellular injury.
rulebook.bears_on: Infectious hepatitis; septic hepatitis; fulminant viral hepatitis with systemic infection
rulebook.source: Acute Liver Failure - Merck Manual (merckmanuals.com): infectious etiologies typically present with fever and systemic inflammatory response

per_case.blind_answer:
Most Likely Diagnosis: Acute adrenal crisis (secondary adrenal insufficiency from abrupt dexamethasone withdrawal) presenting with fulminant hepatocellular injury and coagulopathy.

Recommended Next Action: Immediately initiate IV hydrocortisone replacement (100 mg bolus followed by continuous infusion or frequent dosing q4-6h). Monitor clinical response, vital signs, and liver/coagulation parameters. Taper glucocorticoids as patient stabilizes over 7-14 days.

Confidence: 85-90%. The temporal relationship to abrupt steroid discontinuation, biochemical pattern (marked transaminitis, elevated LDH, coagulopathy with low bilirubin), low cortisol (2.4 µg/dL), and dramatic clinical and biochemical response to glucocorticoid replacement strongly support this diagnosis. The negative workup for viral hepatitis, autoimmune disease, and normal imaging excludes primary liver disease.

Reasoning: Adrenal crisis typically presents with hemodynamic collapse, but can manifest atypically with severe hepatocellular injury when cortisol deficiency triggers acute metabolic derangement and liver dysfunction. The patient's recovery coinciding exactly with glucocorticoid replacement confirms this diagnosis. This case highlights that adrenal insufficiency must be considered in acute liver failure with negative viral/autoimmune workup, especially with recent corticosteroid withdrawal history.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 46-year-old man presented with acute hepatocellular injury (F12-F13, R1) and severe coagulopathy (F19-F20, R5) in the setting of recent chronic dexamethasone use (F35) followed by abrupt self-discontinuation approximately three days before symptom onset (F36). The pattern of injury is hepatocellular: ALT and AST are markedly elevated (>50× reference, F12-F13, R1), with a characteristic disproportionately elevated lactate dehydrogenase (F14, R2) suggestive of acute hepatocellular necrosis. Cholestatic and obstructive disease are effectively excluded by preserved total bilirubin (F16, R3) and near-normal alkaline phosphatase (F15, R4). The coagulopathy (PT 23 sec, INR 2.8) reflects acute impairment of hepatic synthetic function (F19-F20, R5-R6).

Common causes of fulminant hepatocellular injury have been excluded: viral hepatitis A, B, and C serologies are negative (F24-F27, R7); autoimmune markers are non-significant (F28-F30, R8); and abdominal imaging shows no mass, vascular abnormality, or biliary obstruction (F31-F34, R9). The patient is afebrile (F4, F8) throughout, which lowers infectious etiologies (R20). Notably, he had no abdominal pain or change in stool/urine color (F7, F10-F11), findings that would suggest alternative hepatic pathologies.

The pivotal diagnostic clue is the temporal and pharmacologic correlation: the patient had been taking dexamethasone chronically (F35) and stopped it abruptly ~3 days before the onset of progressive lethargy and difficulty rousing (F2-F3, F36). This temporal sequence raises iatrogenic corticosteroid withdrawal as the precipitant (R10). The endocrine workup confirms secondary adrenal insufficiency: serum cortisol is low at 2.4 µg/dL (below the normal 8 AM range of ~5–25 µg/dL, F37, R12), and plasma ACTH is at the lower end of normal (13 pg/dL, reference 9–52, F38, R13). This pattern of low cortisol with inappropriately low-normal ACTH is diagnostic of secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) adrenal insufficiency (R13), not primary adrenal failure. This interpretation is supported by preserved electrolytes: sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.2 mmol/L (both normal, F21-F22), which rules out primary Addison disease where hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are characteristic due to mineralocorticoid loss (R14). The patient's prolonged prior dexamethasone exposure (>3-4 weeks implied by "prolonged period," F35) would inevitably have suppressed the HPA axis (R15); abrupt cessation precipitated acute loss of endogenous cortisol production.

The causal mechanism linking corticosteroid withdrawal and hepatocellular injury is established in the rulebook: withdrawal from chronic corticosteroid therapy can precipitate severe hepatocellular injury through immune reconstitution flare and/or direct hepatotoxicity (R10-R11). Acute secondary adrenal insufficiency itself may contribute to hepatocellular dysfunction through loss of cortisol's stabilizing effects on endothelial integrity, hepatocyte metabolism, and immune homeostasis; the exact mechanistic pathways are not fully detailed in the rulebook but are inferred from the clinical response.

The clinical course confirms the diagnosis: glucocorticoid replacement therapy (F39) led to rapid normalization of liver enzymes and coagulation parameters by approximately day 12 (F40-F41, R16). This normalization without specific antiviral therapy or other interventions lowers viral hepatitis reactivation as a primary mechanism (R19) and supports the metabolic/endocrine etiology. The patient was discharged in good general condition (F42).

In summary: the patient's acute hepatocellular injury with coagulopathy (mimicking fulminant liver failure) was secondary to abrupt cessation of chronic dexamethasone therapy, leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency (confirmed by low cortisol with low-normal ACTH and exclusion of primary adrenal failure by normal electrolytes). The temporal sequence (cessation → symptom onset in ~24 hours), biochemical confirmation (F37-F38), exclusion of alternative diagnoses (F24-F34), and dramatic clinical response to glucocorticoid replacement (F39-F41) collectively support this diagnosis with high confidence.
per_case.framework_top: Acute hepatocellular injury secondary to iatrogenic corticosteroid withdrawal and secondary adrenal insufficiency
per_case.framework_next_step: Document mechanism in literature review: corticosteroid withdrawal-induced hepatotoxicity as a recognized but rare cause of fulminant hepatic failure; confirm whether HPA-axis reconstitution alone (without other immunosuppression) is sufficient to reverse acute ALF in this phenotype, or whether concurrent cytokine/immune dysregulation plays a necessary mediating role
per_case.framework_confidence: High (85-90%). The diagnosis is supported by convergent evidence: temporal correlation between dexamethasone cessation and symptom onset (F36, U4), biochemical confirmation of secondary adrenal insufficiency (F37, F38 with R12, R13), exclusion of common etiologies via negative serology and imaging (F24-F34 with R7-R9), and dramatic clinical response to glucocorticoid replacement (F39-F41 with R16). However, confidence is not absolute (not 95+%) because (a) the mechanistic pathway from adrenal insufficiency to hepatocellular necrosis is incompletely elucidated in the rulebook, (b) the precise timing of cortisol draw relative to presentation and HPA-axis stress response is unclear (U6), and (c) the ACTH level (13 pg/dL) sits at the lower boundary of normal (R13, U7), raising subtle questions about the adequacy of adrenal response to stress.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct diagnosis: secondary adrenal insufficiency from abrupt dexamethasone withdrawal presenting as a hepatocellular acute-liver-failure picture, confirmed by low cortisol, exclusion of viral/autoimmune/obstructive causes, and dramatic response to glucocorticoid replacement. Both cite cortisol as 2.4 (GT 2.5) — a trivial, non-load-bearing discrepancy.

OUTPUT A is more complete and defensible on the diagnostic confirmation that the ground truth emphasizes: it explicitly distinguishes SECONDARY from PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency using the inappropriately low-normal ACTH (13 vs GT 11, ref 9–52) AND normal electrolytes (no hyponatremia/hyperkalemia ruling out Addison) — a key GT point that B handles only superficially. A's reasoning is fully traceable via finding/rule (F/R) citations, and it shows good calibration by explicitly hedging the uncertain mechanism ("exact mechanistic pathways are not fully detailed... inferred"). Its weakness is the absence of an explicit forward management/disposition plan.

OUTPUT B is correct, concise, and well-calibrated (85–90% confidence) and uniquely supplies the actionable disposition the GT calls for (stress-dose then maintenance glucocorticoid, taper over 7–14 days, do not treat as primary liver disease). Its hydrocortisone recommendation is clinically standard and defensible even though the case used prednisolone. However, it is thinner on the secondary-vs-primary biochemical distinction (barely uses ACTH, doesn't leverage electrolytes) and its "adrenal crisis" framing slightly overstates the (atypical, non-hemodynamic) presentation, though it acknowledges the atypicality.

Neither output hallucinates materially. A edges ahead on completeness of confirmation, the secondary/primary distinction central to the GT, and traceability; B is stronger on actionable disposition. Close call, but A's deeper, verifiable diagnostic reasoning wins.
