per_case.prose:
A 41-year-old previously healthy man came to the emergency department after roughly two weeks of feeling unwell. He described daily fevers that tended to spike in the evening and then break with drenching sweats, along with shaking chills, diffuse muscle and joint aches, and a nagging dry cough. He also reported a scratchy, painful throat that made swallowing uncomfortable. He had noticed a faint pink rash that came and went over his upper chest and one thigh, seeming most prominent when his temperature was highest and fading as he cooled down.

About twelve days earlier he had been seen at a walk-in clinic, told he had a chest infection, and started on an oral antibiotic. His symptoms briefly eased but returned within several days, and a second course of a different antibiotic made no difference, prompting his visit to the emergency department.

On arrival his triage vital signs were unremarkable, but during his time in the department his temperature rose to 39.4°C. He did not appear toxic between fever spikes. Examination showed mild pharyngeal erythema without exudate, a few scattered salmon-colored macules over the trunk that were difficult to photograph, and tenderness in several large joints without frank effusion. There was no neck stiffness, no murmur, and the abdomen was soft with mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 26.4 × 10⁹/L with a marked neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin and platelets within normal limits. Liver enzymes were elevated, with an AST of 96 U/L and ALT of 188 U/L; alkaline phosphatase was 688 U/L; total bilirubin was 1.6 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 1.1 mg/dL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was greater than 120 mm/hr and C-reactive protein was elevated. Lactate was mildly raised at 2.1 mmol/L on presentation and normalized after intravenous fluids. Serum ferritin returned strikingly elevated at approximately 22,000 ng/mL. Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were both negative. Blood cultures were drawn. A chest radiograph showed no consolidation, and an abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction.

He was admitted for further evaluation of a prolonged febrile illness.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD). Confirmation: diagnosis of exclusion made on inpatient rheumatology consultation using the Yamaguchi criteria after infectious workup was negative — supported by the classic constellation of quotidian spiking fever >39C, leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, evanescent salmon-colored rash, sore throat, arthralgias, hepatic enzyme derangement, very high ESR, NEGATIVE ANA and rheumatoid factor, and a markedly elevated ferritin (~24,000 ng/mL — extreme hyperferritinemia is a hallmark). Correct disposition: hospital admission; the right management is NOT continued/escalated antibiotics for presumed infection but a trial of systemic corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone ~60 mg/day) after excluding infection and malignancy, with rheumatology follow-up. Outcome in source: dramatic response to steroids within one week, WBC fell ~30% after one day of steroids, remission off steroids at one year. The diagnostic trap is anchoring on infection (urgent care called it pneumonia; ED initially called it viral syndrome / fever of unknown origin) and escalating antibiotics, when the marked hyperferritinemia + negative ANA/RF + evanescent rash + sore throat point to AOSD. NOT to be shown to answering arms.

rulebook.rule: Quotidian spiking fever (>39°C, late afternoon/evening pattern with drenching sweats) raises candidate diagnosis of Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) or acute rheumatic fever
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Acute Rheumatic Fever
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi criteria: fever ≥39°C lasting ≥1 week is a major criterion (AMBOSS); AOSD characterized by high-spiking fevers, transient, lasting typically <4 hours with highest temperatures in late afternoon/early evening (ScienceDirect); Acute rheumatic fever presents with fever as a minor criterion in Jones criteria (CDC)

rulebook.rule: Salmon-colored, non-pruritic evanescent macules appearing during fever spikes and fading as temperature normalizes raise candidate diagnosis of AOSD
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi criteria include typical non-pruritic salmon-colored rash as a major criterion (AMBOSS); AOSD rash is described as salmon-pink, maculopapular lesion involving proximal limbs and trunk, usually coinciding with fever onset (ScienceDirect); evanescent rash in AOSD most prominent when temperature highest and fades as patient cools down (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Evanescent rash that appears with fever spikes and correlates with temperature elevation (via thermal sensitivity) raises candidate diagnosis of evanescent exanthem, AOSD, or acute rheumatic fever
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Acute Rheumatic Fever; Viral exanthem
rulebook.source: Erythema marginatum in rheumatic fever is evanescent, disappearing on exposure to cold and reappearing after hot shower or warm blanket (ScienceDirect); in AOSD, generalized arthralgias/myalgias coincided with temperature elevations in febrile exanthems (NIH PMC); evanescent rashes demonstrate close temporal and thermal relationship with fever (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Myalgia and arthralgia with joint tenderness (without frank effusion) in large joints raise candidate diagnoses of AOSD, acute rheumatic fever, or systemic lupus erythematosus
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Acute Rheumatic Fever; Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi criteria: arthralgia or arthritis lasting ≥2 weeks is a major criterion for AOSD (AMBOSS); AOSD arthritis most commonly affects knees, wrists, ankles (ScienceDirect); SLE manifests with arthralgias/arthritis in 84% of patients (AAFP); acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints as major criterion (CDC)

rulebook.rule: Pharyngitis (sore throat, pharyngeal erythema) without exudate raises candidate diagnoses of acute rheumatic fever (as antecedent), infectious mononucleosis, or systemic inflammation
rulebook.bears_on: Acute Rheumatic Fever; Infectious Mononucleosis; Adult-Onset Still's Disease
rulebook.source: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis; latency period 1-5 weeks (CDC/StatPearls); EBV infectious mononucleosis presents with acute pharyngitis as part of classical triad (AMBOSS); sore throat is a minor criterion in Yamaguchi criteria for AOSD (AMBOSS)

rulebook.rule: Antibiotic-refractory fever (symptom recurrence after two courses of different antibiotics) lowers candidate diagnosis of bacterial infection and raises AOSD or rheumatic fever
rulebook.bears_on: Bacterial infection (lowers); Adult-Onset Still's Disease (raises); Acute Rheumatic Fever (raises)
rulebook.source: AOSD can present as antibiotic-refractory sepsis because it is not an infectious condition; antibiotic-refractory fever is a key diagnostic clue for AOSD (NIH PMC); rheumatic fever is a non-infectious, post-streptococcal inflammatory condition (CDC)

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated serum ferritin (22,000 ng/mL) raises candidate diagnosis of AOSD, macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), or hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Macrophage Activation Syndrome; Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi criteria emphasize markedly elevated serum ferritin exceeding 1,000 ng/mL as distinguishing feature of AOSD (ScienceDirect); ferritin >1,000 ng/mL is a frequent distinguishing feature of AOSD (ScienceDirect); profound hyperferritinemia characterizes secondary HLH/MAS in autoimmune disorders (NIH PMC); ferritin is acute phase reactant elevated during inflammation and macrophage activation (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Elevated transaminases (AST 96, ALT 188 U/L) with cholestasis (elevated ALP 688, bilirubin 1.6 with direct 1.1) raise candidate diagnoses of AOSD, EBV hepatitis, Q fever, or leptospirosis
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV); Q fever; Leptospirosis
rulebook.source: Abnormal liver function tests (elevated ALP and ALT) are a minor Yamaguchi criterion for AOSD (AMBOSS); hepatic inflammation in AOSD shows periportal mononuclear infiltrates and Kupffer-cell hyperplasia (NIH PMC); EBV hepatitis presents with elevated transaminases in 80-90% of cases (AMBOSS); Q fever hepatitis manifests as elevation of ALT and AST (NIH PMC); leptospirosis causes hepatitis in severe disease (CDC)

rulebook.rule: Hepatic cholestasis pattern (elevated alkaline phosphatase >600 U/L relative to transaminases; elevated direct bilirubin) with inflammatory markers raises candidate diagnosis of AOSD, Q fever, or systemic inflammation-mediated intrahepatic cholestasis
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Q fever; Intrahepatic Cholestasis from systemic inflammation
rulebook.source: AOSD abnormal liver function includes elevated alkaline phosphatase (Yamaguchi minor criterion; AMBOSS); Q fever causes hepatic inflammation with elevated transaminases and may present with cholestasis (NIH PMC); intrahepatic cholestasis secondary to sepsis/systemic inflammation occurs via Kupffer cell activation and release of pro-inflammatory mediators (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Marked leukocytosis (WBC 26.4 × 10⁹/L) with marked neutrophil predominance (>80%) raises candidate diagnosis of AOSD or bacterial infection
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi major criterion: leukocytosis ≥10,000/mm³ with granulocytes ≥80% (AMBOSS); Yamaguchi criteria emphasize leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance as major item (AMBOSS); AOSD characterized by neutrophilic leukocytosis (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Preserved hemoglobin and platelet counts (normal) despite marked systemic inflammation and elevated ferritin raise candidate diagnosis of AOSD over hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
rulebook.source: HLH typically presents with cytopenias including anemia and thrombocytopenia (NIH diagnostic criteria); preservation of hemoglobin/platelets despite hyperferritinemia and inflammation is more consistent with AOSD than HLH (contrast with HLH criteria requiring cytopenias)

rulebook.rule: Negative antinuclear antibody (ANA) and negative rheumatoid factor (RF) lower candidate diagnoses of classic SLE and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, but do not exclude seronegative SLE or AOSD
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (lowers); Rheumatoid Arthritis (lowers); Adult-Onset Still's Disease (raises)
rulebook.source: Negative ANA/RF are minor criteria supporting AOSD diagnosis in Yamaguchi framework (AMBOSS); seronegative SLE occurs in 2-5% of lupus cases and presents without ANA positivity (Healthline/NIH PMC); EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria mandate ANA positivity but alternative criteria like SLICC offer flexibility for seronegative cases (NIH PMC); diagnostic challenges in seronegative lupus may involve ANA entrapment in circulating immune complexes (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated ESR (>120 mm/hr) and elevated CRP raise candidate diagnoses of AOSD, acute rheumatic fever, or other systemic inflammatory/infectious processes
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Acute Rheumatic Fever; Systemic inflammation
rulebook.source: Elevated acute phase reactants (ESR and CRP) are minor Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever (CDC); AOSD characterized by elevated ESR and CRP (NIH PMC); elevated inflammatory markers support systemic inflammation across multiple diagnoses

rulebook.rule: Absence of neck stiffness lowers candidate diagnosis of meningitis but does not exclude aseptic meningitis or leptospirosis
rulebook.source: Leptospirosis may present with aseptic meningitis as severe manifestation; presence/absence of neck stiffness not specifically diagnostic (CDC); aseptic meningitis can occur without meningeal signs (general knowledge)

rulebook.rule: Absence of murmur on auscultation lowers candidate diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever with acute carditis, but does not exclude subclinical carditis
rulebook.bears_on: Acute Rheumatic Fever with symptomatic carditis (lowers); Acute Rheumatic Fever with subclinical carditis (neutral)
rulebook.source: Jones criteria include carditis (clinical or subclinical) as major criterion; clinical carditis may present with murmur, but subclinical carditis requires echocardiography for detection (CDC); absence of murmur does not exclude carditis

rulebook.rule: Mild right-upper-quadrant (RUQ) abdominal discomfort without hepatomegaly or biliary obstruction on imaging raises candidate diagnosis of hepatitis from systemic inflammation (AOSD, EBV, Q fever) but lowers acute biliary disease
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (raises); Hepatitis from systemic inflammation (raises); Acute biliary obstruction (lowers)
rulebook.source: RUQ discomfort in AOSD context is typically hepatic inflammation (NIH PMC); negative ultrasound rules out biliary obstruction; abdominal exam with soft abdomen is minor criterion context in Yamaguchi (clinical pearl)

rulebook.rule: No consolidation on chest radiograph lowers candidate diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia but does not exclude viral respiratory involvement or systemic inflammation
rulebook.bears_on: Bacterial pneumonia (lowers); Viral respiratory infection (neutral); Systemic inflammation (neutral)
rulebook.source: Clear CXR in setting of respiratory symptoms and fever supports non-bacterial etiology; typical presentation of AOSD does not include consolidation (clinical feature)

rulebook.rule: Dry cough (non-productive respiratory symptom) without consolidation or pleuritic findings raises candidate diagnosis of systemic inflammation (AOSD, viral infection, early rheumatic fever) over pneumonia
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Viral infection; Pneumonia (lowers)
rulebook.source: AOSD can present with respiratory symptoms in context of systemic inflammation; dry cough typical of viral and inflammatory conditions (clinical pearls)

rulebook.rule: Mildly elevated lactate (2.1 mmol/L on presentation, normalized after fluids) lowers candidate diagnosis of severe sepsis or tissue hypoxia; suggests compensated systemic inflammation or mild dehydration
rulebook.bears_on: Severe sepsis/shock (lowers); Systemic inflammation with adequate perfusion (raises)
rulebook.source: Mild lactate elevation resolving with fluids indicates non-ischemic cause; severe sepsis typically presents with higher lactate and more prolonged elevation (clinical physiology)

rulebook.rule: Age 41 years (adult, not pediatric) raises candidate diagnosis of Adult-Onset Still's Disease over Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis; is compatible with acute rheumatic fever (can occur in adults but more common in children), SLE, and other systemic conditions
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (raises); Acute Rheumatic Fever (neutral); Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (neutral)
rulebook.source: AOSD defined as Still's disease occurring in adults (AMBOSS); acute rheumatic fever epidemiology peaks in children/young adults but can occur in older individuals (CDC)

rulebook.rule: Previously healthy status (no prior immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic illness noted) raises candidate diagnosis of acute autoinflammatory disorder (AOSD) and lowers immunodeficiency-related infections
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (raises); Immunodeficiency-related opportunistic infection (lowers)
rulebook.source: AOSD typically occurs in previously healthy individuals (NORD); absence of immunosuppression lowers likelihood of opportunistic or atypical infections

rulebook.rule: Unprovoked two-week prodrome of constitutional symptoms ('feeling unwell') before overt fever onset raises candidate diagnosis of systemic inflammatory/autoinflammatory condition (AOSD) with gradual disease progression
rulebook.bears_on: Adult-Onset Still's Disease; Systemic inflammatory condition
rulebook.source: AOSD often presents as subacute progressive illness rather than abrupt onset (clinical feature); prodromal malaise common in systemic autoinflammatory conditions

rulebook.rule: Brief initial improvement followed by recurrence of fever and symptoms after first antibiotic course (and failure of second antibiotic) confirms antibiotic-refractory pattern, raising candidate diagnosis of AOSD and lowering bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
rulebook.source: AOSD presenting as antibiotic-refractory sepsis is documented clinical presentation (NIH PMC); initial brief improvement may reflect placebo effect or coincidental fever pattern; subsequent recurrence strongly suggests non-infectious etiology (clinical reasoning)

rulebook.rule: Constellation of quotidian high-grade fever (>39°C), transient salmon-colored rash, arthralgias, marked neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal hemoglobin/platelets, negative ANA/RF, and markedly elevated ferritin (>1,000 ng/mL) meets ≥5 Yamaguchi criteria including ≥2 major items, raising candidate diagnosis of AOSD (diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out infection, malignancy, other rheumatic disease)
rulebook.source: Yamaguchi criteria (sensitivity 96%, specificity 92%) require ≥5 criteria including ≥2 major: fever ≥39°C/≥1 week, arthralgia/arthritis ≥2 weeks, typical salmon rash, leukocytosis ≥10,000/mm³ with granulocytes ≥80%; plus minor: sore throat, lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly, abnormal LFTs, negative ANA/RF (AMBOSS); hyperferritin ≥1,000 ng/mL is frequently present (ScienceDirect)

rulebook.rule: Group A Streptococcus antecedent pharyngitis followed by latency period of 1-5 weeks prior to fever/rash onset raises candidate diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever; however, documented antecedent GAS pharyngitis is not documented in this case (only 'chest infection' diagnosed)
rulebook.direction: raises (if GAS pharyngitis confirmed); lowers (if GAS pharyngitis excluded)
rulebook.source: ARF follows GAS pharyngitis with latency 1-5 weeks, typically 2-4 weeks (CDC/StatPearls); ARF pathophysiology involves molecular mimicry response to bacterial antigens (CDC); diagnosis requires confirmation of antecedent GAS infection (Jones criteria) or recent strep serology

rulebook.rule: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) are in the differential for marked hyperferritinemia but are lowers because hemoglobin and platelet counts are preserved (HLH criteria require cytopenias)
rulebook.bears_on: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis; Macrophage Activation Syndrome (potential but less likely given preserved cytopenias)
rulebook.source: HLH diagnostic criteria include cytopenias (NIH criteria); profound hyperferritinemia can occur in both AOSD and HLH/MAS but cytopenias distinguish HLH (NIH PMC); MAS in autoimmune setting presents with cytopenias and hyperferritinemia (NIH PMC)

rulebook.rule: Blood cultures (pending/unknown result) are needed to definitively lower bacterial infection candidate diagnoses; if sterile, further supports autoinflammatory etiology (AOSD) over bacteremia
rulebook.bears_on: Bacterial sepsis/bloodstream infection (pending result); Adult-Onset Still's Disease (pending result)
rulebook.direction: lowers (if negative: bacterial infection); raises (if negative: AOSD)
rulebook.source: Blood culture status is critical for excluding bacteremia; sterile cultures in antibiotic-refractory fever support AOSD diagnosis (NIH PMC); negative cultures after antibiotic exposure do not exclude AOSD (clinical reasoning)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD). This diagnosis is supported by the classic triad of spiking fevers + evanescent salmon-pink rash + arthralgias, combined with extraordinarily elevated ferritin (~22,000 ng/mL), marked ESR/CRP elevation, hepatic cholestasis, pharyngitis, and failure to respond to antibiotics. Negative ANA and RF exclude typical rheumatologic mimics; the clinical pattern and laboratory abnormalities are autoinflammatory rather than infectious.

Recommended next action: Confirm negative blood cultures. Begin empiric corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) — a dramatic defervescence within 24–48 hours would confirm the diagnosis. Arrange IL-6 or IL-1 inhibitor therapy if conventional steroids fail or for steroid-sparing maintenance.

Confidence: 78%. The ferritin elevation is nearly pathognomonic for AOSD in this clinical context; the rash, fever pattern, and hepatic involvement fit perfectly. Remaining uncertainty stems from alternative systemic autoinflammatory conditions (macrophage activation, periodic fever syndromes) that would show similar but not identical patterns.

Reasoning: AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder of unknown etiology presenting with quotidian spiking fevers, quotidian evanescent rash, and arthralgia/arthritis. Markedly elevated ferritin (>10,000–20,000 ng/mL) is nearly diagnostic. The negative ANA/RF and failure to respond to empiric antibiotics exclude infectious endocarditis and typical rheumatic disease. Liver involvement with cholestatic pattern is common. The young, previously healthy male presentation is typical.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 41-year-old previously healthy man [fact_2] with a two-week prodrome of constitutional malaise [fact_3, fact_22] presenting with quotidian high-grade fever spiking to 39.4°C in the evening with drenching sweats [fact_4, fact_14] meets multiple major Yamaguchi criteria for Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD). 

The cardinal features supporting AOSD diagnosis are: (1) High-spiking fever pattern [fact_4, rule_1] characteristic of AOSD; (2) Salmon-colored, non-pruritic evanescent macules over trunk and thigh [fact_8, fact_17] that correlate temporally with fever spikes [fact_9, rule_2, rule_3]; (3) Myalgia and arthralgia with joint tenderness in large joints without effusion [fact_5, fact_18, rule_4]; (4) Markedly elevated serum ferritin at 22,000 ng/mL [fact_34, rule_7], which far exceeds the Yamaguchi threshold of >1,000 ng/mL; (5) Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 26.4 × 10⁹/L with neutrophil predominance) [fact_22, fact_23, rule_10]; (6) Elevated transaminases and cholestatic pattern [fact_25, fact_26, fact_27, fact_28, fact_29, rule_8, rule_9]; (7) Markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >120 mm/hr, elevated CRP) [fact_30, fact_31, rule_13]; (8) Negative ANA and rheumatoid factor, which are supporting minor criteria for AOSD [fact_35, fact_36, rule_12]; and (9) Preserved hemoglobin and platelet counts despite marked systemic inflammation and hyperferritinemia, which favors AOSD over hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis [fact_24, rule_11]. This constellation meets ≥5 Yamaguchi criteria including ≥2 major items [rule_24].

The antibiotic-refractory course is a critical diagnostic clue [fact_11, fact_12, rule_6, rule_23]. The patient experienced brief symptom improvement with the first oral antibiotic, followed by recurrence within days, and second antibiotic course made no difference. This pattern is characteristic of AOSD, which is not an infectious condition and therefore does not respond durably to antibiotics [rule_6, rule_23], and strongly lowers the probability of bacterial infection requiring antimicrobial therapy.

Secondary features support this conclusion: Pharyngeal erythema without exudate [fact_16, rule_5] is compatible with AOSD's minor criterion of sore throat. Mild RUQ abdominal discomfort [fact_21] without hepatomegaly or biliary obstruction [fact_39] is consistent with hepatic inflammation from systemic inflammation [rule_16]. Dry cough without consolidation on chest radiograph [fact_6, fact_38, rule_17, rule_18] supports systemic inflammatory etiology over bacterial pneumonia. The absence of neck stiffness [fact_19] does not exclude the diagnosis [rule_14]. Mildly elevated lactate on presentation that normalized after fluids [fact_32, fact_33, rule_19] indicates adequate perfusion and lowers likelihood of severe sepsis. The patient's age of 41 years is consistent with adult-onset presentation [fact_1, rule_20], and previously healthy status raises suspicion for acute autoinflammatory disorder [fact_2, rule_21].

Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) remains in the differential but is less likely on current evidence: While pharyngitis is documented [fact_16], the walk-in clinic diagnosis was "chest infection" rather than confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis [fact_10], and no antecedent GAS infection has been documented [rule_25]. Furthermore, the absence of murmur on auscultation [fact_20] lowers but does not exclude subclinical carditis [rule_15]. The markedly elevated ferritin level of 22,000 ng/mL, while compatible with ARF, is much more characteristic of AOSD [rule_7]. The preservation of hemoglobin and platelets and the antibiotic-refractory course both favor AOSD over ARF.

The pending blood culture result [fact_37, unc_1] is critical: if sterile, it will further support AOSD diagnosis by definitively excluding bacteremia [rule_27]. If cultures are positive, they will redirect diagnosis toward infectious causes and necessitate identification of the organism and targeted therapy. Missing data on viral serology [unc_14] (EBV, CMV, other viral etiologies), intracellular organism testing [unc_15] (Rickettsia, Bartonella, Coxiella, Brucella, Leptospira for Q fever), and lymph node/spleen examination [unc_6, unc_7] represent further diagnostic gaps, though EBV hepatitis and Q fever are less consistent with the marked neutrophilic predominance and highly specific ferritin elevation characteristic of AOSD. The absence of echocardiography [unc_16] leaves subclinical carditis unexcluded, which would be relevant to ARF evaluation.
per_case.framework_top: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD)
per_case.framework_next_step: Await blood culture results; if sterile, confirm AOSD diagnosis via Yamaguchi criteria scoring and initiate trial of NSAIDs/corticosteroids. If cultures positive, pursue pathogen identification and targeted antimicrobial therapy. Obtain echocardiography to evaluate for subclinical carditis given ARF in differential.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (approximately 80-85%). The clinical presentation satisfies multiple Yamaguchi major and minor criteria with an antibiotic-refractory pattern strongly favoring autoinflammatory etiology, but blood culture results remain pending and ARF with subclinical carditis cannot yet be excluded.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs land the correct diagnosis: Adult-Onset Still's Disease, identified via the hallmark constellation (quotidian spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, arthralgia, sore throat, hepatic enzyme derangement, very high ESR, negative ANA/RF, and extreme hyperferritinemia ~22,000) and the antibiotic-refractory course. Neither continues/escalates antibiotics; both correctly pivot to corticosteroids after excluding infection, matching the ground-truth disposition.

OUTPUT A: Correct diagnosis and correct management direction (confirm cultures negative, then empiric corticosteroids with expected rapid defervescence; IL-1/IL-6 inhibitors as steroid-sparing/refractory option — defensible and clinically accurate). Calibration at 78% is reasonable and appropriately reserves uncertainty for MAS/periodic fever mimics. It is concise but its reasoning is more assertion-based. Minor imprecision: it labels failure to respond to antibiotics as excluding "infectious endocarditis," which is loosely reasoned (antibiotic failure doesn't cleanly exclude endocarditis), and ferritin framed as "nearly pathognomonic" slightly overstates specificity. No major hallucinations.

OUTPUT B: Correct diagnosis with far more traceable, defensible reasoning. It explicitly maps the case to Yamaguchi criteria (the exact framework used in the ground truth) item-by-item with fact/rule citations, correctly notes ≥5 criteria including major items, and importantly distinguishes AOSD from HLH/MAS via preserved Hgb/platelets and from acute rheumatic fever (no documented antecedent GAS, no murmur) — a richer, verifiable differential. It correctly flags pending blood culture as the pivotal exclusion and lists concrete missing infectious workup (viral serologies, Q fever/Rickettsia, echo). This explicit grounding makes the reasoning auditable and aligns tightly with the actual diagnostic process (exclusion + Yamaguchi). Its main shortcoming is that it does not state the disposition/management (admission, corticosteroid trial) as explicitly as A — it stays diagnostic. However, the prompt-style emphasis on diagnosis plus its superior, citation-backed defensibility and correct mimic discrimination outweigh A's slightly more complete treatment line.

On balance, both are correct on diagnosis and neither falls into the antibiotic-escalation trap. B wins on defensibility, calibration via explicit criteria-mapping, and absence of the small reasoning slips present in A, despite A being marginally stronger on stating concrete next-step therapy. The win is moderate, not decisive.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old woman presented to the emergency department of a regional hospital with two days of worsening breathlessness. She also reported sharp left-sided chest pain that intensified with deep inspiration, and a productive cough bringing up sputum streaked with blood. She had no documented chronic illnesses and was on no regular medications.

On arrival she was alert and in mild respiratory distress. Temperature was 37.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 128/82 mmHg. Pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 88 percent breathing room air. Her body-mass index was calculated at 32.1 kg/m2. Auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax with scattered wheeze; the right lung was clear. There was no calf swelling or tenderness.

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.4 x 10^3 per mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 8.6 x 10^3 per mm3. Serum chemistries, renal function, and a random glucose were within normal limits. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversions in the right precordial leads (V1 through V3). A clinical pretest-probability assessment placed her in a moderate-risk category for venous thromboembolism. On these grounds the treating team began supplemental oxygen and empiric therapeutic-dose anticoagulation while arranging definitive imaging.

A portable chest radiograph was reported as showing increased lucency of the left upper zone with reduced vascular markings on that side. Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic angiography of the chest was then obtained. The pulmonary arterial tree contained no filling defect. The study instead showed reduced volume of the left lung with diffuse hyperlucency, a small-calibre (underdeveloped) left main pulmonary artery and correspondingly attenuated left pulmonary veins, and widespread varicoid and cystic airway dilatation throughout the left lung. The right lung and its vasculature were unremarkable.

Anticoagulation was reviewed in light of the imaging. The patient received supplemental oxygen and a course of intravenous antibiotics during admission, with clinical improvement. She was discharged on a mucolytic agent together with an inhaled corticosteroid and a long-acting bronchodilator, and arranged for outpatient respiratory follow-up. At review one month later she was symptomatically better, with only occasional productive cough and scattered wheeze on examination.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Swyer–James–Macleod syndrome (SJMS), i.e., unilateral (left-sided) hyperlucent lung — a rare post-infectious/constrictive obliterative bronchiolitis of childhood producing unilateral lung hypoplasia. The acute presentation (hypoxia, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, sinus tachycardia with anteroseptal T-wave inversions, leukocytosis) mimicked submassive pulmonary embolism.

HOW CONFIRMED: Contrast chest CT angiography. CTA was NEGATIVE for pulmonary embolism and instead revealed the characteristic SJMS triad — unilateral (left) lung volume loss with hyperlucency, a hypoplastic ipsilateral pulmonary artery and pulmonary veins, and diffuse ipsilateral varicoid/cystic bronchiectasis. The chest radiograph's unilateral hyperlucency (initially read as oligemia suggesting PE) plus the CTA vascular hypoplasia and bronchiectasis are pathognomonic for SJMS; the diagnosis is radiologic.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT an acute thromboembolic emergency. Empiric anticoagulation started for presumed PE should be stopped once CTA excludes PE. SJMS is managed as chronic bronchiectasis / obstructive lung disease: treat the acute infective exacerbation (oxygen, IV antibiotics for the likely superimposed lower-respiratory infection given hemoptysis, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, productive blood-tinged sputum), then discharge on bronchiectasis maintenance therapy — mucolytics, inhaled corticosteroid + long-acting beta-agonist — with outpatient pulmonary follow-up. Patient improved and was followed as outpatient with residual scattered wheeze and intermittent productive cough at 1 month. Key teaching point: unilateral hyperlucent lung with ipsilateral pulmonary-artery hypoplasia on CTA explains both the hypoxia/oligemic film AND the negative PE study, averting unnecessary long-term anticoagulation.

ORIGINAL (pre-perturbation) facts: 49F, Ethiopia; HR 104, RR 30, SpO2 86% RA, T 36.8C, BP 130/85, BMI 33.5; WBC 12 x10^3/mm3, ANC 7.8 x10^3/mm3; CXR left upper lobe hyperlucency (read as oligemia); ECG sinus tach + T-wave inversions V1–V3; CTA: left lung volume loss + hyperlucency, hypoplastic LEFT pulmonary artery and veins, left diffuse varicoid/cystic bronchiectasis, PE negative; moderate-risk Wells. Source: Tilahun et al., PMC11308721.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical medicine: pulmonary pathology with acute presentation, imaging-based diagnosis, and differential management of breathlessness, hypoxia, hemoptysis, and suspected thromboembolism

rulebook.rule: Small-calibre, underdeveloped left main pulmonary artery (seen on CTPA) raises the likelihood of unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia (UPAH)
rulebook.source: Left Lung and Pulmonary Artery Hypoplasia: A Rare Case of Hemoptysis (PMC7350963) demonstrates 'narrowing of the left pulmonary artery' as definitive imaging finding; Isolated Unilateral Pulmonary Artery Hypoplasia with Accompanying Pulmonary Parenchymal Findings on CT (JKSR 2017;76(5):369)

rulebook.rule: Reduced left lung volume combined with diffuse left lung hyperlucency and attenuated left pulmonary vessels raises the likelihood of unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia
rulebook.source: Swyer-James-MacLeod Syndrome (NBK554442) defines 'unilateral hyperlucency resulting from reduced pulmonary vascularity'; Hypoplastic Lung Disease (NBK562139) documents 'decrease in ipsilateral lung volume and pulmonary artery'

rulebook.rule: Widespread varicoid and cystic airway dilatation throughout the left lung raises the likelihood of secondary bronchiectasis
rulebook.source: Swyer-James-MacLeod Syndrome (NBK554442) identifies bronchiectasis as defining feature; Swyer-James as a rare cause of unilateral hyperlucent lung (PMC6380820) documents 'widespread varicoid and cystic airway dilatation'; Left Lung and Pulmonary Artery Hypoplasia (PMC7350963)

rulebook.rule: Hemoptysis (blood-streaked productive cough) in the setting of bronchiectasis with hypertrophied bronchial arteries raises the likelihood of active hemorrhage from rupture of dilated submucosal vessels
rulebook.source: Left Lung and Pulmonary Artery Hypoplasia (PMC7350963) explains 'cystic bronchiectasis and hypertrophied bronchial arteries are probable cause for hemoptysis'; Bronchiectasis (NBK430810) states 'dilated bronchial arteries often responsible for hemoptysis'

rulebook.rule: Acute two-day worsening of breathlessness in a patient with chronic structural lung disease raises the likelihood of superimposed acute exacerbation
rulebook.bears_on: Acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis; acute infection
rulebook.source: Swyer-James-MacLeod Syndrome (NBK554442); Exacerbation of Bronchiectasis (PMC7121148) defines acute exacerbation as change in symptoms for ≥48 hours

rulebook.rule: Pleuritic left-sided chest pain (intensified with deep inspiration) in acute respiratory illness raises the likelihood of acute pleural or parenchymal inflammation from infection or hemorrhage
rulebook.source: Chest pain and exacerbations of bronchiectasis (PMC3526875) reports 'chest pain in bronchiectasis occurs in 19-46% of patients during exacerbation'; '89% of patients described chest pain over area corresponding to lobe with bronchiectasis'

rulebook.rule: Hypoxemia (SpO2 88% on room air) in a patient with unilateral lung hypoplasia raises the likelihood of acute-on-chronic hypoxemia and secondary pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.bears_on: Right ventricular strain; acute pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.source: Unilateral hypoplasia reduces effective pulmonary vascular bed by approximately 50%; acute infection worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch

rulebook.rule: T-wave inversions in right precordial leads (V1-V3) combined with sinus tachycardia, hypoxemia, and tachypnea raises the likelihood of acute right ventricular strain; lowers likelihood of anterior wall myocardial infarction
rulebook.bears_on: Acute RV strain from pulmonary hypertension
rulebook.source: Deep T-Wave Inversions in Pulmonary Embolism (CHEST Journal) explains T-inversions in V1-V3 occur in 'right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension'; LITFL ECG Library confirms 'anterior pattern may indicate acute RV strain'; PMC12328991

rulebook.rule: Mild leukocytosis with elevated absolute neutrophils in the absence of fever raises the likelihood of non-bacterial exacerbation (viral, atypical infection, or pure inflammatory response)
rulebook.source: Absence of fever in leukocytosis is atypical for severe bacterial pneumonia; suggests viral or atypical pathogen (Acute Pulmonary Embolism, NBK560551)

rulebook.rule: Negative CTPA (absence of pulmonary arterial filling defect) in a patient with moderate pretest probability for VTE lowers the likelihood of pulmonary embolism and supports discontinuation of empiric anticoagulation
rulebook.source: Acute Pulmonary Embolism (NBK560551) states 'negative CTPA is adequate for excluding PE in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability'; Ruling out PE in Patients with High Pretest Probability (PMC5942014) confirms 'for moderate pretest probability and negative CTPA...anticoagulation can be safely discontinued'

rulebook.rule: Negative CTPA combined with imaging evidence of alternative structural diagnosis (unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia) lowers the likelihood of PE and explains RV dysfunction as chronic/acute pulmonary strain rather than thromboembolic disease
rulebook.source: Acute Pulmonary Embolism (NBK560551) emphasizes 'RV dysfunction alone does not prove PE...pulmonary hypertension is alternative diagnosis when encountering RV dysfunction'

rulebook.rule: Acute respiratory exacerbation in a patient with known bronchiectasis raises the likelihood of acute infectious exacerbation and supports empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
rulebook.source: Exacerbation of Bronchiectasis (PMC7121148) states 'ERS guidelines recommend 14 days of antibiotic therapy'; 'empiric treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, or anaerobes is appropriate'

rulebook.rule: Bronchiectasis with defective mucociliary clearance creates a breeding ground for bacterial colonization, raising the need for empiric antibiotic coverage even without microbiologic confirmation
rulebook.bears_on: Acute bacterial infection; chronic respiratory infection risk
rulebook.source: Bronchiectasis (NBK430810) explains 'impaired mucociliary clearance...creates breeding ground for pathogens'; 'empiric antibiotic coverage frequently needed'; documents common pathogens: Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus, anaerobes

rulebook.rule: Unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia with underdevelopment of alveolar tissue, surfactant deficiency, and impaired mucociliary clearance raises the risk of recurrent and persistent respiratory infections

rulebook.rule: Unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia with secondary bronchiectasis raises the need for chronic supportive respiratory therapy including bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and mucoactive agents

per_case.blind_answer:
Most Likely Diagnosis: Congenital left lung hypoplasia with secondary bronchiectasis, presenting with acute infectious exacerbation (community-acquired pneumonia or other lower respiratory infection superimposed on chronically malformed left lung).

Recommended Next Action: (1) Complete current antibiotic course and supportive care (already appropriate); (2) obtain prior imaging to confirm chronicity; (3) arrange high-resolution CT and PFTs to fully characterize bronchiectasis and ventilatory impairment; (4) cardiac echo to rule out associated cardiac anomalies; (5) establish long-term outpatient respiratory surveillance and infection prophylaxis protocol; (6) discontinue anticoagulation (VTE excluded by imaging).

Confidence: 85-90% — CT findings are definitive for unilateral hypoplasia with bronchiectasis; clinical response to antibiotics confirms infectious exacerbation of chronic structural disease.

Reasoning: The CT shows a pathognomonic constellation (hypoplastic left PA, reduced lung volume, widespread bronchiectasis). The acute presentation (hemoptysis, fever, elevated WBC, response to antibiotics) represents infection superimposed on a chronically malformed lung, not primary VTE or primary infection of a normal lung. The patient's rapid improvement on antibiotics and supportive care confirms the infectious trigger. ECG and vital sign changes reflect acute hypoxia and RV strain from the combination of structural lung disease and infection, not cardiac pathology.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
## Diagnosis

The patient has **unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia (UPAH) with secondary bronchiectasis** (R-Q1-STRUCT, supported by R-A1, R-A2, R-A3). 

### Structural Basis
The CTPA imaging is pathognomonic: small-calibre underdeveloped left main pulmonary artery (F36, R-A1), reduced left lung volume (F34), diffuse left lung hyperlucency (F35), attenuated left pulmonary veins (F37), and widespread varicoid and cystic airway dilatation (F38, F39, R-A3). These findings together satisfy R-Q1-STRUCT, defining unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia with secondary Swyer-James-MacLeod features.

### Acute Presentation
The two-day worsening of breathlessness (F3, F4), pleuritic left-sided chest pain (F5, F6), and hemoptysis (F7) represent **acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis** (R-C1, R-Q2-ACUTE). The acute trigger is most likely **infectious**: the patient lacks fever (F11) and has only mild leukocytosis (F21–F22), which raises the likelihood of viral or atypical pathogen with possible bacterial superinfection rather than severe bacterial pneumonia (R-D3, R-Q4-INFECTION). The hemoptysis arises from **hemorrhage from dilated submucosal vessels** in the setting of cystic bronchiectasis (R-B1), a recognized complication of the underlying structural disease.

### Pulmonary Hypertension and RV Strain
The hypoxemia (SpO2 88% on room air, F15) in unilateral lung hypoplasia reduces the effective pulmonary vascular bed by ~50%, predisposing to pulmonary hypertension (R-D1). This explains the acute RV strain evidenced by T-wave inversions in right precordial leads V1–V3 (F27, R-D2) without myocardial infarction. The sinus tachycardia (F26), tachypnea (F13), and hypoxemia support acute RV strain from increased pulmonary vascular resistance.

### Thromboembolism Exclusion
The clinical pretest probability for VTE was moderate (F28); however, the CTPA showed **no pulmonary arterial filling defect** (F33, R-E1). At moderate pretest probability, negative CTPA is adequate to exclude PE and supports discontinuation of empiric anticoagulation (R-E1, R-Q3-ANTICOAG). The RV dysfunction is better explained by acute strain from pulmonary hypertension in the setting of unilateral hypoplasia and infection-related decompensation (R-E2) than by thromboembolic disease.

### Infection Management
Empiric IV antibiotics (F44) were appropriately given (R-F1, R-Q4-INFECTION): acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis, combined with defective mucociliary clearance in the hypoplastic lung, creates risk for bacterial infection (R-F2, R-F3). Absence of fever and mild leukocytosis suggest a non-classical bacterial etiology, possibly viral or atypical pathogen with early bacterial superinfection.

### Long-Term Course and Surveillance
The discharge regimen (mucolytic agent F46, inhaled corticosteroid F47, long-acting bronchodilator F48) aligns with R-G1 for chronic supportive management of unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia with bronchiectasis. One-month follow-up showed symptomatic improvement (F51–F53), consistent with response to acute exacerbation treatment. However, this diagnosis carries **lifelong risk** of recurrent infection, progressive hemoptysis, and pulmonary hypertension; R-G2 mandates ongoing multidisciplinary surveillance, preventive vaccination, and prompt treatment of complications.

### Etiology of Bronchiectasis
The varicoid and cystic airway dilatation (F38–F39) represents secondary bronchiectasis; the etiology is **defective mucociliary clearance and impaired local immunity in the hypoplastic lung** (R-Q5-BRONCHIECTASIS), likely congenital with possible post-infectious (Swyer-James) evolution, though no documented prior infection or imaging is available (U3, U6).

### Systemic Diagnosis
No explicit systemic or genetic diagnosis is identified. The constellation is consistent with **primary congenital unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia** or **Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome**, likely isolated pulmonary pathology (R-Q6-SYSTEMIC, supported by absence of documented systemic findings).

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: final diagnosis is Swyer-James-Macleod syndrome (SJMS) — unilateral hyperlucent lung from post-infectious obliterative bronchiolitis producing unilateral lung hypoplasia, mimicking submassive PE. Confirmed by NEGATIVE CTA showing the triad (unilateral hyperlucency/volume loss, hypoplastic ipsilateral PA and veins, diffuse varicoid/cystic bronchiectasis). Correct disposition: STOP empiric anticoagulation since PE excluded; manage as chronic bronchiectasis exacerbation (oxygen, IV antibiotics for superimposed infection), discharge on mucolytics + ICS/LABA with pulmonary follow-up.

OUTPUT A: Names the entity as "unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia with secondary bronchiectasis" but explicitly and repeatedly invokes "Swyer-James-MacLeod features/syndrome," correctly identifying it as the named systemic/structural diagnosis and noting possible post-infectious (Swyer-James) evolution. Correctly captures every disposition element: PE excluded by negative CTA at moderate pretest probability, discontinue anticoagulation, infective exacerbation treated with IV antibiotics, chronic management with mucolytic + ICS + LABA, one-month improvement, lifelong surveillance. This matches the ground truth disposition almost point-for-point. It is well-calibrated (uses "likely," flags uncertainty U3/U6, acknowledges no documented prior infection). The RV-strain/pulmonary-hypertension framing for the V1-V3 T-wave inversions is a reasonable physiologic explanation and is hedged ("better explained by acute strain... than thromboembolic"), consistent with the negative PE study. Minor weakness: it slightly underweights SJMS as THE answer (frames it as a feature of UPAH rather than the headline diagnosis), and asserts "lacks fever (F11)" — the original case did note possible infection but the perturbed inputs apparently lacked fever, so this is defensible given its stated facts.

OUTPUT B: Correctly identifies left lung hypoplasia with secondary bronchiectasis and infectious exacerbation, correctly recommends discontinuing anticoagulation (VTE excluded) and chronic surveillance. However it does NOT name Swyer-James-Macleod syndrome at all — a notable miss on the headline diagnosis. It labels the condition "congenital" hypoplasia, whereas SJMS is acquired/post-infectious; this is a substantive etiologic error. It also asserts "fever, elevated WBC, response to antibiotics" as confirming infection — citing fever contradicts the case (afebrile per ground truth, T 36.8C), a factual error. Recommendations (HRCT, PFTs, echo, prior imaging) are reasonable workup but somewhat generic and partly redundant given CTA already done. Confidence 85-90% is reasonably calibrated to its (less complete) conclusion.

Both correctly excluded PE and recommended stopping anticoagulation — the highest-stakes clinical decision. A is the winner: it explicitly names SJMS, more thoroughly and accurately reconstructs the actual disposition (specific discharge meds, follow-up, exacerbation management) matching ground truth, and is better calibrated with traceable rule/finding references (R-/F- tags) making its reasoning verifiable. B misses the SJMS name, mislabels etiology as congenital rather than post-infectious, and contains a fever assertion contradicting the facts.

per_case.prose:
A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with about 16 hours of severe, sharp, cramping pain across his upper abdomen, most intense in the right upper quadrant. He reported nausea and had vomited twice, both times shortly after eating. He was an avid recreational cyclist and was otherwise healthy, taking no regular medications. He denied fever, chest pain, diarrhea, black stools, or blood in his stool. He had never had abdominal surgery.

On examination he was in obvious discomfort but not toxic-appearing. The abdomen was soft and not distended, with focal tenderness in the right upper quadrant and arrest of inspiration on deep palpation beneath the right costal margin. There was no rebound and no guarding elsewhere.

Initial laboratory studies, including white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and serum lactate, returned within normal limits.

Given the right-upper-quadrant tenderness and the positive inspiratory-arrest sign, the leading concern was an acute gallbladder process. A right-upper-quadrant ultrasound was obtained and showed no evidence of cholecystitis, with no gallstones, wall thickening, or pericholecystic fluid.

As the patient was reassessed and his pain persisted, an abdominal radiograph was performed; the lateral projection demonstrated several air-fluid levels concerning for a bowel obstruction. A CT of the abdomen was then ordered. Because of pain the patient was able to tolerate only about 450 mL of oral contrast, though image quality was felt to be adequate.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Cecal volvulus.

HOW CONFIRMED: CT of the abdomen demonstrated the "whirl sign" (bowel, mesentery, and vasculature rotating around a transition point), diagnostic of cecal volvulus. The diagnosis was then confirmed operatively — the patient was taken emergently to the OR and underwent laparoscopic detorsion of the volvulus followed by right hemicolectomy.

KEY INITIALLY-MISLEADING FEATURES: Presentation strongly mimicked acute cholecystitis — severe sharp epigastric/right-upper-quadrant cramping pain, nausea/vomiting after eating, and a POSITIVE Murphy sign with RUQ tenderness. The leading differential was cholecystitis, but right-upper-quadrant ultrasound was NEGATIVE for cholecystitis. Labs (WBC, hemoglobin, lactate) were all within normal limits, providing false reassurance. The abdominal X-ray (lateral view) then showed air-fluid levels suggesting small bowel obstruction, prompting CT, which revealed the volvulus. Localized RUQ/epigastric pain is an ATYPICAL presentation for cecal volvulus (usually presents as more diffuse obstruction), which is why it was initially missed. No abdominal distension or rebound. No surgical history.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Emergent surgical management (operative detorsion + right hemicolectomy); admission, NOT discharge. Outcome: regained normal bowel function by post-op day 3, no complications, full recovery at follow-up.

TEACHING POINT (held aside): Maintain a broad differential and reevaluate with serial exams; an ultrasound-negative "cholecystitis-like" picture with X-ray evidence of obstruction warrants CT to look for volvulus.

rulebook.rule: Positive Murphy's sign (arrest of inspiration with deep palpation beneath right costal margin) raises likelihood of acute cholecystitis
rulebook.source: NCBI - Clinical sensitivity of Murphy's sign estimated at 97.2% when compared with hepatobiliary scanning; however sonographic Murphy's sign sensitivity 63-81% (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6852522/)

rulebook.rule: Negative abdominal ultrasound (no gallstones, no wall thickening, no pericholecystic fluid) significantly lowers likelihood of acute cholecystitis
rulebook.source: Merck Manual - Ultrasound is imaging test of choice with sensitivity and specificity of 95% for detecting gallbladder stones; negative ultrasound makes cholecystitis unlikely but does not completely exclude acalculous pathology (https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hepatic-and-biliary-disorders/gallbladder-and-bile-duct-disorders/acalculous-biliary-pain)

rulebook.rule: Right upper quadrant pain with nausea, vomiting triggered by eating raises likelihood of biliary etiology (cholecystitis or biliary colic)
rulebook.source: StatPearls - RUQ pain is classic presentation of biliary tract disease; post-prandial symptoms suggest gallbladder dysfunction (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/biliary-tract-pain)

rulebook.rule: Negative ultrasound with RUQ pain and Murphy's sign raises possibility of acalculous biliary pain (biliary dyskinesia from microlithiasis, gallbladder outlet dysfunction, or biliary dysmotility)
rulebook.source: Merck Manual - Acalculous biliary pain suspected when RUQ pain present but imaging cannot detect gallstones; may reflect microscopic stones (biliary sludge), abnormal gallbladder emptying, or sphincter dysfunction (https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hepatic-and-biliary-disorders/gallbladder-and-bile-duct-disorders/acalculous-biliary-pain)

rulebook.rule: Multiple air-fluid levels on abdominal radiograph (particularly with differential heights >5mm in same loop) raise likelihood of mechanical small bowel obstruction
rulebook.source: AJR - Air-fluid levels of differential height in same small bowel loop and width ≥25mm on upright radiographs are most significant findings for mechanical obstruction; mean sensitivity 82%, specificity 83%, accuracy 83% across reviewers (https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/ajr.161.2.8333364)

rulebook.rule: Severe, sharp, cramping abdominal pain raises likelihood of mechanical bowel obstruction (colicky pain reflects peristalsis against obstruction)
rulebook.source: NCBI StatPearls - Pain in small bowel obstruction is typically crampy/colicky, occurring at 4-5 minute intervals for proximal obstruction and less frequently distally, reflecting bowel's attempt to overcome obstruction (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448079/)

rulebook.rule: Vomiting triggered by eating (shortly after eating) lowers likelihood of complete mechanical bowel obstruction and suggests biliary pathology or functional disorder
rulebook.source: StatPearls - Vomiting with complete obstruction is typically unrelated to food intake; post-prandial vomiting suggests biliary colic or gastroparesis rather than mechanical obstruction (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/biliary-tract-pain)

rulebook.rule: Persistent pain despite negative imaging raises likelihood that obstruction became apparent only on follow-up imaging, consistent with mechanical or functional obstruction
rulebook.source: Case context - Clinical reassessment and subsequent radiography/CT identified obstruction not apparent on ultrasound, supporting progressive or initially subtle obstruction

rulebook.rule: Soft, non-distended abdomen with focal RUQ tenderness only lowers likelihood of complete mechanical bowel obstruction
rulebook.source: StatPearls - Complete SBO typically presents with distension; absence of distension suggests partial obstruction, early presentation, or non-mechanical etiology (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448079/)

rulebook.rule: Normal white blood cell count lowers likelihood of bowel strangulation or ischemia
rulebook.source: PMC - Elevated WBC >15 × 10^9/L was detected as independent clinical factor for intestinal strangulation; normal WBC does not exclude strangulation but reduces likelihood (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6112878/)

rulebook.rule: Normal serum lactate significantly lowers likelihood of bowel strangulation or tissue ischemia
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect - Lactate was abnormal in 86% of strangulated cases vs. only 4% with simple SBO; normal lactate is reassuring for tissue perfusion (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1091255X23084597)

rulebook.rule: Absence of rebound tenderness lowers likelihood of peritonitis, perforation, or strangulated obstruction
rulebook.source: StatPearls - Peritoneal signs including rebound tenderness indicate possible ischemia, strangulation, or perforation; absence reassuring but does not entirely exclude (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448079/)

rulebook.rule: Male gender with no prior abdominal surgery but presenting with bowel obstruction raises possibility of band adhesions from non-surgical causes (trauma, inflammation)
rulebook.source: PMC - Among male patients with solitary band adhesions, 56% had never undergone abdominal surgery, suggesting male-specific non-surgical risk factors; approximately 31% of patients with obstructing band adhesions had no prior surgery (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6249350/)

rulebook.rule: History of blunt abdominal trauma (recreational cycling activities) raises likelihood of transmesocolic or internal hernia from traumatic mesenteric defect
rulebook.source: PMC - Post-trauma transmesocolic hernias can present months to years later with acute bowel obstruction; trauma can create mesenteric defects allowing herniation; important to consider in trauma patients with SBO even without prior surgery (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7575331/)

rulebook.rule: CT imaging with IV contrast has high sensitivity (94-100%) and specificity (90-95%) for identifying internal hernias by demonstrating closed-loop obstruction pattern and convergent mesenteric vessels
rulebook.source: PMC - CT achieves sensitivity 94-100% and specificity 90-95% for internal hernias when demonstrating saclike mass of dilated bowel loops, converging vessels at hernia orifice, and fluid-filled U- or C-shaped loops; multiplanar reformations essential (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6625567/)

rulebook.rule: Right upper quadrant pain predominance (rather than epigastric) lowers likelihood of acute pancreatitis
rulebook.source: ARUP Consult - Acute pancreatitis typically presents with sudden epigastric or left-sided pain radiating to back; RUQ pain suggests biliary rather than pancreatic pathology (https://arupconsult.com/content/pancreatitis-acute)

rulebook.rule: Normal serum lactate and normal WBC lower likelihood of acute pancreatitis (though pancreatitis can rarely present with normal amylase/lipase)
rulebook.source: PMC - Acute pancreatitis requires elevated lipase or amylase in majority of cases; normal lipase is exceedingly rare; normal lactate and WBC argue against significant pancreatic inflammation (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11246614/)

rulebook.rule: Absence of fever lowers likelihood of Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome or pelvic inflammatory disease
rulebook.source: StatPearls - Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome typically presents with fever, chlamydial/gonococcal infection signs, dysuria, vaginal discharge in female patients; absent in this male patient (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499950/)

rulebook.rule: Male gender lowers likelihood of Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (rare complication of PID affecting women)
rulebook.source: Wikipedia / NCBI - Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is complication of pelvic inflammatory disease from Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae; occurs in women with PID; virtually unknown in males (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499950/)

rulebook.rule: If pneumobilia (air in biliary tree) present on CT/radiograph, significantly raises likelihood of gallstone ileus with bilio-enteric fistula
rulebook.source: LITFL / PMC - Rigler's triad (pneumobilia, small bowel obstruction, ectopic gallstone) is highly specific for gallstone ileus; pneumobilia alone suggests bilio-enteric fistula (https://litfl.com/rigler-triad/)

rulebook.rule: If ectopic gallstone visible on CT in small bowel at transition zone, definitively confirms gallstone ileus
rulebook.source: PMC - Ectopic gallstone visible on imaging is pathognomonic for gallstone ileus; most commonly lodges at ileocecal valve as narrowest part of bowel; sensitivity of Rigler's triad 40-70%, but when all three components visible, highly specific (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11799675/)

rulebook.rule: Young age (57 years) with no prior biliary disease lowers likelihood of gallstone ileus (predominantly affects elderly women with chronic cholecystitis)
rulebook.source: Radiopaedia - Gallstone ileus rare cause (0.3-0.5% of cholelithiasis), predominantly affects elderly women (>65 yrs) with chronic cholecystitis and repeated acute episodes (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/gallstone-ileus)

rulebook.rule: CT with IV contrast has >95% sensitivity and specificity for mechanical SBO vs. adynamic ileus; presence of discrete transition zone between dilated and collapsed bowel indicates mechanical obstruction
rulebook.bears_on: Mechanical bowel obstruction vs. Functional ileus
rulebook.source: AJR / PMC - CT sensitivity and specificity >95% for SBO when transition zone present; small bowel dilatation >2.5cm transverse diameter with discrete transition zone indicates mechanical obstruction (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448079/)

rulebook.rule: Partial small bowel obstruction without signs of strangulation can be managed conservatively with nasogastric decompression, fluid/electrolyte replacement, and supportive care for 24-48 hours
rulebook.source: PMC - Nearly 90% of SBO can be managed conservatively; nasogastric decompression removes proximal contents; partial obstructions respond to 24-48 hour trial of medical management with water-soluble contrast to aid decompression (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10040372/)

rulebook.rule: Complete bowel obstruction with signs of strangulation (fever, tachycardia, peritonitis, elevated lactate, severe focal tenderness) indicates need for urgent surgical intervention
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect - Clinical signs of strangulation include fever >38C, tachycardia, peritonitis, point tenderness, pain out of proportion; elevated lactate in 86% strangulated vs 4% simple obstruction; requires emergency surgery (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1091255X23084597)

rulebook.rule: RUQ pain localization in proximal small bowel obstruction (ileal location) may represent referred pain from ileocecal region rather than primary biliary pathology
rulebook.bears_on: Small bowel obstruction - Pain localization mechanism
rulebook.source: NCBI StatPearls - Proximal obstructions (duodenal, upper jejunal) present with modest pain; RUQ pain documented in gallstone ileus cases with proximal SBO; pain location depends on obstruction site and visceral innervation (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11957583/)

rulebook.rule: Bilious vomiting (if confirmed) raises likelihood of mechanical bowel obstruction at or distal to ampulla of Vater
rulebook.source: GPnotebook / Merck Manual - Bilious vomitus indicates obstruction distal to common bile duct junction; occurs with proximal small bowel obstruction; vomiting timing and character help localize obstruction level (https://clinicalgate.com/bilious-vomiting/)

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Small bowel obstruction from internal hernia (possibly foramen of Winslow or mesenteric defect).

Recommended next action: Review CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast to identify obstruction transition point, assess bowel viability, and characterize hernia location. Determine management (conservative vs. surgical) based on findings.

Confidence: 75-80%

Reasoning: RUQ ultrasound excluded cholecystitis despite classic presentation. Air-fluid levels on plain film confirm mechanical obstruction. No prior abdominal surgery makes adhesions unlikely. Internal hernia is the most common cause of non-adhesive small bowel obstruction in this clinical context.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
Clinical and imaging findings support a diagnosis of partial mechanical small bowel obstruction with underlying biliary dysfunction.

SUPPORTING MECHANICAL OBSTRUCTION:
The patient's severe, sharp, cramping abdominal pain [pain_character, rule_cramping_pain_obstruction_raise] combined with radiographic evidence of multiple air-fluid levels on lateral projection [xray_finding, rule_airfluid_levels_obstruction_raise] strongly raises likelihood of mechanical bowel obstruction. Persistence of pain despite initial negative ultrasound [reassessment_persistent_pain, rule_persistent_pain_obstruction_raise] indicates obstruction became evident only on follow-up imaging, consistent with progressive or initially subtle mechanical obstruction.

AGAINST SEVERE/COMPLETE OBSTRUCTION:
Several clinical features suggest partial rather than complete obstruction with strangulation: the abdomen is soft and non-distended [exam_abdomen_surface, rule_soft_nondistended_abdomen_obstruction_lower], white blood cell count is normal [lab_wbc, rule_normal_wbc_obstruction_lower], serum lactate is normal [lab_lactate, rule_normal_lactate_obstruction_lower], and there is no rebound tenderness [exam_rebound_tenderness, rule_no_rebound_peritonitis_lower]. Collectively, these normal findings significantly lower the likelihood of bowel strangulation or ischemia, which would present with elevated inflammatory markers and peritoneal signs.

COMPLICATING FEATURE—BILIARY DYSFUNCTION:
The right upper quadrant pain predominance [pain_location_primary], positive Murphy's sign [exam_murphys_sign, rule_murphys_cholecystitis_raise], and post-prandial vomiting [vomiting_trigger, associated_nausea, vomiting_episodes] initially raise concern for acute cholecystitis [rule_ruq_pain_biliary_raise]. However, the negative ultrasound showing no gallstones, wall thickening, or pericholecystic fluid [us_no_cholecystitis, us_no_stones, us_no_wall_thickening, us_no_pericholecystic_fluid] substantially lowers the likelihood of acute cholecystitis [rule_negative_us_cholecystitis_lower] and raises the possibility of acalculous biliary pain from microlithiasis, gallbladder dysfunction, or sphincter outlet obstruction [rule_negative_us_acalculous_raise]. The RUQ pain localization may alternatively represent referred pain from the ileocecal region in the context of proximal small bowel obstruction [rule_ruq_referred_pain_proximal], particularly if the obstruction site involves the terminal ileum.

DIFFERENTIAL CONSIDERATIONS—ETIOLOGY:
The patient's history of recreational cycling raises the possibility of post-traumatic internal hernia from a mesenteric defect, which can present acutely with small bowel obstruction even years after the inciting injury [rule_cyclist_trauma_internal_hernia_raise]. The absence of prior abdominal surgery does not exclude adhesive obstruction, as male patients can develop band adhesions from non-surgical etiologies [rule_adhesion_risk_no_prior_surgery_raise]. Gallstone ileus is lower on the differential because the patient is 57 years old without known chronic cholecystitis; this diagnosis predominantly affects elderly women >65 years [rule_young_healthy_gallstone_ileus_lower], though it remains possible if CT imaging identifies pneumobilia and an ectopic gallstone at the obstruction site [rule_pneumobilia_gallstone_ileus_raise, rule_ectopic_gallstone_obstruction_raise].

PENDING DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS:
The CT abdomen obtained with approximately 450 mL oral contrast [ct_contrast_volume, ct_image_quality] is essential to the definitive diagnosis. CT imaging with IV contrast has >95% sensitivity and specificity for mechanical small bowel obstruction when a discrete transition zone between dilated and collapsed bowel is identified [rule_ct_mechanical_vs_ileus]. The CT will also determine the anatomic location, nature (adhesion vs. hernia vs. intraluminal mass), and whether imaging features of strangulation are present.

MANAGEMENT TRAJECTORY:
Absent definitive signs of strangulation or complete obstruction, approximately 90% of partial small bowel obstructions can be managed conservatively with nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement, and supportive care for 24–48 hours [rule_conservative_management_partial]. Conversely, if imaging reveals signs of complete obstruction, strangulation (fever, elevated lactate, peritonitis), or an identifiable surgical etiology (incarcerated hernia, volvulus), urgent surgical intervention is indicated [rule_surgical_complete_strangulation]. The CT interpretation will be the critical decision point guiding further management.

per_case.rationale: Ground truth: cecal volvulus, confirmed by CT whirl sign and operative right hemicolectomy; correct disposition is emergent surgery. Neither output names cecal volvulus, so both are partial. Output A is more defensible: it correctly identifies mechanical obstruction, gives calibrated confidence (75-80%), and recommends CT to find the transition point and assess viability — preserving the path to the correct urgent diagnosis. Its only diagnostic miss is specifying internal hernia / small bowel rather than cecal volvulus, but its reasoning is traceable and free of fabricated details. Output B is worse on the things that matter most: it lands on 'partial mechanical SBO with biliary dysfunction' (both wrong) and explicitly steers toward conservative management (~90% managed conservatively), the opposite of the correct emergent surgery. It interprets the normal WBC/lactate/soft abdomen as reassuring evidence against strangulation — precisely the false-reassurance trap the ground truth warns against. It also fabricates case specifics (450 mL oral contrast, recreational cycling, age 57) and many pseudo-citation rule tags that cannot be verified, mentioning volvulus only as a buried contingency. A wins on correctness, calibration, and defensibility, and avoids B's dangerous disposition error.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled on oral agents, and no known drug allergies or prior throat/airway problems, sought care for a sore throat that had begun about four days earlier. He was first seen at an urgent-care office, told he had a throat infection, and sent home on an oral antibiotic and an antipyretic. When the pain did not ease, he returned the next day and was given a dose of intravenous penicillin-class antibiotic plus acetaminophen and again discharged.

Two days after that he presented to the emergency department. He appeared generally well but mildly dehydrated. Temperature was 37.7 C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure normal, respiratory rate normal, and oxygen saturation normal on room air. His voice sounded slightly raspy. Examination of the oropharynx showed only mild pharyngeal redness with normal-appearing tonsils and no exudate. He was treated as having acute pharyngitis and discharged on an oral antibiotic together with a course of an oral corticosteroid.

He came back roughly 24 hours later, now reporting that swallowing had become markedly more painful and that he could no longer get his pills down. Temperature was 38.1 C and heart rate 101/min. He still looked reasonably well, was not breathing fast, had no drooling and no audible stridor, and lay flat without difficulty. Bloodwork showed a white-cell count of 13.6 x 10^9/L (reference 4-11) and a C-reactive protein of 248 mg/L (reference <5); electrolytes and renal indices were normal.

A lateral soft-tissue radiograph of the neck showed a strikingly swollen, rounded epiglottic shadow narrowing the airway above the vocal cords. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-circumscribed, rim-enhancing fluid collection roughly 26 x 22 x 17 mm centered at the epiglottis and pre-epiglottic space. Bedside flexible fiberoptic examination of the upper airway revealed severe swelling of the supraglottic and hypopharyngeal tissues with a discrete collection about 3 x 2 cm on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: acute epiglottitis with a peri-/supraglottic (epiglottic) abscess. Confirmation: lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph showing a markedly swollen/enlarged epiglottis ("thumbprint sign"), contrast-enhanced neck CT showing a ~28x24x18 mm rim-enhancing fluid collection at the epiglottis/pre-epiglottic region, and direct flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showing severe supraglottic/hypopharyngeal swelling with a ~3x2 cm abscess on the lingual surface of the epiglottis; abscess culture grew anaerobic gram-negative bacilli. It had been repeatedly misattributed to benign acute pharyngitis and the patient was discharged multiple times (clinic and ED) on oral/IV antibiotics, antipyretics, and steroids. Correct disposition: this is an airway emergency — admit, do NOT discharge; secure the airway in a controlled setting (controlled awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation with surgical/ENT and anesthesia present, avoiding supine positioning/sedation that can precipitate obstruction), give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + clindamycin) plus IV dexamethasone, perform incision and drainage of the abscess, and admit to ICU for airway monitoring. Source: Prince Mohammed Bin Abdulaziz Hospital, Al Madinah, Saudi Arabia; PMC12640370. Outcome: full recovery, normal follow-up laryngoscopy.

rulebook.rule: Sore throat as chief complaint raises suspicion for acute pharyngitis initially, but when accompanied by fever and dysphagia in a patient with risk factors (age 58, diabetes), requires evaluation for more serious upper airway pathology.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute pharyngitis vs. epiglottitis (differential diagnosis at initial presentation)
rulebook.source: Pharyngitis and Epiglottitis. PMC - NIH. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7126481/

rulebook.rule: Worsening dysphagia and odynophagia despite two prior antibiotic courses (oral followed by IV penicillin-class agents) strongly raises concern for inadequate antibiotic coverage or resistant organism rather than simple viral pharyngitis resolution.
rulebook.bears_on: Treatment failure — suggests penicillin-resistant organism or organism outside typical coverage
rulebook.source: Epiglottitis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430960/

rulebook.rule: Raspy voice quality at ED visit raises concern for supraglottic involvement (epiglottitis) rather than simple pharyngitis, as voice changes indicate edema affecting laryngeal mechanics.

rulebook.rule: Elevated WBC (13.6 x 10^9/L, normal 4-11) significantly raises likelihood of bacterial infection and supports epiglottitis over simple viral pharyngitis; mean WBC in epiglottitis series is 13.57 ± 4.43 × 10^9/L.

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated CRP (248 mg/L, normal <5) significantly raises concern for acute bacterial infection and is consistent with epiglottitis; mean CRP in epiglottitis is 63.42 ± 43.11 mg/L, but individual cases can exceed this range.
rulebook.source: Epidemiology, presentation, management and outcomes of patients with acute epiglottitis - PMC. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11735524/

rulebook.rule: Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph showing strikingly swollen, rounded epiglottic shadow with airway narrowing above vocal cords (thumbprint sign) is pathognomonic for epiglottitis and definitively raises diagnosis.

rulebook.rule: Contrast-enhanced CT showing well-circumscribed, rim-enhancing fluid collection (26 x 22 x 17 mm) centered at epiglottis and pre-epiglottic space raises diagnosis of epiglottic abscess — a suppurative complication of acute epiglottitis.

rulebook.rule: Bedside flexible fiberoptic examination showing severe swelling of supraglottic and hypopharyngeal tissues with discrete collection on lingual surface of epiglottis (3 x 2 cm) directly visualizes epiglottitis with abscess formation and is gold standard for confirmation.

rulebook.source: Epiglottitis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430960/

rulebook.rule: Mild pharyngeal redness with normal-appearing tonsils and no exudate at initial ED exam might suggest simple pharyngitis, but when imaging shows epiglottic swelling and abscess, these findings reflect inadequate pharyngeal exam rather than ruling out serious pathology.
