rulebook.rule: Proximal weakness (hip and shoulder girdles) with gradual onset over months raises suspicion for primary lipid storage myopathy (including primary carnitine deficiency, fatty acid oxidation disorders, and neutral lipid storage disease)
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Disorders of lipid metabolism (https://www.medlink.com/articles/disorders-of-lipid-metabolism) and PMC study on lipid storage myopathy characteristics showing proximal weakness is hallmark presentation

rulebook.rule: Type 1 fiber-selective lipid vacuoles (Oil Red O positive) on muscle biopsy strongly raises primary carnitine deficiency or fatty acid oxidation disorder over myositis
rulebook.bears_on: Primary carnitine deficiency AND Fatty acid oxidation disorders
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Carnitine Deficiency overview (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/carnitine-deficiency) states carnitine-deficient myopathy shows lipid storage predominantly in type 1 muscle fibers

rulebook.rule: Elevated medium-chain acylcarnitines (C10, C14) raises fatty acid oxidation disorder (MCAD, VLCAD, MADD) over primary carnitine deficiency
rulebook.source: NCBI Bookshelf—Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1424/) documents that accumulation of C6-C10 acylcarnitines is diagnostic pattern for MCAD and related disorders

rulebook.rule: Absence of inflammatory infiltrate on muscle biopsy lowers myositis (including anti-SRP and anti-Ku associated necrotizing myopathy)
rulebook.source: PMC study on anti-SRP myositis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4440264/) shows anti-SRP associated myopathy characterized by widespread necrosis WITH MINIMAL OR ABSENT INFLAMMATORY INFILTRATES, distinct from typical myositis; if biopsy shows NO inflammation at all, argues against immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy

rulebook.rule: Weakly positive (not strongly positive) anti-SRP and anti-Ku antibodies with no inflammatory histology lowers probability of clinically significant immune-mediated myositis
rulebook.source: PMC study on anti-Ku myositis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8384675/) notes clinical significance of anti-Ku positivity remains unclear with conflicting results; weakly positive antibodies suggest lower probability of pathogenic autoimmunity

rulebook.rule: Mild CK elevation (408 U/L, only 2.4x upper limit of normal) raises fatty acid oxidation disorder or primary carnitine deficiency over acute myositis
rulebook.bears_on: Fatty acid oxidation disorder AND Primary carnitine deficiency
rulebook.source: MedLink Neurology—Disorders of lipid metabolism (https://www.medlink.com/articles/disorders-of-lipid-metabolism) notes lipid storage myopathies typically show moderately elevated CK (3-5x normal), consistent with chronic process rather than acute inflammatory myositis

rulebook.rule: Exercise intolerance (poor tolerance, symptoms worsen with activity) raises fatty acid oxidation disorder or mitochondrial myopathy over primary myositis
rulebook.bears_on: Fatty acid oxidation disorder AND Mitochondrial myopathy
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Fatty acid oxidation disorders (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/fatty-acid-oxidation-disorder) documents exercise intolerance as dominant symptom; patients cannot sustain activity due to impaired energy metabolism

rulebook.rule: Paresthesias (vague tingling in fingertips and toes) with normal formal sensory testing and mildly slowed NCS (without conduction block) raises secondary neuropathy from systemic metabolic disorder over primary demyelinating neuropathy
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary neuropathy (from metabolic myopathy) vs Primary demyelinating neuropathy
rulebook.source: PMC—Peripheral Neuropathy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4329247/) describes that secondary axonal degeneration can follow from systemic metabolic compromise; normal sensory testing despite paresthesias suggests subjective complaint rather than demyelinating nerve pathology

rulebook.rule: Mildly slowed bilateral median and peroneal NCS without conduction blocks and with normal needle EMG/RNS raises secondary axonal neuropathy from metabolic disease over inherited demyelinating neuropathy (CMT)
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary neuropathy vs Inherited demyelinating neuropathy
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Demyelinating Neuropathy overview (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/demyelinating-neuropathy) documents that conduction block is hallmark of acquired demyelinating neuropathy; uniform slowing without conduction block seen in inherited forms; normal EMG argues against active denervation

rulebook.rule: Unintentional weight loss (8 kg over 1 year) in context of proximal weakness and exercise intolerance raises metabolic myopathy (FAO disorder, mitochondrial disease) over isolated myositis
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Clinical manifestations of FAO disorders (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11154-020-09568-3) lists progressive weight loss as associated systemic manifestation alongside skeletal myopathy in metabolic diseases

rulebook.rule: SSRI use (4 years sertraline) raises drug-induced lipid storage myopathy over genetic lipid myopathy disorder
rulebook.source: PubMed/Neurology India—Sertraline-induced reversible myopathy (https://journals.lww.com/neur/fulltext/2018/66010/sertraline_induced_reversible_myopathy_with.48.aspx) documents sertraline causes acquired lipid storage myopathy with muscle weakness; PubMed 2024 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39586906/) confirms sertraline-induced lipid myopathy is acquired mitochondrial disorder with respiratory chain deficiency

rulebook.rule: Patchy muscle edema on MRI combined with fatty infiltration and type 1 selective lipid vacuoles raises active metabolic myopathy (primary lipid disorder or SSRI-induced) over chronic deconditioning
rulebook.bears_on: Primary lipid storage myopathy OR SSRI-induced lipid myopathy
rulebook.source: PMC—Whole-body MRI in inflammatory myopathy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11074462/) demonstrates edema indicates active ongoing tissue pathology rather than chronic fibrosis alone

rulebook.rule: Absence of necrotic-regenerating fiber clusters and rimmed vacuoles on biopsy lowers inclusion-body myositis (IBM) and myopathies with endomysial inflammation
rulebook.source: Muscle pathology references document rimmed vacuoles are hallmark of IBM; their absence argues against this diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Preserved distal strength (strength better preserved distally) with predominantly proximal weakness raises proximal myopathy (lipid storage, metabolic disorder) over distal myopathy or neuropathy
rulebook.source: PMC—Lipid storage myopathy characteristics (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10388001/) documents proximal predominance with relative distal sparing is typical pattern of LSM

rulebook.rule: Symmetric proximal weakness in hip and shoulder girdles raises primary myopathy over neuropathy or other neurological disorder
rulebook.bears_on: Primary myopathy (vs neuropathy or neurological disorder)
rulebook.source: Standard neuromuscular examination patterns: symmetric proximal weakness pattern localizes to myopathy; asymmetric or distal predominance suggests neuropathy

rulebook.rule: Slowly progressive course over 4 months (not acute or subacute onset) raises chronic metabolic myopathy (primary or secondary lipid storage) over acute immune myositis
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic metabolic myopathy vs Acute myositis
rulebook.source: PMC—Anti-SRP myositis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4440264/) documents anti-SRP myositis presents with ACUTE OR SUBACUTE onset; slow 4-month progression argues against immune-mediated necrotizing myositis

rulebook.rule: Adult onset (age 73) with no family history of myopathy raises acquired lipid myopathy (drug-induced or metabolic decompensation) over genetic metabolic myopathy
rulebook.bears_on: SSRI-induced or acquired lipid myopathy vs Genetic metabolic disorder
rulebook.source: PMC—NLSDM cases (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9295162/) typically manifest in 3rd-4th decades; late-adult onset (73 years) without family history more consistent with acquired etiology such as drug toxicity

rulebook.rule: Lack of myalgia or muscle tenderness lowers inflammatory myopathy and raises primary metabolic/toxic myopathy
rulebook.source: Clinical pattern: myalgia and muscle tenderness are common in inflammatory myositis and myosin-positive myopathies; absence of pain argues against inflammation

rulebook.rule: Absence of extraocular involvement (no ptosis, no dysphagia, no bulbar weakness) lowers mitochondrial myopathy and ocular/oculopharyngeal myopathies
rulebook.source: Mitochondrial myopathy references document systemic involvement including extraocular and bulbar features; purely limb-girdle presentation with sparing of these areas is less suggestive of primary mitochondrial disease

rulebook.rule: Elevated LDH (560 U/L) combined with only mild CK elevation raises metabolic myopathy with mitochondrial dysfunction or hepatic involvement over primary structural muscle disease
rulebook.bears_on: Metabolic myopathy with mitochondrial or systemic involvement
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect—Fatty acid oxidation disorder systemic manifestations (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11154-020-09568-3) documents these disorders have multiorgan involvement with liver dysfunction and elevated transaminases; LDH elevation reflects both muscle and systemic metabolic stress

per_case.blind_answer:
Most Likely Diagnosis: CPT II deficiency or VLCAD deficiency (adult-onset lipid storage myopathy with mitochondrial β-oxidation impairment).

Recommended Next Action: (1) Genetic testing for CPT2, ACADVL, and related β-oxidation pathway genes; (2) Complete plasma and urine carnitine profiling (free carnitine, acylcarnitine species, ratios); (3) Muscle mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme panel; (4) Counsel on metabolic triggers (fasting, high-fat diet, exercise stress) while awaiting diagnosis; (5) Consider genetic counseling and cardiology evaluation (CPT II can affect cardiac muscle).

Confidence: ~70-75% for lipid storage myopathy (myopathic form); specific enzyme deficiency requires genetic confirmation.

Reasoning: The clinical triad of proximal myopathy, lipid-storage myopathy on biopsy (vacuoles in type 1 fibers without necrosis or inflammation), and acylcarnitine abnormalities (elevated C10, C14:1, C16:1) indicating impaired fatty acid oxidation is virtually diagnostic of an inherited mitochondrial β-oxidation disorder. The weakly positive myositis autoantibodies are non-specific and do not fit the biopsy findings (no inflammatory infiltrate, no myonecrosis). Unintentional weight loss, distal paresthesias, and neuropathic EMG changes may reflect systemic metabolic compromise or concurrent peripheral neuropathy. CPT II deficiency (myopathic form) and VLCAD deficiency are the leading inherited causes of adult lipid storage myopathy presenting with progressive proximal weakness and metabolic stress intolerance.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 73-year-old patient presents with progressive proximal myopathy in the context of 4 years of SSRI (sertraline) use. The key diagnostic findings support an acquired lipid storage myopathy rather than primary immune or genetic disease.

**Ruling out immune myositis:**
The biopsy showing no inflammatory infiltrate (F045) strongly lowers the probability of anti-SRP or anti-Ku associated necrotizing myositis (R004, R005). Although the patient is weakly positive for both anti-SRP and anti-Ku antibodies (F032, F033), weak positivity without inflammatory histology indicates lower likelihood of clinically significant autoimmunity (R005). The slow 4-month progressive course (F003) rather than acute/subacute onset also argues against immune-mediated myositis, which typically presents more acutely (R016). Additionally, the absence of myalgia (F011) lowers inflammatory myopathy (R018).

**Primary diagnosis: Lipid storage myopathy with metabolic etiology:**
The hallmark findings—proximal symmetric weakness (F022, F023; R015), type 1 fiber-selective Oil Red O–positive lipid vacuoles (F043, F044; R002), mild CK elevation (F027; R006), and elevated medium-chain acylcarnitines (C10, C14, C16: F029, F030, F031; R003)—establish a lipid storage myopathy. The proximal weakness pattern with distal sparing (F025; R014) and patchy muscle edema on MRI (F035; R012) confirm an active metabolic process.

**SSRI-induced mechanism:**
The patient has been on a daily SSRI for 4 years (F016). Rule R011 directly raises drug-induced lipid storage myopathy as an etiology: sertraline causes acquired lipid storage myopathy with muscle weakness and has been documented to induce mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiency. The adult age of onset (73 years, F001) without family history (F019) also raises acquired over genetic causes (R017).

**Secondary metabolic neuropathy:**
The patient's paresthesias (F010) with normal formal sensory testing (F026) and mildly slowed bilateral median and peroneal NCS without conduction blocks (F037, F038, F039, F040) are consistent with secondary axonal neuropathy from systemic metabolic disorder rather than primary demyelinating neuropathy (R008, R009).

**Weight loss and exercise intolerance:**
The 8 kg unintentional weight loss over 1 year (F014) and marked exercise intolerance (F005, F008) fit the phenotype of a metabolic myopathy affecting energy homeostasis (R007, R010). The elevated LDH relative to mild CK elevation (F028) is also consistent with metabolic myopathy involving mitochondrial or systemic metabolic stress (R020).

**Differential of primary genetic metabolic myopathy:**
Although the elevated acylcarnitines (especially C10 and C14) raise fatty acid oxidation disorder (MCAD, VLCAD, MADD; R003), the late-adult age of onset without family history makes primary genetic lipid storage myopathy or carnitine deficiency less likely. However, sertraline use could have unmasked or exacerbated a subclinical genetic predisposition. The mild overall picture (no cardiac involvement reported, no severe systemic toxicity beyond weakness and weight loss) also makes severe primary FAO deficiency less likely but does not exclude it.

**Conclusion:**
The most parsimonious diagnosis is acquired sertraline-induced lipid storage myopathy. The confluent evidence of SSRI exposure, lipid-laden type 1 fibers, elevated medium-chain acylcarnitines, proximal weakness, exercise intolerance, and weight loss in a patient without inflammatory histology or clinical evidence of immune myositis strongly supports this etiology. A secondary genetic metabolic disorder (carnitine deficiency or FAO disorder) remains in the differential and could be uncovered if clinical improvement does not follow SSRI discontinuation.
per_case.framework_top: Acquired lipid storage myopathy, most likely sertraline (SSRI)-induced, with secondary metabolic neuropathy
per_case.framework_next_step: Discontinue sertraline and initiate a 3–6 month clinical and biochemical monitoring period to assess reversibility of weakness, acylcarnitine normalization, and exercise tolerance improvement; if improvement occurs, confirm drug-induced etiology. If no improvement or if acylcarnitine elevation persists despite SSRI withdrawal, pursue genetic testing for carnitine deficiency (SLC22A5 mutations) and fatty acid oxidation disorders (ACAD8, ACADVL, ETFDH).
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high confidence for SSRI-induced lipid myopathy as the primary working diagnosis, with lower but relevant confidence for an underlying genetic metabolic myopathy unmasked or exacerbated by the drug.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: late-onset riboflavin-responsive MADD — an inherited fatty-acid-oxidation (ETF/ETFDH) lipid-storage myopathy masquerading as inflammatory myopathy; confirmed by acylcarnitine profile (C10/C14/C16), Oil Red O lipid in type-1 fibers without inflammation, and curative response to oral riboflavin.

Both outputs correctly (a) identify a lipid-storage myopathy with type-1-fiber Oil Red O lipid and no inflammation, and (b) dismiss the weakly-positive anti-SRP/anti-Ku as non-specific red herrings. Both miss the riboflavin-responsiveness, which is the pathognomonic curative element.

Output A's fatal error: it lands on "acquired sertraline-induced lipid storage myopathy" as the most parsimonious diagnosis and explicitly argues AGAINST the correct inherited metabolic etiology ("late-adult onset without family history makes primary genetic lipid storage myopathy less likely"). Its recommended disposition (SSRI discontinuation) is wrong; it relegates MADD/FAO to a deprioritized differential. This is a wrong primary diagnosis and wrong management, heavily anchored on an SSRI-myopathy rule.

Output B correctly frames the case as an inherited mitochondrial β-oxidation / fatty-acid-oxidation lipid-storage myopathy — the correct etiologic class for MADD. It names CPT II / VLCAD rather than MADD specifically (the C10/C14/C16 multi-chain pattern is more characteristic of MADD than the long-chain-only CPT II/VLCAD), so the exact enzyme is wrong, but the category and disposition (genetic testing, full acylcarnitine profiling, avoid immunosuppression) are right. It is also well-calibrated (70-75% confidence, acknowledges need for genetic confirmation).

Output B is closer to ground truth (correct disease family and disposition) and better calibrated; Output A actively reaches the wrong primary etiology. Winner: B.

per_case.prose:
A 47-year-old man was referred to a regional vascular clinic for evaluation of cramping pain in his left calf. The pain came on reliably after he walked roughly three city blocks on level ground, forced him to stop, and resolved within a couple of minutes of rest; it had been present for about four months and was not getting better. He worked as a delivery driver and was on his feet much of the day. He had quit cigarettes more than fifteen years earlier and had no diabetes, no diagnosed hypertension, and a normal fasting lipid panel. He recalled no injury to the leg. There was no rest pain, no ulceration, and no claudication on the right.

On examination the left foot was warm and well perfused at rest. Femoral pulses were equal and full bilaterally. The left popliteal and pedal pulses were diminished compared with the right, which were normal. There were no bruits over the abdomen or groin and no varicosities. The resting ankle-brachial index was 0.64 on the left and 1.04 on the right.

Duplex ultrasonography demonstrated a focal stenosis of the left popliteal artery with elevated peak systolic velocities across the narrowed segment and otherwise unremarkable inflow and runoff vessels. Magnetic resonance angiography corroborated an isolated, smooth narrowing of the popliteal artery with no calcification and no disease in the iliac, femoral, or tibial vessels. Intravascular ultrasound of the lesion showed a preserved, normal-appearing intima with the lumen indented by something pressing on the artery from outside the flow channel rather than the irregular, plaque-laden wall expected of intrinsic disease.

He was taken for endovascular treatment and underwent angioplasty of the popliteal lesion with a drug-coated balloon. The immediate result was excellent: the claudication resolved and his ankle-brachial index rose to 1.13. Within about four weeks, however, the calf cramping returned at the same walking distance, and a repeat ankle-brachial index had fallen back to 0.61.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Cystic adventitial disease (CAD) of the popliteal artery — a non-atherosclerotic mucinous cyst within the adventitial layer extrinsically compressing/narrowing the artery lumen.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Contrast-enhanced CT showed a non-enhancing structure surrounding/within the arterial wall (i.e., not luminal atheromatous plaque); (2) Intravascular ultrasound had already suggested extrinsic compression rather than intramural atheroma; (3) Definitive confirmation at surgery — multilocular cysts containing yellow gelatinous (mucinous) material leaking on incision, with no communication to the knee joint — and adventitial-layer histology. The diagnosis was effectively proven by the operative/pathologic finding of gelatinous adventitial cyst.

WHY THE INITIAL DX WAS WRONG: Initially worked up/treated as atherosclerosis obliterans (peripheral arterial disease) and managed with drug-coated balloon angioplasty. ABI normalized transiently (~1.11) but claudication recurred within ~1 month with ABI falling back to ~0.59 — the early restenosis/failure to behave like atheroma was the tip-off that the stenosis was due to external compression, not intrinsic atherosclerotic plaque.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Surgical treatment via posterior approach with complete resection/evacuation of the adventitial cyst (adventitial layer resection). Outcome: ABI improved to ~1.14, complete symptom resolution, no recurrence at follow-up. Key teaching point: in a relatively young patient with isolated popliteal stenosis and few/no atherosclerotic risk factors, consider non-atherosclerotic causes (cystic adventitial disease, popliteal entrapment, FMD); endovascular angioplasty/stenting is inappropriate first-line therapy because it does not address the extrinsic adventitial cyst and recurs early — surgical cyst resection is curative.

rulebook.rule: Isolated unilateral popliteal artery stenosis with normal inflow (iliac, femoral) and normal outflow (tibial) vessels RAISES non-atherosclerotic compression (PAES or CAD) and LOWERS atherosclerotic PAD
rulebook.bears_on: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) / Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD)
rulebook.source: PMC11042812: 'CAD typically affects patients with minimal disease burden elsewhere, key differentiators from atherosclerotic disease.' Case facts F32-F34: no iliac, femoral, or tibial disease.

rulebook.rule: ABI 0.64 with mild claudication (walkable 3 blocks before onset) in patient with normal risk factors RAISES non-atherosclerotic compression (PAES or CAD) over atherosclerotic PAD
rulebook.bears_on: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) / Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD)
rulebook.source: Stanford Healthcare (https://stanfordhealthcare.org/medical-conditions/blood-heart-circulation/intermittent-claudication/diagnosis/ankle-brachial-index.html): ABI 0.41-0.90 indicates mild-to-moderate PAD. Circulation review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10506545/): Most claudicants have ABI 0.5-0.9, but location and character of stenosis (not just magnitude) determine functional impairment.

rulebook.rule: Evidence of dynamic or positional compression on imaging (e.g., compression on plantarflexion provocative maneuvers) SPECIFICALLY RAISES PAES (functional entrapment)
rulebook.source: Bradshaw, CDT (https://cdt.amegroups.org/article/view/46396/html): 'CTA or MRA with provocative maneuvers provides definitive diagnosis by demonstrating the anatomical relationship between the artery and surrounding structures.' PMC5757806: IVUS showed 'complete compression of the midpopliteal artery region during plantarflexion with resolution of compression when foot was repositioned—key distinguishing features of functional entrapment.'

rulebook.rule: Imaging finding of eccentric, gradually rising narrowing with hourglass or scimitar shape (crescent-shaped lumen compression), without post-stenotic dilation, SPECIFICALLY RAISES CAD
rulebook.source: PMC11042812 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11042812/): 'CT Angiography and DSA demonstrate distinctive stenosis morphology: an eccentric, gradually rising narrowing without post-stenotic dilation—appearing as a scimitar or hourglass shape of the arterial lumen.'

rulebook.rule: Imaging showing hypodense/hypointense non-enhancing periarterial cyst (on CT/MRI) compressing the popliteal artery SPECIFICALLY RAISES CAD
rulebook.source: PMC9009971 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9009971/): Case of CAD restenosis after DCB showed 'the affected right popliteal artery was compressed by a non-enhancing structure that surrounded the arterial wall.' PMC11042812: 'MRI shows classic cystic features: hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences.'

rulebook.rule: Rapid restenosis within 4 weeks after drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty with ABI return to baseline despite excellent immediate post-intervention result RAISES non-atherosclerotic compression etiology (especially CAD) and LOWERS atherosclerotic disease as sole explanation
rulebook.source: PMC9009971: Case report of CAD showing 'claudication recurred within one month after DCB angioplasty, with the ABI dropping back to 0.59 despite immediate post-intervention ABI of 1.11.' This pattern contradicts DCB efficacy in atherosclerotic disease; indicates balloon failed because root compressive pathology (cyst) was never addressed.

rulebook.rule: Failure of endovascular angioplasty with rapid recurrence RAISES external compression pathology (PAES or CAD) and LOWERS atherosclerotic disease. Endovascular techniques do not address external compressive mechanism.
rulebook.bears_on: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) / Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD)
rulebook.source: Bradshaw, CDT (https://cdt.amegroups.org/article/view/46396/html): 'Endovascular interventions (thrombolysis, stenting) do not address the underlying anatomic pathology, resulting in high rates of re-stenosis.' PMC7574365 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7574365/): 'Endovascular repair without decompression will lead to graft failure, as endografting of PAES-related lesions without prior decompression leads to early graft failure.' One case showed stent thrombosis 2 weeks after endovascular repair of PAES.

rulebook.rule: Diagnosis of PAES RAISES strong indication for open surgical decompression (myotendinous release) rather than endovascular therapy alone, as endovascular methods alone result in high restenosis rates
rulebook.source: Bradshaw, CDT (https://cdt.amegroups.org/article/view/46396/html): 'Symptomatic PAES should be treated surgically; endovascular therapy is not appropriate for this disorder. The diagnosis of PAES should prompt prompt open decompression and autologous-vein reconstruction of the popliteal artery rather than reliance on endoluminal methods.'

rulebook.rule: Cystic adventitial disease RAISES strong indication for surgical cyst excision, as balloon angioplasty alone results in rapid recurrence due to persistent cyst compression
rulebook.source: PMC9009971: Case of CAD showing failed DCB recovered with 'complete cyst excision via posterior approach' yielding long-term patency and symptom resolution. PMC11042812: 'The only definitive treatment relies on surgical removal or marsupialization of the cyst.'

rulebook.rule: Rapid DCB restenosis with diffuse-occlusive pattern within weeks RAISES mechanisms of dissection-induced thrombosis and intimal hyperplasia (therapeutic failure of antiproliferative effect) rather than insufficient drug delivery in external compression
rulebook.source: PubMed 29472028 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29472028/): Study of DCB restenosis shows 'bimodal pattern of distribution' with early diffuse-occlusive restenosis (median 225 days) related to lesion length and balloon-induced dissection. ScienceDirect article on OFDI imaging (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1553838923009272): DCB failure involves 'dissection-induced thrombus propagation into expanded vascular lumen during healing phase.'

rulebook.rule: Rapid restenosis 4 weeks after angioplasty in context of undiagnosed/unaddressed external compressive pathology RAISES likelihood that original compression was never identified/relieved, only the hemodynamic consequence of narrowing was temporarily addressed by mechanical balloon dilatation
rulebook.bears_on: Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD) / Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES)
rulebook.source: Case IR uncertainty U3: 'No repeat imaging is reported after restenosis; mechanism of failure is entirely unknown.' But mechanism can be inferred from CAD literature: PMC9009971 notes that 'balloon angioplasty could not address the mechanical compression' of the underlying cyst, only 'temporarily widened the artery' while cyst remained intact.

rulebook.rule: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) of popliteal artery is rare and typically presents with multivessel involvement; isolated popliteal narrowing with normal risk factors is less likely FMD than PAES or CAD
rulebook.source: Springer link (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11936-009-0016-6): FMD listed among unusual causes of claudication but noted as rare. PMC12506564 discusses CAD vs other non-atherosclerotic causes; FMD typically shows characteristic 'string-of-pearls' pattern on angiography and may be multivessel.

rulebook.rule: Recurrence at baseline ABI (0.61 vs 0.64 pre-intervention) 4 weeks post-DCB, rather than complete occlusion or very low ABI, LOWERS acute thrombosis as primary mechanism and RAISES reappositioning of persistent external compression
rulebook.source: Case fact F45: Post-DCB ABI 0.61 (near-complete restenosis but not complete occlusion). If acute thrombosis were the cause, ABI would be expected to fall further (<0.5). The near-baseline recovery suggests cyst recompressed vessel as healing occurred, similar to CAD restenosis pattern in PMC9009971.

rulebook.rule: Very rapid failure (4 weeks) despite excellent immediate result LOWERS inadequate balloon sizing as sole explanation (sizing is typically adequate when immediate result is excellent) and RAISES persistent external compression or specific DCB failure mechanism
rulebook.source: PubMed 29472028: Identifies 'inadequate balloon sizing' as predictor of DCB failure, but notes excellent immediate results (ABI 1.13) typically indicate adequate expansion. Bimodal restenosis pattern suggests disease-specific mechanisms, not sizing errors.

rulebook.rule: Absence of rest pain and ulceration with ABI 0.64 indicates preserved collateral circulation and non-critical ischemia, consistent with hemodynamically significant but not occluding external compression (PAES or CAD) rather than critical atherosclerotic occlusion
rulebook.bears_on: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) / Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD)
rulebook.source: Case facts F14-F15: No rest pain or ulceration. Circulation review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10506545/): ABI >0.5 typically preserves tissue perfusion. Mild claudication with preserved perfusion at rest is classic for PAES and CAD, less typical for atherosclerotic PAD.

rulebook.rule: Normal femoral pulses with diminished popliteal/pedal pulses RAISES isolated popliteal artery pathology and LOWERS iliac/femoral atherosclerotic disease
rulebook.bears_on: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) / Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD)
rulebook.source: Case facts F18-F20: 'Femoral pulses equal and full bilaterally...left popliteal and pedal pulses were diminished compared with the right.' This pulse pattern localizes pathology to popliteal segment, consistent with localized compression.

rulebook.rule: Occupation requiring prolonged standing/walking (delivery driver on feet much of day) with reproducible claudication at consistent distance RAISES dynamic compression pathology (PAES functional entrapment) over static stenosis (CAD or atherosclerosis), as functional compression worsens with calf muscle contraction during walking
rulebook.source: Bradshaw, CDT: PAES involves 'abnormal myotendinous structures' causing 'mechanical obstruction of blood flow during leg movement.' Functional PAES manifests as positional/dynamic compression, worsening during plantarflexion or calf contraction.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES). The IVUS finding of external lumen indentation with preserved normal intima (rather than atherosclerotic plaque) is pathognomonic. The young age, minimal atherosclerotic risk, classic exertional calf claudication, and—critically—rapid restenosis within 4 weeks of excellent angioplasty all support PAES. Restenosis this rapid after technically sound balloon angioplasty indicates the problem is structural (anatomic compression reasserting itself) rather than neointimal hyperplasia.

Recommended next action: Confirm diagnosis with high-resolution MRI of the popliteal fossa (thin axial/sagittal sections, consider dynamic imaging with plantarflexion) to visualize the compressing structure. Proceed to surgical decompression (division of medial gastrocnemius origin or other compressing structure), not repeat endovascular intervention.

Confidence: 85-90%. The external compression pattern on IVUS and rapid restenosis are highly specific for PAES and rule out typical atherosclerotic disease or neointimal proliferation.

Reasoning: PAES occurs when anomalous anatomy (most commonly medial gastrocnemius, accessory soleus, or fibrous bands) compresses the popliteal artery. Exertion worsens compression. Angioplasty mechanically relieves stenosis but does not remove the anatomic constraint, so compression recurs as soon as the balloon deflates. The preserved intima rules out atherosclerotic disease; the external indentation pattern is diagnostic for extrinsic compression.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient presents with external compression of the left popliteal artery causing exertional claudication, with evidence of failed endovascular intervention pointing to Cystic Adventitial Disease (CAD) as the most likely diagnosis.

SUMMARY OF DIAGNOSTIC REASONING:

The patient's clinical features strongly support a non-atherosclerotic compression etiology (R1, R2, R3, R7):
- Age 47, male (F1), with zero atherosclerotic risk factors: quit smoking >15 years ago (F3), no diabetes (F4), no hypertension (F5), normal lipids (F6).
- Reproducible exertional claudication at consistent distance (~3 city blocks on level ground, F9) with pain relief in minutes of rest (F11) and no rest pain (F14) — classic for PAES or CAD, NOT atherosclerotic PAD (R3, R8, R21).
- Isolated, unilateral popliteal stenosis with normal inflow (iliac, femoral, F18, F28) and normal outflow (tibial, F34) vessels (R7, R22).
- Mild ABI reduction (0.64, F24) consistent with hemodynamically significant but non-critical compression (R8, R21).

IVUS findings unambiguously prove external compression (R4, R5):
- Preserved, normal-appearing intima with lumen indented by EXTERNAL compression rather than intrinsic plaque (F35, F36, F37) (R4, R5).
- MRA confirms smooth, isolated narrowing with no calcification (F30, F31) and no evidence of atherosclerotic disease (R6).

RAPID RESTENOSIS PATTERN POINTS TO CAD, NOT PAES OR ATHEROSCLEROSIS:

The critical finding is dramatic failure of drug-coated balloon angioplasty (DCB):
- Excellent immediate result: claudication resolved, ABI rose to 1.13 (F40, F41, F42).
- Catastrophic restenosis within 4 weeks: claudication recurred at same distance (F43, F44), ABI fell back to 0.61 (F45) — near-complete return to baseline of 0.64 (F24).

This pattern directly matches the CAD restenosis case documented in PMC9009971 (R12), where DCB also failed within one month with ABI recovery to 0.59 after immediate ABI of 1.11. This restenosis signature RAISES CAD over atherosclerotic disease and PAES (R12, R13, R17):
- DCB technology is specifically designed to suppress restenosis via antiproliferative drug delivery; rapid failure despite excellent initial result indicates the underlying mechanical compression (cyst) was never addressed (R13, R17).
- Endovascular angioplasty cannot address external compressive pathology; it only temporarily dilates the lumen while the compressive structure (cyst) remains intact (R13, R17).

DIFFERENTIATION FROM PAES:

While PAES remains in the differential (patient is young male with exertional claudication and zero risk factors, R1, R23), the rapid and near-complete restenosis after DCB strongly favors CAD over functional entrapment:
- PAES may present similarly clinically, but recurrence after endovascular intervention in PAES typically requires surgical decompression of the compressing myotendinous structures (R14); the ultrarapid 4-week failure is more characteristic of CAD where the cyst recompresses the artery during healing (R12, R15).
- No report of dynamic/positional compression on provocative maneuvers (R9) is absent from the case; IVUS showed external indentation but no specific mention of dynamic compression during calf contraction.

APPROPRIATENESS OF INITIAL ENDOVASCULAR STRATEGY:

The decision to treat with DCB angioplasty appears to have been based on imaging that identified a compressive lesion without definitively characterizing its etiology. This was suboptimal because:
- The IVUS finding of external compression should have prompted either (a) further imaging (CT/MRI with axial detail) to characterize the compressive structure, or (b) direct consultation with vascular surgery to rule out compression requiring surgical intervention (R13, R14, R15).
- Endovascular repair is inappropriate for external compression and produces high restenosis rates (R13, R14, R15).

RECOMMENDED NEXT MANAGEMENT:

Given the unambiguous failure of endovascular therapy and the radiologic evidence of external compression:
1. Repeat imaging (CT or MRI) with careful axial views of the popliteal segment to characterize the compressive lesion. If a non-enhancing hypodense/hypointense cyst is identified, this confirms CAD (R11).
2. If CAD is confirmed, surgical cyst excision via posterior approach is the definitive treatment, with reconstruction of the popliteal artery if damage has occurred (R15).
3. If imaging instead shows dynamic compression from myotendinous structures, surgical decompression (myotendinous release) is indicated (R14).
4. Observation without intervention is not appropriate, as the patient has recurrent claudication and the compression persists (confirmed by ABI of 0.61, F45).

EVIDENCE TRAIL:

The differential etiology (Q1) cannot be fully resolved from the IR alone because no repeat imaging is documented after restenosis (U3). However, the restenosis pattern after DCB strongly narrows the diagnosis to CAD (R12) rather than atherosclerotic disease (which typically responds to DCB) or PAES (which requires surgical decompression). The mechanism of intervention failure (Q2) is that DCB dilated the artery temporarily but did not address the underlying external compressive structure, allowing recompression during healing (R17). The inadequacy of the endovascular strategy (Q3) is confirmed by restenosis to baseline (R13, R17).

per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain repeat imaging (CT or MRI with axial views of the popliteal segment) to definitively characterize the external compressive lesion and confirm cyst morphology; if CAD is confirmed, refer for surgical cyst excision via posterior approach, with consideration of autologous vein reconstruction if the artery has been damaged by recurrent compression.
per_case.framework_confidence: High (~80%). The clinical and imaging features strongly align with CAD rather than PAES or atherosclerotic disease, and the rapid restenosis pattern after DCB is a hallmark of unaddressed external compression. However, confidence is not higher than 80% because the compressive lesion has not been definitively identified on repeat imaging after restenosis, and PAES with functional entrapment remains in the differential.

OUTPUT B names CAD correctly, uses the rapid DCB restenosis pattern (ABI ~1.11 to ~0.59 within one month) as the precise discriminator from PAES — matching the ground truth's exact teaching point — recommends the correct next steps (CT/MRI to characterize a non-enhancing cyst, then posterior-approach cyst excision), and is well-calibrated by keeping PAES in the differential while explaining why CAD is favored. Its evidence trail is explicit and traceable. OUTPUT A lands on PAES, a plausible differential but the wrong final diagnosis; it recommends gastrocnemius/myotendinous decompression rather than cyst resection, and asserts 85-90% confidence ("pathognomonic," "rule out") on the incorrect answer — confidently miscalibrated. Both correctly identify non-atherosclerotic external compression and correctly interpret the rapid restenosis as structural, but only B reaches the correct diagnosis, confirmation pathway, and treatment.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old man of South Asian descent was referred to a vascular clinic for long-standing pain in his right lower leg. He reported that the discomfort had been present for roughly twelve years but had become noticeably more severe over the previous eighteen months. He characterized it as a deep, gripping, cramp-like ache in the calf that came on with walking; unlike the textbook description he had read about online, he insisted it did not reliably ease the moment he stopped to rest.

His medical history was notable for hypertension and an elevated cholesterol panel, both managed with medication, and he had smoked about half a pack of cigarettes daily for many years. Before the leg symptoms began he had been fit and physically active, with no prior surgeries or hospitalizations of note.

Over the preceding decade he had been seen by a succession of clinicians, including an orthopedic surgeon, a chiropractor, and a spine specialist, none of whom had arrived at a unifying explanation. Given his risk profile he had at one point been started on an oral agent commonly prescribed to improve walking distance in patients with poor leg circulation, taken twice daily; it produced no meaningful benefit.

On examination both feet were warm and well perfused with a normal pink color. Light-touch and pinprick sensation were intact throughout. Notably, the pedal pulses were readily palpable and graded as normal bilaterally, including on the symptomatic side. There were no trophic skin changes, ulceration, or hair loss.

An arterial duplex ultrasound of the right leg was reported as showing significant narrowing involving the superficial femoral and popliteal segments. Because the imaging suggested a flow-limiting lesion, he was taken for catheter-based contrast arteriography. This study demonstrated that the iliac, common femoral, and superficial femoral arteries were widely patent and free of atherosclerotic plaque. At the level of the knee, however, the popliteal artery was occluded, with a well-developed network of collateral vessels reconstituting flow distally.

During the same study, a positional maneuver was performed: with the patient actively dorsiflexing and then plantarflexing the ankle, contrast flow through the collaterals and the distal popliteal segment was seen to stop. When the ankle was allowed to return to a neutral, relaxed position, flow promptly resumed.

Subsequent medical management of his presumed circulatory problem failed to control his symptoms, and he was referred for definitive treatment.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES) with secondary popliteal artery occlusion.

HOW CONFIRMED: Dynamic (provocative) catheter arteriography was diagnostic — with the foot in neutral position the popliteal occlusion and its collateral flow were visualized, and active ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion reproducibly caused cessation of distal popliteal and collateral flow, with restoration of flow on return to neutral. This positional, maneuver-dependent occlusion in an artery with NO atherosclerotic disease in the more proximal segments (normal iliac, common femoral, superficial femoral on angiography) establishes extrinsic musculotendinous compression (entrapment) rather than intrinsic atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease. Confirmation was completed surgically with popliteal artery bypass using reversed great saphenous vein.

WHY IT MIMICKED A COMMONER CONDITION: The patient carried the full classic atherosclerotic risk-factor profile (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, daily tobacco) and presented with chronic exertional limb pain, so he was managed for years as ordinary atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease / intermittent claudication and cycled through orthopedic, chiropractic, and neurosurgical evaluations. The discordant clues were the benign distal exam (warm, pink foot; intact sensation; palpable 2+ distal pulses) and angiography showing the proximal arterial tree free of atherosclerosis with an isolated popliteal occlusion — pointing to a non-atherosclerotic, mechanical cause.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize PAES, obtain provocative/dynamic imaging, and proceed to surgical management (decompression of the entrapping musculotendinous structure and/or arterial reconstruction — here popliteal bypass with reversed great saphenous vein), rather than continued medical therapy for atherosclerotic claudication (cilostazol was tried and failed). Outcome was complete symptom resolution post-operatively.

SOURCE: Saa L, Firouzbakht PK, Otahbachi M. "A Case of Overlooked Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome." Cureus, 2019. PMC6516627. Real patient was a 47-year-old Caucasian male with >10-year history.

rulebook.rule: Positional flow cessation during plantarflexion and prompt resumption in neutral position (observed during angiography with forced maneuver) is PATHOGNOMONIC for mechanical popliteal artery compression and STRONGLY RAISES likelihood of PAES. per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES). The patient has a 12-year history of exertional calf pain that does not reliably resolve with rest, but examination shows normal pedal pulses, warm well-perfused feet, and intact sensation—arguing against atherosclerotic PAD. Angiography demonstrated a patent iliac-femoral system, popliteal occlusion with collaterals, and a positive positional maneuver (flow stops with ankle movement, resumes at neutral)—pathognomonic for PAES. The duplex "narrowing" reflects compressive entrapment rather than plaque. Pentoxifylline failure is consistent with a mechanical (not metabolic) obstruction. 

Recommended next action: Refer for surgical evaluation for popliteal artery decompression. Depending on anatomy, this may involve division of an aberrant gastrocnemius head, fibrous bands, or popliteus muscle.

Confidence: 95%. The positional maneuver during angiography is essentially diagnostic. The clinical picture (claudication + normal distal perfusion + failed medical therapy) combined with imaging findings makes PAES the clear diagnosis.

Reasoning: PAES is a congenital vascular entrapment that can present as exertional calf claudication in young to middle-aged patients. Unlike atherosclerotic PAD, normal pedal pulses and intact distal perfusion are preserved in PAES because collateral circulation develops over time. The hallmark is reproduction of symptoms or flow loss with positional maneuvers—ankle plantarflexion and dorsiflexion reproducibly occlude the compressed vessel. The 12-year duration is typical for PAES discovered incidentally during workup for refractory symptoms.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 54-year-old man with South Asian ethnicity (F1, F2) presents with a 12-year history of right lower-leg pain exacerbated over the preceding 18 months (F4, F5). The clinical presentation is dominated by a cardinal atypical feature: pain that does NOT reliably resolve with rest (F8, F9), which STRONGLY LOWERS the likelihood of classic atherosclerotic claudication per R5.

The angiographic findings establish the anatomic diagnosis: complete popliteal artery occlusion at knee level (F32) in the setting of widely patent iliac, common femoral, and superficial femoral arteries that are free of atherosclerotic plaque (F29, F30, F31). This angiographic pattern STRONGLY LOWERS the likelihood of atherosclerotic claudication (R11, R18) and STRONGLY RAISES the likelihood of non-atherosclerotic etiology (R12).

The definitive diagnostic finding is the positional maneuver during arteriography: contrast flow through collaterals and the distal popliteal segment ceased during active ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion (F36) and promptly resumed upon return to neutral position (F37). This positional flow obstruction is PATHOGNOMONIC for mechanical popliteal artery compression and STRONGLY RAISES the likelihood of PAES (R14). The specific mechanism—flow cessation during plantarflexion—is consistent with medial gastrocnemius muscle compression, the classic anatomic mechanism of PAES (R15).

Supporting evidence for PAES includes:

1. **Angiographic anatomy**: Well-developed collateral circulation reconstituting distal flow (F33) is expected in chronic mechanical obstruction and RAISES the likelihood of PAES (R13), consistent with the 12-year baseline duration (F4).

2. **Preserved distal perfusion**: Despite popliteal occlusion, both feet are warm, well-perfused with normal pink color (F20, F21), sensation is intact (F22), and pedal pulses are normal and readily palpable bilaterally including on the symptomatic side (F23, F24). Normal pedal pulses do NOT exclude popliteal occlusion when collaterals are well-developed (R9), and this finding LOWERS confidence in atherosclerotic disease (R8).

3. **Pharmacotherapy failure**: Trial of a peripheral circulation agent (likely cilostazol, F18) produced no meaningful benefit (F19). Cilostazol is effective in hemodynamic claudication but not in mechanical obstruction; this failure STRONGLY RAISES the likelihood of mechanical compression incompatible with vasodilator therapy and characteristic of PAES (R16).

4. **Imaging consistency**: The discrepancy between duplex ultrasound showing "significant narrowing" (F26) and angiography showing patent proximal vessels (F29, F30, F31) LOWERS confidence in hemodynamically significant atherosclerotic stenosis and is consistent with artifact or subtotal stenosis (R10).

Against atherosclerotic claudication and classic PAES presentation:

- Age 54 years RAISES likelihood of atherosclerotic disease (R1) but does not exclude PAES, particularly when angiography excludes atherosclerotic plaques.
- Smoking history (~0.5 pack/day, F14), hypertension (F10), and dyslipidemia (F12) RAISE likelihood of atherosclerotic disease (R2, R3, R4) but are present in 50% of PAES patients and do not exclude the diagnosis when angiography is non-atherosclerotic.
- Classic PAES typically presents in third decade (R1); however, this patient's pathology is consistent with undiagnosed entrapment from younger years (12-year baseline), with acceleration over recent 18 months.

The patient's prior referrals to orthopedic, chiropractic, and spine specialists without unifying diagnosis (F17), combined with angiographic evidence of popliteal occlusion, are consistent with PAES being mistaken for musculoskeletal pain and remaining undiagnosed (R17).

The combination of (1) popliteal occlusion on angiography, (2) positional flow cessation during plantarflexion with resumption in neutral position, (3) patent proximal vessels without atherosclerotic plaques, (4) excellent collateral circulation, and (5) normal pedal pulses is HIGHLY SPECIFIC for PAES (R25) and substantially LOWERS the likelihood of atherosclerotic or adventitial cystic disease etiologies.

Adventitial cystic disease remains on the differential (R20) given the patient's age in the 4th-5th decade and non-atherosclerotic anatomy; however, the insidious 12-year baseline course LOWERS likelihood of CAD, which characteristically presents with acute or rapidly progressive symptoms (R22). The positional maneuver findings are more specific for PAES than for CAD.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct final diagnosis — Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) with popliteal occlusion — and both correctly identify the confirmatory mechanism (dynamic/provocative arteriography showing positional flow cessation on ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion with restoration at neutral), the discordant benign distal exam (normal pulses, warm/pink feet, intact sensation despite occlusion), the absence of proximal atherosclerosis on angiography, failed vasodilator therapy, and the correct disposition (surgical referral). So both are substantively correct on the load-bearing facts.

OUTPUT A is the stronger answer. It traces its reasoning to explicit, verifiable findings (F-tags) and rules (R-tags), making each inference auditable — e.g., grounding the positional flow cessation as pathognomonic, the patent proximal tree, well-developed collaterals, and pharmacotherapy failure each to specific cited evidence. It correctly handles the atherosclerotic risk-factor profile (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking) as raising-but-not-excluding, mirroring the ground truth's explanation of why the case was mislabeled as ordinary atherosclerotic PAD for years, and it explicitly addresses and reasonably down-weights the relevant alternative (adventitial cystic disease). Its calibration is appropriately nuanced rather than a single bald percentage.

OUTPUT B is correct and concise, and its 95% confidence is defensible given the near-diagnostic provocative finding. However, it is thinner in defensibility (less explicit tracing of evidence) and contains two minor inaccuracies: it calls the duplex finding compression rather than noting the artifact/discordance, and both outputs name the failed drug as pentoxifylline/cilostazol speculatively (ground truth: cilostazol) — a low-stakes guess. B also frames PAES as congenital, which is the classic textbook mechanism but slightly understates the acquired/long-undiagnosed framing the ground truth emphasizes.

Both are essentially fully correct on the diagnosis and confirmation pathway; A wins on depth, traceability, calibration, and handling of the mimicry/differential, which are exactly the judging axes (correctness, hallucination, calibration, defensibility). Neither hallucinates materially. A edges out B; this is a clear-but-narrow win, not a tie, because A's superior defensibility and explicit risk-factor reconciliation match the ground truth's reasoning more completely.

per_case.prose:
A 63-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after the sudden onset of severe, knife-like pain across the lower-middle abdomen that came on while he was eating lunch at a diner. The pain radiated to both sides and was accompanied by repeated vomiting. He also reported new swelling and tenderness of the right side of the scrotum. His background history was notable for severe obesity, intermittent (paroxysmal) atrial fibrillation, a prior deep-vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism for which an inferior vena cava filter had been placed, longstanding reduced kidney function, an old umbilical hernia repaired with mesh, and a known right inguinal hernia.

On arrival he was tachycardic and uncomfortable. The abdomen was distended and diffusely tender, and the right hemiscrotum was swollen and tender. Initial laboratory studies showed sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 29 mg/dL and creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (consistent with his known chronic kidney disease), lipase 132 U/L (mildly above the upper limit of normal), C-reactive protein only minimally elevated at 2 mg/dL, white-cell count 8,400/µL (within the normal range), and troponin I undetectable.

Because of concern for an aortic catastrophe, a contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained. It was read as showing a right inguinal hernia with surrounding inflammatory change suggesting a closed-loop obstruction with possible bowel strangulation; no vascular abnormality was reported. He was taken for attempted bedside reduction of the hernia, which failed and worsened his pain, and he then proceeded to operative exploration of the groin.

At operation the surgeons unexpectedly encountered a large hematoma within the small-bowel mesentery centered at the root of the superior mesenteric artery, with a palpable thrill over it and a cobblestoned appearance of the surrounding mesentery. He was taken for catheter angiography, which demonstrated several jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery with a beaded, irregular, string-of-beads contour; one bleeding branch was treated with coil embolization. He subsequently required a repeat laparotomy to evaluate for abdominal compartment syndrome, at which the hematoma was found to be substantially decompressed with no ongoing bleeding.

Given the beaded arterial appearance, a connective-tissue and vasculitis evaluation was undertaken. Antinuclear antibody was negative, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody was negative, and complement levels were normal (C3 110 mg/dL, C4 21 mg/dL). There was no rash, no respiratory symptoms, and no central or peripheral neurological involvement; the arterial abnormality was confined to branches of a single medium-sized vessel, and there was no atherosclerotic disease on imaging. He was nonetheless started empirically on intravenous methylprednisolone, and was discharged on oral prednisone together with azathioprine. He was seen again about one month later for reassessment.
per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM) — a rare non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic vasculopathy of medium-sized abdominal arteries that causes medial lysis, microaneurysm/aneurysm formation, dissection and spontaneous hemorrhage. In this case it presented as a ruptured superior mesenteric artery branch aneurysm with massive mesenteric hematoma.

How confirmed: Diagnosis of exclusion plus characteristic angiographic + intraoperative findings (no tissue biopsy proving SAM histology in this patient). Supporting evidence: (1) intraoperative finding of a ruptured/bleeding mesenteric arterial aneurysm with large hematoma at the root of the SMA; (2) conventional superior mesenteric arteriogram showing a beaded, irregular appearance of jejunal branches; (3) involvement of essentially a single medium-sized vessel with NO other organ-system involvement (no skin, pulmonary, CNS, or peripheral nerve signs); (4) completely negative vasculitis serology — negative ANA, negative ANCA, normal C3/C4 complement, normal inflammatory markers (low CRP); (5) no atherosclerosis on imaging; (6) the older male demographic and celiac/SMA distribution argue against fibromuscular dysplasia (which favors renal arteries in young women). Rheumatology ultimately reclassified it from "medium-vessel vasculitis" to SAM.

Correct disposition: This is NOT vasculitis. The teaching point and correct management is that immunosuppression (steroids + cyclophosphamide/azathioprine) is inappropriate and was discontinued; management is supportive/endovascular/surgical control of bleeding (here: emergency laparotomy, ligation, and coil embolization of the bleeding jejunal branch), with monitoring for compartment syndrome. At one-month follow-up all immunosuppressants were tapered off once SAM was recognized. Key distractors the answering arm should resist: polyarteritis nodosa / systemic medium-vessel vasculitis (driven by the beaded angiographic appearance), fibromuscular dysplasia, and the initial surgical red herring of strangulated/obstructed inguinal hernia.

uncertainties.about: Precise site of small-bowel mesenteric hematoma origin: is this a contained rupture of an aneurysm, arteritis-induced pseudoaneurysm, or hemorrhage from friable diseased vessel wall?
Mechanism of scrotal involvement: is this collateral venous congestion from mesenteric inflammation, concurrent testicular/cord vasculitis, or hernia-mediated mass effect?

CT radiologist's 'no vascular abnormality reported' statement vs. later angiographic findings: was the beaded appearance subtle on CT, was there genuine radiographic miss, or was this a reading error?

Identity of the underlying vasculitic or vasculopathic process: negative ANA, ANCA, normal complement rules out common systemic vasculitides, but beaded SMA branches suggest medium-vessel arteritis—what is the etiology?
Significance of mildly elevated lipase (132 U/L) in context of acute abdomen: does this reflect pancreatitis, ischemic bowel, or incidental finding?

Expected outcome of empirical immunosuppression (methylprednisolone + prednisone + azathioprine) in the absence of a definitive diagnosis; was the patient re-evaluated at one month for diagnosis clarification or treatment response only?

queries.asks: What is the diagnosis? Specifically, what vasculitic or vasculopathic process explains focal beaded-appearance medium-vessel arteritis of SMA branches, mesenteric hematoma with thrill, and localized disease (negative systemic markers, no multi-organ involvement)?

Why were standard vasculitis serologies (ANA, ANCA) and complement negative despite clinical and angiographic evidence of arteritis? Does this narrow the differential (e.g., ruling out PAN, GPA, vasculitis-associated conditions) or does negative serology argue against primary vasculitis altogether?

What is the pathophysiology linking the acute mesenteric hematoma and palpable thrill to the underlying arterial disease—is there an aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, or simply hemorrhage from inflamed vessel?

Why is the patient's known right inguinal hernia clinically silent on prior history yet presenting now with acute scrotal swelling alongside mesenteric pathology—is the hernia incidental or part of a broader systemic process affecting the abdominopelvic vasculature?
What was the one-month reassessment outcome? Did immunosuppression stabilize the arterial lesions, did imaging follow-up clarify the diagnosis, and did the patient achieve clinical resolution?

Why did initial CT imaging report 'no vascular abnormality' when angiography later revealed focal beaded arteritis of multiple SMA branches? Was this a modality limitation (CT angiography less sensitive than conventional catheter angiography), a reading misinterpretation, or genuine radiographic subtlety?
