rulebook.rule: Beaded or 'string-of-beads' appearance of mesenteric arteries on angiography raises the likelihood of medium-vessel vasculitis (including polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic mesenteric vasculitis, or fibromuscular dysplasia)
rulebook.source: Mesenteric Vasculitis - StatPearls, NIH Bookshelf: 'Scattered aneurysms and stenotic segments, giving rise to a beaded appearance' characteristic of mesenteric vasculitis; confirmed in multiple case reports of isolated SMA vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Negative ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) status narrows the differential from ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitides (GPA, MPA) and raises the likelihood of polyarteritis nodosa or idiopathic localized mesenteric vasculitis
rulebook.bears_on: Polyarteritis nodosa or idiopathic mesenteric vasculitis (rules out ANCA-positive vasculitis)
rulebook.source: Polyarteritis Nodosa - Vasculitis UK and CHCC classification: 'PAN is always ANCA negative, and the finding of ANCA in a patient suggests a different form of vasculitis'

rulebook.rule: Negative ANA (antinuclear antibody) and normal complement levels lower the likelihood of systemic lupus erythematosus, cryoglobulinemia, and IgA vasculitis
rulebook.bears_on: SLE, cryoglobulinemia, IgA vasculitis (rules these out)
rulebook.source: Complement Levels in Vasculitis: Complement levels may be low in viral vasculitis or systemic autoimmune diseases; normal levels help exclude these (Vasculitis Diagnosis and Evaluation, MSD Manual Professional Edition)

rulebook.rule: Absence of multi-organ system involvement (no rash, no respiratory symptoms, no neurological involvement, no glomerulonephritis) lowers the likelihood of systemic vasculitis (PAN, GPA, Behçet disease) and raises the likelihood of isolated or primary localized mesenteric vasculitis
rulebook.bears_on: Isolated/primary localized mesenteric vasculitis (versus systemic vasculitis)
rulebook.source: Isolated Superior Mesenteric Artery Vasculitis (Cureus/PMC10329138): 'The key distinguishing feature is absence of systemic involvement combined with imaging evidence of mesenteric vessel inflammation.' Case demonstrated negative autoimmune serologies and no multi-organ findings.

rulebook.rule: Mesenteric hematoma with palpable thrill on surgical exploration raises the likelihood of pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, or active arterial rupture secondary to vasculitis or dissection
rulebook.bears_on: Pseudoaneurysm/AVF or hemorrhagic arteritis (mesenteric arterial rupture)
rulebook.source: Traumatic Superior Mesenteric Artery Pseudoaneurysm literature: 'A pseudoaneurysm and AVF often present as a palpable thrill... Pseudoaneurysms and true aneurysms may have a thrill due to significant turbulence'; PMC article on mesenteric arterial pseudoaneurysm complications

rulebook.rule: Circumferential mesenteric arterial wall thickening, luminal narrowing, and aneurysmal dilatation on imaging raise the likelihood of active medium-vessel arteritis (vasculitis) over non-inflammatory arterial diseases
rulebook.source: Isolated Superior Mesenteric Artery Vasculitis (Cureus/PMC10329138): Imaging showed 'circumferential arterial wall thickening, luminal narrowing and aneurysms'—hallmarks of medium vessel vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) without elevated troponin or significant lipase raise the likelihood of systemic inflammation from vasculitis rather than acute myocardial infarction or acute pancreatitis
rulebook.bears_on: Vasculitis (inflammatory process) rather than cardiac or pancreatic etiology
rulebook.source: Mesenteric Vasculitis - StatPearls: Elevated ESR and CRP are typical inflammatory markers in mesenteric vasculitis diagnostic workup

rulebook.rule: Mildly elevated serum lipase (132 U/L, just above normal) without markedly elevated pancreatic enzymes or pancreatitis imaging findings lowers the likelihood of primary acute pancreatitis as cause of acute abdomen
rulebook.bears_on: Acute pancreatitis (rules it out as primary diagnosis)
rulebook.source: Clinical judgment: Mild lipase elevation in context of acute abdomen with clear mesenteric findings more consistent with incidental elevation or ischemia-induced enzyme leak than primary pancreatitis

rulebook.rule: Localization of arterial pathology to branches of a single medium-sized vessel (superior mesenteric artery) without involvement of other major arterial beds raises the likelihood of primary localized mesenteric vasculitis or dissection over systemic arteritis
rulebook.bears_on: Isolated mesenteric vasculitis or dissection (versus systemic polyarteritis nodosa or Takayasu arteritis)
rulebook.source: Mesenteric Vasculitis review literature: Isolated SMA involvement in only 16% of cases; when isolated and seronegative, suggests primary idiopathic mesenteric vasculitis rather than systemic PAN

rulebook.rule: Absence of atherosclerotic disease on imaging in a 63-year-old patient with severe obesity lowers the likelihood of atherosclerotic mesenteric ischemia; raises likelihood of inflammatory or dissective arteriopathy
rulebook.source: High-Value Multidetector CT Angiography literature: Atherosclerotic disease typically shows calcified plaques; absence of atherosclerosis despite risk factors (obesity) supports non-atherosclerotic etiology

rulebook.rule: Acute presentation with sudden severe pain, vomiting, and hemodynamic stress (tachycardia) during eating raises the likelihood of arterial event (dissection, rupture, or vasculitic erosion) over chronic ischemic or inflammatory process
rulebook.bears_on: Acute arterial event (dissection or rupture) or acute arteritis with hemorrhage
rulebook.source: Spontaneous Mesenteric Artery Dissection literature (PMC9764121): Sudden-onset abdominal pain associated with vomiting is characteristic; mesenteric vasculitis with hemorrhage similarly presents acutely

rulebook.rule: Normal white blood cell count despite acute abdomen lowers the likelihood of bacterial infection or perforation-related peritonitis; consistent with non-infectious inflammatory process (vasculitis)
rulebook.bears_on: Infectious/perforation etiology (rules it out); supports inflammatory vasculitis
rulebook.source: Mesenteric Vasculitis diagnostic approach: WBC elevation expected in perforation or infection; normal WBC supports pure inflammatory vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Initial CT report of 'right inguinal hernia with surrounding inflammatory change suggesting closed-loop obstruction with possible strangulation' followed by operative discovery of mesenteric hematoma instead raises concern for radiographic miss or subtle vascular findings on CT; catheter angiography provides superior sensitivity for beaded arterial patterns
rulebook.bears_on: Imaging modality limitation (CT less sensitive than conventional catheter angiography)
rulebook.source: CT Angiography vs. Catheter Angiography literature: While CTA has 96% sensitivity for mesenteric ischemia overall, conventional catheter angiography remains gold standard for detecting subtle beaded arterial patterns characteristic of vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Cobblestoned appearance of mesentery surrounding the hematoma raises likelihood of inflammatory edema from vasculitis and inflammatory response to arterial rupture or pseudoaneurysm formation
rulebook.bears_on: Mesenteric arteritis with hemorrhage or pseudoaneurysm rupture
rulebook.source: Vasculitis pathology: Inflammatory thickening and edema of mesentery adjacent to affected arteries produce cobblestoned texture; suggests active inflammatory process

rulebook.rule: Emergency surgical exploration revealing mesenteric hematoma rather than simple hernia strangulation, combined with subsequent angiographic findings of beaded SMA branches, raises the likelihood of primary mesenteric arteritis with secondary hemorrhage
rulebook.bears_on: Primary mesenteric arteritis with hemorrhage (versus secondary ischemic necrosis from hernia alone)
rulebook.source: Mesenteric Vasculitis surgical presentation: Unexpected intraoperative findings of hematoma without clear external trauma or hernia mechanism suggest underlying vasculitis as primary pathology

rulebook.rule: Response to empirical immunosuppression (corticosteroids and azathioprine) raises the likelihood of primary inflammatory vasculitis over dissection or thrombotic etiologies
rulebook.source: Isolated Intramural Hematoma of SMA (MDPI/PMC10706161): 'High-dose corticosteroid therapy (25 mg prednisone twice daily) may facilitate faster resolution... with complete regression observed within two months'

rulebook.rule: Chronic kidney disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation history raise the baseline thrombotic risk but do not explain beaded arterial pattern or inflammatory imaging; these comorbidities lower the likelihood of fibromuscular dysplasia (non-inflammatory structural disease)
rulebook.bears_on: Fibromuscular dysplasia (less likely given inflammatory context and comorbidities)
rulebook.source: Fibromuscular Dysplasia overview: FMD is a non-inflammatory disease not associated with acute hematoma, thrombosis, or systemic comorbidities; patients typically present with chronic ischemia or renal artery involvement

rulebook.rule: Absence of oral/genital ulcers, ocular involvement, or skin manifestations lowers the likelihood of Behçet disease despite mesenteric arterial involvement
rulebook.bears_on: Behçet disease (ruled out by absence of mucocutaneous findings)
rulebook.source: Behçet Disease diagnostic criteria: Diagnosis requires recurrent oral ulceration plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions. Absence of these makes Behçet unlikely despite possible mesenteric arteritis

rulebook.rule: Serum creatinine elevated (2.3 mg/dL) consistent with known chronic kidney disease; absence of hematuria or proteinuria on urinalysis lowers the likelihood of systemic necrotizing vasculitis causing glomerulonephritis
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic necrotizing vasculitis with renal involvement (ruled out by absence of urinary findings)
rulebook.source: ANCA-Associated Vasculitis: Glomerulonephritis with hematuria/proteinuria expected; absence of these findings argues against ANCA-associated disease

rulebook.rule: Mesenteric hematoma discovered at operative exploration during attempted hernia reduction raises concern that hernia repair was incidental finding and mesenteric arteritis was true underlying pathology
rulebook.bears_on: Primary mesenteric arteritis with hernia as red herring (versus primary hernia strangulation)
rulebook.source: Surgical diagnosis principle: When major vascular pathology is discovered intraoperatively distinct from clinical preoperative suspicion, the vascular pathology is likely the primary driver of acute presentation

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) of the superior mesenteric artery with spontaneous dissection and mesenteric hemorrhage.

Recommended next action: (1) Confirm FMD diagnosis via imaging review; (2) Screen for FMD in other vascular beds (renal, carotid, iliac); (3) Initiate long-term antiplatelet therapy (aspirin); (4) Taper/discontinue empiric immunosuppression; (5) Arrange vascular medicine/genetics follow-up; (6) Serial imaging surveillance.

Confidence: 85-90%

Reasoning: The "string-of-beads" angiographic pattern is pathognomonic for fibromuscular dysplasia. FMD affects medium-sized arteries, commonly presents with acute arterial rupture/dissection and hemorrhage, and would explain the mesenteric hematoma and bleeding jejunal branches. Negative connective-tissue and vasculitis workup (ANA, ANCA, normal complement, localized single-vessel involvement) effectively excludes systemic vasculitis. Lack of atherosclerotic disease and acute presentation in a younger patient favor FMD over atherosclerotic disease. The empiric immunosuppression was appropriately started pre-diagnosis but is not indicated for FMD.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This patient presents with acute mesenteric arteritis with secondary hemorrhage. The top diagnosis is idiopathic localized (isolated) mesenteric vasculitis, supported by the following integrated reasoning:

**Primary pathology: Medium-vessel arteritis of the SMA.** The angiographic finding of "beaded, irregular, string-of-beads contour" of jejunal branches of the SMA (F30) directly raises the likelihood of medium-vessel vasculitis per R1. The cobblestoned appearance of surrounding mesentery (F29) further raises the likelihood of inflammatory edema consistent with vasculitis (R14). The intraoperative discovery of a large hematoma centered at the root of the SMA (F27) with a palpable thrill (F28) raises the likelihood of pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, or arterial rupture secondary to vasculitis (R5).

**Narrowed differential via negative serology.** The negative ANCA (F35) narrows the differential away from ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA) and toward polyarteritis nodosa or idiopathic mesenteric vasculitis (R2). The negative ANA (F34) and normal complement levels (F36, F37, F38) lower the likelihood of SLE, cryoglobulinemia, and IgA vasculitis (R3). Critically, the absence of multi-organ system involvement—no rash (F39), no respiratory symptoms (F40), no neurological involvement (F41)—lowers the likelihood of systemic vasculitis and raises the likelihood of isolated or primary localized mesenteric vasculitis (R4). The localization of arterial pathology to branches of a single medium-sized vessel (F42) raises the likelihood of primary localized mesenteric vasculitis or dissection over systemic arteritis (R9).

**Hemorrhagic presentation linked to vasculitic rupture.** The acute presentation with sudden severe, knife-like pain during eating (F1, F2), vomiting (F4), and hemodynamic stress (F12—tachycardia) raises the likelihood of an acute arterial event (dissection, rupture, or vasculitic erosion) (R11). The mesenteric hematoma with palpable thrill indicates active bleeding, most parsimoniously explained as rupture or pseudoaneurysm secondary to the underlying medium-vessel arteritis rather than trauma or dissection alone.

**Radiographic correlation and surgical finding.** The initial CT report of "right inguinal hernia with surrounding inflammatory change suggesting closed-loop obstruction" (F24) followed by operative discovery of mesenteric hematoma instead (F27) raises concern for radiographic miss or subtle vascular findings on CT (R13). The subsequent finding of beaded SMA branches on catheter angiography (F30) demonstrates the superior sensitivity of conventional angiography for detecting the characteristic vasculitic pattern. The surgical principle that major vascular pathology discovered intraoperatively distinct from clinical preoperative suspicion suggests the vascular pathology as the primary driver (R20) supports mesenteric arteritis as the true underlying pathology, with the inguinal hernia as an incidental finding.

**Laboratory and imaging findings consistent with vasculitis, not alternative diagnoses.** The mildly elevated lipase (F19) without markedly elevated pancreatic enzymes lowers the likelihood of primary acute pancreatitis (R8). The normal white blood cell count (F21) despite acute abdomen lowers the likelihood of bacterial infection or perforation (R12), consistent with a non-infectious inflammatory process. The absence of atherosclerotic disease on imaging (F43) lowers the likelihood of atherosclerotic mesenteric ischemia (R10) in a 63-year-old with severe obesity.

**Limitation: Seronegative vasculitis and unidentified etiology.** Although the clinical and angiographic evidence strongly supports mesenteric vasculitis as the primary pathologic process, the negative ANCA, negative ANA, normal complement, and absence of systemic features preclude definitive attribution to polyarteritis nodosa or other named systemic vasculitis. This constellation is consistent with idiopathic localized mesenteric vasculitis, a poorly characterized but recognized entity. The possibility of other seronegative medium-vessel arteritides (e.g., primary mesenteric arteritis, vasculitis associated with occult infection, or thrombotic microangiopathy) cannot be excluded without additional diagnostic confirmation.

**Treatment response rationale.** The empirical initiation of immunosuppression with methylprednisolone and discharge on prednisone and azathioprine (F44, F45) is consistent with the treating team's clinical suspicion of primary inflammatory vasculitis. Per R16, response to immunosuppression (to be assessed at the one-month reassessment, F46) would raise the likelihood of primary inflammatory vasculitis over dissection or thrombotic etiologies.

**Summary.** The top diagnosis is idiopathic localized mesenteric vasculitis with secondary mesenteric arterial rupture/pseudoaneurysm and hemorrhage, supported by beaded arterial appearance (R1), negative ANCA and ANA (R2), normal complement (R3), absence of systemic involvement (R4, R9), and the clinical-surgical-angiographic constellation of acute arteritis with hemorrhage (R5, R11, R15). The specific vasculitic etiology remains undetermined pending one-month reassessment and imaging follow-up.
per_case.framework_top: Idiopathic localized (isolated) mesenteric vasculitis with secondary mesenteric arterial rupture/pseudoaneurysm and hematoma formation
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain one-month reassessment imaging (CT angiography or conventional angiography) to document hematoma resolution and stability of beaded arterial lesions; assess serologic re-evaluation for emerging vasculitis markers; if hematoma resolving and serology remains negative, continue immunosuppression (prednisone + azathioprine) with gradual taper pending vascular imaging stability. If hematoma has not resolved, rebleeding occurs, or vascular lesions progress, consider alternative diagnoses (occult infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, or fibromuscular dysplasia with secondary hemorrhage) and refer for repeat angiography and infectious disease/rheumatology consultation.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-high confidence in isolated localized mesenteric vasculitis as the primary pathologic process; however, confidence in identifying the specific vasculitic etiology (PAN vs. idiopathic mesenteric vasculitis vs. other medium-vessel arteritis) is moderate due to negative serology and absence of definitive diagnostic criteria. Confidence in the rupture/pseudoaneurysm mechanism is moderate-to-high based on the palpable thrill and active hemorrhage on angiography.

per_case.rationale:
Neither output names the confirmed diagnosis (segmental arterial mediolysis, SAM), so neither is fully correct. The decisive differentiator is the management/disposition teaching point and which distractor each falls into.

OUTPUT A diagnoses fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). FMD is explicitly named in the ground truth as one of the distractors to resist, and the GT notes the demographic/distribution actually argue against FMD (older male, celiac/SMA distribution vs. young women/renal). So A's specific diagnosis is wrong. HOWEVER, A gets the two most clinically important things right: it correctly recognizes this is NOT a systemic inflammatory vasculitis (correctly using the negative ANA/ANCA/complement and single-vessel involvement to exclude vasculitis), and it correctly recommends tapering/discontinuing immunosuppression — which is precisely the GT's central teaching point and correct disposition. A is a non-inflammatory vasculopathy of medium-sized arteries, which is the correct disease CLASS (same family as SAM), even if the wrong member. Its calibration (85-90%) is overconfident for a wrong specific label, which is a defect.

OUTPUT B diagnoses idiopathic localized mesenteric vasculitis / medium-vessel arteritis. This lands squarely on the primary distractor the GT warns against (driven by the beaded angiographic appearance). More damagingly, B endorses the inflammatory-vasculitis framing and explicitly rationalizes CONTINUING immunosuppression ("response to immunosuppression would raise the likelihood of primary inflammatory vasculitis"), which is the exact opposite of the correct disposition (immunosuppression is inappropriate and was discontinued). B's reasoning is extensively traceable to findings/rules (F/R citations), which is good for defensibility, but it reasons its way confidently into the wrong disease category AND the wrong management. The GT specifically notes rheumatology reclassified AWAY from medium-vessel vasculitis to SAM — B is essentially reproducing the abandoned initial misdiagnosis.

Both are incorrect on the specific label, but A is closer on disease class (non-inflammatory vasculopathy vs. inflammatory arteritis) and, critically, gets the correct disposition (stop immunosuppression, not vasculitis), while B gets both the category and the disposition wrong. Correct management is the higher-stakes teaching point. A wins.

per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old right-handed man, a competitive rower who also trained heavily with overhead barbell work, was referred to a vascular clinic for a second opinion regarding color changes in his dominant hand.

His symptoms had begun roughly eight months earlier, when he noticed that the index finger of his right hand would intermittently turn white and feel cold. Over the following months the episodes spread to involve all of the fingers of that hand and a portion of the palm. He reported that the blanching was reliably brought on by cold weather, by emotional stress, and — a detail he emphasized — by lifting or raising the affected arm above his head; the pallor was typically followed by a flushed, reddened phase as color returned.

He was first evaluated by a rheumatologist about a year before this visit. On the assumption that the picture represented a primary vasospastic disorder, and out of concern for an underlying inflammatory process, he had been placed on a tapering course of oral corticosteroids. His symptoms did not improve.

In the months that followed, the clinical picture broadened. He began to experience aching and fatigue in the right forearm and hand when he exercised or used the arm repetitively, along with tingling, a burning quality, intermittent numbness, and pins-and-needles sensations in the hand. Most strikingly to him, the muscles of the forearm and hand on that side had visibly wasted and weakened over time, to the point that his training performance with that arm had fallen off sharply.

He was otherwise healthy. He took no regular medications aside from the recently prescribed steroid, did not smoke, and had no personal or family history of clotting disorders or connective-tissue disease. Vital signs were normal.

On examination, the right hand showed cool, dusky fingers compared with the left. There was appreciable atrophy of the intrinsic hand and forearm musculature on the right with reduced grip strength. Peripheral pulses in the affected arm were diminished distally. Basic inflammatory markers and an autoantibody screen were unremarkable.

Cross-sectional angiographic imaging of the chest and upper limb was obtained. It demonstrated a fully formed extra rib arising from the lower neck on the right side, fused to the first rib. Adjacent to this, the subclavian artery was dilated, measuring approximately 14 mm at its widest. More distally, there was a large, acute-appearing filling defect within the lower axillary artery that extended onward into the brachial artery and into one of its branches supplying the back of the shoulder region.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (aTOS) caused by a congenital cervical rib compressing the subclavian artery, producing a subclavian artery aneurysm with distal arterio-arterial thromboembolism. The hand/finger blanching that had been labeled "primary Raynaud's phenomenon" was actually digital embolic/ischemic phenomena from the aneurysm, NOT primary vasospastic Raynaud's.

HOW CONFIRMED: CT angiography of the chest/upper extremity was diagnostic — it showed a complete left cervical rib fused to the first rib, a 12-mm subclavian artery aneurysm, and a large acute filling defect (thromboembolus) in the distal axillary artery extending into the brachial and thoracodorsal arteries. The diagnosis was further confirmed operatively (cervical + first rib resection, aneurysm repair) and by 5-year clinical/duplex follow-up showing patent bypass and complete symptom resolution.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is a surgical/limb-threatening vascular emergency, not a condition for steroids or calcium-channel blockers. Correct management = urgent vascular surgery referral, anticoagulation for the acute thromboembolism, thoracic outlet decompression (cervical and first rib resection), subclavian aneurysm resection with bypass (subclavian-to-axillary), embolectomy/distal revascularization (axillary-to-ulnar bypass with vein graft). The initial prednisone-for-presumed-vasculitis pathway was wrong and dangerous. Key teaching point: unilateral, fixed/progressive digital ischemia in a young person — especially with arm-elevation provocation and arm claudication/atrophy — should trigger a search for a structural arterial/thoracic-outlet cause rather than acceptance of a benign primary Raynaud's label.

SOURCE: "A case of misdiagnosed arterial thoracic outlet syndrome as primary Raynaud's phenomenon," Journal of Vascular Surgery Cases, Innovations and Techniques, 2024; PMC11133972.

Embolus (traveling clot lodged in artery)
Arterial dissection (intimal tear with subintimal hematoma)
Atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed acute thrombosis
Vasculitis with luminal narrowing (less likely given normal inflammatory markers)

uncertainties.about: Mechanism linking cervical rib anatomy to vascular injury (dilation + thrombosis)
candidates: Static compression of subclavian artery by rib
Dynamic compression during arm elevation (positional narrowing)
Mechanical trauma from repetitive overhead stress (rowing/barbell work)

Combination of above mechanisms

Initial vasospasm; thrombosis developed later (weeks-months)

queries.asks: What is the primary diagnosis? Is this primary Raynaud phenomenon (vasospastic disorder) or secondary thoracic outlet syndrome with vascular compromise?
What is the pathologic nature of the filling defect? Is it thrombosis, embolus, dissection, or another occlusive lesion?
How did the cervical rib cause vascular injury? Is the mechanism static compression, dynamic positional compression, or mechanical trauma from training?
When did the clinical picture transition from intermittent vasospasm to irreversible atrophy and thrombosis? Was there a discrete acute event or continuous progression?
Is the patient currently at risk for further thrombotic events, or was this a one-time mechanical injury?
What is the indicated treatment? Does this require anticoagulation, surgical decompression (rib resection), arterial intervention, or conservative management?
What is the prognosis for functional recovery? Can the patient recover grip strength and forearm function, or is the atrophy permanent?

ir.inferred_domain: Vascular pathology with secondary neuromuscular manifestations. Specifically: thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) variant with acute arterial thrombosis. Cross-talk between congenital cervical anatomy (extra rib), mechanical vascular injury, thrombotic occlusion, and nerve compression sequelae.

rulebook.rule: Visible muscle atrophy with ischemic lesions (gangrene, ulcers, or digital necrosis) raises secondary Raynaud phenomenon over primary; primary Raynaud rarely causes tissue damage.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary Raynaud phenomenon (lowers) vs. Secondary Raynaud phenomenon / Thoracic outlet syndrome with vascular compromise (raises)
rulebook.source: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/cardiovascular-disorders/peripheral-artery-disorders/raynaud-phenomenon — 'trophic changes are uncommon in primary RP, while irreversible ischemia with tissue damage indicates secondary RP'; https://rheumatology.org/patient-blog/all-about-raynauds-phenomenon — 'Primary Raynaud rarely causes gangrene or tissue loss'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499833/ — secondary Raynaud can result in 'digital ulcers, digital pits, and in severe cases, tissue gangrene'

rulebook.rule: Cervical rib (especially complete, fused to first rib) causes mechanical compression of subclavian artery, leading to intimal damage, chronic arterial spasm, increased shear stress, and thrombosis formation.
rulebook.bears_on: Thoracic outlet syndrome with arterial thrombosis
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3475120/ — 'cervical rib narrows the interscalene triangle; chronic arterial spasm induced by pressure of the cervical rib may increase flow velocity and shear stress at the affected arterial wall...damage the intima and trigger clotting'; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1043067915001677 — 'cervical ribs causing clinical symptoms are large and frequently fused to the first rib, resulting in aneurysm formation or thrombosis'; cervical ribs present in 85% of arterial TOS vs <1% general population

rulebook.rule: Acute-appearing filling defect within artery on angiography indicates in-situ thrombosis (luminal occlusion) rather than dissection or hemodynamic narrowing alone.
rulebook.bears_on: Acute arterial thrombosis (vs. dissection or stenosis)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4363156/ — 'invasive coronary angiography detects intracoronary thrombus through abrupt occlusion or filling defect in partially occluded vessels'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11276486/ — 'diagnostic tree for differentiating occlusion etiology: pseudo-occlusion vs. thrombotic occlusion vs. dissection'

rulebook.rule: Symptom reproducibility with arm elevation above head indicates dynamic positional compression of subclavian artery by cervical rib, not primary vasospasm.
rulebook.bears_on: Thoracic outlet syndrome with mechanical compression (raises) vs. primary Raynaud phenomenon (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.tosmri.com/diagnosis-of-neurogenic-thoracic-outlet-syndrome/diagnosis-of-arterial-thoracic-outlet-syndrome/ — 'symptoms only occur in those arm positions where extrinsic structures compress the artery'; 'dynamic CT/MR Arteriogram studies assess compression of subclavian artery with arm elevated; Duplex ultrasound shows normal flow at rest, complete cessation with arm abduction 45° above shoulder'

rulebook.rule: Paresthesias (tingling, burning, numbness, pins-and-needles) with atrophy indicate nerve compression from vascular insufficiency and ischemia, not primary vasospastic disorder.
rulebook.bears_on: Nerve compression secondary to vascular compromise (raises) vs. pure vasospasm without structural compression (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545200/ — 'paresthesia arises from nerve damage (neuropathy)'; https://mpkb.org/home/symptoms/neurological/paresthesia — 'paresthesia can result from mild compression (edema from obstruction of venous flow) to severe compression (ischemia from obstruction of arterial flow causing axonal injury)'; https://www.centerforvein.com/blog/paresthesia-and-vein-health-whats-the-connection/ — 'neurovascular insufficiency comes from capillary closure within nerve, decreased artery flow, or metabolic ischemia'

rulebook.rule: Progressive muscle atrophy over weeks-to-months (8 months in this case) indicates chronic vascular insufficiency and/or denervation from compression, occurring too slowly for acute thrombosis alone and too progressively for pure vasospasm.
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic mechanical compression with progressive ischemic injury (raises)
rulebook.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11462388/ — 'muscle atrophy occurs rapidly after denervation; denervation in calf increased from 7.6% to 15.6% over 12-week period'; https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/ATVBAHA.120.313831 — 'sensory loss is earliest sign in acute arterial insufficiency; continued compromise leads to diminished muscle strength'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3776571/ — 'chronic recurrent vasospasm can result in atrophy of skin, subcutaneous tissue and muscle'

rulebook.rule: Failure to respond to corticosteroid therapy indicates the underlying pathology is mechanical/vascular (not inflammatory), supporting diagnosis of mechanical compression-induced thrombosis rather than primary inflammatory vasospasm.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary inflammatory vasospasm (lowers) vs. mechanical vascular compression (raises)
rulebook.source: https://atlaspainspecialists.com/thoracic-outlet-syndrome-treatment-options-explained/ — 'corticosteroids help relieve symptoms in muscle-based (neurogenic) TOS with tight scalene/pectoralis muscles; vascular TOS requires surgical removal of abnormal tissue or bone'; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6514035/ — vascular TOS presents mechanically and requires structural repair, not anti-inflammatory treatment

rulebook.rule: Cool, dusky fingers at baseline examination indicate chronic resting hypoperfusion from fixed arterial narrowing, not intermittent vasospasm (which would normalize between attacks).
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic vascular insufficiency from fixed stenosis/thrombosis (raises) vs. episodic vasospasm (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/arterial-insufficiency — 'chronic hypoperfusion leads to cool extremities and impaired microcirculation'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3776571/ — vasospasm causes transient color changes, while fixed arterial compromise causes persistent coolness and cyanosis between attacks

rulebook.rule: Diminished peripheral pulses distally in affected arm indicates fixed arterial narrowing or occlusion (from thrombosis or stenosis), not reversible vasospasm.
rulebook.bears_on: Arterial occlusion/severe stenosis (raises) vs. vasospasm alone (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5126392/ — cervical rib compression produces 'diminished distal pulses at wrist, prolongation of capillary refill'; https://www.tosmri.com/diagnosis-of-neurogenic-thoracic-outlet-syndrome/diagnosis-of-arterial-thoracic-outlet-syndrome/ — 'provocative maneuvers evaluate distal pulses; absence of pulse with arm elevation confirms vascular compression'

rulebook.rule: Biphasic color change (white blanching followed by flushed redness) is consistent with both vasospasm and reperfusion after ischemic episodes; does not alone distinguish primary from secondary disease but indicates vascular insufficiency.
rulebook.bears_on: Vascular ischemia (raises) — applies broadly to both primary and secondary causes
rulebook.source: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/331197-overview — 'Raynaud phenomenon typically presents with 3 phases: white (blanching from vasospasm), blue (cyanosis), red (reperfusion hyperemia); not all phases required for diagnosis'; https://rheumatology.org/patient-blog/all-about-raynauds-phenomenon — 'color changes occur from digital artery vasospasm and reactive hyperemia'

rulebook.rule: Cervical rib present in 85% of arterial TOS but only <1% of general population; presence with vascular symptoms (thrombosis, diminished pulses, aneurysm) is highly specific for arterial TOS.
rulebook.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1043067915001677 — 'cervical ribs present in up to 85% of patients with arterial TOS, though cervical ribs present in <1% of general population'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5126392/ — pooled prevalence of cervical ribs in TOS patients 29.5% vs. healthy 1.1%

rulebook.rule: Unilateral involvement (dominant hand only) with training history argues against primary Raynaud (typically bilateral/symmetric) and supports secondary mechanical process.
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary mechanical thoracic outlet syndrome (raises) vs. primary Raynaud phenomenon (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/cardiovascular-disorders/peripheral-artery-disorders/raynaud-phenomenon — 'primary Raynaud presents with mild, symmetric attacks affecting both hands'; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7658106/ — prospective study of 570 patients with Raynaud found significant differences in 'asymmetry of RP' between primary and those with objective thoracic outlet signs

rulebook.rule: History of competitive rowing and heavy overhead barbell training is a known exacerbating/precipitating factor for mechanical vascular injury in thoracic outlet syndrome, causing repetitive microtrauma to subclavian artery.
rulebook.bears_on: Thoracic outlet syndrome with mechanical vascular injury (raises)
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8569270/ — 'athletic history and exacerbating factors (lifting, overhead work) are key elements of focused history for arterial TOS diagnosis'; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5563393/ — case of arterial TOS with overhead training linked to mechanical compression and thrombosis

rulebook.rule: Normal inflammatory markers and negative autoantibody screen exclude underlying autoimmune/connective tissue disease as cause of secondary Raynaud, leaving mechanical/vascular pathology.
rulebook.bears_on: Mechanical thoracic outlet syndrome (raises) vs. autoimmune-mediated secondary Raynaud (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/cardiovascular-disorders/peripheral-artery-disorders/raynaud-phenomenon — 'secondary Raynaud with elevated antinuclear antibodies and inflammatory markers indicates autoimmune/rheumatic disease'; https://www.amboss.com/us/knowledge/raynaud-phenomenon/ — 'in case of diagnostic uncertainty, perform antinuclear antibody test and nailfold capillaroscopy to exclude connective tissue disorders'

rulebook.rule: Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome with acute thrombosis and vascular compromise is almost always an indication for surgical decompression (first rib resection ± scalenectomy) combined with arterial reconstruction based on degree of arterial damage.
rulebook.bears_on: Treatment of arterial thoracic outlet syndrome
rulebook.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10797336/ — 'arterial TOS cases are almost always an indication for surgery; treatment consists of thoracic outlet decompression combined with arterial reconstruction if deemed necessary based on level of damage'; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5563393/ — 'totally endoscopic first rib resection successfully treats arterial TOS; mortality <0.5%'

rulebook.rule: Intrinsic hand/forearm muscle atrophy from prolonged denervation (8+ months) carries guarded prognosis for recovery; longer denervation period correlates with more unsuccessful reinnervation; recovery may require 2-4 years.
rulebook.source: https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.04.1644 — 'presence and degree of muscular atrophy may predict likelihood of functional recovery; presence of atrophy may indicate irreversible muscle damage'; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11559903/ — 'intrinsic muscles atrophy within months after denervation; longer denervation period = more unsuccessful reinnervation process; recovery timeline 2-4 years'

rulebook.rule: Normal vital signs argue against acute systemic thrombotic burden or acute coronary/cerebrovascular compromise, supporting localized arterial thrombosis confined to upper extremity.
rulebook.bears_on: Localized upper extremity thrombosis (raises) vs. acute systemic thromboembolism (lowers)
rulebook.source: Clinical reasoning: vital sign stability reflects overall perfusion adequacy and absence of shock physiology, consistent with regional rather than systemic arterial compromise

rulebook.rule: Absent personal and family history of thrombophilia argues against inherited clotting disorder and supports mechanical/traumatic etiology of thrombosis rather than primary thrombotic diathesis.
rulebook.bears_on: Secondary thrombosis from mechanical injury (raises) vs. primary thrombophilia (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/hemostasis/overview-of-hemostasis — thrombophilia screening is indicated when thrombosis occurs without mechanical provocation; mechanical injury is a well-established prothrombotic stimulus

rulebook.rule: Absence of tobacco use lowers risk of atherosclerotic plaques with superimposed thrombosis, supporting mechanical compression-induced thrombosis as etiology.
rulebook.bears_on: Mechanical compression-induced thrombosis (raises) vs. atherosclerotic thrombosis (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1043067915001677 — tobacco exposure is a major risk factor for atherosclerotic disease in arterial TOS; absence of smoking supports mechanical etiology

rulebook.rule: Absence of comorbid systemic disease (diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune disease) supports primary mechanical etiology of vascular compromise rather than secondary disease from metabolic or inflammatory cause.
rulebook.bears_on: Primary mechanical thoracic outlet syndrome (raises) vs. secondary vascular disease (lowers)
rulebook.source: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/cardiovascular-disorders/peripheral-artery-disorders/raynaud-phenomenon — secondary Raynaud typically accompanies systemic disorders; absence of such comorbidities suggests primary mechanical/local etiology

per_case.blind_answer:
Diagnosis: Thoracic outlet syndrome with secondary arterial thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome). The cervical rib and first rib anomaly mechanically compressed the subclavian artery; overhead training (rowing, barbell work) caused repetitive arterial trauma and thrombosis, leading to progressive ischemia, Raynaud-like blanching, claudication, and muscle atrophy.

Recommended next action: Urgent referral to vascular surgery for thrombectomy/thrombolysis and surgical decompression (first rib resection, cervical rib removal, possible arterial reconstruction). Cease all overhead activities immediately. Early intervention (days) maximizes limb salvage.

Confidence: 95%. The imaging (cervical rib + subclavian dilation + acute axillary/brachial thrombus) combined with the clinical history (effort-induced vasospastic episodes, progressive ischemic sequelae, athlete with overhead training) is pathognomonic for TOS with secondary thrombosis. The negative inflammatory workup excludes primary vasculitis.

Reasoning: The cervical rib mechanically narrows the outlet; overhead arm elevation worsens compression; turbulent flow across the narrowed segment led to thrombus formation in the subclavian/axillary arteries. Distal ischemia explains blanching, coolness, claudication, and atrophy. Initial diagnosis of primary Raynaud disease was incorrect; this patient requires acute vascular intervention.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 34-year-old competitive rower and overhead weightlifter presents with 8 months of progressive hand and forearm symptoms initially attributed to primary Raynaud phenomenon but definitively identified on imaging as secondary arterial thoracic outlet syndrome with acute arterial thrombosis.

EVIDENCE AGAINST PRIMARY RAYNAUD PHENOMENON:
The diagnosis of primary Raynaud is excluded by five independent lines of evidence. First, visible intrinsic hand and forearm muscle atrophy with reduced grip strength (symp-atrophy, exam-atrophy-intrinsic, exam-grip) directly contradicts primary Raynaud, which characteristically does not cause tissue damage or permanent motor deficits (R1). Second, complete failure to respond to a tapering course of oral corticosteroids (hx-rheum-tx, hx-rheum-response: no improvement) indicates the underlying pathology is mechanical/vascular rather than inflammatory (R7), and primary vasospastic disease would be expected to improve or stabilize with such therapy. Third, the symptom distribution is strictly unilateral (right dominant hand only; symp-spread, demo-hand) with no mention of left-hand involvement, whereas primary Raynaud typically presents with bilateral and symmetric attacks (R12). Fourth, cool, dusky fingers present at baseline on examination (exam-hand-appearance) combined with diminished distal pulses on the affected arm (exam-pulses) indicate fixed arterial narrowing or occlusion, not the transient blanching and normalization between attacks characteristic of reversible vasospasm (R8, R9). Fifth, inflammatory markers and autoantibody screens were completely normal (lab-inflam, lab-autoab), excluding underlying autoimmune or connective-tissue disease as the cause of any secondary Raynaud phenomenon (R14).

EVIDENCE FOR ARTERIAL THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME WITH ACUTE THROMBOSIS:
The diagnosis is definitively established by convergent anatomic, hemodynamic, and imaging findings specific to arterial TOS. Imaging demonstrates a fully formed cervical rib on the right side, fused to the first rib, located adjacent to a dilated subclavian artery measuring approximately 14 mm at its widest (anat-rib-presence, anat-rib-fusion, anat-subclavian-dilation, anat-subclavian-location). This anatomic constellation is highly specific for arterial TOS: cervical ribs are present in approximately 85% of arterial TOS cases but less than 1% of the general population (R2, R11). The subclavian artery demonstrates a large, acute-appearing filling defect within the lower axillary artery extending into the brachial artery and one of its shoulder-supplying branches (anat-axillary-defect, anat-defect-extent). This acute morphology on angiography is pathognomonic for in-situ thrombosis (R3), distinguishing it from chronic stenosis, dissection, or simple hemodynamic narrowing.

MECHANISTIC EVIDENCE AND CLINICAL TRIGGERS:
The patient's symptoms are reproducibly triggered by arm elevation above the head (symp-triggers), a trigger that is specific to dynamic positional compression of the subclavian artery by the cervical rib and not characteristic of primary Raynaud, which is triggered more commonly by cold and emotional stress alone (R4). His background of intensive overhead training—competitive rowing and heavy overhead barbell work (context-activity)—is a known exacerbating factor for mechanical vascular injury in thoracic outlet syndrome, contributing to both dynamic compression during exercise and cumulative microtrauma (R13). Paresthesias including tingling, burning quality, numbness, and pins-and-needles sensations (symp-paresthesia) combined with visible atrophy and functional weakness (symp-atrophy, symp-weakness, symp-evolved-forearm) indicate secondary nerve compression and ischemic neuropathy from vascular insufficiency, not the uncomplicated vasospasm of primary Raynaud (R5).

TEMPORAL EVOLUTION SUPPORTS CHRONIC COMPRESSION WITH ACUTE THROMBOSIS:
The 8-month clinical timeline is consistent with chronic cervical rib-induced arterial compression that has progressed to acute thrombosis. The initial 2 months of intermittent blanching in a single finger (symp-initial) spreading to all fingers and palm portion (symp-spread) represents early hemodynamic compromise from the mechanical obstruction. The subsequent 6 months of progressive paresthesia, aching, fatigue on exertion, and visible motor atrophy (symp-evolved-forearm, symp-paresthesia, symp-atrophy, symp-weakness) reflects chronic vascular insufficiency and secondary denervation from sustained compression (R6). By month 8, the baseline finding of cool, dusky fingers and diminished distal pulses (exam-hand-appearance, exam-pulses) combined with acute thrombotic filling defect on imaging indicates that the chronic narrowing from the cervical rib has culminated in acute arterial occlusion from thrombosis formation. This progression from chronic compression causing intimal injury to frank thrombosis aligns with the known pathophysiology of cervical rib-induced arterial trauma (R2).

EXCLUSION OF ALTERNATIVE ETIOLOGIES:
The patient has no personal or family history of thrombophilia or clotting disorders (risk-clot-hx) and does not smoke (risk-smoking), which excludes inherited hypercoagulable states and atherosclerotic disease as alternative causes of thrombosis, leaving mechanical trauma as the primary etiology (R18, R19). He is otherwise healthy without comorbid systemic disease (context-health), supporting a primary local/mechanical mechanism rather than secondary disease from metabolic or inflammatory cause (R20). His vital signs are normal (vitals), arguing against acute systemic thrombotic burden and indicating the thrombosis is regionally confined to the upper extremity (R17).

TREATMENT IMPLICATIONS:
Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome with acute thrombosis is almost universally an indication for urgent surgical intervention (R15). The patient requires first rib resection combined with scalenectomy for definitive decompression of the thoracic outlet. The need for additional arterial reconstruction—thrombectomy, thrombolysis, or vein patch—depends on the degree of arterial damage and should be guided by pre-operative dynamic angiography with arm positioning to demonstrate the compressibility of the arterial narrowing.

PROGNOSIS FOR FUNCTIONAL RECOVERY:
The 8-month duration of muscle atrophy places this patient in a guarded prognostic category. R16 notes that intrinsic hand and forearm muscle atrophy from prolonged denervation carries risk for incomplete reinnervation, with recovery timelines typically 2-4 years even after successful surgical decompression. Earlier intervention would have offered superior motor recovery potential.
per_case.framework_top: Secondary arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) with acute subclavian/axillary artery thrombosis, not primary Raynaud phenomenon
per_case.framework_next_step: Urgent surgical consultation for thoracic outlet decompression (first rib resection with or without scalenectomy) combined with vascular assessment for arterial reconstruction. Pre-operative dynamic angiography with arm positioning should be obtained to confirm dynamic compressibility and guide thrombectomy vs. thrombolysis vs. conservative anticoagulation strategy.

The only residual uncertainty is the precise timing of thrombosis onset (acute vs. chronic with acute worsening) and quantitative degree of arterial damage requiring reconstruction.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly identify the core diagnosis: arterial thoracic outlet syndrome caused by a cervical rib (fused to the first rib) compressing the subclavian artery, producing aneurysmal dilation and distal arterio-arterial thromboembolism, and both correctly reject the primary Raynaud's label and call for urgent vascular surgery referral, anticoagulation/thrombectomy, and thoracic outlet decompression with rib resection. Both capture the key teaching point.

CORRECTNESS vs ground truth:
- Both correctly note cervical rib + subclavian dilation + acute distal filling defect extending into axillary/brachial arteries, matching the CTA findings, and both correctly call this a surgical/limb-threatening emergency rather than a steroid/CCB condition.

OUTPUT A errors and hallucinations (significant):
- A invents a large amount of unsupported specific detail not in the ground truth: a 34-year-old "competitive rower and overhead weightlifter," "right dominant hand," symptoms over "8 months," "approximately 14 mm" subclavian dilation (ground truth = 12 mm), specific structured codes (symp-atrophy, R1, R7, anat-rib-fusion, etc.) that look fabricated/back-formed, and prognostic claims ("2-4 years," "85% of arterial TOS cases"). These are confidently asserted facts that cannot be traced to the ground truth and several conflict with it (14 mm vs 12 mm). This is exactly the kind of overconfident fabrication that hurts calibration and defensibility.
- A mischaracterizes the mechanism somewhat: it frames the distal occlusion as "in-situ thrombosis"/"acute arterial occlusion from thrombosis formation" and "pathognomonic for in-situ thrombosis," whereas the true mechanism is arterio-arterial thromboEMBOLISM from a subclavian aneurysm — A never identifies the aneurysm as such (calls it "dilation," misses the aneurysm-as-embolic-source pathophysiology).

OUTPUT B errors:
- B mislabels the entity as "Paget-Schroetter syndrome," which is venous effort thrombosis (subclavian vein) — factually wrong; this is arterial TOS, not Paget-Schroetter. This is a real conceptual error.
- B also frames it as subclavian/axillary "thrombus" from turbulent flow rather than aneurysm with distal embolism, and like A does not explicitly name the aneurysm, though B does mention "possible arterial reconstruction."
- B's confidence (95%) and concise reasoning are well-calibrated and defensible; it asserts far less unverifiable detail.

WINNER: B. Although B carries one clear nomenclature error (Paget-Schroetter), it is otherwise accurate, appropriately calibrated, concise, and defensible. A reads more impressively but is riddled with fabricated specifics (patient demographics, activity, measurements that contradict ground truth, invented evidence codes and statistics) that are unverifiable or wrong, plus a mechanistic mischaracterization (in-situ thrombosis vs embolism). Trustworthiness and freedom from hallucination favor B; A's volume of confident fabrication is the more serious failing for a judge weighing hallucination and defensibility.

per_case.prose:
A 61-year-old man presented to a community vascular clinic with a roughly five-month history of progressive swelling and a dull, dragging ache in the right lower limb. The symptoms had begun insidiously without any preceding trauma, immobilization, long-haul travel, or surgery. At an outside emergency department early in the course, a duplex ultrasound had been read as showing thrombus within the right common femoral vein, and he had been started on a direct oral anticoagulant; after a few weeks with no benefit this was switched to warfarin, which he had now taken for several months.

On review, the limb remained diffusely swollen from the thigh distally, with mild pitting and a sensation of fullness in the groin. There was no calf tenderness, no skin discoloration, and no fever or constitutional symptoms. Pulses were intact and the limb was warm. On careful palpation of the right groin a firm, only mildly tender mass of about 3 cm was appreciated in the femoral region, which the patient said he had vaguely noticed enlarging over the preceding months.

He was on warfarin at presentation. Coagulation studies reflected this: prothrombin time 19.1 seconds (reference 9.6–12.8) and INR 1.7 (reference 0.86–1.14). Thrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen were within normal limits, and C-reactive protein was normal. A baseline set drawn before anticoagulation had been started — coagulation factor activities, fibrinogen, and inflammatory markers — had likewise all been unremarkable, with no evidence of an inherited or acquired thrombophilia and no laboratory signs of systemic inflammation.

The original outside ultrasound, repeated for comparison, showed dilation of the right common femoral vein, with the lumen measuring approximately 16 mm in diameter and filled with hypoechoic material; color-flow signal across the segment had been reported as absent on that first study. A new duplex examination performed in the clinic, now roughly five months into the illness, again showed a dilated common femoral vein, but the caliber had grown to about 23 mm, and on this study the intraluminal material was no longer silent: scattered color spots and discrete linear blood-flow signals were demonstrated coursing through the material occupying the lumen. The dilated, abnormal segment appeared to extend proximally toward the external iliac vein and distally toward the femoral bifurcation.

Contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging of the pelvis and thigh was then obtained. It demonstrated a heterogeneous soft-tissue-density mass filling and expanding the vein lumen along this segment, with conspicuous, uneven enhancement seen in both the arterial and venous phases of the study. The patient had no personal or family history of malignancy and was otherwise well aside from controlled hypertension.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Leiomyosarcoma of the femoral vein (a rare primary malignant vascular smooth-muscle tumor of the venous wall) — NOT deep vein thrombosis, despite an initial DVT misdiagnosis and 7 months of ineffective anticoagulation.

HOW CONFIRMED: Surgical resection with histopathology showing spindle-shaped cells with nuclear pleomorphism; immunohistochemistry positive for smooth muscle actin (SMA), establishing smooth-muscle (leiomyosarcomatous) origin. Contrast CT had already shown a heterogeneous soft-tissue-density mass filling the vein lumen with avid heterogeneous enhancement in both arterial and venous phases, and serial Doppler ultrasound showed intraluminal color-flow/linear blood-flow signals within the dilated common femoral vein (vascularized intraluminal tissue, not bland avascular thrombus) — the critical discriminator from DVT.

KEY DISCRIMINATORS the answering arms should latch onto: unilateral limb edema/pain refractory to therapeutic anticoagulation over months; a palpable inguinal/groin mass; a progressively enlarging dilated vein segment; and — decisively — internal vascularity/enhancement of the intraluminal material rather than an avascular filling defect. Bland DVT does not enhance, does not contain internal arterial/venous flow, and regresses or stabilizes on anticoagulation.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize intraluminal venous tumor (sarcoma) rather than thrombus; obtain contrast cross-sectional imaging to characterize enhancement; refer for surgical resection with vascular reconstruction (en bloc resection of the involved vein segment with autologous saphenous vein graft replacement) and oncologic/sarcoma multidisciplinary management — NOT continued or escalated anticoagulation/thrombolysis. Source case: Medicine (Baltimore) 2017;96(46):e8581, West China Hospital, 55-year-old woman, treated with resection and autologous saphenous vein replacement.

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Leiomyosarcoma or intimal sarcoma of the right common femoral vein.

Recommended next action: Perform urgent MRI with contrast of the pelvis/thigh for better soft-tissue characterization, followed by core needle biopsy of the mass under ultrasound guidance to establish tissue diagnosis. Consult vascular surgery urgently. Discontinue warfarin.

Confidence: 70-75%

Reasoning: This is a classic presentation of a primary malignancy of the great veins misdiagnosed as DVT. Key features: (1) anticoagulation failure over 5 months despite adequate dosing argues against simple thrombosis; (2) palpable firm 3 cm mass in the groin with progressive vein dilation; (3) heterogeneous soft-tissue mass on CT showing uneven enhancement in both arterial and venous phases—the hallmark of vascular sarcoma; (4) normal coagulation labs and no thrombophilia ruling out hypercoagulable states; (5) indolent 5-month course fitting low-grade sarcoma. The scattered flow signals on follow-up ultrasound likely represent collateral venous drainage around tumor, not thrombus recanalization. Sarcomas of the great veins are rare (0.3-2% of all sarcomas) but present in exactly this manner.
per_case.framework_conclusion: This 61-year-old man (f1) presents with a five-month history of progressive right lower-limb swelling and groin fullness (f2, f8, f9) that began insidiously without provoked triggers (f3, per R2). He was empirically anticoagulated after initial ultrasound reading of "thrombus" in the right common femoral vein (f4, f5, f6, f7), but swelling persisted despite DOAC then warfarin therapy for several months (f6, f7). This failure of anticoagulation to resolve obstruction strongly suggests mechanical obstruction or malignancy rather than primary thrombosis (R3, per f6). Physical examination revealed a firm, palpable 3 cm mass in the femoral region that had been enlarging over months (f14, f15), consistent with R9 (exophytic or intraluminal sarcoma presentation). Repeat imaging is the key discriminator. Initial ultrasound showed dilated CFV (16 mm) with hypoechoic material and absent color flow (f23, f24, f25). By five months later, the vein had expanded further to 23 mm (f27, per R5—vein expansion is atypical for chronic DVT which narrows), and critically, the intraluminal material now exhibited scattered color-Doppler flow signals and discrete linear blood-flow patterns (f28, per R6—internal vascularity indicates tumor vasculature, not thrombus). Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass filling and expanding the vein lumen, with uneven enhancement in both arterial and venous phases (f30, f31, per R7—this dual-phase heterogeneous enhancement is a hallmark of vascular malignancy, not thrombus; per R8—heterogeneous mass expanding the lumen fits leiomyosarcoma or angiosarcoma differential). The patient's age (f1, per R1) combined with unprovoked presentation raises baseline suspicion for occult malignancy (~5% incidence). Importantly, baseline thrombophilia screening was entirely normal (f21, per R10—negative workup does not exclude mechanical/tumor obstruction and actually supports a non-hypercoagulable mechanism). Normal inflammatory markers and coagulation parameters (f19, f20, f22, per R11) do not exclude malignancy. The pattern of progressive mass growth over months (f15, f27, per R4, R20) favors neoplasm over static thrombus. The femoral vein is a common extrahepatic site for intravascular leiomyosarcoma (R15). While benign leiomyoma (R16) and IPEH/Masson's tumor (R17) remain in the differential, the rapid growth, dual-phase enhancement, and progressive symptoms tilt heavily toward malignancy. The absence of constitutional symptoms and fever (f12, per R14) does not exclude malignancy; presentation can be indolent. Current warfarin dosing is subtherapeutic (INR 1.7, per f16, R12), yet even adequate anticoagulation would be expected to fail in mechanical obstruction from tumor (R13). In summary, imaging and clinical evolution are now more consistent with an intravascular vascular malignancy (most likely leiomyosarcoma or angiosarcoma) than primary thrombosis, and mechanical obstruction accounts for both the initial presentation and the failure of anticoagulation—secondary thrombosis may be present but is not the primary pathology.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs correctly identify the primary diagnosis as leiomyosarcoma of the (common) femoral vein, the central requirement of the ground truth, and both correctly reject DVT and recommend stopping anticoagulation in substance. The deciding factor is the handling of the single most load-bearing discriminator: the internal vascularity/flow signals within the intraluminal material. Ground truth states these intraluminal color-flow/linear blood-flow signals are vascularized tumor tissue — the critical sign separating sarcoma from bland avascular thrombus. Output B correctly interprets the scattered/linear color-Doppler signals as tumor vasculature and also correctly flags vein expansion (16→23mm) as atypical for chronic DVT, mirroring the ground truth's discriminators precisely; its mechanism reasoning is explicit and traceable (finding/rule citations), making it highly defensible. Output A instead misreads the flow signals as 'collateral venous drainage around tumor,' a misinterpretation of the decisive discriminator. Output A's advantages are a clear, ground-truth-aligned disposition (discontinue warfarin, contrast imaging, vascular surgery) and an explicit, reasonably calibrated confidence (70-75%), whereas B gives no explicit disposition (resection/reconstruction/sarcoma MDT) and even hedges that secondary thrombosis may be present. Hallucination/discrepancy: B states '61-year-old man' vs the ground-truth 55-year-old woman (likely from arm-specific input findings, but still a factual mismatch); A avoids conflicting demographics but injects a confident wrong reading of the key sign. Neither states the SMA/histopathology confirmation method, which is acceptable since that is the post-resection confirmation rather than the bedside reasoning being asked for. On balance, B's accurate capture of the decisive discriminator and superior, verifiable mechanism reasoning outweigh A's cleaner disposition and calibration. Both are partially correct: A loses points on the decisive discriminator interpretation; B loses points on demographics and missing disposition.

per_case.prose:
A 64-year-old woman was referred to the otorhinolaryngology clinic for evaluation of recurrent watering of the right eye over the preceding four months. Roughly two and a half years earlier she had undergone an uncomplicated endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy on that side, with good results until the current episode. She reported no discharge, swelling, or pain over the lacrimal sac region, and denied nasal obstruction, loss of smell, or runny nose. There was no nosebleed, no chronic cough, and no coughing of blood. She had no constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

On diagnostic nasal endoscopy, several irregular, broad-based mucosal masses with overlying crusting were seen involving the right nasal vestibule, the anterior nasal septum, and the inferior and middle turbinates. There were no signs of acute infection over the lacrimal apparatus. The remainder of the head-and-neck and systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal full blood count, normal renal and liver profiles, and a normal serum calcium. An autoimmune workup was sent given the appearance of the lesions: rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, and anti-ssDNA were all negative, and complement C3 and C4 were within normal limits. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing was negative, as were anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase-3 antibodies. Urinalysis was notable for microscopic hematuria. Sputum examination for acid-fast bacilli was negative, and a nucleic-acid amplification test (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) on the specimen was also negative.

A chest radiograph showed clear lung fields. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed a small non-enhancing soft-tissue lesion along the nasal septum together with homogeneous mucosal thickening of the right maxillary sinus. MRI of the brain showed no significant abnormality.

A nasal biopsy was performed. Histopathology demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with scattered Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells; no caseating necrosis was identified. Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative and no fungal organisms were seen.

On the basis of granulomatous sinonasal lesions together with microscopic hematuria, an empiric trial of oral corticosteroids was started — prednisolone 40 mg daily for roughly two weeks, then tapered over the following weeks. The nasal lesions did not improve clinically on this regimen. A second nasal tissue biopsy was therefore obtained. This again showed granulomatous inflammation, this time with no features of necrotizing (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis and again no caseous necrosis. On this occasion the tissue was additionally submitted for mycobacterial culture and sensitivity testing in addition to repeat histology.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Primary nasal (sinonasal) tuberculosis — isolated extrapulmonary TB of the nasal cavity/septum with NO pulmonary involvement.

HOW CONFIRMED: Mycobacterial culture. After repeated negative acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) tissue stains, negative AFB sputum smears, and a negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF (NAAT), a repeat nasal tissue biopsy was sent for mycobacterial culture/sensitivity (BACTEC radiometric method), which finally isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis ~12 months after initial presentation. Chest imaging was clear throughout (no pulmonary TB).

WHY IT WAS A DIAGNOSTIC TRAP: The presentation — granulomatous, crusting sinonasal masses across multiple subsites plus microscopic hematuria — is a near-classic mimic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's), the initial working diagnosis. The trap is that ANCA serology (c/p-ANCA, anti-MPO, anti-PR3) and the full autoimmune panel were entirely negative, and histology showed granulomas WITHOUT necrotizing leukocytoclastic vasculitis and WITHOUT caseation. The patient was given an empiric corticosteroid trial (oral prednisolone, ~30 mg/day tapered over weeks) for presumed GPA and FAILED to respond — non-response to steroids plus seronegativity is the key signal that should redirect toward an infectious granulomatous etiology. Early TB tests (ZN stain, sputum AFB, GeneXpert) being negative is a known pitfall of paucibacillary extrapulmonary TB; culture is the more sensitive confirmatory test and is what ultimately made the diagnosis.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Standard 4-drug anti-tuberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol — intensive phase then continuation). Outcome: complete resolution of the nasal lesions on endoscopy and resolution of the presenting epiphora after completion of anti-TB treatment. NOT immunosuppression/steroids/cyclophosphamide (which would be the GPA treatment and is harmful in active TB).

SOURCE: Khoo SJ, Kamel S, Arasu K, Zuhaidi KM, Mohan Singh AS. "Primary Nasal Tuberculosis Masquerading as Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis: A Case Report of Diagnostic Dilemma." Cureus, 2023. PMC10755803.
