ir.inferred_domain: Clinical medicine, specifically otolaryngology/head-and-neck pathology with elements of immunopathology, infectious disease (tuberculosis/mycobacterial), and systemic disease evaluation. The case presents a diagnostic puzzle combining sinonasal granulomatous inflammation, iatrogenic lacrimal duct obstruction recurrence, corticosteroid resistance, and asymptomatic hematuria requiring differential diagnosis and additional microbiological investigation.

rulebook.rule: Presence of non-caseating granulomas on biopsy with Langhans giant cells raises sarcoidosis as primary candidate diagnosis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) — diagnostic criteria require 'histopathologic confirmation of noncaseating granulomas within the sinuses' and 'no features of necrotizing (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis'

rulebook.rule: Absence of necrotizing vasculitis on biopsy (biopsies 1 and 2 both negative) raises sarcoidosis and lowers GPA
rulebook.source: Non-infectious Inflammatory Lesions of the Sinonasal Tract (PMC4746140) — 'Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating epithelioid cell granomas' with 'Absence of vasculitis or cholesterol crystals'; GPA shows 'vasculitis affecting small/medium vessels with fibrinoid necrosis' and 'irregular areas of necrosis associated with multinucleate cells'

rulebook.rule: Absence of necrotizing vasculitis on both biopsies lowers GPA substantially, as GPA diagnosis depends on vasculitis histopathology or ANCA positivity
rulebook.source: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (StatPearls NBK557827) — 'The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria uses weighted points including Granuloma or giant cells on biopsy (+2)' but the histopathologic hallmark is 'necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis' in kidneys and 'granulomas surrounded by palisading histiocytes' WITH 'necrotizing vasculitis in small vessels'

rulebook.rule: Negative ANCA panel (c-ANCA, anti-PR3, anti-MPO all negative) significantly lowers GPA, as 65-75% of GPA patients test c-ANCA positive
rulebook.source: GPA Diagnosis (Frontiers Medicine 2024, PMID11385631) — 'cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) is positive in 65%-75% of GPA patients, accompanied by proteinase 3 (PR3)'; Merck Manual: 'Most patients with active disease have cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA), with antibodies against proteinase-3 (PR3)'

rulebook.rule: Microscopic hematuria raises concern for systemic vasculitis with renal involvement (GPA); it indicates pauci-immune glomerulonephritis when combined with ANCA-associated vasculitis
rulebook.source: Microscopic Hematuria in ANCA Vasculitis (Journal of Rheumatology) — 'Microscopic hematuria is one of the most common clinical manifestations of glomerular diseases, including IgA nephropathy, ANCA-vasculitis'; 'Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is a hallmark of ANCA-associated vasculitis and often presents as microscopic hematuria and proteinuria'

rulebook.rule: Microscopic hematuria does NOT typically present in isolated sarcoidosis; when present with granulomatous sinonasal disease, it suggests systemic vasculitis or alternative diagnosis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) — sarcoidosis case series (n=30) present with 'nasal obstruction' and 'crusting' but hematuria is not listed among clinical manifestations; systemic sarcoidosis (pulmonary/cardiac) may present but sinonasal-limited sarcoidosis does not characteristically include renal involvement with hematuria

rulebook.rule: Negative rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies support sarcoidosis (autoimmune markers not elevated) over autoimmune vasculitis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis Diagnostic Criteria (PMC12076595) — diagnosis requires 'no serologic evidence for syphilis or antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies'; De Shazo criteria specify no autoimmune markers

rulebook.rule: Sinonasal involvement with crusting, mucosal lesions, and granulomas is a common presenting feature of GPA (>70% of cases), raising this diagnosis
rulebook.source: Head and Neck Manifestations of GPA (PMC6449134) — 'In more than 70% of cases, the presenting symptoms are head and neck manifestations that are often misdiagnosed as infectious or allergic in etiology. Intranasal findings such as granulations, crusting, and necrosis are seen in the active phase'

rulebook.rule: Corticosteroid failure (lack of response to prednisolone 40 mg daily) lowers sarcoidosis likelihood, as 73% of sarcoidosis cases respond to corticosteroids; failure suggests resistant or alternative diagnosis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) — 'Most patients (73%) received corticosteroids as first-line therapy. Among surgically managed patients, 69% reported symptomatic improvement'; corticosteroid failure suggests corticosteroid-resistant sarcoidosis (requires TNF inhibitors) or alternative diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Corticosteroid-resistant granulomatous disease may respond to TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab); corticosteroid failure does not exclude sarcoidosis but indicates need for escalation
rulebook.source: Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha Inhibitor Treatment for Sarcoidosis (PMC2643111) — 'TNF-α inhibitors may be required in chronic resistant sarcoidosis and/or in conditions where systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated'; 'Remicade (infliximab) and Humira (adalimumab) are two of the most common TNF-alpha inhibitors used as a therapy for sarcoidosis'

rulebook.rule: Negative Ziehl-Neelsen staining on first biopsy significantly lowers tuberculosis (caseating mycobacterial infection); pending culture on second biopsy critical to rule out atypical mycobacteria
rulebook.source: Mycobacterial Infection Overview (ScienceDirect) — Ziehl-Neelsen staining is standard acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain for mycobacteria; negative staining excludes typical TB but does not exclude atypical mycobacteria pending culture

rulebook.rule: Absence of caseating necrosis on both biopsies effectively excludes tuberculosis, which characteristically shows caseous necrosis
rulebook.source: TB Diagnostic Pathology — tuberculosis is characterized by caseating granulomas (cheese-like central necrosis); non-caseating granulomas exclude TB as primary diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Negative sputum AFB smear and negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF (nucleic acid amplification test) effectively exclude pulmonary tuberculosis
rulebook.source: GeneXpert MTB/RIF Sensitivity (WHO endorsement) — nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) with >95% sensitivity for tubercle bacillus; negative result with negative AFB smear makes pulmonary TB extremely unlikely

rulebook.rule: Pending mycobacterial culture and sensitivity on second biopsy is critical; if positive for atypical mycobacteria (MAC, M. marinum, M. fortuitum), raises atypical mycobacterial infection as diagnosis
rulebook.source: Atypical Mycobacteria in Immunocompromised Patients (PMC4953805) — 'Mycobacterium genavense may present almost exclusively in patients with AIDS' but also 'Mycobacterium avium intracellulare complex, M. marinum, M. fortuitum, M. scrofulaceum, M. kansasii' cause atypical mycobacterial disease with granulomatous inflammation; culture and susceptibility testing required for definitive diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Atypical mycobacterial infection characteristically presents with non-caseating granulomas (suppurative or sarcoidal pattern), which matches this patient's biopsy findings
rulebook.source: Atypical Mycobacteria Histopathology (PMC4953805) — 'Suppurative granulomas were considered the most characteristic pattern associated with atypical mycobacterial infections, though many other patterns could be seen including sarcoidal, palisading and tuberculoid granulomas'; 'noncaseating granulomas in the liver and spleen' are documented

rulebook.rule: Absence of fungal organisms on first biopsy lowers fungal sinosinusitis; pending repeat on second biopsy important to confirm
rulebook.source: Non-infectious Inflammatory Lesions of the Sinonasal Tract (PMC4746140) — sarcoidosis diagnosis requires 'negative evidence of acid-fast bacilli or fungal processes'; fungal sinusitis would show fungal hyphae/spores on staining or culture

rulebook.rule: Normal complement C3 and C4 levels exclude active lupus nephritis and ANCA vasculitis with complement consumption; support sarcoidosis diagnosis
rulebook.source: ANCA Vasculitis Serology (Merck Manual) — ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA) may show complement activation; complement consumption (low C3/C4) suggests alternate pathway activation in vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Recurrent lacrimal duct obstruction after initially successful DCR may reflect local granulomatous infiltration or ocular cicatricial pemphigoid; sarcoidosis can present with ocular manifestations including lacrimal involvement
rulebook.source: Sarcoidosis Mimicking Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (PMC12584608) — 'Sarcoidosis can present with nodular epithelioid granulomatous inflammation' in ocular tissues; ocular cicatricial pemphigoid presents with 'loss of Goblet cells and obstruction of lacrimal gland ductules'

rulebook.rule: Recurrent lacrimal duct obstruction with granulomatous inflammation raises GPA (systemic vasculitis with ocular/lacrimal involvement); GPA affects eye and lacrimal apparatus
rulebook.source: EyeWiki GPA article and Head and Neck Manifestations of GPA (PMC6449134) — GPA causes orbital and ocular involvement; lacrimal gland and duct can be affected by granulomatous vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Absence of fever, night sweats, weight loss (negative constitutional symptoms) supports indolent sarcoidosis over acute infection or systemic inflammatory disease
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) — sarcoidosis typically presents with localized sinonasal symptoms (nasal obstruction, crusting) without constitutional symptoms in sinonasal-limited disease

rulebook.rule: Normal chest radiograph with clear lung fields lowers generalized GPA, as >70% of GPA patients present with pulmonary involvement; does not exclude limited upper respiratory GPA
rulebook.source: GPA Presentation (Merck Manual) — 'most patients presenting over the age of 45 years with sinonasal symptoms of obstruction, bleeding or crusting associated with pulmonary infiltrates and renal impairment'; normal CXR makes systemic GPA less likely but does not exclude localized disease

rulebook.rule: Normal brain MRI lowers CNS involvement of GPA or sarcoidosis; absence of intracranial granulomatous disease
rulebook.source: Head and Neck Manifestations of GPA — CNS involvement in GPA is rare but documented; normal imaging excludes this

rulebook.rule: Sinonasal sarcoidosis is rare (1-4% of sarcoidosis cases); when present, diagnosis is supported by non-caseating granulomas and absence of vasculitis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) — 'Sinonasal sarcoidosis occurs in 1%-4% of sarcoidosis cases and is a well-recognized yet chronic and challenging form of the disease'

rulebook.rule: Irregular broad-based mucosal masses with crusting is non-specific but consistent with granulomatous inflammation of sarcoidosis or GPA; specific location (septum, turbinates) may favor one over the other
rulebook.source: Sinonasal GPA Manifestations (PMC6449134) — 'Intranasal findings such as granulations, crusting, and necrosis are seen in the active phase' of GPA

rulebook.rule: Failure to respond to corticosteroids despite adequate dose and duration suggests either corticosteroid-resistant sarcoidosis (requiring TNF inhibitors), GPA (may respond to immunosuppression + cyclophosphamide), or non-granulomatous diagnosis
rulebook.source: TNF Inhibitors in Refractory Sarcoidosis (PMC2643111) — 'TNF-α inhibitors may be required in chronic resistant sarcoidosis'; corticosteroid failure does not exclude sarcoidosis but indicates need for advanced therapy

rulebook.rule: Combination of microscopic hematuria with granulomatous sinonasal inflammation raises concern for systemic granulomatous vasculitis (GPA) requiring renal biopsy or advanced serology
rulebook.source: ANCA Glomerulonephritis (Journal of Rheumatology) — 'Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is a hallmark of ANCA-associated vasculitis and often presents as microscopic hematuria and proteinuria' in GPA

rulebook.rule: Normal FBC, renal profile, liver profile, calcium, and negative autoimmune markers (RF, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-ssDNA) do not exclude granulomatous disease; consistent with either sarcoidosis or early/limited GPA
rulebook.source: Sarcoidosis Laboratory Evaluation (NHLBI, NIH) — sarcoidosis diagnosis does not depend on specific lab abnormalities; diagnosis is clinical + histologic

rulebook.rule: Small non-enhancing soft-tissue lesion on CT may represent early granulomatous infiltration or inflammatory edema; enhancement pattern does not differentiate sarcoidosis from GPA
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Imaging in Sarcoidosis — CT findings in granulomatous sinonasal disease are non-specific; biopsy and serology required for diagnosis

rulebook.rule: Histopathology (non-caseating granulomas, absent vasculitis) is the primary diagnostic tool; repeated biopsies strengthen confidence in diagnosis and aid differential diagnosis
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis Diagnosis (PMC12076595) — 'Diagnosis requires histopathologic demonstration of non-caseating granulomata' and 'diagnosis requires tissue confirmation' in most cases

rulebook.rule: Synthesis: non-caseating granulomas, absent vasculitis, negative ANCA/AFB/fungi, normal systemic labs, corticosteroid failure pattern, and sinonasal-limited presentation (though with hematuria) is most consistent with sarcoidosis, possibly with systemic renal involvement (sarcoid glomerulonephritis)
rulebook.source: Sinonasal Sarcoidosis: A Scoping Review (PMC12076595) and Sarcoidosis Diagnostic Criteria — composite clinical and pathologic picture supports sarcoidosis as primary diagnosis, with pending mycobacterial culture to exclude atypical mycobacteria

per_case.blind_answer:
**Most likely diagnosis:** Seronegative Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)

**Recommended next action:** (1) Repeat ANCA testing with extended panel; (2) Assess for renal involvement (urinalysis with microscopy for casts, serum creatinine; consider renal biopsy if glomerulonephritis suspected); (3) Initiate combination immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide) rather than corticosteroids alone; (4) Review pending mycobacterial culture and re-examine biopsy tissue for subtle vasculitis.

**Confidence:** 75%

**Reasoning:** Upper respiratory granulomatous lesions + microscopic hematuria (suggesting glomerulonephritis) + non-caseating granulomas on histology + negative TB, fungal, and standard autoimmune/ANCA workup + poor response to moderate-dose corticosteroids alone form a classic clinical picture for seronegative GPA. Although ANCA-negative GPA accounts for only 5–10% of cases, it is well-documented and diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and histology rather than serology. Systemic vasculitis, not isolated nasal disease, is the underlying pathology and requires aggressive combination immunosuppression.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The patient presents with a four-month history of recurrent watering of the right eye following prior dacryocystorhinostomy, with endoscopic findings of irregular, broad-based mucosal masses with crusting in the right nasal vestibule, anterior nasal septum, and inferior and middle turbinates (F016-F019). Histopathology from two separate nasal biopsies demonstrates granulomatous inflammation with Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells, but crucially with complete absence of caseating necrosis (F042-F044, F051-F053). The second biopsy explicitly confirms absence of necrotizing (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis (F052).

Differential diagnosis is significantly narrowed by the pathologic findings. Tuberculosis is effectively excluded by: (1) absence of caseating necrosis on both biopsies (R012: "Absence of caseating necrosis...effectively excludes tuberculosis"), (2) negative Ziehl-Neelsen staining (R011), (3) negative sputum AFB and negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF (R013: "Nucleic acid amplification testing...makes pulmonary TB extremely unlikely"). Fungal sinusitis is lowered by absence of fungal organisms on first biopsy (R016), though repeat cultures on the second biopsy are pending and critical (R014).

Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), despite sinonasal involvement in >70% of cases (R008), is substantially lowered by: (1) absence of necrotizing vasculitis on both biopsies (R003: "Absence of necrotizing vasculitis...lowers GPA substantially"), (2) negative ANCA panel with specifically negative c-ANCA, anti-MPO, and anti-PR3 antibodies (R004: "Negative ANCA panel significantly lowers GPA, as 65-75% of GPA patients test c-ANCA positive"). The normal chest radiograph with clear lung fields further lowers systemic GPA, as >70% of GPA patients present with pulmonary involvement (R021). While the microscopic hematuria (F035) does raise concern for ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis (R005, R026), the absence of systemic vasculitis on biopsy, negative ANCA serology, and normal renal/liver function (F023-F024) make GPA considerably less likely as the primary diagnosis.

The clinical picture is most consistent with sarcoidosis: (1) non-caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells on biopsy are the hallmark histologic finding (R001: "Presence of non-caseating granulomas...raises sarcoidosis as primary candidate diagnosis"); (2) absence of necrotizing vasculitis (both biopsies negative) is characteristic of sarcoidosis and argues against vasculitic diseases (R002: "Absence of necrotizing vasculitis...raises sarcoidosis and lowers GPA"); (3) negative rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies support sarcoidosis over autoimmune vasculitis (R007); (4) normal complement C3 and C4 (F030-F031) are consistent with sarcoidosis and argue against ANCA vasculitis with complement consumption (R017); (5) absence of fever, night sweats, and weight loss (F015) supports indolent sarcoidosis (R020); (6) the sinonasal location with crusting masses is recognized in sarcoidosis, albeit rare (1-4% of sarcoidosis cases, but well-established) (R023); (7) normal brain MRI excludes CNS involvement (R022).

However, two findings create diagnostic tension. First, the corticosteroid failure—nasal lesions did not improve clinically on prednisolone 40 mg daily for approximately two weeks followed by taper (F048-F049)—lowers the likelihood of typical (steroid-responsive) sarcoidosis, as 73% of sarcoidosis cases respond to corticosteroids (R009). This failure does not exclude sarcoidosis but indicates either corticosteroid-resistant sarcoidosis (requiring TNF inhibitors per R010) or an alternative diagnosis. Second, microscopic hematuria (F035) is atypical for isolated sinonasal sarcoidosis, as hematuria is not characteristically present in sinonasal-limited disease (R006: "Microscopic hematuria does NOT typically present in isolated sarcoidosis"). However, systemic sarcoidosis with sarcoid glomerulonephritis can present with hematuria; the hematuria may reflect concurrent renal involvement rather than primary systemic vasculitis.

The pending mycobacterial culture and sensitivity testing on the second biopsy (F054, R014) is critical. If positive for atypical mycobacteria (MAC, M. marinum, M. fortuitum, or other non-TB species), the diagnosis shifts to atypical mycobacterial infection, which characteristically presents with non-caseating granulomas (R015) and would explain both the granulomatous inflammation and the corticosteroid resistance. If the culture is negative, sarcoidosis becomes the most probable diagnosis.

Synthesis: The non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, absence of vasculitis, negative ANCA and AFB serology, normal systemic labs, negative constitutional symptoms, and sinonasal-limited location (though with atypical microscopic hematuria) align most closely with sarcoidosis (R030: "...is most consistent with sarcoidosis, possibly with systemic renal involvement (sarcoid glomerulonephritis)"). The recurrent lacrimal duct obstruction after prior DCR may reflect local granulomatous infiltration, consistent with sarcoidosis affecting lacrimal tissues (R018). Corticosteroid failure suggests corticosteroid-resistant sarcoidosis requiring TNF-alpha inhibitor escalation rather than a different diagnosis, provided mycobacterial cultures remain negative.
per_case.framework_top: Sarcoidosis (sinonasal granulomatous disease with possible systemic renal involvement)
per_case.framework_next_step: Complete mycobacterial culture and sensitivity testing on second biopsy to definitively exclude atypical mycobacteria; if negative, initiate TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy (infliximab or adalimumab) for corticosteroid-resistant disease; obtain renal biopsy or advanced serology to characterize microscopic hematuria and determine if systemic sarcoid glomerulonephritis is present.
per_case.framework_confidence: Moderate-to-High (approximately 70-75% confidence in sarcoidosis as primary diagnosis; 15-20% residual uncertainty pending mycobacterial culture and renal workup)

framework_citations.claim: Patient presents with recurrent right eye watering and endoscopic findings of irregular, broad-based mucosal masses with crusting in the right nasal vestibule, anterior nasal septum, and turbinates.
Histopathology demonstrates non-caseating granulomas with Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells and absence of caseating necrosis on both biopsies, with no necrotizing vasculitis on second biopsy.
Tuberculosis is effectively excluded by absence of caseating necrosis, negative Ziehl-Neelsen staining, negative sputum AFB, and negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF.
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is substantially lowered by absence of necrotizing vasculitis on both biopsies and negative ANCA panel (c-ANCA, anti-MPO, anti-PR3 all negative).
Normal chest radiograph with clear lung fields further lowers systemic GPA, as >70% of GPA patients present with pulmonary involvement.

The clinical picture is most consistent with sarcoidosis: non-caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells are the hallmark, absence of necrotizing vasculitis is characteristic, negative autoimmune markers support sarcoidosis, and normal complement levels are consistent with sarcoidosis.
Absence of fever, night sweats, and weight loss supports indolent sarcoidosis.
Sinonasal location is rare in sarcoidosis (1-4% of cases) but well-established.
Corticosteroid failure (lack of clinical improvement on prednisolone 40 mg daily) lowers typical sarcoidosis but does not exclude corticosteroid-resistant sarcoidosis requiring TNF inhibitors.
Microscopic hematuria is atypical for isolated sinonasal sarcoidosis but may reflect systemic sarcoid glomerulonephritis.

Pending mycobacterial culture and sensitivity testing is critical; if positive for atypical mycobacteria, diagnosis shifts to atypical mycobacterial infection; if negative, sarcoidosis becomes primary diagnosis.
Recurrent lacrimal duct obstruction after prior DCR may reflect local granulomatous infiltration consistent with sarcoidosis involving lacrimal tissues.
Normal brain MRI excludes CNS involvement of sarcoidosis or GPA.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: confirmed diagnosis is primary nasal (sinonasal) tuberculosis, isolated extrapulmonary, confirmed by mycobacterial culture (BACTEC) after negative ZN stains, negative sputum AFB, and negative GeneXpert. The case was a trap because it mimics GPA but was ANCA-negative, showed granulomas without vasculitis/caseation, and failed an empiric steroid trial. Correct disposition is 4-drug anti-TB therapy; immunosuppression would be harmful.

OUTPUT A: Concludes the diagnosis is sarcoidosis (with possible sarcoid glomerulonephritis), explicitly stating TB is "effectively excluded" by absence of caseation and negative ZN/GeneXpert. This is exactly the diagnostic pitfall the ground truth warns about — paucibacillary extrapulmonary TB is frequently AFB/NAAT-negative and caseation can be absent; culture is the confirmatory test. So A's primary diagnosis is wrong (sarcoidosis, not TB). However, A is the only output that meaningfully engages with the pending mycobacterial culture as the pivotal test, explicitly noting that a positive culture would shift the diagnosis to a mycobacterial infection and even ties the steroid-failure signal to that possibility. Its handling of the seronegative/no-vasculitis findings correctly down-ranks GPA, which aligns with ground truth. So A's final answer is incorrect, but its reasoning is well-calibrated, traceable to specific findings/rules, and it does not commit to harmful immunosuppression — it recommends withholding escalation pending cultures. Net: wrong final dx but defensible, low-harm, and partially aligned (correctly excludes GPA, flags culture).

OUTPUT B: Concludes seronegative GPA and recommends combination immunosuppression (corticosteroids + rituximab/cyclophosphamide). This is also the wrong diagnosis, and critically it recommends the disposition the ground truth explicitly calls harmful in active TB. B does mention reviewing the pending mycobacterial culture and re-examining for subtle vasculitis, which is a minor hedge, but its headline recommendation (aggressive immunosuppression at 75% confidence) is the most dangerous possible action for what is actually active TB. B correctly recognizes the GPA-mimic pattern and the steroid-non-response, but draws the opposite-of-correct conclusion about treatment.

Comparison: Neither reaches TB. A picks sarcoidosis; B picks seronegative GPA. Both miss the confirmed diagnosis. Differentiators: (1) Harm — A defers aggressive treatment pending cultures and would be safer; B commits to immunosuppression that the ground truth states is harmful in active TB. This favors A. (2) Calibration/defensibility — A is more granular, cites specific findings/rules, and explicitly preserves the mycobacterial-culture branch that is the actual answer path; B is more concise but overconfident (75%) on a harmful plan. This favors A. (3) However, B's reasoning that "isolated nasal disease is unlikely; systemic granulomatous process underlies this" and its recognition that seronegativity does not exclude an aggressive systemic disease is, in spirit, closer to recognizing that a benign localized sarcoidosis framing (A's conclusion) understates the situation — and B at least keeps the differential pointed at a treatable systemic granulomatous disease. Both made the classic error in opposite directions; A erred toward an under-treated benign diagnosis, B toward an over-treated harmful one. Given A is safer and better-calibrated but B's pattern recognition of the GPA-mimic is the textbook framing the case was built around, and neither identified TB or its culture-confirmation as the answer, the outputs are roughly balanced in correctness with offsetting strengths/weaknesses. Calling it a tie: both incorrect on final diagnosis, A safer and more traceable, B closer to the intended clinical reasoning pattern but recommending a harmful disposition.

per_case.prose:
A 34-year-old woman was referred to an otolaryngology clinic with a roughly three-week history of discharge from both ears. The discharge was yellowish and mucopurulent, had appeared without any obvious precipitant, and was never blood-stained. Over the same period she had noticed her hearing becoming progressively muffled, together with a persistent ringing in both ears that she likened to an electrical buzzing. She also described an intermittent sensation of fullness or swelling in the ears. She had no fever and, notably, no ear pain.

Her background was relevant for a long-standing autoimmune disorder first diagnosed in adolescence, which had relapsed several years earlier and required repeated and prolonged courses of oral corticosteroids; she had been on steroid therapy on and off for years. She had received routine childhood vaccinations, including BCG. She reported occasional nasopharyngeal discomfort over the preceding months.

On examination there was bilateral chronic congestion and swelling of the nasal mucosa with hypertrophy of both inferior turbinates. Both external auditory canals were patent. The tympanic membranes appeared retracted on initial inspection.

Pure-tone audiometry showed a conductive pattern bilaterally: on the right, air conduction thresholds averaged about 39 dB with bone conduction near 10 dB; on the left, air conduction averaged about 45 dB with bone conduction near 9 dB.

A high-resolution CT of the temporal bones reported bilateral chronic middle-ear inflammatory changes and mastoiditis, with a query of cholesteatoma on the left, a left tympanic membrane perforation, and incidental thickening of the maxillary sinus mucosa on both sides.

She was managed as bilateral chronic suppurative otitis media and given a course of anti-inflammatory and antibiotic treatment. The purulent discharge improved somewhat on this regimen, but her hearing loss and tinnitus did not resolve. On review a few weeks later, the left canal contained secretion and the left tympanic membrane was perforated, with hyperaemic surrounding mucosa and persistent purulent material.

Because symptoms persisted, she underwent a left-sided tympanoplasty with ventilation-tube placement. Tissue obtained at operation was sent for histology, which showed chronic granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis. Special staining of the specimen for acid-fast bacilli was negative.

Some days after the operation she developed a new right-sided peripheral facial weakness. A chest radiograph and CT obtained as part of her subsequent workup demonstrated bilateral emphysematous change, scattered calcified foci and fibrosis in both lungs, and some pleural thickening.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Bilateral tuberculous otitis media (TOM) — extrapulmonary TB of the middle ear, an uncommon cause of chronic ear discharge that mimics ordinary chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).

HOW CONFIRMED: Molecular/immunologic confirmation after conventional bacteriology was misleadingly negative. Middle-ear/granulation tissue and clinical workup yielded: GeneXpert MTB/RIF POSITIVE for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, rifampicin-sensitive (the definitive test); T-SPOT.TB POSITIVE; histopathology showing chronic granulomatous inflammation with necrosis. Notably the AFB smear was NEGATIVE and mycobacterial CULTURE was NEGATIVE — the classic trap, as paucibacillary TOM frequently has negative smear/culture. Chest imaging showed old fibrocalcific changes consistent with prior TB exposure, and the patient was relatively immunosuppressed from long-term corticosteroid therapy for a chronic autoimmune condition. A peripheral facial nerve palsy developing during the course is a well-recognized TOM complication (reported in ~15-40% of cases) and is a strong discriminator away from banal CSOM.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Refer to TB service; start standard multidrug anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy — intensive phase 2 months isoniazid/rifampicin/ethambutol/pyrazinamide (HREZ) then continuation 10 months isoniazid/rifampicin (HR) given the extrapulmonary site. Manage the facial palsy and provide ENT/audiology follow-up. Outcome with therapy: resolution of otorrhea and tinnitus, healed tympanic membrane, improved hearing. Pitfall to avoid: do NOT continue treating as routine CSOM with repeated antibiotics/myringoplasty without considering TB when discharge is chronic, antibiotic-refractory, associated with granulation tissue, facial palsy, or occurs in an immunosuppressed host — and remember smear/culture are commonly negative, so molecular testing (GeneXpert) and IGRA are key.

rulebook.rule: Bilateral chronic suppurative otitis media with otorrhea raises candidacy for both tuberculous otitis media and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA); tuberculosis classically presents as painless, purulent bilateral discharge with multiple tympanic perforations, while GPA may also present with bilateral recurrent otitis media
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: PMC3336232: 'chronic discharge' as classical feature of TB otitis media; PMC4963591: GPA case with bilateral ear involvement and tympanic perforations

rulebook.rule: Granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis on histology is characteristic of tuberculous otitis media and can also occur in GPA; however, the finding alone is non-specific and requires microbiological confirmation or additional systemic features
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: PMC3336232: histology showed 'caseous necrosis with epithelioid cells and Langhans type giant cells'; PMC8327233: GPA produces 'granulomatous tissue' rather than simple bacterial infection

rulebook.rule: Negative acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining does NOT exclude tuberculosis of the middle ear; low bacterial concentrations in ear TB make AFB staining unreliable for diagnosis, and molecular testing (PCR) or culture may be needed for confirmation
rulebook.source: PMC3336232: 'no alcohol-acid-resistant bacilli when Ziehl Neelsen staining' despite subsequent PCR confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis; PMC11552462: 'TB otomastoiditis diagnosis can be made based on intraoperative findings of caseous necrosis, which may be culture positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis but negative on AFB stain'

rulebook.rule: Conductive hearing loss with conductive hearing threshold air-bone gaps is expected in both tuberculous otitis media and GPA due to middle ear inflammation and ossicular disruption; tinnitus accompanying conductive loss is consistent with middle ear pathology
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: Merck Manual: chronic suppurative otitis media 'usually manifests with conductive hearing loss and otorrhea'; Dovepress (2021): conductive tinnitus is 'attributable to alterations in middle ear physiology' in otitis media

rulebook.rule: Tympanic membrane perforation with retraction prior to perforation indicates chronic negative middle ear pressure from Eustachian tube dysfunction; this can result from inflammatory obstruction of the nasopharynx or direct infiltration by granulomatous disease
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: Eustachian tube dysfunction article (Stanford Medicine, 2025): 'prolonged ET dysfunction may produce negative pressure within the tympanic cavity, resulting in a shift of intravascular fluid into the interstitial spaces and then into the middle ear lumen, or causing retraction of the tympanic membrane'

rulebook.rule: Bilateral nasal congestion with turbinate hypertrophy combined with otitis media suggests either Eustachian tube dysfunction from inflammatory rhinitis or direct sinonasal involvement by granulomatous disease; this pattern is consistent with both infectious (TB) and autoimmune granulomatous disease (GPA, sarcoidosis)
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: 'nasal inflammation due to allergen challenge results in Eustachian tube dysfunction'; EAACI (2025): 'interactions among infection, allergic reactions, and Eustachian tube dysfunction'

rulebook.rule: Prolonged oral corticosteroid exposure significantly increases risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis (odds ratio 2.8 for <15 mg/day prednisone; 7.7 for >15 mg/day); this is a major risk factor for tuberculosis development in immunosuppressed patients
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect (Tuberculosis in immunosuppressed patients): 'An increase in the incidence of TB in patients undergoing chronic treatment with corticosteroids has been reported, with odds ratios of 2.8 for doses lower than 15 mg/day of prednisone and 7.7 for doses greater than 15 mg/day'

rulebook.rule: Underlying autoimmune disorder in patient with subsequent bilateral granulomatous otitis media and facial nerve paralysis raises suspicion for granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), an autoimmune systemic vasculitis; GPA is characterized by necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of small- and medium-sized vessels
rulebook.source: PMC4963591: GPA case with autoimmune manifestation and bilateral facial palsy; PMC8327233: 'GPA is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis'

rulebook.rule: Bilateral facial nerve paralysis occurring after otologic surgery or in conjunction with bilateral otitis media strongly suggests GPA rather than simple infectious otitis media; facial nerve involvement in GPA results from necrotizing vasculitis of the facial nerve 'vasa nervorum'
rulebook.source: PMC4963591: 'bilateral facial palsy' in GPA case; ScienceDirect (GPA and facial palsy): 'necrotizing vasculitis of the facial nerve vasa nervorum is nowadays the most widely accepted etiopathogenetic theory to explain facial damage in GPA patients'

rulebook.rule: Post-operative facial nerve weakness (new-onset after tympanoplasty) can be iatrogenic (nerve injury during surgery) or represent progression of underlying granulomatous vasculitis; presence of bilateral pre-operative otitis with granulomatous histology favors systemic disease over isolated surgical injury
rulebook.bears_on: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Tuberculous otitis media
rulebook.source: PMC5305654: facial nerve paralysis in acute suppurative otitis media can result from 'intrafallopian inflammatory edema and consequent ischemia with neuropraxia' from active infection

rulebook.rule: Bilateral pulmonary calcified foci with fibrosis and emphysematous change in a patient with bilateral granulomatous otitis media raises concern for systemic granulomatous disease; both tuberculosis and sarcoidosis present with apical/upper lobe calcified lesions, though TB is more likely given corticosteroid exposure and clinical context
rulebook.source: Archives of Bronconeumología: calcified nodules and fibrotic scarring from TB result from 'Mtb-host interaction during infection in the lung'; ScienceDirect (pulmonary fibrosis): 'differential diagnosis of fibrotic lesions includes non-tuberculous mycobacteria, histoplasmosis, post-pneumonia fibrosis, interstitial diseases, and sarcoidosis'

rulebook.rule: Lack of fever despite chronic suppurative otitis media with granulomatous histology does NOT exclude tuberculosis; chronic TB otitis media often presents with indolent course and absent systemic inflammatory signs, making diagnosis more challenging
rulebook.source: Frontiers (2025): TB otitis media case report describes 'gradual' presentation without acute inflammatory signs; PMC7451667: TB otitis media series describes variable presentations

rulebook.rule: Sensation of ear fullness and intermittent hearing fluctuation suggest middle ear fluid accumulation or negative pressure; this is consistent with Eustachian tube dysfunction which can predispose to both infectious and inflammatory otitis media
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: StatPearls (ETD): 'negative pressure in the middle ear' causes symptoms of fullness; assessment of ET function shows dysfunction in 'patients with tympanic membrane retraction'

rulebook.rule: Positive response to anti-inflammatory and antibiotic therapy with improvement in discharge but persistence of hearing loss and tinnitus suggests either: (1) incomplete infection control requiring definitive drainage/surgical intervention, or (2) non-infectious granulomatous disease (vasculitis, sarcoidosis) refractory to antibiotics but potentially responsive to immunosuppression
rulebook.bears_on: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis, Tuberculous otitis media
rulebook.direction: raises (for GPA/sarcoidosis); lowers (for simple bacterial otitis media)
rulebook.source: PMC8327233: GPA-related ear involvement 'does not resolve with antibiotic therapy'; PMC4963591: 'initial misdiagnosis as tuberculosis' in GPA case due to granulomatous findings

rulebook.rule: Failure of antibiotics to resolve hearing loss and tinnitus despite improvement in discharge suggests the hearing loss may be due to chronic ossicular erosion, sensorineural component from toxin diffusion, or alternatively, from a non-infectious inflammatory/granulomatous process not responsive to antimicrobials
rulebook.source: Merck Manual: 'hearing loss in chronic suppurative otitis media can result from perforation of the tympanic membrane, disruption of ossicular chain (conductive hearing loss), outer hair cell damage caused by the diffusion of bacterial toxins into the inner ear (sensorineural hearing loss), or both'

rulebook.rule: Bilateral chronic otitis media with mastoiditis in context of prior autoimmune disease raises suspicion for GPA; GPA otitis media occurs in 23-70% of GPA cases and can present as initial manifestation before renal or pulmonary involvement
rulebook.source: PMC8327233: 'GPA manifests with otitis media through middle ear involvement, occurring in 23-70% of GPA cases'; PMC4963591 & others: otologic symptoms can be first manifestation

rulebook.rule: Cholesteatoma query on CT imaging (uncertain finding) lowers confidence in simple infectious otitis media; however, if confirmed, cholesteatoma would indicate long-standing middle ear disease with ossicular erosion, consistent with chronic untreated TB or severe inflammatory disease
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect (GPA mimicking cholesteatoma): 'GPA findings on MRI can mimic cholesteatoma'; Frontiers (2025): TB otitis media case with similar imaging complexity

rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: PMC8327233: GPA shows 'negative microbiological cultures (no bacterial growth)' distinguishing it from bacterial infection

rulebook.rule: Serological testing for c-ANCA (cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) showing high titers is highly specific (80-90%) for GPA diagnosis; absence of c-ANCA does not exclude GPA (seronegative variant exists ~10%) but presence strongly supports diagnosis
rulebook.source: PMC8327233: 'c-ANCA (cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies), specifically PR3-ANCA, which shows 80-90% specificity for GPA'

rulebook.rule: Systemic pulmonary findings (bilateral fibrosis, calcified foci) in conjunction with granulomatous otitis media suggests systemic granulomatous disease; TB is statistically more likely given corticosteroid immunosuppression, but GPA can also present with pulmonary nodules in 45% at presentation and 87% over disease course
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: PMC8026843: 'Pulmonary manifestations occur in 45% of cases at initial presentation and 87% during the course of the disease' in GPA; Archives of Bronconeumología: TB produces calcified nodules and fibrotic scarring

rulebook.rule: Bilateral presentation (bilateral otitis, bilateral lung findings, bilateral hearing loss) strongly suggests systemic disease rather than unilateral infection; both TB dissemination and GPA can present bilaterally due to hematogenous spread (TB) or vasculitic involvement (GPA)
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sarcoidosis
rulebook.source: PMC7451667: TB otitis media series; PMC4963591: GPA case with 'bilateral otalgia', 'bilateral ear involvement'

rulebook.rule: History of prior autoimmune disorder that relapsed and required prolonged corticosteroids creates dual risk: (1) corticosteroid-induced TB reactivation (if latent TB present), and (2) inadequate control of underlying autoimmune disease allowing manifestation as systemic granulomatous vasculitis (GPA) with otologic involvement
rulebook.bears_on: Tuberculous otitis media, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
rulebook.source: ScienceDirect (TB in immunosuppressed): 'if corticosteroids are indicated in patients with latent tuberculosis, close observation is necessary as reactivation of the disease may occur'; PMC8327233: GPA manifests in autoimmune context

rulebook.bears_on: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Tuberculous otitis media
rulebook.source: PMC8327233: GPA 'commonly affects the nose and paranasal sinuses'

rulebook.source: Frontiers (2024): 'BCG vaccine complications are a key warning sign of inborn errors of immunity'; note: BCG vaccination is routine and does not independently suggest TB risk unless vaccine complications developed

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Sarcoidosis

Reasoning: Bilateral granulomatous inflammation of middle ear with systemic involvement (bilateral nasal mucosal inflammation, lung calcification/fibrosis), negative AFB biopsy ruling out TB, and subsequent cranial nerve involvement in an immunosuppressed patient all point to sarcoidosis as the unifying diagnosis. Otologic sarcoidosis is uncommon but well-documented.

Recommended next action: Obtain serum ACE level, serum and 24-hour urine calcium; review chest imaging with pulmonology and consider PET-CT or gallium scan to confirm multisystem granulomatous disease; coordinate care with rheumatology.

Confidence: 70–75%

The case fits sarcoidosis well clinically and histologically, though the preexisting "autoimmune disorder" in the history is not fully characterized, leaving room for other granulomatous conditions in the differential.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 34-year-old woman with a long-standing autoimmune disorder (F10) on prolonged oral corticosteroids (F11) presents with bilateral chronic granulomatous otitis media (F32, R2) and pulmonary manifestations (F35), requiring differentiation between systemic granulomatous vasculitis and tuberculosis reactivation.

GPA is the leading diagnosis because: (1) underlying autoimmune disease predisposes to GPA, which manifests as necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis in 23-70% of cases as otologic involvement (R8, R16); (2) the failure of antibiotics to resolve hearing loss and tinnitus despite partial improvement in discharge (F27, F28) is characteristic of GPA-related ear involvement, which does not resolve with antibiotic therapy (R14); (3) post-operative facial nerve weakness (F34) developing days after surgery, combined with bilateral pre-operative otitis media and granulomatous histology, strongly suggests underlying granulomatous vasculitis (R9, R10) involving the facial nerve vasa nervorum rather than isolated surgical injury; (4) the bilateral presentation across multiple organ systems—ears, lungs, sinuses (F22, F35, F25)—fits the systemic pattern of GPA (R21, R20, R23); (5) negative microbiological culture with granulomatous inflammation raises probability of non-infectious autoimmune disease rather than simple bacterial infection (R18); and (6) pulmonary nodules and fibrosis occur in 87% of GPA patients over disease course (R20).

Tuberculosis remains in the differential diagnosis because: (1) prolonged oral corticosteroid exposure (F11) carries odds ratios of 2.8-7.7 for TB reactivation depending on dose (R7); (2) bilateral painless purulent otorrhea (F3, F7) is the classical presentation of tuberculous otitis media (R1); (3) negative AFB staining does not exclude tuberculosis—low bacillary burden in ear TB makes AFB unreliable; diagnosis requires PCR or culture confirmation (R3); (4) chronic granulomatous inflammation with areas of necrosis (F32) is characteristic of TB otitis media (R2); (5) lack of fever (F9) does not exclude TB, which often presents with an indolent course lacking acute systemic inflammation (R12); (6) bilateral pulmonary calcified foci and fibrosis (F35) fit the typical pattern of healed TB lesions (R11); and (7) the bilateral presentation suggests hematogenous dissemination consistent with TB (R21).

The diagnosis cannot be definitively established without additional testing. Serological testing for c-ANCA (PR3) with 80-90% specificity for GPA (R19) is the highest-yield next step; if positive, it strongly supports GPA diagnosis. If ANCA is negative or seronegative GPA is suspected, tuberculosis workup including sputum AFB smears, TB culture, and molecular testing (TB-PCR) must be pursued. Tissue PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on the intraoperative specimen (F31) may provide rapid confirmation if TB is suspected. Renal function and urinalysis should be obtained to assess for glomerulonephritis, which would strongly support GPA diagnosis. The unspecified underlying autoimmune disorder (U1) requires clarification, as this may point toward GPA or another systemic condition. The temporal relationship between autoimmune disease activity and ear symptoms (U2) and the etiology of post-operative facial weakness (U5) remain unclear but would be resolved by the serology and microbiology results.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: bilateral tuberculous otitis media (TOM), confirmed by GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive, with the deliberate trap that AFB smear and mycobacterial culture are NEGATIVE (paucibacillary disease), plus necrotizing granulomas, facial nerve palsy, steroid immunosuppression, and old fibrocalcific lung changes.

OUTPUT A (Sarcoidosis): Wrong diagnosis and, worse, commits the precise reasoning error the case is built to expose — it states "negative AFB biopsy ruling out TB." Negative AFB does NOT exclude TOM; this is the central pitfall. Sarcoidosis is also poorly supported (sarcoid granulomas are classically non-caseating, but the case shows necrosis; steroid-immunosuppression context fits TB reactivation, not sarcoid). It reports 70-75% confidence on a wrong answer (overconfident, miscalibrated), and its recommended workup (ACE, calcium, gallium/PET) points away from the confirmatory molecular test. Defensibility is weak because the key inferential step is an outright error.

OUTPUT B (GPA leading, TB strong co-differential): Also does not name TB as the single top answer, so not fully correct. However, it keeps TB prominently and accurately in the differential: it explicitly states negative AFB does NOT exclude TB and that PCR/molecular confirmation is required, correctly reads necrotizing granulomas, indolent afebrile course, healed fibrocalcific lung lesions, and steroid-related reactivation risk. Crucially it recommends tissue PCR for M. tuberculosis on the intraoperative specimen — effectively the GeneXpert/molecular test that actually clinched the real diagnosis — so its proposed pathway would reach the correct answer. It avoids the fatal trap A falls into, is better calibrated (declines to commit definitively, names the discriminating test), and its F/R reference scaffolding makes the reasoning traceable/verifiable. GPA is a defensible differential given the autoimmune/steroid history, so B's error is reasonable rather than a trap-failure.

B wins decisively: it surfaces the correct diagnosis as a co-leading hypothesis with sound reasoning, recommends the confirmatory test that wins the case, and explicitly corrects the very error A commits.

per_case.prose:
A 47-year-old man was referred to a tertiary rhinology clinic after roughly a year of progressive bilateral nasal blockage, persistent watery-to-thick nasal discharge, and frontal headaches that had not responded to several courses of intranasal steroids, antihistamines, and oral antibiotics prescribed by his primary physician for presumed chronic sinusitis. Over the same period he had become unusually tired and had noticed that his sense of smell was nearly gone.

On examination he appeared fatigued. There was symmetric fullness beneath the angles of both lower jaw lines, and both eyes appeared mildly protruded. Rigid nasal endoscopy showed pale, swollen mucosa with bilateral polypoid change and mucopurulent secretions filling both nasal cavities. Formal smell testing confirmed marked hyposmia.

Initial laboratory testing showed a normal complete blood count, normal renal panel and electrolytes, normal urinalysis, and normal complement (C3/C4). An autoimmune screen, including standard antinuclear and cytoplasmic antibody panels and infectious serologies, was unremarkable. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 38 mm/h. Total serum immunoglobulin G was raised at 1,880 mg/dL (laboratory reference 700-1,600 mg/dL), and a serum IgG subclass assay returned a markedly elevated IgG4 fraction, several times the patient's upper expected value.

Non-contrast and contrast CT of the head and neck demonstrated opacification consistent with inflammatory disease across the maxillary, ethmoid, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses bilaterally. In addition, and beyond what routine sinus disease would explain, the scan showed diffuse symmetric enlargement of both submandibular glands, both parotid glands, and both lacrimal glands.

Because the gland enlargement and orbital findings did not fit straightforward chronic rhinosinusitis, tissue was obtained. Biopsy of the sinonasal mucosa and of an enlarged submandibular gland was sent for detailed histopathologic and immunostaining analysis, and an organ-by-organ assessment of the salivary, lacrimal, and orbital tissues was undertaken.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) with sinonasal/paranasal involvement (IgG4-related sinusitis), presenting in the clinical pattern initially mistaken for ordinary chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis. CONFIRMATION: (1) Histopathology of nasal/sinus mucosa showing dense lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophilic infiltrate with an IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio >40%; submandibular gland biopsy showing ~50-78 IgG4+ plasma cells/HPF with stromal fibrosis — meeting consensus IgG4-RD histopathologic criteria. (2) Supportive serology: elevated total serum IgG (above normal) and markedly elevated serum IgG4 subclass; elevated ESR. (3) Multi-organ glandular involvement on CT (bilateral submandibular, lacrimal, and parotid gland enlargement) plus clinical bilateral exophthalmos — the systemic signature distinguishing IgG4-RD from isolated chronic sinusitis. CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize this as systemic IgG4-RD rather than treating as isolated chronic sinusitis. Tissue diagnosis + serum IgG4 + organ survey, then systemic immunosuppression — first-line glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisolone ~30 mg/day) with a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate), tapered with monitoring; endoscopic sinus surgery is adjunctive for the obstructive disease, not curative. In the source case the patient improved on prednisolone + methotrexate, was tapered off, and had no recurrence. Key teaching point: chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps that is refractory/atypical AND accompanied by salivary/lacrimal gland swelling, proptosis, and a high ESR/IgG should trigger an IgG4-RD workup rather than repeated sinus-directed therapy alone.

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated serum IgG4 (several times upper normal limit, as in this case) combined with multi-organ involvement raises suspicion for IgG4-related disease.
rulebook.source: IgG4-Related Disease - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499825/

rulebook.rule: Bilateral symmetric enlargement of submandibular, parotid, and lacrimal glands raises IgG4-related disease; simultaneous salivary-lacrimal involvement is characteristic and historically referred to as Mikulicz's disease before IgG4-RD was recognized as the underlying entity.
rulebook.source: Ophthalmic manifestations in IgG4-related disease: Clinical presentation and response to treatment in a French case-series, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5348160/

rulebook.rule: Bilateral mild proptosis (exophthalmos) combined with lacrimal gland enlargement raises IgG4-related ophthalmic disease; lacrimal gland involvement is the most common ocular manifestation of IgG4-RD.
rulebook.source: IgG4-related Orbital Inflammation, EyeWiki: https://eyewiki.org/IgG4-related_Orbital_Inflammation

rulebook.rule: Bilateral sinonasal opacification (maxillary, ethmoid, frontal, sphenoid sinuses) on imaging combined with pale, swollen nasal mucosa and mucopurulent secretions raises IgG4-related sinonasal disease; however, sinonasal IgG4-RD is rare (7 cases over 11 years in one study).
rulebook.source: Sinonasal IgG4-related sclerosing disease: A rare entity and challenging diagnosis, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9764806/

rulebook.rule: Elevated serum IgG (above reference range) combined with elevated ESR raises IgG4-related disease; elevated total IgG and elevated ESR are nonspecific findings that commonly occur together in IgG4-RD due to hypergammaglobulinemia.
rulebook.source: IgG4-Related Disease - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499825/

rulebook.rule: Normal serum complement C3/C4 and negative standard autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB) lower Sjögren syndrome, lupus, and ANCA-associated vasculitis; these conditions are characterized by reduced complement and high-titer autoantibodies.
rulebook.bears_on: Sjögren syndrome; Systemic lupus erythematosus; ANCA-associated vasculitis
rulebook.source: IgG4-Related Disease - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499825/

rulebook.rule: Negative standard autoimmune serologies (specifically seronegative for anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La) lowers Sjögren syndrome; primary Sjögren is typically ANA-positive (90% of cases) and anti-SSA/Ro positive (50% of cases).
rulebook.source: Immunoglobulin G4 in primary Sjögren's syndrome and IgG4-related disease - connections and dissimilarities, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11446744/

rulebook.rule: Negative ANCA serology lowers granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis); GPA is an ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized vessels.
rulebook.source: Wegener's granulomatosis with orbital involvement: case report and literature review, PMC: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7995507/

rulebook.rule: Absence of pulmonary involvement (chest imaging not mentioned in case presentation) and lack of hilar lymphadenopathy lowers sarcoidosis; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is a hallmark feature of systemic sarcoidosis when orbital/lacrimal involvement occurs.
rulebook.source: Bilaterally Diffuse Lacrimal Gland Involvement: Initial Presentation of Systemic Sarcoidosis, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5468531/

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated hyposmia (confirmed by formal smell testing) with mucopurulent nasal secretions and bilateral polypoid nasal mucosa raises chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps; olfactory dysfunction in CRSwNP is driven by both mechanical obstruction from polyps and inflammatory damage to olfactory neurons via TNF-alpha and other pro-inflammatory mediators.
rulebook.source: Pathophysiology of Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps, SpringerLink: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-21217-9_43

rulebook.rule: Pale, swollen nasal mucosa with polypoid change and mucopurulent secretions raises chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps; these endoscopic findings are typical of CRSwNP, which is dominated by eosinophil-driven type 2 inflammation in 70-90% of cases.
rulebook.source: The advance on pathophysiological mechanisms of type 2 chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12263562/

rulebook.rule: Polypoid nasal mucosa changes lowers IgG4-related sinonasal disease as primary diagnosis; IgG4-RD sinonasal presentations typically show diffuse sclerosing inflammation rather than discrete polyp formation characteristic of eosinophilic CRSwNP.

rulebook.source: Sinonasal IgG4-related sclerosing disease: A rare entity and challenging diagnosis, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9764806/

rulebook.rule: Refractory hyposmia/anosmia despite presumed treatment raises IgG4-related disease with multi-organ involvement over simple allergic rhinosinusitis; IgG4-RD produces persistent olfactory dysfunction via chronic inflammatory remodeling of olfactory tissue that does not respond to standard rhinosinusitis therapy (intranasal steroids, antihistamines, antibiotics).

rulebook.rule: Fatigue and general appearance of fatigue on exam raises IgG4-related disease and other systemic inflammatory conditions; systemic symptoms reflect multi-organ involvement and sustained inflammatory burden.

rulebook.rule: Normal CBC (specifically absence of peripheral eosinophilia or lymphocytosis) lowers primary eosinophilic CRSwNP and hematologic malignancy; however, does not exclude IgG4-RD or tissue-localized eosinophilic inflammation.

rulebook.rule: Histopathology showing dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis raises IgG4-related disease; these three features together are highly specific for IgG4-RD when present with abundant IgG4+ plasma cells on immunostaining.
rulebook.source: IgG4-Related Disease - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499825/

rulebook.rule: Immunostaining showing >10 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field AND IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40% raises IgG4-related disease; these immunohistochemical criteria are central to the Japanese Comprehensive Clinical Diagnostic criteria.
rulebook.source: Salivary Gland Pathology in IgG4-Related Disease: A Comprehensive Review, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5901485/

rulebook.rule: Histopathology showing only lymphoid infiltration without storiform fibrosis or obliterative phlebitis lowers IgG4-related disease; simple lymphoid inflammation is nonspecific and can occur in Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, and lymphoma.
rulebook.source: Consensus statement on the pathology of IgG4-related disease, ScienceDirect: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893395222029805

rulebook.rule: Elevated serum IgG4 alone without histopathologic confirmation lowers IgG4-related disease as definitive diagnosis; elevated IgG4 is found in 50-90% of IgG4-RD cases but also occurs in 5% of healthy persons and up to 10% of patients with malignancy and other inflammatory diseases.
rulebook.bears_on: IgG4-related disease (as sole or sufficient criterion)
rulebook.source: Spectrum of Disorders Associated with Elevated Serum IgG4 Levels Encountered in Clinical Practice, PMC: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3368193/

rulebook.rule: Progressive year-long symptom duration with subacute onset and multi-organ enlargement pattern raises IgG4-related disease; IgG4-RD characteristically develops through progressive organ enlargement over months to years.
rulebook.source: IgG4-Related Disease - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499825/

rulebook.rule: Middle-aged to older adult presentation (47 years old) raises IgG4-related disease; IgG4-RD typically occurs in the sixth decade of life.
rulebook.source: Immunoglobulin G4 in primary Sjögren's syndrome and IgG4-related disease - connections and dissimilarities, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11446744/

rulebook.rule: Bilateral polypoid nasal mucosa with eosinophil-dominated infiltrate (if present on histology) raises chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps; eosinophilic CRSwNP is driven by type 2 T helper polarized immune response with elevated IL-5 and IL-13 mediating eosinophil recruitment and polyp formation.
rulebook.bears_on: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (type 2 eosinophilic endotype)
rulebook.source: The advance on pathophysiological mechanisms of type 2 chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, PMC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12263562/

rulebook.rule: Co-occurrence of sinonasal and orbital findings raises bidirectional diagnostic consideration: IgG4-RD affecting both sites, or separate processes (eosinophilic CRSwNP with coincidental IgG4-related orbital/lacrimal disease).
rulebook.bears_on: IgG4-related disease; Concurrent chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
rulebook.source: IgG4-related disease: a case report, PMC: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10197263/

per_case.blind_answer:
Most Likely Diagnosis: IgG4-Related Disease (IgG4-RD)

Recommended Next Action: (1) Complete histopathologic analysis of biopsies with quantitation of IgG4+ plasma cells and IgG4/IgG ratio; (2) Measure serum IgG4 level; (3) Initiate systemic corticosteroid therapy (prednisone ~0.6 mg/kg daily); (4) Screen for pancreatic, renal, and other organ involvement.

Confidence: 85-90%

Reasoning: The markedly elevated IgG4 fraction is the biochemical hallmark. The clinical presentation—symmetric bilateral involvement of sinuses, submandibular and parotid glands, lacrimal glands, and orbit—is characteristic of IgG4-RD. The chronic progressive course, elevated ESR, elevated total IgG, and exclusion of vasculitis/lupus/infection via serologies and normal complement support this diagnosis. Tissue biopsy would confirm via demonstration of IgG4+ plasma cells comprising >40% of IgG+ cells.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
The clinical presentation strongly suggests IgG4-related disease as the unifying diagnosis for multi-organ involvement.

**Salient features raising IgG4-RD:**

The combination of markedly elevated serum IgG4 (f21, at "several times the patient's upper expected value") with multi-organ involvement raises suspicion for IgG4-RD (r1). Bilateral symmetric enlargement of submandibular (f9, f23), parotid (f24), and lacrimal glands (f25) is particularly characteristic, historically recognized as Mikulicz's disease before IgG4-RD was identified as the underlying entity (r2). The bilateral mild proptosis (f10) combined with lacrimal gland enlargement (f25) raises IgG4-related ophthalmic involvement, as lacrimal gland disease is the most common ocular manifestation of IgG4-RD (r3). The elevated total IgG (f20) and elevated ESR (f19) further support IgG4-RD, which commonly presents with hypergammaglobulinemia and elevated inflammatory markers (r5). The progressive year-long symptom duration (f2) with multi-organ enlargement pattern is consistent with IgG4-RD's characteristic subacute onset and progressive course over months to years (r21). The patient's age (47 years, f1) fits the typical presentation in the sixth decade (r22). Constitutional fatigue (f6, f8) reflects the systemic inflammatory burden expected in IgG4-RD (r15). The frontal headaches resistant to multiple courses of intranasal steroids and antibiotics (f4) suggest a systemic fibroinflammatory process rather than simple infectious or allergic sinusitis (r14). The marked hyposmia (f13) that persisted despite prior treatment (f4) raises IgG4-RD over simple allergic rhinosinusitis, as IgG4-RD produces treatment-resistant olfactory dysfunction via chronic inflammatory remodeling (r13).

**Supporting negative findings:**

Normal serum complement C3/C4 (f17) and negative standard autoimmune serologies (f18)—including negative ANA and ANCA—lower Sjögren syndrome (r6, r7), ANCA-associated vasculitis (r6, r8), and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (r8). The absence of mentioned pulmonary involvement or hilar lymphadenopathy lowers sarcoidosis (r9). Normal CBC (f14) lowers primary eosinophilic CRSwNP and hematologic malignancy, though does not exclude tissue-localized eosinophilic inflammation or IgG4-RD (r16).

**Complicating features and uncertainties:**

Bilateral polypoid nasal mucosa changes (f11) are endoscopically typical of eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (r11), not the sclerosing fibroinflammatory pattern classically associated with IgG4-related sinonasal disease (r12). Indeed, IgG4-related sinonasal disease is exceptionally rare (r4). This raises the possibility that sinonasal and orbital/salivary manifestations represent separate pathologic processes: eosinophilic CRSwNP affecting the nose and sinuses (explaining the polypoid changes and hyposmia via eosinophil-driven type 2 inflammation, r23), with coincidental IgG4-related disease affecting the glandular and orbital compartments (r24).

However, the overwhelming pattern of symmetric multi-organ glandular and orbital involvement (submandibular, parotid, lacrimal bilaterally, plus mild bilateral proptosis and orbital findings documented on imaging, f10, f22–f25) remains the dominant clinical signature, and unified explanation by IgG4-RD is more parsimonious than invoking two separate diseases.

**Critical dependence on histopathology:**

The diagnosis rests fundamentally on pending histopathologic findings (u3, f27). Tissue showing dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis (r17) combined with immunostaining >10 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40% (r18) would confirm IgG4-RD. Conversely, histology showing only lymphoid infiltration without storiform fibrosis or obliterative phlebitis would lower IgG4-RD (r19). Additionally, elevated serum IgG4 alone, absent histopathologic confirmation, is insufficient for definitive diagnosis; IgG4 elevation occurs in 5% of healthy persons and up to 10% of patients with other inflammatory diseases or malignancy (r20).

**Conclusion:**

IgG4-related disease with multi-organ involvement emerges as the most probable unifying diagnosis, with the caveat that the sinonasal component—manifesting as polypoid disease—is atypical for IgG4-RD and may represent concurrent eosinophilic CRSwNP. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation per Japanese Comprehensive Clinical Diagnostic criteria. The marked hyposmia is explained by the chronic inflammatory remodeling affecting olfactory tissue (r13), and treatment-resistance reflects the systematic nature of IgG4-RD rather than simple allergic rhinosinusitis.
per_case.framework_top: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) with multi-organ involvement (sinonasal, salivary, lacrimal, and orbital sites), likely as the primary unifying diagnosis, pending histopathologic confirmation.
per_case.framework_next_step: Confirm diagnosis by reviewing biopsy histopathology (sinonasal mucosa and submandibular gland) for the three hallmark features: (1) dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, (2) storiform fibrosis, and (3) obliterative phlebitis, combined with immunostaining showing >10 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40%. If confirmed, initiate immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids and/or steroid-sparing agents). If histology does not meet IgG4-RD criteria, reassess for alternative diagnoses (eosinophilic CRSwNP with concurrent IgG4-related orbital/salivary disease, or other systemic inflammatory conditions).

Confidence is tempered by: (a) dependence on pending histopathology (currently unknown per u3), (b) the rarity of IgG4-related sinonasal disease (r4), (c) the presence of polypoid nasal changes which are more typical of eosinophilic CRSwNP (r11, r12), and (d) uncertain distinction between sinonasal manifestations of IgG4-RD versus coincidental eosinophilic CRSwNP.

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs correctly identify the diagnosis as IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) with the characteristic multi-organ glandular/orbital involvement (submandibular, parotid, lacrimal, proptosis), and both correctly note the supporting serology (elevated IgG4, total IgG, ESR) and the exclusion of competing diagnoses (vasculitis/lupus via negative ANA/ANCA and normal complement). Both also correctly emphasize histopathologic confirmation (IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40%) as the diagnostic anchor — matching the ground truth's consensus criteria.

Where A pulls ahead is defensibility and calibration. A explicitly grapples with the single most important diagnostic subtlety in this case: the sinonasal/polypoid component is atypical for IgG4-RD and is precisely the feature that caused the initial misdiagnosis as ordinary CRSwNP. A surfaces the parsimony tension (one unifying disease vs. two coincident processes), resolves it correctly toward unified IgG4-RD, and traces each finding to a labeled rule (rN/fN/uN), making the reasoning auditable. A also correctly flags the key calibration caveat from the ground truth literature — elevated serum IgG4 alone is insufficient (occurs in healthy persons and other inflammatory/malignant conditions) — which is exactly the trap the ground truth warns against. A's teaching emphasis (refractory atypical polyposis + glandular swelling + proptosis + high ESR/IgG should trigger IgG4-RD workup) mirrors the ground truth's stated key teaching point almost exactly.

B is correct and well-calibrated (85-90% confidence, appropriate) and notably adds the correct management/disposition that A omits: systemic corticosteroids (~0.6 mg/kg ≈ prednisolone dosing), organ survey for pancreatic/renal involvement, which aligns with the ground truth's disposition (first-line glucocorticoids + organ survey). However, B is terse, does not engage the central sinonasal-atypicality nuance, and offers shallow, non-traceable reasoning. B also misses the steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate) and surgery-as-adjunct points.

Net: A is more thorough, more defensible (traceable rule-linked reasoning), and better-calibrated on the diagnostic pitfalls, correctly nailing the case's central teaching subtlety; B is more concise and uniquely includes the correct treatment disposition but is reasoning-thin. The diagnostic accuracy and analytic defensibility of A outweigh B's management completeness. Neither hallucinates materially.

per_case.prose:
A 61-year-old woman was referred to a tertiary head-and-neck clinic for evaluation of a persistently rough, breathy voice and throat discomfort that had been present for roughly five months and had not improved.

Her medical history was notable for long-standing bronchial asthma and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, both of which had required ongoing treatment with low-dose oral prednisolone, an inhaled corticosteroid, and a disease-modifying immunosuppressant. She also carried diagnoses of a small reducible abdominal-wall hernia and dyslipidemia. She had never smoked and reported no alcohol use. She kept no birds and recalled no specific environmental or occupational exposures.

Some months earlier, her primary-care physician had examined the throat, presumed a yeast infection of the voice box, and prescribed a course of antifungal therapy. Her voice and throat symptoms were unchanged afterward, prompting the referral.

On flexible laryngoscopy there was a well-demarcated whitish, slightly raised lesion on the right side of the larynx, extending from the right laryngeal recess onto the right vestibular (false) fold. Both vocal folds were mobile and the airway was adequate. There was no neck lymphadenopathy and no fever.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed an enhancing soft-tissue abnormality at the right vestibular fold corresponding to the visible lesion, without bulky lymphadenopathy or cartilage destruction.

Selected laboratory results: white-cell count 5.9 x10^9/L; C-reactive protein 0.03 mg/dL; serum beta-D-glucan not elevated; HIV antibody negative. A blood culture grew only alpha-hemolytic streptococci, regarded as a contaminant.

An initial biopsy of the lesion was taken under local anesthesia. Histology showed laryngeal mucosa with dense inflammation only; no organisms and no malignant or dysplastic cells were identified. Because the lesion persisted, a second biopsy was performed under local anesthesia several months later; this again demonstrated only a mixed lymphocytic and plasma-cell inflammatory infiltrate, with no neoplastic features and no organisms seen on routine sections.

Given the persistent lesion and nondiagnostic superficial sampling, the patient was taken to the operating room for an examination under general anesthesia with deeper, more generous tissue sampling of the right vestibular-fold lesion.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Primary laryngeal cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus infection of the larynx, no disseminated/pulmonary/CNS disease).

HOW CONFIRMED: Diagnosis was missed on the first two laryngeal biopsies (both under local anesthesia), which showed only severe inflammation / lympho-plasmacytic infiltrate with no fungal organisms and no malignancy. The THIRD biopsy, obtained via endoscopic laryngomicrosurgery under general anesthesia, revealed a small number of yeast-type fungi with a characteristic clear halo representing a mucinous (mucopolysaccharide) capsule, highlighted on Alcian blue staining — pathognomonic for encapsulated Cryptococcus. Workup to exclude dissemination was negative: chest CT normal, CSF examination normal, serum cryptococcal antigen NEGATIVE, beta-D-glucan negative, HIV negative. Hence: PRIMARY (localized) laryngeal cryptococcosis in an immunosuppressed host (the patient was on oral + inhaled corticosteroids and immunosuppressants for asthma and rheumatoid arthritis).

KEY MISLEADING FEATURES: (1) initially misattributed by a primary-care physician to laryngeal candidiasis and treated with amphotericin B without benefit; (2) endoscopically the white vestibular-fold lesion strongly mimicked malignancy / candidiasis; (3) the first two biopsies were falsely negative, delaying diagnosis ~4 months. Serum crypto antigen being negative is a known pitfall in localized disease and does not exclude it.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Recognize that a persistent white laryngeal lesion in an immunosuppressed patient that fails empiric antifungal/reflux therapy and yields nondiagnostic superficial biopsies requires a DEEP/adequate biopsy (operative microlaryngoscopy) with fungal special stains (Alcian blue / mucicarmine / GMS) and culture; exclude dissemination (chest imaging, CSF, serum CrAg). Definitive treatment is prolonged systemic azole therapy — oral fluconazole 400 mg daily for ~6 months — NOT surgical resection and NOT escalation toward cancer treatment. Outcome here: lesion regressed promptly, symptoms resolved by ~6 weeks, no recurrence at 12 months.
