rulebook.rule: Acute onset progressive angioedema (lips, tongue, floor of mouth) over hours in an adult without prior history and with absent urticaria/pruritus/wheeze raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency or hereditary angioedema type I/II rather than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired C1-INH deficiency; HAE Type I/II
rulebook.source: Hereditary angioedema (DermNetNZ): HAE presents as recurrent angioedema without urticaria or pruritus; Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency with lymphoma (PMC2399707): angioedema without hives typical of acquired deficiency

rulebook.rule: Markedly reduced C4 (3 mg/dL) and low C1-esterase inhibitor functional activity (15%) during acute angioedema episode strongly raises the candidate diagnosis of either Type II HAE (normal/elevated C1-INH protein but low function) or acquired C1-INH deficiency.
rulebook.bears_on: HAE Type I/II; Acquired C1-INH deficiency
rulebook.source: Hereditary Angioedema — StatPearls (NIH/NCBI): diagnostic criteria for HAE-C1INH require low C4 and low functional C1-INH; The diagnosis of hereditary angioedema with C1 inhibitor deficiency (Springer): low C4 establishes HAE-C1INH type

rulebook.rule: Discordance between low C1-INH functional activity (15-30%) and low C1-INH protein level (13 mg/dL, reference 21-39) — with protein level reduced but not severely — lowers the confidence in Type I HAE (which shows marked reduction in protein) and raises the probability of Type II HAE (dysfunctional protein secreted at reduced level) or acquired deficiency.
rulebook.bears_on: HAE Type I; HAE Type II; Acquired C1-INH deficiency
rulebook.source: Hereditary Angioedema — StatPearls: Type I shows truncated/misfolded proteins with marked deficiency; Type II shows normal or elevated protein but low activity; Evaluating functional C1INH with multiple laboratory methods (PMC12417112): phenotyping discordant results

rulebook.rule: Absence of positive family history (no childhood swelling episodes, no affected relatives) combined with adult-onset angioedema substantially lowers the probability of Type I or Type II hereditary angioedema and raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency.
rulebook.bears_on: HAE Type I/II; Acquired C1-INH deficiency
rulebook.source: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency with lymphoma (PMC2399707): negative family history and adult-onset angioedema mark acquired form; Hereditary Angioedema — StatPearls: HAE types are autosomal dominant with family history

rulebook.rule: Severe reduction in total complement (CH50 <10 U/mL, reference 31-60) combined with low C4 raises the candidate diagnosis of Type I/II HAE or acquired C1-INH deficiency (which consume complement through classical pathway activation).
rulebook.bears_on: HAE Type I/II; Acquired C1-INH deficiency
rulebook.source: Hereditary Angioedema — StatPearls: C1-INH deficiency leads to uncontrolled classical pathway activation and complement consumption

rulebook.rule: Clonal B-cell population (CD19+CD20+FMC7+kappa-restricted; CD5-CD10-CD23-CD43-) in bone marrow at 10-15% cellularity raises the candidate diagnosis of B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, particularly splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL).
rulebook.bears_on: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma; B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
rulebook.source: CD5 expression identifies a subset of splenic marginal zone lymphomas (Haematologica): SMZL phenotype is CD5-, CD23-, and typically FMC7+; Pathology Outlines — Splenic marginal zone lymphoma: characteristic phenotype CD19+CD20+FMC7+ without CD5/CD10

rulebook.rule: CD5 and CD23 co-negativity with CD19+CD20+ and FMC7 positivity strongly distinguishes splenic marginal zone lymphoma from CLL/SLL (which are CD5+CD23+) and mantle cell lymphoma.
rulebook.source: CD5 expression identifies a subset of splenic marginal zone lymphomas (Haematologica): CD5/CD23 negativity with FMC7+ distinguishes SMZL; Differential diagnosis of CLL/SLL and other indolent lymphomas (PMC7810253): CLL markers include CD5+CD23+

rulebook.rule: Marked splenomegaly (21.5 cm craniocaudal dimension) combined with clonal B-cell population in bone marrow raises the candidate diagnosis of splenic marginal zone lymphoma.
rulebook.source: Splenic Lymphomas Presenting as Splenomegaly (CancerNetwork): splenomegaly and B-cell clonal proliferation suggest splenic lymphoma; Pathology Outlines — Splenic marginal zone lymphoma: splenic involvement is defining feature

rulebook.rule: Wedge-shaped hypodensity consistent with splenic infarct in a patient with massive splenomegaly and clonal B-cell disorder raises the candidate diagnosis of splenic marginal zone lymphoma with vascular complications from lymphomatous infiltration.
rulebook.source: Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes of Splenic Infarction in Cancer Patients (ASH): lymphoma is recognized etiology of splenic infarct; Splenic infarction attributed to lymphomatous infiltration with vascular compromise; Isolated Splenic Infarcts as Presentation of DLBCL (PMC12646813)

rulebook.rule: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive Coombs-IgG, elevated reticulocyte count, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin) developing 20 months after initial angioedema episodes raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency with secondary B-cell lymphoproliferation and autoimmune hemolysis.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired C1-INH deficiency with B-cell lymphoma; Autoimmune hemolytic anemia secondary to lymphoma
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia in Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma (ResearchGate): AIHA frequently co-occurs with NHL; Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia overview (ScienceDirect): AIHA driven by dysregulated B-lymphocyte activity

rulebook.rule: IgG-mediated positive Coombs test raises the candidate diagnosis of complement-independent extravascular hemolysis (RBC destruction by splenic macrophages) rather than complement-dependent intravascular hemolysis (which typically involves IgM).
rulebook.bears_on: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia subtype (warm vs cold)
rulebook.source: Three different pathways of IgM-antibody-dependent hemolysis (Frontiers): IgM-mediated hemolysis occurs predominantly via complement; Complement inhibitors to treat IgM-mediated hemolysis (Haematologica): IgM is primary mediator of complement-dependent hemolysis

rulebook.rule: Moderate anemia (Hgb 7.4 g/dL) with elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, and elevated reticulocyte count raises the candidate diagnosis of active hemolysis, consistent with autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia overview (ScienceDirect): elevated LDH and low haptoglobin are markers of hemolysis; elevated reticulocyte count reflects bone marrow response to anemia

rulebook.rule: Association of B-cell lymphoproliferation (10-15% clonal B cells) with both acquired C1-INH deficiency (low C4, low functional C1-INH) and autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive Coombs-IgG) raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency secondary to an underlying B-cell lymphoma rather than primary idiopathic HAE.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired C1-INH deficiency secondary to lymphoma
rulebook.source: Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency and lymphoproliferative disorders: A tight relationship (ScienceDirect): acquired C1-INH deficiency most commonly associated with B-cell malignancy; Acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency in lymphomas (PubMed26795750): prevalence 10.2% in DLBCL, 4.1% in CLL, predominantly in indolent splenic MZL

rulebook.rule: Adult-onset recurrent angioedema (months 0-5) unresponsive to antihistamines and corticosteroids, followed 20 months later by autoimmune hemolytic anemia and clonal B-cell proliferation, raises the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency driven by occult lymphoproliferative disease detected late.
rulebook.bears_on: Acquired C1-INH deficiency; Splenic marginal zone lymphoma or other B-cell NHL
rulebook.source: TYPE I HEREDITARY VS ACQUIRED ANGIOEDEMA ONSET IN OLDER ADULTHOOD (Annals of Allergy): acquired angioedema occurs later in life and is linked to lymphoproliferative disorders; Malignancy and immune disorders in hereditary angioedema (Springer): 35% malignancy risk in acquired C1-INH deficiency

rulebook.rule: No monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis during acute admission lowers but does not exclude the candidate diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency with lymphoproliferation, as paraprotein may be absent in 10-15% clonal populations or detectable only by more sensitive methods (immunofixation, free light chain assay).
rulebook.source: Acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency or serendipity? (PMC1770271): paraprotein may not be evident on standard electrophoresis despite underlying B-cell clone

rulebook.rule: Absence of significant lymphadenopathy on imaging combined with splenomegaly and clonal B cells in marrow raises the candidate diagnosis of splenic marginal zone lymphoma with predominant splenic involvement (as opposed to nodal lymphomas with systemic adenopathy).
rulebook.source: Splenic Lymphomas Presenting as Splenomegaly (CancerNetwork): SMZL characteristically involves spleen with minimal nodal disease; Pathology Outlines — Splenic marginal zone lymphoma: splenic-based presentation

rulebook.rule: Hypercellular bone marrow with preserved trilineage maturation and 10-15% abnormal B-lymphoid population lowers the probability of myelodysplastic syndrome or aplastic anemia and raises the probability of B-cell lymphoproliferation with reactive marrow response.
rulebook.bears_on: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma; B-cell NHL
rulebook.source: Clinical analysis of 20 patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (Medicine): marrow involvement in NHL shows clonal B-cell population with preserved maturation

rulebook.rule: Hepatitis C antibody negativity substantially lowers the candidate diagnosis of hepatitis C-associated lymphoproliferation (e.g., Type II mixed cryoglobulinemia with HCV-driven B-cell expansion).
rulebook.source: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia in Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma (ResearchGate): HCV associated with certain lymphoproliferative disorders; standard screening excludes HCV etiology

rulebook.rule: Treatment response: normalization of C1-INH activity and C4 following chemotherapy for lymphoma raises the candidate diagnosis that the C1-INH deficiency was acquired secondary to the lymphoproliferative disorder rather than primary hereditary deficiency.
rulebook.source: Acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency in lymphomas (PubMed26795750): in DLBCL patients successfully treated with chemotherapy, complete normalization of C1 INH activity and C4 observed; in splenic MZL, deficiency persisted after splenectomy

rulebook.rule: Clinical presentation: emergency intubation for airway compromise from rapidly progressive oropharyngeal angioedema, rapid resolution with swelling control (next morning), and absence of systemic features of anaphylaxis (no hypotension, no wheeze) raises the candidate diagnosis of C1-INH deficiency-mediated bradykinin-driven angioedema rather than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
rulebook.source: Hereditary angioedema (DermNetNZ): HAE presents as recurrent localized angioedema without systemic anaphylaxis features; Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency (Wikipedia): bradykinin-mediated edema without urticaria or systemic symptoms

per_case.blind_answer:
**Most Likely Diagnosis:** Acquired Angioedema (AAE) secondary to marginal zone lymphoma or other B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. The clonal B-cell population is driving both C1-INH deficiency (via consumption/inactivation or autoantibody production) and immune dysregulation manifesting as autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

**Recommended Next Action:** (1) Establish lymphoma diagnosis with excisional lymph node biopsy and/or repeat bone marrow biopsy with molecular clonality studies; (2) Stage disease with PET-CT; (3) Initiate treatment of the underlying lymphoproliferation, as angioedema management alone will fail while the malignancy persists.

**Confidence:** 85-90%

**Reasoning:** HAE-C1INH alone would explain the initial presentation, but the temporal appearance of a clonal B-cell disorder 20 months later, combined with acquired autoimmune hemolytic anemia and persistent C1-INH dysfunction, indicates the C1-INH deficiency is acquired, not hereditary. The B-cell clone is pathogenic and must be treated to resolve the angioedema. The phenotype (CD5−, CD10−, CD23−, CD43−, kappa-restricted) is consistent with marginal zone lymphoma, a known trigger of AAE. Splenomegaly with infarction further supports lymphoproliferative disease.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 61-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with two distinct but temporally linked disease processes unified by a single underlying cause.

Initial Presentation (Months 0-5): Adult-onset recurrent angioedema
The patient experienced acute progressive swelling of the lips, tongue, and floor of mouth (F003) without urticaria, pruritus, or wheeze (F005-F007), requiring emergent intubation (F004) with rapid resolution by the next morning (F012). This clinical phenotype strongly raises C1-INH-mediated angioedema rather than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (R020). Laboratory studies showed markedly reduced C4 at 3 mg/dL (F014) and low C1-INH functional activity at 15% (F015), both supporting hereditary angioedema (HAE) Type I/II or acquired C1-INH deficiency (R002). However, the absence of childhood swelling episodes (F021), lack of family history (F022), and adult-onset presentation (F001) substantially lower the probability of hereditary HAE and raise acquired C1-INH deficiency (R004). The recurrent episodes over 5 months (F023-F024) were refractory to antihistamines and corticosteroids (F025), further supporting a complement-mediated mechanism rather than allergic disease.

Interval Findings (Outpatient allergy clinic visit, between phases):
Repeat testing demonstrated persistent abnormality: C4 remained low at 4 mg/dL (F017), C1-INH functional activity was 30% (F018), C1-INH protein was low at 13 mg/dL (F019), and total complement (CH50) was severely reduced at <10 U/mL (F020). The discordance between low functional activity (15-30%) and low but not severely low protein level (13 mg/dL, ref 21-39) is more consistent with acquired C1-INH deficiency or Type II HAE than Type I HAE, which typically shows marked protein depletion (R003).

Late Presentation (Month 20): Overt hematologic malignancy with secondary immune complications
The patient returned with several weeks of fatigue, exertional dyspnea (F027-F028), and dark urine (F029) indicative of hemolysis. Laboratory assessment revealed moderate anemia (hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, F032), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (320 U/L, F033), and severely reduced haptoglobin (19 mg/dL, F034)—all consistent with active hemolysis (R012). The direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG (F036) with elevated reticulocyte count (F037), confirming autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Notably, the IgG-mediated mechanism indicates extravascular (splenic) hemolysis rather than complement-dependent intravascular hemolysis (R011).

Physical examination revealed massive splenomegaly palpable below the costal margin (F038), measuring 21.5 cm in craniocaudal dimension on CT (F039). Imaging also identified a wedge-shaped hypodensity consistent with splenic infarction (F040), but no significant lymphadenopathy (F041). Bone marrow was hypercellular with preserved trilineage maturation and contained an abnormal mature B-lymphoid population estimated at 10-15% of cellularity (F042-F043).

Flow cytometry identified a clonal B-cell population expressing CD19, CD20, and FMC7 with surface kappa light-chain restriction, while lacking CD5, CD10, CD23, and CD43 (F044-F052). This immunophenotype is diagnostic of splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL): the CD5- and CD23- profile with CD19+CD20+FMC7+ expression strongly distinguishes SMZL from chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (which are CD5+CD23+) and mantle cell lymphoma (R007). The combination of marked splenomegaly, clonal B-cell population, and absence of significant nodal disease is characteristic of SMZL with splenic-predominant involvement (R008, R016). The wedge-shaped splenic infarction is consistent with lymphomatous infiltration causing vascular compromise (R009).

Unifying Diagnosis:
The constellation of findings indicates acquired C1-INH deficiency SECONDARY to SMZL. The temporal sequence—early angioedema driven by complement dysregulation (months 0-5), latent lymphoproliferation, followed by overt AIHA and splenic complications at month 20—is characteristic of acquired C1-INH deficiency arising from an underlying B-cell malignancy (R014). The presence of both C1-INH deficiency (persistently low C4, low functional C1-INH, severely reduced CH50) and B-cell lymphoproliferation (10-15% clonal B cells with SMZL phenotype) occurring in the same patient with concurrent AIHA raises the candidate diagnosis that the C1-INH deficiency is secondary to the lymphoproliferative disorder rather than primary hereditary disease (R013). The AIHA in this context is secondary to dysregulated B-cell activity and complement activation abnormality (R010).

Supporting evidence includes:
- Negative hepatitis C antibody (F053), lowering the probability of HCV-associated lymphoproliferation (R018).
- Absence of monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis (F013), which does not exclude acquired C1-INH deficiency with small clonal populations detectable only by more sensitive methods (R015).
- Hypercellular marrow with preserved trilineage maturation and 10-15% abnormal B cells, consistent with B-cell lymphoproliferation rather than myelodysplasia (R017).

The diagnosis of acquired C1-INH deficiency secondary to SMZL can be definitively confirmed by successful normalization of C1-INH activity and C4 following treatment of the underlying lymphoma (R019).
per_case.framework_top: Acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency secondary to splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL), complicated by warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgG-mediated extravascular hemolysis) and splenic infarction
per_case.framework_next_step: Perform bone marrow biopsy with morphology and immunohistochemistry to confirm SMZL diagnosis and exclude other lymphoproliferative entities. Initiate treatment of underlying lymphoma (chemotherapy and/or splenectomy given massive splenomegaly with infarction). Reassess C1-INH levels and functional activity post-treatment to confirm acquired secondary deficiency (normalization following successful lymphoma treatment would validate this diagnosis per R019). Consider complement inhibitor therapy for angioedema if recurrent episodes occur during cancer treatment.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs reach the correct core diagnosis — acquired C1-INH deficiency (acquired angioedema) secondary to a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder — and both correctly conclude that the angioedema is not allergic/hereditary and that the underlying lymphoma must be treated. Output A is accurate and well-calibrated (85-90%) but hedges ("marginal zone lymphoma or other B-cell LPD"), and its recommended next steps (excisional lymph node biopsy + PET-CT) are a poor fit for this splenic/marrow-based case with no significant lymphadenopathy. Output B commits firmly and correctly to splenic marginal zone lymphoma, traces every finding (complement pattern, AIHA with DAT IgG+ extravascular hemolysis, massive splenomegaly + infarct, 10-15% clonal marrow B-cells), and correctly uses the CD5−/CD10−/CD23−/CD43−, CD19+CD20+FMC7+ kappa immunophenotype to distinguish SMZL from CLL/SLL and mantle cell — matching the ground truth differential. B also gives the correct confirmatory logic (C1-INH/C4 normalization after lymphoma treatment). Neither output explicitly names the undetectable C1q, the single best discriminator highlighted in the ground truth, though B reasons around the protein/function discordance. B's F/R codes and minor numeric differences (C4 3-4 vs <2, spleen 21.5 vs 20.3 cm) reflect the case-harness vignette rather than factual hallucinations. B is more complete, more firmly correct, and more traceable/defensible.

per_case.prose:
A 53-year-old man was referred to an allergy and immunology clinic for evaluation of a long-standing, recurrent skin eruption that had repeatedly failed to respond to treatment.

He reported that since early childhood — by his account beginning around the age of five — he had experienced recurring crops of raised, pink-red, hive-like welts over his trunk and limbs. He emphasized that, unlike ordinary hives, the lesions did not itch. The eruptions came and went in episodes lasting one to three days and were frequently accompanied by low-grade fevers and aching, swollen joints, particularly the wrists, fingers, and knees. He had noticed over the years that the flares were more likely after exposure to cold air and tended to ease when he kept warm.

Over more than two decades he had also developed slowly worsening hearing in both ears, now requiring hearing aids.

His medical history was notable for repeated, inconclusive evaluations. In his mid-twenties he had been hospitalized for disabling joint pain but left without a diagnosis; he improved temporarily on antibiotics and a course of corticosteroids. Roughly twenty years later a skin biopsy was read as consistent with "urticarial vasculitis," and he was again treated with corticosteroids with only transient benefit. In the year before this referral he had been tried on weekly low-dose methotrexate together with an oral JAK inhibitor for about a week, without improvement.

Family history was striking. He described numerous relatives across several generations — by his count more than a dozen — with a similar combination of a non-itchy hive-like rash, recurrent fevers, joint pains, eye complaints, and hearing loss; many were still living.

On examination he was afebrile at the visit. The skin showed scattered non-pruritic, urticaria-like plaques on the forearms and shins. There was no angioedema and no wheeze. Examination was otherwise unremarkable apart from reduced hearing.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count. Inflammatory markers were elevated: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 52 mm/h (reference <15), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 31.4 mg/L (reference <3.0), interleukin-6 10.8 pg/mL (reference <5.9), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha 9.4 pg/mL (reference <8.1). Antinuclear antibody was positive at a titer of 1:80, with a weakly positive anti-Jo-1 result; the remainder of an extended autoimmune panel was unremarkable. Complement levels and C1-inhibitor function were normal.

Plain radiographs of the hands, wrists, and knees showed mild osteoarthritic change and osteopenia.

A repeat skin biopsy demonstrated a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate; there were no fibrinoid necrosis, no leukocytoclasis, and no other features of a true vasculitis.
per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndrome (CAPS), a hereditary autoinflammatory disorder, in the Muckle-Wells syndrome end of the spectrum (recurrent urticarial rash + periodic fever/arthralgia + progressive sensorineural hearing loss + AD family history). CONFIRMATION: genetic testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic gain-of-function variant in the NLRP3 (cryopyrin/CIAS1) gene — c.778C>T, p.(Arg260Trp), exon 3 — segregating with an extensive autosomal-dominant pedigree (17 affected members across generations). Supporting: skin biopsy showed a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate WITHOUT features of true vasculitis (i.e., the prior 'urticarial vasculitis' label was wrong); elevated IL-6, hsCRP, ESR, and TNF-alpha consistent with IL-1-driven systemic inflammation; lifelong cold/stimulus-associated non-pruritic urticarial rash from early childhood; failure of immunosuppression (steroids, methotrexate, tofacitinib). CORRECT DISPOSITION: recognize as an IL-1-mediated autoinflammatory syndrome rather than chronic urticaria/urticarial vasculitis or an autoimmune connective-tissue disease (the weakly positive ANA/anti-Jo-1 are red herrings); refer to clinical immunology/genetics, counsel the autosomal-dominant family, and treat with an IL-1 inhibitor (anakinra/canakinumab/rilonacept) to control inflammation and prevent progressive organ damage (notably further hearing loss and AA amyloidosis). NOT chronic spontaneous urticaria, NOT urticarial vasculitis, NOT an inflammatory myopathy/connective-tissue disease.

ir.inferred_domain: Immunology / Rheumatology: systemic inflammatory disease with multi-organ involvement (dermatologic, articular, otologic), putative autoinflammatory/autoimmune etiology, likely monogenic hereditary syndrome given strong familial clustering with identical phenotype across multiple generations.

Specific composition of 'extended autoimmune panel': which antibodies tested beyond ANA and anti-Jo-1?
Histopathologic discordance: F15 shows 'urticarial vasculitis' ~20 years ago; F37-40 show perivascular infiltrate WITHOUT vasculitis features. Same lesion or disease evolution?

Mechanism of cold-responsiveness: cold-induced urticaria, vasodilatory rebound, cryoprecipitable protein activation, or immune trigger?
Methotrexate dose definition: 'low-dose' typically 7.5-25 mg/week; exact dose not specified

rulebook.rule: Cold-responsive, non-pruritic urticarial rash with 1–3 day flare episodes following cold exposure raises CAPS (FCAS/MWS/CINCA) diagnosis via NLRP3 mutations causing cryo-sensitive inflammasome assembly and IL-1β release triggered by cold-induced NLRP3 aggregation.
rulebook.source: Cryo-sensitive aggregation triggers NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (eLife 2022) — demonstrates Ca²⁺-dependent NLRP3-mutant inflammasome assembly with cold-triggered IL-1β release; confirmed in Cold-induced urticaria with familial transmission (NCBI PMC3307481) and Neonatal familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (NCBI PMC12731731)

rulebook.rule: Bilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss over 20+ years starting from inner ear inflammation at high frequencies (>4 kHz) and progressing to lower frequencies raises MWS (intermediate CAPS phenotype) diagnosis, as hearing loss is a hallmark of MWS/CINCA but not FCAS and not present in TRAPS.
rulebook.source: Early detection of sensorineural hearing loss in Muckle-Wells-syndrome (NCBI PMC4632838) — HF-PTA testing achieved 100% sensitivity for detecting high-frequency hearing loss; anti-IL-1 therapy improved or stabilized hearing in 91% of MWS patients; Muckle-Wells syndrome in an Indian family (NCBI PMC4943435) confirms hearing loss as cardinal MWS feature; Understanding Muckle-Wells Syndrome (Arthritis Foundation) — lists 'sensorineural hearing loss' as distinguishing feature

rulebook.rule: Non-pruritic, pink-red hive-like welts without itch (unlike ordinary urticaria) on trunk and limbs raise CAPS diagnosis, consistent with 'neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis' (perivascular/interstitial neutrophilic infiltrates without vessel wall destruction).
rulebook.source: Dermatologic and Dermatopathologic Features of Monogenic Autoinflammatory Diseases (Frontiers Immunology 2019, NCBI PMC9524803) — describes CAPS lesions as 'pink or pale red macules or slightly raised papules/plaques…typically not itchy or with only slight pruritus…individual lesions resolve within 24–48 hours'; Cutaneous Manifestations of Autoinflammatory Diseases (NCBI PMC9524803) — 'dense interstitial and perivascular neutrophilic infiltrations' without leukocytoclasis or fibrinoid necrosis

rulebook.rule: Perivascular inflammatory infiltrate WITHOUT fibrinoid necrosis or leukocytoclasis on repeat skin biopsy lowers true vasculitis and urticarial vasculitis diagnoses, and instead raises non-vasculitic autoinflammatory urticarial dermatosis (CAPS or similar monogenic autoinflammatory disease).
rulebook.bears_on: True vasculitis / Urticarial vasculitis (excludes); raises CAPS diagnosis
rulebook.source: Vasculitis in Systemic Autoinflammatory Diseases (Frontiers Pediatrics 2018) — fibrinoid necrosis is always absent in CAPS; leukocytoclasia is frequently observed in CAPS but WITHOUT vessel wall destruction; The histological assessment of cutaneous vasculitis (Histopathology 2010) — fibrinoid necrosis confirms true vasculitis; in absence of fibrinoid necrosis diagnosis of cutaneous vasculitis becomes difficult; Urticarial vasculitis (JACI 2022) — UV requires leukocytoclasia in 76% and fibrin deposits in 27.9% vs. CAPS which shows neither

rulebook.rule: Elevated IL-6 (10.8 pg/mL, ~1.8× ULN) and TNF-α (9.4 pg/mL, mildly elevated) with NORMAL CBC and normal complement raises NLRP3-driven autoinflammatory disease (CAPS) diagnosis, as IL-1β-mediated inflammasome activation drives IL-6/TNF-α elevation independent of hematologic abnormality or complement consumption.
rulebook.source: The discovery of NLRP3 and its function in cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (NCBI PMC10950545) — NLRP3 inflammasome leads to excessive IL-1β production; IL-6 and TNF-α can be elevated independently of CBC abnormality in autoinflammatory conditions; Aseptic Meningitis in Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases (NCBI PMC7398045) — IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α mediate inflammation in FMF/CINCA; IL-6 and TNF-α May Correlate with Activity and Severity (NCBI PMC4694713) — elevated cytokines reflect disease activity separate from hematologic indices

rulebook.rule: Striking familial pattern across multiple generations (>12 affected relatives with identical phenotype constellation: non-itchy rash, fever, joint pain, eye complaints, hearing loss) with disease onset in early childhood (~age 5) raises autosomal-dominant monogenic inheritance (NLRP3, TNFRSF1A, or MEFV-related disorder).
rulebook.source: Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes (Medscape/eMedicine) — TRAPS inherited as autosomal-dominant; >50 known TNFRSF1A mutations; Periodic fever syndromes: beyond the single gene paradigm (2019) — hereditary periodic fever syndromes show clear monogenic inheritance with strong familial clustering; Clinical Genetic Testing of Periodic Fever Syndromes (NCBI PMC3581266) — monogenic periodic fevers display multi-generational family patterns

rulebook.rule: Failure to respond to methotrexate and transient JAK inhibitor trial (~1 week, discontinued without adequate duration) raises IL-1-driven autoinflammatory disease (CAPS), as IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) provide rapid and dramatic response, while conventional DMARDs and JAK inhibitors are ineffective in true CAPS.
rulebook.source: IL-1 Inhibitors in the Treatment of Monogenic Periodic Fever Syndromes (Frontiers Immunology 2020) — all FCAS, MWS, NOMID respond dramatically and invariably to IL-1 blockade; this is a KEY diagnostic feature; Anakinra Therapy for Non-cancer Inflammatory Diseases (Frontiers Pharmacology 2018) — anakinra provides rapid reduction in CAPS disease severity; Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Fever Syndrome and the Nervous System (NCBI PMC6132776) — IL-1β blockade reverses neurologic inflammation and hearing impairment in CAPS

rulebook.rule: Low-titer ANA (1:80) and weakly positive anti-Jo-1 without myositis features lower classic systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or antisynthetase syndrome; these findings are incidental/secondary in CAPS and do not indicate primary autoimmune disease driving the phenotype.
rulebook.bears_on: Systemic lupus erythematosus / Antisynthetase syndrome (excludes as primary diagnosis); supports CAPS
rulebook.source: What does it mean if a patient is positive for anti-Jo-1 in routine hospital practice (NCBI PMC6058461) — positive anti-Jo-1 is only weakly predictive for ILD; weak positivity should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of active myositic disease without supporting clinical/lab evidence; Clinical Characteristics of Patients With Anti-Jo-1 Antibodies (NCBI PMC3380442) — anti-Jo-1 without myositis reflects predisposition to antisynthetase syndrome, not active disease

rulebook.rule: Normal complement levels and normal C1-inhibitor function lower immune complex-mediated vasculitis (SLE, cryoglobulinemia, urticarial vasculitis with complement deposition) and hereditary angioedema; supports innate inflammasome-driven autoinflammatory disease without immune complex deposition.
rulebook.bears_on: Immune complex vasculitis / Hereditary angioedema (excludes); supports NLRP3 autoinflammatory pathophysiology
rulebook.source: Vasculitis in Systemic Autoinflammatory Diseases (Frontiers Pediatrics 2018) — CAPS typically present with normal complement; complement consumption occurs in immune complex vasculitis but not IL-1β-driven inflammasome disease

rulebook.rule: Elevated acute-phase reactants (ESR 52 mm/h, hs-CRP 31.4 mg/L, both ~10× ULN) indicate active systemic inflammation; consistent with hereditary periodic fever syndromes (CAPS, TRAPS, FMF) and raises persistent low-grade inflammatory state typical of monogenic autoinflammatory disorders.
rulebook.bears_on: Hereditary periodic fever syndrome / Systemic autoinflammatory disease
rulebook.source: Serum Levels of IL-6 and TNF-α May Correlate with Activity and Severity (NCBI PMC4694713) — elevated acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) correlate with disease activity in autoinflammatory disorders; Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes (Medscape) — elevated inflammatory markers characteristic of CAPS, TRAPS, FMF

rulebook.rule: Recurrent low-grade fevers and polyarthralgias with joint swelling (wrists, fingers, knees) accompanying rash flares raise fever-driven systemic autoinflammatory syndrome (CAPS, TRAPS, FMF) rather than non-systemic chronic urticaria or allergic disease.
rulebook.source: CAPS (Muckle-Wells Syndrome in an Indian family, NCBI PMC4943435) — fever, arthralgia, arthritis are cardinal features; Understanding Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (Arthritis Foundation) — FCAS features include fever and joint pain accompanying rash; TRAPS (NORD — Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome) — fever in 88%, limb pain (arthralgia) in 85% of TRAPS patients

rulebook.rule: Hearing loss + continuous systemic symptoms (not just cold-triggered) + intermediate disease severity raise MWS (intermediate CAPS phenotype) over FCAS (cold-triggered, milder, no hearing loss).
rulebook.bears_on: Muckle-Wells syndrome (MWS) versus Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (FCAS)
rulebook.source: Understanding Muckle-Wells Syndrome (Arthritis Foundation) versus Understanding Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (Arthritis Foundation) — MWS features: fever, urticaria, joint pain, conjunctivitis, hearing loss; FCAS: cold-induced episodes only, no hearing loss; FCAS is the mildest form of CAPS; Muckle–Wells syndrome (Wikipedia) — MWS is intermediate phenotype with hearing loss as distinguishing feature

rulebook.rule: Non-migratory urticarial rash with evanescent lesions lasting 1–3 days lowers TRAPS diagnosis, which typically presents with migratory erythematous or urticarial rash that persists for days to weeks; TRAPS hearing loss also not reported.
rulebook.bears_on: Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS) (excludes)
rulebook.source: TNF Receptor Associated Periodic Syndrome — Overview (ScienceDirect) — TRAPS rash is migratory; Diagnosis and Management of CAPS (NCBI PMC7794776) — key distinguishing feature: TRAPS rash is migratory (unlike CAPS); TRAPS common features: fever 88%, limb pain 85%, abdominal pain 74%, rash 63%; hearing loss NOT listed as typical TRAPS feature

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis, pericarditis), erysipelas-like erythema, or severe abdominal pain episodes lowers Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) diagnosis; FMF also presents with amyloidosis risk over multi-decade disease course, but this patient has mild osteoarthritic change only.
rulebook.source: FMF clinical features (Medscape/eMedicine, CAPS diagnostic criteria NCBI PMC7794776) — FMF characterized by recurrent fever, serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis, pericarditis), erysipelas-like rash on lower legs/dorsal feet, arthritis, amyloidosis risk; this patient lacks documented serosal involvement and classic erysipelas-like pattern

rulebook.rule: Prior biopsy (~20 years ago) read as 'urticarial vasculitis' (which required fibrinoid necrosis/leukocytoclasis for diagnosis in 2003 standards) versus current biopsy showing perivascular infiltrate WITHOUT true vasculitis features suggests either: (A) reclassification of prior lesion as non-vasculitic autoinflammatory dermatosis (CAPS-like), (B) disease evolution from vasculitic to non-vasculitic histology, or (C) sampling of different lesion phases. Current biopsy (non-vasculitic) consistent with CAPS diagnosis.
rulebook.bears_on: Distinction between prior misclassification and current disease state; supports CAPS
rulebook.source: Histopathology of Vasculitis: Classification (Indian Journal Dermatopathology 2022) — fibrinoid necrosis defines true vasculitis; in absence of fibrinoid necrosis diagnosis becomes difficult; A novel histopathological scoring system (NCBI PMC8099228) — differences between UV and chronic urticaria samples include leukocytoclasia (76% in UV vs 3.9% in CSU) and fibrin deposits (27.9% in UV vs 9.7% in CSU); CAPS shows sparse or absent fibrinoid necrosis despite perivascular neutrophils

rulebook.rule: Disease duration of 48+ years (from age ~5 to 53) with early childhood onset in early childhood suggests chronic hereditary condition rather than acquired autoimmune disease, adult-onset disorder, or infection-triggered syndrome.
rulebook.source: Clinical Genetic Testing of Periodic Fever Syndromes (NCBI PMC3581266) — hereditary periodic fever syndromes typically present in childhood with lifelong course; CAPS phenotypes often manifest in infancy or early childhood and persist throughout life unless treated

rulebook.rule: Absence of angioedema, wheeze, or documented IgE-mediated allergic features lowers allergic urticaria, hereditary angioedema, and IgE-mediated autoinflammatory diseases; supports innate inflammasome-driven CAPS.
rulebook.bears_on: Allergic urticaria / Hereditary angioedema / IgE-mediated disease (excludes)
rulebook.source: Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome overview (DermNet, NORD) — FCAS/CAPS present with urticarial rash WITHOUT angioedema or allergic features; Hereditary C1-inhibitor deficiency (angioedema) presents with recurrent angioedema as primary feature, absent in this patient

rulebook.rule: Afebrile at examination despite history of recurrent low-grade fevers is consistent with periodic/episodic fever pattern rather than continuous fever; typical of CAPS, TRAPS, and FMF which feature fever episodes interspersed with afebrile intervals.
rulebook.source: CAPS clinical presentations (Frontiers Pediatrics 2018, NORD FCAS) — CAPS characterized by episodic fever and systemic symptoms with afebrile intervals between flares; not continuous fever

rulebook.rule: Failure of methotrexate and brief JAK inhibitor trial (insufficient duration) WITHOUT prior trial of IL-1 inhibitor (anakinra or canakinumab) raises strong recommendation for IL-1 blockade diagnostic/therapeutic trial; anticipated dramatic response would confirm CAPS diagnosis and establish IL-1 as pathogenic driver.
rulebook.bears_on: Muckle-Wells syndrome / CAPS diagnosis (therapeutic diagnostic criterion)
rulebook.source: IL-1 Inhibitors in the Treatment of Monogenic Periodic Fever Syndromes (Frontiers Immunology 2020) — all FCAS, MWS, NOMID respond dramatically and invariably to IL-1 blockade; this is a key diagnostic feature; Canakinumab for the treatment of different refractory autoinflammatory disorders (NCBI PMC4191365) — IL-1 blockade provides rapid symptom improvement in CAPS

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (FCAS) or Muckle-Wells Syndrome (MWS, if sensorineural hearing loss confirmed). The classic triad of cold-triggered non-pruritic urticarial rash, systemic autoinflammation (fever, arthritis, elevated IL-6/TNF-α), and strong autosomal-dominant family history is pathognomonic. Progressive sensorineural hearing loss tips toward MWS. The perivascular infiltrate without vasculitic features on biopsy, and marked resistance to corticosteroids/methotrexate, are consistent with autoinflammatory disease.

Recommended next action: (1) NLRP3 genetic sequencing; (2) Audiometry to confirm sensorineural component; (3) Ophthalmology evaluation for uveitis; (4) Initiate IL-1 inhibitor (anakinra or canakinumab). Rapid clinical and laboratory response to IL-1 inhibition would both treat and confirm diagnosis.

Confidence: 80–85%. Cold trigger, non-pruritic rash, autoinflammatory biomarkers, family history, and biopsy pattern are highly suggestive. Hearing loss and positive ANA add some uncertainty but fit the MWS phenotype. Genetic confirmation needed.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 53-year-old man with 48-year disease duration (F4, F12, R16) presenting with non-pruritic, pink-red hive-like welts without itch on trunk and limbs (F5, F6, R3) in 1–3 day episodes (F7) accompanying low-grade fever and polyarthralgia (F8, F9, R11), cold-responsiveness (F10, R1), bilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss over 20+ years (F11, R2), striking familial inheritance of identical phenotype across multiple generations in >12 living relatives (F18, F19, F20, R6), and failure of methotrexate and brief JAK inhibitor therapy (F17, R7) is most consistent with Muckle-Wells Syndrome (MWS), an intermediate CAPS phenotype driven by NLRP3-associated inflammasome hyperactivation.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE:

1. **Clinical phenotype strongly raises MWS (R12):** The presence of hearing loss (F11) combined with continuous systemic symptoms (fever, arthralgia, rash) and intermediate disease severity distinguish MWS from the milder FCAS phenotype (which lacks hearing loss) and from CINCA/NOMID (which presents earlier, more severely, often with meningitis).

2. **Non-pruritic neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis consistent with CAPS (R3, R4):** The rash is explicitly non-pruritic (F5), unlike ordinary urticaria, and histology shows perivascular inflammatory infiltrate without fibrinoid necrosis, leukocytoclasis, or true vasculitis features (F37, F38, F39, F40). These histopathologic findings lower true vasculitis (R4) and instead raise CAPS diagnosis via the neutrophilic infiltrate pattern characteristic of autoinflammatory, not autoimmune, disease.

3. **Cold-responsiveness raises NLRP3-mediated autoinflammation (R1):** The patient's report of flares with cold exposure and improvement with warmth (F10) is a hallmark trigger for NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated disease; cold induces NLRP3 aggregation and IL-1β release in genetically susceptible individuals (R1).

4. **Elevated IL-6 and TNF-α with normal CBC and complement raise NLRP3 autoinflammatory disease (R5):** The pattern of IL-6 10.8 pg/mL (~1.8× ULN), TNF-α 9.4 pg/mL (mildly elevated) (F29, F30), normal CBC (F26), and normal complement (F34, F35) is consistent with IL-1β-driven inflammasome activation independent of hematologic abnormality or complement consumption (R5). This pattern disfavors immune complex–mediated vasculitis or systemic lupus erythematosus.

5. **DMARD refractoriness and IL-1 blockade responsiveness anticipated (R7, R19):** The failure to respond to methotrexate (F17) and the inadequate, brief trial of JAK inhibitor (~1 week) (F17) without prior IL-1 inhibitor trial (R7) raise strong expectation for dramatic response to IL-1 blockade—a diagnostic hallmark of CAPS (R19). Conventional DMARDs are ineffective in true CAPS; IL-1 inhibitors provide rapid and invariable response in all FCAS, MWS, and NOMID patients.

6. **Monogenic inheritance pattern with early childhood onset (R6, R16):** The striking familial pattern across multiple generations (>12 affected relatives) (F18, F19) with identical phenotype constellation including non-itchy rash, fever, joint pain, eye complaints, and hearing loss (F20), combined with disease onset in early childhood (~age 5) (F4), is consistent with autosomal-dominant monogenic inheritance—the hallmark of NLRP3-driven CAPS (R6) and early-onset lifelong chronic disease (R16).

7. **Low-titer ANA and weak anti-Jo-1 are incidental, not primary (R8):** The low-titer ANA (1:80) and weakly positive anti-Jo-1 (F31, F32) without myositis features or myopathy lower classic systemic lupus erythematosus or antisynthetase syndrome (R8) and are consistent with secondary autoimmune serology in CAPS without driving the phenotype.

8. **Elevated acute-phase reactants reflect ongoing autoinflammation (R10):** The elevated ESR 52 mm/h and hs-CRP 31.4 mg/L (both ~10× ULN) (F27, F28) are consistent with persistent low-grade inflammatory state typical of monogenic autoinflammatory disorders (R10).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS EXCLUSION:

- **TRAPS (Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome) is less likely (R13):** The evanescent, non-migratory urticarial rash lasting 1–3 days (F7) contrasts with TRAPS rash, which is migratory and persists days to weeks (R13). Hearing loss is not a typical TRAPS feature.

- **FMF (Familial Mediterranean Fever) is less likely (R14):** The absence of documented serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis, pericarditis), erysipelas-like erythema, or severe abdominal pain episodes, combined with lack of amyloidosis risk (only mild osteoarthritic change noted) (F36), lowers FMF (R14).

- **Immune complex–mediated vasculitis is excluded (R4, R9):** The non-vasculitic histology (no fibrinoid necrosis, no leukocytoclasis) (F38, F39, F40) and normal complement with normal C1-inhibitor (F34, F35) lower immune complex vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, and hereditary angioedema (R9).

- **Allergic urticaria or IgE-mediated disease is excluded (R17):** The absence of angioedema (F23), wheeze (F24), or documented allergic features (R17) lowers allergic disease.

CAVEAT—HISTOPATHOLOGIC DISCORDANCE (R15, U4):

The prior biopsy ~20 years ago was read as "urticarial vasculitis" (F15), whereas the current biopsy shows perivascular infiltrate without true vasculitis features (F37–F40). This discordance may reflect: (A) reclassification of the prior lesion under modern CAPS criteria (recognizing it as non-vasculitic autoinflammatory dermatosis), (B) disease evolution from vasculitic to non-vasculitic histology, or (C) sampling of different lesion phases. The current non-vasculitic histology is consistent with CAPS (R4, R15).

CONCLUSION:

MWS (intermediate CAPS phenotype driven by NLRP3 mutations) is the unifying diagnosis integrating rash morphology, hearing loss, fever, polyarthralgia, cold-responsiveness, non-vasculitic histology, DMARD refractoriness, anticipated IL-1 responsiveness, monogenic inheritance, and cytokinemic profile. Confirmation requires NLRP3 gene sequencing and/or a diagnostic trial of IL-1 inhibitor therapy, which is expected to produce rapid, dramatic clinical improvement (R19).
per_case.framework_top: Muckle-Wells Syndrome (MWS; intermediate phenotype of Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndrome, NLRP3-driven autoinflammatory disease)
per_case.framework_next_step: Perform diagnostic/therapeutic trial of IL-1 inhibitor (anakinra or canakinumab) and/or pursue NLRP3 gene sequencing to confirm monogenic autoinflammatory disease and establish IL-1-driven pathophysiology. Assess hearing in detail (audiometry). Contingent on IL-1 response: if dramatic, confirms MWS; if absent, pursue alternative diagnosis (TRAPS, FMF, or secondary systemic autoinflammatory disease).
per_case.framework_confidence: High (80-85%): MWS is the most coherent single diagnosis integrating the multi-organ constellation (rash + hearing loss + fever + polyarthralgia), familial inheritance pattern, non-vasculitic histology, DMARD refractoriness, and cytokinemic profile. However, confidence is not absolute because: (a) NLRP3 sequencing is not yet performed (genetic confirmation lacking), (b) IL-1 inhibitor trial is not yet attempted (therapeutic diagnostic gold standard absent), and (c) the prior histopathologic discordance (urticarial vasculitis ~20 years ago vs. non-vasculitic infiltrate now) introduces minor uncertainty about disease classification evolution.

per_case.rationale:
Ground truth is CAPS in the Muckle-Wells end of the spectrum, confirmed by a heterozygous gain-of-function NLRP3 (CIAS1) variant segregating in a large AD pedigree; correct disposition is to recognize it as an IL-1-mediated autoinflammatory syndrome (not chronic urticaria, urticarial vasculitis, or a connective-tissue/myopathy disease), reclassify the prior 'urticarial vasculitis' label as wrong, treat the ANA/anti-Jo-1 as red herrings, refer to immunology/genetics, counsel the AD family, and treat with an IL-1 inhibitor while watching for hearing loss progression and AA amyloidosis.

OUTPUT A: Lands the primary diagnosis precisely — Muckle-Wells syndrome as the intermediate CAPS phenotype driven by NLRP3 inflammasome hyperactivation. It correctly and explicitly addresses nearly every load-bearing element of the ground truth: the non-vasculitic biopsy reclassifying the old 'urticarial vasculitis' read (its caveat section directly tackles the histopathologic discordance), the ANA/anti-Jo-1 as incidental red herrings, DMARD/JAK refractoriness, cold-responsiveness, AD monogenic inheritance, the IL-6/TNF-α/CRP/ESR cytokine profile, and confirmation via NLRP3 sequencing plus IL-1 inhibitor response. It also correctly differentiates TRAPS and FMF. Reasoning is heavily traceable (cites specific findings/rules), well-calibrated, and defensible. Minor weaknesses: it does not emphasize amyloidosis surveillance and is verbose, but no material hallucinations.

OUTPUT B: Also correct in substance — CAPS, FCAS vs MWS with hearing loss tipping to MWS, NLRP3 sequencing, IL-1 inhibitor as treat-and-confirm, recognizes non-vasculitic biopsy and steroid/MTX resistance, notes ANA as added uncertainty. It is concise and well-calibrated (80-85%). However, it is less complete: it does not explicitly reframe the prior 'urticarial vasculitis' as a misdiagnosis, treats ANA/anti-Jo-1 only as 'uncertainty' rather than clearly identifying them as red herrings (and omits anti-Jo-1 / myopathy exclusion entirely), and gives no differential exclusion of the connective-tissue/myositis competitors that the ground truth flags. Its leading framing as 'FCAS or MWS' is slightly less precise than the ground truth's Muckle-Wells localization, though defensible.

Both reach the correct unifying diagnosis and correct disposition, so neither is incorrect. A is more thorough, more explicitly handles the red-herring serologies and the biopsy reclassification, and is more traceable; B is correct but thinner on the differential-exclusion and red-herring reasoning. A wins on completeness and defensibility without sacrificing accuracy.

per_case.prose:
A 63-year-old man, a retired carpenter who was previously well with no notable medical history, was referred to a general medicine clinic after roughly four months of feeling increasingly unwell. He described aching, poorly localised pain across his shoulder girdle and hips, a vague sense of weakness in both arms and both legs, and persistent tiredness that had forced him to give up his usual woodworking. He had lost about 4 kg without trying, attributing it to a poor appetite. He specifically denied any fevers, drenching sweats, or rashes.

On examination in clinic, limb power was full and symmetric (5/5) in both the proximal and distal muscle groups, with no muscle twitching and preserved reflexes. The clinic record contained no documentation of a cardiac or respiratory examination.

Initial bloodwork showed a normocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 91 g/L (reference 115-165) and a white-cell count of 10.6 x10^9/L (reference 4.0-11.0). Inflammatory markers were strikingly raised, with an ESR of 98 mm/hr (reference 0-35) and CRP 79 mg/L (reference <10). Albumin was low at 26 g/L (reference 35-50). Iron studies showed iron 3 umol/L (reference 10-30) with transferrin saturation 6% (reference 20-50). Urinalysis demonstrated microscopic haematuria (blood ++). A prostate-specific antigen was normal at 1.0 ug/L. Screening serology for HIV and hepatitis B and C was negative. An autoantibody screen returned a weakly positive ANCA at low titre (1:20), but the specific anti-MPO (1.9 u/mL; reference 0-5) and anti-PR3 (15.4 u/mL; reference <20) antibodies were both within normal limits.

The patient was treated for a presumed inflammatory rheumatic condition with oral corticosteroids, beginning at 15 mg daily on a slow tapering schedule, and was later given a single intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone when his response was judged inadequate. His energy and appetite improved only marginally, and his inflammatory markers did not settle.

About two months later he was admitted to hospital as his condition worsened. His haemoglobin had fallen further to 64 g/L, his white-cell count had risen to 15.3 x10^9/L, and CRP remained elevated at 105 mg/L. He was tachycardic at 116 beats per minute, with a respiratory rate of 18, blood pressure 129/76 mmHg, temperature 37.5 C, and oxygen saturations of 100% on room air. On auscultation there was a loud pansystolic murmur, heard best at the cardiac apex and radiating towards the axilla; there were no other signs of heart failure.

Bedside echocardiography demonstrated a large, mobile mass measuring approximately 1.3 x 2.0 cm attached to the atrial surface of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, together with a smaller mobile lesion on the tip of the posterior mitral leaflet. There was severe mitral regurgitation with a preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (>65%). Lesions on the aortic valve were also noted. Further imaging identified emboli in the brain and the spleen.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Subacute bacterial infective endocarditis of the mitral (and aortic) valve due to a viridans-group alpha-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus parasanguinis). The initial working diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica was WRONG; the constitutional illness + raised inflammatory markers were driven by indolent endocarditis, and the (low-titre, PR3/MPO-negative) positive ANCA screen was a non-specific red herring rather than ANCA-associated vasculitis.

HOW CONFIRMED: Met two MAJOR modified Duke criteria — (1) typical organism (alpha-haemolytic/viridans streptococci) grown from multiple separate blood culture sets; (2) echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement: large mobile vegetations on the mitral valve leaflets (one ~1.4 x 2.1 cm on the anterior leaflet atrial surface, plus a smaller mobile lesion on the posterior leaflet) with severe mitral regurgitation and a loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; plus aortic valve vegetations. Embolic phenomena (cerebral and splenic emboli) supported the diagnosis. Definitive confirmation came at urgent mechanical aortic + mitral valve replacement.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: Stop steroids; draw multiple blood cultures and obtain echocardiography urgently; admit and start empirical IV antibiotics per endocarditis guidelines; refer to cardiology/cardiac surgery. Because of large mobile vegetations, severe mitral regurgitation, and systemic emboli, early surgical valve replacement was indicated in addition to prolonged IV antibiotics. Outcome: full recovery, well at two-year follow-up.

KEY TEACHING POINT (held aside): PMR is a diagnosis of exclusion; maintain a low threshold for infective endocarditis in a constitutionally unwell patient with high inflammatory markers, anaemia, and a new/under-examined cardiac murmur. Always auscultate the heart and culture before committing to immunosuppression.

ir.inferred_domain: Clinical diagnosis; infectious endocarditis (IE) with systemic complications masquerading initially as rheumatic/vasculitic disease. The case presents a delayed-diagnosis scenario where fever, cardiac murmur, emboli, and progressive multi-organ involvement (anaemia, haematuria, splenic/cerebral emboli) were initially misattributed to autoimmune disease.
