queries.asks: What is the unifying diagnosis that explains the constellation of initial findings (shoulder-hip pain, bilateral arm-leg weakness, fatigue, 4 kg weight loss, normocytic anaemia, elevated inflammatory markers ESR 98 and CRP 79, low albumin, iron deficiency pattern, microscopic haematuria) without fever or systemic features at presentation?

Why was the initial presentation misinterpreted as an autoimmune rheumatic condition (leading to steroid therapy) when the ANCA was weakly positive at low titre with normal anti-MPO and anti-PR3 antibodies? What triggered the initial presumptive diagnosis?

What is the nature and pathophysiological basis of the cardiac masses (vegetation vs thrombus vs other)? Are they consistent with infective endocarditis (IE), and if so, what is the likely microbial organism?

What is the mechanism of progressive anaemia (91 g/L → 64 g/L in 2 months) with normocytic morphology and concurrent iron deficiency pattern? Is this acute blood loss from IE, haemolysis, or chronic disease anaemia?

How did infective endocarditis evade diagnosis at initial presentation despite apparent fever, developing murmur, and embolic phenomena? What were the diagnostic blind spots (missing cardiac/respiratory exams, late imaging)?

What is the clinical significance of low-titre, weakly positive ANCA with normal ANCA component antibodies in the setting of confirmed IE? Does this represent false positivity, cross-reactivity, or rare ANCA specificity?
Did corticosteroid therapy delay diagnosis, alter natural history, or worsen the IE by immunosuppression? Was steroid escalation (methylprednisolone) contraindicated?

What is the nature of embolic complications (septic vs sterile vegetation emboli vs thromboembolism) and their distribution (brain and spleen)? Are lesions acute or chronic, and do they require intervention?

Should blood cultures have been obtained at initial clinic presentation, and what organism(s) would be expected based on presentation and risk factors (elderly, no immunosuppression, no IV drug use documented)?

What is the appropriate management pathway (antibiotic therapy duration, consideration of surgical valve replacement, treatment of emboli, monitoring for relapse) and estimated prognosis given the delayed diagnosis and prior corticosteroid exposure?

rulebook.rule: Echocardiographic evidence of a mobile, oscillating mass attached to a valve or supporting structure (vegetation) on transthoracic or transesophageal echo significantly raises the likelihood of infective endocarditis. TEE is more sensitive than TTE for detecting vegetations, abscesses, and prosthetic valve involvement.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NCBI Bookshelf NBK557641): 'A vacillating intra-cardiac mass fixed to a valve, supporting structure, or implanted material' is a major diagnostic criterion; TEE shows 'higher sensitivity than TTE' for endocardial complications

rulebook.rule: Two or more positive blood cultures (drawn >12 hours apart) for typical endocarditis pathogens (viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, S. aureus, HACEK, enterococci) from separate venipunctures constitute a major diagnostic criterion. Three sets of cultures detect 96-98% of bacteremia.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NCBI Bookshelf NBK470547): 'positive blood cultures' with typical organisms from 'separate cultures or persistently positive cultures' meet major criteria; ESC guidelines recommend ≥3 sets with 10ml blood

rulebook.rule: A new or worsening pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur heard best at the cardiac apex, radiating to the axilla, indicates mitral regurgitation and suggests acute valvular damage from vegetation, endocarditis abscess, or valve perforation.
rulebook.source: Merck Manual Professional (Mitral Regurgitation): 'holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur, heard best at the apex with diaphragm...radiating towards the axilla' indicates MR; Infective Pseudoaneurysm of Anterior Mitral Leaflet (NCBI PMC4939257) documents vegetations causing acute regurgitation

rulebook.rule: Vegetations >10 mm diameter are associated with higher risk of septic emboli (septic fragments dislodging to brain, spleen, lungs, kidneys) and are independent predictors of mortality in endocarditis.
rulebook.source: Management of Septic Emboli in Infectious Endocarditis (Aalaei-Andabili 2017, Wiley): 'vegetation length over 10 mm' is independent predictor of mortality; Septic Embolism StatPearls (NCBI NBK549827) documents 44% of IE patients experience major embolic events

rulebook.rule: Septic emboli to the brain cause acute ischemic stroke through vascular occlusion or brain abscess formation. Cerebral complications occur in 55% of IE cases, with acute neurologic deficit secondary to septic emboli presenting symptomatically in 20% of IE patients.
rulebook.source: Septic Embolism StatPearls (NCBI NBK549827): 'Cerebral complications can occur in 55% of patients with IE and acute neurologic deficit secondary to septic emboli may be the presenting symptom in 20% of cases'; 'areas where emboli were found include: the brain (26.3%)'

rulebook.rule: Septic emboli to the spleen result in splenic infarction (40% of IE cases with emboli) and splenic abscess (5% of splenic emboli). Splenic imaging abnormalities are markers of systemic embolic disease in IE.
rulebook.source: Septic Embolism StatPearls (NCBI NBK549827): 'Embolism to the spleen can result in splenic infarction in 40% of patients, with splenic abscess occurring in 5% of these patients'; documented embolism site 'spleen (6.8%)' of IE cohort

rulebook.rule: Normocytic anemia in the setting of chronic infection/inflammation is consistent with anemia of chronic disease. In subacute IE (lasting weeks to months), normocytic-normochromic anemia results from shortened RBC lifespan and iron sequestration in macrophages due to chronic bacterial infection.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NCBI NBK557641): 'More specifically, cases with more subacute-chronic presentations may have normocytic anemia consistent with anemia of chronic disease'; Anemia and Transfusion in Infective Endocarditis (NCBI PMC12230846): 'anemia of chronic disease...conditions associated with anemia of chronic disease include chronic bacterial endocarditis'

rulebook.rule: True iron deficiency pattern (low serum iron, low transferrin saturation) coexisting with anemia may result from chronic, minor gastrointestinal or valve-related blood loss from vegetations, or from vegetations causing vascular damage. Iron deficiency anemia can be a rare but significant presenting feature of subacute bacterial endocarditis.
rulebook.source: Iron Deficiency Anemia in Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis (NCBI PMC11676614): 'Unexplained iron deficiency anemia, especially when persistent and accompanied by systemic symptoms, should prompt consideration of infective endocarditis'; Infective Endocarditis Presenting as Unexplained Iron Deficiency Anaemia (NCBI PMC12410828): documents cases of IE with 'progressive iron deficiency anemia'

rulebook.rule: Microscopic haematuria results from immune complex deposition on the glomerular basement membrane. In IE, circulating immune complexes (bacterial antigen-antibody complexes) trigger immune complex glomerulonephritis, which may manifest as haematuria and/or proteinuria without embolic disease.
rulebook.source: AJKD Atlas: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis-Associated Glomerulonephritis: 'Immune complexes related to infectious endocarditis cause proliferative lesions, supported by...immunoglobulin and complement staining by immunofluorescence'; 'Hematuria and mild proteinuria are commonly present in endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis'; Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis StatPearls: 'right-sided infective endocarditis commonly presents with...anaemia and microscopic haematuria—the latter possibly due to immune complex deposition'

rulebook.rule: Constitutional symptoms of fatigue, malaise, vague weakness, and weight loss (>4 kg unintentional) are nonspecific but common in endocarditis, present in up to 44% of IE cases. These symptoms reflect systemic infection, anemia, and chronic inflammation.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Endocarditis (NCBI NBK499844): 'Associated symptoms of infective endocarditis are often nonspecific and include fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, chills, nausea, and vomiting'; 'constitutional symptoms of weight loss, anorexia, and myalgias are not uncommon and can exist in up to 44% of cases'; StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NCBI NBK557641): 'Systemic manifestations include fever, malaise, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and breathlessness'

rulebook.rule: Fever ≥38°C is a minor Duke criterion for IE, present in >95% of unselected IE patients in general populations. However, in elderly patients, fever is frequently absent, making atypical presentations common. Absence of fever should not exclude IE in older adults.
rulebook.direction: raises or lowers depending on age
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NCBI NBK557641): 'Fever present in >95% of patients'; Infective Endocarditis in the Elderly (NCBI PMC9224959): 'Fever, the most common initial symptom in general populations, is frequently absent in elderly patients'; 'In elderly patients, anemia and weight loss are occasionally the only or the most striking symptoms'

rulebook.rule: In elderly patients (age >60), absence of fever does NOT exclude infective endocarditis. Atypical presentations with only nonspecific constitutional symptoms (fatigue, anemia, weight loss, anorexia) are characteristic. The differential includes neoplasia and wasting syndrome when fever is absent.
rulebook.direction: raises (or prevents lowering by fever absence)
rulebook.source: Infective Endocarditis in the Elderly (NCBI PMC9224959): 'one of the most distinctive features in elderly patients is the absence of fever'; 'In such cases, the clinical reasoning process leads to a hypothesis of wasting syndrome or neoplastic disease, especially when there is no fever'; 'The diagnosis of IE in the elderly is rarely straightforward and is often delayed or overlooked'

rulebook.rule: Weakly positive ANCA (typically PR3-ANCA, occurring in 18-43% of IE patients) can mimic ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV). ANCA positivity in IE is likely due to bacteria triggering autoantibody production through molecular mimicry or TLR activation. However, ANCA component antibody titers (anti-PR3, anti-MPO) may be within normal limits despite positive ANCA staining (low-titre, weakly positive).
rulebook.source: PLOS ONE: Infective Endocarditis with Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (PMC3934949): 'All 13 ANCA-positive patients were PR3-ANCA-positive...PR3-ANCA predominance'; 'ANCA positivity was found in 18-43% of patients with infective endocarditis'; Springer: Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies in IE (10.1007/s10067-022-06240-w): bacteria trigger autoantibody production via 'indirect molecular simulation' and TLR activation; case review documented 33.3% of tested IE patients ANCA-positive

rulebook.rule: Weakly positive ANCA at low titre (e.g., 1:20) combined with normal anti-MPO and anti-PR3 antibody levels (<20 u/mL) is atypical for primary ANCA-associated vasculitis and should raise suspicion for IE masquerading as vasculitis. In genuine AAV, component antibody titers are typically elevated.
rulebook.source: PMC: Infective Endocarditis Mimicking ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (PMC7373528): documents cases where IE patients had positive ANCA staining but misdiagnosis as AAV led to inappropriate corticosteroid therapy; standard AAV diagnostic criteria require elevated anti-PR3 or anti-MPO, not just ANCA staining

rulebook.rule: Misdiagnosis of IE as ANCA-associated vasculitis and treatment with corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy without antibiotics can worsen IE, lead to disease progression, septic complications, and death. Four of eight documented IE patients treated initially with immunosuppression for presumed vasculitis died.
rulebook.source: PMC: Infective Endocarditis Mimicking ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (PMC7373528): 'the misdiagnosis of an infectious disease as AAV and the administration of immunosuppressive therapy could worsen the infection and lead to disastrous consequences'; 'there have been 8 cases of IE with positive ANCA...treated initially with immunosuppression...Four of these patients eventually died'

rulebook.rule: Corticosteroid therapy for presumed autoimmune/rheumatic disease can mask IE clinical signs and delay diagnosis. One documented case involved 9-month diagnostic delay when corticosteroids masked IE, and delayed diagnosis (≥4 weeks from symptom onset) correlates with worse renal and systemic outcomes.
rulebook.source: PMC: Immunosuppressant Use in IE-Associated GN (PMC12307529): 'Delayed diagnosis of infective endocarditis (≥ 4 weeks from symptom onset) was observed in 71 cases...and was associated with worse renal outcomes'; Q Fever Endocarditis Case Report (PubMed 2729329): documented 9-month delay when corticosteroids masked endocarditis; ScienceDirect: 'When Steroids Stop Working' (2024): endocarditis is 'the great mimicker' of vasculitis

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented cardiac examination or early echocardiography in patients with acute constitutional symptoms, anaemia, and systemic inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP markedly elevated) represents a critical diagnostic gap. Normal or absent echocardiography does NOT exclude endocarditis; TEE is more sensitive than TTE and should be obtained if clinical suspicion remains high.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NBK470547): 'Echocardiography...should be performed in all patients with suspected bacterial endocarditis'; TEE demonstrates 'higher sensitivity than TTE' and better detects abscesses/perforations; Clinical case of IE Presenting as Unexplained Iron Deficiency (NCBI PMC12410828): 'Initial transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was unremarkable...Only transoesophageal echocardiography and CT coronary angiography revealed vegetations'

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated ESR (>50 mm/hr, e.g., 98) and CRP (>50 mg/L, e.g., 79) indicate active systemic inflammation. These are nonspecific but common in IE and are supporting evidence for chronic systemic infection. Persistently elevated or rising inflammatory markers despite steroid therapy suggest inadequate treatment of underlying infection.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): established IE 'often cause...increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, increased immunoglobulin levels, and the presence of circulating immune complexes'; elevated markers persistent despite treatment suggest infection not controlled

rulebook.rule: Low serum albumin (26 g/L; normal 35-50) in the setting of marked inflammatory markers (high ESR/CRP) reflects both acute-phase response (albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant) and chronic nutritional depletion from prolonged systemic illness. In IE with 4-month symptom duration, low albumin indicates chronic catabolism.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Endocarditis (NBK499844) and Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): chronic infection causes 'anorexia' and systemic symptoms reflecting prolonged inflammatory state; low albumin reflects both acute-phase suppression and chronic nutritional depletion typical of subacute IE

rulebook.rule: Persistent positive blood cultures (positive on days 1 and 2+) strongly support endocarditis diagnosis (likelihood ratios 1.78-9.60 depending on organism). Culture clearance by day 2 argues against IE for most organisms except streptococci (which naturally clear rapidly regardless of IE presence). Single positive culture (1 of 4 bottles) argues against IE (negative LR ~0.1).
rulebook.source: PMC: Interpreting Blood Culture Results as Early Guidance for IE (PMC12046426): 'Only 1 of 4 blood culture bottles positive...provides strong evidence against endocarditis...negative LR of approximately 0.1'; 'Conversely, 4 of 4 bottles positive increases endocarditis likelihood...LR 4.21-5.35'; 'Persistent bacteremia (positive ≥2 days) supports an endocarditis diagnosis, with likelihood ratios ranging from 1.78 to 9.60'

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented cardiac/respiratory examination during initial presentation with constitutional symptoms prevents detection of endocarditis stigmata (new murmur, heart failure signs, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions). Physical findings are present in ~85% of IE cases. Missing this opportunity delays diagnosis.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NBK470547): 'cardiac murmurs...in about 85% of patients'; StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): detailed list of physical findings (Osler nodes, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages) that aid diagnosis; absent documentation = lost diagnostic opportunity

rulebook.rule: WBC count at upper limit of normal or mildly elevated (10.6 x10^9/L, normal 4.0-11.0) can occur in both inflammatory and infectious conditions. Rising WBC over time (e.g., 10.6 → 15.3 in 2 months) despite steroid therapy argues against autoimmune disease and suggests progressive bacterial infection.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NBK470547): elevated WBC is nonspecific but common in IE; progressive elevation despite immunosuppression argues for infection over autoimmune etiology

rulebook.rule: Progressive worsening of anemia (Hb 91 → 64 g/L over 2 months) despite treatment with steroids or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents indicates ongoing blood loss, hemolysis, or bone marrow suppression from chronic infection. This trajectory supports IE over autoimmune disease (which typically responds to steroids).
rulebook.source: Anemia and Transfusion in Infective Endocarditis (NCBI PMC12230846): 'anemia may result from hemolysis or bone marrow suppression due to inflammation'; progressive anemia despite treatment indicates mechanism not responsive to anti-inflammatory therapy, suggesting ongoing infection

rulebook.rule: Marked elevation in inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) that fail to improve despite adequate corticosteroid therapy (15 mg daily + methylprednisolone pulse) suggests the diagnosis is NOT primarily autoimmune inflammation but rather infectious disease. Endocarditis characteristically fails to improve with steroids alone.
rulebook.source: PMC: When Steroids Stop Working – Infective Endocarditis (ScienceDirect 2024): 'endocarditis, the great mimicker' often treated as vasculitis with steroids; 'when his response was judged inadequate' and markers persist, diagnosis should be reconsidered for infection; Q Fever Endocarditis case (PubMed 2729329): apparent paradoxical response to steroids masked underlying IE

rulebook.rule: Negative screening for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C does not exclude endocarditis but indicates IE is not secondary to immunosuppression or chronic viral infection. Community-acquired bacterial endocarditis (streptococci, staphylococci) occurs in immunocompetent individuals.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): typical IE pathogens (viridans streptococci, S. aureus) occur in immunocompetent hosts; HIV/HBV/HCV seronegative patients are at risk for community-acquired bacterial IE

rulebook.rule: Normal PSA (1.0 ug/L) argues against prostate as source of haematuria or systemic inflammation. This helps exclude benign prostatic disease or prostate cancer as alternative diagnoses for haematuria and constitutional symptoms.
rulebook.bears_on: Supports IE diagnosis (by excluding urologic mimickers)
rulebook.source: Clinical evaluation: normal PSA excludes common urologic causes of haematuria and systemic symptoms, directing diagnosis toward hematologic or cardiac sources

rulebook.rule: Presence of vegetations on multiple valves (mitral AND aortic) indicates more aggressive, disseminated infection. Multivalvular endocarditis increases severity and risk of acute heart failure, embolic complications, and mortality. Aortic valve involvement adds risk of aortic root abscess and conduction abnormalities.
rulebook.source: Analysis of Clinical Features and Outcomes of IE with Very Large Vegetations (NCBI PMC11266946): multivalvular involvement associated with higher complication rates; Mitral and Aortic Valve Lesions case reports (NCBI PMC4939257, PMC12410292): document accelerated deterioration with bivalvular disease

rulebook.rule: Large (>13 mm), mobile vegetations on mitral valve anterior leaflet have high risk of embolization because of: (a) size enabling fragmentation, (b) mobility with each heartbeat creating mechanical stress, (c) anterior leaflet location with direct blood flow dynamics favoring dislodgement.
rulebook.bears_on: Infective endocarditis with high embolic risk
rulebook.source: Analysis of Clinical Features and Outcomes of IE with Very Large Vegetations (NCBI PMC11266946): 'very large vegetations' (>10 mm) associated with embolic events and mortality; 3D Imaging of Mitral Valve Perforation (NCBI PMC12410292): documentation of large anterior leaflet vegetation causing acute pathology

rulebook.rule: Severe mitral regurgitation (large regurgitant jet, hyperdynamic left ventricle) in acute IE results from vegetation destruction of leaflet tissue, perforation, or rupture of chordae tendineae. Severity correlates with risk of acute pulmonary edema and hemodynamic compromise.
rulebook.source: Merck Manual: Mitral Regurgitation can result from 'infective endocarditis'; Chordae Tendinea Rupture and Pulmonary Valve Vegetation in Pediatric Endocarditis (NCBI PMC11070895): documents valve tissue destruction by vegetations causing severe regurgitation

rulebook.rule: Preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (>65%) despite severe mitral regurgitation indicates acute-onset disease before the left ventricle has dilated. This pattern suggests acute IE with recent valve damage, rather than chronic rheumatic or degenerative disease (which causes LV dilation and EF reduction).
rulebook.source: Hemodynamic physiology: acute, severe MR → volume overload without chronic compensation → preserved EF initially; chronic MR → LV dilation with reduced EF; IE case patterns (NCBI PMC11070895, NCBI PMC11448373) show preserved function in acute presentations

rulebook.rule: Fall in hemoglobin from 91 to 64 g/L (27 g/L drop) in 2 months indicates severe, progressive blood loss or hemolysis. This rate of deterioration is unusual for simple iron deficiency (which develops over months) and suggests acute hemolysis from mechanical trauma (vegetation), septic microinfarcts, or ongoing acute bleeding.
rulebook.source: Hemolytic Anemia in IE: vegetation mechanical trauma causes RBC destruction; Anemia and Transfusion in Infective Endocarditis (NCBI PMC12230846): 'hemolysis or bone marrow suppression due to inflammation'; rapid decline suggests acute process

rulebook.rule: Tachycardia (116 bpm) at hospital admission in context of fever, anemia, and cardiac pathology indicates sympathetic response to hemodynamic compromise, anemia, and/or sepsis. HR >100 is common in IE and correlates with disease severity.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): systemic infection triggers tachycardia; elevated HR typical in IE with fever and hemodynamic derangement from valve disease

rulebook.rule: Low-grade temperature (37.5°C) at hospital admission in an elderly patient with 4 months of constitutional symptoms does not exclude IE. Low-grade fever can reflect chronic adaptation or temperature dysregulation in elderly. Combined with other findings (anaemia, murmur, emboli), this should raise IE suspicion.
rulebook.source: Infective Endocarditis in the Elderly (NCBI PMC9224959): 'Fever, the most common initial symptom in general populations, is frequently absent in elderly patients'; 'In elderly patients, anemia and weight loss are occasionally the only...striking symptoms'

rulebook.rule: Occupational history of manual labor (carpentry) may increase minor trauma to hands/fingers, creating transient bacteremia risk (e.g., from oral streptococci colonization entering through small wounds). While not a major risk factor, occupational injury combined with poor oral hygiene increases seeding risk.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Endocarditis (NBK499844): predisposing conditions include 'valvular abnormalities' and 'IV drug use'; occupational injury creating transient bacteremia is a recognized (though minor) pathway to seeding

rulebook.rule: History of previous good health with no prior documented cardiac disease suggests this is native valve endocarditis rather than prosthetic valve IE. Native valve IE has different epidemiology (more streptococci, less virulent) and somewhat better prognosis than prosthetic valve IE.
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NBK470547): 'Prosthetic valve endocarditis...demonstrates highest mortality (~30%)'; native valve IE has lower mortality; absence of prior documented murmurs/disease indicates likely native valve involvement

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented IV drug use history reduces risk of Staphylococcus aureus (typical in IVDU-related IE) and Pseudomonas. Community-acquired native valve IE in non-IVDU elderly patients is more likely caused by viridans group streptococci, S. gallolyticus, or other oral commensals.
rulebook.bears_on: Community-acquired native valve IE (likely streptococcal etiology)
rulebook.source: StatPearls Bacterial Endocarditis (NBK470547): 'Two or more positive blood cultures for typical endocarditis pathogens: viridans group streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK...typical of community-acquired native valve IE'; IV drug use associated with S. aureus predominance

rulebook.rule: Age 63 years is above the threshold where IE presentation becomes atypical and nonspecific. In elderly patients, absence of fever, presence of only constitutional symptoms, and prevalence of baseline cardiac abnormalities (murmurs, degenerative changes) create diagnostic confusion mimicking neoplasia or wasting syndrome.
rulebook.source: Infective Endocarditis in the Elderly (NCBI PMC9224959): 'Diagnosis of IE in elderly patients is challenging due to the atypical presentation of the disease'; 'the clinical reasoning process leads to a hypothesis of wasting syndrome or neoplastic disease, especially when there is no fever'; 'The diagnosis of IE in the elderly is rarely straightforward and is often delayed'

rulebook.rule: Four-month duration of symptoms with gradual onset of constitutional symptoms, anaemia, and weight loss is classic for SUBACUTE infective endocarditis. This contrasts with acute IE (days-weeks presentation with fulminant sepsis). Subacute IE mimics chronic inflammatory diseases (vasculitis, rheumatic conditions).
rulebook.source: StatPearls Infectious Endocarditis (NBK557641): 'Subacute infective endocarditis may cause symptoms such as fatigue, mild fever, a moderately fast heart rate, weight loss, sweating, and a low red blood cell count (anemia)'; subacute presentations often misdiagnosed as autoimmune disease

per_case.blind_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: Infective endocarditis, likely streptococcal or enterococcal species.

Recommended next action: (1) Blood cultures if not already obtained; (2) Start empiric IV antibiotics immediately (ceftriaxone + gentamicin or vancomycin based on local resistance patterns); (3) Cardiac surgery consultation for valve replacement assessment given large vegetations (1.3 × 2.0 cm), severe MR, and systemic emboli indicating high embolic risk; (4) Transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude paravalvular abscesses and better characterize valve involvement; (5) Neurology/neuroradiology evaluation of cerebral emboli.

Confidence: 95%

Reasoning: Valve vegetations with septic emboli (brain, spleen) and severe mitral regurgitation are pathognomonic for endocarditis. The subacute presentation over four months, systemic inflammatory markers, new pansystolic murmur, microscopic hematuria (immune complex GN), anemia of chronic inflammation, and failure to respond to corticosteroids all support endocarditis rather than primary rheumatologic disease. The initial misdiagnosis as inflammatory rheumatic disease is understandable given prominent systemic inflammation and microscopic hematuria, but echocardiographic evidence of vegetations and emboli is diagnostic.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 63-year-old man presents a classic case of subacute infective endocarditis initially misdiagnosed as autoimmune vasculitis. The diagnosis is supported by multiple layers of evidence:

MAJOR ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC CRITERION (R1): Bedside echocardiography demonstrated a large mobile mass (1.3 x 2.0 cm) attached to the anterior mitral valve leaflet (F58) and a smaller mobile lesion on the posterior mitral leaflet (F59), with severe mitral regurgitation (F60). These are pathognomonic vegetations meeting the major diagnostic criterion for IE (R1), supported by the new pansystolic murmur heard best at the apex radiating to the axilla (F53, F54, F55), which indicates acute mitral regurgitation consistent with vegetation damage (R3).

EMBOLIC COMPLICATIONS: The presence of septic emboli in the brain (F63) and spleen (F64) further confirms active IE. Cerebral septic emboli occur in 55% of IE cases (R5), and splenic emboli in 40% of IE cases with embolic phenomena (R6). The large vegetation size (>10 mm, here 1.3 x 2.0 cm = 13 x 20 mm) is an independent predictor of mortality and systemic emboli (R4), with anterior mitral leaflet location conferring highest embolization risk due to blood flow dynamics (R28).

SUBACUTE PRESENTATION WITH CONSTITUTIONAL SYMPTOMS: The four-month duration (F4) of progressive aching pain (F5, F6), fatigue (F9), unintentional weight loss of 4 kg (F10), and loss of appetite are hallmark constitutional symptoms of subacute IE (R10, R38). These symptoms are present in up to 44% of IE cases and reflect systemic infection and anemia (R10). The patient's age (63 years; F1) places him in the cohort where IE presentations are atypical and nonspecific (R12, R37): he explicitly denied fever (F12), yet presented with only constitutional symptoms—a pattern characteristic of elderly patients where fever is frequently absent, and diagnosis is often delayed (R11, R12).

PROGRESSIVE ANEMIA AND IRON DEFICIENCY: The normocytic anemia at presentation (Hb 91 g/L; F21) is consistent with anemia of chronic disease secondary to subacute IE (R7). The concurrent iron deficiency pattern (serum iron 3 umol/L, transferrin saturation 6%; F27, F28) suggests chronic minor blood loss from vegetations or vascular damage—a recognized presenting feature of subacute bacterial endocarditis (R8). The rapid deterioration to 64 g/L over two months (F45) indicates progressive hemolysis or ongoing acute blood loss from vegetation, accelerated by the hemodynamic stress of severe MR (R31).

ELEVATED INFLAMMATORY MARKERS UNRESPONSIVE TO STEROIDS: Markedly elevated ESR 98 mm/hr and CRP 79 mg/L (F23, F24) are consistent with IE-driven systemic inflammation (R18). Critically, these markers failed to improve despite corticosteroid therapy (15 mg daily plus intramuscular methylprednisolone; F38, F39) and remained elevated at CRP 105 mg/L on admission (F47). This failure to respond to immunosuppression is a major red flag suggesting the diagnosis is infectious, not autoimmune (R24). In genuine ANCA-associated vasculitis, such inflammation typically resolves with steroids—the persistent elevation argues against vasculitis and toward endocarditis.

MISDIAGNOSIS AS ANCA VASCULITIS: The initial diagnosis of "presumed inflammatory rheumatic condition" (F37) was informed by a weakly positive ANCA at low titre 1:20 (F34). However, anti-MPO and anti-PR3 were both within normal limits (F35, F36). This discordance—weakly positive ANCA staining with normal component antibody titers—is atypical for primary ANCA-associated vasculitis and highly suggestive of IE masquerading as vasculitis (R13, R14). ANCA positivity occurs in 18-43% of IE patients due to bacterial molecular mimicry and TLR activation (R13). This misattribution of ANCA positivity to AAV led to immunosuppressive therapy without antibiotics—a treatment known to worsen IE (R15). Published case series document that four of eight IE patients initially treated with immunosuppression for presumed vasculitis died (R15).

DIAGNOSTIC DELAYS AND DOCUMENTATION GAPS: The absence of cardiac and respiratory examination documentation at initial clinic presentation (F19, F20) was a critical missed opportunity, as cardiac murmurs and other stigmata are present in ~85% of IE cases (R21). This examination gap likely contributed to the delayed detection of the pansystolic murmur, which only became documented at hospital admission two months later. Additionally, the case does not report blood culture results, which are required for the full Duke criteria diagnostic algorithm. However, the echocardiographic findings (major criterion) combined with the clinical presentation (new murmur, constitutional symptoms, emboli, positive ANCA staining) meet diagnostic criteria independently.

SUPPORTING FEATURES: The low albumin (26 g/L; F26) reflects both acute-phase response and chronic cachexia from four months of systemic illness (R19). The rising WBC (10.6 → 15.3 x10^9/L; F22, F46) despite steroid therapy argues against autoimmune disease and supports progressive infection (R22). The multivalvular involvement (mitral AND aortic lesions; F62) indicates disseminated, aggressive infection with higher risk of complications (R27). The preserved LVEF >65% despite severe MR (F61) suggests acute-onset valve damage before compensatory LV dilation, typical of acute IE superimposed on previously normal valves (R30), consistent with the patient's history of prior good health (F3; R35). The tachycardia (HR 116; F48) at admission reflects sympathetic response to hemodynamic compromise and sepsis (R32).

EXCLUDED MIMICKERS: Negative serology for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C (F31, F32, F33) excludes secondary immunosuppression as a contributor; this is community-acquired bacterial IE (R25). Normal PSA (F30) excludes genitourinary sources of haematuria (R26). The microscopic haematuria (F29) is explained by immune complex glomerulonephritis secondary to circulating IE-associated antigen-antibody complexes, not primary urologic disease (R9).

ORGANISM PREDICTION: Absence of documented IV drug use and the elderly, community-acquired, native valve presentation (R36) predict viridans group streptococci, S. gallolyticus, or less likely S. aureus as the causative organism. Blood cultures remain the gold standard for organism identification and would determine definitive antibiotic selection.

PROGNOSIS IMPACT: The delayed diagnosis (four months before hospitalization, steroid therapy without antibiotics for weeks to months) has worsened prognosis. Documented delayed IE diagnosis (≥4 weeks from symptom onset) correlates with worse renal and systemic outcomes (R16). The large vegetation size, multivalvular involvement, embolic complications, severe MR, and prior immunosuppression all indicate a high-risk presentation requiring urgent surgical consideration alongside aggressive antibiotic therapy.

In summary, the echocardiographic finding of large mobile mitral vegetations with severe MR (major criterion per R1, R3) combined with the clinical syndrome of subacute IE (constitutional symptoms, anemia, emboli, new murmur, elevated inflammatory markers refractory to steroids), the atypical elderly presentation (R11, R12, R37), the misattributed ANCA positivity (R13, R14), and the documented diagnostic delay (R16, R21) converge on a single diagnosis: infective endocarditis, complicated by systemic septic emboli and iatrogenic delay in appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
per_case.framework_top: Infective endocarditis (IE), subacute presentation with native mitral valve (and aortic valve) vegetations, complicated by systemic septic emboli (brain and spleen), severe anemia, and iatrogenic diagnostic delay due to misdiagnosis as ANCA-associated vasculitis.
per_case.framework_next_step: Obtain blood cultures (if not already done) immediately to identify organism and guide antibiotic selection; initiate IV antibiotics covering typical community-acquired native valve pathogens (viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, S. aureus) pending culture results; arrange urgent cardiothoracic surgery consultation to assess for surgical intervention (vegetation size >13 mm, multivalvular involvement, severe MR, septic emboli indicate high-risk features); neuroimaging follow-up to characterize brain emboli and assess for mycotic aneurysm risk; and transition from corticosteroids to appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
per_case.framework_confidence: High confidence (85-90%) for IE diagnosis based on echocardiographic major criterion (large mobile vegetations with severe MR), clinical major criterion (pansystolic murmur), supporting criteria (anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, embolic complications, constitutional symptoms, subacute 4-month timeline, elderly patient with atypical presentation). Confidence is qualified by absence of organism identification (blood cultures not documented in case) and missing blood culture data required for full Duke criteria, but echocardiographic findings are pathognomonic.

per_case.rationale: Both outputs reach the correct core diagnosis: subacute infective endocarditis due to viridans/streptococcal organisms, with vegetations, severe MR, and septic emboli, and both correctly identify that the autoimmune/rheumatic working diagnosis was wrong and that steroids were inappropriate without antibiotics. Output A is concise, well-calibrated (95%), and gives the cleanest actionable disposition (blood cultures, specific empiric IV regimens, cardiac surgery consult, TEE, neuro eval) with low hallucination risk; its vegetation size (1.3x2.0 cm) closely matches ground truth (1.4x2.1 cm). However, A omits two load-bearing ground-truth elements: the multivalvular (mitral AND aortic) involvement and an explicit organism-level prediction, and it does not surface the ANCA-as-red-herring nuance. Output B captures substantially more of the ground truth's central content: multivalvular mitral+aortic involvement, a correct organism prediction (viridans group streptococci, S. gallolyticus), the ANCA red-herring framing (low-titre positive ANCA with normal MPO/PR3 being non-specific rather than true AAV), the two-major-Duke-criteria structure, and the embolic confirmation. B's weaknesses are real: it over-emphasizes ANCA-associated vasculitis as the misdiagnosis whereas ground truth states the working diagnosis was PMR (B does mention the "inflammatory rheumatic condition" framing, so this is partial rather than wrong), and it leans heavily on numerous very precise statistics tied to internal R-citations (e.g., 55% cerebral emboli, 18-43% ANCA, "four of eight died") whose provenance cannot be verified, creating calibration/hallucination risk. On balance B aligns with more of the decisive ground-truth facts (organism, multivalvular, ANCA nuance, criteria structure) while still being clinically correct, edging out A despite A's superior concision, calibration, and disposition crispness. Close call.

per_case.prose:
A 58-year-old man was referred to a general internal medicine clinic for evaluation of several weeks of loose, watery stools without blood, weight stable, no recent travel or sick contacts.

His past history was dominated by a long-standing mood and anxiety problem. For roughly twelve years he had carried diagnoses of recurrent depression and an anxiety disorder, including one prolonged inpatient psychiatric admission a few years earlier for a major depressive episode. Over those years he had described recurrent spells, several times per week to several times per month, often waking him at night, consisting of intense anxiety and a sense of dread together with nausea and occasional vomiting, fine tremor, and pounding palpitations. The spells had been attributed to panic attacks and managed by his psychiatry team. His current regimen was venlafaxine 150 mg daily, clonazepam 0.5 mg at night as needed, and a low bedtime dose of extended-release quetiapine.

He also had a five-year history of hypertension that had been described as somewhat difficult to control on his current agents, along with dyslipidemia and lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic enlargement.

In clinic his blood pressure was elevated and his pulse was mildly tachycardic between episodes; he appeared anxious but was alert and oriented. General and abdominal examination was unremarkable. Because the new bowel symptoms were unexplained, abdominal cross-sectional imaging was obtained.

CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large left adrenal mass measuring approximately 16 x 15 cm, together with two low-density lesions in the liver measuring about 2.0 and 2.6 cm. Subsequent MRI confirmed the adrenal mass and identified an additional small hepatic lesion of roughly 0.6 cm. Functional imaging with FDG-PET/CT showed avid tracer uptake within the left adrenal mass.

Twenty-four-hour urine and paired plasma studies were obtained:
- Urine normetanephrine: 228,000 nmol/day (reference < 240)
- Urine metanephrine: 91,000 nmol/day (reference < 275)
- Urine dopamine: 8,100 nmol/day (reference < 2,570)
- Urine norepinephrine: 1,240 nmol/day (reference < 440)
- Urine epinephrine: 2,510 nmol/day (reference < 110)
- Plasma free normetanephrine: 705 nmol/L (reference < 1.20)
- Plasma free metanephrine: 171 nmol/L (reference < 0.48)

Routine chemistries and blood counts were otherwise unremarkable.
per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Malignant (metastatic) pheochromocytoma of the adrenal gland, which had masqueraded for over a decade as a refractory primary anxiety/panic disorder.

HOW CONFIRMED: (1) Biochemistry — grossly elevated 24-hour urinary and plasma fractionated metanephrines/catecholamines (urine normetanephrine, metanephrine, dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine all far above reference; plasma free normetanephrine and metanephrine hundreds-fold above the upper limit). (2) Imaging — large unilateral adrenal mass with avid FDG-PET uptake plus multiple liver lesions. (3) Histopathology after adrenalectomy — pheochromocytoma with lymphovascular invasion, and synchronous hepatic metastases (resected at partial hepatectomy), establishing the MALIGNANT variant. (4) Confirmatory functional cure — catecholamine/metanephrine values normalized after tumor + metastasis resection and panic attacks resolved, allowing psychiatric medications to be largely discontinued. Hereditary panel of 14 pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma genes (incl. SDHB, SDHD, VHL, RET, NF1) was NEGATIVE — i.e., apparently sporadic.

CORRECT DISPOSITION: This is NOT a psychiatric problem. The correct action is to STOP escalating psychiatric therapy and instead screen biochemically for a catecholamine-secreting tumor (plasma free or 24-h urinary fractionated metanephrines), localize with cross-sectional imaging, refer to endocrine surgery, institute pre-operative alpha-adrenergic blockade (then beta-blockade) before resection, and resect both the primary adrenal tumor and metastatic disease. Lifelong oncologic/biochemical surveillance is required because the tumor is malignant/metastatic. Recognizing the mimic matters: long-standing panic/anxiety REFRACTORY to medication, especially with paroxysmal palpitations/tremor/diaphoresis, headache, hypertension, and an adrenal mass, should trigger pheochromocytoma workup rather than further psychotropic escalation.

ORIGINAL (unperturbed) details for reference: 64-year-old man, 13-year psychiatric history (depression + anxiety/panic disorder, prior inpatient stay), 5-yr hypertension; on venlafaxine 187.5 mg/day, clonazepam 0.5 mg qhs, quetiapine XR 25 mg/day. New-onset diarrhea triggered CT showing an 18.2 x 16.3 cm left adrenal mass + two liver lesions (2.2, 2.5 cm); MRI found a third 0.5 cm hepatic lesion; FDG-PET SUVmax 7.8. Source: Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism Case Reports, 2018 (PMC5890079), Centre hospitalier de l'Universite de Montreal, Canada.

uncertainties.about: Precise onset date of the initial psychiatric symptoms 12 years ago and whether any precipitating event or medical workup was done at that time
Whether the recent diarrhea represents a new symptom or exacerbation of chronic symptoms (timeline relative to psychiatric history)
Whether the patient was screened for secondary causes of hypertension during the 5-year history (including pheochromocytoma)
Whether the fine tremor was characterized further (rest vs. action, amplitude, distribution)
Whether glucose homeostasis was assessed (blood glucose on labs, given alpha-adrenergic hyperactivity)
Nature and imaging characteristics of the three liver lesions (cystic vs. solid, enhancement pattern, follow-up imaging)
Whether genetic testing (RET, SDH, NF1) was pursued or planned, given tumor size and metastatic pattern
Tumor tissue diagnosis (core biopsy, fine-needle aspiration) and pathologic confirmation of pheochromocytoma
Whether imaging of thorax and other sites was performed to fully stage disease

queries.asks: Is the clinical presentation (paroxysmal episodes of anxiety, tremor, palpitations, dread, nausea) consistent with pheochromocytoma or another catecholamine-excess state?
Does the pattern of catecholamine metabolites and the relative elevation of epinephrine vs. norepinephrine indicate the adrenal origin and specific tumor secretion profile?
What is the malignancy risk assessment for this adrenal mass, and does the presence of liver lesions indicate metastatic pheochromocytoma (malignant pheochromocytoma)?
What is the mechanism by which catecholamine excess produces diarrhea and how does this relate to the patient's GI symptoms?
How did psychiatric misattribution occur (diagnostic capture), and what are the clinical red flags in the symptom complex that should have prompted endocrine evaluation sooner?
What is the appropriate perioperative management strategy for adrenalectomy in the context of severe catecholamine excess and metastatic disease?
Are there genetic predisposition syndromes associated with early-onset pheochromocytoma, and is testing indicated?

rulebook.rule: Paroxysmal episodes of intense anxiety, dread, and sense of impending doom (several times per week to monthly) RAISES suspicion for pheochromocytoma; episodes triggered by catecholamine release rather than emotional stress, and unresponsive to standard anxiolytics are key distinguishing features.
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma: The Challenge of Paroxysmal Symptoms, Clinical Advisor; Unusual presentation of pheochromocytoma: thirteen years of anxiety requiring psychiatric treatment, Endocrinology Diabetes & Metabolism Case Reports 2018; PMC29644077

rulebook.rule: Paroxysmal palpitations, tremor, nausea, and vomiting occurring during anxiety episodes RAISES suspicion for pheochromocytoma; these catecholamine-mediated symptoms are accompanied by autonomic activation distinct from psychologically-triggered panic.
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertensive Crises in a Previously Healthy Woman: A Case Report, PMC12867173; PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: AN ENDOCRINE STRESS MIMICKING DISORDER, PMC2693284

rulebook.rule: Nocturnal episodes awakening the patient from sleep RAISES suspicion for pheochromocytoma; classic presentation includes nocturnal hypertension with palpitations and panic-like symptoms lasting 5-20 minutes, whereas psychologically-driven panic typically shows emotional triggers and anticipatory anxiety.
rulebook.source: Pheochromocytoma associated with nocturnal hypertension, PubMed 8012072; Symptoms of Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland, Adrenal.com; Top 5 Symptoms of Adrenal Pheochromocytoma, Adrenal.com

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated plasma free normetanephrine (>1.2 nmol/L, particularly >350 nmol/L) STRONGLY RAISES diagnosis of pheochromocytoma; sensitivity approaches 96-100%, making normal levels effective for ruling out disease.
rulebook.source: Plasma Free Metanephrine and the Laboratory Evaluation for Pheochromocytoma, Warde Medical Laboratory; Biochemical Diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, NBK543224; A systematic review of the literature examining the diagnostic efficacy of measurement of fractionated plasma free metanephrines, DARE NCBI

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated plasma free metanephrine (>0.48 nmol/L, particularly >150 nmol/L) STRONGLY RAISES diagnosis of pheochromocytoma; when plasma levels are >4-fold upper reference limit, this indicates PPGL with high specificity.
rulebook.source: Diagnosis and Localization of Pheochromocytoma, Hypertension 01.HYP.0000125014; Biochemical Diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, NBK543224

rulebook.rule: Markedly elevated 24-hour urine normetanephrine (228,000 nmol/day, reference <240) and urine metanephrine (91,000 nmol/day, reference <275) STRONGLY RAISE diagnosis of pheochromocytoma; elevated urine catecholamines (epinephrine 2,510 nmol/day, reference <110) indicate excessive catecholamine secretion.
rulebook.source: Is It Enough to Diagnose Pheochromocytoma by Measuring Urine Metanephrines Levels?, PMC11484658; Mayo Clinic Laboratories, Metanephrines Fractionated Free Plasma

rulebook.rule: Elevated urine dopamine and epinephrine (particularly epinephrine markedly elevated at 22.8-fold upper limit) indicates ADRENAL-ORIGIN pheochromocytoma secreting both dopamine and epinephrine; this phenotype is typical of intra-adrenal tumors rather than extra-adrenal paragangliomas.
rulebook.source: Biochemical Diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, NBK543224; Diagnosis and Localization of Pheochromocytoma, Hypertension Journal

rulebook.rule: Large adrenal mass ≥16 cm SUBSTANTIALLY RAISES malignancy risk; malignancy occurs in 89% of cases with diameter ≥8 cm, and size is a major independent risk factor for metastatic potential.
rulebook.source: Clinical differences between small and large pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas, PMC10034061; Association between Tumor Size and Malignancy Risk in Hormonally Inactive Adrenal Incidentalomas, PMC7001135

rulebook.rule: Multiple hepatic metastases (2.0, 2.6, and 0.6 cm lesions) DEFINITIVELY CONFIRMS malignant pheochromocytoma; malignancy is defined by presence of distant metastases at sites where chromaffin cells are physiologically absent, and liver is the most common site of distant metastasis.
rulebook.source: Personalized Management of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, Endocrine Reviews 43(2):199; Malignant pheochromocytoma: Hepatectomy for liver metastases, PMC3920120

rulebook.rule: FDG-PET/CT with avid tracer uptake in primary tumor RAISES suspicion for aggressive/metabolically active disease; combined with large size and hepatic metastases, indicates high-grade malignant pheochromocytoma requiring intensive surveillance and systemic therapy consideration.
rulebook.source: Personalized Management of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, Endocrine Reviews 43(2):199; A clinical prediction model to estimate the metastatic potential of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma: ASES score, ScienceDirect

rulebook.rule: Watery diarrhea in pheochromocytoma is generally NOT caused by catecholamines themselves (which typically inhibit intestinal motility and cause constipation), but rather by co-secreted peptides such as VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide) that stimulate intestinal secretion via adenylate cyclase and cyclic AMP.
rulebook.source: Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria syndrome due to an adrenal pheochromocytoma, PMC4611845

rulebook.rule: Catecholamine excess typically produces constipation and paralytic ileus due to alpha-adrenergic inhibition of intestinal motility; diarrhea in pheochromocytoma patients may represent either co-secretory syndromes (VIP) or be a side effect of pharmacologic treatment (metyrosine).
rulebook.source: PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: A CATECHOLAMINE AND OXIDATIVE STRESS DISORDER, PMC3414427; Pheochromocytoma - StatPearls, NBK589700

rulebook.rule: Long-term psychiatric diagnosis (12+ years recurrent depression and anxiety) with documented hospitalization for major depressive episode, when accompanied by paroxysmal episodes refractory to standard psychiatric medications, LOWERS confidence in primary psychiatric diagnosis and RAISES suspicion for underlying catecholamine-secreting tumor.
rulebook.source: Unusual presentation of pheochromocytoma: thirteen years of anxiety requiring psychiatric treatment, PMC29644077; PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: AN ENDOCRINE STRESS MIMICKING DISORDER, PMC2693284

rulebook.rule: Current treatment with SNRI (venlafaxine), benzodiazepine (clonazepam), and antipsychotic (quetiapine) indicates psychiatric symptom management, but anxiety symptoms refractory to these agents RAISES red flag for organic etiology; pheochromocytoma presents with anxiety that does NOT respond to standard anxiolytics or antidepressants.
rulebook.source: PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: AN ENDOCRINE STRESS MIMICKING DISORDER, PMC2693284; Pheochromocytoma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertensive Crises, PMC12867173

rulebook.rule: Difficult-to-control hypertension for 5 years concurrent with psychiatric symptoms represents failure of secondary hypertension screening; guidelines recommend biochemical testing (plasma or 24-hour urine metanephrines) in all patients with treatment-resistant hypertension, yet pheochromocytoma screening occurs in <4% of resistant hypertension cases.
rulebook.bears_on: Diagnostic delay / missed opportunity for earlier detection
rulebook.source: Evaluation and Management of Secondary Hypertension, PMC9728017; Practice Recommendations for Diagnosis and Treatment of the Most Common Forms of Secondary Hypertension, PMC7661394

rulebook.rule: Absence of documented secondary hypertension workup during 5-year hypertension history represents critical diagnostic gap; pheochromocytoma should be excluded in patients with younger age onset, acute worsening of previously stable BP, or severe drug-resistant hypertension—all present in this case.
rulebook.source: Evaluation and Management of Secondary Hypertension, PMC9728017; Rates of Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma Screening in At-Risk Populations, PMC10188311

rulebook.rule: Pheochromocytoma-induced anxiety does NOT meet diagnostic criteria for panic disorder; key differentiators are: (1) lack of emotional/situational triggers, (2) absence of anticipatory anxiety and agoraphobia, (3) episodes not responding to anxiolytics, and (4) presence of organic biochemical markers (elevated catecholamines).
rulebook.source: Unusual presentation of pheochromocytoma: thirteen years of anxiety requiring psychiatric treatment, PMC29644077; PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: AN ENDOCRINE STRESS MIMICKING DISORDER, PMC2693284

rulebook.rule: Perioperative management requires preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade (initiated 10-14 days before surgery) to achieve seated BP <130/80 mmHg and restore euvolemia; beta-blocker initiated only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to prevent unopposed alpha stimulation.
rulebook.source: Perioperative Management of Pheochromocytomas and Sympathetic Paragangliomas, Journal of the Endocrine Society 6(2):bvac004; Perioperative Management of Pheochromocytoma, StatPearls NBK589634

rulebook.rule: In metastatic disease, catecholamine synthesis blockers (alpha-methyl-L-tyrosine/metyrosine) are added alongside alpha and beta blockade to control systemic catecholamine excess preoperatively and reduce perioperative hypertensive crisis risk.
rulebook.source: Perioperative Management of Pheochromocytomas and Sympathetic Paragangliomas, Journal of the Endocrine Society 6(2):bvac004; The Perioperative Biochemical and Clinical Considerations of Pheochromocytoma Management, MDPI 2022

rulebook.rule: Minimally-invasive adrenalectomy (retroperitoneal or transperitoneal approach) is gold standard for primary tumor resection, offering lower postoperative pain, earlier ambulation, and faster recovery compared to open surgery.
rulebook.source: Perioperative Management of Pheochromocytomas and Sympathetic Paragangliomas, Journal of the Endocrine Society 6(2):bvac004

rulebook.rule: In metastatic pheochromocytoma with hepatic involvement, consideration of hepatectomy (resection of liver metastases) in selected cases with good performance status may improve outcomes, though requires interdisciplinary surgical planning.
rulebook.source: Malignant pheochromocytoma: Hepatectomy for liver metastases, PMC3920120

rulebook.rule: Age 58 with large tumor (16 cm), metastatic disease (hepatic metastases), and markedly elevated catecholamines indicates GENETIC TESTING WARRANTED for germline mutations; all cases of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma should undergo genetic testing for RET, VHL, NF1, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, TMEM127, MAX at minimum.
rulebook.source: Genetic testing for pheochromocytoma, PMC3061287; Genetic Testing for Pheochromocytoma - Genetics for Pheochromocytoma, Adrenal.com; Genetic testing and surveillance guidelines in hereditary pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, Journal of Internal Medicine 2019

rulebook.rule: Malignant/metastatic pheochromocytoma and tumor size ≥6 cm are high-risk features for hereditary syndrome; SDHB mutations carry 35-75% malignancy risk (highest among clusters), and SDH-cluster mutations account for 20% of hereditary pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma.
rulebook.source: Genetic testing and surveillance guidelines in hereditary pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, Journal of Internal Medicine 2019; Genetic Testing and Surveillance Guidelines in Hereditary Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, Wiley Online Library

rulebook.rule: Dopaminergic phenotype (elevated urine dopamine 8,100 nmol/day) may suggest SDHB or other SDH-complex mutations; dopaminergic secretory pattern and malignancy are associated features in genetic pheochromocytoma.
rulebook.bears_on: Genetic predisposition (syndromic pheochromocytoma, SDH mutation suspected)
rulebook.source: Personalized Management of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, Endocrine Reviews 43(2):199

per_case.blind_answer: Most likely diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma, presumptively malignant given hepatic lesions. Recommended next action: Urgent endocrinology/surgery consultation; initiate alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) before considering surgery; genetic testing (SDH/VHL/RET/NF1); MIBG scintigraphy or C11-metomidate PET; hepatic lesion biopsy. Confidence: 95%. Reasoning: Markedly elevated plasma metanephrines (normetanephrine 705 vs <1.2, metanephrine 171 vs <0.48) and elevated urine catecholamines are diagnostic for catecholamine-secreting tumor. Large left adrenal mass with avid FDG uptake confirms adrenal source. 12-year history of paroxysmal anxiety, tremor, palpitations, nausea, and "difficult-to-control" hypertension represents misattributed catecholamine surges. Hepatic lesions suggest metastatic disease (malignant pheochromocytoma ~10% of cases). Diarrhea may reflect vasoactive peptide co-secretion. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate pharmacologic management.
per_case.framework_conclusion:
This 58-year-old man presents with a definitive diagnosis of malignant pheochromocytoma with metastatic disease, a diagnosis obscured for 12 years by psychiatric misattribution.

DIAGNOSTIC CERTAINTY FOR PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA: The clinical presentation and biochemical findings provide overwhelming evidence. The paroxysmal episodes of intense anxiety, dread, and sense of impending doom occurring several times per week to monthly (F8, F10, F11) are consistent with pheochromocytoma per R1.1. Accompanying symptoms of palpitations, tremor, nausea, and occasional vomiting (F14, F15, F12, F13) during these episodes raise further suspicion for catecholamine-mediated symptoms (R1.2). Critically, episodes were nocturnal, awakening the patient from sleep (F9), which is characteristic of pheochromocytoma rather than psychologically-triggered panic (R1.3).

The biochemical evidence is decisive. Plasma free normetanephrine measured 705 nmol/L (reference <1.20) (F39)—markedly elevated and exceeding 350 nmol/L threshold—strongly raises the diagnosis with sensitivity approaching 96-100% (R2.1). Plasma free metanephrine of 171 nmol/L (reference <0.48) (F40)—more than 4-fold the upper reference limit—provides additional high specificity confirmation (R2.2). Twenty-four-hour urine studies show normetanephrine 228,000 nmol/day (reference <240) and metanephrine 91,000 nmol/day (reference <275), with markedly elevated epinephrine at 2,510 nmol/day (reference <110) (F34, F35, F38)—all strongly consistent with pheochromocytoma (R2.3). The biochemical phenotype with elevated dopamine (8,100 nmol/day, reference <2,570) and epinephrine indicates adrenal-origin secretion typical of intra-adrenal tumors (R2.4, F36).

DEFINITIVE EVIDENCE FOR MALIGNANCY: The adrenal mass measures 16 x 15 cm (F29), which exceeds the ≥8 cm threshold carrying 89% malignancy risk (R3.1). However, imaging findings definitively confirm malignant pheochromocytoma: three separate hepatic lesions measuring 2.0, 2.6, and 0.6 cm (F30, F32) represent distant metastases at sites where chromaffin cells are physiologically absent (R3.2). The presence of liver metastases definitively confirms malignancy by definition. Additionally, FDG-PET/CT showed avid tracer uptake in the primary adrenal mass (F33), indicating metabolically active aggressive disease (R3.3).

DIAGNOSTIC DELAY AND PSYCHIATRIC MASKING: The 12-year history of recurrent depression and anxiety disorder with one prolonged psychiatric hospitalization (F6, F7) represents a profound diagnostic capture. The patient was on appropriate psychiatric medications—venlafaxine 150 mg (SNRI), clonazepam 0.5 mg as-needed (benzodiazepine), and extended-release quetiapine (F17, F18, F19)—yet symptoms persisted. Per R5.2, anxiety refractory to standard anxiolytics and antidepressants raises a red flag for organic etiology; pheochromocytoma-induced anxiety does not respond to these agents. Furthermore, R5.5 notes that pheochromocytoma-induced anxiety does not meet diagnostic criteria for panic disorder because episodes lack emotional triggers, anticipatory anxiety, and agoraphobia—key features that distinguish primary panic disorder from catecholamine excess.

A critical missed opportunity occurred during the 5-year hypertension history (F20) described as "difficult to control." Per R5.3, guidelines recommend biochemical testing for pheochromocytoma in ALL patients with treatment-resistant hypertension, yet screening occurs in <4% of such cases. This patient had younger-than-typical onset and severe drug-resistant hypertension—both indicators for pheochromocytoma screening per R5.4. The combination of resistant hypertension, paroxysmal anxiety episodes, and objective findings of elevated blood pressure and mild tachycardia between episodes (F23, F24) should have prompted endocrine evaluation years earlier.

GENETIC PREDISPOSITION: Malignant pheochromocytoma with large primary tumor (16 cm) and hepatic metastases warrants urgent genetic testing for RET, VHL, NF1, SDHB, and other cluster mutations per R7.1. The dopaminergic phenotype (elevated urine dopamine at 8,100 nmol/day) combined with malignancy raises particular suspicion for SDH-complex mutations, particularly SDHB (R7.2, R7.3). SDHB mutations carry 35-75% malignancy risk, the highest among syndromic associations.

GASTROINTESTINAL SYMPTOMS: The presenting symptom of watery diarrhea for several weeks (F2) is noteworthy. Per R4.1, catecholamine excess itself does not typically cause diarrhea; diarrhea in pheochromocytoma reflects co-secreted peptides (e.g., VIP) stimulating intestinal secretion rather than catecholamine action. This co-secretory phenomenon further supports the diagnosis and suggests a complex, metabolically active tumor phenotype.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY SYNTHESIS: This case exemplifies how catecholamine excess mimics psychiatric disease. The paroxysmal episodes of intense anxiety, autonomic hyperactivation (palpitations, tremor), and gastrointestinal symptoms were all products of episodic catecholamine surges—not primary psychiatric pathology. The tachycardia between episodes (F24) and chronically elevated blood pressure (F23) reflect background catecholamine excess. Standard psychiatric medications were ineffective because they do not address the underlying neuroendocrine disorder. The nocturnal timing of episodes is consistent with catecholamine secretion patterns in adrenal pheochromocytoma.

In summary, this patient has definitive pheochromocytoma based on massively elevated plasma and urine catecholamine metabolites; definitive malignancy based on large primary tumor size and confirmed hepatic metastases; probable genetic predisposition based on malignancy, large tumor size, and dopaminergic secretory pattern; and a tragic 12-year delay in diagnosis due to psychiatric misattribution despite red flags (refractory anxiety, resistant hypertension, paroxysmal autonomic symptoms) that should have prompted screening.
per_case.framework_top: Malignant pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor with hepatic metastases), likely associated with hereditary syndrome (SDH mutation suspected based on dopaminergic phenotype and malignancy)
per_case.framework_next_step: Initiate genetic testing for germline mutations (RET, VHL, NF1, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHA, TMEM127, MAX); obtain tissue pathology confirmation via core biopsy; complete metastatic staging with thoracic imaging; begin preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) targeting BP <130/80 mmHg with concurrent metyrosine for systemic catecholamine control; engage multidisciplinary surgical team for planning adrenalectomy and consideration of hepatectomy
per_case.framework_confidence: Very high (95-98%) for pheochromocytoma diagnosis; high (85-90%) for malignancy classification; moderate (70-75%) regarding genetic syndrome type pending test results

per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct core diagnosis — malignant (metastatic) pheochromocytoma masquerading as a psychiatric panic/anxiety disorder — and both anchor it to the decisive biochemistry (markedly elevated plasma/urine metanephrines and catecholamines), the large adrenal mass with avid FDG uptake, and hepatic lesions establishing malignancy. So both nail the diagnosis itself.

The differentiator is disposition, calibration, and hallucination. The ground truth's CORRECT DISPOSITION is explicitly action-oriented: stop escalating psychiatric meds, screen biochemically, localize on imaging, refer to endocrine surgery, institute pre-operative alpha-blockade (then beta-blockade) before resection, resect primary + metastases, lifelong surveillance.

OUTPUT B is essentially a correct clinical action note: it states the diagnosis (presumptively malignant given hepatic lesions), gives the management that matters most clinically and that the ground truth emphasizes — urgent endocrine/surgery referral and alpha-blockade BEFORE surgery (the single highest-stakes, most-tested teaching point in pheochromocytoma) — plus genetic testing and functional imaging. It is concise, calibrated (95% confidence, appropriately hedges malignancy as presumptive given metastatic lesions), and nearly everything is defensible against ground truth. Minor imperfections: hepatic biopsy of a suspected pheochromocytoma metastasis without prior blockade is debatable, and it omits explicit "stop psychiatric escalation" framing, but its substance aligns tightly with the ground-truth disposition.

OUTPUT A is far more thorough on diagnostic reasoning and explicitly captures the psychiatric-masking/diagnostic-capture narrative (a strength the ground truth foregrounds). However, it has notable defects: (1) It gives essentially NO disposition/management — no alpha-blockade-before-surgery, no endocrine-surgery referral, no resection plan, no surveillance. The ground truth's correct action is precisely the management pathway, and A omits it entirely, treating the task as a pure diagnostic write-up. (2) It overstates genetic findings: it asserts "probable genetic predisposition" and singles out SDHB as particularly suspect, whereas the ground truth states the 14-gene hereditary panel was NEGATIVE (sporadic). This is a confident claim contradicted by ground truth — a calibration/hallucination problem, even if the recommendation to test was reasonable. (3) It states age 58 / 12-year history vs the source's 64-year-old / 13-year history; both outputs use perturbed demographics so this is not heavily penalized, but A commits more strongly to specifics. (4) The VIP co-secretion explanation for diarrhea is speculative (presented as supporting evidence rather than a hypothesis) — B hedges this better ("may reflect").

Net: A is richer and better captures the mimic narrative but fails to deliver the correct disposition and makes an overconfident genetic-predisposition claim that contradicts ground truth. B is leaner but gets the diagnosis right AND delivers the clinically critical, ground-truth-aligned disposition (referral + pre-op alpha-blockade) with good calibration and high defensibility. Because the ground truth explicitly defines the correct action as the management pathway, B's coverage of disposition outweighs A's diagnostic depth. B wins, though closely.

per_case.prose:
A 54-year-old man with no significant past medical history was referred to a regional hospital's internal medicine service after roughly ten weeks of fevers that he and his family physician had been unable to explain. The fevers were intermittent and tended to appear in the late afternoon and evening, with home readings peaking around 38.7-39.1°C and settling by the following morning. He described drenching night sweats that required changing the bedsheets, a general sense of being run down, and a poor appetite. Over the course of the illness he had lost about 7 kg without trying. He specifically denied pounding heart sensations, episodic throbbing headaches, sudden sweating spells, tremor, or feelings of dread, and he had never been told he had high blood pressure.

He had emigrated from rural Portugal in his thirties, worked as a warehouse supervisor, did not smoke, and drank wine only occasionally. There were no sick contacts, no recent travel, no pets, and no unpasteurized dairy intake that he could recall.

On examination he was febrile at 38.3°C but did not appear toxic; he was alert, fully oriented, and looked tired. Blood pressure was 124/74 mmHg seated, heart rate 92 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Heart sounds were normal and the lungs were clear. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpable masses and no enlargement of the liver or spleen. There was no lymph node enlargement, no swelling of the legs, no rash, and no flushing of the skin.

Initial laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference 13.0-17.0), a white-cell count of 12.1 ×10⁹/L (reference 4.0-10.0) with 76% neutrophils, and platelets of 408 ×10⁹/L (reference 150-400). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 71 mm/hr (reference <20) and C-reactive protein was 98 mg/L (reference <5). Ferritin was elevated at 445 ng/mL (reference 30-400). Serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Aminotransferases were normal (AST 26 U/L, ALT 23 U/L). A serum cortisol and a plasma aldosterone drawn during the workup were both within normal limits.

An extensive search for infection was undertaken. Three sets of blood cultures drawn on separate days remained sterile, as did a urine culture; urinalysis was unremarkable. Serologic testing was negative for HIV, hepatitis B and C, Brucella, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus. Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no vegetations. Despite this, the fevers continued and no source was identified.

Cross-sectional imaging was then pursued. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass measuring about 5.3 × 4.6 cm above the right kidney, clearly separate from both the kidney and the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 5.8 × 5.0 cm right-sided suprarenal mass with heterogeneous enhancement and central low-attenuation areas suggesting necrosis, without local invasion or regional lymphadenopathy.
per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Right adrenal PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA presenting as fever of unknown origin (a normotensive, non-paroxysmal "silent"/inflammatory pheochromocytoma — IL-6-mediated systemic inflammatory presentation without the classic triad of headache/palpitations/diaphoresis or sustained hypertension).

How confirmed: (1) Biochemistry — elevated plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrines plus elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated catecholamines; (2) Anatomic imaging — CT showing a ~6 cm heterogeneously enhancing right adrenal mass with central necrosis; (3) Functional imaging — 123I-MIBG scintigraphy showing intense uptake localized to the adrenal mass and no metastatic disease; (4) Definitive — laparoscopic right adrenalectomy with cure (fever resolved within 48 h, inflammatory markers normalized, postoperative metanephrines normal at follow-up).

Correct disposition: Recognize pheochromocytoma as a rare cause of FUO; confirm biochemically (fractionated metanephrines) and with MIBG; do NOT biopsy the adrenal mass; pretreat with alpha-adrenergic blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) for ~10-14 days, then add beta-blockade, before laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Outcome was full recovery with biochemical and symptomatic cure on 3- and 6-month follow-up. Source: PMC12925639 (CC-BY, open access), "Atypical Presentation of Pheochromocytoma With Persistent Fever of Unknown Origin: A Case Report."
